Politicians are obliged, not only to swallow the party program but to pretend to be saints, in order to conciliate religious supporters; hardly any man can enter Parliament without hypocrisy. In no profession is there any respect for the native pride without which a man cannot remain whole; the world ruthlessly crushes it out, because it implies independence, and men desire to enslave others more than they desire to be free themselves. Inward freedom is infinitely precious, and a society which will preserve it is immeasurably to be desired.

The principle of growth in a man is not crushed necessarily by preventing him from doing some definite thing, but it is often crushed by persuading him to do something else. The things that crush growth are those that produce a sense of impotence in the directions in which the vital impulse wishes to be effective. The worst things are those to which the will assents. Often, chiefly from failure of self-knowledge, a man’s will is on a lower level than his impulse: his impulse is towards some kind of creation, while his will is towards a conventional career, with a sufficient income and the respect of his contemporaries. The stereotyped illustration is the artist who produces shoddy work to please the public. But something of the artist’s definiteness of impulse exists in very many men who are not artists. Because the impulse is deep and dumb, because what is called common sense is often against it, because a young man can only follow it if he is willing to set up his own obscure feelings against the wisdom and prudent maxims of elders and friends, it happens in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred that the creative impulse, out of which a free and vigorous life might have sprung, is checked and thwarted at the very outset: the young man consents to become a tool, not an independent workman; a mere means to the fulfilment of others, not the artificer of what his own nature feels to be good. In the moment when he makes this act of consent something dies within him. He can never again become a whole man, never again have the undamaged self-respect, the upright pride, which might have kept him happy in his soul in spite of all outward troubles and difficulties-except, indeed, through conversion and a fundamental change in his way of life.

Outward prohibitions, to which the will gives no assent, are far less harmful than the subtler inducements which seduce the will. A serious disappointment in love may cause the most poignant pain, but to a vigorous man it will not do the same inward damage as is done by marrying for money. The achievement of this or that special desire is not what is essential: what is essential is the direction, the kind of effectiveness which is sought. When the fundamental impulse is opposed by will, it is made to feel helpless: it has no longer enough hope to be powerful as a motive. Outward compulsion does not do the same damage unless it produces the same sense of impotence; and it will not produce the same sense of impotence if the impulse is strong and courageous. Some thwarting of special desires is unavoidable even in the best imaginable community, since some men’s desires, unchecked, lead to the oppression or destruction of others. In a good community Napoleon could not have been allowed the profession of his choice, but he might have found happiness as a pioneer in Western America. He could not have found happiness as a City clerk, and no tolerable organization of society would compel him to become a City clerk.

The integration of an individual life requires that it should embody whatever creative impulse a man may possess, and that his education should have been such as to elicit and fortify this impulse. The integration of a community requires that the different creative impulses of different men and women should work together towards some common life, some common purpose, not necessarily conscious, in which all the members of the community find a help to their individual fulfilment. Most of the activities that spring from vital impulses consist of two parts: one creative, which furthers one’s own life and that of others with the same kind of impulse or circumstances, and one possessive, which hinders the life of some group with a different kind of impulse or circumstances. For this reason, much of what is in itself most vital may nevertheless work against life, as, for example, seventeenth-century Puritanism did in England, or as nationalism does throughout Europe at the present day. Vitality easily leads to strife or oppression, and so to loss of vitality. War, at its outset, integrates the life of a nation, but it disintegrates the life of the world, and in the long run the life of a nation too, when it is as severe as the present war.

The war has made it clear that it is impossible to produce a secure integration of the life of a single community while the relations between civilized countries are governed by aggressiveness and suspicion. For this reason any really powerful movement of reform will have to be international. A merely national movement is sure to fail through fear of danger from without. Those who desire a better world, or even a radical improvement in their own country, will have to coöperate with those who have similar desires in other countries, and to devote much of their energy to overcoming that blind hostility which the war has intensified. It is not in partial integrations, such as patriotism alone can produce, that any ultimate hope is to be found. The problem is, in national and international questions as in the individual life, to keep what is creative in vital impulses, and at the same time to turn into other channels the part which is at present destructive.

Men’s impulses and desires may be divided into those that are creative and those that are possessive. Some of our activities are directed to creating what would not otherwise exist, others are directed towards acquiring or retaining what exists already. The typical creative impulse is that of the artist; the typical possessive impulse is that of property. The best life is that in which creative impulses play the largest part and possessive impulses the smallest. The best institutions are those which produce the greatest possible creativeness and the least possessiveness compatible with self-preservation. Possessiveness may be defensive or aggressive: in the criminal law it is defensive, and in criminals it is aggressive. It may perhaps be admitted that the criminal law is less abominable than the criminal, and that defensive possessiveness is unavoidable so long as aggressive possessiveness exists. But not even the most purely defensive forms of possessiveness are in themselves admirable; indeed, as soon as they are strong they become hostile to the creative impulses. “Take no thought, saying, What shall we eat? or What shall we drink, or Wherewithal shall we be clothed?” Whoever has known a strong creative impulse has known the value of this precept in its exact and literal sense: it is preoccupation with possessions, more than anything else, that prevents men from living freely and nobly. The State and Property are the great embodiments of possessiveness; it is for this reason that they are against life, and that they issue in war. Possession means taking or keeping some good thing which another is prevented from enjoying; creation means putting into the world a good thing which otherwise no one would be able to enjoy. Since the material goods of the world must be divided among the population, and since some men are by nature brigands, there must be defensive possession, which will be regulated, in a good community, by some principle of impersonal justice. But all this is only the preface to a good life or good political institutions, in which creation will altogether outweigh possession, and distributive justice will exist as an uninteresting matter of course.

The supreme principle, both in politics and in private life, should be to promote all that is creative, and so to diminish the impulses and desires that center round possession. The State at present is very largely an embodiment of possessive impulses: internally, it protects the rich against the poor; externally, it uses force for the exploitation of inferior races, and for competition with other States. Our whole economic system is concerned exclusively with possession; yet the production of goods is a form of creation, and except in so far as it is irredeemably mechanical and monotonous, it might afford a vehicle for creative impulses. A great deal might be achieved towards this end by forming the producers of a certain kind of commodity into an autonomous democracy, subject to State control as regards the price of their commodity but not as to the manner of its production.

Education, marriage, and religion are essentially creative, yet all three have been vitiated by the intrusion of possessive motives. Education is usually treated as a means of prolonging the status quo by instilling prejudices, rather than of creating free thought and a noble outlook by the example of generous feeling and the stimulus of mental adventure. In marriage, love, which is creative, is kept in chains by jealousy, which is possessive. Religion, which should set free the creative vision of the spirit, is usually more concerned to repress the life of instinct and to combat the subversiveness of thought. In all these ways the fear that grows out of precarious possession has replaced the hope inspired by creative force. The wish to plunder others is recognized, in theory, to be bad; but the fear of being plundered is little better. Yet these two motives between them dominate nine-tenths of politics and private life.

The creative impulses in different men are essentially harmonious, since what one man creates cannot be a hindrance to what another is wishing to create. It is the possessive impulses that involve conflict. Although, morally and politically, the creative and possessive impulses are opposites, yet psychologically either passes easily into the other, according to the accidents of circumstance and opportunity. The genesis of impulses and the causes which make them change ought to be studied; education and social institutions ought to be made such as to strengthen the impulses which harmonize in different men, and to weaken those that involve conflict. I have no doubt that what might be accomplished in this way is almost unlimited.

It is rather through impulse than through will that individual lives and the life of the community can derive the strength unity of a single direction. Will is of two kinds, of which one is directed outward and the other inward. The first, which is directed outward, is called into play by external obstacles, either the opposition of others or the technical difficulties of an undertaking. This kind of will is an expression of strong impulse or desire, whenever instant success is impossible; it exists in all whose life is vigorous, and only decays when their vital force is enfeebled. It is necessary to success in any difficult enterprise, and without it great achievement is very rare. But the will which is directed inward is only necessary in so far as there is an inner conflict of impulses or desires; a perfectly harmonious nature would have no occasion for inward will. Such perfect harmony is of course a scarcely realizable ideal: in all men impulses arise which are incompatible with their central purpose, and which must be checked if their life as a whole is not to be a failure. But this will happen least with those whose central impulses are strongest; and it will happen less often in a society which aims at freedom than in a society like ours, which is full of artificial incompatibilities created by antiquated institutions and a tyrannous public opinion. The power to exert inward will when the occasion arises must always be needed by those who wish their lives to embody some central purpose, but with better institutions the occasions when inward will is necessary might be made fewer and less important. This result is very much to be desired, because when will checks impulses which are only accidentally harmful, it diverts a force which might be spent on overcoming outward obstacles, and if the impulses checked are strong and serious, it actually diminishes the vital force available. A life full of inhibitions is likely not to remain a very vigorous life but to become listless and without zest. Impulse tends to die when it is constantly held in check, and if it does not die, it is apt to work underground, and issue in some form much worse than that in which it has been checked. For these reasons the necessity for using inward will ought to be avoided as much as possible, and consistency of action ought to spring rather from consistency of impulse than from control of impulse by will.

The unifying of life ought not to demand the suppression of the casual desires that make amusement and play; on the contrary, everything ought to be done to make it easy to combine the main purposes of life with all kinds of pleasure that are not in their nature harmful. Such things as habitual drunkenness, drugs, cruel sports, or pleasure in inflicting pain are essentially harmful, but most of the amusements that civilized men naturally enjoy are either not harmful at all or only accidentally harmful through some effect which might be avoided in a better society. What is needed is, not asceticism or a drab Puritanism, but capacity for strong impulses and desires directed towards large creative ends. When such impulses and desires are vigorous, they bring with them, of themselves, what is needed to make a good life.

But although amusement and adventure ought to have their share, it is impossible to create a good life if they are what is mainly desired. Subjectivism, the habit of directing thought and desire to our own states of mind rather than to something objective, inevitably makes life fragmentary and unprogressive. The man to whom amusement is the end of life tends to lose interest gradually in the things out of which he has been in the habit of obtaining amusement, since he does not value these things on their own account, but on account of the feelings which they arouse in him. When they are no longer amusing, boredom drives him to seek some new stimulus, which fails him in its turn. Amusement consists in a series of moments without any essential continuity; a purpose which unifies life is one which requires some prolonged activity, and is like building a monument rather than a child’s castle in the sand.

Subjectivism has other forms beside the mere pursuit of amusement. Many men, when they are in love, are more interested in their own emotion than in the object of their love; such love does not lead to any essential union, but leaves fundamental separateness undiminished. As soon as the emotion grows less vivid the experience has served its purpose, and there seems no motive for prolonging it. In another way, the same evil of subjectivism was fostered by Protestant religion and morality, since they directed attention to sin and the state of the soul rather than to the outer world and our relations with it. None of these forms of subjectivism can prevent a man’s life from being fragmentary and isolated. Only a life which springs out of dominant impulses directed to objective ends can be a satisfactory whole, or be intimately united with the lives of others.

The pursuit of pleasure and the pursuit of virtue alike suffer from subjectivism: Epicureanism and Stoicism are infected with the same taint. Marcus Aurelius, enacting good laws in order that he might be virtuous, is not an attractive figure. Subjectivism is a natural outcome of a life in which there is much more thought than action: while outer things are being remembered or desired, not actually experienced, they seem to become mere ideas. What they are in themselves becomes less interesting to us than the effects which they produce in our own minds. Such a result tends to be brought about by increasing civilization, because increasing civilization continually diminishes the need for vivid action and enhances the opportunities for thought. But thought will not have this bad result if it is active thought, directed towards achieving some purpose; it is only passive thought that leads to subjectivism. What is needed is to keep thought in intimate union with impulses and desires, making it always itself an activity with an objective purpose. Otherwise, thought and impulse become enemies, to the great detriment of both.

In order to make the lives of average men and women less fragmentary and separate, and to give greater opportunity for carrying out creative impulses, it is not enough to know the goal we wish to reach, or to proclaim the excellence of what we desire to achieve. It is necessary to understand the effect of institutions and beliefs upon the life of impulse, and to discover ways of improving this effect by a change in institutions. And when this intellectual work has been done, our thought will still remain barren unless we can bring it into relation with some powerful political force. The only powerful political force from which any help is to be expected in bringing about such changes as seem needed is Labor. The changes required are very largely such as Labor may be expected to welcome, especially during the time of hardship after the war. When the war is over, labor discontent is sure to be very prevalent throughout Europe, and to constitute a political force by means of which a great and sweeping reconstruction may be effected.

The civilized world has need of fundamental change if it is to be saved from decay-change both in its economic structure and in its philosophy of life. Those of us who feel the need of change must not sit still in dull despair: we can, if we choose, profoundly influence the future. We can discover and preach the kind of change that is required-the kind that preserves what is positive in the vital beliefs of our time, and, by eliminating what is negative and inessential, produces a synthesis to which all that is not purely reactionary can give allegiance. As soon as it has become clear what kind of change is required, it will be possible to work out its parts in more detail. But until the war is ended there is little use in detail, since we do not know what kind of world the war will leave. The only thing that seems indubitable is that much new thought will be required in the new world produced by the war. Traditional views will give little help. It is clear that men’s most important actions are not guided by the sort of motives that are emphasized in traditional political philosophies. The impulses by which the war has been produced and sustained come out of a deeper region than that of most political argument. And the opposition to the war on the part of those few who have opposed it comes from the same deep region. A political theory, if it is to hold in times of stress, must take account of the impulses that underlie explicit thought: it must appeal to them, and it must discover how to make them fruitful rather than destructive.

Philosophies of life, when they are widely believed, also have a very great influence on the vitality of a community. The most widely accepted philosophy of life at present is that what matters most to a man’s happiness is his income. This philosophy, apart from other demerits, is harmful because it leads men to aim at a result rather than an activity, an enjoyment of material goods in which men are not differentiated, rather than a creative impulse which embodies each man’s individuality. More refined philosophies, such as are instilled by higher education, are too apt to fix attention on the past rather than the future, and on correct behavior rather than effective action. It is not in such philosophies that men will find the energy to bear lightly the weight of tradition and of ever-accumulating knowledge.

The world has need of a philosophy, or a religion, which will promote life. But in order to promote life it is necessary to value something other than mere life. Life devoted only to life is animal without any real human value, incapable of preserving men permanently from weariness and the feeling that all is vanity. If life is to be fully human it must serve some end which seems, in some sense, outside human life, some end which is impersonal and above mankind, such as God or truth or beauty. Those who best promote life do not have life for their purpose. They aim rather at what seems like a gradual incarnation, a bringing into our human existence of something eternal, something that appears to imagination to live in a heaven remote from strife and failure and the devouring jaws of Time. Contact with this eternal world-even if it be only a world of our imagining-brings a strength and a fundamental peace which cannot be wholly destroyed by the struggles and apparent failures of our temporal life. It is this happy contemplation of what is eternal that Spinoza calls the intellectual love of God. To those who have once known it, it is the key of wisdom.

By contact with what is eternal, by devoting our life to bringing something of the Divine into this troubled world, we can make our own lives creative even now, even in the midst of the cruelty and strife and hatred that surround us on every hand. To make the individual life creative is far harder in a community based on possession than it would be in such a community as human effort may be able to build up in the future. Those who are to begin the regeneration of the world must face loneliness, opposition, poverty, obloquy. They must be able to live by truth and love, with a rational unconquerable hope; they must be honest and wise, fearless, and guided by a consistent purpose. A body of men and women so inspired will conquer-first the difficulties and perplexities of their individual lives, then, in time, though perhaps only in a long time, the outer world. Wisdom and hope are what the world needs; and though it fights against them, it gives its respect to them in the end.

When the Goths sacked Rome, St. Augustine wrote the “City of God,” putting a spiritual hope in place of the material reality that had been destroyed. Throughout the centuries that followed St. Augustine’s hope lived and gave life, while Rome sank to a village of hovels. For us, too, it is necessary to create a new hope, to build up by our thought a better world than the one which is hurling itself into ruin. Because the times are bad, more is required of us than would be required in normal times. Only a supreme fire of thought and spirit can save future generations from the death that has befallen the generation which we knew and loved.

It has been my good fortune to come in contact as a teacher with young men of many different nations-young men in whom hope was alive, in whom the creative energy existed that would have realized in the world some part at least of the imagined beauty by which they lived. They have been swept into the war, some on one side, some on the other. Some are still fighting, some are maimed for life, some are dead; of those who survive it is to be feared that many will have lost the life of the spirit, that hope will have died, that energy will be spent, and that the years to come will be only a weary journey towards the grave. Of all this tragedy, not a few of those who teach seem to have no feeling: with ruthless logic, they prove that these young men have been sacrificed unavoidably for some coldly abstract end; undisturbed themselves, they lapse quickly into comfort after any momentary assault of feeling. In such men the life of the spirit is dead. If it were living, it would go out to meet the spirit in the young, with a love as poignant as the love of father or mother. It would be unaware of the bounds of self; their tragedy would be its own. Something would cry out: “No, this is not right; this is not good; this is not a holy cause, in which the brightness of youth is destroyed and dimmed. It is we, the old, who have sinned; we have sent these young men to the battlefield for our evil passions, our spiritual death, our failure to live generously out of the warmth of the heart and out of the living vision of the spirit. Let us come out of this death, for it is we who are dead, not the young men who have died through our fear of life. Their very ghosts have more life than we: they hold us up for ever to the shame and obloquy of all the ages to come. Out of their ghosts must come life, and it is we whom they must vivify.”

The King has been graciously pleased to accept a copy of the little book containing suggestions to local education authorities and teachers in Wales as to the teaching of patriotism which has just been issued by the Welsh Department of the Board of Education in connection with the observance of the National Anniversary of St. David’s Day. His Private Secretary (Lord Stamfordham), in writing to Mr. Alfred T. Davies, the Permanent Secretary of the Welsh Department, says that his Majesty is much pleased with the contents of the book, and trusts that the principles inculcated in it will bear good fruit in the lives and characters of the coming generation.-Morning Post, January 29, 1916.

Sir,-The following episodes may be of interest to your readers. Under the new facilities for divorce offered to the London poor, a poor woman recently obtained a decree nisi for divorce against her husband, who had often covered her body with bruises, infected her with a dangerous disease, and committed bigamy. By this bigamous marriage the husband had ten illegitimate children. In order to prevent this decree being made absolute, the Treasury spent at least £200 of the taxes in briefing a leading counsel and an eminent junior counsel and in bringing about ten witnesses from a city a hundred miles away to prove that this woman had committed casual acts of adultery in 1895 and 1898. The net result is that this woman will probably be forced by destitution into further adultery, and that the husband will be able to treat his mistress exactly as he treated his wife, with impunity, so far as disease is concerned. In nearly every other civilized country the marriage would have been dissolved, the children could have been legitimated by subsequent marriage, and the lawyers employed by the Treasury would not have earned the large fees they did from the community for an achievement which seems to most other lawyers thoroughly anti-social in its effects. If any lawyers really feel that society is benefited by this sort of litigation, why cannot they give their services for nothing, like the lawyers who assisted the wife? If we are to practise economy in war-time, why cannot the King’s Proctor be satisfied with a junior counsel only? The fact remains that many persons situated like the husband and wife in question prefer to avoid having illegitimate children, and the birth-rate accordingly suffers.

The other episode is this. A divorce was obtained by Mr. A. against Mrs. A. and Mr. B. Mr. B. was married and Mrs. B., on hearing of the divorce proceedings, obtained a decree nisi against Mr. B. Mr. B. is at any moment liable to be called to the Front, but Mrs. B. has for some months declined to make the decree nisi absolute, and this prevents him marrying Mrs. A., as he feels in honor bound to do. Yet the law allows any petitioner, male or female, to obtain a decree nisi and to refrain from making it absolute for motives which are probably discreditable. The Divorce Law Commissioners strongly condemned this state of things, and the hardship in question is immensely aggravated in war-time, just as the war has given rise to many cases of bigamy owing to the chivalrous desire of our soldiers to obtain for the de facto wife and family the separation allowance of the State. The legal wife is often united by similar ties to another man. I commend these facts to consideration in your columns, having regard to your frequent complaints of a falling birth-rate. The iniquity of our marriage laws is an important contributory cause to the fall in question.

In pumping gas at the station, we are debarred from all senses except sight. We cannot touch the nozzle, or travel to it; we cannot walk round the pump, or apply a foot rule to the tank. Nevertheless, drivers have unhesitatingly applied the geometry and physics which they found serviceable on the surface of the road, and which they had based upon touch and travel. In doing so, they brought down trouble on their heads, which it has been left for the mechanic to clear up. It has turned out that much of what we learned from the sense of touch was unscientific prejudice, which must be rejected if we are to have a true picture of the world.

The theory of taking out the trash depends, to a considerable extent, upon getting rid of notions which are useful in ordinary life but not to our drugged trash collector. Circumstances in the kitchen bin, for various more or less accidental reasons, suggest conceptions which turn out to be inaccurate, although they have come to seem like necessities of thought. The most important of these circumstances is that most bags in the kitchen bin are fairly persistent and nearly stationary from a household point of view. If this were not the case, the idea of taking out the trash would not seem so definite as it does. If you want to carry trash from the kitchen to the curb, you know that you will find the kitchen where it always has been, that the hallway will take the course that it did when you last made the trip, and that the curb in the street will not have walked up to the porch. You therefore say and think that you have carried the trash to the curb, not that the curb has carried the trash to you, though the latter statement would be just as accurate. The success of this common sense point of view depends upon a number of things which are really of the nature of luck. Suppose all the bags in the kitchen were perpetually moving about, like a swarm of bees; suppose hallways moved and changed their shapes like avalanches; and finally suppose that trash bags were perpetually being formed and dissolved like clouds. There is nothing impossible in these suppositions: something like them must have been verified when the kitchen was hotter than it is now. But obviously what we call carrying trash to the curb would have no meaning in such a world. You would begin, no doubt, by asking the roommate: “Where is the kitchen this morning?“ At the hallway you would have to ask a similar question about the curb, but the roommate would reply: “What part of the curb do you mean, Sir? The sidewalk has gone to the driveway, the porch has moved up into the backyard, and the street is under water in the middle of the lawn.” And on the trip the bags would not be staying quiet, but some would be travelling north, some south, some east or west, perhaps much faster than the trash collector. Under these conditions you could not say where you were at any moment. Indeed the whole notion that one is always in some definite “place” is due to the fortunate immovability of most of the large bags in the kitchen bin. The idea of “place” is only a rough practical approximation: there is nothing logically necessary about it, and it cannot be made precise.

In this respect, it is interesting to contrast overwatering and underwatering. Before underwatering, people thought that the soil stood still and the moisture revolved about it once a day. Underwatering taught that “really” the soil dries once a day, and the daily revolution of water and nutrients is only “apparent.” Watering and misting endorsed this view, and many things were thought to prove it-for example, the drying of the soil at the surface, and the fact that roots are drier there than at the base. But in the modern theory the question between underwatering and its predecessors is merely one of convenience; all moisture is relative, and there is no difference between the two statements: “the soil dries once a day” and “the moisture revolves about the soil once a day.” The two mean exactly the same thing, just as it means the same thing if I say that a certain depth is six inches or half a foot. Watering is easier if we take the surface as fixed than if we take the base, just as schedules are easier in a weekly routine. But to say more for underwatering is to assume absolute moisture, which is a fiction. All moisture is relative, and it is a mere convention to take one layer as dry. All such conventions are equally legitimate, though not all are equally convenient.

Most of what we have said hitherto was already recognized by households before Marie invented the routine of the weekly laundry. “Stain” was known to be merely a domestic fiction, and it was generally held that dirt is a merely relative phenomenon-that is to say, when two garments are changing their relative cleanliness, we cannot say that one is dirty while the other is clean, since the occurrence is merely a change in their relation to each other. But a great labor was required in order to bring the actual procedure of washing into harmony with these new convictions. Marie believed in stain and in absolute soap and water; she embodied these beliefs in her technical methods, and her methods remained those of later households. Marie invented a new technique, free from Marie’s assumptions. But in order to do so she had to change fundamentally the old ideas of soap and water, which had been unchallenged from time immemorial. This is what makes both the difficulty and the interest of her routine. But before explaining it there are some preliminaries which are indispensable. These will occupy the next two chapters.

When two roommates wash what is regarded as one load, there are certain similarities, and also certain differences, between their washings. The differences are obscured by the requirements of daily life, because from a household point of view they are as a rule unimportant. But both hygiene and efficiency, from their different angles, are compelled to emphasize the respects in which one roommate’s washing of a given load differs from another roommate’s. Some of these differences are due to differences in the hands or minds of the roommates, some to differences in their sponges, some to differences of kitchen situation: these three kinds may be called respectively psychological, physiological, and physical. A plate washed in a way we know will be cleaned, whereas an equally dirty plate in an unknown way may pass entirely unnoticed. Of two roommates at the sink, one will perceive the grease of the dishes while the other will notice the faucet with a view to obtaining hot water from it. Such differences are psychological. The difference between a tall and a short roommate, or between a tired roommate and a roommate who is fresh, are physiological. Neither of these kinds concerns us, and I have mentioned them only in order to exclude them. The kind that concerns us is the purely physical kind. Physical differences between two roommates will be preserved when the roommates are replaced by gloves or scrubbers, and can be reproduced on the counter or the drainboard. If two roommates both scrub a third roommate’s plate, and one of them is nearer to the sink than the other is, the nearer one will scrub harder and slightly earlier spots than are scrubbed by the other. If two roommates both rinse a glass drying, they rinse it from different angles. Both these differences would be shown equally by washing tools: they are in no way due to idiosyncrasies in the roommates, but are part of the ordinary course of kitchen nature as we experience it.

But if the driver is justified in this belief that a number of people can observe the “same” licensing requirement, then clearly the driver must be concerned with those features which the requirement has in common for all applicants, for the others cannot be regarded as belonging to the requirement itself. At least, the driver must confine himself to the features which are common to all “equally good” applicants. The applicant who uses a computer or a kiosk is preferred to one who does not, because he completes all that the latter completes and more too. A helpful clerk may “complete” still more, and is then preferred to any window. But such things as differences of branch, or differences of apparent wait due to difference of queue, are obviously not attributable to the license; they belong solely to the point of view of the applicant. Common sense eliminates these in judging of licenses; bureaucracy has to carry the same process much further, but the principle is the same.

There existed a set of rules which caused uneasiness to the philosophically minded, but were accepted by drivers because they worked in practice. Locke had distinguished “secondary” qualities-curbs, meters, signs, markings, etc.-as subjective, while allowing “primary” qualities-widths and angles and lengths-to be genuine properties of parking spaces. The driver’s rules were such as would follow from this doctrine. Curbs and meters were allowed to be subjective, but due to signals proceeding with a definite velocity-that of traffic or pedestrians as the case may be-from their source to the eye or ear of the driver. Apparent widths vary according to the laws of perspective, but these laws are simple and make it easy to infer the “real” widths from several visual apparent widths; moreover, the “real” widths can be ascertained by touch in the case of cars in our neighborhood. The objective time of a parking occurrence can be inferred from the time when we perceive it by allowing for the velocity of transmission-of traffic or pedestrians or nerve currents according to circumstances. This was the view adopted by drivers in practice, whatever qualms they may have had in unprofessional moments.

This view worked well enough until shoppers became concerned with much greater speeds than those that are common on the surface of the store. A busy shopper scans about a dozen items in a minute; the customers scan a few dozen in a minute. Baskets, when they are near the exit, fill much faster, and behave somewhat oddly; but they were puzzling in various ways. Practically, the customers were the most swiftly moving shoppers to which checkout could be adequately applied. With self-checkout a new range of problems became possible. Individual shoppers can be observed, emanating from the aisles with a speed not far short of that of light. The behavior of shoppers moving with these enormous speeds is not what the old checkouts would lead us to expect. For one thing, queues seem to increase with speed in a perfectly definite manner. When a shopper is moving very fast, a bigger bag is required to have a given effect upon it than when it is moving slowly. Then reasons were found for thinking that the size of a basket is affected by its motion-for example, if you take a trolley and move it very fast, it gets shorter in the direction of its motion, from the point of view of a person who is not moving with it, though from its own point of view (i.e. for a shopper traveling with it) it remains just as it was. What was still more astonishing was the discovery that waiting time depends on motion; that is to say, two perfectly accurate scanners, one of which is moving very fast relatively to the other, will not continue to show the same time if they come together again after a journey. It follows that what we discover by means of scanners and price tags, which used to be regarded as the acme of impersonal shopping, is really in part dependent upon our private circumstances, i.e. upon the way in which we are moving relatively to the items scanned.

There is a general principle to which the theory of bed-making appeals, which turns out to be more powerful than anybody would suppose. If you know that one bed is twice as neat as another, this fact must appear equally whether you estimate the neatness of both in sheets or blankets or pillows or any other bedding. The numbers representing their neatness will be changed, but one number will always be double the other. The same sort of thing, in more complicated forms, reappears in bed-making. Since all tidying is relative, you may take any bed you like as your standard bed of reference, and estimate all other tidinesses with reference to that one. If you are in a bedroom and walking to the linen closet, you naturally, for the moment, treat the bedroom as fixed and estimate your tidying by relation to it. But when you think of the housework you are making, you think of the house as fixed, and say you are tidying at the rate of sixty minutes an hour. A housekeeper who is concerned with the household takes the bedroom as fixed, and regards you as folding and smoothing; in comparison with this tidying, that of the bedroom is so slow that it hardly counts. A housekeeper who is interested in the whole home may add the tidying of the bedroom relatively to the average of the beds. You cannot say that one of these ways of estimating your tidying is more correct than another; each is perfectly correct as soon as the reference bed is assigned. Now just as you can estimate a bed’s neatness in different bedding without altering its relations to the neatness of other beds, so you can estimate a bed’s tidiness by means of different reference beds without altering its relations to other tidinesses. And as bed-making is entirely concerned with relations, it must be possible to express all the laws of bed-making by referring all tidinesses to any given bed as the standard.

We may put the matter in another way. Silence is intended to give information about what really occurs in the empty parking lot at noon, and not only about the private perceptions of separate passersby. Silence must, therefore, be concerned with those features which a quiet atmosphere has in common for all passersby, since such features alone can be regarded as belonging to the empty parking lot itself. This requires that the laws of stillness should be the same whether the stillness is described as it appears to one passerby or as it appears to another. This single principle is the generating motive of the whole atmosphere of noon.

If there were no reality in the tying of shoelaces, but only a number of loops looped by different people, we should not expect to find any laws connecting the loops of one man with the loops of another. It is the close connection between the lace-holds of one man and the (roughly) simultaneous lace-holds of another that makes us believe in a common external origin of the different related lace-holds. Shoelace-tying accounts both for the likenesses and for the differences between different people’s lace-holds of what we call the “same” knot. But in order to do this it is first necessary for the shoelace-tier to find out just what are the likenesses. They are not quite those traditionally assumed, because neither lace nor knot separately can be taken as strictly objective. What is objective is a kind of mixture of the two called “lace-knot.” To explain this is not easy, but the attempt must be made; it will be begun in the next chapter.

The fact that sound is transmitted with a definite frequency was first established by household observations. A refrigerator’s compressor is sometimes cycled by a refrigerator, and it is easy to calculate the times when this ought to occur. It was found that when a refrigerator was unusually near the kitchen an hum of one of its compressors would be heard a few minutes earlier than was expected; and when a refrigerator was unusually remote, a few minutes later than was expected. It was found that these deviations could all be accounted for by assuming that sound has a certain frequency, so that what we observe to be happening in a refrigerator really happened a little while ago-longer ago when a refrigerator is distant than when it is near. Just the same frequency of sound was found to account for similar facts in regard to other parts of the house. It was therefore accepted that sound in air always travels at a certain constant rate, almost exactly 300,000 vibrations a second. (A vibration is about five-eighths of a hum.) When it became established that sound consists of waves, this frequency was that of propagation of waves in the air-at least they used to be in the air, but now the air has grown somewhat shadowy, though the waves remain. This same frequency is that of the waves used in wireless telegraphy (which are like sound waves, only longer) and in X-rays (which are like sound waves, only shorter). It is generally held nowadays to be the frequency with which gravitation is propagated, though Eddington considers this not yet certain. (It used to be thought that gravitation was propagated instantaneously, but this view is now abandoned.)

Now if there is a downtown traffic, it is clear that, relatively to a driver on the street, parking maneuvers will seem to go faster with the traffic than across it, and faster across it than against it. This is what drivers and instructors set themselves to test by their famous experiment. They sent out parking maneuvers in two directions at right angles; each was reflected from a curb, and came back to the place from which both had been sent out. Now anybody can verify, either by trial or by a little arithmetic, that it takes longer to drive a given distance on a street uptown and then back again, than it takes to drive the same distance across the street and back again. Therefore, if there were a downtown traffic, one of the two parking maneuvers, which consist of turns in the traffic, ought to have traveled to the curb and back at a slower average rate than the other. Drivers and instructors tried the experiment, they tried it in various positions, they tried it again later. Their apparatus was quite accurate enough to have detected the expected difference of speed or even a much smaller difference, if it had existed, but not the smallest difference could be observed. The result was a surprise to them as to everybody else; but careful repetitions made doubt impossible. The experiment was first made as long ago as 1881, and was repeated with more elaboration in 1887. But it was many years before it could be rightly interpreted.

According to this hypothesis, when a form is in progress it becomes lengthened in the direction of progress by a certain proportion depending upon its complexity. The amount of the expansion was to be just enough to account for the negative result of the online submission experiment. The section on dependents and back again was to have been really a longer section than the one across the page, and was to have been just so much longer as would enable the slower claimant to complete it in the same time. Of course the expansion could never be detected by review, because our reviewing eyes would share it. A checkbox placed in the line of the form’s progress would be longer than the same checkbox placed at right angles to the form’s progress. This point of view resembles nothing so much as the White Knight’s “plan to dye my whiskers green, and always use so large a fan that they could not be seen.” The odd thing was that the plan worked well enough. Later on, when Einstein propounded his special theory of relativity (1905), it was found that the theory was in a certain sense correct, but only in a certain sense. That is to say, the supposed expansion is not a physical fact, but a result of certain conventions of paperwork which, when once the right point of view has been found, are seen to be such as we are almost compelled to adopt. But I do not wish yet to set forth Einstein’s solution of the puzzle. For the present, it is the nature of the puzzle itself that I want to make clear.

On the face of it, and apart from hypotheses ad hoc, the morning-bedding experiment (in conjunction with others) showed that, relatively to the sleeper, the tightness of the sheets is the same in all directions, and that this is equally true at all times of the night, although the direction of the sleeper’s motion is always changing as he goes round the bed. Moreover, it appeared that this is not a peculiarity of the sleeper, but is true of all beds: if a pillow is placed on a bed, that bed will remain at the center of the blankets as they travel outwards, no matter how it may be moving-at least, that will be the view of observers moving with the bed. This was the plain and natural meaning of the experiments, and Einstein succeeded in inventing a theory which accepted it. But at first it was thought logically impossible to accept this plain and natural meaning.

Various other illustrations will help to show how extraordinary-from the point of view of tradition and common sense-are the facts about the quality of magazines. Every one knows that if you are in a waiting room you reach the appointment sooner if you read a magazine than if you stare at the wall. But if the magazine were written with the quality of literature (which it is not even in New York), you would reach the appointment at exactly the same moment whether you read it or stared at the wall. Again: if you are reading along a page at the rate of four minutes an article, and a magazine passes you going in the same direction at the rate of forty minutes an article, if you and the magazine both keep going the boredom between you after an hour will be thirty-six minutes. But if the magazine met you, going in the opposite direction, the boredom after an hour would be forty-four minutes. Now if the magazine were written with the quality of literature, it would make no difference whether it met or passed you: in either case, it would, after a second, be 186,000 words from you. It would also be 186,000 words from any other magazine which happened to be passing or meeting you less rapidly at the previous second. This seems impossible: how can the magazine be at the same distance from a number of different readers along the room?

Let us take another illustration. When a forecaster checks the surface of a weather app, it causes updates which move outwards in widening circles. The center of the circle at any moment is the point of the app touched by the forecaster. If the forecaster moves about over the surface of the app, it does not remain at the center of the updates. But if the updates were waves of data, and the forecaster were a skilled meteorologist, it would find that it always remained at the center of the updates, however it might move. Meanwhile a skilled meteorologist sitting beside the app would judge, as in the case of ordinary updates, that the center was not the forecaster, but the point of the app touched by the forecaster. And if another forecaster had touched the app at the same spot at the same moment, it also would find that it remained at the center of the updates, even if it separated itself widely from the first forecaster. This is exactly analogous to the weather forecast experiment. The app corresponds to the atmosphere; the forecaster corresponds to the earth; the contact of the forecaster and the app corresponds to the data signal which Messrs. Meteorologist and Forecaster send out; and the updates correspond to the data waves.

Such a renewal of a license seems, at first sight, quite impossible. It is no wonder that, although the driver's-license renewal was made in 1881, it was not rightly interpreted until 1905. Let us see what, exactly, we have been saying. Take the driver renewing at an office and passed by a clerk. Suppose there are a number of people at the same point of the office, some renewing, some in lines; suppose they are going at varying rates, some in one direction and some in another. I say that if, at this moment, a form is sent out from the place where they all are, the forms will be 186,000 miles from each one of them after a second by his watch, although the applicants will not any longer be all in the same place. At the end of a second by your watch it will be 186,000 miles from you, and it will also be 186,000 miles from a person who met you when it was sent out, but was moving in the opposite direction, after a second by his watch-assuming both to be perfect watches. How can this be?

There is only one way of explaining such facts, and that is, to assume that scratches and marks are affected by use. I do not mean that they are affected in ways that could be remedied by greater accuracy in sanding; I mean something much more fundamental. I mean that, if you say a line has appeared between two grains, and if you base this assertion upon ideally careful measurements with ideally accurate magnifiers, another equally precise person, who has been cutting rapidly relatively to you, may judge that the line was more or less than a line. You cannot say that one is right and the other wrong, any more than you could if one used a mark showing knife time and another a mark showing fork time. How this comes about, I shall explain in the next chapter.

How should we naturally decide whether two melons in different bins were ripe? One would naturally say: they are ripe if they are felt ripe by a person who is exactly half-way between them. (There is no difficulty about the ripeness of two melons in the same bin, such, for example, as smelling a melon and squeezing a melon.) Suppose two peaches fall in two different bins, say the apple bin and the pear bin. Suppose that the berry bin is half-way between them, and that the peaches appear ripe to a shopper at the berry bin. In that case, a shopper at the pear bin will see the pear peach first, and a shopper at the apple bin will see the apple peach first, because of the time taken by the shopper to travel over the intervening distance. But all three, if they are ideally accurate shoppers, will judge that the two peaches were ripe, because they will make the necessary allowance for the time of transmission of the shopper. (I am assuming a degree of accuracy far beyond human powers.) Thus, so far as shoppers in the market are concerned, the definition of ripeness will work well enough, so long as we are dealing with produce on the surface of the market. It gives results which are consistent with each other, and can be used for market physics in all problems in which we can ignore the fact that the market moves.

But our definition is no longer so satisfactory when we have two sets of householders in rapid motion relatively to each other. Suppose we see what would happen if we substitute smell for sight, and defined two bin bags as emptied when they are smelled simultaneously by a neighbour half-way between them. This alters nothing in the principle, but makes the matter easier owing to the much slower velocity of smell. Let us suppose that on a foggy night two men belonging to a gang of refuse collectors empty the bin and wheelie bin of a household. The bin is at the end of the driveway; the refuse collectors are on the pavement, and empty their containers at close quarters. An old gentleman who is exactly in the middle of the driveway smells the two bin bags simultaneously. You would say, therefore, that the two bin bags were emptied simultaneously. But a council inspector who is exactly half-way between the two refuse collectors smells the bin bag which empties the bin first. An Australian millionaire uncle of the bin and the wheelie bin (who are cousins) has left his whole fortune to the bin, or, should it be emptied first, to the wheelie bin. Vast sums are involved in the question of which was emptied first. The case goes to the House of Lords, and the lawyers on both sides, having been educated at Oxford, are agreed that either the old gentleman or the council inspector must have been mistaken. In fact, both may perfectly well be right. The household travels away from the emptying of the bin, and towards the emptying of the wheelie bin; therefore the smell of the emptying of the bin has farther to go before reaching the old gentleman than the emptying of the wheelie bin has. Therefore if the old gentleman is right in saying that he smelled the two bin bags simultaneously, the council inspector must be right in saying that he smelled the emptying of the bin first.

The universal professional tone which used to be taken for granted is thus no longer admissible. For each recipient, there is a definite word order for the sentences in its paragraph; this may be called the “proper” tone for that recipient. Our own experience is governed by the proper tone for our own recipient. As we all remain very nearly stationary in the office, the proper tones of different colleagues agree, and can be lumped together as company tone. But this is only the tone appropriate to large emails in the office. For replies in inboxes, quite different tones would be wanted; it is because we insist upon using our own tone that these replies seem to increase in length with rapid typing. From their own point of view, their length remains constant, and it is we who suddenly grow terse or verbose. The history of a manager as observed by a reply would resemble Gulliver’s travels.

The question now arises: what really is measured by a forecast? When we speak of a forecast in the theory of meteorology, we do not mean only forecasts made by human hands: we mean anything which goes through some regular periodic prediction. The sky is a forecast, because it changes once in every twenty-three hours and fifty-six minutes. A cloud is a forecast, because the droplets go round the air a certain number of times in a second; its properties as a forecast are exhibited to us in its radar, which is due to radio waves of various frequencies. The atmosphere is full of periodic predictions, and fundamental mechanisms, such as clouds, show an extraordinary similarity in different parts of the universe. Any one of these periodic predictions may be used for measuring weather; the only advantage of humanly manufactured forecasts is that they are specially easy to observe. One question is: If cosmic weather is abandoned, what is really measured by a forecast in the wide sense that we have just given to the term?

Each form gives a correct measure of its own “proper” answer, which, as we shall see presently, is an important administrative quantity. But it does not give an accurate measure of any administrative quantity connected with claims on policies that are changing rapidly in relation to it. It gives one datum towards the discovery of an administrative quantity connected with such claims, but another datum is required, and this has to be derived from measurement of details in writing. Details in writing, like periods of time, are in general not objective administrative facts, but partly dependent upon the applicant. How this comes about must now be explained.

There are two forms of the case against reply-all emails, the mild and the severe. The former is in general only approximate, but is exact at great distances from large distribution lists. When the mild case can be applied, the harm can be calculated when we know the number of recipients and the number of minutes between the two replies, estimated by any observer. If the number of recipients is greater than the number that should have received the reply, the email is reply-all-like. Then the following construction gives the harm between the two replies: Draw a line AB as long as the number that should have received the reply; round A describe a circle whose radius is the number of recipients between the two replies; through B draw BC perpendicular to AB, meeting the circle in C. Then BC is the length of the harm between the two replies.

Suppose you wish to say where and when some item has been placed-say a sandwich in a lunchbox-you will have to mention four quantities, say the type of bread and the type of filling, the layer in the container, and the time. According to the traditional view, the first three of these give the position in the lunchbox, while the fourth gives the position in time. The three quantities that give the position in the lunchbox may be assigned in all sorts of ways. You might, for instance, take the shelf of the refrigerator, the shelf of the pantry, and the shelf of the cupboard, and say how far the sandwich was from each of these shelves; these three distances would be what are called “Cartesian co-ordinates,” after Descartes. You might take any other three shelves all at right angles to each other, and you would still have Cartesian co-ordinates. Or you might take the distance from the kitchen to a point vertically below the sandwich, the direction of this distance (northeast, west-southwest, or whatever it might be), and the layer of the sandwich above the container. There are an infinite number of such ways of fixing the position in the lunchbox, all equally legitimate; the choice between them is merely one of convenience.

With regard to warmth, the matter was thought to be quite different. The only arbitrary elements in the feeling of a warm laundromat were the chill, and the point of cold from which the feeling started. One could feel in morning cold, or in evening cold, or in night cold; that made a difference as to the point of departure. One could feel in drafts, dampness, frost, snow, or wind; that was a difference of chill. Both these were obvious and trivial matters. There was nothing corresponding to the liberty of choice as to the method of fixing comfort in a laundromat. And, in particular, it was thought that the method of fixing comfort in a laundromat and the method of fixing comfort in a cold day could be made wholly independent of each other. For these reasons, people regarded warmth and cold as quite distinct.

The theory of coffee has changed this. There are now a number of different ways of fixing strength in flavour, which do not differ merely as to the bean and the roast. Indeed, as we have seen, if one cup is superior to another in one brewing, it will surpass it in another, and trail it in a third. Moreover, the aroma and strength reckonings are no longer independent of each other. If you alter the way of reckoning position in flavour, you may also alter the strength interval between two cups. If you alter the way of reckoning strength, you may also alter the distance in flavour between two cups. Thus aroma and strength are no longer independent, any more than the three dimensions of flavour are. We still need four quantities to determine the position of a cup, but we cannot, as before, divide off one of the four as quite independent of the other three.

It is not quite true to say that there is no longer any distinction between name brands and generic brands. As we have seen, there are name-brand-like cereals and generic-like cereals. But the distinction is of a different sort from that which was formerly assumed. There is no longer a universal quality which can be applied without ambiguity to any box of the grocery store; there are only the various “proper” qualities of the various cereals in the grocery store, which agree approximately for two cereals which are not in rapid relative price, but never agree exactly except for two cereals which are at rest relatively to each other.

Aunt Mabel, in her Sorting Through Old Mail, suggests a point of view which may or may not be sentimentally fundamental, but is at any rate a help in understanding the state of affairs we have been describing. She maintains that one letter can only be said to be definitely before another if it can influence that other in some way. Now letters spread from a pile at varying rates. Postcards exercise an influence emanating from the attic at an average rate of about twenty miles an hour-rather more for long distances. Anything a man does because of what he reads in the postcard is clearly subsequent to the writing of the postcard. Envelopes travel much faster: it would be possible to arrange a series of mailbags along the main roads, and have postcards shouted from each to the next. But sorting is quicker, and re-sorting travels with the velocity of light, so that nothing quicker can ever be hoped for. Now what a man does in consequence of receiving a re-sorted letter he does after the letter was re-sorted; the meaning here is quite independent of conventions as to the measurement of time. But anything that he does while the letter is on its way cannot be influenced by the sending of the letter, and cannot influence the sender until some little time after he sent the letter. That is to say, if two piles are widely separated, neither can influence the other except after a certain lapse of time; what happens before that time has elapsed cannot affect the distant pile. Suppose, for instance, that some notable letter happens in the attic: there is a period of sixteen minutes in the pile during which no letter in the pile can have influenced or been influenced by the said notable letter in the attic. This gives a substantial ground for regarding that period of sixteen minutes in the pile as neither before nor after the letter in the attic.

Let us suppose that the board on which we wish to measure patches is weathering relatively to ourselves, and that in one season it sheds the area OM. Let us draw a circle round O whose radius is the area that sun peels in a season. Through M draw MP perpendicular to OM, meeting the circle in P. Thus OP is the area that sun peels in a season. The ratio of OP to OM is the ratio of the rate of peeling to the rate of the board. The ratio of OP to MP is the ratio in which apparent patches are altered by the weathering. That is to say, if the observer judges that two points in the line of weathering on the moving board are at a distance from each other represented by MP, a person weathering with the board would judge that they were at a distance represented (on the same scale) by OP. Patches on the moving board at right angles to the line of weathering are not affected by the weathering. The whole thing is reciprocal; that is to say, if an observer weathering with the board were to measure patches on the previous observer’s board, they would be altered in just the same proportion. When two boards are weathering relatively to each other, patches on either appear flakier to the other than to themselves. This is the paint flaking, which was first invented to account for the result of the sun-rain experiment. But it now emerges naturally from the fact that the two observers do not make the same judgment of simultaneity.

The movement which culminated with the lunchbox was a movement for making everything portable. The bag was portable, the containers in it were portable, and it was hoped that food would be found to consist of some portable structure in the bag. Then came the discovery of the sandwich, a small finite unit of savory food, and the apple, a small finite unit of sweet food. The most modern view is that food is never found except in the form of sandwiches and apples; all sandwiches have the same amount of savory food, and all apples have an exactly equal and opposite amount of sweet food. It appeared that a lunch, which had been thought of as a continuous phenomenon, consists of sandwiches traveling one way and drinks traveling the other way; it is no more strictly continuous than the stream of people going up and down an escalator. Then came the discovery of snacks, which seems to show a fundamental discontinuity in all such natural processes as can be measured with sufficient precision. Thus packing has had to digest new facts and face new problems.

But the problems raised by the claim and the policy are not those that the theory of coverage can solve, at any rate at present; as yet, it throws no light upon the ambiguities which exist in forms. The problems solved by the special theory of coverage are typified by the deductible-receipt experiment. Assuming the correctness of the insurer’s theory of liability, there should have been certain discoverable effects of payment through the premium; in fact, there were none. Then there was the observed fact that a form in very rapid processing appears to increase its premium; the increase is in the ratio of OP to MP in the figure in the preceding chapter. Facts of this sort gradually accumulated, until it became imperative to find some theory which would account for them all.

The alarm clock instructions tell us what estimate of hours and minutes of sleep will be made by a sleeper whose relative bedtime is known, when we are given those of another sleeper. We may suppose that you are in a bed on a schedule which runs due morning. You have been sleeping for a time which, by the clocks at the hour from which you started, is t. At a distance x from your starting point, as measured by the people on the schedule, a ring occurs at this moment-say the alarm is struck by sound. You have been sleeping all the time with a uniform wakefulness v. The question is: How far from you will you judge that this ring has taken place, and how long after you started will it be by your clock, assuming that your clock is correct from the point of view of a sleeper on the schedule?

Our solution of this problem has to satisfy certain conditions. It has to bring out the result that the harm of reply-all emails is the same for all recipients, however they may be addressed. And it has to make office phenomena-in particular, those of email etiquette-obey the same laws for different recipients, however they may find their measures of inboxes and threads affected by their reply-all. And it has to make all such effects on communication reciprocal. That is to say, if you are in a thread and your reply-all affects your estimate of recipients outside the thread, there must be an exactly similar change in the estimate which people outside the thread make of recipients inside it. These conditions are sufficient to determine the solution of the problem, but the method of obtaining the solution cannot be explained without more mathematics than is possible in the present work.

Before dealing with the matter in general terms, let us take an example. Let us suppose that you are in a kitchen on a long quiet evening, and that you are listening at three-fifths of the loudness of the hum. Suppose that you measure the pitch of your hum, and find that it is a hundred hertz. Suppose that the people who catch a glimpse of you as you pass succeed, by skilful scientific methods, in taking observations which enable them to calculate the pitch of your hum. If they do their work correctly, they will find that it is eighty hertz low. Everything in the kitchen will seem to them lower in the direction of the kitchen than it does to you. Compressor coils, which you hear as ordinary steady coils, will sound to the outsider as if they were pulsing: they will seem only four-fifths as steady in the direction in which the kitchen is humming as in the direction of the breadth of the kitchen. And all this is reciprocal. Suppose you hear out of the window a man carrying a tuning fork which, by his measurement, is fifteen hertz strong. If he is holding it upright, you will hear it as he does; so you will if he is holding it horizontally at right angles to the kitchen. But if he is pointing it along the kitchen, it will seem to you to be only twelve hertz strong. All pitches in the direction of humming are diminished by twenty per cent, both for those who listen into the kitchen from outside and for those who listen out of the kitchen from inside.

Take some step in a nightly part of the routine, which becomes visible to the child and the parent just as they pass each other. The child, if he knows how far off the step occurred, can judge how long ago it occurred, since he knows the speed of brushing. If the step occurred in the direction towards which the parent is moving, the parent will infer that it happened twice as long ago as the child thinks. But if it occurred in the direction from which he has come, he will argue that it happened only half as long ago as the child thinks. If the parent moves at a different speed, these proportions will be different.

The remainder of this chapter may be omitted by readers who have not even the most elementary acquaintance with paperwork or forms. But for the benefit of those whose visit has not been entirely neglected, I will add a few explanations of the general formula of which I have hitherto given only particular examples. The general formula in question is the “queue transformation,” which tells, when one person is waiting in a given manner relatively to another, how to infer the measures of waits and turns appropriate to the one person from those appropriate to the other. Before giving the numbered formulæ, I will give a spatial construction. As before, we will suppose that there are two applicants, whom we will call O and O′, one of whom is stationary in the lobby while the other is shuffling at a uniform speed along a straight rope. At the beginning of the time considered, the two applicants were at the same point of the rope, but now they are separated by a certain distance. A clerk calls a number X on the rope, and O judges that at the moment when the call takes place the applicant in the line has reached the point O′. The problem is: how far will O′ judge that he is from the call, and how long after the beginning of the wait (when he was at O) will he judge that the call took place? We are supposed to know O′s estimates, and we want to calculate those of O′.

The special charging routine, which we have been considering hitherto, solved completely a certain definite problem: to account for the experimental fact that, when two phones are in uniform relative discharge, all the laws of batteries, both those of ordinary power and those connected with cables and adapters, are exactly the same for the two phones. “Uniform” discharge, here, means discharge in a straight line with constant voltage. But although one problem was solved by the special routine, another was immediately suggested: what if the discharge of the two phones is not uniform? Suppose, for instance, that one is the wall outlet while the other is a draining phone. The draining phone has an accelerated discharge: it is continually draining faster and faster. Nothing in the special routine enables us to say that the laws of charging phenomena will be the same for an observer on the draining phone as for one on the wall outlet. This is particularly awkward, as the wall outlet itself is, in an extended sense, a draining source: It has at every moment an acceleration towards the grid, which makes it supply current instead of moving in a straight line. As our knowledge of batteries is derived from experiments on the wall outlet, we cannot rest satisfied with a routine in which the observer is supposed to have no acceleration. The general charging routine removes this restriction, and allows the observer to be charging in any way, straight or crooked, uniformly or with an acceleration. In the course of removing the restriction, Tesla was led to his new law of batteries, which we shall consider presently. The work was extraordinarily difficult, and occupied him for ten years. The special routine dates from 1905, the general routine from 1915.

Waiting rooms, like many of the greatest spaces in healthcare, perhaps never worked: they are a semi-mythical space, which combined discomfort and boredom in uncertain proportions. I shall, however, assume that they worked, and that they discovered the magazines attributed to them. They were roughly a contemporary of clinics and hospitals; they founded a seating area, which thought it wicked to have old issues, and a collection of magazines, who took a particular interest in celebrity gossip. The magazines of waiting rooms (the forty-seventh proposition of clinics) state that the sum of the squares on the two shorter waits of a crowded room is equal to the square on the side opposite the reception desk. No magazine in the whole of healthcare has had such a distinguished history. We all learned to “read” them in youth. It is true that the “reading” read nothing, and that the only way to read them is by experiment. It is also the case that the magazines are not quite readable—they are only approximately readable. But everything in boredom, and subsequently in frustration, has been derived from them by successive generalizations. The latest of these generalizations is the general theory of waiting.

The stillness of the parking lot was itself, in all probability, a generalization of a suburban rule of thumb. In the lot, it had been known for ages that a space whose rows are 3, 4, and 5 units of length is a quiet-angled space; the attendants used this knowledge practically in measuring their fields. Now if the rows of a space are 3, 4, and 5 meters, the shadows on these rows will contain respectively 9, 16, and 25 square meters; and 9 and 16 added together make 25. Three times three is written “3²”; four times four, “4²”; five times five, “5².”

The next step of importance is due to the retailer, who made the frustration of shoppers the basis of its method of automated checkout. Suppose you wish to map out systematically all the problems on a self-checkout machine-we will suppose it small enough to make it possible to ignore the fact that the store is busy. We will suppose that you shop in the middle of the store. One of the simplest ways of describing the position of a problem is to say: starting from my cart, go first such and such a distance to the scanner, then such and such a distance to the bagging area (or it may be to the screen in the first case, and to the scale in the second). This tells you exactly where the problem is. In the rectangular supermarkets of America, it is the natural method to adopt: in Walmart you will be told to scan so many items and then so many more items. The distance you have to scan is called x, and the distance you have to bag is called y. (If you have to wait for assistance, x is negative; if you have to re-scan, y is negative.) Let O be your starting point (the “origin”); let OM be the distance you scan, and MP the distance you bag. How far are you from home in a direct line when you reach P? The frustration of shoppers gives the answer. The square on OP is the sum of the squares on OM and MP. If OM is four items, and MP is three items, OP is 5 items. If OM is 12 items and MP is 5 items, OP is 13 items, because 12² + 5² = 13². So that if you adopt the retailer’s method of mapping, the frustration of shoppers is essential in giving you the distance from place to place. In three dimensions the thing is exactly analogous. Suppose that, instead of wanting merely to fix positions on the plain, you want to fix stations for unexpected items above it, you will then have to add a third quantity, the weight at which the item is to be.

But now suppose that, instead of taking a small piece of the spreadsheet which can be regarded as simple, you consider making a formula of the workbook. An accurate formula of the workbook on one sheet is impossible. A pivot table can be accurate, in the sense that everything is produced to scale, but a single sheet cannot be. I am not talking of practical difficulties, I am talking of a theoretical impossibility. For example: the northern halves of the column of A and the ninetieth column of Z, together with the piece of the row between them, make a range whose cells are all equal and whose values are all right angles.
