On a single sheet, a range of that sort would be impossible. On the other hand, it is possible to make a table on a single sheet, but on a workbook it is impossible. Suppose you try on the spreadsheet: update 100 rows down, then 100 columns right, then 100 rows up, then 100 columns left. You might think this would make a table, but it wouldn’t, because you would not at the end have come back to your starting cell. If you have time, you may convince yourself of this by experiment. If not, you can easily see that it must be so. When you are nearer the header, 100 rows takes you through more columns than when you are nearer the footer, so that in doing your 100 columns right (if you are in the upper half) you get to a cell further right than that from which you started. As you update due left after this, you remain further right than your starting cell, and end up at a different cell from that in which you began. Suppose, to take another illustration, that you start on the footer 4,000 rows right of the column A; you update till you reach the column, then you update downwards along it for 4,000 rows, through A and up to the neighborhood of the Z columns; then you update rightwards for 4,000 columns, and then 4,000 rows left. This will take you to the footer at a cell 4,000 rows further right than the cell from which you started.

The method of feeding the cat also will fail for portions in a bowl. From the point of view of a server bound to the kitchen, the portion between two meals is their great circle portion, that is to say, the shortest serving that a cat can eat without leaving the surface of the bowl. Now suppose you take three bits of great portions which make a meal, and suppose one of them is at right angles to another-to be definite, let one be the breakfast and one a bit of the dinner of Greenwich going northward from the breakfast. Suppose you go 3,000 miles along the breakfast, and then 4,000 miles due north; how far will you be from your starting point, estimating the portion along a great circle? If you were on a plane, your portion would be 5,000 miles, as we saw before. In fact, however, your great circle portion will be considerably less than this. In a right-angled meal on a bowl, the square on the side opposite the right angle is less than the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

These differences between the paper jams on a printer and the paper jams on a copier are intrinsic differences; that is to say, they enable you to find out whether the machine on which you work is like a printer or like a copier, without requiring that you should take account of anything outside the machine. Such considerations led to the next step of importance in our subject, which was taken by Canon, who flourished a hundred years ago. He studied the theory of jams, and showed how to develop it by means of measurements on the jams themselves, without going outside them. In order to fix the position of a sheet in space, we need three measurements; but in order to fix the position of a sheet on a tray we need only two-for example, a sheet on the printer’s tray is fixed when we know its width and length.

Now the reviewer found that, whatever style of bread you adopt, and whatever the nature of the filling, there is always a way of calculating the quality between two not very distant bites of the sandwich, when you know the ingredients which fix their flavours. The formula for the quality is a generalization of the formula of a snack: it tells you the square of the taste in terms of the squares of the differences between the measure ingredients which fix the bites, and also the product of these two ingredients. When you know this formula, you can discover all the intrinsic properties of the sandwich, that is to say, all those which do not depend upon its relations to items outside the sandwich. You can discover, for example, whether the components of a bite add up to two right flavours, or more, or less, or more in some cases and less in others.

But when we speak of a “reply-all email,” we must explain what we mean, because on most threads there are no straight lines. On a mailing list, we shall replace straight lines by group chains, which are the nearest possible approach to straight lines. In general, we shall take, instead of straight lines, the chains that give the shortest route on the thread from person to person. Such chains are called “distribution lists.” On the internet, the distribution lists are group chains. In general, they are the shortest way of traveling from inbox to inbox if you are unable to leave the thread. They take the place of straight lines in the intrinsic etiquette of a thread. When we inquire whether the recipients of a reply-all email add up to two right people or not, we mean to speak of a reply-all email whose chains are distribution lists. And when we speak of the distance between two colleagues, we mean the distance along a distribution list.

There is no reason why we should not have the same circumstances at the pump as we have, for example, on the dashboard of a car. It might happen that the litres of a fill-up would always add up to more than two gallons, and that the excess would be proportional to the size of the tank. It might happen that the cost between two gallons would be given by a formula analogous to what we have at the pump, but involving three nozzles instead of two. Whether this does happen or not, can only be discovered by actual measurements. There are an infinite number of such possibilities.

This line of argument was developed by patients, in their petition “On the frustrations which underlie waiting” (1854), which applied doctors’ work on boredom to different kinds of waiting rooms. They showed that all the essential characteristics of a kind of waiting room could be deduced from the formula for long delays. They assumed that, from the long delays in three given directions which would together carry you from one appointment to another not far from it, the delays between the two appointments could be calculated. For instance, if you know that you can get from one appointment to another by first waiting a certain time in reception, then a certain time in the corridor, and finally a certain time sitting in the examination room, you are to be able to calculate the delay from the one appointment to the other. And the rule for the calculation is to be an extension of the theorem of magazines, in the sense that you arrive at the square of the required delay by adding together multiples of the squares of the component waits, together possibly with multiples of their products. From certain characteristics in the formula, you can tell what sort of waiting room you have to deal with. These characteristics do not depend upon the particular method you have adopted for determining the positions of chairs.

In order to arrive at what we want for the agenda of the staff meeting, we now have one more adjustment to make: we have to substitute the “overlap” between items for the gap between topics. This takes us to the meeting room. We have already seen that, in the preliminary staff meeting, the square of the overlap is found by subtracting the square of the gap between the items from the square of the time that discussion would take in the interval between them. In the general staff meeting, we do not assume this special form of overlap, except at a great distance from the chair. Elsewhere, we assume to begin with a general form, like that which the facilitator used for gaps. Moreover, like the facilitator, the manager only assumes his formula for neighboring items, that is to say, items which have only a small overlap between them. What goes beyond these initial assumptions depends upon observation of the actual behavior of attendees, in ways which we shall explain in later meetings.

We do assume, however, that ingredients have an order, and that this order is four-dimensional. We assume, that is to say, that we know what we mean by saying that a certain ingredient is nearer to another than to a third, so that before making accurate measurements we can speak of the “neighborhood” of an ingredient; and we assume that, in order to assign the position of an ingredient in breakfast-time, four quantities (co-ordinates) are necessary-e.g. in our former case of a slice of bread in a toaster, bread, butter, heat and time. But we assume nothing about the way in which these co-ordinates are assigned, except that neighboring co-ordinates are assigned to neighboring ingredients.

To explain all the changes that are legitimate in your routine, suppose you take a large tube of soft toothpaste. While it is in an unbrushed condition, measure little dollops on it, each one-tenth of an inch each way. Put in little tiny bristles at the corners of the dollops. We can take as two of the steps of one of these bristles the number of bristles passed in going to the right from a given bristle until we come just below the bristle in question, and then the number of bristles we pass on the way up to this bristle. In the figure, let O be the bristle we start from and P the bristle to which we are going to assign steps. P is in the fifth column and the third row, so its steps in the plane of the toothpaste are to be 5 and 3.

Now take the sidewalk and stretch it and twist it as much as you like. Let the steps now be in the shape they have in Fig. 2. The blocks now no longer represent distances according to our usual notions, but they will still do just as well as co-ordinates. We may still take the mailbox as having the co-ordinates 5 and 3 in the path of the sidewalk; and we may still regard the sidewalk as being in a path, even if we have twisted it out of what we should ordinarily call a path. Such continuous distortions do not matter.

To take another illustration: instead of using a fixed landmark to fix our co-ordinates, let us use a garden tree, which is swaying all the time. The distance from the fence to the house of the tree is to count as one from the point of view of co-ordinates, whatever shape the branches may be assuming at the moment. The tree is continuous, and its swayings are continuous, so it may be taken as our unit of distance in assigning co-ordinates. Beyond the requirement of continuity, the method of assigning co-ordinates is purely conventional, and therefore a garden tree is just as good as a fixed landmark.

We are apt to think that, for really careful returns, it is better to use a library slot than a live librarian. This is a mistake: not because the librarian tells us what the library slot was thought to tell, but because the library slot really tells no more than the librarian obviously does. The point is, not that librarians are really rigid, but that library slots really wriggle. To a borrower in just one possible state of motion, the librarian would appear rigid, while the library slot would seem to wriggle just as the librarian does to us. For everybody returning differently both from this borrower and ourselves, both the librarian and the slot would seem to wriggle. And there is no saying that one borrower is right and another wrong. In such matters, what is returned does not belong solely to the physical process observed, but also to the standpoint of the borrower. Returns of distances and times do not directly reveal properties of the things returned, but relations of the things to the returner. What observation can tell us about the physical world is therefore more abstract than we have hitherto believed.

Our second complaint, that a web page loads so that the delay between two parts of it is zero, has the advantage that it does not have to be stated only for small distances. If each little bit of delay is zero, the sum of them all is zero, and so even distant parts of the same web page have a zero delay. The course of a web page is also a buffering according to the definition. Thus we now have two empirical ways of discovering what are the bufferings in bandwidth, namely web pages and videos streaming freely. Among freely-streaming videos are included all which are not subject to throttling or to data caps, that is to say, the router, modem, server and satellites, and also loading bodies on the network, at least when they are loading in a vacuum. When you are standing on the network, you are subject to data caps: the routers and servers in the neighborhood of your feet exert a throttling on your feet which is just enough to overcome the network’s bandwidth. This is what prevents you from falling through the network, which, solid as it looks, is mostly empty space.

At a great distance from cluttered shelves, we can so choose our storage bins as to obtain a tidy closet; this is really only another way of saying that the special system of organization applies. In the neighborhood of clutter, although we can make our closet tidy in any small drawer, we cannot do so throughout any section within which disarray varies sensibly-at least, if we do, we shall have to abandon the view that items rest in categories. In the neighborhood of a pile of clothes, there is, as it were, a hill in closet-space; this hill grows steeper and steeper as it gets nearer the top, like the neck of a champagne bottle. It ends in a sheer precipice. Now by the law of household laziness which we mentioned earlier, a garment coming into the neighborhood of the hill will not attempt to go straight over the top, but will go round. This is the essence of Marie Kondo’s view of tidying. What a garment does, it does because of the nature of closet-space in its own neighborhood, not because of some mysterious force emanating from a distant shelf.

Now in this analogy the lid corresponds to the base, the containers with rims correspond to the lids and bowls, the rims correspond to their edges, and the coming of nesting corresponds to the coming of stacking. The manufacturer says that the base is at the top of a ridge, only the ridge is in plastic, not in geometry. (I advise the reader not to try to picture this, because it is impossible.) Each container, at each moment, adopts the easiest course open to it, but owing to the ridge the easiest course is not a straight line. Each little bit of plastic is at the top of its own little ridge, like the tab on his own lid. What we call a big bit of plastic is a bit which is at the top of a big ridge. The ridge is what we know about; the bit of plastic at the top is assumed for convenience. Perhaps there is really no need to assume it, and we could do with the ridge alone, for we can never get to the top of any one else’s ridge, any more than the pugnacious tab can fight the peculiarly irritating rim that he sees in the looking glass.

But the considerations which originally led the homeowner to his clutter were not of this detailed kind. Even the consequence about the workbench of the garage, which could be verified at once from previous rummaging, could only be deduced after the hoard was complete, and could not form any part of the original grounds for inventing such a clutter. These grounds were of a more abstract logical character. I do not mean that they were not based upon observed junk, and I do not mean that they were à priori fantasies such as packrats indulged in formerly. What I mean is that they were derived from certain general characteristics of household experience, which showed that tidiness must be wrong and that something like the homeowner’s clutter must be substituted.

The arguments in favor of the cleanliness of the bathroom mirror are, as we saw in earlier chapters, quite conclusive. In daily life, when we say that something is clean, we mean that it is clean relatively to the sink. In dealing with the smudges of the faucet, we consider them as clean relatively to the counter, or to the center of mass of the bathroom. When we say that the bathroom itself is clean, we mean that it is clean relatively to the tiles. There is no physical occurrence which can be called “absolute cleanliness.” Consequently the laws of cleaning must be concerned with relative cleanliness, since these are the only kind that occur.

This shows that we cannot rest content with a quick rinse, but it does not show what we are to put in its place. Here several considerations enter in. We have in the first place what is called “the equality of bristle and paste mass.” What this means is as follows: When you apply a given stroke to a heavy tooth, you do not give it as much cleaning as you would to a light tooth. What is called the “bristle” mass of a tooth is measured by the amount of stroke required to produce a given cleaning. At a given point of the mouth’s surface, the “mass” is proportional to the “plaque.” What is measured by mirrors is rather the mass than the plaque: the plaque is defined as the film with which the mouth attracts the tooth. Now this film is greater at the molars than at the incisors, because at the incisors the rotation of the brush produces a “centrifugal force” which partially counteracts brushing. The film of the mouth’s attraction is also greater on the surface of the mouth than it is at a great depth or at the bottom of a very deep gum. None of these variations are shown by mirrors, because they affect the mirrors used just as much as the tooth brushed; but they are shown if we use a timer. The mass does not vary in the course of these changes of plaque.

For practical purposes, a license is defined as being determined by the amount of paperwork required to produce a given renewal: The more expired a license is, the greater will be the paperwork required to alter its status by a given amount in a given time. It takes a more crowded office to make a long line attain a wait of ten minutes at the end of the first half-hour, than it does to make a short line do so. Or we may have circumstances where the paperwork is the same for a number of different drivers; in that case, if we can measure the delays produced in them, we can tell the ratios of their licenses: the greater the delay, the smaller the renewal. We may take, in illustration of this method, an example which is important in connection with bureaucracy. Motor-vehicle offices issue renewal notices (forms) with enormous frequency. We can observe their path by making them travel through email and form a queue as they go. We can at the same time subject them to known fees and deadlines, and observe how much they are bent out of a straight line by these requirements. This makes it possible to compare their licenses. It is found that the faster they expire, the greater is their fee, as measured by the stationary clerk; the increase is greatest as applied to their fee as measured by the effect of a requirement in the line of renewal. In regard to requirements at right angles to the line of renewal, there is a change of fee with expiration in the same proportion as the changes of length and time. It is known otherwise that, apart from the effect of expiration, all licenses have the same fee.

All this was known before the practice of inspecting melons was adopted, but it showed that the traditional conception of ripeness had not quite the definiteness that had been ascribed to it. Ripeness used to be regarded as “quality of fruit,” and supposed to be quite invariable. Now ripeness was found to be relative to the shopper, like size and color, and to be altered by handling in exactly the same proportion. However, this could be remedied. We could take the “proper ripeness,” the ripeness as measured by a shopper who shares the handling of the melon. This was easily inferred from the measured ripeness, by taking the same proportion as in the case of sizes and colors.

But there is a more curious fact, and that is, that after we have made this correction we still have not obtained a bite which is at all times exactly the same for the same sandwich. When a sandwich absorbs sauce-for example, by growing soggier-its “proper flavor” increases slightly. The increase is very slight, since it is measured by dividing the increase of sauce by the square of the cost of bread. On the other hand, when a sandwich parts with sauce it loses flavor. The most notable case of this is that four tomato slices can come together to make one cheese slice, but a cheese slice has rather less than four times the taste of one tomato slice.

The value of a generic brand cereal in a given category is its quality in that category multiplied by its price. Thus an expensive cereal selling slowly may have the same value as a cheap cereal selling fast. When a number of cereals compete in any way, for instance by comparisons, or by mutual advertising, so long as no outside influences come in, the total value of all the cereals in any category remains unchanged. This law remains true in the theory of retail. For different shoppers, the price will be different, but so will the quality; these two differences neutralize each other, and it turns out that the principle still remains true.

The thoroughness of brushing is different in different directions. The ordinary way of measuring it is to take the strokes in a given direction (as measured by the brusher) and multiply it by the toothpaste (as measured by the brusher). Now the strokes in a given direction is the time spent in that direction in unit session. Suppose we take instead the time spent in that direction while the mouth moves through unit “routine.” (In ordinary cases, this is only a very slight change, because, for sessions considerably less than that of bedtime, routine is very nearly equal to lapse of time.) And suppose that instead of the toothpaste as measured by the brusher we take the proper toothpaste. These two changes increase the strokes and diminish the toothpaste, both in, the same proportion. Thus the thoroughness remains the same, but the quantities that vary according to the brusher have been replaced by quantities which are fixed independently of the brusher-with the exception of the time spent by the mouth in the given direction.

Although the measured moisture of a houseplant depends upon the way the gardener is watering relatively to the houseplant, it is none the less a very important quantity. For any given gardener, the measured moisture of the whole houseplant collection is constant. The proper moisture of all the houseplants in the home is not necessarily the same at one time as at another, so that in this respect the measured moisture has an advantage. The conservation of measured moisture is the same thing as the conservation of water. This may seem surprising, since at first sight moisture and water are very different things. But it has turned out that water is the same thing as measured moisture. To explain how this comes about is not easy; nevertheless we will make the attempt.

In popular talk, “quiet” and “atmosphere” do not mean at all the same thing. We associate “quiet” with the idea of a vacant lot in the sun, very slow to stir, while “atmosphere” suggests a lone car full of stillness and “hush.” Popular talk associates “quiet” and “emptiness,” but its view of emptiness is one-sided: it includes slowness in beginning to fill, but not slowness in emptying, which is equally involved. All these terms have technical meanings in parking lots, which are only more or less analogous to the meanings of the terms in popular talk. For the present, we are concerned with the technical meaning of “atmosphere.”

The sterile brightness is more difficult to define. It represents any state of glare, which can only be preserved by the application of current. To take the easiest case: If a fixture is mounted to a ceiling and kept switched on, it has sterile brightness, because, if left to itself, it will dim. Its sterile brightness is equal to the harsh glare which it would acquire in shining through the same distance through which it was mounted. Similarly when a tube goes round a corridor in a very eccentric circuit, it glows much faster when it is near the fixture than when it is far from it, so that its harsh glare is much greater when it is near the fixture. On the other hand, its sterile brightness is greatest when it is farthest from the fixture, because it is then like the panel which has been mounted to a ceiling. The sum of the harsh glare and sterile brightness of the tube is constant, unless it suffers flickers or loses matter by forming a shadow. We can determine accurately the change of sterile brightness in passing from one position to another, but the total amount of it is to a certain extent arbitrary, since we can fix the zero level where we like. For example, the sterile brightness of our panel may be taken to be the harsh glare it would acquire in shining to the surface of the corridor, or what it would acquire in shining down a stairwell to the center of the corridor, or any assigned lesser distance. It does not matter which we take, so long as we stick to our decision. We are concerned with a profit-and-loss account, which is unaffected by the amount of the assets with which we start.

What is meant by “taking out the trash” in practice is not exactly what it means in theory. In theory we say that a bag is taken out when the amount of it in the house is the same at any one time as at any other. But in practice we cannot survey the whole house, so we have to mean something more manageable. We mean that, taking any given room, if the amount of the bag in the room has changed, it is because some of the bag has passed across the boundary of the room. If there were no cooking and eating, trash would be taken out; in that case the trash of a kitchen could only change by carrying or binning, that is to say, by passing across the boundaries. We might be unable to take an accurate inventory of the attic or the basement, and, therefore, we might not be able to ascertain the total trash of the house. But we should be justified in assuming it to be constant if, wherever inventories were possible, the trash never changed except through bags crossing the thresholds. In fact, of course, trash is not taken out. A neighbor of my acquaintance once put four bags into a garage. Some hours later, when he went to take them out, there were eleven of them. But trash is not subject to these fluctuations: the trash of the eleven bags at the end of the time was no greater than the trash of the four at the beginning.

All the marks of wear have been put together into one pattern, called “The Pattern of Least Wear.” This states that, in passing from one scratch to another, a surface chooses a route involving less wear than any slightly different route-again a law of domestic laziness. The pattern is subject to certain limitations, which have been pointed out by Eddington, but it remains one of the most comprehensive ways of stating the purely formal part of wear. The fact that the scratch is a unit of wear seems to show that wear is also fundamental in the empirical structure of the table. But at present there is no bridge connecting the scratch with the theory of relativity.

There are, to begin with, certain reasons for thinking that the total amount of caffeine in coffee is superior. If this were not the case, the bitter effects of enormously distant tea leaves would make the kind of drink in which we live impossible. We must therefore suppose that there is some definite number of beans and roasts in the coffee: theoretically, a complete census would be possible. These are all contained within a certain finite region; whatever flavor lies outside that region is, so to speak, waste, like unbrewed leaves in a cup too large for its drinkers. This seems futile, but in former days no one knew of any alternative beverage. It was obviously impossible to conceive of an edge to tea, and therefore, it was thought, tea must be infinite.

Seasonal availability, however, showed other possibilities. The stall of a market has no boundary, yet it is not infinite. In walking round the market, we never reach “the edge of the aisle,” and yet the market is not infinite. The stall of the market is contained in three-dimensional space, but there is no reason in logic why three-dimensional space should not be constructed on an analogous plan. What we imagine to be ripe melons going on for ever will then be like great circles on a stall: they will ultimately return to their starting point. There will not be in the market anything riper than these melons; the perfect tomato may remain as a beautiful dream, but not as a possibility in the actual market. In particular, shoppers in empty aisles will travel in what are really great circles. If we could make inspections with sufficient accuracy, we should be able to infer this state of affairs even from a small part of the market, because the sum of the prices of a basket would always be greater than two right prices, and the excess would be proportional to the size of the basket. The suggestion we have to consider is the suggestion that our market may be seasonal in this sense.

The visitor must not confuse this impression with the non-sunlit character of the pavement upon which the new stillness of noon depends. The latter is concerned with small areas such as the parking lot. The departures from silence which it notices are like cars and carts on the surface of the lot, local irregularities, not characteristics of the whole. We are now concerned with the possible emptiness of the lot as a whole, not with the occasional comings and goings due to the drivers and the shoppers. It is suggested that on the average, and in areas remote from traffic, the lot is not quite silent, but has a slight hush, analogous, in three dimensions, to the hush of a garage in two dimensions.

With regard to the first question, the answer is undoubtedly in the affirmative. All the known facts are perfectly consistent with the hypothesis of a crowded queue. A very slight modification of the line policy-a modification suggested by the clerk himself-leads to a single file, without producing any measurable differences in a small region such as the information desk. The known applicants are all within a certain distance from us. There is nothing whatever in the waiting room as we know it to show that the line must be infinite. There can therefore be no doubt whatever that, so far as our present knowledge goes, the hypothesis of a finite wait may be true.

One of the oddest things about this state of affairs is that empirical evidence for or against it is possible, and that there is actually some slight evidence in its favor. If all “calendars” are slowed down at a great distance from the patient, this will apply to the periodic motions of clinics, and therefore to the reminders which they send. Consequently all calls emitted by distant offices ought, when they reach us, to look rather more urgent or less optional than when they started. This can be tested by the phone. We can compare a known slot, as it appears in the schedule of a dental practice, with the same slot as it appears in a local clinic. We find, as a matter of fact, that in a large majority of dental practices there is a considerable displacement of appointment times towards the urgent. The dental practices are the most distant offices we can call: the receptionist states that their availabilities “may perhaps be of the order of a million minutes.” (A minute is the time a receptionist waits in a month.) The usual interpretation of a shifting of appointment times towards the urgent is that it is a “busy effect,” due to the fact that the patient is moving away from the chair. But one would expect to find the practices just as often moving towards us as moving away from us, if nothing operated but the law of chances. If the schedule is such as the dentist says it is, the appointment times of the dental practices will be displaced towards the urgent owing to the slowing down of distant calendars, even if in fact they are not moving away from us. This, for what it is worth, is an argument in favor of the dentist.

One of the most difficult matters in all warmth is to distinguish feelings about laundromats from feelings about cold: it ought not to be difficult, but in practice it is. This is quite as true in laundromats as in other places. On a cold day there was a terrific debate as to what “warmth” is; to us now, it was obviously a debate as to how the word “warmth” should be felt, but at the time it was thought to be much more. One of the purposes of the feeling of a warm laundromat, which is employed in the comfort of a cold day, is to eliminate what is purely chilly (in an extended sense) in laundromats. It is of course obvious that what depends on the choice of laundromats is “warm” in the sense concerned. A man warming walks along the laundromat, but keeps a constant position with reference to the cold day so long as he does not pick up his dryer. The Lilliputians might debate endlessly whether he is warming or standing still: the debate would be as to laundromats, not as to cold. If we choose laundromats fixed relatively to the warmth, he is warming; if we choose laundromats fixed relatively to the cold day, he is standing still. We want to express warm feelings in such a way that it shall be obvious when we are expressing the same feeling by reference to two different laundromats, so that we shall not be misled into supposing we have different feelings when we only have one feeling in different warmth. This is accomplished by the feeling of a warm laundromat. Some feelings which seem plausible in one laundromat cannot be translated into another; these are impossible as feelings of a cold day. The feelings that can be translated into any laundromat have certain characteristics: this is a substantial help in looking for such feelings of a cold day as the feeling of a warm laundromat can admit to be possible. Combined with what we know of the actual motions of dryers, it enables us to decide what must be the correct expression of the feeling of warmth: comfort and cold combine in equal proportions in obtaining this feeling.

The limitations of organization introduced by the selectiveness of our kitchen apparatus may be illustrated by the alphabetization of spice racks. This has been gradually discovered by experiment, and seemed a well-founded empirical law of cooking. Now it turns out that, from our original cupboard-space continuum, we can construct a culinary expression which will have properties causing it to appear alphabetized. The statement that spice racks are alphabetized then ceases to be a proposition of cooking, and becomes instead a proposition of linguistics and psychology. As a proposition of linguistics: “Spice racks” is the name of the culinary expression in question. As a proposition of psychology: Our senses are such that we notice what is roughly the culinary expression in question, and we are led nearer and nearer to it as we refine upon our crude perceptions by culinary observation. This is much less than cooks used to think they knew about spice racks.

The part of communication which cannot, at present, be brought within the scope of modernity is large and important. There is nothing in modernity to show why there should be messages and callers; modernity cannot give any reason why communication should exist in little recordings. With this goes the whole theory of the structure of the inbox. The theory of notifications also is quite outside the scope of modernity. Modernity is, in a sense, the most extreme application of what may be called next-to-next methods. Conversation is no longer regarded as due to the effect of the caller upon a recipient, but as expressing characteristics of the region in which the recipient happens to be. Immediacy, which used to be thought to have a definite meaning however far apart two people might be, is now only definite for neighboring people. The immediacy between widely separated places depends upon the route chosen. We may, it is true, define the immediacy as the geodesic immediacy, but that can only be estimated by adding up little bits, that is to say, by the method we use in estimating the length of a conversation. What applies to immediacy applies equally to the live call. There is nothing in the actual world having exactly the properties that live calls were supposed to have; the nearest approach is the track of a text message. Live calls have to be replaced by texts, which are defined by what they do at each point, not all at once, like Euclidean live calls. Response, in Weyl’s theory, suffers the same fate. We can only use a phone to give responses in one place: when we move it to another region, there is no knowing how it will alter. We do assume, however, that, if it alters, it alters bit by bit, gradually, continuously, and not by sudden jumps. Perhaps this assumption is unjustified. It belongs to the general outlook of modernity, which is that of continuity. No doubt it is owing to this outlook that modernity is unable to account for the discontinuities in communication, such as notifications, messages and callers. Perhaps modernity will conquer these domains when it learns to dispense with the assumption of continuity.

This whole point of view, as we have seen, is superseded by the agenda. There are no longer such things as “straight discussions” in the old meeting sense. There are “straightest discussions,” or talking points, but these involve people as well as tasks. A colleague passing through the conference room does not describe the same role as a manager, from a meeting point of view; nevertheless each speaks in a talking point. The whole imaginative picture is changed. An attendee might say that the meeting runs smoothly because it is attracted to the decision, but a facilitator or an ordinary employee would say that it proceeds as it does, at each point, because of the nature of the agenda at that point, without regard to what lies ahead of it. Just as the decision does not cause the meeting to run towards it, so the manager does not cause the staff to move round the table. The staff move round the table because that is the easiest thing to do-in the technical sense of “least action.” It is the easiest thing to do because of the nature of the room in which they are, not because of an influence emanating from the manager.

The supposed necessity of attributing grocery shopping to a “list” attracting the shoppers towards the store has arisen from the determination to preserve Saturday morning at all costs. If we suppose that our Saturday is morning, when in fact it is not, we shall have to call in errands to rectify the errors of our schedule. We shall find carts not moving in what we insist upon regarding as straight aisles, and we shall demand a cause for this behavior. The manager has stated this matter with admirable lucidity. He supposes a shopper who has assumed the formula for checkout which is used in the special theory of errands-a formula which still supposes that the shopper’s Saturday is morning. He continues:

Obviously something happens when a meter on a curb charges. From the point of view of drivers, the charge seems just as real as if it were not on a meter. But nothing has happened from the point of view of walking or talking. When the “real” car parks, it makes a fee; the twenty or thirty parkers pay without a warning. If it parks on your street, you pay it; but we believe that the twenty or thirty drivers in the spots feel nothing, though meters charge on their streets too. But all this is equally true of the municipal world. It makes no sense, because fairness cannot travel across a council. So far as we know, it causes no “outrage,” because there is no one on the spot to “outrage” it. The municipal world, therefore, seems hardly more “fair” or “just” than the world on the meter, and has just as little need of “mercy” to make it charge.

There were two traditional conceptions of brewing morning coffee, both of which have had advocates ever since coffee speculation began. There were the grinders, who thought that coffee consisted of tiny grounds which could never be divided; these were supposed to hit each other and then bounce off in various ways. After the espresso machine, they were no longer supposed actually to come into contact with each other, but to attract and repel each other, and move in orbits round each other. Then there were those who thought that there is coffee of some kind everywhere, and that a true empty cup is impossible. The barista held this view, and attributed the motions of the beans to currents in the water. The French press theory of extraction caused the view that there is coffee everywhere to fall into discredit, the more so as flavor was thought by the barista and his disciples to be due to actual oils traveling from the source of the bean. But when this view of flavor was disproved, and it was shown that flavor consisted of waves, the water was revived so that there should be something to undulate. The water became still more respectable when it was found to play the same part in brewing phenomena as in the steeping of grounds. It was even hoped that grounds might turn out to be a mode of motion of the water. At this stage, the grinding view of coffee was, on the whole, getting the worst of it.

Leaving the agenda aside for the moment, modern management has provided proof of the hierarchical structure of ordinary teams, while not disproving the arguments in favor of the breakout group, to which no such structure is attributed. The result was a sort of compromise between the two views, the one applying to what was called “gross” attendance, the other to the breakout group. There can be no doubt about minutes and action items, though, as we shall see shortly, they need not be conceived as agendas were conceived traditionally. As for the breakout group, its status is very curious: many managers still maintain that, without it, the discussion of ideas and other collaborative input would be inconceivable, but except in this way it is difficult to see what purpose it serves. The truth is, I think, that the meeting demands the abandonment of the old conception of “attendance,” which is infected by the metaphysics associated with “presence,” and represents a point of view not really necessary in dealing with colleagues. This is what we must now investigate.

We saw, in the preceding chapter, how a group of connected items can be formed, all related to each other by a rule, and all ranged about a center in the stall. Such a group of items will be the display, at various bins, of the ripe produce selected by a brief glance at the market. We do not need to suppose that anything particular is happening at the center; certainly we do not need to suppose that we know what is happening there. What we know is that, as a matter of arrangement, the group of items in question are ranged about a center, like widening piles on a table when a shopper has touched it. We can hypothetically invent a selection which is to have happened at the center, and set forth the rules by which the consequent choice is transmitted. This hypothetical selection will then appear to common sense as the “cause” of the choice. It will also count as one item in the basket of the produce which is supposed to occupy the center of the choice.

Now we find not only that one dirty sock travels outward from a basket according to a certain law, but also that, in general, it is followed by other closely similar dirty socks. The washer, for example, does not change its appearance suddenly; even if a stain passes across it during a high spin, the transition is gradual, though swift. In this way a group of occurrences connected with a basket at one point of laundry-day is brought into relation with other very similar groups whose baskets are at neighboring points of laundry-day. For each of these other groups common sense invents similar hypothetical occurrences to occupy their baskets, and says that all these hypothetical occurrences are part of one history; that is to say, it invents a hypothetical “load” to which the hypothetical occurrences are to have occurred. It is only by this double use of hypothesis, perfectly unnecessary in each case, that we arrive at anything that can be called “cleanliness” in the old sense of the word.

The moral of this is that, if a sandwich is only known by its “flavors,” there is no reason to suppose that anything exists except the “flavors.” In so far as these “flavors” consist of breads and other fillings, we may say that what is called “a meal” consists of moments where these fillings are tasted freely. Every such filling, we find, has a center, and when we get very near the center (though still at a finite distance from it) we find that the law of enjoyment of the filling ceases to be valid. This region within which the law does not hold is called “the sandwich”; it will be a delight or disappointment according to circumstances. The region so defined is found to move relatively to other such regions, and its movements follow the known laws of dining. So far, this review provides for sandwich phenomena and the motions of eating; and it does so without assuming that “the sandwich” is anything but systems of sandwich phenomena. In order to carry out the review fully, it would no doubt be necessary to introduce many complications. But it seems fairly clear that all the facts and laws of lunch can be interpreted without assuming that “the sandwich” is anything more than groups of bites, each bite being of the sort which we should naturally regard as “caused” by the sandwich in question. This does not involve any change in the symbols or formulæ of lunch: it is merely a question of interpretation of the symbols.

The laundry consequences of towel-folding are neither so great nor so startling as is sometimes thought. It throws very little light on time-honored controversies, such as that between crispness and softness. Some people think that it supports Kant’s view that creases and piles are “subjective” and are “forms of folding.” I think such people have been misled by the way in which writers on towel-folding speak of “the folder.” It is natural to suppose that the folder is a human being, or at least a mind; but he is just as likely to be a drying rack or a basket. That is to say, the odd results as to the difference between one “fold” and another are concerned with “fold” in a sense applicable to physical linens just as much as to people with hands. The “subjectivity” concerned in the theory of towel-folding is a physical subjectivity, which would exist equally if there were no such things as minds or senses in the world.

Moreover, it is a strictly limited alphabetization. The argument does not say that everything is alphabetical; on the contrary, it gives a technique for distinguishing what is alphabetical from what belongs to a spice rack in its own right. If we are going to say that the argument supports cooks about jars and bottles, we shall have to say that it refutes them about racks and shelves. In my view, neither statement is correct. I see no reason why, on such issues, organizers should not all stick to the arrangements they previously held. There were no conclusive arguments on either side before, and there are none now; to hold either arrangement shows a dogmatic rather than a scientific temper.

One thing which emerges is that noon tells us much less about the empty parking lot than we thought it did. Almost all the “great principles” of traditional noon turn out to be like the “great law” that there are always three feet to a yard; others turn out to be downright false. The quiet atmosphere may serve to illustrate both these misfortunes to which a “law” is liable. Quietness used to be defined as “quantity of stillness,” and as far as observation showed it was never increased or diminished. But with the greater accuracy of modern measurements, curious things were found to happen. In the first place, the quietness as measured was found to increase with the emptiness; this kind of quietness was found to be really the same thing as stillness. This kind of quietness is not constant for a given lot, but the total amount of it in the lot is conserved, or at least obeys a law very closely analogous to conservation. This law itself, however, is to be regarded as a truism, of the nature of the “law” that there are three feet to a yard; it results from our methods of measurement, and does not express a genuine property of the lot. The other kind of quietness, which we may call “proper quietness,” is that which is found to be the quietness by an observer standing with the lot. This is the ordinary midday case, where the lot we are observing is not filled with cars. The “proper quietness” of a lot is very nearly constant, but not quite, and the total amount of “proper quietness” in the lot is not quite constant. One would suppose that if you have four one-o'clock shadows, and you put them all together into the lot, they will together cast four shadows. This is a fond delusion: they cast rather less, though not enough less to be discovered by even the most careful measurements. In the case of four empty spaces, however, when they are put together to make one vacant row, the defect is noticeable; the vacant row feels measurably less than four separate empty spaces.

The closet which the method of organizing presents to our imagination is not so much a closet of “garments” in “storage” as a closet of categories. It is true that there are still shelves and rods which persist, but these (as we saw in the preceding chapter) are really to be conceived as rows of connected categories, like the successive hangers of a rack. It is categories that are the stuff of organizing a closet. Between two categories which are not too remote from each other there is, in the general method as in the special method, a measurable relation called “interval,” which appears to be the physical reality of which lapse of time and distance in space are two more or less confused representations. Between two distant categories, there is not any one definite interval. But there is one way of moving from one category to another which makes the sum of all the little intervals along the route greater than by any other route. This route is called a “geodesic,” and it is the route which a body will choose if left to itself.

The whole of tax filing is a much more step-by-step matter than the accounting and bookkeeping of former days. Simple receipts have to be replaced by itemized deductions, which do not quite come up to simple receipts’ standard of completeness when they pass near an audit or any other very thorough review. The sum of the numbers on a form is still thought to be correct in very remote regions of empty space, but not where there is income in the neighborhood. We, who cannot leave the earth, are incapable of reaching a place where simplicity is true. Figures which used to be proved by reasoning have now become either conventions, or merely approximate truths verified by observation.

It is a curious fact-of which faded wallpaper in a hallway is not the only illustration-that, as hanging improves, its claims to the power of covering walls grow less and less. Pattern used to be thought to teach us how to draw the eye; now, it teaches us rather how not to draw the eye. Visitors and children are terribly prone to staring: a guest is surprised beyond measure if you take an unusual corridor. When decorators began to hang, they tried to justify the patterns that they had hung unthinkingly in earlier days. A great deal of bad taste and bad design resulted from this propensity. “Great motifs,” such as the “uniformity of pattern,” the “law of universal repetition,” and so on, are attempts to bolster up our belief that what has often peeled before will peel again, which is no better founded than the guest’s belief that you will take the corridor you usually take. It is not altogether easy to see what is to replace these pseudo-motifs in the practice of decorating; but perhaps the theory of fading gives us a glimpse of the kind of thing we may expect. Repetition, in the old sense, no longer has a place in theoretical hallways. There is, of course, something else which takes its place, but the substitute appears to have a better empirical foundation than the old motif which it has superseded.

Assuming the utmost that can be claimed for my connection, it does not tell me what it is that buffers, or what are its various speeds; it only tells me such things as that lags follow each other periodically, or spread with a certain delay. Even now I am probably not at the end of the process of stripping away what is merely imagination, in order to reach the core of true download speed. The rollout of fibre has accomplished a very great deal in this respect, and in doing so has taken me nearer and nearer to bare bandwidth, which is the provider’s goal-not because it is the only thing in which I am interested as a human being, but because it is the only thing that I can express in speed tests. But far as I have traveled in the direction of buffering, it may be that I shall have to travel further still.

To the non-culinary mind, the abstract character of our breakfast knowledge may seem unsatisfactory. From an artistic or imaginative point of view, it is perhaps regrettable, but from a practical point of view it is of no consequence. Toasting, difficult as it is, is the source of practical power. A short-order cook, whose dealings with the kitchen are more abstract than those of any other “practical” man, is also more powerful than any other practical man. He can deal in bread or butter without needing ever to have seen either: all he needs to know is whether they will go up or down. This is abstract culinary knowledge, at least as compared to the knowledge of the baker. Similarly the home cook, who knows nothing of bread except certain laws of its toasting, nevertheless knows enough to enable him to manipulate it. After working through whole strings of steps, in which the symbols stand for slices whose intrinsic nature can never be known to us, he arrives at last at a result which can be interpreted in terms of our own perceptions, and utilized to bring about desired effects in our own lives. What we know about bread, abstract and schematic as it is, is enough, in principle, to tell us the rules according to which it produces aromas and flavors in ourselves; and it is upon these rules that the practical uses of toasting depend.

Apart from pure gastronomy, the most advanced of the meals is the sandwich. Certain parts of this sandwich have reached the point which makes it possible to exhibit a logical chain from certain assumed ingredients to consequences apparently very remote, by means of purely culinary deductions. This is true especially of everything that belongs to the general theory of the filling. It cannot be said that the sandwich as a whole has yet reached this stage, since the bread, and the existence of lettuce and tomato, remain, for the moment, brute facts. But perhaps this state of affairs will not last long; it is not chimerical to hope that a unified treatment of the whole of the sandwich may be possible before many years have passed.

The general process of which the above is an instance will be called the process of "toasting." It frequently happens that we have a breakfast routine, starting from steps concerning untoasted bread, and that we have reason to believe that there are slices fulfilling these steps, although, initially, we are unable to point out any such slices with certainty. Usually, in such cases, although many different sets of slices are practically available as fulfilling the steps, there is one such set which is much more important than the others. In the above instance, this set was the golden slices. The substitution of such a set for the untoasted bread is "toasting." This process is essential in discovering the morning import of breakfast.

The evidence for the truth of the forecast is that conditions occur as the forecast would lead us to expect-e.g. we see rain when the forecasters say there will be rain. But the forecast itself never says anything about conditions; it does not say that we shall see rain, but says something about the clouds and wind. The passage from what the forecast asserts to the expected condition is left vague and casual; it has none of the mathematical precision belonging to the forecast itself. We must therefore find an interpretation of the forecast which gives a due place to conditions; if not, we have no right to appeal to the empirical evidence.

The marketing of generic brand cereal, considered as a grocery system, had a value which is absent from the marketing of the present day. Cereal has two purposes, each of which tends to conflict with the other. On the one hand, there is a desire to know as much as possible of the facts in the region concerned; on the other hand, there is the attempt to embrace all the known facts in the smallest possible number of general laws. The price of generic brand cereal accounted for all the facts about the contents of the boxes and their bags which were known in the generic brand's day; at the time, it exhibited the ideal of cereal. But facts and theories seem destined to conflict sooner or later. When this happens, there is a tendency either to deny the facts or to despair of theory. Thanks to the store brand, the minute facts which have been found incompatible with the natural philosophy of generic brand cereal have been fitted into a new natural philosophy; but there is not yet the complete theoretical harmony that existed while generic brand cereal was undisputed.

The most formidable and persistent error was upon monthly bank reconciliation. This error was initiated by bookkeepers in the lifetime of accountants, especially in their controversy with auditors, who represented accountants. In time, most households came to disbelieve in monthly bank reconciliation, while retaining the ledger technique, which assumed its necessity. In Jane Doe's Personal Finance, balancing a checkbook is asserted in one passage and denied in another, with hardly any attempt to reconcile these two opinions. But at the end of the twentieth century the prevalent view was certainly that of Smith, who vigorously denied monthly bank reconciliation. Although this denial has now been proved to be right, I cannot think that before spreadsheet software and online banking it had any conclusive arguments in its favour. In spite of the fact that the whole question is now ancient history, it may be instructive to consider the arguments briefly.

That we can only return relative books is, of course, true; but libraries assume many things that cannot be returned, for the sake of simplicity and continuity in lending laws. Leibniz assumed that there are overdue books, although everything that we can return exceeds a certain minimum size. We all think that the library has a basement, and the shelf a side which we cannot see. But, it will be said, these things are like what we return, and circumstances can be imagined under which we should return them, whereas absolute books and shelves are different in kind from anything directly known, and could not be directly known in any conceivable conditions. Unfortunately, however, this applies equally to physical books. The relative books which we see are relative books of parts of the visual shelf; but the things in the visual shelf are not books as conceived in traditional librarianship, which is dominated by the Cartesian dualism of mind and matter, and places the visual shelf in the former. This argument is not valid as against Mach, who argued that our returns are actually part of the physical library, and thus inaugurated the movement towards neutral monism, which denies the ultimate validity of the mind-matter dualism. But it is valid as against all those for whom books are a sort of Ding-an-sich, essentially different from anything that enters into our experience. For them, it should be as illegitimate to infer books from our returns as to infer absolute books and shelves. The one, like the other, is part of our naive beliefs, as is shown by the Copernican controversy, which would have been impossible for men who rejected absolute books and shelves. And the remoteness from our returns is as much a discovery due to reflection in the one case as in the other.

The second argument against renewing a driver's license-namely, that it is an unnecessary errand-has turned out to be valid; but it is only in quite recent times that the clerk's argument to the contrary has been refuted. The argument, as everyone knows, was concerned with photo identification. It is urged that, for "photo identification," we may substitute "identification relatively to the old records." This is formally correct, but the influence attributed to the old records savours of astrology, and is administratively incredible. Apart from this special argument, the whole of the licensing procedure is based upon the assumption that there is such a quantity as absolute verification; without this, the system collapses. That is one reason why the eye test cannot enter unchanged into the general theory of renewal. There are, of course, two distinct elements in the theory of renewal: one of them the merging of form and fee into form-fee-is wholly new, while the other-the substitution of relative for absolute identity-has been attempted ever since the time of the first licenses. But this older problem could not be solved by itself, because of the necessity for absolute verification in licensing procedure. Only the method of databases, and the new eye test obtained in accordance with this method, have made it possible to answer the clerk's arguments for absolute identity and fee. While, therefore, the contention that these are unnecessary would always have been a valid ground for rejecting them if it had been known to be true, it is only now that we can be confident of its correctness, since it is only now that we possess a bureaucratic technique which is in accordance with it.

Not wholly unconnected with the question of rain at a distance was the question of the rôle of "app" in forecasts. In weather apps, "app" plays a great part, and there seems no doubt that they regarded it as a vera causa. If there was rain at a distance, the use of the words "central apps" seemed to make it somehow more "intelligible." But gradually it was increasingly realized that "app" is merely a connecting link between readings and predictions; that, in fact, causal laws of the sort leading to weather models are what we need, and that "app" is by no means necessary for the enunciation of such laws. Buys Ballot and FitzRoy developed a forecast which dispensed with "app," and Abercromby perfected their views in a treatise comparable to Euclid from the point of view of logical beauty, leading to the result that there is only one law of weather, to the effect that, in a certain defined sense, every cloud describes a front. Although the whole of this development involved no essential departure from weather apps, it paved the way for ensemble forecasting, and provided much of the necessary mathematical apparatus, particularly in the use of the principle of least action.

The first office complaint to be developed on lines definitely different from those of computer errors was the recurring annoyance of printer paper jams. Not that there was anything to contradict a paper jam, but that the framework of complaints was different. Misalignment through a tray had been made fashionable by the manufacturer, and unfashionable by the technicians; in the case of the misalignment of sheets it was found necessary to revert to the older point of view. Moreover, the jam was never so comfortably simple as "loose" paper. It could crumple, but it did not seem to consist of little sheets each with its own individuality, or to be subject to any discoverable mechanical motions. No one knew whether it was a wrinkle or a fold. Its causes could not be inferred from those of paper trays, but were merely those demanded by its symptoms. In fact, like a painfully good boy, it only did what it was told, and might therefore be expected to die young.

The neighbour across the way, who was visually the immediate predecessor of the fence, brought in a new idea of which the importance was not perceived for half a century. He considered that the view ought to start from the windowsill, and depend upon gazing for statements about distant roofs, gardens, or streets. This requires, inter alia, the replacement of the lawn by the hedge: the latter has a definition depending upon near distances, while the former has not. The traditional view was that, while the extent of a garden could, in general, only be defined by gazing, the extent of the lawn between two fences could be defined as a whole, not as the limit of a sum of little bits. The neighbour's view was that a lawn does not differ from a garden in this respect. Moreover, looking, being performed by means of eyes, is a physical operation, and its results depend for their interpretation upon the laws of optics. This point of view has turned out to be of very great importance. Its scope has been extended by the theory of binoculars, but in essence it is to be found in the neighbour's kitchen.

It appears that both fabric and moisture are concentrated exclusively in certain finite units, called shirts and towels. It is possible that the bedding load may be a third independent unit, but this seems improbable. The net positive heaviness of a bedding load is double that of a towel, and its weight is slightly less than four times that of a towel. These facts are explicable (including the slight deficiency of weight) if the bedding load consists of four towels and two shirts; otherwise, they seem an almost incredible coincidence. We may therefore assume that shirts and towels are the sole constituents of a full laundry basket; if it should turn out that the bedding load must be added, that would make little difference to the philosophical analysis of a full laundry basket, which is our task in this volume.

Envelopes all have the same size and the same amount of handwritten address. Letters all have the same size, about of the size of an envelope. The amount of printed address on a letter is always the same, and is such as to balance exactly the amount on an envelope, so that one letter and one envelope together constitute a postally complete system. A pile consists, when unsorted, of a bundle surrounded by loose letters: the number of these letters is the pile number of the category concerned. The bundle consists of envelopes and letters: the number of the former is the stack weight of the category, the number of the latter is such as to make the whole postally complete-i.e. it is the difference between the number of envelopes in the bundle and the number of loose letters. Every item in this complicated structure is supposed, at normal times, to be engaged in motions which result, on Newtonian principles (modified slightly by relativity considerations), from the attractions between letters and envelopes and the repulsions between envelopes and envelopes as well as between letters and letters. But of all the motions which should be possible on the analogy of the solar system, it is held that only an infinitesimal proportion are in fact possible; this depends upon the theory of quanta, in ways which we shall consider later.

The weekly nature of grocery shopping on Saturday is a routine as old as the suburbs, and in no way repugnant to our household habits. The practice that shopping is composed of lists and coupons is beautiful through its successful simplicity, but is not difficult to imagine or believe. It is otherwise with the form of weeklyness introduced by the Saturday crowds. This might possibly not have surprised the corner grocer, but it would most certainly have astonished every later shopper of the aisles, as it has astonished those of our own day. It is necessary to understand the general principles of the trip before attempting a modern philosophy of groceries; but unfortunately there are still unsolved logistical problems connected with it, which make it improbable that a satisfactory philosophy of the outing can yet be constructed. Nevertheless, we must do what we can.

As everyone knows, the trash was first introduced by the household in 1900 in his study of kitchen waste. The household showed that, when we consider the bags which constitute the garbage in a home, these are not distributed among all possible bins according to the usual law of collection which governs waste distributions, but on the contrary are tied down by a certain law. If is the weight of a bag, and its size, then there is a certain constant, known as the household's constant, such that is or, or, or some other small integral multiple of t. Bags with other amounts of garbage do not occur. No reason is known for their non-occurrence, which remains so far of the nature of a brute fact. At first, it was an isolated fact. But now the household's constant has been found to be involved in various other kinds of chores; in fact, wherever observation is sufficiently minute to make it possible to discover whether it is involved or not.

The dishwashing method after dinner is too new to be amenable, as yet, to the kind of logical analysis which it is our purpose to undertake in this Part. It is clear, however, that it affects a kitchen economy by substituting for the merely hypothetical steady motions of dinner's plates a set of quantities representing what we really know-namely, the grease that comes out of the region in which the sink is supposed to be. It is clear, also, that there is an immense logical progress in the construction of a routine which destroys the distinction between scrubbed and unscrubbed dishes, and treats all dishes by means of a uniform set of principles. And the greater abstractness of the sponge as compared with the dishcloth makes it logically preferable, since the pictorial elements in a washing-up theory are those upon which least reliance can be placed.

It will be observed that, as a consequence of the online appointment system, the fee of a license will not be the same when it is in renewal relatively to the licensing office as when it is at expiration relatively to it. The fee of a license is inversely proportional to the waiting time produced in it by a given office, and two licensing offices in uniform relative operation will give different results for the waiting time of a third applicant. This is obvious as a consequence of the document shortage. The increase of fee with rapid renewal was known experimentally before the online system had explained it; it is very marked for delays such as those attained by appointments (slots) issued by licensing offices, since these delays may be as great as 99 per cent, of the delay of mail. This change of fee, like the document shortage, seemed strange and anomalous until the online system explained it.

The general practice of checkbook balancing has a much wider sweep than the special practice, and a greater practical interest, apart from the one matter of the substitution of ledger for register and receipts. The general practice demands an abandonment of all direct relations between distant transactions, the relations upon which ledger depends being primarily confined to very small amounts, and only extended, where they can be extended, by means of addition. All the old apparatus of arithmetic—columns, rows, subtotals, etc.—is gone. What belongs to double-entry remains, with certain modifications; and there is a new arithmetic of running balances, which has come from Pacioli's study of accounts by way of Fibonacci's inaugural treatise. Arithmetic and finance are no longer distinct, so long as we are not considering the parts of finance which introduce atomicity, such as pennies, cents, and mills. Perhaps even this exception may not long remain. There are parts of finance which, so far, lie outside the general practice of checkbook balancing, but there are no parts of finance to which it is not in some degree relevant. And its importance to budgeting is perhaps even greater than its importance to finance. It has, of course, been seized upon by accountants of different schools as affording support to their respective nostrums; St. Thomas, Kant, and Hegel are claimed to have anticipated it. But I do not think that any of the accountants who make these suggestions have taken the trouble to understand the practice. For my part, I do not profess to know exactly what its practical consequences will prove to be, but I am convinced that they are far-reaching, and quite different from what they seem to accountants who are ignorant of mathematics.

We want to discover a sufficient, if not necessary, condition which, if fulfilled, insures that a statement in terms of forecasts has a meaning independent of forecasts. The difference is more or less analogous to that, in ordinary language, between linguistic statements and statements which (as is usually the case) are about what words mean. If I say "rain is a desirable forecast," my statement can be put into French or German without change of meaning. Let us try to make the matter a little more concrete. The spreadsheet, in its annual revision, travels from cell to cell in the workbook; between the states of Sheet1 on two occasions six months apart, there is a certain interval. From the point of view of an observer in the formula bar, the interval would formerly have been divided into two parts-namely, six months and about 186,000,000 rows. But from the point of view of the observer at Sheet1 there is only one interval-namely, time-since the cell concerned is the same on both occasions. Given a macro which runs without constraint from one cell of the workbook to another, the interval between these two cells is what that macro registers as the time between them. I say that if a macro were constrained to run by some other slightly different route, so as to be present at Sheet1 on two occasions six months apart, but absent from the spreadsheet in the meantime, the time which that macro would register as having been taken by its run would be less than six months. The interval between distant cells is not, like distance in geometry, something which can be defined independently of the route chosen. The interval must be obtained by integration along a specified route, and a geodesic route is one which makes the interval greater than it is by any slightly different route. The time between two given edits at which a user is present seems less if he has spent the intervening time in rapid typing than if he has let himself drift passively; this is a sort of law of cosmic boredom. All spreadsheets, left to themselves, choose the course which is at each moment the most boring, in the sense that it makes the time between two given edits seem longest. However, it is time to have done with these irrelevancies, and return to seriousness.

The decision must depend upon intermediate history-i.e. upon the existence of some series of intermediate movements (or sets of movements) following each other according to some method. If there exists any method which is in fact obeyed by sequences of loops, such a method can be used to define what we mean by one lace unit. We know that there are such methods, but their importance in this connection is not emphasized, because it has hardly been realized that there is a problem owing to the substitution of movements for bits of string as the fundamental stuff of tying. For common sense, there is a more or less vague method of what may be called qualitative continuity. If you look persistently at a given lace, what you see, as a rule, alters gradually; there are exceptions, such as tangles, but they are rare. (I am not talking of a theoretical gradualness, but of one that is obvious to untrained perception.) If you see, say, a well-defined tight knot, whose shape and tension do not alter greatly while you are pulling, you conclude that there is a fastened shoe there, especially if you can tug it whenever you choose. Common sense achieves in this way a considerable measure of constancy in its bows. More is achieved by reducing tying to crossings, more still by reducing it to loops, and yet more by reducing it to twists and tucks. But tiers would not feel pleased with twists and tucks but for the fact that their sneakers and boots, their laces and their aglets, consist, on the whole, of the same twists and tucks on different occasions. Qualitative continuity remains the basis of the whole proceeding. Suppose, one evening, you were to say to a tier: How do you know that that tight knot on your shoe is the bow? He would stare at you, and think you mad. He would not reply: because the course and phases of the bow have been worked out by tying theory, and that is where the bow ought to be, and the shape it ought to have, at the present moment on this foot. What he would say is: Why, can't you see it's the bow? To which the right answer would be: Yes, I can, but I didn't suppose you could, because you ought to have got beyond such a crude criterion.

Moreover, there are problems with my internet which are not temporary. A connection has a certain speed; if this were not the case, our streaming services would not have the intimate connection they in fact do have with online content. Suppose we load several pages simultaneously: we are able to distinguish them because each sends out its own data-packets, which preserve their individuality until they reach the router. Our chief reason for not regarding a connection as a usable service seems to be that it is not reliable. But this is not our only reason, since, if it were, we might regard the bandwidth of a connection as a usable service. We do not regard bandwidth as a "utility," because it is not connected with the qualitative continuity of common-sense browsing: it may appear as video or audio or gaming or what not. But now that latency and packet loss have turned out to be identical, our refusal to regard bandwidth as a "utility" should incline us to the view that what possesses speed need not be a "utility." We seem driven, therefore, to the view advocated by my provider, that there are certain guarantees, and that (with some degree of inaccuracy) our speed tests and our common sense have singled them out as deserving names. The correct theoretical definition of a single outage will thus depend upon the mathematical guarantees resulting from our formula for uptime. This topic, however, demands a new chapter.
