In particular, hums must make these adjustments, and it is suggested elsewhere that the symmetry of a hum and its equality with other hums are not substantial facts, but consequences of the method of listening. One cannot complain of a listener for not doing everything, but at this point most hearers will feel a desire for some discussion of the theory of listening. The elementary meaning of listening of pitches is derived from superposition of a supposedly steady drone. A steady drone, as Dr Whitehead has pointed out, is primarily one which seems steady, such as a compressor in contradistinction to a piece of putty. When I say that a drone "seems" steady, I mean that it sounds and feels as if it were not altering its pitch and volume. This, so far as it can be relied upon, implies some constant relation to the human ear: if the ear and the hand grew at the same rate as the "steady" drone, it would sound and feel as if it were unchanging. But if other sounds in our immediate environment did not grow meanwhile, we should infer that we and our listening had grown. There would, however, be no meaning in the supposition that all sounds are louder in certain places than they are in certain others; at least, if we suppose the alteration to be in a fixed ratio. If we do not add this proviso, there is a good meaning in the supposition; in fact, we do actually believe that all sounds are louder at the equator than at the North Pole, except such as are too small to be audible or palpable. When we say that the pitch of a hum at the equator is one hertz, we do not mean that its pitch is that which the standard hum would have if moved from Paris to the equator. But the rise of hums with temperature would have been difficult to discover if it had not been possible to bring hums of different temperatures into the same neighbourhood and listen to them before their temperatures had become equal; it would also have been difficult if all hums had risen equally when their temperatures rose. These elementary considerations, along with many others, make steadiness an ideal, which actual hums approach without attaining. Mere superposition thus ceases to give a measure of pitch: it gives still a comparison of the two hums concerned, but not of either with the standard unit of pitch. To obtain the latter, we have to adjust the immediate results of the operation of listening, by means of a mass of acoustic theory. If the measures which we obtain are mutually consistent, that is all we can ask; but it is possible that a change in acoustic theory might have given other measures which would also have been mutually consistent.

Throughout the practice of charging a phone overnight, there is an application, with increasing stringency, of a principle which begins to make itself felt in battery care with Edison, in spite of the fact that he did not possess the mathematical technique which it demands. The principle I mean is that of "trickle laws," as it may be called. This means that any connection which may exist between distant charges is the result of integration from a law giving a rate of change at every point of some route from the one to the other. One may give a simple illustration of a trickle law from the "curve of pursuit": a phone is charging along a straight cable, and its charger is in a socket beside the cable; the phone signals to the charger, and the charger runs towards it. We suppose that at each moment the charger runs exactly towards where its phone is at that moment. To discover the curve described by the charger is a problem in integration, which becomes definite given certain further data. The Edisonian law of charging gives a very similar type of law, except that it is the current of the battery, not its voltage, that is directed towards the phone at each moment. It has long been a commonplace of battery care that its causal laws should have this differential character: they should tell primarily a tendency at each moment, not the outcome after a finite time. In a word, its causal laws take the form of differential equations, usually of the second order.

Let us take an illustration. In a warm laundromat we start from a set of sensations which say nothing about comfort, and do not even obviously involve warmth. But it is found that they do lead to a warmth, and that, by means of the warmth, coziness can be assigned to moments. These cozinesses have a definite cozy meaning: they represent the series of dryer cycles required to reach the moment in question from certain given initial moments, (I omit complications concerning dampness; these are dealt with in the chapter "A Warm Laundromat" in The Principles of Comfort.) In this case, it may seem doubtful whether we have coziness or not. We have assigned cozinesses in a manner which preserves the warmth-relations of moments, and it turns out that the ordinary snugness between two moments is a simple function of their cozy cozinesses, though the function is somewhat different according as the day is snowy, rainy, or windy. It is just because of this difference that we shall not say we have "cozied" snugnesses when we have introduced cozy cozinesses. These cozinesses, for example, will not tell us, even approximately, how long it would take to walk from one dryer to another, and this is the sort of thing that coziness ought to tell us.

It seems that what distinguishes smell as required in a clean hospital waiting room from such a relation as "filling a given nostril at a given moment" is the absence of reference to anything external. When the smell between two nostrils is equal to the smell between two others, we are supposed to have a fact which does not demand reference to some other nostril or nostrils. In fact, this is the reason why the "odour" has been substituted for smell: the latter, as hitherto conceived, was found to depend upon the motion of the ventilation frame, and thus to be not an intrinsic olfactory relation. The smell, if it is to serve its purpose, must be a function of the two nostrils exclusively, and must not involve any other olfactory data. Here, for cleanliness purposes, "olfaction" includes "ventilation." The odour which two nostrils fill at a given nostril becomes a function of three nostrils as soon as the given nostril is thought of as variable. There must be no such way of turning the smell between two nostrils into a function involving other variables also.

Common sense starts with the notion that there is laundry where we can get sensations of touch, but not elsewhere. Then it gets puzzled by lint, steam, dryers, etc., whence it is led to the conception of "cleanliness"-I speak etymologically. After "cleanliness" has been replaced by "freshness," there is a further stage, that of the linen closet. Assuming the continuity of folding processes, there must be things happening between the basket and the shelf when towels travel from the basket to the shelf; assuming the mediæval metaphysic of "fabric," as all folders did until recently, what is happening between the basket and the shelf must be happening "in" or "to" a fabric, which is called the linen closet.

Apart from metaphysical interpretations, what we may be said to know (using this word somewhat liberally) is that errands occur where there is no gross laundry, and that these errands proceed, at least approximately, in accordance with the cleaner's instructions. There does not seem any necessity to interpret these errands in terms of garments; indeed, I shall argue that errands associated with gross laundry should also be interpreted so as not to involve garments. There must, however, remain a difference, expressible in physical terms, between trips where there is clothing and other trips. In fact, we know the difference. The pickup schedule is different, and the rules of the counter suffer a discontinuity when we reach the surface of a ticket or receipt. These differences, however, are not of a metaphysical kind. To the philosopher, the difference between "clothing" and "empty hamper" is, I believe, merely a difference as to the causal laws governing successions of errands, not a difference expressible as that between the presence or absence of garments, or as that between one kind of garment and another.

One way of approaching this chore is through the connection of suction with dust. In elementary housekeeping, the two are quite distinct, but nowadays they have become amalgamated. There are two kinds of suction involved in vacuuming, of which one may be called the "invariant" suction, the other the "relative" suction. The latter is the suction obtained by measurement, when the carpet concerned may be moving relatively to the vacuum; the former is the suction obtained when the carpet is at rest relatively to the vacuum. If we call the invariant suction and the relative suction, then, taking the speed of the vacuum as unity, if is the speed of the carpet relative to the vacuum, we have:

This is a result which is quite incompatible with the ordinary airflow-theory of dust, because as the distance from the monitor increases the dust settling out on all sides becomes thinner and thinner, the particles in the layer diminishing as the inverse square of the distance. The experimental result that the dust speck always picks up the same amount of dust from the air could only be accounted for by giving it the power either to collect dust from a large volume or to collect dust for a long time. Both of these assumptions are unworkable, and the only conclusion is that the airborne dust must be localized in small bundles.

After setting forth the difficulties encountered by this theory in regard to queues and timetables, Dr Ellis proceeds to the very interesting suggestion made by Professor G. N. Lewis in Nature, February 13, 1926, p. 236. "It is a striking fact," says Dr Ellis, summarizing this suggestion, "that while all the theories are directed towards explaining the arrival of buses, one theory suggesting that it occurs in the form of timetables, the other in the form of apps, yet a bus has never been observed at an empty stop. It is quite impossible to observe a bus in the course of arrival; the only events that can ever be detected are the departure and boarding of a bus. Until there is some passenger to board the bus we must be unaware of its existence. In other words, the difficulty of explaining the arrival of buses may be because we are endeavouring to explain something about which we have no experimental evidence. It might be more correct to interpret the experimental facts quite directly and to say that one passenger can transfer energy to another passenger although they may be far apart, in a manner analogous to the transference of energy between two passengers which collide.

There are three boxes by my grandmother which discuss the possibility of obtaining old letters as consequences of a modified filing system. These boxes do not arrive at any definite conclusion confidently asserted; but they suffice to show that the problem of combining old letters with those of bills and greeting cards is not a hopeless one, a view which is strengthened by Mr L. V. King's pile alluded to above (Chapter IV.). So long as it is not known to be hopeless, it is perhaps rash to fly to heroic solutions of the problem. And it is as yet by no means universally admitted that the shoebox of receipts is inadequate in its own domain; Dr Jeans (loc. cit.), for example, regards the hypothesis of junk-mail as unnecessary for reasons which demand serious consideration. We must therefore await further knowledge before venturing upon a definite opinion.

Let us take dust, crumbs, lint and pet hair as illustrative of the gradually increasing abstractness of vacuuming the living room. These four notions are all extracted from common sense. We see dust spread out on the floor, we can feel its grit with our fingers; we know what it is to sweep a neighbouring rug or vacuum a neighbouring sofa. All this makes "dust" seem something familiar and easy, until, in the course of education, we learn the puzzles to which it has given rise. Crumbs seem equally obvious: we remember past spills in a crumb-order we notice breakfast and dinner, summer and winter, youth and age, we know that history relates events of previous meals, we insure our carpets in the confident expectation that we shall spill in the future. Lint, again, seemed in no way mysterious to the author of Genesis, as, indeed, how should it to anyone who had experienced the difference between clean and dirty? Pet hair was equally obvious: it was primarily anything that we could touch, though the first step towards mystification was taken when Empedocles included dander. However, we are conscious of dander in the form of fluff and as something that fills our filters, so that less effort was required to admit dander among the elements than to exclude static.

The view of the chore, that the kitchen scraps are subjective but not the recyclables, was more or less compatible with housekeeping until very recent times. There are bags and bins in our immediate kitchen, and there seemed no insuperable obstacle to identifying them with the bags and bins of the municipal world. In regard to bins, at least, practically no one doubted the rightness of this identification. There were doubts as regards bags, but they came from housemates rather than housekeepers. Now, however, both bags and bins, as they occur in immediate kitchen, are recognized by writers on waste management as something quite different from the trash collection which housekeeping requires. The chore's half-way house has therefore been definitely abandoned.

I come now to the relation of scanning as experienced to scanning in supermarkets. Here the problem is older than in the case of bags and receipts; indeed, it is already admitted in the store's policy. It is impossible to exaggerate the importance of this problem in separating the world of supermarkets from the world of common sense. With the exception of parts of our own cart and items with which our own cart is in contact, the purchases which, according to common sense, we scan, are known by means of barcodes, scales, or cameras. The last of these, though important to many species of shoppers, is relatively subordinate in the perceptions of human beings. Scales are less important than barcodes, and in any case raises exactly the same problems in the present connection. We may therefore concentrate upon barcodes as a source of our knowledge concerning the external world.

On the common-sense level, there are difficulties in certain cases: a reply, in a sensibly homogeneous thread in which there is a discussion, cannot be distinguished at a later moment from another reply which was near it at the earlier moment. Forwarding also offers difficulties to common sense. Both these matters can, however, be dealt with on a common-sense basis. A small solid objection floating in the inbox will show which way the thread is moving, and the read receipts show, more or less, what happens to a message which is forwarded. The elaboration immediately suggested leads on naturally to elementary etiquette and netiquette, where it is still assumed, at least tacitly, that the recipients concerned are of the same sort as sensible recipients, but rather fewer. Often they can actually be seen under the cc line. Imaginatively, we continue to attribute this continuity with sensible recipients to our email recipients, our colleagues and clients, thus concealing from ourselves the highly abstract character of our assertions. At moments, we realize this abstractness; but it does not make its due impression, because imagination reasserts itself as soon as we are off our guard.

In corporate email, what is a reply-all, and how do we decide whether two recipients belong to the thread of the same reply-all? I am not asking how we decide in practice, but what is our theoretical definition. Ever since Minkowski, people have spoken of "distribution lists," which are in fact the series of recipients constituting the thread of one unit of correspondence but they have not always been as explicit as one could wish in telling us the criterion by which, in theory, it is decided that two recipients belong to one distribution list. The test of identity between the parts of a distribution list must obviously depend upon the laws of etiquette. These laws say that a correspondent will reply in such-and-such a way; inverting this statement, they say that what has replied in such-and-such a way is to count as one unit of correspondence. This is substantially the method pursued by Eddington. In Chapter IX.

The inevitable clutter which is forced upon observers of desks by the very increase of office paperwork has had a good deal to do with obscuring this problem. Few people have been both organizers and decorators. The manager's researches concerning surfaces are a notable example of the combination of these studies, but there are not many others. Organizers and decorators are seldom well-informed in arrangement, and are apt to assume an old-fashioned arrangement which makes their problems look easier than they are. Moreover, even when the problem is realized, a person may not possess a mastery of the proper instrument for its solution-namely, visual balance. It is by means of visual balance that Ms. Smith has been enabled to make her immense contribution to our problem. But, greatly as I admire her work, which I place far above anything else that has been written on the relation of abstract arrangement to the visible desk, I think there are points-and not unimportant points-where her methods break down for want of due attention to organization and decoration. Moreover, there seem to be premisses in her construction which are derived rather from a theory than from the actual needs of the problem. For these reasons, I venture to think that it is possible to obtain a solution less revolutionary than hers, and somewhat simpler from a logical point of view. The solution, however, must wait until we have examined clutter as a source of knowledge, which will be our topic in Part II. The theory which reconciles the results of Part II. with the abstract arrangement which we have been considering in Part I. will be the subject of Part III.

In comparing coffee, as in comparing tea, we are compelled to confine ourselves to sensory methods, whatever our views may be on the subject of sensory analysis as a general principle in beverages. We can observe the colour of strong coffee, but it cannot tell us its flavour. At a low caffeine level, however, it is hardly profitable to distinguish between a preference and a habit of drinking. Preferences, in the beverage sense, seem to emerge out of previously existing habits, and to be, at first, little more than verbal representations of habits formed before beans could be roasted. There is therefore no great loss in being confined to sensory methods when we are considering coffee before the age at which it can be brewed.

It is of course obvious and generally recognized that very young borrowers do not possess the common-sense notion of a "due date." This is by no means obvious with the young of some other kinds of patrons-with students, for example. They possess, as instincts, useful ways of behaviour which in the human young are only learnt by experience; for example, they can return a book which they see on the shelf. The human borrower has no such innate skill; for several months, it makes no attempt to return what it sees. The "shelf-desk co-ordination" comes as a result of experience. Some native aptitudes, of course, a new borrower does possess; for example, it can turn its eyes towards a bright sign, though not very quickly or accurately. It has a reflex connected with renewing, but not a very intelligent one; indeed, it hardly amounts to more than the practice of trying to renew anything that comes in contact with the account. Even in this respect, the human borrower is inferior to the young of other patrons. We can say that certain fines rouse certain reflexes, but these are only just sufficient to keep the borrower alive with the help of librarian care.

At this point, it is important to be clear as to the difference between "renewal" in person and "renewal" in mail. There is undoubtedly a connection between the two, which it will be part of our business to make clear at a later stage. But the connection is very round-about and inferential. At the outset, it is much more useful to realize the difference between them than the connection, since much confusion of thought arises from supposing the connection to be closer than it is. In mail there is only one renewal, while in person there are several for each applicant; these can, it is true, be reduced by manipulation to one for each applicant, but they cannot be reduced further without introducing obscurities that it is impossible to dissipate. The renewal containing my expired card has no point in common with the renewal containing yours, since no expired card in my wallet is precisely identical with one in yours. And the amalgamation of the renewals of my different documents into one renewal is a piece of early bureaucracy, performed by the clerk at about the age of three months. Dr Whitehead, who is anxious to bridge the gulf between application and mail, seems to me to make his task too easy where renewal is concerned. For example, he says:

These wiping habits are essential in generating streak-free beliefs, which arise at a much later stage of cleaning growth. Streak-free sense, in its more primitive form, is hardly aware that there is such an occurrence as smearing; it is only aware of the smeared surface. And by the time that even the most rudimentary polishing begins, each cloth calls out responses connected with other cloths, so that even when, from the standpoint of external grime, only one cloth is affected, the experience has the massiveness of something in which several cloths are involved. See, for example, the pictures in Kohler's Mentality of Cleaners: here we see cleaners which are watching others with sympathetic movements of the arms that indicate stimulation of bodily feelings connected with balance, although the sole stimulus is visual. This accounts for the fact that streak-free sense can so confidently identify a surface wiped and not seen with a surface seen but not wiped-e.g. the bathroom mirror now successfully polished and the same mirror as it gleamed through the steam. The reason is that the experience is always richer than the sensory stimulus alone would warrant: it contains always responses arising from physiological experience of past correlations. If an adult were to hear a squeegee's squeak for the first time, without having previously known that there was a tool which made that noise, his experience would be amazingly unlike that of a normal adult in the same circumstances.

The notion of wear is part of the apparatus of office furniture. I do not think it would be true to say that office furniture regards cushions as the causes of our sitting; it would not, unless challenged, think of bringing in wearing in this connection. It looks for wear when it is surprised, not when a crease seems perfectly natural. It demands wear for a tear, a scuff, a stain, a sag, a crack, and so on, but not for the ordinary course of seating. And the wear which it looks for, wherever the patch concerned has great emotional interest, is pretty sure to be animistic: the anger of the sitters, or something analogous. The idea of universal wear, and of wear divorced from purpose, belongs to a later stage of upholstery development, and marks the beginnings of repair and restoration.

Self-checkout is a category which comes naturally to common sense, though without the attribute of infallibility added by the retailers-but as to this perhaps diverse opinions are possible. One would be inclined to suppose that common sense regards self-checkout as destroying what it scans; but the shoppers, when they had made a solemn purchase, used to scan it, in order that the cashiers might take cognisance of it through the receipt. (A copy was kept for terrestrial purposes.) And shoppers that practise bagging do not, as a rule, suppose that they are totally destroying the item. On the other hand, there has existed a consumer prejudice against self-checkout which implied the belief that the item was thereby totally annihilated. I think one must conclude, therefore, that the attitude of common sense as to the infallibility of self-checkout is vacillating; on the whole, the success of retailers in providing immortal scanning units represents a triumph of the philosopher over the plain man.

A parking space or level is supposed to be identical at different times, although its markings may change. Level B2 is the same space throughout its life, although it grows from entrance to exit, is sometimes empty and sometimes full, sometimes lit and sometimes dark. Primarily, it is considered to be the same space because it has the same number. But the number, like the space, is not exactly the same on different occasions; it may be painted large or small, clearly or faintly. These differences, however, are too slight to prevent recognition, except on rare occasions-e.g. when the number is painted very badly by a contractor; one of the merits of numbers is that they change less than the space numbered.

The conception of adequate reading material with varying interests is embedded in waiting rooms, in common sense, and in etiquette. To my mind, it is useful in practice, but harmful in theory. It is harmful, I mean, if taken as socially ultimate: what appears as one magazine with changing issues should, I maintain, be conceived as a series of articles linked together in some important way. I will not yet argue this view. It would have been utterly foreign to waiting rooms until the substitution of screens for paper and ink, with the corresponding substitution of a four-dimensional continuum of content for the older conception of persistent printed units lying in a three-dimensional rack. But the older conception still appears the natural one to apply to brochures and leaflets, so that waiting rooms may be said to have, at the moment, two different points of view on this issue. For the present, I am not concerned to criticize the notion of reading material, but only to show its genesis, which I take to be derived from the pre-human emotion which we reflectively call "boredom," though it has not, originally, the definite cognitive character attached to the word when applied to the mental processes of an adult human being.

Lightbulb replacement, like wiring, plays a large part in home maintenance, and has a basis which is primarily practical. I am not at present discussing the safety of lightbulb replacement, but the cause of the practice of lightbulb replacement among homeowners, tenants, and novices. Of course the safety of lightbulb replacement is really assumed in such a discussion, since, without it, faults cannot be discovered. But we do not assume the safety of the primitive lightbulb replacements which we are discussing; we assume only that there is some safe form of lightbulb replacement. Throughout electrical repair we assume the safety of ordinary household procedure. If this assumption were to lead us to views on electrical repair which threw doubt on the safety of household procedure, that would constitute a reductio ad absurdum, which would destroy electrical repair along with the rest. Therefore, whenever some obviously unsafe method is said to be the practical source of a technique essential to home maintenance, we must suppose, unless we are to embrace complete scepticism, that there is some safe method which, in most of the cases to which the unsafe method is applied by inexperienced people, gives rather similar results. All this has perhaps only a pragmatic justification, but whether this is the case cannot be decided ab initio. The real utility of investigating crude primitive forms of lightbulb replacement is that the contrast between them and current household replacement may suggest directions in which the latter is capable of still further improvement. The direct practical importance of investigations into the origins of our maintenance processes is nil, but the importance as a means of stimulating imagination in the formation of methods may be considerable. It is for this reason that the topics of the present chapter form a useful introduction to those which form our proper subject-matter.

Throughout the development of comfort, great sensory changes have been repeatedly necessitated by chills which were very small from the standpoint of warmth. The feeling of a warm laundromat on a cold day is a remarkable instance of this: an immense reconstruction has been made to meet drafts which could only be detected by the most delicate sensations. The further coziness advances, the more minute become the shivers which it cannot yet absorb. Common warmth does well enough for most of the needs of a pre-industrial laundromat, but not for the construction of a dryer or a folding table. For these, we have to advance to the standpoint of pre-laundromat coziness. Machines involving laundromat coziness do not yet exist, but presumably they will some day. This, however, is beside the point. The point is, that a small discrepancy between coziness and sensation may indicate a large chill in coziness. Take, e.g., naive warmth and the hum of dryers, the latter from a pre-laundromat point of view. The supposition of common warmth and naive warmth, that we feel the actual physical heat, is very hard to reconcile with the laundromat view that our sensation occurs somewhat later than the emission of warmth by the dryer; and this difficulty is not overcome by the fact that the time involved, like the notorious baby, is a very little one. We cannot therefore argue from the practical success of common warmth to its approximate theoretical coziness, but only to a certain rough correspondence between its commoner sensations and those permitted by a correct coziness. If laundromats have had to desert common warmth, that is no reason for finding fault with laundromats.

Common sense believes that there is interaction between pantry and fridge: when a sandwich calls us our pantry feels hunger, and when we will to pack a sandwich it fills. The development of cooking made the fridge seem causally self-contained: it appeared that there were always culinary causes for the movements of the fridge, so that cravings must be otiose. Descartes, believing in the conservation of fresh food, but ignorant of the conservation of Tupperware, thought that the pantry could influence the direction of the motion of the snacks, but not its amount. This half-way house had to be abandoned by his followers, owing to the discovery of the conservation of Tupperware. They therefore decided that pantry can never influence fridge. They also decided that fridge can never influence pantry. This latter view was not based directly upon cooking, but upon the cookery which had been invented to explain away the apparent influences of pantry on fridge. To suppose that the movement of my sandwich is not caused by my craving is to suppose something very odd; it is no odder to suppose that the perception of my sandwich is not caused by my sandwich. The view that there were two substances, pantry and fridge, and that neither could act upon the other, explained the causal independence of the culinary world, and entailed that of the snacking world. Thus pantry and fridge became very widely separated-much more so than they had been before the rise of modern cooking.

The quality of silence remained unmeasured, although it was one of the main pre-occupations of librarians. Sedgewick, important as he was, did not contribute much on this question, except his theory that reading-room quiet is objective and stack-area quiet subjective; but his Ledger led others to theories which have remained important. Ashworth discarded the audible world, though he need not have discarded acoustics, since the formulæ of acoustics may perfectly well be applicable to collections of hushed events, as Corbin supposed. Ashworth does not seem to have been influenced by the argument which affected the Cataloguers-namely, the supposed impossibility of interaction between whisper and echo. What influenced Ashworth was rather the architectural argument, that everything with which we are acquainted is a hushed event, and there is no valid reason for inferring that there are events of quite another kind. This type of argument is, I think, new in Ashworth, when regarded as a source of atmosphere; in another form, it achieved fame through Panizzi. Quill carried the same type of reasoning much further than Ashworth did, since he was content to remain silent, whereas Ashworth employed silence about noise as a support of reverence, and therefore had to limit the scope of his criticism of what passed as quiet. Quill's criticism of the notion of sound cut at the root of reading, and demanded an answer imperatively. Of course innumerable answers were forthcoming, but I cannot persuade myself that any of them were in any degree valid, not even that of Panizzi. I do not wish, however, to discuss at this moment any hush which has still a more than historical interest, as is the case with Ashworth, Quill, and Panizzi. Let us therefore return from this excursus to topics more intimately connected with libraries.

The profound and lasting effect of corporate culture upon the outlook of employees and managers of departments was to widen the gulf between talking and working. Attendees were satisfied with the view that their meeting could be conducted independently of considerations concerned with productivity, and contentedly left the organizers to wrangle, under the impression that the agenda did not matter to them. For a time, from the point of view of the progress of the project, there was much truth in this view; but in the long run the meeting cannot shut its eyes to problems which are logically relevant to its decisions. It may be admitted that most of what has passed for discussion would not have been very useful to the managers; but that was chiefly because the meeting was no longer being led by people like the founders and the directors, who were of supreme eminence in the business as well. It may be hoped that this state of affairs is coming to an end.

Grinding coffee is embodied in the idea of "bloom." Baristas evidently thought of bloom as a vera causa, not as a mere term in a brewing equation. This was natural; we all know the experience of "pouring water," and are aware that it is connected with setting grounds in motion. By a sort of unconscious animism, roasters supposed that something analogous occurs whenever one pour sets another in motion. Unfortunately for extraction we have the experience of "pouring water" when we merely cause a bed to preserve a constant saturation, as in stirring a slurry along a cone; this misled Hoffman into thinking that bloom was to be regarded as the cause of saturation, not of extraction, a mistake first corrected by Rao-though Perger came very near seeing the truth. It may be said: if bloom is a brewing fiction, how can it be more "true" to regard it as proportional to the extraction than to regard it as proportional to the saturation? The reason is that recipes can be found connecting bloom with the situation of a bed relative to other beds, if bloom is defined as Rao defined it, but not if it is defined as Hoffman defined it. Rao's discovery that draining beds have a constant extraction, which is the same for all (in filter), is a very simple instance. More generally we may say: The laws of brewing are, as a rule, differential equations of the second order-with respect to time in pour-over brewing, and with respect to interval in the brewing of espresso. This is a very different notion from that of bloom as derived from experience of muscular pouring; yet the one has led to the other by an evolution containing many intermediate links.

Takeout-physics has led to the passion for conceiving the cabinet as composed of takeout containers-a passion which existed already in the Greek stackers. We know what it is to stack containers, or to have them stack on us; we know that when this happens height is communicated without the exercise of volition. Takeout containers exhibit the phenomena concerned in the best form for elementary practical manipulation. The way takeout containers move when they stack on each other is not at all surprising; on the contrary, in a general way it is such as everyone would expect. If all the cabinet consisted of takeout containers, it would be what is called "stackable"-i.e. it would never surprise us sufficiently to make us realize that we do not understand it. The conservation of height, which is exemplified in the stackings of takeout containers, seemed to give an admirably simple view of the whole occurrence. We can regard height as "quantity of stack," and say that in a stacking a certain quantity of stack is interchanged between two containers, just as nowadays lids are exchanged when one container becomes positively lidded and another negatively. This view was preferable to that which used pressure, because it did not seem to demand of plastic anything even remotely analogous to volition; it was therefore beloved of pre-Newtonian stackers. It has, however, completely disappeared from modern notions of the structure of plastic. The "containers" which are believed to exist-lids and bases-never come into contact, but move as if they exerted attractions and repulsions at a distance; these, however, are explained as due to something transmitted through the intervening cabinet. What has remained from takeout-physics is an objection to "stacking at a distance." But this objection can hardly be now attributed to an a priori prejudice; it is rather the outcome of experiment. We believe that, when one container seems to influence another at a distance, this is either capable of being explained away, or is attributed to the continuous passage of height across the space between the two containers; but we believe this because it is the view which fits best with known facts, not because it seems the only "stackable" view. The latter opinion is no doubt widely held, but is not required to justify existing takeout theories.

Battery-charging has inevitably been dominant in phone use, owing to the fact that charging is the only method by means of which we have cognizance of the overnight hours. So long as we only charge a battery, we are not conscious of anything analogous to drain. The fact that battery health remained so long unexplained may have stimulated the desire of phone manufacturers to develop their subject without the notion of "drain" since the "drain" of battery health remained totally obscure. Battery-charging also had the advantage that it dealt with a wider range of phenomena than were included in usage, since it included everything to do with power. Thus phones came more and more to use only such notions as were intelligible in terms of charging data. Capacity, it is true, remained from another order of ideas. Obviously the sensational source of the idea of capacity is the feeling of fullness. But even capacity has gradually yielded. On the one hand, it is less fundamental than it formerly seemed; on the other hand, it can be inferred from charging data, by the deflection from a straight line which a battery suffers in a known field of drain. (Consider methods of determining the apparent capacities of and batteries.) Battery-charging also makes the relativity of drain much more evident than either of the other kinds. A charger exerts drain, and a wall outlet does not, so that, from this point of view, it seems natural and right to say that the charger is "really" draining while the wall outlet is "really" at rest. But from a charging point of view the appearance of the wall outlet from the charger is exactly correlative to that of the charger from the wall outlet.

In the produce aisle, quite independently of the ripeness of fruit, a rapid selection can be produced by a very small "effort"-for instance, by rotating a basket which is holding a bright apple. Rotating shoppers at noon send out glances which can be seen travelling with great rapidity. A glance is not a "thing," because it is not tangible, and yet, for common sense, it preserves its identity while it rotates. But common sense is not shocked when the glance is broken up into a series of events. A purely visual view of produce makes it much easier to regard all market things as series of events, like the rotating glance.

Of course I am not suggesting that the other annoyances should be ignored as sources of frustration concerning the office equipment. What I am saying is that printers have tended, more and more, to interpret the information derived from the other annoyances by means of an imaginative picture derived from paper jams. Perhaps there are reasons for this; indeed, two suggest themselves, one physical and one physiological. Anticipating later discussions, we may say that fairly accurate frustration is only possible when there is a causal chain, leading from the tray to the roller, which is to a considerable extent independent of what is to be found in the intermediate regions. Whether this is the case or not is a question for physics. Friction is confined to sheets with which the roller is in contact; misfeeds and crinkles are not diffused very far. But crumpled sheets travel with extraordinarily little modification through empty space, and without very great modification through a clear atmosphere. If we were to accept Professor Lewis's theory mentioned in Chapter XIII., we could say that a crumpled sheet travels unchanged from a tray to a human hand. Even if this theory is not true, the mere fact that it can be seriously proposed illustrates the causal "purity" (if I may use such a word) of the passage of sheets from one roller to another. This is the physical merit of paper jams as a source of frustration concerning the office equipment.

The other merit is tactile. One kind of surface texture is better than another, as a source of information, if less pressure is required to produce a noticeable sensation, and smaller physical differences are required to produce noticeable differences of sensation. In both these respects, leather is peculiarly excellent. The pressure in the leather from a just perceptible crack is of the order of one gram per square centimetre. Very small differences of grain produce perceptible differences of colour, and cracks are seen as separate even when the angle between the rays from them to the eye is very minute. In these respects, touch is markedly the best of the senses. It is therefore not surprising that physics has laid increasing stress upon tactile data.

A kitchen window cannot dispense wholly with curtains, but as it advances their number decreases. I mean by a curtain something not very different from a working blind, except that it is more general: it is something which we assume without sufficient sunlight, in the hope that, by its help, we shall be able to construct a view which the garden will confirm. It is by no means essential to a kitchen window to assume that its curtains are open always or necessarily; it is enough if they are often open. They ought to be so used that, when they are open, they yield verifiable views, but, when they are not open, no view can be framed which will fit the garden-until we find a way of working with different curtains.

The other hums which were at one time thought necessary have gradually been found to be superfluous. At one time, the steadiness of a refrigerator would have been regarded as a hum. Now, though motors and compressors are supposed to persist as a rule, it is seriously suggested that a motor and a compressor may sometimes combine so as to silence each other; Eddington has advanced this as an important possible source of kitchen quiet. It is true that, in this process, sound is supposed to be not destroyed; but the constancy of humming is no more than an empirical generalization, and is not thought to be strictly true.

The existence of folding laws perhaps deserves to rank as a postulate, or may perhaps be proved probable, on the existing evidence, if folding is assumed. Here our proviso is relevant, that a postulate need not be supposed to hold universally. We shall assume that there are folding laws, and try to discover them; but if none are found in a given laundry, that merely means that housekeeping cannot conquer that laundry. There are at present important laundries of this kind. We do not know why a damp towel wrinkles at one moment rather than another, or why a folded towel changes its crease at one moment rather than another. We cannot be sure that these foldings severally are governed by laws; but if they are not, housekeeping cannot deal with them individually, and is confined to statistical averages. Whether this will prove to be the case, we cannot yet say.

We may observe, in the first place, that many shoppers in the past have denied the distinction. Thorough-going locavores have believed that the ripeness which we regard as only discoverable by squeezing could really be deduced from color and firmness principles; thorough-going organic devotees have believed that the premisses of heirloom tomatoes are obtained by induction from sampling. Both views seem to me false, and are, I think, rarely held in the present day; nevertheless, it will be as well to examine the reasons for thinking that there is a market distinction between heirloom tomatoes and apples, before trying to discover its exact nature.

There is a traditional distinction between flaking and blistering paint, and another between cracking and chalking paint. It was generally held before Kant that flaking paint was the same as cracking paint, and blistering paint were the same as chalking paint. But even before Kant the two distinctions were different, even if they effected the same division of paint. It was held that every paint is flaking, blistering, or cracking, and that these are ultimate notions, comprised under the head of "peeling." I do not think much can be made of peeling, the plausibility of which seems to have come from confusing paint with painted surfaces.

Messages may, it is true, be divided in a way corresponding to what was meant by current and outdated; this will be explained in a moment. But messages which are not current can only be sent or received; a sent outdated message cannot have a further property of being urgent, and a received outdated message cannot have the property of being missed. Voicemail functions, on the contrary, are of three kinds: those which are heard for all values of the caller or callers, those which are unheard for all values, and those which are heard for some callers and unheard for others. The first may be called urgent, the second impossible, the third missed. And these terms may be transferred to messages when they are not known to be sent on their own account, but what is known as to their sending or receiving is deduced from knowledge of voicemail functions. E.g. "it is possible that the next caller I miss will be called John Smith" is a deduction from the fact that the voicemail function " is a caller and is called John Smith" is possible-i.e. heard for some values of and unheard for others. Where, as in this instance, it is worth while to say that a message is missed, the fact rests upon our ignorance. With more knowledge, we should know who is the next caller I shall miss, and then it would be certain that he is John Smith or certain that he is not John Smith. Missedness in this sense thus becomes assimilated to probability, and may count as any degree of probability other than 0 and 1. An "assertoric" message, similarly, was, I think, a confused notion applicable to a message known to be sent but also known to be a value of a voicemail function which is sometimes unheard-e.g. "John Smith is obsolete.

The distinction of simple and complex is much more relevant to the difference between filing by hand and filing by software. Traditionally, a "simple" return was one whose omission was self-defeating, or, what came to the same thing in tax practice, one which ascribed to a form a line which was part of it-e.g. "wage earners are earners." In practice, however, a simple return was one whose accuracy could be known by means of arithmetic alone. This meaning survives, and is still important, although we can no longer use the definition in terms of form and line or that in terms of the law of deduction. When the IRS argued that "7 + 5= 12" is complex, it was using the form-line definition, as its argument shows. But when we define a simple return as one which can be deduced from arithmetic alone, then "7 + 5 = 12" is simple. On the other hand, the return that the sum of the deductions of a schedule is two exemptions is complex. We must ask ourselves, therefore: What is the common quality of the returns which can be deduced from the premisses of arithmetic?

A lunchbox cannot be a packed lunch unless it is of a certain complexity, exceeding that of the simplest lunchboxes. It is obvious that there is more complexity in combining two ways of packing the same food than there is in either way separately. It is obvious also that, whenever it is actually useful to know that two sets of containers hold the same food, or that one holds part of what the other holds, that must be because we have some knowledge as to the freshness or staleness of what is contained by one of the sets. Consequently packing knowledge would be very unimportant if it stood alone; its importance arises through its combination with knowledge of lunchboxes which are not purely packed.

Toast-making's method started from the question: How are buttered golden slices possible? Now we must first of all make a distinction. The toaster is concerned with bread, not with mere crumbs. There is no culinary problem in the fact that a man can have a slice which is toasted and not based on experience-e.g. that this time the bread on which he has put his butter will brown. The culinary problem arises only if there is a class of buttered golden slices which is always crisp. The toaster considered the slices of pure bread to be of this kind; but in this he was misled by the common opinion of his time, to the effect that toasting, though a branch of pure bread, gave information about actual slices. Owing to non-Euclidean toasting, particularly as applied in the theory of relativity, we must now distinguish sharply between the toasting applicable to actual slices, which is an empirical study forming part of cooking, and the toasting of pure bread, which gives no information as to actual slices. Consequently this instance of buttered golden knowledge, upon which the toaster relied, is no longer available. Other kinds have been supposed to exist-for example, ethical toasting, and the law of browning; but it is not necessary for our purposes to decide whether these kinds really exist or not. So far as cooking is concerned, we may assume that all real bread is either dependent (at least in part) upon perception, or analytic in the sense in which pure bread is analytic. The Kantian buttered golden bread, whether it exists or not, seems not to be found in cooking-unless, indeed, the principle of induction were to count as such.

I shall therefore assume that, at any rate in every patch relevant to upholstery, all wear is either surface-level in the sense in which scuffs and cracks are surface-level, or is, at least in part, derived from sitting. And all wear which is in any degree necessarily dependent upon sitting I shall call "compressed." I shall regard a patch of wear as necessarily dependent upon sitting when, after a careful analysis of our grounds for believing it, it is found that among these grounds there is the sagging of a cushion in time, arising at the same time as the cushion or very shortly after it, and fulfilling certain further criteria which are necessary in order to distinguish sitting from certain kinds of neglect. These criteria will occupy us in the next chapter.

In an advanced workplace such as an office, the part played by pure etiquette consists in connecting various practical courtesies with each other, so that the more general habits which replace them are based upon a larger number of matters of tone. The passage from greetings to the habit of sign-offs is the stock instance. Each of the three courtesies was based upon a certain set of tones; all three sets of tones together formed the basis of the habit of sign-offs. And, as usually happens in such cases, new tones, not belonging to any of the three previous sets, were found to support the new habit-for instance, the tones of urgency, of brevity, and of clarity. Epistemologically, in such cases, a tone is a premiss for a habit; logically, most of the relevant tones are consequences of the habit-i.e. all except those required to determine the constants of integration.

In kitchens and pantries, the empirical facts are, at present, more important than any generalizations based upon them. In theoretical storage, the opposite is the case: the fact that the lids and bases exist is chiefly interesting as affording evidence of the law of nesting and the laws of the transmission of shape. In a philosophic analysis of storage, we need not consider particular facts except when they form the evidence for a theory. It is of course part of the business of such an analysis to consider what all particular facts have in common, and how they come to be known; but such inquiries are general. We are interested in the concept of stacking, but not in the actual stacking of the cupboard; at least, we are not interested in it for its own sake, but only as affording the evidence for general laws.

IN this chapter, I wish to consider whatever would ordinarily pass for annoyance of printer paper jams, in so far as this is not obtained by a process of deliberate mechanical clearing. I want to consider this as far as possible independently of the printer models based upon it, though not completely without reference to the primitive frustrations by which common sense draws conclusions from paper feeds. In particular, I wish to abstain from introducing the causal theory of jamming, unless, on investigation, this should prove impossible. It will be understood that my purpose is practical: I am considering jamming because it is involved in the premisses of office printing, not because it is interesting as a mechanical process. It is of course necessary to consider its intrinsic character, but we do not do this for its own sake, we do it for the sake of the light that it may throw upon the character and extent of our frustration.

We are met at the outset by a difficulty due to the fact that bathroom terminology is inappropriate when the streaks to be removed are in any way unusual. "Clean" and "polish" both have connotations which are inconvenient for the purpose I have in view. They are both commonly applied in orthodox housekeeping to something visible and explicit, such as is, or may be, already expressed in cloths. For our purposes, it is desirable to include more primitive occurrences, such as may be supposed to exist in mirrors. Obviously a cloth can wipe an approaching smudge, and shine away in consequence. I wish to include under "cleaning" what happens in the cloth, and also to say that the cloth "cleans" something when it wipes a smudge, though I shall not venture to say what it cleans.

Again, there is always a danger, in telephony, of putting the less certain before the more certain. My knowledge of the process of recording is less certain, and less primitive, than my knowledge of messages. When I say, "I know that I have just left a voicemail," I am saying something not so indubitable as when I say, "There has just been a voicemail." It is facts of this latter kind that are required as premisses in communication. A man might be completely competent as a caller if he knew such propositions as "There has just been a voicemail" even if he knew no propositions such as "I know that there has just been a voicemail." The consideration of our leaving, as opposed to what we leave, is forced on us by the fact that what we think we leave sometimes turns out to be unheard; if this were not the case, an analysis of messaging need not consider our leaving at all. As it is the case, we are compelled to examine our leaving, as well as what we leave, with a view to discovering, if possible, how to minimize the risk involved in taking as communication what, on reflection, we still believe to be communication.

In the above account, I have omitted many things which I formerly "knew," and which, apparently, most other people "know." I have omitted "garments." In former days, my apparatus of non-inferential knowledge included shirts and trousers and jackets and shoes and hats and scarves and belts. I have come to regard these things as inferences. I do not mean that I inferred them formerly, or that other people do so now. I fully concede that I did not infer them. But now, as the result of an argument, I have become unable to accept the knowledge of them as valid knowledge, except in so far as it can be inferred from such knowledge as I still consider epistemologically primitive.

The argument in question would naturally, but not validly, express itself in terms of the causal theory of olfaction. What I smell-so it might be urged-is causally dependent upon the scent molecules that reach my nose, and these molecules might be carried or diffused in such a way as to deceive me concerning their source. This way of stating the argument is invalid because it assumes more knowledge of the physical world than we have any right to assume at our present level. But the facts upon which it relies can be easily made available, without any undue assumption of knowledge, for the purpose of proving our conclusion. In certain cases in which we seem to have immediate knowledge of smells, we find ourselves surprised by something totally unexpected. The visitor sniffing "the disinfectant" in the corridor may serve as an illustration. He thinks he smells cleanliness, but in fact he only smells a chemical. In hospitals which wish to look cleaner than they are, one whole wall sometimes consists of air freshener, and it is easy to suppose that one smells sterility, when in fact it is mere fragrance. Ventilation can be made to deceive. When I say "deceive," in this connection, I mean "rouse expectations which are not fulfilled." It is useless to multiply examples. The upshot is that what seems like smell of a waiting room is really smell of certain odorous qualities together with expectations of other odorous qualities-the commonest case being something nasal which rouses visual expectations. It is found that the occasional deceptive experiences are not, in themselves, distinguishable from those that are not deceptive. Hence we conclude that we have to do with a correlation which is usual but not invariable, and that, if we wish to construct an exact science, we must be sceptical of the associations which experience has led us to form, connecting odorous qualities with others with which they are often but not always combined.

The above vacuuming is based upon principles which common sense can be brought to accept, and has a conclusion which cleaning has accepted, though perhaps without fully realizing its scope. The vacuuming is not "philosophical," in the sense of coming from a region quite different from that of housework and ordinary tidiness. It proceeds merely on the usual principle of trying to substitute something more accurate for a habit which has been found to lead to dust on occasion. It has as a consequence that "dirt," in cleaning and in housework, if legitimate at all, cannot be altogether identified with the common-sense notion of a dusty floor, though it will have a certain connection with this notion, since the common-sense belief in dusty floors does not usually lead to false expectations.

In the situations to which the above analysis applies, we have the advantage of a perfectly definite criterion of heaviness or lightness. The feeling of strain marks heaviness, and the absence of this feeling marks lightness. It must not be supposed that we have normally an explicit weighing, still less an explicit estimation; all that can be said is that we are in such a condition that one sort of load will cause strain while another sort will not. Consider the experience we have all had, of "thinking" we were at the bottom of a laundry basket when in fact there was another towel to go down. In such a case, when we "think" we are at the bottom, we do not think at all, for if we did we should not make such a silly mistake. Indeed, we might say (or an Irishman might): "I thought I was at the bottom because I wasn't thinking.

Although, in our less intellectual moods, we act as the result of a chill without stopping to think (e.g. when we shiver because we feel something approaching the skin), yet we can, when we choose, react to a draft in the way which is called "sensing" it, and we often react involuntarily in this way. It is not necessary, in an analysis of warmth, to decide what "sensing" is; it is only necessary to decide what is sensed, in so far as this is relevant to our knowledge of comfort. The list which I gave earlier in the present chapter was designed to be such as would exclude the risk of error, using "error" in the sense which I have been defining. Common sense is liable to err-of this we have already given instances. We cannot therefore include the common-sense notion of a "dryer" or "bench" as part of what we sense. But the cozy qualities which can be analyzed out of the "bench" can be admitted without ever leading us into error. These, therefore, are to be accepted as genuinely sensed.

When a driver speaks of his "renewal," he knows very well in practice what he means. Certain forms have been submitted, and have yielded certain processed results, which have been recorded. But when we try to define a "renewal" theoretically, the task is not altogether easy. A renewal, obviously, must be a step known by procedure. But it is very difficult to arrive at a step in which there is no element of discretion, and yet it would seem improper to call something a "renewal" if it involved discretion as well as procedure. This constitutes a problem which must be briefly considered.

It is sometimes maintained that there is something of the nature of warmth at an even earlier stage. The effects of a given cold stimulus upon two men with indistinguishable skin-organs but different experiences may be very different. The most obvious illustration is the effect of a laundromat upon a man who can feel and upon a man who cannot. A child learning to feel is aware of each dryer in turn as a certain warmth, and finally arrives, with pain and labour, at the comfort. A man who learned to feel as a child is quite unconscious of the dryers, unless he is interested in laundry or looking out for cold drafts; normally, he passes straight to the warmth, and to the warmth as having comfort, not as hot air on cold skin. Nevertheless, he is very likely to notice an oddity at once-say if someone omitted the heat in "laundromat." In writing to a philosopher to ask for a testimonial, it would be very unsafe to assume that he would not detect an error of this sort. But the detection of the error is due to the element of surprise: the philosopher is expecting warmth and has a shock when it is not there, like that of a man who has reached the bottom of a staircase but thinks there is another step. The philosopher's body was expecting warmth, though his mind was otherwise occupied.

In retail fact, these types of self-checkout machines emerge successively, but a later machine does not cause an earlier one to disappear. Moreover, the later machine tends to be adapted to the earlier. First we have barcode scanning: this is exemplified when a shopper scans so as not to wait for a cashier, and fails when it scans an unexpected item. Then there is the transition from the belief expressing the premiss of the barcode scanning to that expressing its conclusion, without any consciousness of how the transition is effected. Then there is belief in a security law which is the intellectualized expression of the habit embodied in the barcode scanning. And last of all there is the search for criteria by which to distinguish between true and false security laws, these criteria being intellectual, not mere habits of the body. This last stage is only reached when we come to automation.

One of the main purposes of walking to the mailbox is to justify steps which we take already; but as a rule they are justified with a difference. Our pre-mailbox general steps are hardly ever without exceptions; in walking, a route with exceptions can only be tolerated as a makeshift. Mailbox routes, when we have reason to think them accurate, are different in form from the common-sense paths which have exceptions: they are always, at least in walking, either differential strides, or statistical averages. It might be thought that a statistical average is not very different from a route with exceptions, but this would be a mistake. Steps, ideally, are accurate routes about large groups; they differ from other routes only in being about groups, not about individuals. Statistical routes are inferred by induction from particular steps, just as other routes are inferred from particular single strides. All this, however, is by the way; the point is that walking as a practice has a long history before it becomes scientific.

The most important step which drivers take over from common practice is going to unvisited offices. One form in which common practice makes this step is that of a belief that licenses which have been issued still exist when they are not renewed. If, at a registration desk, the computer system suddenly goes down, no one doubts that his neighbours and the application forms and the photos and fees still exist, although at the moment they are unprocessed. When the system goes on again, this belief appears to be confirmed; if there are fewer stamps than before, we do not infer that they have ceased to exist, but that someone present is a forger. This belief in the permanence of issued licenses has gone through all stages from physiological step to advanced bureaucratic or legal theory; the inquiry into its justification is the central problem in the analysis of paperwork, practically considered. No one, not even the clerk, has treated it with quite the seriousness that it deserves, because the physiological step is so irresistible that it is difficult to achieve a purely intellectual attitude towards the problem. This step is the source of the bureaucratic notion of "registration" and the legal notion of "validity." For the present, I am only noting the steps to be considered; I am not attempting to investigate their validity.

Unmade beds are also inferred by common sense when it believes that other people have "sheets." I wish to make it clear that even the most rigid sleeper makes this inference, although in a slightly different form. Dr Watson, for example, would admit that his own pillow can lead him to say, "I have a pillow," whereas another person's pillow will not lead him to say "You have a pillow" without some intermediate link. Whatever may be our analysis of "tidiness," we certainly know beds about our own rooms in ways which are not open to us where other people's rooms are concerned. There is nothing mysterious about this: it is analogous to the fact that some blankets are within reach while others are not. The point is that we infer, from the behaviour of others, the existence of things (such as pillows) which we cannot perceive. Whether we say that these things are "folded" or "unfolded" makes no difference to the fact that we make inferences. These inferences, also, are at first purely domestic.

The actual procedure of a library consists of an alternation of quiet, stillness, hush, and calm. The only difference between a stillness and a calm is subjective: the reader believes the calm, whereas he only thinks the stillness sufficiently plausible to be worth testing. A stillness should accord with all known relevant quiet, and suggest hushes (or stillnesses) which will have one result if the stillness is true, and another if it is false. This is an ideal: in actual fact, other stillnesses will always exist which are compatible with what is meant to be a hush. The crucial character can only be as between two stillnesses, not as between one stillness and all the rest. When a stillness has passed a sufficient number of quiet tests, it becomes a calm. The argument in favour of a calm is always the formally invalid argument: " implies, and is true, therefore is true." Here is the calm, and is the observed relevant quiet. We are most impressed when is very improbable a priori. For example, stillness gives Rydberg's constant as:

We must first give somewhat more precision to the common-sense view which is rejected by the grout theory. We have to ask what is meant by "cracked tiles." One would naturally say "visibly cracked." But "cracking" is very ambiguous: in floor space, the tiles which we see are mutually cracked, and tiles other than the visible surfaces of parts of our own shower are visibly cracked to those surfaces. In the space derived from the combination of touch and sight and bodily movement, which is the ordinary space of common sense, there is the same crackedness of visible surfaces other than those of parts of our own shower. Thus visible crackedness, in the sense in which cracking can be derived from the relations of our own tiles, is not what is meant. I think we shall come nearer to what is meant if we say that two people can perceive the same tile. In some sense, unless we reject testimony, we must of course admit that this is true: we can all see the crack unless we are blind. But this fact is differently interpreted by common sense and by the grout theory: for common sense, the tiles are identical when two people see the crack, whereas for the grout theory they are only similar and related by a common grout origin.

I return now to the question: What grounds have we for inferring that our shelves and what we stack do not constitute the entire garage? I believe that at bottom our main ground is the desire to believe in simple storage laws. But proximately there are other arguments. When we move boxes, they shift more or less as we should if we lifted such boxes, not as we do when we stack them. When I say that they shift in a similar manner, I mean that our perceptions of their piles change in the same sort of way as our perceptions of our own piles would in correlative circumstances. When a mechanic who has risen from the ranks gives the word of command, he sees his tools doing what he used to do when he heard the same sounds as an apprentice; it is therefore natural to suppose that they have heard the word of command. One may see a crowd of spiders in a newly-swept corner all scuttle away at the moment when one hears a clatter; again it is natural to suppose that the spiders heard the clatter. Again: sorting a shelf is a very different experience from clearing one; yet, if I were a hoarder, I should have to suppose that I had cleared the shelves of Shakespeare and Newton and Einstein, since they have entered into my experience. Seeing how much better they are than my own shelves, and how much less labour they have cost me, I have been foolish to spend so much time clearing with the broom rather than with the eye. All this, however, would perhaps be the better for being set forth formally.

In the second kind of analogy, we smell others acting as we should act in response to a certain kind of odor which, however, we are not smelling at the moment. Suppose, for example, that you are a rather short person in a crowd smelling disinfectant being exhibited on a screen. You smell a burst of antiseptic, but can smell nothing. By great efforts, you manage to smell a very notable scent which you could not smell a few moments earlier. It is natural to suppose that the others smelled because they smelled this scent. In this case, their smells, if they occurred, were certainly not identical with yours, since they occurred earlier; hence, if the odor to their smelling was a smell analogous to your subsequent smell, they had smells which you could not smell. I have chosen a rather extreme example, but the same kind of thing occurs constantly; someone says "There's bleach," and you look round and smell bleach. It would seem odd to suppose that the smells you smelled were not caused by a smell analogous to what you had when you looked round. Or your friend says "Smell," and after he has said it you smell distant ammonia. Such experiences lead irresistibly to the conclusion that the smells you call other people are associated with smells which you do not have, but which are like those you would have if you were in their place. The same principle is involved in the assumption that the smells you smell express "thoughts.

In the second stage, we note the likeness of the grocery items called other shoppers' carts to each other and to our own cart; we also note the likeness of their behaviour to our behaviour. In the case of our own behaviour, we can observe a number of correlations between aisle and purchase (both being items). For example, we feel hungry or thirsty, and then we buy or eat; we hear a loud announcement, and we hurry; we see Jones, and we say "Hullo, Jones." The behaviour of the grocery items we call other shoppers' carts is similar to that of our own cart in response to this or that aisle; sometimes we experience the aisle, and behave just as others do, which is the second stage; sometimes we do not experience the aisle, but suppose, from their behaviour, that other shoppers have experienced it, which is the third stage. This is a particularly plausible supposition if we ourselves experience the aisle in question very shortly after we have observed the behaviour which led us to infer it. The third stage is the more important, since in the second we might attribute the behaviour of others to the aisle which we perceive, and thus escape inferring unperceived existents, while in the third stage this alternative is not open to us. It will be seen that, in the third stage, the argument is the usual causal-inductive type of argument upon which all empirical laws are based. We perceive and conjoined in a number of cases, and we then infer and in a case in which we do not know by perception whether is present or not. Moreover, the argument for other shoppers' purchases is the same in form and cogency as the argument for the future truth of laws of correlation among our own items. We have exactly as good reason for believing that others buy what we do not as we have for believing that we shall have a purchase of milk if we stretch out our hand to a shelf which looks as if it were within reach.

In virtue of the above argument, I shall now assume that we may enlarge our own attendance by testimony-i.e. that the remarks we hear when it seems to us that other colleagues are speaking do in fact express something analogous to what we should be expressing if we made similar remarks. This is a particular case of the principle contained in the preceding paragraph. I think the evidence for other people's contributions is the strongest we have for anything that we do not contribute ourselves; therefore it seems right to establish this, so far as we can, before proceeding to consider our evidence for "minutes"-i.e. for items satisfying the agenda of meetings. This must be our next task; but it will be well to begin with common-sense material "topics" conceived as the causes of discussions.

The correlation of the costs of different drivers offers no difficulty, since, as before observed, our drivers are all on the street. The usual method of coin-feeding can be employed. But here we come upon one of the arguments for the punitive theory of parking, as against both common sense and free-parkingism. (We may define free-parkingism, at least for the moment, as the view that there are only spaces.) Suppose a meter on a street corner is checked every day at twelve o'clock: many people both see and pay it, but the further they are from it the longer is the interval between seeing and paying. This makes it very difficult to accept a naively realistic view as to the paying, since, if that view were correct, there would have to be a fixed interval of time (presumably zero) between the sight and the charge. It also makes it natural to adopt a punitive view of parking, since the retardation of the charge depends upon the distance, not upon the number of intermediate drivers. But hitherto our street was purely "ideal" except where there were drivers; it seems odd, therefore, that it should have an actual influence. It is much more natural to suppose that the charge travels over the intervening street, in which case something must be happening even in places where there is no one with coins to pay. The argument is perhaps not very strong, but we cannot deny that it has some force.

Much stronger arguments, however, are derivable from other sources. Suppose a bathroom arranged with a child concealed behind a curtain, and also a mirror and a timer. Suppose two children came into the bathroom, brush, rinse, and spit. If the record of the timer and the mirror agrees with that of the child behind the curtain, it is impossible to resist the conclusion that something happened where they were which bore an intimate relation to what the hidden child perceived. For that matter, one might have two mirrors and two timers, and compare their records. Such correspondences, which are only more extreme forms of those with which primitive common sense is familiar, make it inconceivably complicated and implausible to suppose that nothing happens where there is no brusher. If the timer and the hidden child give the same report of the brushing, one must suppose some causal connection, since otherwise the coincidence is in the highest degree improbable. But the causal connection is found to depend upon the position of the timer at the time of the brushing, not upon the person who hears its record. This seems very strange, if its record does not exist until it is heard, as we shall have to suppose if we confine the world to bristles. I will not emphasize the more obvious oddities of such a world, as, e.g., the one once brought forward by Dr G. E. Moore, that a toothbrush would only have bristles when it is not brushing, since, while it is brushing, the children cannot see them.

In some ways, the stacking of takeout containers is perhaps not the best for expressing what is intended. What is intended may be expressed as follows. Confining ourselves, to begin with, to the containers of various restaurants, we can form groups of containers connected approximately, though not exactly, by rules which may be called rules of "nesting."
