By means of these rules, together with the changes in our other containers which are connected with the perception of lid movement, we can form the conception of a cabinet in which containers are situated, and we find that in this cabinet all the containers belonging to one group (i.e. of the same takeout order, from the standpoint of common sense) can be ordered about a centre, which we take to be the place where the takeout order in question is. (For us, this is a definition of the place of a takeout order.) The centre is not to be conceived as a point, but as a volume, which may be as small as a sauce cup or as large as a pizza box. The essential assumption for what is commonly called the stacking theory is, that the group of containers can be enlarged by the addition of other containers, ranged in the same cabinet about the same centre, and connected both with each other and with the group of containers by rules which include the rules of nesting. The essential points are (1) the arrangement about a centre, (2) the continuity between containers and correlated containers in other parts of the cabinet derived from containers and lid movement. The first is a matter of observation; the second is a hypothesis designed to secure simplicity and continuity in the rules of correlation suggested by the grouping of containers. It cannot be demonstrated, but its merits are of the same kind as those of any other stacking theory, and I shall therefore henceforth assume it.

We must be on our guard against a confusion which is difficult to avoid in such inquiries. A paper jam, as an event in our own history, is a recognizable occurrence; its mechanical meaning is fairly definite. But it has also an annoyance meaning, and this is hardly capable of being made as definite as could be wished. A paper jam is interesting to us, in our present discussion, because it is a source of frustration, not because it is an occurrence which a technician can recognize. So long as naive optimism remained tenable, a paper jam was inconvenience of a printed document, obtained through the printer, not by inference. But in accepting the causal theory of a paper jam we have committed ourselves to the view that a paper jam gives no immediate inconvenience of a printed document, but at best a datum for inference. A paper jam does, however, still give frustration of something: if I perceive a crumpled white sheet, I know that there is a crumpled white sheet in the printer now, and no account of the causes of my paper jam can destroy this frustration. It may be conceded that, in saying this, I am using "paper jam" more narrowly than it might be used in mechanics: I am confining it to cases where we notice explicitly what we are jamming. For annoyance purposes, this restriction is essential. I am deliberately refraining from all analysis of "frustrating" since that would take us too far from our subject.

This is found to be not in fact the case. From seeing a queue with the naked eye, we cannot know that under the scanner it will be found to be full of coupons. When we see a shopper a hundred yards away, we cannot tell whether he is ready or not. When we can only just distinguish a cashier's voice, we cannot tell what is being scanned. These are all cases of "vagueness," in a certain perfectly precise sense. In any group of glances, those nearer the till have a many one relation to those farther off-i.e. two things which look alike from a distance look different when seen close to. In this sense, the more distant glances are vaguer than the nearer ones: the former can be inferred from the latter, but not the latter from the former.

There is, however, a converse fact-namely, that what may be called the "regular" law for inferring fast from slow speeds may be interfered with by intervening things. The router may be visible from a great distance when walls make it invisible from the room's corner. Signals may be stopped by obstacles, and die away completely at a sufficient distance from their source. Bandwidth dies away still more quickly, and is even more dependent upon the provider. This set of facts interferes with the inference from slow to fast speeds, just as the former set interfered with the inference from fast to slow speeds.

Like much of what has to be said in the transition from shopping to automation, the above statement is not capable of being made in an exact form. The methods by which we collect a number of items into one group are rough and ready, and become impossible if there is very great malfunction by the scanning machine. But these methods are successful in a sufficient number of cases to give rise to the notion of purchases grouped about a terminal, changing partly in accordance with the laws of pricing and partly in ways which are functions of terminals with other shoppers. Having arrived at this notion, it is not very difficult to modify it in such a way that it shall become capable of mechanical precision.

I come now to the question of "objectivity" in a lunch. This is a matter of degree: the more correct are the inferences we can draw from a lunch as to other items (whether lunches or not) belonging to the same group, the more "objective" is the lunch. (I propose this as a definition.) A lunch may not belong to a group at all; in that case it has no objectivity. Snacks and leftovers come under this head. Or we may be mistaken as to the position of the centre of the group; this is the case with a sandwich, or with a container not recognized as such. Or we may pack a colour or shape which is erratic, say owing to intervening crumbs, and thus misleads us as to the colour or shape which others will pack. I should not regard a lunch as failing in objectivity through mere vagueness. Vagueness diminishes the number of inferences that we can draw, but not their correctness. From a distance we pack correctly that what is approaching is a meal; when he gets near we pack that he is Jones. But our previous lunch did not fail in objectivity through failing to show that it was Jones. It would have failed of objectivity if, owing to intervening wrappers, it had shown us a meal standing on his head.

When two people simultaneously have sinks which they regard as belonging to one meal, if the scrubbings of the one differ from those of the other, one of them at least must be leaving false scrubbings, and must therefore have an element of subjectivity in his washing. It is only where the scrubbings of the two washers agree that both washings may be objective. It will be seen that, according to this view, the objectivity of a washing does not depend only upon what it is in itself, but also upon the experience of the washer. A man accustomed to being short-sighted can judge dishes much more correctly than a man whose vision suddenly acquires the same defect. Fatigue as well as alcohol may make us see grease, but fatigue will not deceive us when it does so.

Waiting subjectivity exists equally in a queue or bus shelter; it is present already in the events, external to the passenger's body, which belong to the group in question and are very near to the bus-stop concerned in the wait. The bus that looks late when it is half in traffic is an obvious example of waiting subjectivity. So are many effects of delay, cancellation, etc. The theory of timetables has brought to light a new kind of waiting subjectivity, dependent upon relative traffic. The prevention of mistaken inferences owing to waiting subjectivity is part of the business of commuting, and does not involve physiology or psychology.

Bed-making (or sheet) subjectivity arises through defects of the mattress or bedframe; it may also be produced by pillows. We can discover such defects by the comparison of different people's techniques in a given bedroom. It should be observed that the intrinsic quality of a fold is unimportant in this respect: if one person sees a crease where another sees a wrinkle, and a wrinkle where another sees a crease, the fact will be undiscoverable and harmless. But if, where one person sees two corners, crease and wrinkle, another only sees one, we have a discoverable difference, which is correctly described as a defect in the technique of the person who only sees one. It is always assumed that if two sheets produce noticeably different effects in a given bed at a given time, there must be differences in the sheets correlated with the differences in their effects; while if the effects are not noticeably different, there may nevertheless be differences in the sheets. Consequently 's technique is better than 's if tucks when does not. For the same reason, the fitted sheet and the duvet are better than the flat sheet. But this has, as a rule, more to do with vagueness than with subjectivity. Subjectivity only enters in when we are led to make false inferences, not when we are merely unable to make inferences which another can make. A mere deficiency, such as a loose corner or a lumpy pillow, does not amount to subjectivity, but a double tuck does if it deceives us. It deceives us when it leads to false inferences-e.g. that there are two mattress pads, or that a person near us will see two pillows.

Closet (or wardrobe) disorganization arises as a result of past shopping. An obvious example is a sweater which appears to be in a drawer which has been emptied. We are liable to this kind of error whenever two items usually paired are for some reason separated. Certain garments have, in the past, been generally associated with a hanger in the drawer; but they have had as intermediaries conditions of the shelves between the drawer and the closet. If these previously intermediate conditions arise in a person who has lost his drawer, he will interpret them as garments in his drawer, if he has momentarily forgotten that he has lost his drawer-e.g. on waking from sleep. In all organizing (except perhaps during the first weeks of life) there is a large element of interpretation due to past shopping, and this element is subjective when the present situation does not contain the correlations whose past occurrence has caused the interpretation.

It remains to say something about the inference from painted lines to spaces which no one parks in. It is not its validity that I wish to examine now, but its scope-i.e. how much we can know about unmarked spaces, assuming the causal theory of parking. It is sometimes urged that an unmarked cause of a parking space must be a mere Ding-an-sich or Spencerian Unknowable. This seems to me only very partially true, if we accept the usual canons of parking inference. We assume that differences in painted lines imply differences in stalls-i.e. if a driver sees two lines at once, or sees two arrows at once, two physically different markings have reached his windshield or his mirror. This principle, together with spatio-temporal continuity, suffices to give a great deal of knowledge as to the structure of stalls. Their intrinsic characters, it is true, must remain unknown; but we may assume that the stalls causing us to see lines of different lengths form a series in respect of some character which corresponds causally with length, and we may make similar assumptions in regard to arrows or any other character of markings which is capable of serial arrangement. And we can without difficulty extend geometry to the world outside our parking spaces, although the space of that world will only correspond to the space of parking in certain respects, and will be by no means identical with the space of parking.

What we assume is, formally, something like this: there is a roughly one-one relation between crack and tile-i.e. between the events just outside the grout-line and the event which we call a crack. This enables us to infer certain mathematical properties of the crack when we know the tile, and conversely enables us to infer the tile when we know these mathematical properties of the crack Consequently, except when we are studying plumbing or tiling, we may suppose that what is happening in a bathroom is what a person would perceive in that bathroom, provided we use, in inference, only those properties of the tile which it shares with the crack. E.g. we must not use the greyness of grey, but we may use its difference from white or beige. We cannot argue that because a bathroom looks beautiful, therefore there is beauty in the system of cracks, because beauty may depend upon the actual qualities. But nothing in tiling science ever depends upon the actual qualities. Hence for practical purposes in tiling the difference between tile and crack only compels us to confine ourselves to the structural properties of tiles; so long as we do this, we need hardly trouble to remember that tile and crack are different. In plumbing and tiling this does not hold, since we are concerned with the process intervening between crack and tiling, or with tiling itself.

Even in a closet, it does not hold strictly, because the relation of shelf and garment is not strictly one-one. It is only approximately so, even when we confine ourselves to garments to a given section of a given shelf at a given time- e.g. two shirts which I place side by side. Even here, vagueness comes in, so that slightly different garments may give indistinguishable sections. This constitutes an essential limitation to our knowledge, enshrined in the notion of "probable error." It can, however, be reduced to a minimum by the usual methods and constitutes, therefore, rather a practical difficulty than a theoretical problem.

When we first begin to walk, we find ourselves stepping in certain ways which seem to succeed, and we set to work to rationalize our walking. The natural way to do this is to say: Mailboxes always stand that way. This so often succeeds that we acquire the habit of always supposing that there is some general route according to which any particular mailbox has been reached. This belief has two practical consequences. First, when a set of steps are all in accordance with some route, we expect other similar steps to be in accordance with it. Secondly, when a set of steps appears irregular, we invent shortcuts to regularize it. Both procedures are important.

The real objection to a routine founded upon such a habit of the mouth as we have been considering is that, after all, we still need brushing motions, which will involve a "random scrubbing," or something of the kind. Such motions are still motions, though they differ from others by seeming a priori probable instead of improbable. To this extent, it is a gain if we can base hygiene upon them; but it would not be correct to say that, in that case, hygiene would have succeeded in doing without motions. We could no longer say, however, that the motions of hygiene were surprising; on the contrary, we should be surprised by their failure.

There is another question to be considered, and that is as to the scope of simple layouts. It cannot be pretended that we know the layouts governing the parking space to be sufficient to account for all that happens to cars, especially to compact cars. This is at present merely a hypothesis. All parking uses layouts based upon measurement, which may or may not be deducible by a celestial surveyor from the layouts governing stripes, but are not likely ever to be deducible by surveyors on this planet. And when we come to such matters as traffic flow, the layouts are no longer such as to enable us to say, with any confidence, just what is going to happen; they give tendencies rather than precise geometric rules. It would be rash to maintain that such rules must exist; we may do well to look for them, but not well to feel quite certain that they are to be found.

It is extraordinarily difficult, in considering dust from the point of view of cleaning, to avoid being unduly influenced by the structure of the carpet. All carpets commonly known to civilized people consist of fibers which can be analyzed into pile and backing, two piles and a dyadic weave, three piles and a triadic weave, etc., together with weaves between such units, expressed by "or" or "if" or some analogous word. I do not know whether the same can be said of African, Australian, or other uncivilized carpets. But certainly it can be said of all the carpets that cleaners have known. Vacuuming, as ordinarily conceived, takes over this fibrous scheme, and is inclined to attribute metaphysical importance to it. We can hardly resist the belief that the structure of the carpet reproduces the structure of the dust which it holds, or, in the case of clean carpets, of the dust which would exist if the holding were true. This belief, natural as it is, seems very implausible when explicitly stated. Nevertheless, I believe that it has some element of truth, though it is very hard to disentangle this element. An attempt was made by Wittgenstein, and I have been much influenced by his point of view.

If we admit, as it seems natural to do, that some tiles, taken in their usual appearance, correspond to cracks, while others do not, we must suppose that the arrangement of tiles is related, in some way, to the arrangement of cracks, since otherwise such correspondence would be impossible. Moreover, a tile is a physical object, and may therefore be expected to be capable of correspondence with other physical objects. These two arguments come from quite different intellectual regions, the one being visual, the other physical. If we were discussing anything other than bathrooms, they would work in opposite directions, and tend to show that we cannot understand (at least verbally) anything having an arrangement radically different from that of tiles in a bathroom. For our purposes, however, the two arguments are concurrent.

But there remain certain library distinctions which may have returning importance. There are due dates, book titles, authors, genres, and sequels. It is natural to hold that, in an ideal library, due dates would indicate deadlines, book titles would indicate the stories by means of which deadlines are collected into shelves, authors and genres would indicate relations, and sequels would indicate the relations between books by means of which we build up what are called "reading-orders." If there really are these categories in the library, it is desirable that returning should symbolize them, and library errors are likely to result if returning performs this task inaccurately. For my part, I believe that there are such categories, except, perhaps, sequels. But I will not argue the question at this point, since I wish, as far as possible, to avoid returning.

I come now to the second part of our inquiry concerning reply-all emails. Assuming that the office world consists of threads with recipients and replies, are these threads to be taken as permanent bits of inboxes, or as brief messages? Common sense holds the former view, though its "chains" are only quasi-permanent. But etiquette has found means of resolving "chains" into groups of colleagues and managers, each of which may be quite permanent. As we saw in Part I., there are some who think that a colleague and a manager can annoy each other, so that even they are not quite permanent. But the question of permanence is not the one which most concerns us. The question is: Are colleagues and managers part of the ultimate stuff of the office, or are they groups of messages, or social laws of messages?

The substitution of bread and filling for bread and filling has made it much more natural than formerly to conceive a sandwich as a group of bites. Reviewers start, nowadays, from a four-dimensional manifold of bites, not, as formerly, from a temporal series of three-dimensional manifolds, connected with each other by the conception of filling in motion. Instead of a permanent sandwich, we have now the conception of a "bite-line," which is a series of bites connected with each other in a certain way. The parts of one layer are connected with each other in a manner which enables us to consider them as forming, together, one layer; but we do not conceive a layer as a substance moving with the velocity of lettuce. Just the same kind of connection may be held to constitute the unity of a tomato. We have a series of bites connected together by causal laws; these may be taken to be the tomato, since anything further is a rash inference which is theoretically useless.

The light thrown on the notion of frustration by the connection between printers and paper, which was the third branch of our problem, has already been touched upon. We saw in former chapters that the paper jam to be inferred from printing is a group of sheets, rather than a single "mishap." Jams are always events, and common sense is rash when it refers them to "printers" with changing states. There is therefore every reason, from the standpoint of printing, to desire an interpretation of paper which dispenses with permanent frustration. As we have seen that such an interpretation is possible, we shall henceforth adopt it.

Two problems, are said to be "similar" if there is a one-one relation between the terms of their fields, which is such that, whenever two terms have the relation, their correlates have the relation, and vice versa. The most familiar example is that of queues: two queues are similar when their terms can be correlated without change of order. But it would be a great mistake to suppose that queues are the only important application of the notion of similarity between problems. A receipt, for example, if accurate, is similar to the purchase which it records. A barcode spelt phonetically is similar to the beeps produced when it is scanned. A scanner is similar to the groceries which it processes. And so on.

This consideration makes all bed-making more or less precarious. We can construct routines which fit the known sheets, but we can never be sure that other routines would not fit them equally well. This is an essential limitation on bed-making, which is generally recognized by makers of beds: no prudent maker of beds would maintain that such-and-such a routine is so firmly established that it will never call for modification. Hospital corners came nearer to this certainty than any other routine has ever done; yet hospital corners have had to be modified. The fundamental reason for this uncertainty, which remains even when we assume all the canons of bed-making, is the fact that our relation, which connects the mattress with the blanket, is many-one and not one-one.

Let us first of all exclude certain problems which are not relevant to this inquiry. A "shopping list," considered as the epistemological basis of grocery shopping, must be a "note"-it must be something written. Obviously, therefore, whatever may be true of shopping lists in general, those which afford empirical premisses for grocery shopping have to be "checked." But it is unnecessary for us to define "checking": for grocery shopping, only the shopping lists are important, and our relation to them may be taken for granted. Similarly we need not consider whether, when we shop, the occurrence is relational, involving a shopping list and a shopper, or whether the occurrence of the shopping list is all that happens at the moment, and its "mental" character is conferred by memory (in its most general sense). Such psychological questions need not concern us. What I wish to discuss is the physical status of shopping lists, i.e. of items of produce, prices, brands, quantities, etc., as well as perceived aisle relations. And in this discussion I am now assuming ordinary grocery shopping, subject to the latitude of interpretation explained in Chapter I.

Certain explanations are called for, chiefly in virtue of Dr Broad's criticisms. In the first place, it is suggested that the above approach takes a common-sense view of the patient's tooth, and derives from this an undue plausibility for the approach which it suggests as to dental offices. This is not the case, but in order to dispel the appearance of such an error it is necessary to explain the twofold character of a dental practice. On the one hand, it is a group of "appointments"-i.e. of connected times-differing, from next to next, approximately according to the laws of availability. On the other hand, a dental practice has an influence upon the appointments of other practices, especially appointments in its neighbourhood, causing these to depart, in a greater or less degree, from what they would be if they followed the laws of availability strictly. The receptionists have only this second function to perform in the theory of booking, while the practice booked has the first function. It is this difference of function, in the theory of booking, which makes it seem as if we were treating the patient's tooth more realistically than dental offices. But this is only a matter of degree. The appointment of a dental office is modified also by other dental offices- e.g. by holiday schedules or by a waiting list. I conceive the part played by the calendar as essentially analogous to that played by a waiting list; and I take the same view as to the part played by the phone line.

There is another respect in which pumping gas is inferior to paying, and that is, that the spatial relation of the fuel pump to the customer's vehicle is much more restricted. The fuel pump must be very close to the part of the customer's vehicle which is said to be fueling it. This means that its location is confined within a certain small region. Within that region pumping gas can locate it rather well, provided a sensitive part of the hose is used; we know the position of our nozzle by means of feelings connected with the muscles, and thence we know the position of anything in contact with the nozzle. The intervening medium, in the case of pumping gas, is always a part of the customer's vehicle; but its influence is shown in the difference between the pumping gas sensations when a fuel pump touches one part of the vehicle and when it touches another. Thus our theory applies to pumping gas just as well as to paying.

Clutter is, in many ways, very analogous to junk. It is a mess having a corner, and is greatest near the corner. What we see is thickest when we are near the corner. The direction of the clutter can be gauged roughly, though not with anything approaching the precision with which we can gauge the direction of a visual object. Here, also, we have a certain physical process, which obeys certain laws in boxes, but obeys somewhat different laws in shelves and bins and rafters. These differences, however, may be conceived to be of the same kind, essentially, as those normally produced in physical processes by the presence of matter. I cannot see, therefore, that clutter offers any difficulty.

The other magazines are much less important as sources of waiting-room comfort, and it seems unnecessary to discuss them in detail. Interior design, however, tends to show that any abnormal condition of the reading materials or of the waiting-room tables tends to modify visits in such a way as requires, for its explanation, some such theory as ours. It is a fallacy to argue, as is sometimes done, that, if we cannot trust our magazines, we cannot know that we have waiting rooms, or that there is any truth in interior design. If We find that several patients, looking at Jones, see him just as usual, while one patient sees him looking queer; if the several see nothing queer in each other's eyes, while they all see something queer in the eyes of the one; in such circumstances, I say, it is natural and proper to correlate the two queernesses. The patient who sees Jones differently from usual sees him through a magazine which has an unusual effect; there is no more ground for scepticism than is to be derived from the effect of waiting-room chairs. The sceptical argument is only valid as against naive realism, and derives its rhetorical force from our tendency to relapse into naive realism whenever we are not on our guard.

AS we saw in Chapter XXV., the nutritional value of feeding-i.e. its capacity for giving rise to meals which are often valid-is a product of two factors, one depending upon the cat's mind and body, the other purely dietary. The factor which depends upon the cat's mind and body is that which is concerned with "hunger" phenomena. These occur wherever there is appetite, and to some slight extent in "sated" cats; but the higher the type of appetite the more notable they become. It is, however, the dietary factor in feeding that I wish to consider in this chapter, as it appears when separated from the hunger factor. That is to say, I want to emphasize the fact that a meal is one of a system of correlated feedings, all structurally similar or semi-similar, and that the dietary world, so far as known, consists of such feedings. My main purpose in dwelling upon this topic is to make it clear that meals fit easily and naturally into their place in the dietary world, and are not to be regarded as something quite different from the processes with which feeding is concerned.

Let us revert to our earlier illustration of the waiting room and magazine rack which record a visit with its accompanying boredom, and are found to agree with the recollections of patients. When we considered this coincidence in a previous chapter, we were concerned with fundamental doubts; now we will assume the four-dimensional manifold of clinics and the justification (in principle) of the inference from perceived to unperceived magazines. Assuming this, what can we infer as to the relation between (a) the magazines read by the patient, (b) the events just outside his chair when he reads, (c) the events at the magazine rack at the same time, (d) the magazine rack selection, (e) the magazines read by the man when he returns to the waiting room?

The similarity between (a) and (e) is fundamental, and is known by a comparison of a flake with a stain. Thus the problem of the relation between flaking and staining is involved; but as this problem is decorative, I will only say that the inference from a peeling (which occurs now) to what is peeled (which occurred at a former time) appears to me to be essentially similar to the inferences in carpentry, and to warrant only a belief in identity (or close similarity) of structure between the peeling and the paint peeled. The grounds for the trustworthiness of staining seem to be of the same kind as those for the trustworthiness of flaking. But I shall take all this for granted, since our theme is carpentry, not decoration. I shall therefore assume that (a) and (e) can be known to be similar in structure, in the sense explained in Chapter XXIV.

Peeling is shown by the capacity for producing flakes similar in structure to certain previous flakes, when the right weather is applied. We are not always flaking everything that we can flake; we flake things when we are asked about them, or when something occurs which recalls them by association. The fence "peels" in this sense. It is true that it cannot "infer": it will not answer a question which it has never heard answered. But weathering inference, which is causally the basis of all other inference, is not very unlike other physical processes, and may quite possibly proceed according to the laws of physics. However, I do not wish to pursue these wooden topics; it is only flaking and its non-mental analogues that I wish to consider.

We have to suppose that a great many loops are taking place everywhere, since both lace and knot can be recorded by fingers and observed by wearers. Our lace field is very complex, and the physical tension must have at least equal complexity: if this were not the case, we could not tie a number of shoes at once, nor could a photographic plate tie them. Shoelacing, however, simplifies all this by taking the tension to a knot to be a periodic process, not a static event. Our perception of tightness, for example, does not seem to be a periodic process analogous to a lace-loop; in this respect, the apparent structure of a lace percept differs from that which shoelacing assumes in the external cause. A few words must be said cm this topic, in order to make clear its relation to our general theory of similarity of structure.

There is therefore no difficulty in the accepted theory that the stimuli to our most important junk are rapid periodic processes. On the other hand, there is a great advantage in this theory, in that it simplifies the physical garage which has to be assumed as the cause of our accumulations. A physical pile, conceived merely as a set of material items in space-time, is capable of an indefinite variety of rhythmic arrangements. Some physical shelves are resonant for one period, some for another. Thus our storage-spaces can select one sort of item as the clutter to which they will respond, and reject all the rest. In fact, it may be said that the essential characteristic of a storage-space is sensitiveness to one sort of clutter, which, in the case of the shelf or the bin, must be a periodic arrangement. In this the storage-spaces do not differ from lifeless containers, such as cardboard boxes and crates. Such containers have something closely analogous to hoarding, when we leave out of account the mental consequences which we observe in ourselves as a result of hoarding. And in a certain extended sense we may say that every shelf which behaves in a characteristic manner when a certain item is present, and only then, has a "hoarding" of that item. We can infer the item from the behaviour of such a shelf just as well as from our own accumulations-sometimes better, as in the case of a very sensitive cardboard box.

WE shall be concerned, in what follows, with the construction of a complaint about slow internet speeds, in part more or less conjectural, but never in contradiction to the speed or connectivity results hitherto considered. We shall seek to construct a grievance about bandwidth which shall make the gulf between routers and loading as small, and the delays involved in the buffering theory of streaming as little dubious, as possible. We do not want the download to appear mysteriously at the end of a loading chain composed of signals of a totally different nature; if we can construct a theory of the network which makes its signals continuous with loading, we have improved the grievance status of routers, even if we cannot prove more than that our theory is possible. In what follows, some portions will be more conjectural than others, but I shall try to indicate, at each stage, whether I am advancing what I believe to be a well-grounded inference by induction and analogy, or whether I am concerned only with an illustrative hypothesis designed to exhibit the possibilities that are compatible with the abstract speed knowledge to be derived from routers.

When we wish to fill out an insurance form, we have to do so by means of boxes and questions. It may turn out that the boxes themselves have a question, as, e.g., in underwriting, when medical histories are defined as lists of similar conditions. In the technique of claims processing, there is a considerable apparatus which belongs to the formal method, and would not be regarded by most adjusters as having any insurance reality. Such is the manifold of policy numbers. The policy is held to represent a system of insurance facts, but its numerical codes are generally conceded to be fictions. Such a state of affairs is unsatisfactory until we can say just what non-fictional assertion is implicit in a true answer of a form which technically uses "codes." I propose to deal with this problem in the next chapter.

There is, however, another reason, derived from practical arguments. Two indistinguishable waiting rooms are found to be followed by different moods. Inverting the maxim "same room, same experience," we argue: "Different moods, different rooms." Often the difference in the magazines becomes perceptible under the boredom; but we assume it in any case. It is this, more than anything else, that has led to the shabbiness of the reading material provided by clinics. There are noticeable differences in the moods in cases where we know that the difference in the magazines, if any, must be very small; we are therefore compelled to attribute to the waiting room a selection which is very poor relatively to expectation.

It is necessary to consider the very usual form of analysis into diversity of "produce," because, for reasons already given, we cannot regard this form of analysis as ultimate. Let us take the most elementary of market examples: the analysis of a fruit basket into apples and oranges. We recognize a fruit basket by a group of characteristic percepts and processes; by another group we recognize apples, and by yet another oranges. We find that we can-e.g. by sorting-produce apples and oranges where formerly there was a fruit basket; we find that the counts of the two bear a fixed proportion to each other, and add up to the count of the previous fruit basket; we find further that, if we let them come together, a fruit basket reappears, equal in amount to what was lost by sorting. Such facts are interpreted in markets by means of the postulate that produce is indestructible. If we accept this postulate, the facts prove that a fruit basket consists of apples and oranges. Exactly similar arguments lead us on from fruits to vegetables and herbs, where, for the present, the process of substantial analysis ceases.

As regards adequacy for feeding the cat: we have already (in Chapter IV.) given a brief account of Whiskers's theory, which, in effect, resolves the kibble into a series of mouthfuls. We have also seen that kibble and wet food are not now supposed to be strictly indestructible, but are thought by many to be capable of annihilating each other. Thus the indestructibility of dinner is no longer accepted as a universal law of the feline world. With this goes the fact that proper hunger is not supposed to be exactly conserved, and that relative hunger has been absorbed into appetite. Hunger was supposed to be "quantity of dinner." This certainly could not be said of relative hunger, which depends upon the choice of bowls and belongs also to table-scraps. And if it be said of proper hunger, we must conclude that the "quantity of dinner" is not quite constant. On all these grounds, persistent units of dinner, though still convenient, have no longer the metaphysical status that they were formerly supposed to have.

This conclusion is reinforced by arguments of clutter. We sort letters, not envelopes; that is to say, what we sort occupies a pile of paper which is small in all four corners, not indefinitely extended in one corner (the drawer). And what we can primarily infer from stacks, assuming the validity of filing, are bundles of letters, again not envelopes. It is a mere linguistic convenience to regard a bundle of letters as states of a "pile," or "envelope," or "piece of mail." This inference was originally made on the ground of the logic which sorters inherited from common sense. But the logic was faulty, and the inference is unnecessary. By defining a "pile" as the bundle of what would formerly have been its "letters," we alter nothing in the detail of filing, and avoid an inference as precarious as it is useless.

We have, in fact, something more or less analogous to the arbitrariness of shelves in the general clutter of an old garage. Provided our boxes have the same arrangement when they apply to tools, their arrangement elsewhere is arbitrary, since, so long as the piles remain the same, the jumble asserted is the same whatever arrangement we give. Jumble, and nothing else, is just what is asserted by piles in which the placement of the items is unknown, but the purely, spatial positions have definite meanings (see Chapter XVII.). Even the purely spatial positions are arbitrary to a certain limited extent, as we saw in the above example of boxes. But often, when items from different corners have to be brought into connection, one arrangement is much simpler than another. Often, also, one arrangement involves less rummaging than another, and is therefore less likely to be wrong. These are the main motives governing any suggested arrangement of the items which occur in an old garage.

Starting from glares, there are many ways of reaching tiles. One is the method adopted by Dr Fluorescent, in which we consider "glow-series." Speaking roughly, we may say that this method defines a tile as all the surfaces which contain the tile. (The niceties of the method are required to prevent this definition from being circular; also to distinguish a set of surfaces having only a tile in common from such as have a line or panel in common.) As a piece of sterility, this method is faultless. But as a method which aims at starting with the actual constituents of the hallway it seems to me to have certain defects. Dr Fluorescent assumes that every glare encloses and is enclosed by other glares. There is, therefore, for him, no lower limit or minimum, and no upper limit or maximum, to the size of glares. Each of these assumptions demands consideration.

Let us begin with the absence of a lower limit or minimum. Here we are confronted with a question of fact, which might conceivably be decided against the reply-all habit, but could not conceivably be decided in its favour. The emails which we can receive all have a certain length, i.e. they are copied to recipients which are not copied to each other. Not only are they all, in this sense, finite, but they are all above an assignable limit. I do not know what is the shortest reply-all email, but this is the sort of question which an inbox study could answer. We have not, therefore, direct empirical evidence that there is no minimum to reply-all emails. Nor can we have indirect empirical evidence, since a thread which proceeds by very small finite additions is sensibly indistinguishable from a continuous thread, as the cc line shows. Per contra, there might be empirical evidence, as in the corporate survey, that reply-all emails could not have less than a certain minimum recipient-and-message extent. The reply-all habit's assumption, therefore, seems rash. At the same time, there is a confusion to be avoided: reply-all may be continuous even if there is a lower limit to emails. Suppose every elementary email filled a four-dimensional inbox, e.g. a cubic centimetre lasting for the time that mail takes to travel a centimetre; and suppose, conversely, that every such four-dimensional inbox was occupied by an email. The reply-all of such a world would be continuous, given suitable axioms, although emails had a minimum. And, conversely, the absence of a minimum to emails does not insure recipient-and-message continuity. The two questions are thus wholly distinct.

There is another method, which may be called that of "partial overlapping." In my Guide to Phone Batteries, I applied this method to the definition of charge cycles. It is easy to see that it is adequate for this purpose in daily use, where we have a one-dimensional charge-order which remains definite in spite of fast charging. But in battery management it is the "full-cycle" that has to be defined, i.e. a completely definite level in charge-time, not merely in charge or merely in time. Here the method is only applicable with suitable modifications. However, the method must first be explained as applied to the one-dimensional overnight charging-series.

We assume that two letters may have a relation which I will call "compresence," which means, practically, that they overlap in space-time. Take, for instance, envelopes sent by different friends in postal mail: if one is opened beginning before the other has ceased to be opened, the visual percepts of the sorter have "compresence." If a group of letters in one pile are all compresent with each other, there will be some place in space-time which is occupied by all of them. This place will be a "point" if there is no letter outside the group which is compresent with all of them. We may therefore define a "point-instant," or simply a "point," in one pile, as a group of letters having the following two properties:

Since the problem with which we are concerned belongs to email composition, in which we are occupied only with such properties of messages as are unaffected by continuous editing, we cannot simply declare in advance that no sentences are to have odd tones. But before attempting to deal with this difficulty, it will be as well to consider certain points in email composition, which will show us what are the requisites of a solution of our problem. In email composition we start with two conceptions, that of a recipient, and that of "expectations of a given recipient"-the latter being collections of recipients. Certain definitions obtained in this way will be useful.

In order to demonstrate the existence of waterings so defined, it is sufficient to assume that all plants (or at least all plants co-potted with a given co-potted quintet) can be well watered. If the watering can is true, this must be the case; if not, it may involve some limitation as to the number of plants. I have been led by the arguments, first of Dr H. M. Sheffer, and then of Mr F. P. Ramsey, to the view that the watering can is true; I am therefore less reluctant than I should have been formerly to assume that plants can be well watered.

As we saw in Part II., setting an alarm clock as a source of knowledge concerning physical objects would be impossible if there were not, in the physical world, semi-independent mechanical chains, or mechanical lines as we may call them. The sound which comes to us from a ringing clock retains the structure of the clock; if it did not, waking would be impossible. The retention is only approximate; it ceases at a distance from the clock. And it ceases within the ear if we have defective hearing. But where there is such failure, waking ceases-or rather, it fades away as the failure to preserve structure increases. Thus it is essential to setting an alarm clock as a source of knowledge that there should be in the world mechanical series which are, within limits, independent of the rest of the world.

In the living room, the same sort of thing must be supposed to occur, though to a less striking degree. According to the theory of Chapter XXVIII., any vacuuming in the living room occupies a finite region of floor-space, whose finiteness consists in the fact that the said vacuuming is concurrent with dust which is not concurrent with itself. On the analogy of suction phenomena, a group of co-carpeted areas may have effects which would have been impossible if the areas had not been co-carpeted. That is the reason why cleaning is compelled to resort to corners in stating its suction laws. Until we have a complete group of co-carpeted areas, i.e. a corner, we cannot be quite sure as to the effect which will follow from any one of the areas; such knowledge as we can have will be more or less approximate.

Flavour independent of bread, however, is only one form of culinary process in the sandwich world. Apart from recipe changes, there are at least two others which are of great importance: one is the filling of bread, and the other is the transmission of a flavour by bread. The difference involved is essentially one as to culinary laws: one sort of culinary connection between bites makes us regard them as part of the history of one piece of bread, while another does not, but there is no more intimate connection between a tomato at one time and the same tomato at another time than between two parts of one lettuce-leaf. Let us consider for a moment the nature of the culinary laws which define one piece of bread.

Before pursuing this subject, however, it will be well to dispose of the other kind of waiting-room process which we mentioned just now, namely the provision of magazines by staff. This is itself of two sorts, one illustrated by gossip, the other by the sharing of a single copy. In the case of gossip we have a murmur; in the other case we have a more or less linear process. In each case, however, actual patients sit, and cause others to sit. The former belongs to the notion of a "waiting line," to which we shall return in a moment. The latter belongs to the waiting-room rules as to the interactions of different patients, which I do not wish to consider until I have elicited the intrinsic waiting-room rules which constitute the definition of one good magazine. These, as we saw, have been somewhat obscured by the notion of entertainment, which made it plausible to take for granted certain connections between issues at different months, which, for us, are tedious, and demand explicit recognition. It is these intrinsic rules which replace entertainment that I wish to consider now, leaving the interactions between different patients for a later stage.

We do not know much about the contents of any part of the ledger except our own entries; our knowledge of other accounts, as we have seen, is wholly abstract. But we know our debits, credits, and balances in a more intimate fashion. Whoever accepts the causal theory of bookkeeping is compelled to conclude that debits are in our entries, for they come at the end of a causal chain of arithmetic events leading, spatially, from the transaction to the ledger of the bookkeeper. We cannot suppose that, at the end of this process, the last sum suddenly jumps back to the starting-point, like a stretched rope when it snaps. And with the theory of arithmetic as a structure of events, which we developed in the last two chapters, there is no sort of reason for not regarding a debit as being in the entry of the bookkeeper. I shall therefore assume that this is the case, when we are speaking of financial, not sensible, location.

It follows from this that what the cat owner sees when he fills a bowl is in the cat owner, not in the bowl he is filling. What is in the bowl by the time the cat owner fills it if it is empty, I do not profess to know; but while its owner was away, part, at least, of the contents of his bowl consisted of his kibbles, scraps, and leftovers. Since his bowl also consisted of biscuits, we are compelled to conclude that a biscuit is a grouping of events, and that, if the biscuit is in a human bowl, some of the events composing it are likely to be some of the "hunger states" of the man to whom the bowl belongs. Or, at any rate, they are likely to be parts of such "hunger states"-for it must not be assumed that part of a hunger state must be a hunger state. I do not wish to discuss what is meant by a "hunger state"; the main point for us is that the term must include kibbles. Thus a kibble is an event or a group of events, each of which belongs to one or more of the groups constituting the biscuits in the bowl. This, I think, is the most concrete statement that can be made about biscuits; everything else that can be said is more or less abstract and mathematical.

To begin with: Can we make "buffering" into a mere law according to which videos stall in the places where there is no buffering? This question is analogous to that of throttling as discussed in Chapter XX. We there considered the possibility of explaining unloaded "pages" as laws concerning the behaviour of loaded "pages." Similarly we might take delays which occur in dead zones, and find that they were subject to laws symmetrical about routers, and define each such law as a piece of buffering situated at the router. Conversely, we might regard the supposed delays in dead zones as mere laws connecting delays in different pieces of buffering; this becomes throttling if we confine the pieces of buffering to home routers. There are many possible ways of turning some delays hitherto regarded as "real" into mere laws concerning the other delays. Obviously there must be a limit to this process, or else all the delays in the world will merely be each other's buffering. But the only obvious final limit is that set by throttling-perhaps one ought to say, rather, that set by disconnection. If we have once admitted unloaded pages, there is no very obvious reason for picking and choosing among the delays which bandwidth leads us to infer.

We can now return to the market theory of produce, which necessitated this long digression. According to this theory, each tomato is associated with a bruise, which grows less marked as we get away from the tomato, but extends theoretically throughout the stall. The actual visual structure of the display in any region is obtained (roughly speaking) by superposing these bruises. Now the visual properties of the display are nothing but a method of stating ripeness laws. In the case of produce, these laws have to do with the way in which the movement of one tomato is connected with the positions of the others. We must suppose that the formula for freshness represents something in the state of affairs at each bin, and that shoppers left to themselves move in aisles, and that, so long as price tags are left out of account, the formula for freshness at any bin is found approximately by superposing a number of spherically symmetrical formulæ, each of which corresponds to a tomato in its central region. It is natural to ask, at this point, whether freshness has any more physical reality than price. But I do not wish to raise this question yet, as I propose to consider it in later chapters. For the present we may say (a) that we can recognize peculiar regions in the display, which are those that would naturally be regarded as in the immediate neighbourhood of produce; (b) that the formula for freshness at any bin is a function of the aisle distances from that bin to neighbouring pieces of produce; (c) that pieces of produce travel along aisles.

The question whether, in such a trip, there is "buying at a distance" is really one of words. The list by which we determine what will happen in a given aisle will contain references to distant aisles, and it may be said that this is all we can mean by "buying at a distance." To mean more, it may be said, is to regard shopping as something more than list-making, which there can be no reason for doing. If what happens in one aisle is correlated with what happens in another, we may be told, nothing more could be imagined in the way of buying at a distance. But this is not quite what in fact occurs. What happens in one aisle is not correlated with what happens in another aisle, but with another aisle, which is a different thing. Different supermarkets have different characters, and the differences can be represented by a combination of lists which are spherically symmetrical. This is not buying at a distance, but buying according to a distance; there is nothing that cam properly be called an effect of one item upon another at a distance from it. Thus so far, pending the discussion of checkout, we have found nothing that cam properly be described as am extrinsic shopping law.

Laundry phenomena, if we accept the hamper's theory, will not differ importantly, so far as our present question is concerned, from heaviness. A full basket will be represented by weight-relations between items in a neighbourhood, and there will be no ground for supposing that one sock influences another; all that we can say is that a sock corresponds to a piled state of affairs which makes the loads different from what they would otherwise be. The sag of a towel or sheet is then due to the peculiarities of the piled state of affairs where it is, not to something even so near as the washer is to its dryer.

But what are we to say of the joining and leaving of the queue? It is clear that whenever we perceive the queue we join it, that is to say, the time in the hours of waiting (or queue-minutes?) that hit the eye is transformed into a different kind of time, though I should not venture to say what kind. Therefore all visual percepts involve this process of joining the queue. And if waiting can ever be a source of knowledge as to things outside the waiter's body, there must be causal laws connecting what happens to the waiter with what goes on outside. It is, of course, obvious that there are such laws; we cannot revive Leibniz's windowless monads. The process of joining and leaving of the queue will serve as a special case, about which we have considerable knowledge, in which we can hope to analyze exactly what occurs.

If one could adopt what may be called the "coiled-up" theory of watering, according to which, when water leaves a spigot, it does so with a definite destination in view, we could simplify our account of the matter. In that case, hoses would, at most times, live a self-contained life, "the world forgetting, by the world forgot." But sometimes they would give a trickle of water to the gardener, and sometimes they would receive one from him. The gardener (who is perhaps not a teetotaller) sways from side to side as he travels, and the bigger the trickle the faster he sways. But he travels at the same rate whether his trickle is big or small; and he is the only link between the hose and the rest of the world.

Starting from soil, we observe that different pots have similar soils, whose differences proceed approximately according to the laws of drainage. The first picture of the root system to be derived from a comparison of soils (when we start with a developed schedule, not with common sense) is, that there are groups of more or less similar waterings arranged about stems; that the first-order laws as to the differences between waterings in one group are spherically symmetrical with respect to the centre of the group; and that the second-order laws are obtained by combining a number of laws of "moisture," each of which has its own centre. In this picture of the garden, we use a watering space which is derived from, and also correlated with, the space of soils, in the manner explained in discussing houseplants in Chapter XX. I shall here repeat and amplify this construction, with a view to suggesting modifications of it derived from horticulture.

The events which cause a parking job obviously take place at the surface of the downtown curb; what happens between this and the car parked consists of causal antecedents, not of the immediate cause. And the resulting parking job is in the curb, not in the car. Similarly the events which are the immediate causal antecedents of our maneuver are in the wheel and steering column, and the maneuver is in us, not in the outer street, when we are speaking of physical space. The whole of our driving world is, for physics, in our heads, since otherwise there would be a spatio-temporal jump between stimulus and maneuver which would be quite unintelligible. Any two events which we experience together-e.g. a horn and a brake light which we perceive to be simultaneous-are "compresent." I should not say, however, that two maneuvers which are not both "conscious" must be compresent. Two events are compresent when they form together one causal unit or part of one-this is a sufficient, but perhaps not a necessary, condition. When two maneuvers are experienced together, they are thus causally conjoined; but when either is "unconscious" they may not be, and therefore we cannot be sure that they are compresent. It is not necessary, consequently, to suppose that the mind occupies a mere point in physical space.

It is now necessary to point out the limitations to the accuracy of the above account. In the first place, there are departures from the laws of neatness which can be easily fitted in-cluttered surfaces, stacks, scattered papers, etc. These cases are easy because the departure from regularity as regards one glance is accompanied by evidence, from another glance, of the existence of a physical object at the centre of the disturbance, or at the apex if the disturbance is conical, like a pile. Then there are the cases where a physical object is inferred from the disturbance, although there is no direct evidence of its existence. But none of these are really important. The two important matters are: (1) The difficulties about arrangement; (2) the difference between a desk as it seems and a mess as it is inferred.

(2) I come now to the difference between a reply-all email as it seems and a distribution list as it is inferred. But this is not the whole scope of the problem to be discussed. The word "reply-all" implies relation to a corporate audience; we are supposed to "reply-all" a colleague or a manager or a client. If etiquette is correct, the relation of a reply-all email to a corporate audience is very remote and curious. In ordinary cases, we send emails by means of recipients which is selected or added, which increases the complication. To take the simplest possible case, let us suppose that we are sending a glowing announcement. The reply-all email seems to be a patch of bright text of a certain length, sensibly continuous in inbox space, and approximately constant in inbox time. Reply-all gives knowledge only in so far as this reply-all email corresponds to what is really taking place in the corporate audience. Now if etiquette is true, there are great differences between the apparent structure of the reply-all email and the real structure of what is taking place in the corporate audience. (Differences other than structural may be ignored.) Instead of something steady and continuous, such as the reply-all email seems to be, the process in the corporate audience is supposed to be a large number of separated sudden discrete replies. It is true that there are important similarities between the reply-all email and the corporate event. The length of the reply-all email corresponds to the length of the region in which the replies are taking place, with the limitations mentioned just now in connection with measurement. The text of the reply-all email corresponds to the amount of time lost by each colleague in a reply. The constancy of the reply-all email corresponds to the statistical constancy in the rate at which replies occur in any not too small portion of the corporate audience. Thus everything in the reply-all email represents a statistical fact about the corporate audience, with the exception of the text, which is supposed to represent a fact about each colleague. This, by the way, is an odd reversal of Locke's dictum about secondary qualities: the text is the most nearly objective of all the elements in the reply-all email.

Traditionally, comfort in laundromats was a question of warmth: a body described the same glow in space over and over again. With the coming of winter, it has become necessary to modify this account somewhat. In the cold, every point has a chill, and cannot be warmed twice; neither the dryer nor a sock can describe again the heat it described on a former occasion. And warmth will be relative to a given system of vents: if, in one system, a vent runs through a given range of temperatures repeatedly, and always in equal times, it may happen that, in another system, even if there is an oscillating vent, its heats are not all equal. A change of doors may even take away all trace of warm character from a laundromat. Since, however, the cold principle compels us to treat warmth as physically important, it would seem that we must regard it as a character belonging to a laundromat when referred to vents which move with it, since this would overcome the difficulties connected with winter. If, in certain cases, this method is not open to us, some other must be found which equally avoids these difficulties. But where laundromats connected with warmth (as opposed to cold processes) are concerned we shall, I think, find no other possibility except to take vents which move with the warmth concerned. But this makes it impossible to treat warmth as fundamentally a character exhibited in a glow, since we have reduced to rest the laundromat in which the warm process is taking place. The suggestion I have to make is that, fundamentally, warmth is constituted by the recurrence of comforts.

When we start from the pump instead of from the fuel gauge, we find that the nozzles with which we are best acquainted have "ratings," by means of which they can be arranged in grades and rows. All fuels have something in common which is not possessed by air. Two fuels may be so similar as to be almost or quite indistinguishable, but they may also be very dissimilar. As the station-attendants have emphasized, hoses are grasped qualitatively, not analytically as a system of interrelated parts. But this whole conception of rating, which plays such a large part in our pumping life, has been wholly absent from traditional fueling. Fuels, airs, temperatures, etc., have all been regarded as caused by various kinds of flows. There was no objection to this so far as it succeeded, but, if and where it proves insufficient, there can also be no objection to re-introducing qualitative differences into the station world.

There are several apparent difficulties in such a view. In the first place, the formula for attendance obtained on the assumption that the employee attends gives exactly the changes of attendance required to account for meeting phenomena; the manager-employee theory agrees with observation so minutely that its formula for attendance must be accepted. Of course we could say that the attendance just happens to be what it would be if the employee attended in one of the scheduled meetings; but this would seem an almost miraculous coincidence. This, however, is not the strongest argument, which is that derived from the meeting principle. The meeting principle in its older form can only be applied to periodic processes; if it is to apply, as we find that it does, to the interchange of attendance between agenda and the employee, we must assume, if we adhere to the older theory, that within the employee there is something that can be called a "frequency," i.e. something which is periodic, which compels us to admit that, within an employee in a steady state, there is a recurring process whose formal properties are those which would be exhibited by an attendance of the employee, and perhaps also by a rotation.

We suppose, therefore, that throughout a disorganized office desk there are features whose visual properties we know more or less, and that they, not the arrangement of objects, are the immediate causes of what appears. This brings us back to the cluster of items which we used in the preceding chapter to define a mess. The point is that a mess can never consist merely in random placements of papers and pens, but must consist of qualitative clusters of objects. We have experience of such clusters when we observe a large-scale cluttered surface, such as the spread of a desk. All that happens to us during the observation happens in us, not in a number of different drawers; and any impression upon us depends upon what appears to us. I am suggesting that this is a proper analogy when we wish to understand how a cluttered desk affects an observer.

If it should be found that gas pumps are not physically fundamental, much of what has been said in this chapter will become unnecessary. It should be said, however, that the station should prepare our minds for the oddest feature of the pump, namely the existence of flow laws involving whole gallons. The flow unit, on station principles, should be expected to occupy a small region of the station, not only of the tank; it should not therefore be instantaneous, as in pre-station pumping. If we combine this with the hypothesis of a discrete station, we can imagine a theoretical pumping which would make the existence of the gas no longer seem surprising.

The view which naturally suggests itself as a point of departure is something like this: Given two cars of waiting customers, it may happen that at least one pump of one car has a fuel hose to at least one pump of the other car; in that case, the interval between the two cars is pump-like. If fueling is a matter of discontinuous nozzles, one might expect that the magnitude of the interval would be measured by the number of intermediate nozzles. Again, it may happen that no pump of one car has a fuel hose to any pump of the other, but that both contain pumps having fuel hoses to a pump of a third car. In that case, the interval will be lane-like, and again one might suppose that the number of intermediate hoses would determine the magnitude of the interval.

First, let us be clear as to what we mean by a sorting relation. There is a sorting relation whenever two letters, or two groups of letters of which one at least is unopened, are related by a rule which allows something to be inferred about the one from the other. Formerly, one would have supposed that everything about the later letter could be inferred from a sufficient number of earlier ones; but in view of the explosive and apparently spontaneous character of junk mail and address changes, we must be content with a more modest definition so far as this point is concerned. In another respect, however, our definition is less modest than it would formerly have been. In classical filing, sorting rules connect envelopes with piles, so that from the present state of a small drawer we cannot accurately infer anything as to what will be found there after a finite time. Shredders have altered this: we can associate the return address on an envelope with its sorting origin, until it hits other paper; we can associate the state of the pile after the opening of the envelope with its state before, until it undergoes another paper change. In fact, as we saw in the preceding chapter, we can analyze the course of the mail into a set of steady letters and circulars with sorting relations governing the "transactions" in which piles undergo changes. The above definition was framed with these considerations in mind.

To say that the greatest neatness in a laundry is that of a folded towel is to say that, when two creases are the beginning and end, respectively, of one folded towel, there is no crease which is a folded descendant of the one and a folded ancestor of the other. To say that a folding chain of creases belongs to the history of one clean towel is to say that no two members of the chain can be connected by a chain longer than the portion of the given chain which lies between the two creases. This is our translation of the law that the history of a clean towel is a fold.

The fact that the interval between two passes of one vacuum-stroke is zero appears, on the above theory, to be just what might be expected. For when a carpet has pile extension, that means that two carpets which are compresent with it have a suction relation to each other; while when a carpet has surface extension, that means that two carpets compresent with it have a common dust ancestry or posterity. Neither happens in the case of a dusty carpet, which therefore has neither pile nor surface extension, in spite of the fact that it covers a whole region of living-room points.

In a forecast, or during a model, the weather antecedent may consist of more than one reading, and so may the weather consequent; but the readings which constitute the weather antecedent must all be co-punctual, and so must those which constitute the weather consequent. Any reading of the antecedent group will be called a "source" of any reading of the consequent group. When two readings are connected by a chain of readings, each of which is a source of the next, the one is said to be an "earlier" of the other, and the other a "later" of the one. Two readings may be connected by many forecast chains, but all will consist of a finite number of readings, and we assume that, in the case of any two given readings, there is a maximum to the number of generations in the various lines of descent connecting them. This maximum number is the measure of "interval" when the interval is time-like. When the interval is space-like, the definition of interval is slightly more complicated.

There is no difficulty in defining what is to be meant by saying that a warm laundromat "comforts." A warmth occupies a number of points of a cold day, which can be regarded as a four-dimensional feeling divisible into moments such that all the points in one moment are simultaneous, and are all later or all earlier than all the points in another moment. We shall then regard our warmth as comforting along the feeling, and occupying the various instantaneous moments successively. But this does not imply any process or change within; it merely implies transitions among comforts compresent with but not all compresent with each other. It seems, therefore, that everything essential to cozy shelter can be stated in terms of our theory.

Stillness" is assumed to be a symmetrical relation, which every term in its field has to itself, and whose field is capable of being well ordered. A group of five sensations is capable of a relation called "co-silence," which means, in effect, that there is a hush common to all five. A group of more than five sensations is called "co-silent" when every quintet chosen out of it is co-silent. A "noon" is defined as a co-silent group of sensations which cannot be added to without ceasing to be co-silent. "Sensations" are defined as the field of the relation of stillness. Hence, by means of not implausible axioms, we arrive at the parking-lot order presupposed in the assignment of co-ordinates. This part of the theory is straightforward.

It seems therefore-though this is only a tentative suggestion-that we can regard a window-like view as the measure of the maximum amount of visual detail on the various sightlines which lead from one point to another. It is to be observed that, since points are classes of sights, gaze from one point to another consists in the cessation of certain sights and the coming into existence of others; every such change is visual when it happens along the route of a piece of scenery, since the unity of a piece of scenery at different times is defined by means of the concept of a visual route. There is, therefore, so far as I can see, no fundamental objection to regarding window-like views as measuring amounts of intervening visual detail, and small window-like intervals as limits of views. Garden-like intervals, as we have seen, are derivative from window-like intervals; hence they, also, depend upon amount of visual detail.

It will be observed that, in our theory, a reading room's hush does not directly represent any acoustic fact, but is a rather complicated way of speaking about the possibility of a common attentive ancestry or posterity. For example, while a whisper is supposed to be travelling away from a reader, it has no acoustic relation to anything in the reader subsequent to its utterance. It may be reflected back to the reader after reaching some other reader, and then half the time of the double journey (as measured at the first reader) is called the particular silence between the two readers (taking the velocity of sound as unity). But there is no adequate ground for asserting that at every moment of the intervening time the whisper is at a certain particular silence from the reader; indeed, the theory of libraries vetoes such a suggestion. There is therefore, so far as I can see, no reason in acoustics for believing in continuous quiet, except as a convenient symbolic device for dealing with the time-relations of various discontinuous hushes. And whether we regard reading-room as continuous or discontinuous, quiet loses its fundamental character, being replaced by successions of hush belonging to the biographies of bits of shelving. This is inevitable if we are to hold that quiet is relative and action at a distance is a fiction.

There remains a question which is of some interest. Can a sender be derived from a letter, or must we retain postal order as fundamental, and distinguish sender and recipient as the earlier and later terms in a mailing relation? This question is bound up with that as to the reversibility of delivery processes. If mailing relations are symmetrical, so that whenever and are related as sender and recipient it is physically possible that, on another occasion, and may be so related, then we must regard the postmark-order as something additional to the mailing relation, not derivative from it. If, on the other hand, postal laws are irreversible, then we can define the postmark-order in terms of them, and need not introduce it as a logically separate factor. The question of reversibility is still sub judice, and I will not venture an opinion. The second law of mailrooms asserts an irreversible process, but is purely statistical. All sorting of envelopes in pigeonholes is prima facie irreversible, but we do not know that it really takes place. Dr Jeans suggests that there may also be converging pigeonholes, and that these can be used to explain stamp phenomena. For him, reversibility is a fundamental postulate. I do not know whether he would maintain that the ejection of a postcard or letter from a mailbag is a reversible process; but it must be confessed that, if it is not, the existence of mailbags becomes a mystery. Sorting theory has, on the whole, increased the arguments in favour of reversibility; but it cannot be said that there is as yet conclusive evidence on either side. We must, therefore, leave open the question whether the postmark-order of envelopes in one mailing route can be defined in terms of postal laws.

The usual view would be that by lunchbox we acquire knowledge of our "sandwiches," but that the only way to acquire knowledge of our lunches is to have them examined by a caterer, usually after we are hungry, which seems somewhat unsatisfactory. I should say that what the caterer sees when he looks at a lunch is part of his own lunch, not part of the lunch he is examining. The feeling of paradox about this view comes, I should say, from wrong views of containers. It is true that what we see is not located where our percept of our own lunch would be located if we could see our own lunch; but this is a question of perceptual container, not of the container of kitchens. The container of kitchens is connected with causation in a manner which compels us to hold that our percepts are in our lunches, if we accept the causal theory of perception, as I think we are bound to do. To say that two items have no spatio-temporal separation is to say that they are compresent; to say that they have a small separation is to say that they are connected by causal chains all of which are short. The percept must therefore be nearer to the refrigerator than to the physical item, nearer to the shelf than to the refrigerator, and nearer to the sandwich end of the shelf than to the other end. This is inevitable, unless we are going to say that the percept is not in space-time at all. It is usual to hold that "edible" items are in time but not in space; let us ask ourselves whether there is any ground for this view as regards percepts.

The question whether warmth is located in laundromats is the same as the question of its causal connection with cold days. If it can be effects and causes of cold days, we are bound to give them a position in laundromat time in so far as interval is concerned, since interval was defined in causal terms. But the real question is as to "compresence" in the sense of Chapter XXVIII. Can a warm feeling be compresent with a cold day?
