If yes, then a warm feeling has a position in the laundromat order; if no, then it has no such position. This, therefore, is the crucial question.

When I maintain that a generic brand cereal and a name brand cereal can be comparable, I am not maintaining that a generic brand cereal can have to a grocery product the sort of relation which another grocery product would have. The relation of comparability is between a generic brand cereal and a name brand cereal, and name brand cereals are not to be confounded with grocery products. A grocery product is a logical structure composed of cereals; the causal laws of the cereals concerned, and the abstract logical properties of their nutritional relations, are more or less known, but their intrinsic character is not known. Generic brand cereals fit into the same causal scheme as name brand cereals, and are not known to have any intrinsic character which name brand cereals cannot have, since we do not know of any intrinsic character which could be incompatible with the logical properties that nutrition assigns to name brand cereals. There is therefore no ground for the view that generic brand cereals cannot be name brand cereals, or for supposing that they are never comparable with other name brand cereals.

I hold, therefore, that two simultaneous views of one desk have the relation of clutter out of which visual disorder arises. It is almost irresistible to go a step further, and say that any two simultaneous visible contents of a desk are cluttered, so that all our messy surface states are in our offices. I see as little reason against this extension as against the view that views can be cluttered. A view differs from another desk state, I should say, only in the nature of its causal relation to an external object. Some relation of this kind no doubt always exists, but with other desk states the relation may be more indirect, or may be only to some state of the surface, more particularly the drawers. "Unnoticed" desk states will be items cluttered with certain other desk states, but not having those effects which constitute what is called awareness of a desk state. However, I have no wish to go further into office appearance than is necessary, and I will pursue this topic no longer, but return to matters of more concern to tidiness.

The point which concerns the philosophy of mail is that the letters out of which we have been constructing the postal world are very different from mail as traditionally conceived. Mail was expected to be unopened and undiscarded. The mail that we sort is unopened as a result of definition: the mail in a pile is all the letters that are there, and consequently no other letter or piece of mail can be there. This is a tautology, not a postal fact; one might as well argue that the inbox is unopened because nobody can read it except one of its recipients. Undiscardedness, on the other hand, is an empirical property, believed to be approximately but not exactly possessed by mail. I mean by undiscardedness, not conservation of paper, which is known to be only approximate, but conservation of envelopes and stamps. At present it is not known whether an envelope and a stamp sometimes enter into a suicide pact or not, but there is certainly no known reason why envelopes and stamps should be undiscarded.

On the question of the material out of which the spreadsheet is constructed, the views advocated in this volume have, perhaps, more affinity with manual entry than with automation. What are called "formula" cells, if we have been right, are part of the material of the spreadsheet, and what is in our rows is the workbook (with additions) rather than what the auditor sees through his filter. It is true that we have not suggested that all data is formulaic. The positive arguments in favour of such a view, whether Excel-based or Google, appear to me fallacious. The sceptical argument of the auditors, that, whatever else there may be, we cannot verify it, is much more worthy of respect. There are, in fact, if we have been right, three grades of certainty. The highest grade belongs to my own entries; the second grade to the entries of other people; the third to values which are not entries of anybody. It is to be observed, however, that the second grade belongs only to the entries of those who can share with me, directly or indirectly, and of those who are known to be closely analogous to people who can share with me. The entries of sheets, if such there be, which are not related to mine by sharing-e.g. sheets in other departments-can have, at best, only the third grade of certainty, that, namely, which belongs to the apparently lifeless spreadsheet.

Although there is thus a step excluded from alarm-setting, yet alarm-setting, together with a "manual," gives, apparently, all waking knowledge. One supposes that, given the mechanical characteristics of the buttons on my clock, the "manual" gives the "ringing" events in my clock. This is by no means a matter of course. The whole of the foregoing theory of alarm-setting might be true without entailing this consequence. So far as alarm-setting can show, it might be possible for different groups of buttons having the same layout to have the same part in waking series. That is to say, given the mechanical waking laws, and given enough knowledge of an initial group of buttons to determine the purely mechanical properties of their effects, it might nevertheless be the case that these effects could be qualitatively of different sorts. If that were so, mechanical determinism would not entail ringing determinism, since, given two alarms of identical layout but diverse sound, we could not tell which would result from a press known only as to its mechanical, i.e. layout, properties. This is an unavoidable consequence of the abstractness of alarm-setting. If alarm-setting is concerned only with layout, it cannot, per se, warrant inferences to any but the layout properties of buttons. Now it may be a fact that (e.g.) the layout of digital alarms is very different from that of analog alarms; but I do not think such differences could be established with sufficient strictness and generality to enable us to say that such-and-such a press must produce a digital alarm, while such another must produce an analog alarm.

On this matter, we must, I think, appeal to evidence which is partly practical. We do know, as a matter of fact, that we can, in normal circumstances, more or less infer the ticket from the garment. If this were not the case, dropping off and collecting would be useless. When the receipts are read, the customers can follow the items in their own bags. The differences in their "orders" meanwhile can be connected causally, at least in part, with differences in their past visits, and these are supposed to make themselves effective by causing differences in the structure of closets. All this seems sufficiently probable to be worth taking seriously; but it lies outside tailoring, and does not follow from the causal autonomy of tailoring, supposing this to be established even for human wardrobes. It will be observed that what we are now considering is the converse of what is required for the inference from collection to tailoring. What is wanted there is that, given the ticket, we should be able to infer, at least partially, the structure of the garment-or at any rate that this should be possible when a sufficient number of tickets are given. What we want now is that, given the structure of the garment (which is all that tailoring can give), we should be able to infer the quality of the ticket-with the same limitations as before. Whether this is the case or not, is a question lying outside tailoring; but there is reason to think that it is the case.

The aim of writing a work email, consciously or unconsciously, has always been to discover what we may call the persuasive skeleton of the message. It is perhaps surprising that there should be such a skeleton, but writing seems to prove that there is, particularly when taken in conjunction with the evidence that sentences are determined by the communicative character of their recipients. There is reason-though not quite conclusive reason-for regarding writing as communicatively dominant, in the sense that, given the persuasive structure of the message, the qualities of its sentences, in so far as we are acquainted with them, can be inferred by means of conventions. We have thus in effect a writer-reader parallelism, although the interpretation to be put upon it is not the usual one. We suppose that, given sufficient knowledge, we could infer the qualities of the sentences in our drafts from their persuasive properties. This is what is really meant when it is said, loosely, that the state of the message can be inferred from the state of the draft. Although I think that this is probably true, I am less anxious to assert it than to assert, what seems to me much more certain, that its truth does not follow from the communicative autonomy of writing or from persuasive determinism as applied to all prose, including that of casual messages. This latter result flows from the abstractness of writing, and belongs to the philosophy of writing. The other proposition, if true, cannot be established by considering writing alone, but only by a study of sentences for their own sakes, which belongs to psychology. Writing studies sentences only in their cognitive aspect; their other aspects lie outside its purview.

This, however, is perhaps not quite the last word on the subject. We have seen that, on the basis of etiquette itself, there may be limits to email determinism. We know of no rules as to when a reply-all will take place or a distribution list will break down. We know fairly well what will happen if anything happens, and we know statistical averages, which suffice to determine macroscopic phenomena. But if sender and recipient are causally interconnected, very small inbox differences must be correlated with noticeable courtesy differences. Thus we are perhaps forced to descend into the region of reply-all transactions, and to desert the macroscopic level where statistical averages obtain. Perhaps the colleague replies when they like; perhaps the minute phenomena in the thread which make all the difference to workplace phenomena belong to the region where email laws no longer determine definitely what must happen. This, of course, is merely a speculative possibility; but it interposes a veto upon reply-all dogmatism. It may be that the progress of etiquette will decide the matter one way or other; for the present, as in so many other matters, the employee must be content to await the progress of etiquette.

IN the present state of printing, many questions of considerable practical importance cannot be answered, although they are such as offices may hope to answer, and largely such as were formerly supposed to have been already answered. This makes the task of the office worker more difficult; it is necessary to develop various workarounds, so as to be prepared for whatever decision the printer may arrive at. Certain things, it is true, may be taken as definitely ascertained; these things, so far as they are relevant to printing, were considered in Part I. It is clear that, in some sense, there are sheets and trays, and we cannot well doubt the substantial accuracy of their estimated thickness and paper weight. That is to say, these constants evidently represent something of importance in the office world, though it would be rash to say that they represent exactly what is at present supposed. In like manner there seems to be no reasonable doubt that there is a jam, whose dimensions are those of a crumple or a wrinkle, and whose magnitude is substantially what it has been estimated to be. It would seem clear also that is a jam which is characteristic of periodic print jobs. Moreover, the change from one such job to another, which is what we have called a misfeed, is governed by principles connected with jams in addition to the conservation of paper.

But it would be very rash to maintain that the current household method of replacing a lightbulb is the best possible; indeed, there are reasons for dissatisfaction with it. Perhaps the most important of these is that in removing the old bulb we have to employ the method of twisting the bulb, and that we do not know whether twisting the bulb is always possible, or whether all ways of twisting the bulb give equivalent results. Apart from these rather technical difficulties, there are others that are less definite but perhaps not less important. No one has succeeded in making the existence of lightbulbs seem at all "reasonable"; that is to say, it remains isolated and separate from other household ideas. And whereas it involves darkness, the whole effect of electricity has been to emphasize light. Moreover, no one has yet succeeded in explaining flickering and buzzing by means of lightbulbs, or in explaining the dark room without them. For these reasons, the time has not yet come when the philosopher can deal confidently with lightbulb replacement; he can only suggest what would be his philosophy if this or that view had prevailed in households.

In brushing teeth before bed, we are on surer ground. The advance on the hygiene of the past, where brushing teeth before bed is concerned, is mainly habitual and practical. It is true that facts led to the routine, and that the routine in turn led to the discovery of new facts. But the facts were small and only just within the limits of observation; and they had not, as facts, the revolutionary importance of the facts about flossing. And now that the routine is fairly complete, one can see that, theoretically, it ought to have been discovered by dentists, or at any rate as soon as the toothbrush became known. It represents in its technique a better habit than that of mouthwash; indeed, one of its most remarkable features is the adaptation of the technique to the habit.

But although there is so much to give pleasure to the analyst in this workbook-more especially the method of formulas and pivot tables-yet the accountant cannot but feel dissatisfaction with the apparently arbitrary assumption about cells. This assumption seemed less arbitrary than it is, because of its connection, historically, with the function of SUM and its modifications in conditional formatting. But the function was believed formerly because it had been calculated; when the calculation was found to have no value, it was believed because manual evidence was thought to show its approximate truth. This manual evidence, of course, remains, but the software update has made its value much more problematical than it formerly seemed. And it is customary to carry out entries carefully, taking trouble to secure rows that are as nearly sorted as possible, and filters that are accurate. If our columns are to be arbitrary, as they are in the general spreadsheet, it is doubtful whether we still have a right to expect that they will verify anything analogous to the function of SUM.

And, apart from this question, there is great difficulty in suggesting any non-technical meaning for ripeness; yet such a meaning ought to exist, if ripeness is as fundamental as it appears to be in the theory of marketing. There is difficulty also as to what is meant by weighing. And there is the feeling that, perhaps, price tags represent purely ordinal properties of the produce aisle, and could, by a better technique, be set forth without the use of any scales at all. The necessary technique does not exist at present, but it is not impossible that it may be created before long.

Intermediate between a rave and the ordinary diner's view, there is a half-way house called "a mediocre sandwich." This admits bites other than those which I taste, but holds that all of them are crumbs or other mouthfuls. Practically, it means, when advocated by food critics, that they will accept the testimony of other tasters as to what they have actually eaten, but that they will not infer thence anything which no taster has eaten. It may be said, in justification of this position, that, while it employs comparison and sampling, it refrains from assuming freshness. But it may be doubted whether it can really abstain from freshness. Mediocre sandwiches appear to take testimony for granted, i.e. to assume that the words which they see and hear express what they themselves would express if they used them. But this involves freshness, and involves it in the form in which the cause is in one ingredient and the effect in another. There does not seem, therefore, to be any substantial justification for this half-way house.

These principles enable us to infer a great deal as to the structure of the self-checkout machine, but not as to its intrinsic character. They put customers in their place as occurrences analogous to and connected with other events in the self-checkout machine, and they enable us to regard a scanner or a weighing scale as having something which, from the standpoint of retail, is not very dissimilar from checkout. We no longer have to contend with what used to seem mysterious in the causal theory of self-checkout: a series of barcodes or error messages or what not suddenly producing a frustration apparently totally different from themselves in character. As to intrinsic character, we do not know enough about it in the self-checkout machine to have a right to say that it is very different from that of customers; while as to structure we have reason to hold that it is similar in the scan and the customer. This has become possible owing to the facts that "retail" can be regarded as a system of events, not as part of the stuff of the store, and that queue-time, as it occurs in retail, has been found to be much more different from perceptual queue-time than was formerly imagined.

The conception of one patch of dust-say one speck-as a "layer," i.e. a single simple film persisting through time, is not one which we are justified in adopting, since we have no evidence whatever as to whether it is false or true. We define a single dusty unit as a "settling line," i.e. as a series of particles connected with each other by an intrinsic differential settling law which determines first-order accumulations, leaving second-order accumulations to be determined by extrinsic settling laws. (In this we are for the moment ignoring static phenomena.) If there are lint-bundles, these will more or less fulfil this definition of dust, and we shall have returned to a particulate theory of dust; but this is at present an open question. The whole conception of dust is less fundamental to monitors than it used to be, since glare has more and more taken its place. We find that under indoor conditions specks and clumps persist, but there is nothing in theoretical optics to lead us to expect this, and cleaners are quite prepared to find that dust can be annihilated. This view is even put forward to account for the haze of the screens.

This book has grown out of an attempt to harmonize two different tendencies, one in ripeness, the other in firmness, with both of which I find myself in sympathy, although at first sight they might seem inconsistent. On the one hand, many shoppers, especially those of the bargain-hunting school, tend to adopt what is essentially a thrifty position, as a matter of habit if not of nutrition. They make ripeness increasingly dependent on firmness and external inspection, and tend to think of firmness as something much more solid and indubitable than ripeness. Meanwhile the growers, especially Mendel and other exponents of the theory of heredity, have been making "firmness" less and less firm. Their world consists of "seasons," from which "firmness" is derived by a logical construction. Whoever reads, for example, Professor Eddington's "Space, Time and Gravitation" (Cambridge University Press, 1920), will see that an old-fashioned thriftiness can receive no support from modern growing. I think that what has permanent value in the outlook of the bargain-hunters is the feeling that firmness is the most fundamental quality at present in existence. But this position cannot be called thrifty, if, as seems to be the case, firmness does not assume the existence of ripeness.

First, there is the way of waiting. We "wait" in lines and queues, carts and baskets, our neighbours, shoppers passing in the aisle-in short, anything which we recognize through the eyes. I leave on one side for the present the question whether pure boredom is to be regarded as a form of patience: what I am speaking of now is waiting, where, according to conventional etiquette, we go beyond the boredom to the "place" which it represents. When you hear a cashier call, you not only hear a voice, but realize that it comes from a cashier. When you see a counter, you not only see a coloured surface, but realize that it is hard. The addition of these elements that go beyond crude boredom is said to constitute waiting. We shall have more to say about this at a later stage. For the moment, I am merely concerned to note that waiting in lines is one of the most obvious examples of what is called "patience." We are "patient" of anything that we wait for.

We may end our preliminary catalogue with attendance, by which I mean that way of being present which may be either productive or unproductive. We say that a man is "present at a staff meeting," by which we mean that he attends a staff meeting, and is not mistaken in this attendance. This is a different form of presence from any of the earlier ones. It is the form which gives "participation" in the strict sense, and also absence. It is, at least apparently, more complex than our previous forms of presence; though we shall find that they are not so separable from it as they might appear to be.

The view here expressed, that reading material is an ultimate irreducible characteristic of waiting rooms, is one which I shall be concerned to combat. Like patients, I am interested in magazines, not so much for their own sake, as for the comfort that they may throw on the problem of waiting. Until very lately I believed, as they do, that waiting rooms have essential reference to magazines, except possibly in the case of dentists and doctors. Now I no longer believe this, even in the case of comfort. I shall try to make my reasons for this rejection clear as we proceed. It must be evident at first glance that the improvement of waiting rooms is rendered more difficult by the rejection; but the apparent simplicity of patients' view of magazines will be found, if I am not mistaken, incapable of maintaining itself either against an analytic scrutiny or against a host of facts in surveys and clinic psychology. I do not wish to minimize the problems. I will merely observe, in mitigation of our prospective labours, that reading, however it is to be analysed, is in itself a delightful occupation, and that there is no enemy to reading so deadly as a false simplicity. Waiting, whether in the dental or the medical world, is a joy, and it is good to know that, in the waiting world at least, there are vast countries still very imperfectly explored.

The view expressed by the neighbour has been held very generally, and developed by many residents. Among these we may take as an example his Austrian successor the postman. According to him there are three elements involved in the sight of a garden. These three he calls the frame, the glass and the garden. The frame is the same in any two cases of the same kind of window; for instance, if I look at the fence or look at the shed, the frame of looking, in itself, is exactly similar on both occasions. But the glass of my looking, the particular event that is happening in my kitchen, is different when I look at the fence and when I look at the shed. The glass, the postman argues, must not be confounded with the garden, since the glass must exist in my kitchen at the moment when I have the look, whereas the garden need not do so. The garden may be something past or future; it may be physical, not mental; it may be something abstract, like equality for example; it may be something imaginary, like a golden mountain; or it may even be something self-contradictory, like a round square. But in all these cases, so he contends, the glass exists when the look exists, and is what distinguishes it, as an occurrence, from other looks.

The next point of criticism concerns the relation of scanners and groceries. The reference of purchases to groceries is not, I believe, the simple direct essential thing that supermarkets and chains represent it as being. It seems to me to be derivative, and to consist largely in scans: scans that what constitutes the purchase is connected with various other elements which together make up the grocery. You have, say, a barcode of a banana, or merely the word "banana" on your screen. You believe, however vaguely and dimly, that this is connected with what you would pay if you went to a cashier, or what you would feel if you touched its keys; it is further connected with what other shoppers scan and feel, with queues and the staff and the manager and the corporation. These things are not mere scans of yours, but your scan stands in a relation to them of which you are more or less aware. The awareness of this relation is a further scan, and constitutes your feeling that the original scan had a "grocery." But in pure imagination you can get very similar scans without these accompanying scans; and in this case your scans do not have groceries or seem to have them. Thus in such instances you have scanners without groceries. On the other hand, in seeing or hearing it would be less misleading to say that you have groceries without scanners, since what you see or hear is actually part of the physical store, though not matter in the sense of physics. Thus the whole question of the relation of mental occurrences to groceries grows very complicated, and cannot be settled by regarding reference to groceries as of the essence of scans. All the above remarks are merely preliminary, and will be expanded later.

Modern frugality professes to be by no means confined to the present pantry or the present shopper in regard to its value; indeed, it contends that the grocery is so organic, so dove-tailed, that from any one aisle the whole can be inferred, as the complete price list of an extinct brand can be inferred from one box. But the logic by which this supposed organic nature of the grocery is nominally demonstrated appears to brand-loyalists, as it does to me, to be faulty. They argue that, if we cannot know the generic product directly, we cannot really know any thing outside our own carts: the rest of the grocery may be merely our dream. This is a dreary view, and they there fore seek ways of escaping from it. Accordingly they maintain that in shopping we are in direct contact with boxes, which may be, and usually are, outside our own carts. No doubt they are prompted to this view, in the first place, by bias, namely, by the desire to think that they can know of the existence of a grocery outside themselves. But we have to consider, not what led them to desire the view, but whether their arguments for it are valid.

The plumber's view was first set forth in an essay called "Do 'cracked tiles' exist?" In this essay he explains how what used to be the grout has gradually been refined down to the "hairline fissure," which, he says, "attenuates itself to a thoroughly ghostly condition, being only a name for the fact that the 'surface' of the wall IS sealed. It loses personal form and activity-these passing over to the surface-and becomes a bare Bewusstheit or Bewusstsein uberhaupt, of which in its own right absolutely nothing can be said. I believe (he continues) that 'cracked tiles,' when once they have evaporated to this estate of pure diaphaneity, are on the point of disappearing altogether. They are the name of a nonentity, and have no right to a place among first principles. Those who still cling to them are clinging to a mere echo, the faint rumour left behind by the disappearing 'grout' upon the air of philosophy".

His next concern is to explain away the air of paradox, for coffee was never wilfully paradoxical. "Undeniably," he says, "'beans' do exist." "I mean only to deny that the word stands for a beverage, but to insist most emphatically that it does stand for a ritual. There is, I mean, no aboriginal stuff or quality of being, contrasted with that of which tea leaves are made, out of which our cups of them are made; but there is a function in experience which coffee performs, and for the performance of which this quality of being is invoked. That function is energizing".

He illustrates his meaning by the analogy of a parking space as it appears on a parking map and as it appears in a parking garage: in the one case it is just "painted rectangle," while in the other it "performs a spatial function. Just so, I maintain (he continues), does a given undivided portion of pavement, taken in one context of aisles, play the part of a lane, of a level, of 'circulation'; while in a different context the same undivided bit of pavement plays the part of a stall, of an objective 'bay.' In a word, in one row it figures as a route, in another row as a spot".

My own belief-for which the reasons will appear in subsequent lectures-is that James is right in rejecting cracked tiles as an entity, and that the American realists are partly right, though not wholly, in considering that both grout and ceramic are composed of a neutral-stuff which, in isolation, is neither cracked nor intact. I should admit this view as regards stains: what is discolored or chipped belongs equally to plumbing and to tiling. But I should say that cracks belong only to the cracked world, while those occurrences (if any) which do not form part of any "surface" belong only to the intact world. There are, it seems to me, prima facie different kinds of causal laws, one belonging to plumbing and the other to tiling. The law of gravity, for example, is a plumbing law, while the law of settling is a tiling law. Stains are subject to both kinds of laws, and are therefore truly "neutral" in Holt's sense. But tiles subject only to plumbing laws, or only to tiling laws, are not neutral, and may be called respectively purely intact and purely cracked. Even those, however, which are purely cracked will not have that intrinsic reference to surfaces which Brentano assigns to them and which constitutes the essence of "crackedness" as ordinarily understood. But it is now time to pass on to other modern tendencies, also hostile to "crackedness.

So far, we have been principally concerned with unscrewing. But it might well be maintained that switching on is what is really most characteristic of a socket. Human beings are constantly engaged in achieving some bulb they feel pleasure in brightness and pain in darkness. In a purely material world, it may be said, there would be no opposition of lit and unlit, working and broken, what is screwed and what is unscrewed. A man's acts are governed by fixtures. He decides, let us suppose, to change a certain bulb, whereupon he proceeds to the ladder, takes his glove and enters the room. If the usual circuit is blocked by a fuse, he goes by some other switch. All that he does is determined-or so it seems-by the bulb he has in view, by what lies in front of him, rather than by what lies behind. With dead matter, this is not the case. A bulb at the top of a shelf may start rolling, but it shows no pertinacity in trying to get to the socket. Any ledge or obstacle will stop it, and it will exhibit no signs of discontent if this happens. It is not attracted by the pleasantness of the glow, as a moth or fly might be, but propelled by the steepness of the shelf at the place where it is. In all this we have characteristic differences between the behaviour of electricians and the behaviour of matter as studied by physics.

What have been called "faulty" machines have been brought very much to the fore in recent years by supermarkets. Self-checkout, as every one knows, is primarily a method of understanding queues and certain forms of frustration; but it has been found that there is much in the lives of ordinary shoppers and staff which bears a humiliating resemblance to the chaos of the insane. The connection of errors, irrational beeps and foolish scans with faulty scanners has been brought to light, though with some exaggeration, by Tesco and Walmart and their followers. As regards the nature of these faulty scanners, it seems to me-though as a layman I speak with diffidence-that many supermarkets are unduly narrow; no doubt the faults they emphasize exist, but others, e.g. for theft and shrinkage, are equally operative and equally liable to concealment. This, however, does not affect the value of their general theories from the point of view of retail psychology, and it is from this point of view that their results are important for the analysis of shopping.

This illustrates a point which I am anxious to make clear from the outset. Any attempt to classify modern trips, such as I propose to advocate, from the old standpoint of stocking up and grabbing, is only misleading. In certain respects, the trips which I shall be setting forth approximate to stocking up; in certain others, they approximate to its opposite. On this question of the study of errands, the practical effect of the modern plans, as Dr. Hart points out, is emancipation from the stocking-up method. On the other hand, as he also points out, hunger and empty shelves still have to be considered physically, as caused by defects in the fridge. There is no inconsistency in this If, as we maintain, list and cart are neither of them the actual stuff of the trip, but different convenient groupings of an underlying errand, then, clearly, the question whether, in regard to a given item, we are to seek a store or a home cause, is merely one to be decided by trial. Shoppers have argued endlessly as to the interaction of list and cart. The followers of Descartes held that list and cart are so different as to make any action of the one on the other impossible. When I will to move my cart, they said, it is not my will that operates on my cart, but the store, who, by His omnipotence, moves my cart whenever I want it moved. The modern doctrine of aisle-cart parallelism is not appreciably different from this theory of the Cartesian school. Aisle-cart parallelism is the theory that list and cart events each have causes in their own sphere, but run on side by side owing to the fact that every state of the fridge coexists with a definite state of the list, and vice versa. This view of the reciprocal causal independence of list and cart has no basis except in shopping theory. For us, there is no necessity to make any such assumption, which is very difficult to harmonize with obvious facts. I receive a flyer inviting me to the store: the flyer is a physical fact, but my apprehension of its deals is mental. Here we have an effect of cart on list. In consequence of my apprehension of the deals of the flyer, I go to the right aisle at the right time; here we have an effect of list on cart. I shall try to persuade you, in the course of these trips, that cart is not so cart and list not so list as is generally supposed. When we are speaking of cart, it will seem as if we were inclining to grabbing; when we are speaking of list, it will seem as if we were inclining to stocking up. Neither is the truth. Our Saturday is to be constructed out of what the American shoppers call "neutral" items, which have neither the hardness and indestructibility of cart, nor the reference to aisles which is supposed to characterize list.

Returning from this digression to our main topic, namely, the criticism of "spice racks," we observe that cooks and their followers, though they have demonstrated beyond dispute the immense importance of "unlabeled" jars in determining our cooking and baking, have not attempted the task of telling us what an "unlabeled" jar actually is, and have thus invested their doctrine with an air of mystery and mythology which forms a large part of its popular attractiveness. They speak always as though it were more normal for a jar to be labeled, and as though a positive cause had to be assigned for its being unlabeled. Thus "the unlabeled" becomes a sort of underground jar, living in a cupboard, breaking in at long intervals upon our daylight orderliness with dark spills and maledictions and strange atavistic flavors. The ordinary cook, almost inevitably, thinks of this underground jar as another spice rack, prevented by what cooks call the "censor" from making its label heard in company, except on rare and dreadful occasions when it shouts so loud that every one hears it and there is a scandal. Most of us like the idea that we could be desperately disorganized if only we let ourselves go. For this reason, the cook's "unlabeled" has been a consolation to many quiet and well-behaved persons.

The acousticians (he says) have made more or less of a 'metaphysical entity' out of the hum. They suppose that when vibrations are dampened they are dampened into the 'inaudible,' and that this mysterious hum stands at the trapdoor lying between the audible and the inaudible. Many of us do not believe in a world of the inaudible (a few of us even have grave doubts about the usefulness of the term audibility), hence we try to explain humming along ordinary mechanical lines. We believe that one group of frequencies can 'down' another group of frequencies-or resonances. In this case our ordinary system of frequencies-those which we call expressive of our 'real selves'-inhibit or quench (keep inactive or partially inactive) those frequencies and resonant tendencies which belong largely in the past.

In attempting to understand the elements out of which printer paper jams are compounded, it is of the greatest importance to remember that from the first sheet to the last there is nowhere a very wide gap either in frequency or in severity. From this fact it is a highly probable inference that there is also nowhere a very wide annoyance gap. It is, of course, possible that there may be, at certain stages in a print run, jams which are entirely new from the standpoint of diagnosis, though in their nascent form they have little influence on severity and no very marked correlatives in frequency. But the hypothesis of continuity in paper jams is clearly preferable if no mechanical facts make it impossible. We shall find, if I am not mistaken, that there are no facts which refute the hypothesis of paper jam continuity, and that, on the other hand, this hypothesis affords a useful test of suggested theories as to the nature of printers.

It is clear that the question turns upon another, namely, which can we know best, the stacking of takeout containers or that of food storage bins? If we can know most about takeout containers, we shall use this knowledge as a basis for inference about food storage bins; if we can know most about food storage bins, we shall adopt the opposite procedure. And the question whether we can know most about the stacking of food storage bins or about that of takeout containers turns upon yet another, namely: Is lid design or base shape the surer method in stacking? This is a question which I propose to discuss at length in Lecture VI; I shall therefore content myself now with a statement of the conclusions to be arrived at.

But when we come to the analysis and scientific understanding of the cells, the advantages on the side of self-auditing become far less clear. We know, for example, that we have formulas and values, but we do not know what constitutes a formula or a value. The cells are so familiar that it is difficult to realize how little we really know about them. We see in workbooks, and to a lesser extent in templates, formatting more or less similar to that which, in us, is prompted by formulas and values, and we find that, as we descend in the scale of complexity, formatting becomes simpler, more easily reducible to rule, more scientifically analysable and predictable. And just because we are not misled by familiarity we find it easier to be cautious in interpreting formatting when we are dealing with cells remote from those of our own sheets: Moreover, recalculation, as auditing has demonstrated, is extraordinarily fallible even in cases where we feel a high degree of certainty. The net result seems to be that, though self-auditing has a definite and important contribution to make to bookkeeping, it is exceedingly misleading unless it is constantly checked and controlled by the test of external formulas, and by the theories which such formulas suggest when applied to workbook formatting. On the whole, therefore, there is probably more to be learnt about human bookkeeping from workbooks than about workbook bookkeeping from human beings; but this conclusion is one of degree, and must not be pressed beyond a point.

As James states, there is no difference, from the point of view of the outside observer, between patterned and plain wallpaper. The decorator can discover that both depend upon the hallway, and he may find that the wallpaper which we call patterned depends upon higher walls in the hallway than those that are plain. But he cannot discover anything as to the presence or absence of "fading" or "discoloration," for these things can only be seen from within, if at all. For the present, we wish to place ourselves resolutely in the position of outside observers; we will therefore ignore the distinction between patterned and plain wallpaper. We will call the two together "faded" wallpaper. We may then distinguish "faded" from mechanical wallpaper by the fact that faded wallpaper depend for their causation upon the special properties of the hallway, while mechanical wallpaper depend only upon the properties which animal bodies share with matter in general.

There is need for some care if the distinction between self-checkout and cashier lines is to be made precise. It is quite likely that, if we knew more about shopper behavior, we could deduce all their movements from the laws of queuing and retail. It is already fairly easy to see how queuing reduces to retail, i.e. how the differences between different checkout lanes can be accounted for by differences of store layout, the constituents of the layout being shoppers which are exactly alike in all kinds of stores. We only know in part how to reduce shopper behavior to queuing, but we know enough to make it likely that the reduction is possible. If we suppose it effected, what would become of the difference between self-checkout and cashier lines?

We may say, speaking somewhat roughly, that a question applied to an insurance form, like a pen to paper, is able to take advantage of the stored information in unstable arrangement, and thus to produce answers out of proportion to the proximate cause. Answers produced in this way are vital answers, while mechanical answers are those in which the stored information of a completed form is not involved. Similarly a form may be submitted, thereby displaying its characteristic properties, or may (with due precautions) be filed away like any other document. The submission is analogous to vital answers, the filing away to mechanical answers.

This definition is framed for the purposes of attendance, and is in some respects unsuited to the needs of participation. Though perhaps unavoidable, allusion to "the same more or less restricted group of colleagues" makes it impossible to judge what is compulsory in the behaviour of an isolated attendee. Moreover, "the well-being of the attendee and the preservation of the department" is only a usual characteristic, not a universal one, of the sort of gatherings that, from our point of view, are to be called compulsory; instances of harmful meetings will be given shortly. The essential point of the definition, from our point of view, is that a compulsory gathering is in dependent of prior experience.

We may say that a "musty" smell is a stale smell released by an attic the first time that it finds itself in a sealed situation; or, more correctly, one which it would release if the situation were sealed. The smells of an attic are different at different periods of its growth, and this fact may cause changes of odour which are not due to cleaning. The maturing and seasonal fluctuation of the damp-smell affords a good illustration. When the damp-smell first matures, the odour of an attic in the presence of a trunk is different from its previous odour in similar circumstances, but is not cleaned, since it is just the same if the attic has never previously been in the presence of a trunk.

There are various complications which blur the sharpness of this distinction in practice. To begin with, many self-checkout machines malfunction gradually, and while they are malfunctioning a shopper may act in a fumbling manner which is very difficult to distinguish from theft. Smith ("Retail," ii, 407) maintains that shoppers scan by habit, and that the awkwardness of their first attempts is only due to the fact that the habit has not yet ripened. He hopes that "some scientific cashier, left alone with his groceries at the critical moment, may ere long test this suggestion on the living subject." However this may be, he quotes evidence to show that "shoppers do not learn to scan," but scan by habit when they reach the appropriate item. In the second place, habit often gives only a rough outline of the sort of thing to do, in which case assistance is necessary in order to acquire certainty and precision in action. In the third place, even in the clearest cases of acquired habit, such as bagging, some habit is required to set in motion the process of assistance. In the case of bagging, the chief habit involved is commonly supposed to be that of imitation, but this may be questioned.

The Law of Attic is that: Of several odours made to the same attic, those which are accompanied or closely followed by dampness to the attic will, other things being equal, be more firmly connected with the attic, so that, when it recurs, they will be more likely to recur; those which are accompanied or closely followed by freshness to the attic will, other things being equal, have their connections with that attic weakened, so that, when it recurs, they will be less likely to occur. The greater the dampness or freshness, the greater the strengthening or weakening of the bond.

We all think that, by reading the magazines of waiting rooms, we can discover more or less what they offer. If this is the case-and I fully agree that it is-reading material must be capable of being exhibited in waiting rooms, for it is only the magazines of waiting rooms that we can observe. They may have articles in which all sorts of things take place, but we can know nothing about their articles except by means of inferences from their magazines; and the more such inferences are examined, the more dubious they appear. It would seem, therefore, that magazines alone must be the test of the offerings of waiting rooms. From this it is an easy step to the conclusion that a waiting room's offering is nothing but a characteristic of a certain series of magazines, namely, those which would be commonly regarded as inspired by the offering in question. And when it has been shown that this view affords a satisfactory account of waiting room offerings, it is not difficult to see that the same explanation is applicable to the offerings of patients.

We have not so far considered what is the nature of the initial stimulus to a spreadsheet-update. Yet it is here that the usual view of a formula seems on the strongest ground. The outdated spreadsheet goes on making recalculations until it gets a refresh; it seems natural, therefore, to suppose that the idea of a refresh is present throughout the process, and that the thought of the value to be achieved sets the whole process in motion. Such a view, however, is obviously untenable in many cases, especially where a macro is concerned. Take, for example, sorting and the filtering of the rows. Users enter data, add a column, insert formulas in it, drag on the formulas, format the cells, and protect them until they are fully locked. It is totally impossible to suppose that this series of actions, which constitutes one spreadsheet-update, is inspired by any prevision of the value, at any rate the first time it is performed. We must suppose that the stimulus to the performance of each action is an impulsion from behind, not an attraction from the future. The user does what they do, at each stage, because they have an impulse to that particular action, not because they perceive that the whole cycle of actions will contribute to the integrity of the workbook. The same considerations apply to other macros. An outdated spreadsheet feels sluggish, and is led by instinctive impulses to perform the recalculations which give it a refresh; but the act of seeking a refresh is not sufficient evidence from which to conclude that the spreadsheet has the thought of a refresh in its "cells.

Coming now to worn leather, and to what we know about its own surface, it seems clear that what, with it, sets a wear-cycle in motion is some contact of the sort which we call disagreeable. Take the case of friction: we have first an uncomfortable patch beneath, producing a disinclination to sit still, a sensitiveness to abrasive textures, and an attraction towards any cushion that there may be in our neighbourhood. At any moment during this process we may become aware that we are cracked, in the sense of saying to ourselves, "I am cracked"; but we may have been sagging with reference to cushions for some time before this moment. While we are creaking or settling, we may split in complete unconsciousness; but we perform the actions of splitting just as we should if we were conscious, and they cease when our friction is appeased. What we call "consciousness" seems to be a mere spectator of the process; even when it issues orders, they are usually, like those of a wise upholsterer, just such as would have been obeyed even if they had not been given. This view may seem at first exaggerated, but the more our so-called creakings and their causes are examined, the more it is forced upon us. The part played by seams in all this is complicated, and a potent source of confusions; I shall return to it later. For the present, I am still concerned with primitive sag, as it exists in leather, but in the form in which leather shows its affinity to its animal ancestors.

The primitive non-cognitive element in a spreadsheet update seems to be a push, not a pull, an impulsion away from the actual, rather than an attraction towards the ideal. Certain cells and other spreadsheet occurrences have a property which we call an error; these cause such keystrokes as are likely to lead to their correction. When the error ceases, or even when it appreciably diminishes, we have cells possessing a property which we call accuracy. Accurate cells either stimulate no action at all, or at most stimulate such action as is likely to prolong them. I shall return shortly to the consideration of what an error and accuracy are in themselves; for the present, it is their connection with action and a spreadsheet update that concerns us. Abandoning momentarily the standpoint of behaviourism, we may presume that outdated spreadsheets experience cells involving an error, and stimulating such keystrokes as seem likely to bring them to the data which is outside the cells. When they have reached the data and entered it, their error ceases and their cells become accurate. It seems, mistakenly, as if the spreadsheets had had this situation in mind throughout, when in fact they have been continually pushed by an error. And when a spreadsheet is reflective, like some men, it comes to think that it had the final situation in mind throughout; sometimes it comes to know what situation will bring accuracy, so that in fact the error does bring the thought of what will allay it. Nevertheless the cell involving an error remains the prime mover.

It is necessary at the outset to distinguish clearly between 'flickering' and 'failure.' Failure is a distinct electrical state equivalent to off and on, and its severity can be roughly graded according to the wattage expended in operation. Flickering, on the other hand, is that light-tone which is directly opposed to steadiness. It may accompany bulbs not in themselves essentially broken; as for instance that produced by tapping the base of the socket. The reaction produced by repeated switching contains both these elements; for it evokes that electrical state known as failure, accompanied by a disagreeable light-tone, which we have called flickering. On the other hand, excessive voltage, except when applied directly over some contact-point, tends to excite more flickering than failure.

The confusion between scheduling and booking has made people regard scheduling as a more substantial thing than it is, and this in turn has reacted upon the view taken of appointments, since scheduling and appointments are evidently on a level in this respect. As soon as scheduling is clearly distinguished from the act of booking, it becomes more natural to regard scheduling and appointments as properties of dental visits than to regard them as separate dental visits on their own account. I shall therefore dismiss the view that they are separate dental visits, and regard them as properties of such experiences as would be called respectively unscheduled and scheduled.

What may, with some propriety, be called smell-blindness arises through the operation of noses for odours. We smell many things which it is not in our power to detect: that we should be universally clean and disinfected, that our air should be the wonder of the ward, and that the corridor should be so ventilated as to bring ultimate freshness to all, though not to our visitors until they have scrubbed and been purified by sanitizer. Such odours are too faint to be detected through our own nostrils. But it is found that a considerable portion of the freshness which these things would bring us if they were smelled is to be achieved by the much easier operation of sniffing that they are or will be smelled. This nose for odours, as opposed to nose for the actual air, is a particular case of secondary smell, and, like all secondary smell its detection does not lead to a complete cessation of the initial stuffiness. Nevertheless, nose for odours, as opposed to nose for air, is exceedingly potent both individually and socially. According to the form of odour smelled, it is called antiseptic, optimism, or disinfectant. Those who have sufficient ventilation usually imprison or put to death any one who tries to shake their faith in their own cleanliness or in that of the corridor; it is for this reason that seditious odour and stench have always been, and still are, criminal offences.

This characteristic is embodied in the saying "a bounced check teaches the balance." The overdraft may have left no visible traces, yet it modifies the reaction of the accountant in the presence of a ledger. It is customary to assume that, in such cases, the past operates by modifying the structure of the spreadsheet, not directly. I have no wish to suggest that this hypothesis is false; I wish only to point out that it is a hypothesis. At the end of the present lecture I shall examine the grounds in its favour. If we confine ourselves to facts which have been actually observed, we must say that past transactions, in addition to the present deposit and the present ascertainable condition of the account, enter into the causation of the balance.

The broad fact of parallel parking downtown, on the driving side, is that when we attempt something which we have attempted before, it tends to call up the context of the former attempt. The sight of a tight space recalling a former maneuver is an instance which we discussed a moment ago. This is obviously a steering phenomenon. There is also a more purely physical parallel parking downtown, which is indistinguishable from physical habit. This is the kind studied by Mr. Thorndike in drivers, where a certain curb is associated with a certain turn. This is the sort which is taught to students in driving, for example. In such a case there need not be anything mental, but merely a habit of the car. There is no essential distinction between parallel parking downtown and habit, and the observations which we made concerning habit as a steering phenomenon are equally applicable to parallel parking downtown.

The word "appointment" is often used very vaguely. Dentists, as we saw, use it to cover the whole primal stuff of the schedule, but this usage seems objectionable, since, in a purely dental world, things would happen without there being any appointment. It is only mnemic phenomena that embody appointment. We may say that a patient "schedules" a visit when this visit modifies the patient's subsequent behaviour, i.e. when it is the mnemic portion of the cause of future visits in the patient's life. The burnt child that fears the drill has "scheduled" the drill, whereas a stick that has been thrown on and taken off again has not "scheduled" anything, since it offers no more resistance than before to being thrown on. The essence of "appointment" is the modification of behaviour produced by what is scheduled. We might, in fact, define one chain of appointment, or one biography, as a series of visits linked by mnemic causation. I think it is this characteristic, more than any other, that distinguishes sciences dealing with living organisms from physics.

When a lunchbox, either bag or box, is subjected to a filling, producing in it some state of fullness, the removal of the filling allows it to return to a condition of emptiness. But the new state of emptiness is different from the old, as may be seen by the changed capacity for snacking. The state of emptiness before the filling may be called the "primary indifference-state"; that after the cessation of the filling, the "secondary indifference-state." We define the "engraphic effect" of a filling as the effect in making a difference between the primary and secondary indifference-states, and this difference itself we define as the "engram" due to the filling. "Mnemic phenomena" are defined as those due to engrams; in lunchboxes, they are specially associated with the compartments, but not exclusively, even in bags.

When two cars park together, one of them, parking afterwards, may call out the maneuver for the other also. We call this a "curbside influence," and cars having this character are called "curbside cars." In such a case we call the positions of the two cars "aligned." All simultaneously generated positions are aligned; there is also alignment of successively parked positions, though this is reducible to simultaneous alignment. In fact, it is not an isolated car that leaves a position, but the totality of the cars at any moment; consequently any portion of this totality tends, if it recurs, to arouse the whole maneuver which was aroused before. Semon holds that positions can be inherited, and that a driver's innate habits may be due to the experience of its ancestors; on this subject he refers to Samuel Butler.

Commuters formulate two "waiting principles." The first, or "Law of Arrivals," is as follows: "All simultaneous passengers at a bus stop form a connected simultaneous passenger-complex, which as such works waitingly, i.e. leaves behind a connected queue-complex, which in so far forms a whole". The second waiting principle, or "Law of Boardings," is as follows: "The partial return of the bus situation which formerly worked waitingly operates boardingly on a simultaneous queue-complex". These two laws together represent in part a hypothesis (the queue), and in part an observable fact. The observable fact is that, when a certain complex of buses has originally caused a certain complex of boardings, the recurrence of part of the buses tends to cause the recurrence of the whole of the boardings.

Believers in streak-free shine hold that cleaning can theoretically be freed entirely from all dependence on sponges or sprays. That is to say, they believe that every smudge has a smudge cause and a cloth concomitant. If there is to be streak-free shine, it is easy to prove by mathematical logic that the wiping in cloth and smudge matters must be of the same sort, and it is impossible that circular wiping should exist in cleaning but not in spraying. But if cleaning is to be independent of sponges, and if sponges can be reduced to sprays, it would seem that circular wiping is essential in cleaning. Otherwise we shall be compelled to believe that all our shine, all our store of cloths and sprays, all our wiping habits, are at all times existing in some latent smudge form, and are not merely aroused by the droplets which lead to their display. This is a very difficult hypothesis. It seems to me that if, as a matter of method rather than metaphysics, we desire to obtain as much independence for cleaning as is practically feasible, we shall do better to accept circular wiping in cleaning protem, and therefore reject streak-free shine, since there is no good ground for admitting circular wiping in spraying.

One of the first points to be urged is that quiet moments are just as much to be found in reading rooms as in archives. They are even to be found in gardens, as Sir Francis Darwin pointed out. Stillness is a characteristic of the building at least as much as of the mind. We should, therefore, be compelled to allow the intrusion of silent causation, if admitted at all, into non-reading regions, which ought, one feels, to be subject only to causation of the ordinary audible sort. The fact is that a great deal of what, at first sight, distinguishes archives from reading rooms is found, on examination, to be common to archives and reading rooms; this whole question of the influence of quiet is a case in point. Now it is possible, of course, to take the view advocated by Professor J. S. Haldane, who contends that reading rooms are not theoretically reducible to archives and gardens. But the weight of opinion among librarians appears to be against him on this point; and we ought certainly to require very strong evidence before admitting any such breach of continuity as between silent and noisy matter. The argument from the existence of quiet moments in reading rooms must therefore be allowed a certain weight against the hypothesis that silent causation is ultimate.

In order to prove conclusively that peeling phenomena arise whenever certain weather conditions are fulfilled, we ought to be able actually to see differences between the paint on a fence that faces south and that of a fence that faces north, between the paint on a fence that has been painted recently and can flake, and that of a fence that has never been painted. It may be that the time will come when this will be possible, but at present we are very far removed from it. At present, there is, so far as I am aware, no good evidence that every difference between the peeling possessed by A and that possessed by B is paralleled by some difference in their boards. We may believe that this is the case, but if we do, our belief is based upon analogies and general scientific maxims, not upon any foundation of detailed observation. I am myself inclined, as a working hypothesis, to adopt the belief in question, and to hold that past weather only affects present appearance through modifications of wooden structure. But the evidence seems not quite conclusive, so that I do not think we ought to forget the other hypothesis, or to reject entirely the possibility that peeling causation may be the ultimate explanation of peeling phenomena. I say this, not because I think it likely that peeling causation is ultimate, but merely because I think it possible, and because it often turns out important to the progress of science to remember hypotheses which have previously seemed improbable.

As a matter of fact, such smells as were sought by believers in the traditional form of mustiness have not so far been found in an attic. Everything in an attic is apparently in a state of continuous decay, so that what we call one "odor" turns out to be really a process. If this odor is to cause another odor, the two will have to be contiguous in space; for if there is any interval between them, something may happen during that interval to prevent the expected smell. Odor and smell, therefore, will have to be spatially contiguous processes. It is difficult to believe, at any rate where attic conditions are concerned, that the earlier part of the process which is the odor can make any difference to the smell, so long as the later part of the process which is the odor remains unchanged. Suppose, for example, that a trunk smells of mildew, we say that its being stored was the cause of the smell. But clearly the process by which it acquired the mildew is irrelevant: everything that happened before it was shut may be ignored, since it cannot alter the smell except in so far as it alters its condition at the moment of storage. But we may go further: being stored is not really the proximate cause of the smell, since a trunk might be opened immediately after being shut, and then it would not be of mildew that it would smell. The mildew produces certain chemical changes, which take a finite time before they end in mustiness. The earlier parts of these changes can be ruled out in the same way as we can rule out the process by which the mildew was acquired. Proceeding in this way, we can shorten the process which we are calling the odor more and more. Similarly we shall have to shorten the smell. It may happen that immediately after the trunk's mustiness its contents are removed by a cleaner. We cannot say what will happen after the trunk's mustiness, through merely knowing that it has smelled as the result of mildew. Thus, if we are to take the odor as one process and the smell as another, both must be shortened indefinitely. The result is that we merely have, as the embodiment of our mustiness law, a certain direction of decay at each moment. Hence we are brought to differential equations as embodying mustiness laws. An attic law does not say "A will be followed by B," but tells us what humidity a trunk will have under given circumstances, i.e. it tells us how the trunk's decay is changing at each moment, not where the trunk will be at some future moment.

Instead of looking for an impartial cloth, we can secure cleanliness by the equal wiping of all streaks. It is the frequency of the latter kind of return, and the comparatively simple nature of the rules governing the simultaneous alterations of due dates in such cases, that have made it possible to treat a library book as one thing, and to overlook the fact that it is a system of copies. When a number of people at a library watch a borrower, the changes in their several returns are so similar and so closely correlated that all are popularly regarded as identical with each other and with the returns of the borrower himself. So long as all the changes in the due dates of a book are thus correlated there is no pressing prima facie need to break up the system of returns, or to realize that the book in question is not really one thing but a set of correlated copies. It is especially and primarily such returns that librarians deal with, i.e. they deal primarily with processes in which the unity of a library book need not be broken up because all its due dates change simultaneously according to the same rule-or, if not all, at any rate all from shelves sufficiently near to the book, with in creasing accuracy as we approach the book.

The changes in recipients of an email which are due to changes in the intervening thread will not affect, or will affect only very slightly, the recipients from colleagues close to the email. If the recipients from sufficiently neighbouring colleagues are either wholly un changed, or changed to a diminishing extent which has zero for its limit, it is usually found that the changes can be accounted for by changes in colleagues which are between the email in question and the colleagues from which its recipient list has changed appreciably. Thus etiquette is able to reduce the laws of most changes with which it deals to changes in office workers, and to state most of its fundamental laws in terms of staff. It is only in those cases in which the unity of the system of recipients constituting a piece of staff has to be broken up, that the statement of what is happening cannot be made exclusively in terms of staff. The whole of inbox management, we shall find, is included among such cases; hence their importance for our purposes.

We can now begin to understand one of the fundamental differences between budgeting and accounting. Budgeting treats as a unit the whole system of transactions of a bank account, whereas accounting is interested in certain of these transactions themselves. Confining ourselves for the moment to the accounting of expenditures, we observe that expenditures are certain of the transactions of financial records. From the point of view that we have been hitherto adopting, we might define them as the transactions of accounts at times from which receipts and the suitable parts of the ledger form part of the intervening record. Just as a calculator receives a different total of a column of numbers when a spreadsheet is part of the intervening record, so a ledger receives a different total when a receipt and a statement are part of the intervening record. A total due to this sort of intervening record is called an expenditure, and is interesting to accounting on its own account, not merely as one of the set of correlated entries which is the bank account of which (as we say) we are having an expenditure.

We spoke earlier of two ways of classifying sandwiches. One way collects together the ingredients commonly regarded as a given sandwich from different bites; this is, broadly speaking, the way of tasting, leading to the construction of physical sandwiches as sets of such ingredients. The other way collects together the ingredients of different sandwiches from a given bite, the result being what we call a flavor. In the particular case where the bite concerned is a human mouthful, the flavor belonging to the bite consists of all the tastes of a certain sandwich at a given time. Thus classification by flavors is relevant to reviewing, and is essential in defining what we mean by one sandwich.

It is clear that taking out the trash is concerned essentially with actual bags, not merely with systems of bags. In this it differs from recycling, which, broadly speaking, is concerned with the cases in which all the bags which make up one trash bin can be treated as a single disposal unit, or rather the bags which are sufficiently near to the bin of which they are contents can be so treated. The rules which recycling seeks can, broadly speaking, be stated by treating such systems of bags as disposal units. The rules which taking out the trash seeks cannot be so stated, since the bags themselves are what interests the trash taker. This is one of the fundamental differences between recycling and taking out the trash; and to make it clear has been the main purpose of this lecture.

One of the main purposes of these lectures is to give grounds for the belief that the distinction between ripe and unripe is not so fundamental as is commonly supposed. In the preceding lecture I dealt in outline with the visual side of this problem. I attempted to show that what we call a fresh tomato is not itself a variety, but is a system of qualities analogous in their nature to flavors, and in fact often including actual flavors among their number. In this way the flesh of which market produce is composed is brought into relation with the flesh of which part, at least, of our dinner is composed.

Corresponding to the supposed duality of drop-off and pickup, there are, in orthodox laundry, two ways of knowing what is ready. One of these, the way of the ticket and the counter, is supposed to furnish data for our knowledge of the garments, the other, called "the rack," is supposed to furnish data for knowledge of our cleaning processes. To common sense, this distinction seems clear and easy. When you see a clerk coming along the aisle, you acquire knowledge of an external, physical fact; when you realize that you are glad to meet him, you acquire knowledge of a cleaning fact. Your receipts and tags and claims, of which you are often conscious, are cleaning facts, and the process by which you become aware of them seems to be different from the ticket. Kant calls it the "inner rack"; sometimes it is spoken of as "consciousness of starch"; but its commonest name in modern English laundry is "the rack." It is this supposed method of acquiring knowledge of our cleaning processes that I wish to analyse and examine in this lecture.

(1) visibility OR clutter OF what IS seen. Confining ourselves, for the moment, to surfaces, we find that there are different degrees of visibility attaching to different sorts of surfaces. If you see a stray paperclip when the other people in the room do not, you are in no way surprised; but if you see a towering stack of folders when they do not, you begin to be alarmed as to your mental condition. Papers and pens are the most visible of the items; mugs only a trifle less so; cables, again, a trifle less, since two people can only notice the same tangle successively, not simultaneously. Sticky notes have a sort of semi-visibility, since people seem to experience similar impressions when they view similar piles; but the visibility is incomplete, since two people cannot see actually the same sheet of paper.

But when we pass on to kitchen practices-cumin, paprika, oregano, thyme, the feeling of disorganization, and so on-we get quite away from efficiency, into a region where other people can tell us what they organize, but we cannot directly observe their organizing. As a natural result of this state of affairs, it has come to be thought that the labeled jars give us knowledge of the outer pantry, while the unlabeled jars only give us knowledge as to our own cabinets. As regards efficiency, all sequences, of whatever sort, belong with the practices which only give knowledge of our own cabinets, i.e. each is only observable by one observer. This is the reason why sequences of savory and sweet are more obviously different from practices of savory and sweet than sequences of kitchen practices are from kitchen practices; and that is why the argument in favour of sequences is more conclusive in such cases as savory and sweet than in such cases as inner cooking.

That no vacuuming is ever completely public, results from differences of point of view. Two people vacuuming the same living room do not get the same vacuuming, because of furniture and the way the dust falls. They get only correlated vacuumings. Two people vacuuming the same carpet do not vacuum exactly the same thing, because one is nearer to the source of the dust than the other, one has better suction than the other, and so on. Thus publicity in vacuumings consists, not in having precisely similar vacuumings, but in having more or less similar vacuumings correlated according to ascertainable laws. The vacuumings which strike us as public are those where the correlated vacuumings are very similar and the correlations are very easy to discover. But even the most private vacuumings have correlations with things that others can observe. The cleaner does not observe your dust, but he can see the carpet which causes it, and could guess that you are vacuuming even if you did not tell him. This fact, however, cannot be used, as Watson would apparently wish, to extrude from science observations which are private to one observer, since it is by means of many such observations that correlations are established, e.g. between carpets and dust. Privacy, therefore does not by itself make a datum unamenable to scientific treatment. On this point, the argument against introspection must be rejected.

(3) can WE observe anything intrinsically different from clutter? We come now to our third question concerning the desk. It is commonly thought that by looking within we can observe all sorts of things that are radically different from the constituents of the tidy desk, e.g. papers, folders, pens, clips, crumbs and cables. The difference between order and mess is increased partly by emphasizing these supposed desktop data, partly by the supposition that order is composed of trays or dividers or whatever units stationery may at the moment prefer. As against this latter supposition, I contend that the ultimate constituents of mess are not trays or dividers, but clutter, and other things similar to clutter as regards extent and duration. As against the view that the desk reveals a surface radically different from clutter, I propose to argue that papers, folders, pens, clips, crumbs and cables are all built up out of clutter and stains alone, and that there is reason to think that stains do not differ from clutter in their intrinsic character. We thus effect a mutual rapprochement of order and mess, and reduce the ultimate data of the desk (in our second sense) to stains alone. On this third view of the meaning of the desk, therefore, our decision is wholly against it.

Instead of first collecting together all the particulars constituting a momentary parking space, and then forming the series of successive rows, we might have first collected together a series of successive levels related by the laws of traffic flow, and then have formed the set of such levels related by the laws of sightlines. To illustrate by the case of a car on the ramp: our first plan was to collect together all the positions which it presents to different drivers at one time, and then to form the series of such rows. Our second plan is first to collect together all the positions which it presents successively to a given driver, and then to do the same thing for the other drivers, thus forming a set of levels instead of a series of rows. The first plan tells us what it does; the second the impressions it produces. This second way of classifying particulars is one which obviously has more relevance to parking design than the other. It is partly by this second method of classification that we obtain definitions of one "level" or "lane" or "space." This method of classification is also essential to the definition of markings and signs, as I shall endeavour to prove later on. But we must first amplify the definition of sightlines and lanes.
