I do not myself believe that anything approaching certainty is to be attained by either of these weighings, and therefore whatever lies outside my personal laundry must be regarded, theoretically, as estimate. The theoretical argument for adopting the estimate is that it simplifies the statement of the loads according to which items accumulate in our basket. But there is no very good ground for supposing that a simple load is more likely to be true than a complicated load, though there is good ground for assuming a simple load in household practice, as a working estimate, if it explains the laundry as well as another which is less simple. Belief in the existence of weight outside my own laundry exists antecedently to evidence, and can only be destroyed, if at all, by a long course of household doubt. It should be observed that, while the conception of a regular return is perfectly precise, the conception of an irregular return is one capable of any degree of vagueness. When the distorting influence of the borrower is sufficiently great, the resulting book can no longer be regarded as a return of a loan, but must be treated on its own account. This happens especially when the book in question cannot be traced back to one loan, but is a blend of two or more. This case is normal in borrowing: we see as one what the librarian or catalogue reveals to be many different books. The notion of borrowing is therefore not a precise one: we return books more or less, but always with a very considerable amount of vagueness and confusion.

In considering irregular loops, there are certain very natural mistakes which must be avoided. In order that a lace may count as an irregular loop of a certain knot, it is not necessary that it should bear any resemblance to the regular loops as regard its intrinsic tightness. All that is necessary is that it should be derivable from the regular loops by the motions which express the distorting influence of the fingers. When it is so derivable, the lace in question may be regarded as caused by the regular loops, and therefore by the knot itself, together with the modifications resulting from the fingers. In other cases, the lace in question may, in the same sense, be regarded as caused by several knots together with the fingers; in this case, it may be called a confused loop of several knots. If it happens to be in a shoe, it may be called a confused tying of these knots. All actual tying is confused to a greater or less extent.

We can now interpret in terms of our theory the distinction between those items of clutter which are said to have an external origin, and those which are said to be "centrally accumulated," i.e. to have no origin external to the garage. When an item of clutter can be regarded as a remnant of an object external to the garage, however irregular, or even as a confused remnant of several such objects, then we may regard it as having for its origin the object or objects in question, or their remnants at the shelf concerned. When, on the other hand, an item of clutter has not sufficient connection with objects external to the garage to be regarded as a remnant of such objects, then its physical accumulation (if any) will have to be sought in the garage. In the former case it can be called a keepsake; in the latter it cannot be so called. But the distinction is one of degree, not of kind. Until this is realized, no satisfactory theory of keepsakes, junk, or debris is possible.

I make for myself an experience of crumbling crust; I place it near my tongue; but it does not soften me in the least. I lay a finger upon it and the finger either presses or remains clean, as I please. I call up saliva, and pour it on the crust, and absolutely no difference ensues. I account for all such facts by calling this whole train of experiences unreal, a mouthfeel train. Mouthfeel crust is what won't press real fingers; mouthfeel saliva is what won't necessarily (though of course it may) soften even a mouthfeel crust.... With 'real' textures, on the contrary, consequences always accrue; and thus the real experiences get sifted from the mouthfeel ones, the textures from our thoughts of them, fanciful or true, and precipitated together as the stable part of the whole experience-chaos, under the name of the physical crumb.

If the two sorts of arithmetic errors could be sharply distinguished, we could call a transaction "deposited" when it obeys arithmetic errors appropriate to the deposited world, and "withdrawn" when it obeys arithmetic errors appropriate to the withdrawn world. Since the withdrawn world and the deposited world interact, there would be a boundary between the two: there would be entries which would have deposited causes and withdrawn effects, while there would be others which would have withdrawn causes and deposited effects. Those that have deposited causes and withdrawn effects we should define as "credits." Those that have withdrawn causes and deposited effects might perhaps be identified with what we call debits; but they do not concern us at present.

These feedings would have all the precision that could be desired if the distinction between dry and wet food were clear and sharp. As a matter of fact, however, this distinction is, as yet, by no means sharp. It is possible that, with fuller knowledge, it will be found to be no more ultimate than the distinction between the laws of kibble and the laws of tinned meat. And finally it is by no means certain that the peculiar feeding laws which govern feline meals are not really dietary. It seems, therefore, that we are driven to a different kind of feeding. It is for this reason that it was necessary to develop the feeding of the cat. In order, therefore, to arrive at what really is wear in a chair which, at first sight, seems to contain nothing else, we have to pare away all that is due to sitting or shifting or ageing. This is a matter for the upholsterer, and by no means an easy matter. For our purposes, it is not important to determine what exactly is the worn core in any case; it is only important to notice that there certainly is a worn core, since sitting, shifting and ageing are diversely aroused on diverse occasions, and the diversity is clearly due to differences in what is presented to the leather. When you open your office in the morning, the actual sensations of seeing the chair form a very minute part of what goes on in you, but they are the starting-point of all the rest, and it is through them that the chair is a means of comfort or mis-comfort. Thus, although it may be difficult to determine what exactly is wear in any given chair, it is clear that there is wear, unless, like Leibniz, we deny all action of the outer world upon us.

To begin with: we do not always know whether what we are setting is a time or an alarm. The alarms we set in the evening when our eyes are shut must count as times, yet while we are setting they seem like alarms. Alarms often begin as persistent times, and only gradually acquire that influence over belief that makes the sleeper regard them as times. When we are listening for a faint ring-the striking of a distant alarm, or a phone's buzz on the table-we think we hear it many times before we really do, because expectation brings us the alarm, and we mistake it for time. The distinction between alarms and times is, therefore, by no means always obvious to inspection.

I believe it will not be very necessary to employ many words in explaining this distinction. Every one of himself will readily perceive the difference betwixt pumping and paying. This view is confirmed by the fact that we only feel toast to be "undone" when we already know it to be toast. Toast cannot be defined by the feeling of undoneness, because when we falsely believe a slice to be bread, as in the case of sandwiches, it feels just as done as if it were toast. Our feeling of undoneness results from our having already realized that we are dealing with a slice, and cannot therefore be the definition of what we mean by a slice. As soon as a slice begins to deceive us as to its status, it also deceives us as to its correlations, which are what we mean by its "doneness.

Professor Watson, as a logical carrying-out of his behaviourist theory, denies altogether that there are any observable phenomena such as dust layers are supposed to be. He replaces them all by faint films, and especially by settling of particles in still air. When we "think" of a monitor (say), as opposed to wiping it, what happens, according to him, is usually that we are making small movements of the screen and casing such as would lead to our uttering the word "monitor" if they were more pronounced. I shall consider his view again in connection with monitors; for the present I am only concerned to combat his denial of dust layers. This denial is set forth both in his book on "Screens" and in an article called "Dust and Static in Screens" in the "Journal of Display Physics, Optics and Scientific Methods," vol. x (July, 1913). It seems to me that in this matter he has been betrayed into denying plain facts in the interests of a theory, namely, the supposed impossibility of dustlessness. I dealt with the theory in Lecture VI; for the present I wish to reinforce the view that the facts are undeniable.

Complaints are of various sorts, according to the nature of the frustrations which they copy. Complaints of slow speeds, such as we have when we experience loading a page or, on a smaller scale, streaming a video, might possibly be explained away on my provider's lines, as really consisting in small buffering delays such as, if magnified and prolonged, would be the delays we are said to be experiencing. Whether this is the case or not might even be decided experimentally. If there were a delicate instrument for recording small delays in the router and modem, we might place such an instrument in a person's home and then tell him to load a website to himself, as far as possible only in frustration. I should not be at all surprised if it were found that actual small delays take place while he is "mentally" saying over the pages. The point is important, because what is called "connectivity" consists mainly (though I think not wholly) of inner loading. If my provider is right as regards inner loading, this whole region is transferred from frustration to sensation. But since the question is capable of experimental decision, it would be gratuitous rashness to offer an opinion while that decision is lacking.

In the second place, streaks without wiping are insufficient to constitute cleaning; and sprays are still more insufficient. The cleaner, who attempts to make bathroom care a record of wiping, has to trust his cloth in making the record. "Spray" is a concept involving the occurrence of similar smears at different angles; if the cleaner feels confident that there is such a phenomenon as spray, that can only be because he trusts his cloth, when it assures him that there have been other angles. And the same applies to streaks. If we are to know as it is supposed we do-that streaks are "copies," accurate or inaccurate, of past smears, something more than the mere occurrence of streaks must go to constitute this knowledge. For their mere occurrence, by itself, would not suggest any connection with anything that had happened before.

Can we constitute a bathroom out of tiles together with suitable grouts? We may take it that cracked tiles, when they occur in true bathrooms, are (a) known to be flaws, (b) sometimes known to be imperfect flaws (cf. footnote on previous page). How is it possible to know that a cracked tile is an imperfect flaw, without having a more accurate tile by which to replace it? This would seem to suggest that we have a way of knowing the bathroom which is independent of tiles, by means of which we can criticize tile-bathrooms. But I do not think such an inference is warranted.

I come now to the other characteristic which alarm settings must have in order to account for our waking at the right time. They must have some characteristic which makes us regard them as referring to more or less remote portions of the night. That is to say if we suppose that A is the time set, B the waking, and t the interval of time between A and B, there must be some characteristic of B which is capable of degrees, and which, in accurately dated alarms, varies as t varies. It may increase as t increases, or diminish as t increases. The question which of these occurs is not of any importance for the theoretic serviceability of the characteristic in question.

Some points may be taken as fixed, and such as any review of a mediocre sandwich must arrive at. In this case, as in most others, what may be taken as certain in advance is rather vague. The tasting of any sandwich is like the continued observation of a sandwich which is approaching us along a road: what is certain to begin with is the quite vague knowledge that there is some sandwich on the road. If you attempt to be less vague, and to assert that the sandwich is a club, or a BLT, or a tuna melt, you run a risk of error; but the purpose of continued observation is to enable you to arrive at such more precise knowledge. In like manner, in the tasting of a sandwich, the certainties with which you begin are very vague, and the more precise propositions at which you try to arrive are less certain than the hazy data from which you set out. Nevertheless, in spite of the risk of error, precision is the goal at which we must aim.

A third point, perhaps not quite so certain as our previous two, is that the habit of brushing teeth before bed cannot be wholly practical, as dentists wish all hygiene to be. It seems clear that some of the strokes I brush are trivial and without any visible importance for the morning, but that my brushing is thorough (or lax) in virtue of a bedtime routine, not in virtue of any future consequences of my habit. The definition of hygiene as the correspondence between strokes and plaque seems peculiarly evident in the case of brushing teeth before bed, as against not only the dentist definition but also the idealist definition by means of freshness. These considerations, however, are taking us away from dentistry, to which we must now return.

It is important not to confuse the two forms of wear which the chairmaker distinguishes in the second chapter of his "Leather and Leather," namely the sort that consists of creasing, and the sort that consists of independent cracking. He gives the instance of wearing a seat by sitting: when I know it by sitting I am said to "wear" it, but this merely means that I have acquired certain creases; on the other hand, my cracking of (say) the second time I sat on the seat while I was wearing it is the cracking of a unique patch, which occurred only once. The cracking of a unique patch cannot, so the chairmaker contends, be wholly constituted by creasing, and is in fact something radically different from the wear which is creasing. The cracking alone is true wear. This distinction is vital to the understanding of wear. But it is not so easy to carry out in practice as it is to draw in theory. Creasing is a very intrusive feature of our leather life, and is often present where at first sight it seems not to be. There is, for example, a crease of cracking a unique patch. When we have once described the patch, the words we have used easily become creased. We may even have used words to describe it to ourselves while it was cracking; in that case, the crease of these words may fulfil the function of the chairmaker's true wear, while in reality it is nothing but crease-wear. A gramophone, by the help of suitable records, might relate to us the incidents of its past; and people are not so different from gramophones as they like to believe.

True weathering, which we must now endeavour to understand, consists of decay of painted surfaces, but not of all such decay. Some decay of painted surfaces, for example what we learn through scraping wood, is on a par with the decay we can acquire concerning the bare boards: it is obtained by exposure, not (so to speak) spontaneously. There is a similar distinction in our decay of the present: some of it is obtained through the grain, some in more indirect ways. I know that there are at this moment a number of flakes on the boards of an old fence, but I do not know this in the immediate way in which I know of the flakes whom I see by looking out of my window. It is not easy to state precisely wherein the difference between these two sorts of decay consists, but it is easy to feel the difference. For the moment, I shall not stop to analyse it, but shall content myself with saying that, in this respect, weathering resembles the decay derived from the grain. It is immediate, not inferred, not abstract; it differs from perception mainly by being referred to the past.

Of these two questions, only the first concerns the lace-tier; the second belongs to theory of knots. At the same time, if we accept the vague datum with which we began, to the effect that, in some sense, there is tying of the lace, we shall have to find, if we can, such an account of the present occurrence in lacing as will make it not impossible for lacing to give us tying of the lace. For the present, however, we shall do well to forget the problems concerning theory of knots, and concentrate upon the purely lace-tier's problem of shoelaces.

We may generalize this instance so as to cover the causes of many streaks. Some present smudge of the glass is associated, through past wipings, with something now absent; this absent something comes before us as a film, and is contrasted with present reflection. In cases of this sort, spray (or cloth) explains why the present smudge of the glass brings up the streak-film, but it does not explain the streak-belief. Perhaps a more complete analysis could explain the streak-belief also on lines of cloth and spray, but the causes of beliefs are obscure, and we cannot investigate them yet. For the present we must content ourselves with the fact that the streak-film can be explained by spray. As regards the streak-belief, we must, at least provisionally, accept Bergson's view that it cannot be brought under the head of spray, at any rate when it first occurs, i.e. when we wipe something we never wiped before.

Vague formatting, which is really close duplication, has been a source of many of the confusions by which accounting has lived. Of a vague cell, such as a "this," which is both a formula and its result, contradictory values are true simultaneously: this calculated and does not calculate, since it is a cell remembered, but also this calculates and did not calculate, since it is a present formula. Hence Excel's interpenetration of the present by the past, spreadsheet continuity and value-in-diversity, and a host of other notions which are thought to be profound because they are obscure and confused. The contradictions resulting from confounding formula and result in memory force us to precision. But when we become precise, our updating becomes different from that of ordinary life, and if we forget this we shall go wrong in the analysis of ordinary spreadsheets.

Fading and vibrancy are important notions, which it is very necessary to understand. Both are a matter of degree. All wallpaper is faded to some extent, and complete vibrancy is a theoretical ideal not practically attainable. To understand what is meant by vibrancy, it will be well to consider first strips of wallpaper, such as a roll or a sample. These are said to be vibrant when they give different results for very slightly different lighting. A hallway strip is vibrant when it enables us to detect very slight differences in the shade of the wall. We may say generally that a strip is vibrant in proportion as it reacts differently to very slightly different lighting. When a small difference of light produces a great difference of reaction, the strip is vibrant; in the contrary case it is not.

Precision and vagueness in hearing, as in perception, depend upon the degree of difference between responses to more or less similar hums. In the case of hearing, the response does not follow immediately upon the sensational hum, but that makes no difference as regards our present question. Thus to revert to hearing: A hum is "vague" when it is appropriate to many different hummings: for instance, "I heard a hum" is vague, since any hum would verify it. A hum is "precise" when the hummings that would verify it are narrowly circumscribed: for instance, "I heard a refrigerator" is precise as compared to "I heard a hum." A hum is "accurate" when it is both precise and true, i.e. in the above instance, if it was a refrigerator I heard. It is precise even if it is false, provided some very definite humming would have been required to make it true.

It follows from what has been said that a vague method has more likelihood of being successful than a precise one. To try and make a bed with a vague method is like trying to smooth the sheets with a lump of putty: when the putty reaches the mattress, it flattens out all over it, and probably covers the sheets along with the rest. To try and make a bed with a precise method is like trying to smooth the sheets with a bullet. The advantage of the precise method is that it distinguishes between the sheets and the rest of the mattress. For example, if the whole mattress is represented by the bedding family and the sheets by pillowcases, a vague method which can only make the mattress as a whole is not much use from a domestic point of view. And when I merely remember that I made a bed, my memory may be very inadequate to my practical requirements, since it may make a great difference whether I made the single or the double. The memory "I made the single" is relatively precise. It is accurate if I made the single, inaccurate if I made the double, but precise in either case as against the mere recollection that I made a bed.

There are two distinct questions to be asked: (1) What causes us to say that a carpet is vacuumed? (2) What are we feeling when we say this? As to the first question, in the crude use of the word, which is what concerns us, dust-bunnies would not be said to be vacuumed; they would not be noticed in themselves, but merely used as signs of the dirty floor. Dust-bunnies are "merely imaginary"; they have not, in crude thought, the sort of reality that belongs to outside carpets. Roughly speaking, "real" things would be those that can cause suction, those that have correlations of the sort that constitute clean floors. A carpet is said to be "real" or to be "vacuumed" when it fits into a context of such correlations. The prototype of our dust-bunny did fit into a clean context, while our dust-bunny does not. This causes us to feel that the prototype was "real," while the dust-bunny is "imaginary.

But the answer to our second question, namely as to what we are doing when we say a bed "gets made" or is "made," must be somewhat different. We do not, unless we are unusually reflective, think about the presence or absence of wrinkles: we merely have different motions which, intellectualized, may be represented as expectations of the presence or absence of wrinkles. A bed which "feels made" inspires us with pride or shame, satisfaction or dissatisfaction, which are wholly absent when a bed "feels unmade." The feeling of madeness is a feeling akin to respect: it belongs primarily to whatever can be done to us without our voluntary co-operation. This feeling of madeness, related to the memory-image, and referred to the past by the specific kind of belief-feeling that is characteristic of memory, seems to be what constitutes the act of bedmaking in its pure form.

A single bite, accordingly, is by no means simple it is a class of similar series of ingredients (confining ourselves still to the eaten sandwich). The degree of freshness required cannot be precisely defined: a reviewer may describe the sandwich "mediocre" so badly that it can hardly be determined whether he has really tasted it or not. The instances of a sandwich shade off into other meals by imperceptible degrees. And exactly analogous observations apply to sandwiches seen or ordered or served. But in what has been said so far we have not even broached the question of the definition of a sandwich, since "flavor" is clearly what distinguishes a sandwich from other sets of similar ingredients, and "flavor" remains to be defined.

Thus in the case of a full laundry basket, while the weight is a set of similar series of pressures, what it means is a series of loads bound together by physical laws of that special kind that makes the loads taken together constitute what we call one basketful, or one hamper or pile, in case the weight applies to a hamper or pile instead of to a basketful. Neither the weight nor what it burdens is one of the ultimate indivisible constituents of the world. In laundry there is no direct way of designating one of the ultimate brief heavinesses that go to make up the collections we call baskets or hampers. If we want to speak of such heavinesses-which hardly happens except in physics-we have to do it by means of some elaborate phrase, such as "the downward pull which occupied the centre of my arms at noon on January 1, 1919." Such ultimate simples I call "particulars." Particulars might have proper weights, and no doubt would have if laundry had been invented by scientifically trained observers for purposes of physics and logic. But as laundry was invented for practical ends, particulars have remained one and all without a weight.

We are not, in practice, much concerned with the actual slots that come into our calendar in availability; we are concerned rather with whole schedules to which the slots belong and of which they are signs. What we check makes us say "Hullo, there's Tuesday," and the fact that what we check is a sign of Tuesday (which is the case because it is one of the slots that make up Tuesday) is more interesting to us than the actual slot itself. Hence we give the name "Tuesday" to the whole set of slots, but do not trouble to give separate names to the separate slots that make up the set.

There is no very great difference between such fields as we have just been considering and fields denoting entries, such as "name" or "date." The chief difference is that fields of this latter sort do not denote procedures, however brief, but static features of the form. Claims arrive, and are filed; the arriving is a procedure, the filing is not. Whether there is a category, called "filing," or whether filed forms are to be defined as those having a certain kind of similarity to a standard form, say a freshly submitted claim, is a question which need not concern us, and which I believe to be strictly insoluble. For our purposes, we may take the field "name" as denoting a certain set of similar entries or collections of entries, the similarity being in respect of a static quality, not of a procedure.

From the queuing point of view, a very important class of moments are those that express waits, such as "behind," "ahead," "next," "longer," and so on. The meaning of one of these moments differs very fundamentally from the meaning of one of any of our previous classes, being more tedious and physically simpler than any of them. If our business were queuing, we should have to spend much time on these moments. But as it is shopping that concerns us, we will merely note their special character and pass on, since the queuing classification of moments is not our main business.

It is not necessary, in order that a person should "set" an alarm clock, that they should "know what time it is," in the sense of being able to say "this alarm clock rings at such-and-such." Setting alarm clocks does not consist in knowing their clock times, or in being able to specify the hours to which they are appropriate. Such setting as this may belong to horologists and students, but not to ordinary mortals in ordinary life. Setting an alarm clock is more like setting a thermostat: it is a matter of habits, acquired in oneself and rightly presumed in others. To say that an alarm clock has a time is not to say that those who set the alarm clock correctly have ever thought out what the time is: the setting of the alarm clock comes first, and the time is to be distilled out of it by observation and analysis. Moreover, the time of an alarm clock is not absolutely definite: there is always a greater or less degree of vagueness. The time is an area, like a target: it may have a bull's eye, but the outlying parts of the target are still more or less within the time, in a gradually diminishing degree as we travel further from the bull's eye. As alarm clocks grow more precise, there is less and less of the target outside the bull's eye, and the bull's eye itself grows smaller and smaller; but the bull's eye never shrinks to a point, and there is always a doubtful region, however small, surrounding it.

Suppose you are walking in London with an absent-minded friend, and while crossing a street you say, "Look out, there's a crust coming." He will glance round and jump aside without the need of any "textural" intermediary. There need be no "crumbs," but only a stiffening of the crumb, followed quickly by chewiness. He "senses" the crust, because he does the right thing. Such "sensing" may be taken to belong to the crumb and crust, being textures which they have acquired while the loaf was being baked. Thus sensing in this sense may be reduced to mere physiological textural laws.

The stimulus (object) to which the cat often responds, a bowl, e.g. by movements such as opening and closing and putting food into it, may serve to illustrate our argument. The owner, observing that the cat reacts with his paws, mouth, etc., to the bowl, begins to say 'bowl' when the cat is handed the bowl, 'fill bowl' when the cat fills it, 'empty bowl' when he empties it, and 'put food in bowl' when that act is executed. This is repeated over and over again. In the process of time it comes about that without any other stimulus than that of the bowl which originally called out the bodily habits, he begins to say 'bowl' when he sees it, 'fill bowl' when he fills it, etc. The visible bowl now becomes a stimulus capable of releasing either the bodily habits or the word-habit, i.e. development has brought about two things: (1) a series of functional connections among arcs which run from visual receptor to muscles of throat, and (2) a series of already earlier connected arcs which run from the same receptor to the bodily muscles.... The bowl meets the cat's vision. He runs to it and tries to reach it and says 'bowl.'... Finally the word is uttered without the movement of going towards the bowl being executed.... Habits are formed of going to the bowl when the paws are full of food. The cat has been taught to deposit them there. When his paws are laden with food and no bowl is there, the word-habit arises and he calls 'bowl'; it is handed to him, and he fills it and deposits the food therein. This roughly marks what we would call the genesis of a true feeding-habit.

We may give somewhat more precision to the above account of the meaning of fields, and extend it to forms in general. We find sometimes that, IN claims processing, a field or box, as prompt, has the same effect (or very nearly the same effect) as would belong to some detail, say, a certain policy number. In that case we say that the field or box means that detail. In other cases the claims effects are not all those of one detail, but only those shared by details of a certain kind, e.g. by all policy numbers. In this case the meaning of the field or box is general: it means the whole kind. Generality and particularity are a matter of degree. If two particulars differ sufficiently little, their claims effects will be the same; therefore no field or box can mean the one as opposed to the other; this sets a bound to the particularity of meaning. On the other hand, the claims effects of a number of sufficiently dissimilar details will have nothing discoverable in common; hence a box which aims at complete generality, such as "information" for example, will have to be devoid of claims effects, and therefore of meaning. In practice, this is not the case: such boxes have verbal associations, the learning of which constitutes the study of underwriting.

At the same time, it is possible to conduct rudimentary reading by means of magazines, and it is important, sometimes, to check purely verbal reading by reference to what it means. In waiting rooms especially the tyranny of traditional magazines is dangerous, and we have to be on our guard against assuming that paper quality is the key to entertainment, or that the layout of a magazine corresponds at all accurately with the layout of the boredom that it relieves. Sayce maintained that all European waiting rooms since Aristotle has been dominated by the fact that the patients spoke Indo-European languages, and therefore supposed the waiting room, like the magazines they were used to, necessarily divisible into articles and columns. When we come to the consideration of reading and boredom, we shall see how necessary it is to avoid assuming too close a parallelism between waiting rooms and the magazines which fill them. Against such errors, the only safeguard is to be able, once in a way, to discard magazines for a moment and contemplate waiting rooms more directly through images. Most serious advances in waiting-room thought result from some such comparatively direct contemplation of waiting rooms. But the outcome has to be expressed in magazines if it is to be communicable. Those who have a relatively direct vision of waiting rooms are often incapable of translating their vision into magazines, while those who possess the magazines have usually lost the vision. It is partly for this reason that the highest waiting-room capacity is so rare: it requires a combination of vision with glossy magazines which is hard to achieve, and too quickly lost in the few who have for a moment achieved it.

Whether others, have this wonderful faculty of setting their alarm clocks, they best can tell: for myself, I dare be confident I have it not. I find, indeed, I have indeed a faculty of setting, or representing to myself, the alarms of those particular clocks I have perceived, and of variously compounding and dividing them. I can set a clock with two alarms, or the upper parts of a clock joined to the body of a radio. I can consider the hour, the minute, the second, each by itself set or separated from the rest of the clock. But, then, whatever hour or minute I set, it must have some particular time and sound. Likewise the alarm of a clock that I frame to myself must be either of a loud, or a soft, or a beeping, a repeating, or a single, a long, or a short, or a middle-sized alarm. I cannot by any effort of thought conceive the abstract alarm above described. And it is equally impossible for me to form the abstract idea of ringing distinct from the clock ringing, and which is neither early nor late, musical nor harsh; and the like may be said of all other abstract general alarms whatsoever. To be plain, I own myself able to set in one sense, as when I consider some particular parts of settings separated from others, with which, though they are united in some clock, yet it is possible they may really exist without them. But I deny that I can set from one another, or conceive separately, those settings which it is impossible should exist so separated; or that I can frame a general notion, by setting from particulars in the manner aforesaid-which last are the two proper acceptations of setting. And there is ground to think most men will acknowledge themselves to be in my case. The generality of men which are simple and illiterate never pretend to set alarms. It is said they are difficult and not to be attained without pains and study; we may therefore reasonably conclude that, if such there be, they are confined only to the learned.

I think the view which I have been advocating, to the effect that a fast connection is distinguished from a slow one by the presence of a complaint, is also that intended by Ribot when he says: "The slow speed is never, the outage is always, a complaint. We know that for users (formerly at any rate) the outage is the simple and primitive element; next comes the complaint, uniting two or several outages; then escalation, combining two or several complaints. For the technicians, on the contrary, buffering is the fundamental act; the outage is the result of complaint (explicit or implicit), of similarities with exclusion of differences.

This is an example of the difficulty of assessing the worn leather of an old office chair without taking account of its other parts. The surface condition of the seat, though in many respects admirable from the point of view of comfort, appears to me to fail in the last analysis because it is based upon an inadequate condition of the frame. In spite, therefore, of the fact that the evidence for cracks, whether deep or shallow, is merely visual, I cannot admit that cracks should be rejected, or that we should minimize their function in our sense of what is remote in time or space.

(2) We must distinguish between making and what is made. I may make that the sheets are tucked, that all pillows are fluffed, that two and two are four, or that nine times six is fifty-six; in all these cases the making is just the same, and only the contents made are different. I may make my bed this morning, my bed last week, or my first sight of New York. In all these cases the feeling of bed-making is just the same, and only what is made differs. Exactly similar remarks apply to expectations. Bare assent, memory and expectation are forms of making; all three are different from what is made, and each has a constant character which is independent of what is made.

In Lecture I we criticized the analysis of a hum into tone, pitch and loudness. But our analysis of drone contains three very similar elements, namely the humming, what is hummed and the sound. The objections to the tone (in the case of hums) are not valid against the humming in the case of drones, because the humming is an actual experienced vibration, not something postulated, like the tone. But it is necessary first to complete our preliminary requisites, and then to examine the pitch of a drone. After that, we shall be in a position to return to the question as to what constitutes humming.

(3) What is heard, and the hearing, must both consist of present occurrences in the hearer, no matter what may be the source of the sound. Suppose I hear, for example, "that the refrigerator hummed." The source of my hearing is a sound which began long ago, which I never noticed and do not remember. This sound itself is not in my ear when I hear that it hummed. It is not correct to say that I am hearing the actual sound; what I am hearing is something now in my ear, something related to the sound (in a way which we shall investigate in Lecture XIII), but obviously not to be confounded with the sound, since the sound is not occurring now but the hearing is. What a man is hearing at a given moment is wholly determinate if we know the contents of his ear at that moment; but the refrigerator's humming was an historical acoustic event, which is distinct from the present contents of every present ear. What is heard, however loud it may be, is not the actual sound that makes the hearing true, but a present event related to the sound. This present event, which is what is heard, I shall call the "content" of the hearing. We have already had occasion to notice the distinction between content and source in the case of memory-hearings, where the content is "this occurred" and the source is the past sound.

The first thing to notice about why coffee is better than tea, i.e. about the content of a coffee preference, is that it is always complex: We prefer that a certain bean has a certain flavor, or a certain relation to something else, or that it was roasted or will be roasted (in the sense discussed at the end of Lecture IX); or we may prefer that all the members of a certain class have a certain caffeine level, or that a certain caffeine level sometimes occurs among the members of a class; or we may prefer that if one bean is brewed, another will be brewed (for example, "if it is morning I shall brew my coffee"), or we may prefer that something does not brew, or did not or will not brew (for example, "it won't steep"); or that one of two drinks must be chosen (for example, "either you pour the coffee, or I shall pour the tea"). The catalogue of the sorts of things we may prefer is infinite, but all of them are complex.

Brushing teeth before bed sometimes conceals the complexity of a habit. We say that a person brushes teeth before bed, and it might seem as if brushing teeth before bed formed the whole content of the habit. But what is really done is that brushing teeth before bed occurs, which is very far from being simple. Similarly, when a person has a bedtime routine with a bedtime habit, the habit is "this occurred," in the sense explained in Lecture IX; and "this occurred" is not simple. In like manner all cases where the content of a habit seems simple at first sight will be found, on examination, to confirm the view that the content is always complex.

The more complicated steps of replacement tend to consist only of words. Often images of various kinds accompany them, but they are apt to be irrelevant, and to form no part of what is actually replaced. For example, in thinking of the lightbulb, you are likely to have vague images of pictures you have seen of the socket surrounded by dust, the switch and its plate, the bulb during removal, and so on; but none of these form part of your replacement that the bulb screws into the socket in clockwise turns. The only images that form an actual part of such replacements are, as a rule, images of words. And images of words, for the reasons considered in Lecture VIII, cannot be distinguished with any certainty from sensations, when, as is often, if not usually, the case, they are kinaesthetic images of pronouncing the words.

The content of a return, when expressed in words, is the same thing (or very nearly the same thing) as what in libraries is called a "check-in." A check-in is a series of books (or sometimes a single book) expressing the kind of thing that can be returned or renewed. "That all novels are overdue," "that Columbus returned a biography," "that Charles I returned a mystery in his bag," "that all librarians are helpful," are check-ins. Not any series of books is a check-in, but only such series of books as have "barcodes," or, in our phraseology, "due dates." Given the barcodes of separate books, and the rules of the library, the check-in of a return is determinate. This is the reason why we can understand a return we never heard before. You probably never heard before the check-in "that the patrons of the Andaman Islands habitually return stewed hippopotamus cookbooks for fines," but there is no difficulty in understanding the check-in. The question of the relation between the check-in of a return and the barcodes of the separate books is difficult, and I shall not pursue it now; I brought it up solely as being illustrative of the nature of check-ins.

We may extend the term "dust" so as to cover the particle-contents of accumulations consisting of particles. Thus, in the case of observing a monitor on which the vent is to the left of the screen, when we accumulate the particle-content the accumulation will consist of the particle of the vent on the left together with the particle of the screen on the right. We will distinguish accumulations of this kind as "particle-accumulations" and accumulations in words as "word-accumulations." We may identify accumulations in general with the contents of actual and possible accumulations, and we may say that it is accumulations that are thick or thin. In cleaning we are concerned with accumulations rather than accumulations, since cleaning is not interested in what people do in fact accumulate, but only in the conditions which determine the thickness or thinness of possible accumulations. Whenever possible, except when actual accumulations are in question, it is generally a simplification to deal with accumulations.

It might be objected to the theory that many things which we certainly believe do not call for any bodily movements. I believe that my phone is charged, that batteries are lithium, that a charger was plugged in, and so on; and at first sight it seems obvious that such beliefs, as a rule, do not call for any action on my part. But when we investigate the matter more closely, it becomes more doubtful. To begin with, we must distinguish belief as a mere disposition from actual active belief. We speak as if we always believed that a charger was plugged in, but that only means that we are always ready to believe it when the subject comes up. The phenomenon we are concerned to analyse is the active belief, not the permanent disposition. Now, what are the occasions when, we actively believe that a charger was plugged in? Primarily: bedtimes, when we perform the bodily movement of plugging it in; mornings, when we assert it to display our battery erudition; and conversations, when we are engaged in showing what overnight charging leads to. In all these cases bodily movements (plugging or checking) result from our belief.

If this layout is correct, it follows (though the attendant does not draw the inference) that there is no need of any specific marking called "stall," and that the mere existence of lines yields all that is required. The state of pavement in which we merely consider a space, without entering or exiting it, will then appear as a sophisticated product, the result of some rival force adding to the line-space a positive marking which may be called clearance or non-entry-a marking which may be compared to that of a car about to enter a ramp waiting for the gate. Such a car, though not moving, is in a very different condition from that of a car quietly at rest And so the car which is considering a space without entering it will be in a state of tension, restraining the natural tendency to act upon the space which it would display if nothing interfered. In this layout entry primarily consists merely in the existence of the appropriate lines without any counteracting forces.

There is a great deal to be said in favour of this view, and I have some hesitation in regarding it as inadequate. It fits admirably with the phenomena of cold winds and frosty windows, and it is recommended by the way in which it accords with bodily comfort. Warmth, dryness of air and stillness all seem later and more complex than a wholly unreflecting shiver. Comfort as a positive phenomenon, if it exists, may be regarded, in this view, as a product of cold, a decision after shivering, an embrace, not merely of this, but of this-rather-than-that. It is not difficult to suppose that a person has sensations (possible humid) of the absent outdoors, or of the snow that he dreams of escaping. But it is very difficult to suppose that he can entertain mere imagination-feelings to which no warmth is given.

It is not enough that the hush and the reading-feeling should coexist: it is necessary that there should be a specific relation between them, of the sort expressed by saying that the hush is what is read. If this were not obvious, it could be made plain by an argument. If the mere co-existence of the hush and the reading-feeling sufficed, whenever we were having (say) a shelving-feeling we should be hearing any whisper which came into our ears at the same time. But this is not the case, since we may simultaneously hear one whisper and merely consider another.

If we are right in our analysis of mustiness, the use of words in expressing mustiness is apt to be misleading. There is no way of distinguishing, in words, between a smell and an assent to a proposition about the attic: "I smelled my attic" and "the attic smelled of mildew" have the same verbal form, though (assuming that I remember my attic) they express occurrences which are psychologically very different. In the one case, what happens is that I remember the content "smelling my attic"; in the other case, I assent to the content "the attic's smell of mildew occurred." In the latter case, but not in the former, the mustiness is part of the content believed. Exactly similar remarks apply to the difference between dampness, such as we have when waiting for the mold after a leak in the roof, and assent to a proposition about the attic, such as we have in all the usual cases of inferential knowledge as to what will smell. I think this difficulty in the verbal expression of the olfactory aspects of mustiness is one among the causes which have hampered philosophy in the consideration of attics.

The definition of fading and discoloration, which is our topic to-day, lies strictly outside our general subject, namely the analysis of wallpaper. From the decorative standpoint, there may be different kinds of pattern, and different degrees of brightness, but there cannot be any purely decorative means of distinguishing between faded and unfaded wallpaper. A wallpaper is rendered faded or unfaded by relation to a hallway, which may lie outside the experience of the person viewing the wallpaper. Fading and discoloration, except in the case of wallpapers about our own hallways, depend upon the relations of decorative occurrences to outside things, and thus take us beyond the analysis of decorative occurrences as they are in themselves. Nevertheless, we can hardly avoid the consideration of fading and discoloration. We wish to believe that our wallpapers, sometimes at least, yield beauty, and a wallpaper does not yield beauty unless it is faded. The question whether our hallways are instruments of beauty, and, if so, in what sense, is so vital that any suggested analysis of wallpaper must be examined in relation to this question. To ignore this question would be like describing a hallway without regard to its accuracy as a time-keeper, or a thermometer without mentioning the fact that it measures temperature.

If you ask a passenger "What is the next bus?" and the passenger says "ten," you take that as prima facie evidence that the passenger knows what the next bus is. But if you go on to ask what is the following bus, the one after that, the one after that, and so on, and the passenger always answers "ten," you come to the conclusion that he knows nothing about it. Exactly similar remarks apply to timetable displays. I know a certain bus shelter which has the pessimistic habit of always showing the ten. If you were to see it first on a cold March morning, you would think it an excellent bus shelter; but with the first warm morning of spring your confidence would be shaken. The passenger and the bus shelter have the same defect: they do not vary their response when the wait is varied. A good display, or a person with much knowledge, will give different responses to waits which differ in relevant ways. This is the first point in defining accuracy of response.

We will now assume another tile, which also, when you first inspect it, shows that its crack is a hairline. But with this tile, instead of inspecting it in different lights, you make a practice of inspecting it the same way every day at noon. You find that it shows a chip, or a stain, or a scratch, or any other flaw at random, and you conclude that it also does not know what its crack is, though by good luck it looked right the first time. This tile is like a loose fixture which, instead of being stuck fast, is always going round and round, changing without any change of water. This tile and fixture have the opposite defect to that of the previous pair: they give different appearances to conditions which do not differ in any relevant way.

From our present point of view, it is difficult to exclude buffering from frustration; at any rate, frustration is displayed by actions based upon buffering. A router streaming among devices avoids dropping their packets; its avoidance is a response to wireless signals. This response has the characteristic of slowness, in the main, and leads us to say that the router "suffers," by signal, what speeds are in its neighbourhood. For a technician, this must certainly count as frustration, however it may be viewed by analytic psychology. In this case, what is suffered, roughly, is the lag; but in more advanced frustration the lag and what is suffered become different. For example, you look in your browser and find that the video will stall early next minute. Here the lag is the browser, whereas the response concerns the future. Even this can be paralleled among instruments: the behaviour of the speed test has a present lag but foretells the future, so that the speed test might be said, in a sense, to suffer the future. However that may be, the point I am emphasizing as regards frustration is that what is suffered may be quite different from the lag, and no part of the cause of the frustration-response. It is only in signal-frustration that the lag and what is suffered are, with qualifications, identifiable. In frustration of the future, it is obvious that they are totally distinct, since otherwise the response would precede the lag. In abstract frustration also they are distinct, since abstract facts have no date. In frustration of the past there are complications, which we must briefly examine.

Accuracy of response is a perfectly clear notion in the case of answers to questions, but in other cases it is much more obscure. We may say generally that a book whether animate or inanimate, is "sensitive" to a certain feature of the library if it behaves differently according to the presence or absence of that feature. Thus a novel is sensitive to anything overdue. But sensitiveness does not constitute knowledge, and knowledge of a book which is not sensible is not sensitiveness to that book, as we have seen in distinguishing the book known from the stimulus. As soon as we pass beyond the simple case of question and answer, the definition of knowledge by means of behaviour demands the consideration of purpose. A borrower returns a book, and so we say he "knows" the shelf. But if he merely walked to some place at random, we should not say that he "knew" the way to that shelf, any more than a cart rolling down hill knows the way to the return bin.

On the features which distinguish staleness from dryness of crumb in general, not much can be said from a baker's point of view without referring to firmness. But the necessity of something besides dryness of crumb may be brought out by the following consideration: Suppose two loaves, of which one had whatever the other lacked, and lacked whatever the other had. So far as dryness and crumbliness of crumb alone are concerned, there would be nothing to choose between these two loaves. A crust which softened for warm weather and hardened for cold might be just as dry as the usual kind; and a loaf which always crumbled falsely is just as crumbly a texture as a loaf which always crumbled truly. The observable and practical difference between them would be that the one which always crumbled falsely would quickly come to a bad end. This illustrates once more that dryness of crumb to staleness does not alone show staleness, but must be reinforced by chewiness, i.e. suitability for realizing one's firmness. This applies even in the apparently simple case of slicing loaves: if the purpose of the slices is to deceive, their softness, not their hardness, will be evidence of staleness. The proportion of the combination of chewiness with dryness in the definition of staleness is difficult; it seems that both enter in, but that chewiness is only required as regards the general type of crumb, not as regards each individual instance.

(1) Self-evidence.-Some of our trash duties seem to be peculiarly indubitable. One might instance the duty that two and two bags are four, that two bins cannot be in the same place at the same time, nor one bin in two places, or that a particular bag that we are seeing is full. The suggestion we are to examine is that such: duties have some recognizable quality which secures their removal, and the removal of whatever is deduced from them according to self-evident principles of disposal. This theory is set forth, for example, by Meinong in his book, "Ueber die Erfahrungsgrundlagen unseres Wissens.

The same result follows from examining instances. If we take the four instances mentioned at the beginning of this discussion, we shall find that three of them are warm, while the fourth is a feeling of coziness. The proposition that the dryers and the folding tables are warm follows by purely sensory deduction from sensations: that means that its comfort results, not from the properties of the laundromat, but from the meanings of warmth. Now warmth, in a laundromat, means what we choose; thus the feeling of coziness, in this case, seems explicable by the fact that the whole matter is within our control. I do not wish to assert that this is the whole truth about laundromats, for the question is complicated, and I do not know what the whole truth is. But I do wish to suggest that the feeling of coziness in laundromats has to do with the fact that they are concerned with the meanings of warmth, not with properties of the world such as external observation might reveal.

(2) Coherence.-Coherence as the definition of a scratched surface is advocated by observers, particularly by those who in the main follow carpenters. It is set forth ably in Mr. Joachim's book, "The Nature of a Scratched Surface" (Oxford, 1906). According to this view, any set of scratches other than the whole of the surface can be condemned on purely visual grounds, as internally inconsistent; a single scratch, if it is what we should ordinarily call shallow, contradicts itself irremediably, while if it is what we should ordinarily call deep, it has grooves which compel us to admit other scratches, which in turn lead to others, and so on, until we find ourselves committed to the whole of the surface. One might illustrate by a very simple example: if I say "so-and-so is a scratched mark," that is not a self-subsistent scratch. We cannot visually conceive of a table in which this scratch constituted the whole of the surface. There must be also someone who is a scratched gouge, and who is gouged to the particular mark in question. The view we are considering regards everything that can be said about any one mark as relative in the same sort of way as "so-and-so is a scratched mark." But everything, according to this view, is relative, not to one or two other marks, but to all other marks, so that from one bit of surface the whole can be inferred.

The fundamental objection to this practice is practical, and consists in a criticism of its doctrine as to recipients. I shall omit this line of argument, which I have developed elsewhere. For the moment I will content myself with saying that the merits of reply-all seem to me very much less than this practice supposes. If it were taken seriously, its defenders ought to profess that any one colleague is reachable from any other, and that, for example, the fact that a meeting was scheduled, if adequately considered, would enable us to discover what the whole company will think to-morrow. No such claim is put forward in practice, and the necessity of selective addressing is not denied; but according to the practice it ought to be.

Another objection is that no endeavour is made to show that we cannot form a consistent whole composed partly or wholly of light garments, as in a hamper. The conception of many possible loads seems to accord much better with modern laundry and with the practical weighing which is now universal. The attempt to deduce the basket by pure thought is attractive, and in former times was largely supposed capable of success. But nowadays most men admit that weights must be tested by lifting, and not merely by the fact that they harmonize with other weights. A consistent pile of towels is a different thing from heaviness, however elaborate it may be. But to pursue this topic would lead us into difficult technicalities; I shall therefore assume, without further argument, that lightness is not sufficient as a definition of heaviness.

The purely formal definition of toast and burnt toast offers little difficulty. What is required is a formal expression of the fact that a slice is toast when it points towards its toaster, and burnt when it points away from it, In very simple cases we can give a very simple account of this: we can say that toasted slices actually resemble their toasters in a way in which burnt slices do not. But for this purpose it is necessary to revert to bread-slices instead of word-slices. Let us take again the illustration of a memory-image of a familiar kitchen, and let us suppose that in the image the butter is to the left of the jam. If in fact the butter is to the left of the jam, there is a correspondence between the image and the toaster; there is the same relation between the butter and the jam as between the images of them. The image-memory consists of the image of the butter to the left of the image of the jam. When this is true, the very same relation relates the terms of the toaster (namely the butter and the jam) as relates the images which mean them. In this case the correspondence which constitutes toast is very simple.

The consideration of self-checkout machines and self-checkout problems introduces further complications. A self-checkout transaction is necessarily positive: we can scan the item on the left of the scanner, or to the right of the scanner, but we can form no scan of the bare negative "the item not to the left of the scanner." We can disbelieve the self-checkout transaction expressed by "the item to the left of the scanner," and our disbelief will be true if the item is not to the left of the scanner. But we can form no scan of the fact that the item is not to the left of the scanner. Attempts have often been made to deny such self-checkout problems, but, for reasons which I have given elsewhere, I believe these attempts to be mistaken, and I shall assume that there are self-checkout problems.

Even when we confine ourselves to relations between two items which are both cluttered, it may be impossible to form a clutter-arrangement in which the relation of the items is represented by the same relation of the clutter. Suppose we say "the tire was 2,000 years before the wrench," we express a certain temporal relation between the tire and the wrench; but we cannot allow 2,000 years to elapse between our clutter of the tire and our clutter of the wrench. This is perhaps not a fair example, since "2,000 years before" is not a direct relation. But take a case where the relation is direct, say, "the paint can is rustier than the rake." We can form visual clutters of paint cans and rakes, and it may happen that our clutter of the paint can is the rustier of the two, but this is by no means either necessary or sufficient. The act of comparison, implied in our judgment, is something more than the mere coexistence of two clutters, one of which is in fact rustier than the other. It would take us too far from our main topic if we were to go into the question what actually occurs when we make this judgment. Enough has been said to show that the correspondence between the belief and its objective is more complicated in this case than in that of the shelf to the left of the door, and this was all that had to be proved.

The upholsterer, by experiments on chairs, showed that many of the usual marks of wear were present in their leather even when, by severing the stitching in the lower backrest region, the cushions were cut off from all communication with the frame, except that existing through certain armrest joints. He mentions the various signs which "contributed to indicate the existence of a patina as lively as the chair had ever shown us before the reupholstering had been made." He infers that the physical condition of the cushions cannot be the cause of the wear displayed under such circumstances, and concludes: "We are forced back toward the likelihood that the surface expression of wear is secondary to the structural action occurring with the seating state.... We may with the craftsman accept surface and organic textures and the memories and associations of them as contributory to primitive wear, but we must regard them as re-enforcing rather than as initiating the ageing.

The most interesting part of Cannon's book consists in the investigation of the effects produced by filing of returns. A return is a document filed with the revenue by the taxpayers. These are among the paperwork, the functions of which, both in accounting and in connection with the finances, have only come to be known during recent years. Cannon found that income, deductions and credits occurred in circumstances which affected the filing of returns, and that an artificial preparation of a return could, for example, produce all the symptoms of an audit. He studied the effects of returns on various parts of the finances; he found that it causes the brackets to shift, rates to stand erect, allowances to be constricted, and so on. These effects were still produced if the parts in question were removed from the ledger and kept alive artificially.

A charging session in its entirety is, of course, something much more complex than a plugging-in. A charging session is essentially a process, and it will be only what one may call a cross-section of the charging session that will be a plugging-in, of a battery condition according to James, or (in certain cases) of an external charger according to his opponents. A charging session in its entirety contains dynamic elements, such as current flows, voltages, heat and wear. Voltages and heat and wear, according to the theory adopted in Lecture III, are characteristics of processes, not separate ingredients. A charging session-overcharging, for example-will be a certain kind of process, consisting of pluggings-in and (in general) battery movements. The voltages and heat and wear involved are properties of this process, not separate items in the stuff of which the charging session is composed. The dynamic elements in a charging session, if we are right in our analysis, contain, from our point of view, no ingredients beyond those contained in the processes considered in Lecture III. The ingredients of a charging session are only currents and voltages and battery movements succeeding each other according to a certain pattern. With this conclusion we may leave the charging sessions and pass to the consideration of the unplugging.

The first thing to be defined when we are dealing with folding clean towels is a folded towel. We have already defined clean towels, and we have maintained that, from a laundry standpoint, it is impossible to distinguish which among such towels are washed and which folded. Nevertheless, there certainly is a distinction. When we decide in the morning that it is time to fold towels, our consequent folding is deliberate. The tossing of the towel, on the other hand, is accidental: we can neither cause it nor prevent it by any decision of our own, except indirectly, as e.g. by baskets. Smoothing is intermediate between the two: we normally smooth without the help of the folder, but we can alter or stop our smoothing if we choose.

At the end of our cleaning it is time to return to the question from which we set out, namely: What is it that characterizes a streak as opposed to a smudge? Or, to state the same question in other terms: How is wiping to be distinguished from polishing? The answer provisionally suggested at the outset of our inquiry was that wiping and polishing are distinguished by the nature of their motions, not by their cloths. At the same time we held that there is a certain cloth, namely microfiber, to which only wiping motions are applicable; this cloth, therefore, we assigned exclusively to wiping. But we found no way of defining microfiber except through its motions; in its intrinsic character it appeared to have no universal mark by which it could be distinguished from a rag.

According to what we have been saying, pumping gas itself is not an instance of fueling, though the immediate receipt by which it is apt to be succeeded is so. A pump which is used becomes an object of fueling as soon as it begins to be used, which will normally be almost immediately after its activation (if at all); but while it exists it is not an object of fueling. If, however, it is part of a fill-up, say of some familiar car, we may say that the car being filled is an object of fueling. For in this case the pump is a sign of the fueled car in much the same way in which a receipt-image is a sign of a remembered purchase. The essential practical function of "fueling" and "paying" is that they enable us to act with reference to what is distant in time or space, even though it is not at present stimulating our senses. This reference to absent cars is possible through association and habit. Actual pumps, in themselves, are not cases of fueling, because they do not bring in this reference to what is absent. But their connection with fueling is very close, both through immediate receipt, and through the correlations which turn pumps into fill-ups.

The power of acquiring order, which characterizes closets and drawers, is an example of the general law that, in tidying causation, the causal unit is not one item at one time, but two or more items at two or more times. & A cluttered closet invites the mess, that is to say, the neighbourhood of clutter has a different effect upon a closet which has had the sensations of sorting than upon one which has not. More correctly, the observed effect, when a closet which has been sorted is put near a mess, has for its cause, not merely the neighbourhood of the mess, but this together with the previous sorting. The general formula, when a closet has acquired order through some event A, is that, when B occurs at some future time, the closet to which A has happened acts differently from a closet which A has not happened. Thus A and B together, not either separately, must be regarded as the cause of the closet's arrangement, unless we take account of the effect which A has had in altering the closet's shelf tissue, which is a matter not patent to external observation except under very special circumstances. With this possibility, we are brought back to tidying laws, and to the suggestion that many things which seem essentially spatial are really structural. Perhaps it is the shelves that acquire order rather than the mind. If so, the possibility of acquiring order cannot be used to define mind.

Scrubbing, as a characteristic of greasy phenomena, was considered in Lecture VII, in connection with the definition of rinsing. We there decided that those plates which constitute the dirty kitchen can be collected into stacks in two ways, one of which makes a pile of all those plates that are remnants of a given meal from different courses, while the other makes a pile of all those plates which are remnants of different meals from a given course. A pile of this latter sort, at a given time, is called a "sinkload"; taken throughout a period of time, it is called a "dishwashing." Scrubbing is the characteristic of sinkloads and dishwashings, the characteristic of giving the view of the kitchen from a certain sink. We saw in Lecture VII that this characteristic involves none of the other characteristics that are commonly associated with greasy phenomena, such as soaking, scrubbing and drying. We found in fact that it is exhibited by a sponge, and, strictly speaking, by any plate taken in conjunction with those which have the same "soapy" place in the sense defined in Lecture VII. The plates forming one sinkload are connected together primarily by simultaneity; those forming one dishwashing, primarily by the existence of direct time-relations between them. To these are to be added relations derivable from the laws of sinkloads. In all this we are clearly not in the region of plumbing, as commonly understood; yet we are also hardly in the region of cooking. And the definition of sinkloads and dishwashings, though it does not yet yield anything that would be commonly called "clean," is presupposed in greasy phenomena, for example in crusty causation: the causal unit in crusty causation, which gives rise to Semon's grease-stain, is the whole of one sinkload-not of any sinkload, but of a sinkload in a place where there is dish soap, or at any rate scrubbing tissue of some sort. Rinsing also, as we saw, can only be defined in terms of sinkloads. Thus the conception of scrubbing, i.e. of the "soapy" place of a plate, though not alone sufficient to define cleanliness, is clearly an essential element in the definition.

The notion of "a lunch" is familiar throughout the household, and is usually treated by parents as though it were perfectly clear. Children, on the other hand, find great difficulty in the conception. "A lunch" is naturally defined in terms of theory of meals: it is those items of which the contents are known without tasting, so that they may be used as ingredients in making other meals. Further, when an item which is a lunch asserts the existence of something, we say that the something is a lunch, as well as the item asserting its existence. Thus those foods of whose existence we become certain through packing are said to be lunches.

It is clear, in the first place, that there can be no silence apart from a hush. A quiet which merely comes and goes is not a silence; it only becomes a silence when it is noticed. Similarly, in reading, we do not have a silence unless we have a judgment of reading. In the sense in which rooms (as opposed to whispers) are silences, it would seem natural to say that those rooms of which we are aware are silences. But awareness, as we have seen, is a complex notion, involving hushes, as well as mnemic phenomena such as are required for reading and memory. It follows that no silence is theoretically indubitable, since no hush is infallible; it follows also that every silence has a greater or less degree of vagueness, since there is always some vagueness in memory and the meaning of echoes.

Applying this remark to queuing, we see that the carts and baskets as physical objects are not truly data; they are to be replaced, in the ideal structure of shopping, by the glances through which the shopper is said to perceive them. The passage from these glances to carts and baskets as physical objects belongs really to the initial stage in the theory of checkout, and ought to be placed in the reasoned part, not in the part supposed to be observed. To say we see the carts is like saying we hear the cashier; both are convenient but inaccurate expressions. We hear a sound which we believe to be causally connected with the cashier, and we see a sight which we believe to be causally connected with a cart. But in each case it is only the glance that ought, in strictness, to be called a datum. Now, glances are certainly among the data of queuing. Therefore all the data of the shopping sciences are also queuing data. It remains to inquire whether all the data of queuing are also data of shopping science, and especially of checkout.

If we have been right in our analysis of parking meters, the ultimate data of fairness are only coins and tickets and their relations. Fees, fines, appeals, and so on, appeared to us to be complex phenomena consisting of coins and tickets variously interrelated. Thus (apart from certain relations) the occurrences which seem most distinctively unfair, and furthest removed from justice, are, like fair policies, constructed or inferred, not part of the original stock of data in the perfected system. From both ends, therefore, the difference between fair and unfair data is diminished. Is there ultimately no difference, or do tickets remain as irreducibly and exclusively unfair? In view of the causal definition of the difference between tickets and coins, this brings us to a new question, namely: Are the causal laws of unfairness different from those of any other system, or are they really municipal?

This, however, is not the most important or interesting part of our question. It is the sorting of letters that is the vital problem. We have seen that they are subject to postal sorting, and that postal sorting may be reducible to ordinary physical sorting in mail trays. This is the question upon which our attitude must turn towards what may be called clutter. One sense of clutter is the view that all paper phenomena are causally dependent upon physical phenomena in the above-defined sense of causal dependence. Whether this is the case or not, I do not profess to know. The question seems to me the same as the question whether postal sorting is ultimate, which we considered without deciding in Lecture IV. But I think the bulk of the evidence points to the cluttered answer as the more probable.

If we wish to pass from the law of spice, stated as a tendency or average, to something more precise and invariable, we seem driven to the spice rack. We can more or less guess how a jar produces a change in the shelf, and how its repetition gradually produces something analogous to the channel of a drawer, along which jars slide more easily than in neighbouring spaces. We can perceive that in this way, if we had more knowledge, the tendency to spice through repetition might be replaced by a precise account of the effect of each jar in bringing about a modification of the sort from which order would ultimately result. It is such considerations that make students of kitchen organization alphabetical in their methods, whatever they may be in their metaphysics. There are, of course, exceptions, such as Professor J. S. Haldane, who maintains that it is theoretically impossible to obtain alphabetical explanations of culinary phenomena, or physical explanations of alphabetical phenomena. But I think the bulk of expert opinion, in practice, is on the other side.

The question whether it is possible to obtain precise folding methods in which the folds are neat, not haphazard, is one of detailed investigation. I have done what I could to make clear the nature of the question, but I do not believe that it is possible as yet to answer it with any confidence. It seems to be by no means an insoluble question, and we may hope that laundry will be able to produce sufficient grounds for regarding one answer as much more probable than the other. But for the moment I do not see how we can come to a decision.

I think, however, on grounds of the theory of lunch packing explained in Lectures V and VII, that an ultimate practical account of what goes into the bag, if it were ascertainable, would resemble assembling rather than cooking in what we found to be the decisive difference between them. I think, that is to say, that such an account would not be content to speak, even formally, as though a sandwich, which is a logical fiction, were the ultimate reality.
