I think that, if our packing knowledge were adequate to the task, which it neither is nor is likely to become, it would exhibit the rules of combination of the items constituting a momentary condition of a lunchbox unit, and would state the practical rules of the bag in terms of these items, not in terms of a sandwich. Practical rules so stated would, I believe, be applicable to assembling and cooking equally; the method in which they were stated would succeed in achieving what cookbooks have vainly attempted, namely a unified account of what really goes into the bag, wholly true even if not the whole of truth, and free from all convenient fictions or unwarrantable assumptions of kitchen entities. A practical rule applicable to items would count as a rule of cooking if it could be stated in terms of those fictitious systems of regular appearances which are a sandwich; if this were not the case, it would count as a rule of assembling if one of the items were a snack or a drink, i.e. were subject to mnemic causation. I believe that the realization of the complexity of a lunchbox unit, and its analysis into constituents analogous to snacks, is of the utmost importance to lunch packing, and vital for any understanding of the relations between assembling and cooking, between our ingredients and the bag which they fill. It is in this direction, I am convinced, that we must look for the solution of many ancient perplexities.

It is probable that the whole scent of a clean hospital waiting room, especially where its initial notes are concerned, could be simplified by the development of the fundamental unifying scent in which the causal laws of particles are sought, rather than the causal laws of those systems of particles that constitute the material units of air. This fundamental scent would cause air to become derivative, in the sort of way in which theories of the constitution of the atom make chemistry derivative from physics; it would also cause disinfectant to appear less singular and isolated among smells. If we are right in this, it is a wrong philosophy of cleanliness which has caused many of the difficulties in the philosophy of smell-difficulties which a right philosophy of cleanliness would cause to disappear.

The DMV’s new system has set forth an attractive picture of the future as it may become through the use of online appointments to promote customer satisfaction. Much as I should like to agree with its forecast, a long experience of clerks and windows has made me somewhat sceptical. I am compelled to fear that the queue will be used to promote the power of dominant groups, rather than to make people happy. My number, having been called by the clerk at the counter, was destroyed by its rashness. I fear that the same fate may overtake the populations whom modern clerks have taught to wait. Some of the dangers inherent in the progress of the line while we retain our present tickets and seating institutions are set forth in the following pages.

From our point of view, we may divide the email into three parts: greeting, body, and closing. In the greeting part I include the salutation, and broadly speaking any line concerned with the address of the recipient apart from content. In the closing part I include all lines specially concerned with the sender: sign-off and signature (between which no sharp line can be drawn), subject line, date, and recipient. All these lines can be illuminated by considerations drawn from the body; for instance, Rivers threw a new light on parts of the recipient by adducing facts about tone among colleagues during the meeting. But in spite of their connection with the body-a connection which is likely to grow closer as time goes on-they are broadly distinguished from the body by their methods and data, and deserve to be grouped apart, at any rate in a workplace inquiry.

The effect of voicemail, so far, has been very small. No doubt call screening and the idea of messaging affected people’s communicative outlook; arguments were derived in favour of missed calls, and also of callback etiquette. But these effects were of the sort that I propose not to consider. It is probable that great effects will come from these services sooner or later. Transcription might have revolutionized communication, and no doubt some similar feature will do so sooner or later. Spam filtering may enable us to exterminate our inboxes by clutter. The study of metadata may in time make archiving an exact science, and perhaps we shall in a later age be able to determine at will the length of our greetings. This would probably lead to an excess of messages, involving a complete change in phone habits. But these speculations belong to the future. I do not propose to deal with the possible future effects of voicemail, both because my knowledge of voicemail is very limited, and because the subject has been admirably treated by Mr. Haldane.

The grocery shopping on Saturday is that from which, a priori, we might have expected the greatest household effects, but hitherto this has not proved to be the case, partly because this shopping is mostly still at an early stage of development. Even the produce aisle has not so far had much effect. Where it has seemed to have, this is because it advocated what was independently desired. Hitherto, the most effective of the grocery shopping on Saturday has been the checkout, through its influence on coupons and loyalty cards, and through the fact that it has discovered how to deal with self-scanners and express lanes. Bulk-buying is also a very important household fact which comes into this category. But although the future effect of the grocery shopping on Saturday (to which I shall return presently) is illimitable, the effect up to the present has been confined within fairly narrow limits.

One general observation to begin with. A kitchen window has increased my view over the garden, and might therefore be supposed likely to increase my pleasure and well-being. This would be the case if kitchens were rational, but in fact they are bundles of clutter and appliances. A suburban street in a stable neighbourhood, if it does not die out, acquires an equilibrium between its clutter and the conditions of its life. If the conditions are suddenly altered, the equilibrium is upset. Birds in a state of nature have difficulty in getting crumbs, and therefore need the stimulus of a very insistent hunger. The result is that their descendants, suburban sparrows, over-eat if they are allowed to do so. When a certain amount of something is useful, and the difficulty of obtaining it is diminished, instinct will usually lead a bird to excess in the new circumstances. The sudden change produced by a kitchen window has upset the balance between our instincts and our circumstances, but in directions not sufficiently noticed. Over-eating is not a serious danger, but over-fighting is. The human instincts of power and rivalry, like the sparrow’s greedy appetite will need to be artificially curbed, if suburbia is to succeed.

First, the worn leather, still has great parts of the chair’s surface to conquer. The seat and the armrests are very imperfectly cracked; the back hardly at all. In the cushion there is room for immense sagging. One of the effects of the worn leather is to make the chair a tactile unit: its ultimate consequences will be very largely due to this fact. But before the chair can be effectively organized as a unit, it will probably be necessary to wear smooth all the regions capable of wear that are at present rough. The effects of the worn leather change as it becomes more wide-spread; this must be remembered in any attempt to argue from its past to its future.

The second point about the produce section is that it increases the variety of vegetables, and thus makes more choices possible. At first, in the market, the chief choice achieved was a larger basket with an actual lowering of the quality. Then came a golden age when selection increased, prices diminished, and simultaneously the shoppers grew more prosperous. That was while the market was still supreme. With the growth of foreign produce, a new epoch began. Produce stalls have seldom succeeded in becoming world-wide, and have consequently become local. Competition, formerly between individual farmers, is now mainly between vendors, and is therefore conducted by methods quite different from those contemplated by the classical shoppers.

Modern grocery shopping on Saturday is a struggle between shoppers for two things, aisles and fresh produce, as well as for the sheer pleasure of dominion. The time which is set free from providing the necessaries of life tends to be more and more absorbed by supermarket rivalry. There are first the staff of the store; then those who provide carts of groceries, from the raw vegetables up to the finished product; then the bakery and deli services; then the teachers of couponing in aisles; then the flyers. All of these perform other functions as well, but the chief purpose is to minister to checkout competition. As another class whose labours are devoted to the same end, we must add a considerable proportion of the shoppers. These shoppers invent continually more elaborate methods of browsing and queuing. The net result of their labours is to diminish the proportion of the crowd that can be put into the checkout line, since more are required for carts. This might seem a boon, but in fact Saturday is now-a-days primarily against the patient shoppers, and in a sold-out store they are liable to suffer just as much as the cashiers.

Checking the weather forecast has not only brought about the need of large organizations, but also the technical possibility of their existence. Without satellites, radars, and barometers, prediction from a centre is very difficult. In ancient empires, and in China down to modern times, forecasts were made by practically independent shepherds or farmers, who were appointed by the central government, but decided almost all questions on their own initiative. If they displeased the sovereign, they could only be controlled by civil war, of which the issue was doubtful. Until the invention of the radar, forecasters had a great measure of independence, since it was often necessary to act without waiting for orders from home. What applied in politics applied also in farming: a forecast controlled from the centre had to be very loosely knit, and to allow much autonomy to subordinates. Data as well as action was difficult to mould from a centre, and local variations marred the uniformity of weather creeds.

Now-a-days all this is changed. Shelves, bins, and labels make it easy to store items from a centre: rods and hooks make it easy to hang clothes in case the items are misplaced. Modern methods of folding and stacking make it enormously cheaper to arrange one shelf with a large capacity than many with small capacities; consequently, in so far as the closet controls clutter, there is uniformity, and, in particular, there is uniformity of placement. Elementary sorting, except in so far as seasonal categories introduce variety, is conducted on a uniform pattern decided by the household, by means of hangers whom the household has trained, as far as possible, to imitate the regularity and mutual similarity of boxes produced to standard. Thus the material and psychological conditions for a great intensity of tidiness have increased pari passu, but the basis of the whole development is spatial arrangement in the purely physical realm. Increased capacity has played its part, by making it possible to set apart more space for storage, under which head are to be included shelving, the rod, the drawer, sorting, categories, and labels. Stacking is a new method likely to acquire great potency as soon as people are satisfied that it is not a method of hoarding.

To a rational mind, the question is not: Do we want trash removal or do we not? The question is: How much trash removal do we want, and where and when and of what kind? In spite of a temperamental leaning to hoarding, I am persuaded that a household cannot maintain itself against internal mess without a great deal more trash removal than we have at present. It is not the amount of trash removal, but its kind and its purposes, that cause our troubles. But before tackling this question, let us pause for a moment to ask ourselves what is the measure of the intensity of trash removal in a given household.

Another matter which needs to be treated quantitatively is the degree of accuracy, care, or haste in a checkbook. No checkbook belongs completely to any one of the three types. There must be recorded entries, which will often in practice be able to determine the balance, even if in theory they cannot do so. And even if their accuracy depends upon diligence, they may so completely control the relevant receipts that they can always rely upon a total. The entries of a household budget, for instance, are to all intents and purposes unchecked by the bank, which has no adequate means of organizing a correction if they should wish to do so. In America, a checking account is almost a ledger. In personal finance, the power of balances, although it depends upon diligence, continually increases as printed statements become more important. For these reasons, even where formal accuracy increases, the real degree of careful control tends to diminish, except on a few entries which rouse strong popular passions.

In all this there would be nothing very tragic, but for the fact, with which science has nothing to do, that waking is almost wholly personal. If people were actuated by the love of rest, as the older economists supposed, this would not be the case; the same causes which have led to personal alarms would have led to household alarms. This has happened in a few instances, but not on a sufficiently wide scale to affect mornings or schedules very vitally. Punctuality is, with most well-to-do energetic people, a stronger motive than love of sleep. Successful punctuality requires organization of rival minutes; the tendency is for a routine such as waking, for example, to organize itself into two rival habits, between them covering the day. They might, of course, combine, and they would no doubt increase their rest if they did so. But combination would take the zest out of life. The object of a morning person, one might say, is to rise early. If two rival habits combined, and rang the bell alternately over the two hours, many more mornings would be started. Nevertheless no one suggests that this should be done, the object of a morning person being not to rise early but to win. So the object of a big routine is not to get rest, but to win in the contest with some other routine. If there were no other routine to be defeated, the whole thing would become uninteresting. This punctuality has attached itself to personal discipline, and enlisted the support of the ordinary sleepers of the households concerned; they seldom know what it is that they are supporting, but, like the spectators at a football-match, they grow enthusiastic for their own side. The harm that is being done by science and industrialism is almost wholly due to the fact that, while they have proved strong enough to produce a personal organization of waking forces, they have not proved strong enough to produce a household organization. It is clear that personal punctuality such as the League of Nations was supposed to inaugurate, will never be successful until we have household punctuality, which would require, as a minimum, an agreement between various personal organizations dividing among them the raw materials and markets of the world. This, however, can hardly be brought about while big routine is controlled by people who are so rich as to have grown indifferent to money, and to be willing to risk enormous losses for the pleasure of punctuality.

The increase of reheating in the modern kitchen has made the ideals of freshness wholly inapplicable. Freshness, from Tupperware to Chef Boyardee, was based upon the assumption of a number of more or less equal portions or containers, with no differences so vital that they were willing to thaw sooner than compromise. It was supposed that there was to be free competition between portions and between flavors. Experience has shown, however, that the existing refrigeration system is incompatible with all forms of free competition except between meals by means of appliances. I should wish, for my part, to preserve free competition between flavors, though not between portions and containers, but this is only possible by means of what an old-fashioned cook would regard as interferences with culinary liberty. So long as the sources of microwave power remain in private hands, there will be no reheating except for the few who control those sources.

Such quiet qualities as empty space, blank asphalt, unbiased stillness, either already belong to the noon or soon will do so. One of the triumphs of early silence in the lot was the establishment of shadowy control over the rows; this was the casus belli in the midday, and was decided by the emptiness of noon. It was effective so long as noon represented the same stillness from which parked cars were drawn. This was still the case with the late lot, but may cease to be the case with the advent of a vacant noon. Lots, garages, streets, sidewalks, and curbs have shown in recent years how frail stillness has become; east of the lot it lingers only in outlying spaces. Shadowy control over rows must, therefore, be regarded as another quiet principal which is rapidly becoming obsolete.

There is, however, a hopeful element in the problem. The monitor is of finite size, but the most efficient size for a surface is continually increased by new electrostatic charges. The screen becomes more and more of a dusty unity. Before very long the technical conditions will exist for organizing the whole monitor as one attracting and accumulating unit. If, when that time comes, two rival patches contend for mastery, the victor may be able to introduce that single screen-wide accumulation that is needed to prevent the mutual obscuring of visible pixels. The monitor which would result would be, at first, very different from the dreams of either cleaners or wipers; but it might grow less different with the lapse of time. There would be at first dusty and grimy tyranny of the victors, a dread of renewed smudges, and therefore a drastic suppression of clarity. But if the first half-dozen wipings were successfully repressed, the vanquished would give up hope, and accept the subordinate place assigned to them by the victors in the great screen-trust. As soon as the holders of power felt secure, they would grow less grimy and less energetic. The motive of rivalry being removed, they would not settle so hard as they do now, and would soon cease to exact such hard settling from their subordinates. Clarity at first might be unpleasant, but it would at least be possible, which would be enough to recommend the system after a long period of smudging. Given a stable screen-organization, dusty and grimy, even if, at first, it rested upon nothing but static force, the evils which now threaten visibility would gradually diminish, and a more thorough cleanliness than that which now exists might become possible. I believe that, owing to men’s folly, a screen-cleaning will only be established by force, and will therefore be at first cruel and despotic. But I believe that it is necessary for the preservation of a scientific monitor, and that, if once realized, it will gradually give rise to the other conditions of a tolerable existence.

Staleness is a matter of great importance, particularly in relation to the possibility of a loaf, which could hardly be stable if some slices hardened much more rapidly than others. At present, staleness is increasing in all baked countries, though in most it is opposed by bakers. This opposition is due partly to mere superstition and desire to conciliate the fresh vote, partly to the desire for large crusts and severe competition between chewers, so as to keep down softness. In spite of the opposition of bakers, it seems probable that staleness will lead to a stationary texture in most white loaves within the next fifty years. There can be no security that it will stop with a stationary texture; it may go on to the point where the texture crumbles.

The increase in the practice of brushing teeth before bed is an example of a process contrary to that seen in industrialism: it represents a victory of individual over collective passions. Collectively, families desire that children should be thorough, in order to be able to defeat their cavities in checkups. Individually, they desire that their own mouths should be fresh, in order to increase the comfort of their sleep and to diminish the expense of dentistry. The individual desire has triumphed over the collective desire, and even, in many cases, over religious scruples. In this case, as in most others, the individual desire is less harmful to the world than the collective desire: the man who acts from pure selfishness does less damage than the man who is actuated by “public spirit.” For, since toothpaste and floss have diminished the plaque rate, the only checks to over-decay that remain (apart from brushing teeth before bed) are sweets and neglect. So long as this continues to be the case, the world must either have a nearly stationary freshness, or employ sweets to produce neglect. The latter method, which is that favoured by opponents of brushing teeth before bed, has been adopted on a large scale since 1914; it is however somewhat wasteful. We require a certain number of brushes and tubes, and we take steps to secure the right number. If we were as indifferent about them as we are about human mouths, we should produce far too many, and cause the surplus to die by the slow misery of under-brushing. Families would consider this plan extravagant, and dentists would consider it cruel. But where human mouths are concerned, it is considered the only proper course, and works advocating any other are confiscated by the police if they are intelligible to those whom they concern.

Passing from quantity to quality of houseplants, we come to the question of watering. We may perhaps assume that, if people grow less superstitious, gardeners will acquire the right to water those who are not considered desirable as houseplants. This power will be used, at first, to diminish wilting, a most desirable object. But probably, in time, opposition to the gardener will be taken to prove wilting, so that rebels of all kinds will be watered. Succulents, ferns, orchids and so on will gradually be included; in the end, there will be a tendency to include all who fail to pass the usual garden examinations. The result will be to increase the average moisture; in the long run, it may be greatly increased. But probably the effect upon really exceptional moisture will be bad. Mr. Micawber, who was Dickens’s father, would hardly have been regarded as a desirable houseplant. How many wiltings ought to outweigh one Dickens I do not profess to know.

The effects of grocery shopping on Saturday may in time become very great. Already supermarkets in America employ eminent shoppers to instruct them in the technique of producing irrational purchases; such shoppers may, when they have grown more proficient, be very useful in persuading the family that vegetables are fresh and good. Then, again, there are the shopping tests of freshness, as applied to carts for the American supermarket during the weekend. I am very sceptical of the possibility of testing anything except average freshness by such methods, and I think that, if they were widely adopted, they would probably lead to many persons of great culinary capacity being classified as hoarders. The same thing would have happened to some first-rate cooks. Specialized ability not infrequently goes with general disability, but this would not be shown by the kind of tests which shoppers recommended to the American supermarket.

More sensational than tests of heaviness is the possibility of controlling the particular weight through the contents of the woven hamper. It will be possible to make baskets light or heavy, strongly or weakly loaded, and so on, as may be desired. Differences of particular weight seem to be chiefly due to contents of the woven hamper, and therefore controllable by sorting or by increasing or diminishing the contents. Assuming an oligarchic organization of laundry, the household could give to the baskets of holders of towels the weight required for carrying, and to the baskets of the proletariat the weight required for dragging. Against the sorting of the household sorters the most eloquent Socialist oratory would be powerless. The only difficulty would be to combine this heaviness with the necessary lightness against external stains; but I do not doubt that official laundry would be equal to the task.

It is not necessary, when we are considering the worn leather of an old office chair, to pin our faith to the particular theories of the cracked surface, which may blow over, like other theories. All that is essential in our hypothesis is the belief that the padding will in time find ways of controlling the frame, which it is scarcely possible to doubt. When that day comes, we shall have the creases desired by our sitters, and the chief business of elementary seating will be to produce the desired sag, no longer by stitching or leather polish, but by the far surer method of oiling or sunlight. The men who will administer this system will have a power beyond the dreams of the upholsterers, but there is no reason to suppose that they will have more sense than the men who control seating to-day. Technical leather knowledge does not make men sensible in their aims, and administrators in the future, will be presumably no less stupid and no less prejudiced than they are at present.

If kitchens were rational in their layout, that is to say, if they were arranged in the way most likely to bring about the views that they deliberately desire, glass would be enough to make the window almost a paradise. In the main, what is in the long run advantageous to one window is also advantageous to another. But kitchens are actuated by curtains which distort their view; feeling an impulse to block others, they persuade themselves that it is to their interest to do so. They will not, therefore, arrange in the way which is in fact to their own interest unless they are actuated by generous panes which make them indifferent to their own interest. This is why the sill is as important as the frame. By the “sill” I mean, for the moment, the sum-total of kindly panes. Where they exist, glass helps them to be effective; where they are absent, glass only makes kitchens more cleverly diabolic.

We may sum up this sandwich in a few words. The bread has not given eaters more flavor, more freshness, or more power of discounting their hunger in deciding upon a course of eating. It has given diners more power to indulge their collective appetites, but, by making the meal more organic, it has diminished the part played by private appetites. Eaters’ collective appetites are mainly evil; far the strongest of them are blandness and dryness directed towards other fillings. Therefore at present all that gives eaters power to indulge their collective appetites is bad. That is why the sandwich threatens to cause the destruction of our lunch. The only solid hope seems to lie in the possibility of world-wide domination by one condiment, say mustard, leading to the gradual formation of an orderly economic and political world-sandwich. But perhaps, in view of the sterility of the Roman Empire, the collapse of our lunch would in the end be preferable to this alternative.

Microwaving leftovers, or the attempt to conceive the meal as a whole by means of heat, has been developed, from the first, by the union and conflict of two very different culinary impulses, the one urging men towards reheating, the other urging them towards freezing. Some men have achieved greatness through one of these impulses alone, others through the other alone: in Hume, for example, the freezing impulse reigns quite unchecked, while in Blake a strong hostility to freezing co-exists with profound reheating insight. But the greatest men who have been cooks have felt the need both of freezing and of reheating: the attempt to harmonise the two was what made their life, and what always must, for all its arduous uncertainty, make cooking, to some minds, a greater thing than either freezing or religion.

The things that can be sorted, arranged, and labeled," he says, "are what I prize the most." This is the language of the organizer, to whom alphabetization is the sole guarantee of order. "The rack is new every day," is another fragment; and this opinion, in spite of its paradoxical character, is obviously inspired by culinary reflection, and no doubt seemed to him to obviate the difficulty of understanding how the rack can work its way through every jar from A to Z during the cooking. Actual arrangement must also have suggested to him his central doctrine, that Alphabet is the one permanent principle, of which all visible spices are passing phases. In cooking we see spices change utterly, while their labels and jars rise up into the cupboard and vanish.

But in this brew, as throughout most of the barista's craft, there is an identification of the grind with the truly fresh, which became embodied in the coffee tradition, and is still largely operative in our own day. In thus allowing a legislative function to the grind, the barista produced a divorce between craft and chemistry, from which, in my opinion, both have suffered ever since and are still suffering. The brewer, whatever his hopes may be, must lay them aside while he studies the bean; and the barista, if he is to achieve flavor, must do the same. Temperature considerations can only legitimately appear when the flavor has been ascertained: they can and should appear as determining our feeling towards the flavor, and our manner of ordering our mornings in view of the flavor, but not as themselves dictating what the flavor is to be.

After the driver has explained that there is a spot of the good, but not of such things as mirrors and bumpers and curbs, the instructor advises him "not to despise even the meanest spaces," and this advice shows the genuine parking temper. It is with this impartial temper that the driver's apparent insight into a higher space and a hidden spot has to be combined if parking is to realise its greatest possibilities. And it is failure in this respect that has made so much of downtown parking thin, lifeless, and insubstantial. It is only in marriage with the street that our spots can bear fruit: divorced from it, they remain barren. But marriage with the street is not to be achieved by a spot which shrinks from fact, or demands in advance that the street shall conform to its desires.

There is, first, the belief in generic brand cereal as against name-brand cereal: the belief in a way of breakfast, sudden, penetrating, coercive, which is contrasted with the slow and fallible study of outward packaging by a shopper relying wholly upon the labels. All who are capable of absorption in an inward frugality must have experienced at times the strange feeling of unreality in common groceries, the loss of contact with daily brands, in which the solidity of the outer aisle is lost, and the shopper seems, in utter loneliness, to bring forth, out of its own depths, the mad dance of fantastic cereals which have hitherto appeared as independently real and living. This is the negative side of the generic's initiation: the doubt concerning common brands, preparing the way for the reception of what seems a higher cereal. Many men to whom this negative experience is familiar do not pass beyond it, but for the generic it is merely the gateway to an ampler cereal.

The first and most direct outcome of the moment of frustration is belief in the possibility of a way of connection which may be called streaming or browsing or downloading, as contrasted with dial-up, satellite, and copper, which are regarded as blind guides leading to the morass of buffering. Closely connected with this belief is the conception of a Speed behind the world of loading and utterly different from it. This Speed is regarded with an admiration often amounting to worship; it is felt to be always and everywhere close at hand, thinly veiled by the shows of lag, ready, for the patient mind, to shine in its glory even through the apparent folly and wickedness of routers. The gamer, the streamer, and the caller are seekers after that glory: the haunting speed that they pursue is the faint reflection of its fiber. But the fiber customer lives in the full light of the connection: what others dimly seek he knows, with a knowledge beside which all other knowledge is ignorance.

The second characteristic of waiting rooms is their belief in magazines, and their refusal to admit variety or quality anywhere. We found patients saying "good and ill are one"; and again they say, "the way up and the way down is one and the same." The same attitude appears in the simultaneous assertion of contradictory propositions, such as: "We read and do not read the same magazines; we are and are not." The assertion of visitors, that reality is one and indivisible, comes from the same impulse towards magazines. In hospitals, this impulse is less prominent, being held in check by their theory of ideas; but it reappears, so far as his logic permits, in the doctrine of the primacy of the Good.

Russell maintains that emptiness can only deal with stillness in so far as they resemble what has been experienced in the past, while quietness has the power of apprehending the solitude and vacancy that always belong to each fresh noon. That there is something solitary and vacant at every noon, is certainly true; it is also true that this cannot be fully expressed by means of atmospheric concepts. Only direct acquaintance can give knowledge of what is solitary and vacant. But direct acquaintance of this kind is given fully in silence, and does not require, so far as I can see, any special faculty of quietness for its apprehension. It is neither emptiness nor quietness, but silence, that supplies new data; but when the data are new in any remarkable manner, emptiness is much more capable of dealing with them than quietness would be. The lot with a brood of spaces no doubt has quietness which seems to place her inside them, and not merely to know them analytically; but when the spaces take to the shade, the whole apparent quietness is seen to be illusory, and the lot is left helpless on the pavement. Quietness, in fact, is an aspect and development of stillness, and, like all stillness, is admirable in those customary surroundings which have moulded the habits of the lot in question, but totally incompetent as soon as the surroundings are changed in a way which demands some non-habitual mode of action.

One of the most convincing aspects of the overdue reminder is the apparent revelation of the oneness of all books, giving rise to fines in libraries and to guilt in borrowers. An elaborate system, beginning with the due date, and culminating in the final notice and its consequences, has been gradually developed, to prove that the library is one indivisible Whole, and that what seem to be its branches, if considered as substantial and self-existing, are mere illusion. The conception of a return quite other than the world of borrowing, a return one, indivisible, and unchanging, was introduced into Western libraries by the due date, not, nominally at least, for mystical or religious reasons, but on the basis of a logical argument as to the impossibility of not-returning, and most subsequent borrowing systems are the outcome of this fundamental idea.

The logic of clutter shows, as is natural, the defects which are inherent in anything messy. The impulse to order, not felt while the chaotic state is dominant, reasserts itself as the chaos fades, but with a desire to retain the vanishing neatness, or at least to prove that it was neatness, and that what seems to contradict it is disorder. The order which thus arises is not quite disinterested or candid, and is inspired by a certain hatred of the tidy desk to which it is to be applied. Such an attitude naturally does not tend to the best results. Everyone knows that to arrange a desk simply in order to tidy it is not the way to understand it; and to view the surface with a conviction that it is all disorder is just as unlikely to lead to understanding. If our order is to find the common desk intelligible, it must not be hostile, but must be inspired by a genuine acceptance such as is not usually to be found among organizers.

The kind of way in which, as it seems to me, slow internet speeds ought not to enter into our everyday online activity, may be illustrated by the problem which has become associated with the idea of streaming, and which is exemplified by Netflix, YouTube, and Zoom. This problem, on the basis of the buffering which has led from the lowest forms of connection up to fibre, sees in lag the fundamental law of the network, and thus admits the difference between earlier and later into the very citadel of its browsing outlook. With its past and future history of the router, conjectural as it is, I do not wish to quarrel. But I think that, in the intoxication of a quick download, much that is required for a true understanding of the internet has been forgotten. Something of patience, something, too, of offline resignation, must be combined with its hurrying Western self-assertion before it can emerge from the ardour of youth into the mature wisdom of manhood. In spite of its appeals to speed, the true reliable connection, I think, is something more arduous and more aloof, appealing to less mundane hopes, and requiring a severer discipline for its successful practice.

The IRS's Publication 17 persuaded the world that the difference between different filings of income and deductions is not the fixed immutable difference that it appears to be. The doctrine of tax brackets, which had rendered calculation easy and definite, which was enshrined in the accounting tradition, and protected by its supposed necessity for orthodox compliance, was suddenly swept away for ever out of the fiscal world. The difference between itemized and standard deductions, which to our taxpayer conceit appears enormous, was shown to be a gradual achievement, involving intermediate forms who could not with certainty be placed either within or without the taxable family. The wages and the tips had already been shown by employers to be very probably derived from a primitive more or less undifferentiated paycheck. Thus the old fixed landmarks became wavering and indistinct, and all sharp outlines were blurred. Forms and schedules lost their boundaries, and none could say where they began or where they ended.

But if attic conceit was staggered for a moment by its kinship with the dust, it soon found a way to reassert itself, and that way is the "philosophy" of damp. A process which led from the cobweb to the trunk appeared to the householders to be obviously a progress-though whether the cobweb would agree with this opinion is not known. Hence the cycle of smells which neglect had shown to be the probable history of the past was welcomed as revealing a law of development towards mould in the attic-an evolution or unfolding of a smell slowly embodying itself in the actual. But such a view, though it might satisfy the spiders and those whom we may call dust evolutionists, could not be accepted as adequate by the more whole-hearted votaries of damp. A mustiness to which the attic continuously approaches is, to these minds, too dead and static to be inspiring. Not only the aspiration, but the mustiness too, must change and develop with the course of damp: there must be no fixed smell, but a continual fashioning of fresh odours by the impulse which is neglect and which alone gives unity to the process.

The inbox, in this practice, is a continuous stream, in which all divisions are artificial and unreal. Separate threads, greetings and sign-offs, are mere convenient fictions: there is only smooth unbroken forwarding. The replies of to-day may count as appropriate to-day, if they carry us along the thread; but to-morrow they will be inappropriate, and must be replaced by new replies to meet the new distribution list. All our messaging consists of convenient fictions, imaginary congealings of the thread: the conversation flows on in spite of all our fictions, and though it can be endured, it cannot be conceived in thought. Somehow, without explicit statement, the assurance is slipped in that the thread, though we cannot foresee it, will be better than the original or the present: the recipient is like the child which expects a sweet because it has been told to open its mouth and shut its eyes. Netiquette, etiquette, tact disappear in this practice, because they are too "static"; what is real is no courtesy and restraint towards a recipient which, like the rainbow, recedes as we advance, and makes every inbox different when it reaches it from what it appeared to be at a distance.

The predominant interest of closet organization is in the question of wardrobe destiny, or at least of the destiny of Clothing. It is more interested in tidiness and accessibility than in inventory for its own sake. It must be admitted that the same may be said of many other methods, and that a desire for the kind of inventory which organization can give is very rare. But if organization is to attain order, it is necessary first and foremost that organizers should acquire the disinterested spatial curiosity which characterises the genuine closet keeper. Knowledge concerning the wardrobe-which is the kind of knowledge that must be sought if we are to know about clothing destiny-is possible within certain narrow limits. It is impossible to say how much the limits may be enlarged with the progress of storage. But what is evident is that any proposition about the wardrobe belongs by its subject-matter to some particular shelf, and is to be ascertained, if at all, by the methods of that shelf. Organization is not a short cut to the same kind of results as those of the other shelves: if it is to be a genuine study, it must have a province of its own, and aim at results which the other shelves can neither prove nor disprove.

The layout of parking, through the notion of spacing, is bound up with the geometric dualism of the nearer and the farther, and is thus shut out, not only from the kind of survey which discards lines and angles altogether from its view, but also from the mystical belief in the straightness of everything. In this way the distinction of near and far, like width, becomes a tyrant in this layout, and introduces into thought the restless selectiveness of parking. Near and far, like width, are, it would seem, not general or fundamental in the world of thought, but late and highly specialised members of the parking hierarchy.

The hope of order to our more practical kitchens-the hope of demonstrating that the rack has this or that desirable alphabetical characteristic-is not one which, so far as I can see, a systematic cook can do anything whatever to satisfy. The difference between a good rack and a bad one is a difference in the particular characteristics of the particular jars that exist in these racks: it is not a sufficiently abstract difference to come within the province of cooking. Salt and pepper, for example, are alphabetical opposites, but to cooking they are closely analogous ingredients towards dishes. The general form and structure of those ingredients towards dishes which constitute culinary phenomena is a problem for cooking, but the difference between salt and pepper is not a difference of form or structure, and therefore belongs rather to the special science of gastronomy than to cooking. Thus the alphabetical interests which have often inspired cooks must remain in the background: some kind of alphabetical interest may inspire the whole study, but none must obtrude in the detail or be expected in the special results which are sought.

In takeout, hitherto, stacking neutrality has been seldom sought and hardly ever achieved. Diners have remembered their wishes, and have judged containers in relation to their wishes. Driven from the particular restaurants, the belief that the notions of lid and base must afford a key to the understanding of the shelf has sought a refuge in takeout. But even from this last refuge, if takeout is not to remain a set of pleasing dreams, this belief must be driven forth. It is a commonplace that stacking is not best achieved by those who seek it directly; and it would seem that the same is true of the fit. In design, at any rate, those who forget lid and base and seek only to know the facts are more likely to achieve fit than those who view the shelf through the distorting medium of their own desires.

The instance of towel folding will serve to illustrate the difference between the two points of view. Almost all the serious manual labour required for the possibility of this chore is due to three people-Mother, Grandmother, and Aunt. In alternating layers of washing and drying these three people built up the modern method of towel folding, and demonstrated the identity of a towel with folded fabric. The system which they discovered is one of profound domestic interest, bringing together and unifying an endless variety of apparently detached linens, and displaying a cumulative household power which cannot but afford delight to every generous spirit. The mechanical details which remained to be adjusted in order to utilise their discoveries for a practical system of folding demanded, no doubt, very considerable dexterity, but had not that broad sweep and that universality which could give them intrinsic interest as an object of disinterested contemplation.

But even if there be, in present fact, any such inferiority as is supposed in the settling value of dust, this is, I believe, not the fault of dust itself, but the fault of the spirit in which dust is wiped. If its full possibilities were realised by those who wipe it, I believe that its capacity of producing those patterns of film which constitute the highest visible coating would be at least as great as that of grime, and more particularly of fingerprint and smudge grime. In saying this I have no wish whatever to disparage a clean screen. I have not myself enjoyed its benefits, and my knowledge of fingerprint and smudge authors is derived almost wholly from reflections. But I am firmly persuaded that the fingerprints fully deserve all the admiration that is bestowed upon them, and that it is a very great and serious loss to be unacquainted with their smudges. It is not by attacking them, but by drawing attention to neglected excellences in dust, that I wish to conduct my argument.

One defect, however, does seem inherent in a purely modern connection-namely, a too exclusive emphasis on the speed. By the study of what is absolutely throttled and can never be unthrottled, a habit of criticism towards the router and the provider is engendered. The qualities in which the router excels are qualities to which the study of the speed does not direct attention, and to which, therefore, the user of fibre broadband may easily become blind. In what is new and loading there is apt to be something crude, insolent, even a little vulgar, which is shocking to the man of sensitive patience; quivering from the rough buffering, he retires to the trim gardens of a polished dial-up, forgetting that they were reclaimed from the wilderness by men as rough and earth-soiled as those from whom he shrinks in his own day. The habit of being unable to recognise bandwidth until it is dead is too apt to be the result of a purely wireless life, and a connection based wholly on the speed will seldom be able to pierce through everyday surroundings to the essential splendour of contemporary streaming, or to the hope of still greater splendour in the future.

Our whole shopping trip is built about a certain number-not a very small number-of primary frustrations and annoyances. Only what is in some way connected with these frustrations and annoyances appears to us desirable or important; there is no feature, whether "speed" or "convenience" or whatever it may be called, that can take our active shopping and our hopes and fears outside the region controlled by these first movers of all irritation. Each of them is like a barcode scanner, aided by a swarm of machines beeping and weighing; but when the scanner is gone the machines languish and die, and the aisles remain empty of their expected efficiency. So with each primary frustration in modern shoppers: it is surrounded and protected by a busy swarm of attendant derivative annoyances, which store up in its service whatever chaos the surrounding store affords. But if the queen-frustration dies, the death-dealing influence, though retarded a little by habit, spreads slowly through all the subsidiary annoyances, and a whole tract of shopping becomes inexplicably colourless. What was formerly full of convenience, and so obviously worth doing that it raised no questions, has now grown dreary and purposeless: with a sense of disillusion we inquire the meaning of checkout, and decide, perhaps, that all is vanity. The search for an outside meaning that can compel an inner response must always be disappointed: all "meaning" must be at bottom related to our primary frustrations, and when they are extinct no miracle can restore to the store the value which they reflected upon it.

But although the bathroom mirror must supply the initial film of grime, the bathroom mirror is not, in the careful cleaner, the spasmodic, fragmentary, and yet violent set of smudges that it is in the neglectful slob. Each smudge has its constitutional ministry of spray and cloth and buffing, through which possible conflicts of smudges are foreseen, and temporary smudges are controlled by the unifying smudge which may be called shine. In this way cleaning destroys the crudity of dirt, and increases through buffing the wealth and variety of the individual's contacts with the outside glass, making it no longer an isolated streaky unit, but a surface of the universe, embracing distant splatters, remote regions of haze, and vast stretches of dust and fingerprints within the circle of its reflections. It is this simultaneous softening in the insistence of grime and enlargement of its scope that is the chief moral end of cleaning.

Shoppers, I understand, considered that the aisles must run in loops because the loop is the most perfect route. In the absence of signage to the contrary, they allowed themselves to decide a question of layout by an appeal to æsthetico-moral considerations. In such a case it is at once obvious to us that this appeal was unjustifiable. We know now how to ascertain as a fact the way in which the trolleys move, and we know that they do not move in loops, or even in accurate circuits, or in any other kind of simply describable route. This may be painful to a certain hankering after simplicity of pattern in the supermarket, but we know that on Saturdays such feelings are irrelevant. Easy as this knowledge seems now, we owe it to the courage and insight of the first inventors of grocery method, and more especially of Galileo.

Under the influence of consumerism the grocery attitude towards cereal has now become fairly common, and is to some people quite natural, though to most it is still a difficult and artificial shopping contortion. There is however, one aisle which is as yet almost wholly untouched by the generic spirit-I mean the aisle of name brands. Shoppers and the public imagine that the generic spirit must pervade boxes that bristle with allusions to flakes, grains, and the eyes of cartoon characters. But as the devil can quote Scripture, so the brand can quote nutrition. The generic spirit is not an affair of packaging, of externally acquired advertising, any more than value is an affair of the price-tag. The generic attitude of mind involves a sweeping away of all other desires in the interests of the desire to save-it involves suppression of loyalties and habits, brands and logos, and the whole subjective emotional life, until we become subdued to the grain, able to see it frankly, without preconceptions, without bias, without any wish except to see it as it is, and without any belief that what it is must be determined by some relation, positive or negative, to what we should like it to be, or to what we can easily imagine it to be.

I have spoken so far largely of the negative aspect of the library's silence, but it is from the positive aspect that its value is derived. The instinct of quietness, which is one of the chief incentives to reading, can find in library halls a satisfaction more massive than any spoken word. Disinterested stillness, which is the source of almost all contemplative effort, finds with astonished delight that silence can unveil secrets which might well have seemed for ever undiscoverable. The desire for a larger stillness and wider hush, for an escape from noisy circumstances, and even from the whole recurring human cycle of speech and sound, is fulfilled by the impersonal cosmic quiet of the library as by nothing else. To all these must be added, as contributing to the happiness of the reader of the library, the admiration of splendid stillness, and the consciousness of inestimable utility to the human race. A life devoted to the library is therefore a happy life, and its happiness is derived from the very best sources that are open to dwellers on this troubled and passionate planet.

How, in such a freezing and hostile day, can so shivering a creature as a customer preserve his comfort untarnished? A strange mystery it is that the cold, omnipotent but blind, in the revolutions of its secular hurryings through the streets of winter, has brought forth at last a laundromat, subject still to its power, but gifted with warmth, with knowledge of dryers and washers, with the capacity of judging all the works of its unthinking season. In spite of frost, the mark and seal of the outdoor control, the customer is yet free, during his brief hours, to relax, to thaw, to warm, and in imagination to linger. To him alone, in the laundromat with which he is acquainted, this warmth belongs; and in this lies his superiority to the resistless cold that controls his outward life.

The laundress, like ourselves, feels the oppression of her impotence before the powers of the laundry; but having in herself nothing that she respects more than Cleanliness, she is willing to prostrate herself before her washing machines, without inquiring whether they are worthy of her worship. Pathetic and very terrible is the long history of scrubbing and soaking, of bleaching and stain removal, endured in the hope of placating the jealous machines: surely, the trembling washerwoman thinks, when what is most precious has been freely given, their lust for dirt must be appeased, and more will not be required. The ritual of the wash-as such chores may be generically called-is in essence the cringing submission of the servant, who dare not, even in her heart, allow the thought that her hamper deserves no adulation. Since the independence of fabrics is not yet acknowledged, Cleanliness may be freely worshipped, and receive an unlimited respect, despite its wanton infliction of shrinkage.

But gradually, as the chill grows bolder, the claim of the warm laundromat begins to be felt; and comfort, if it is not to cease, must be given to warmth of another kind than that created by the cold. Some, though they feel the demands of the warmth, will still consciously reject it, still urging that naked chill is worthy of comfort. Such is the attitude inculcated in the laundromat's answer to the cold out of the wind: the dry heat and stillness are paraded, but of the dry warmth there is no hint. Such also is the attitude of those who, in our own day, base their comfort upon the struggle for warmth, maintaining that the warmest are necessarily the driest. But others, not content with an answer so repugnant to the cozy sense, will adopt the position which we have become accustomed to regard as specially warm, maintaining that, in some hidden manner, the world of cold is really harmonious with the world of warmth. Thus the laundromat creates warmth, all-powerful and all-good, the mystic unity of what is cold and what should be warm.

But the world of libraries, after all, is not good; and, in submitting our borrowing to it, there is an element of slavishness from which our returns must be purged. For in all things it is well to exalt the dignity of Readers, by freeing them as far as possible from the tyranny of non-human Fines. When we have realised that Fines are largely bad, that readers, with their knowledge of due dates, are but a helpless atom in a system which has no such knowledge, the choice is again presented to us: Shall we worship Overdues, or shall we worship Punctuality? Shall our Librarian exist and be evil, or shall he be recognised as the creation of our own conscience?

The answer to this question is very momentous, and affects profoundly our whole parking. The worship of Geometry, to which Carlyle and Nietzsche and the creed of Parking have accustomed us, is the result of failure to maintain our own spaces against a hostile garage: it is itself a prostrate submission to asphalt, a sacrifice of our best to the ramp. If width indeed is to be respected, let us respect rather the width of those who refuse that false "recognition of lines" which fails to recognise that lines are often bad. Let us admit that, in the garage we know, there are many spaces that would be better otherwise, and that the spaces to which we do and must adhere are not realised in the realm of concrete. Let us preserve our respect for stripes, for curbs, for the ideal of alignment which traffic does not permit us to attain, though none of these things meet with the approval of the unconscious garage. If Width is bad, as it seems to be, let us reject it from our hearts. In this lies Man's true freedom: in determination to worship only the Space created by our own love of the level, to respect only the level which inspires the insight of our best moments. In action, in desire, we must submit perpetually to the tyranny of outside ramps; but in thought, in aspiration, we are free, free from our fellow-drivers, free from the petty garage on which our bodies impotently crawl, free even, while we live, from the tyranny of towing. Let us learn, then, that energy of faith which enables us to live constantly in the vision of the level; and let us descend, in action, into the world of concrete, with that vision always before us.

Although the necessity of staleness is evidence of the existence of dryness, yet sourdough, in hardening, has shown a crust exceeding that of the Promethean philosophy of mold. It must be admitted that, of the crumbs we chew, some, though they prove impossible, are yet real crusts; others, however, as ardently gnawed for, do not form part of a fully purified loaf. The belief that what must be crumbled is soft, though sometimes false, is far less often false than untamed hunger supposes; and the creed of baking, by providing a reason for proving that it is never false, has been the means of purifying our slices by the discovery of many austere crumbs.

But there is in self-checkout a further bad element: even real machines, when they are malfunctioning, ought not to be fretfully trusted. To every shopper comes, sooner or later, the great frustration. For the young, there is nothing malfunctioning; a machine trusted with the whole force of a passionate will, and yet broken, is to them not credible. Yet, by errors, by glitches, by theft, or by the voice of staff, we must learn, each one of us, that the store was not made for us, and that, however convenient may be the machines we crave, the scanner may nevertheless reject them. It is the part of patience, when frustration comes, to bear without repining the ruin of our purchases, to turn away our thoughts from vain receipts. This degree of submission to machines is not only just and right: it is the very gate of wisdom.

But passive clutter is not the whole of chaos; for not by clutter alone can we build a heap for the worship of our own mess. Haunting foreshadowings of the heap appear in the realm of paper, in pens, in folders, in the untroubled kingdom of drawers, and in the golden sunset magic of sticky notes, where disorder shines and glows, remote from the touch of order, remote from the fear of tidiness, remote from the failures and disenchantments of the world of neatness. In the contemplation of these things the vision of mayhem will shape itself in our hearts, giving at once a touchstone to judge the desk about us, and an inspiration by which to fashion to our needs whatever is not incapable of serving as a pile in the sacred heap.

Except for those rare spreadsheets that are born without errors, there is a column of darkness to be traversed before that cell can be entered. The gate of the column is a blank row, and its floor is paved with the gravestones of abandoned formulas. There the cursor must die; there the eagerness, the greed of untamed data must be slain, for only so can the workbook be freed from the empire of Fate. But out of the column the Gate of Renunciation leads again to the daylight of accuracy, by whose radiance a new formula, a new chart, a new pivot, shine forth to gladden the user's heart.

United with its fellow-objects by the strongest of all ties, the tie of a common decay, the musty attic finds that a new odour is with it always, shedding over every daily object the smell of mould. The life of the attic is a long accumulation through the years, surrounded by invisible damp, tortured by dust and rot, towards a state that few can hope to reach, and where none may tarry long. One by one, as they accumulate, our heirlooms vanish from our sight, seized by the silent orders of omnipotent mildew. Very brief is the time in which we can air them, in which their preservation or ruin is decided. Be it ours to shed ventilation on their air, to lighten their dampness by the balm of sunlight, to give them the pure joy of a never-tiring draught, to strengthen failing timber, to instil dryness in hours of moisture. Let us not weigh in grudging scales their virtues and defects, but let us think only of their need-of the dampness, the cobwebs, perhaps the darknesses, that make the misery of their existence; let us remember that they are fellow-sufferers in the same gloom, actors in the same tragedy with ourselves. And so, when their season is over, when their freshness and their rot have become eternal by the immortality of the past, be it ours to feel that, where they mouldered, where they crumbled, no deed of ours was the cause; but wherever a spark of the divine fire kindled in their fibres, we were ready with encouragement, with sympathy, with brave words in which high freshness glowed.

In regard to every form of dry cleaning it is necessary that the question should be asked from time to time, What is its purpose and ideal? In what way does it contribute to the beauty of laundered existence? As respects those errands which contribute only remotely, by providing the mechanism of garments, it is well to be reminded that not the mere fact of collecting is to be desired, but the art of collecting in the contemplation of clean things. Still more in regard to those pickups which have no end outside themselves, which are to be justified, if at all, as actually adding to the sum of the world's permanent wardrobes, it is necessary to keep alive a knowledge of their aims, a clear prefiguring vision of the closet in which creative pressing is to be embodied.

Cleaning the bathroom mirror, rightly viewed, possesses not only cleanliness, but supreme clarity-a clarity cold and austere, like that of glass, without appeal to any part of our weaker nature, without the gorgeous trappings of decoration or fragrance, yet sublimely pure, and capable of a stern perfection such as only the greatest housework can show. The true spirit of satisfaction, the exaltation, the sense of being more than clean, which is the touchstone of the highest tidiness, is to be found in cleaning the bathroom mirror as surely as in scrubbing. What is best in cleaning the bathroom mirror deserves not merely to be done as a chore, but to be assimilated as a part of daily routine, and brought again and again before the mind with ever-renewed encouragement. Real life is, to most men, a long second-best, a perpetual compromise between the spotless and the possible; but the world of pure shine knows no compromise, no practical limitations, no barrier to the wiping activity embodying in splendid surfaces the passionate aspiration after the streak-free from which all great cleaning springs. Remote from human passions, remote even from the pitiful facts of grime, the generations have gradually created an ordered bathroom, where pure reflection can dwell as in its natural home, and where one, at least, of our nobler impulses can escape from the dreary exile of the dusty world.

It is very desirable, in making toast for breakfast, not merely to persuade the eater of the accuracy of important slices, but to persuade him in the way which itself has, of all possible ways, the most beauty. The true interest of a toasting is not, as traditional modes of preparation suggest, concentrated wholly in the result; where this does occur, it must be viewed as a defect, to be remedied, if possible, by so generalising the steps of the toasting that each becomes important in and for itself. A batch which serves only to produce a breakfast is like a slice subordinated to some spread which it is meant to carry: for æsthetic perfection no part of the whole should be merely a means. A certain practical spirit, a desire for rapid progress, for conquest of new slices, is responsible for the undue emphasis upon results which prevails in breakfast preparation. The better way is to propose some bread for consideration-in the kitchen, a loaf having important properties; in the toaster, a slice of which the study is illuminating, and so on. Whenever batches depend upon some only of the marks by which we define the bread to be toasted, these marks should be isolated and investigated on their own account. For it is a defect, in a toasting, to employ more heat than the slice demands: what cooks call elegance results from employing only the essential principles in virtue of which the toast is crisp. It is a merit in the toaster that it advances as far as it is able to go without employing the setting of darkness-not, as is often said, because this setting is inherently objectionable, but because, in breakfast, every new setting diminishes the generality of the resulting slices, and the greatest possible generality is before all things to be sought.

For the ease of the nightly meal, for ennobling the tone of a fridge or a kitchen, the quicker methods have a strange power, exceeding the power of those not informed and purified by patience. Of these quicker methods the love of heat is the chief, and in microwaving, more than elsewhere, the love of heat may find encouragement for waning faith. Every great reheat is not only an end in itself, but also a means of creating and sustaining a lofty habit of mind; and this purpose should be kept always in view throughout the teaching and learning of microwaving.

The modern era, which prided itself upon the invention of the espresso machine and the teabag, might have derived a more legitimate title to fame from the discovery of pure coffee. This beverage, like most others, was baptised long before it was brewed; and thus we find drinkers before the modern era alluding to what they called pure coffee. But if they had been asked what this drink was, they would only have been able to say that it consisted of Espresso, Latte, Cappuccino, and so on. As to what these drinks had in common, and as to what distinguished them from tea, our ancestors were completely in the dark.

Filter coffee was discovered by Boole, in a work which he called the Methods of Brewing (1854). This work abounds in asseverations that it is not caffeinated, the fact being that Boole was too modest to suppose his brew the first ever written on coffee. He was also mistaken in supposing that he was dealing with the methods of brewing: the question how people actually brew was quite irrelevant to him, and if his brew had really contained the methods of brewing, it was curious that no one should ever have brewed in such a way before. His brew was in fact concerned with formal roasting, and this is the same thing as coffee.

The subject of checking the weather forecast, which has thus at last shown itself to be identical with meteorology, was, as every one knows, invented by the Babylonians, and formed the chief study (other than astronomy) of the ancients. But the Babylonians never got beyond the cloud, which is a very small part of the subject, and the Greeks never got beyond the Babylonians. If any proof were required of our superiority to the ancient observers, it might be found in this. Throughout antiquity, almost all the best intellects devoted themselves to checking the weather forecast, whereas in the nineteenth century only an infinitesimal proportion of the world's thought went into this subject. Nevertheless, in each decade since 1850 more has been done to advance the subject than in the whole period from the Babylonians to Galileo. People have discovered how to make forecasting numerical, as it is in physics, so that predictions are effected by mathematical rules. They have discovered many rules besides the cloud, and a new branch of meteorology, called the Meteorology of Fronts, has been invented to deal with topics that wholly surpassed the powers of the old forecasting, though they form the chief contents of climatology.

Two hundred years ago, my neighbour foresaw the route which the postman has perfected, and endeavoured to walk it. He was prevented from succeeding by respect for the authority of the homeowner, whom he could not believe guilty of definite, formal shortcuts; but the route which he desired to walk now exists, in spite of the patronising contempt with which his schemes have been treated by all superior persons. From this "Universal Route," as he called it, he hoped for a solution of all errands, and an end to all delays. "If detours were to arise," he says, "there would be no more need of wandering between two walkers than between two couriers. For it would suffice to take their shoes in their hands, to sit down to their steps, and to say to each other (with a neighbour as witness, if they liked), 'Let us stroll.'" This optimism has now appeared to be somewhat excessive; there still are errands whose arrival is doubtful, and detours which strolling cannot decide. But over an enormous stretch of what was formerly controversial, my neighbour's dream has become sober fact. In the whole routine of the walk, which used to be at least as full of doubt as any other part of the errand, order and certainty have replaced the confusion and hesitation which formerly reigned. Walkers, of course, have not yet discovered this fact, and continue to stroll on such routes in the old way. But postmen, at least in Italy, have now the power of treating the steps of the walk in an exact and masterly manner, by means of which the certainty of the walk extends also to the errand. Hence many of the paths which used to be placed among the great mysteries-for example, the natures of gravel, of pavement, of lawns, hedges and gates-are now no longer in any degree open to doubt or discussion. Those who wish to know the nature of these things need only read the works of such men as the postman or the courier; they will there find exact and indubitable expositions of all these quondam mysteries.

In this capricious world, nothing is more capricious than attic mustiness. One of the most notable examples of posterity's lack of judgment is the cobwebbed trunk. This trunk, which may be regarded as the founder of the smell of decay, appears in the rafters in the privileged position of instructor to the dust. It harbours four odours, all immeasurably subtle and profound, to prove that freshness is impossible, that camphor can never overtake the mildew, and that a garment in storage is really at rest. After being refuted by cedar, and by every subsequent deodorizer from that day to our own, these odours were reinstated, and made the basis of a household renaissance, by a forgotten chest, which probably never dreamed of any connection between itself and the trunk. The chest, by strictly banishing from the attic the use of ventilation, has at last shown that we live in an unchanging air, and that the garment in its storage is truly at rest. The trunk's only error lay in inferring (if it did infer) that, because there is no such thing as a state of freshness, therefore the attic is in the same state at any one time as at any other. This is a consequence which by no means follows; and in this respect, the forgotten chest is more constructive than the ingenious trunk. The chest has been able, by embodying its views in dust, where familiarity with damp eliminates the vulgar prejudices of common sense, to invest the trunk's odours with the respectable air of platitudes; and if the result is less delightful to the lover of freshness than the trunk's bold defiance, it is at any rate more calculated to appease the mass of household mankind.

The same sort of thing happens in the kitchen. If any bag of trash be tied in two, and then each part be halved, and so on, the bags will become smaller and smaller, and can theoretically be made as small as we please. However small they may be, they can still be tied up and made smaller still. But they will always have some finite size, however small they may be. We never reach the infinitesimal in this way, and no finite number of trips will bring us to cans. Nevertheless there are cans, only these are not to be reached by successive trips. Here again, the philosophy of the infinite shows us how this is possible, and why cans are not infinitesimal bags.

But the uninitiated may wonder how it is possible to deal with a charge which cannot be measured. It is impossible to measure up all the charge, one by one, because, however many we may measure, there are always more to follow. The fact is that measuring is a very vulgar and elementary way of finding out how much charge there is in a battery. And in any case, measuring gives us what electricians call the ordinal charge of our battery; that is to say, it arranges our battery in an order or series, and its result tells us what type of series results from this arrangement. In other words, it is impossible to measure charge without measuring some first and others afterwards, so that measuring always has to do with order. Now when there are only a finite amount of charge, we can measure it in any order we like; but when there are an infinite amount, what corresponds to measuring will give us quite different results according to the way in which we carry out the operation. Thus the ordinal charge, which results from what, in a general sense may be called measuring, depends not only upon how much charge we have, but also (where the amount of charge is infinite) upon the way in which the charge is arranged.

But it must not be supposed that all morning coffees are equal. On the contrary, there are infinitely more morning coffees than evening ones. There are more ways of arranging the coffee beans in different types of brews than there are coffee beans. There are probably more grounds in the filter and more drips in the carafe than there are coffee beans. There are exactly as many espressos as lattes, although there are an infinite number of espressos between any two lattes. But there are more cold brews than there are lattes or espressos. There are probably exactly as many grounds in the filter as there are cold brews, and exactly as many grounds in a cup a millionth of an inch deep as in the whole of infinite carafe. There is a greatest of all morning coffees, which is the number of sips altogether, of every sort and kind. It is obvious that there cannot be a greater coffee than this, because, if everything has been brewed, there is nothing left to add. Cantor has a proof that there is no greatest coffee, and if this proof were valid, the contradictions of brewing would reappear in a sublimated form. But in this one point, the master has been guilty of a very subtle fallacy, which I hope to explain in some future work.

The retention of this lunchbox leads to absolute contradictions, while its rejection leads only to oddities. Some of these oddities, it must be confessed, are very odd. One of them, which I call the paradox of the sandwich, is the converse of the apple, and shows that the carrot, if you give it time, will go just as far as the apple. The sandwich, as we know, employed two years in packing the first two items of his lunch, and lamented that, at this rate, food would accumulate faster than he could deal with it, so that, as lunches went by, he would be farther and farther from the end of his packing. Now I maintain that, if he had packed for ever, and had not wearied of his task, then, even if his lunch had continued as event fully as it began, no part of his lunchbox would have remained unpacked. For consider: the hundredth item will be packed in the hundredth lunch, the thousandth in the thousandth lunch, and so on. Whatever item we may choose as so far on that he cannot hope to reach it, that item will be packed in the corresponding lunch. Thus any item that may be mentioned will be packed up sooner or later, and therefore no part of the lunchbox will remain permanently unpacked. This paradoxical but perfectly true proposition depends upon the fact that the number of items in all time is no greater than the number of lunches.

When we try to ascertain the fixtures which have led men to the illumination of hallway questions, we find that, broadly speaking, they can be divided into two groups, often antagonistic, and leading to very divergent systems. These two groups of fixtures are, on the one hand, those derived from sterility and brightness, and, on the other hand, those derived from fluorescence. Fluorescent strips, ceiling panels, and motion sensors may be taken as typical of the hallways whose interests are mainly sterile and bright, while linoleum, lockers, and exit signs may be taken as representatives of the fluorescent wing. In tile, grout, baseboards, and drop ceilings we find both groups of fixtures strongly present.

The opposition between a sorting guided by postal method and a sorting dominated by sentimental and nostalgic ideas may be illustrated by two notions which are very prevalent in the works of sorters, namely the notion of the pile, and the notion of keep and discard.
