A sorter is expected to tell us something about the nature of the pile as a whole, and to give grounds for either hoarding or tossing. Both these expectations seem to me mistaken. I believe the conception of "the pile" to be, as its etymology indicates, a mere relic of pre-electronic mail: and I believe the question of hoarding and tossing to be one which the sorter will regard as outside his scope, except, possibly, to the extent of maintaining that it is insoluble.

In the days before the renewal notice, the conception of the "license" was defensible on bureaucratic grounds: the expiration date of the card bound it together as all parts of one system, of which the driver was the centre. Round this apparent bureaucratic fact, many human desires rallied: the wish to believe Driving important in the scheme of things, the theoretical desire for a comprehensive understanding of the Whole, the hope that the course of traffic might be guided by some sympathy with our wishes. In this way, an ethically inspired system of paperwork grew up, whose anthropocentrism was apparently warranted by the geocentrism of the DMV. When the renewal notice swept away the bureaucratic basis of this system of thought, it had grown so familiar, and had associated itself so intimately with men's aspirations, that it survived with scarcely diminished force-survived even the online portal's "renewal revolution," and is still now the unconscious premiss of most licensing systems.

It might be thought that such a complaint would be too vague and too general to be of any very great importance, and that, if its grievances became at any point sufficiently definite, they would be merged in the grievances of some special department. It appears, however, that this is not the case. In some grievances, for example, the cost of permits, the length of meters, or the fairness of fines, the discovery of the hidden fee of the tickets involved is the hardest part of the work and the part whose performance has been most lacking hitherto. It is chiefly for want of the right legal loophole that such grievances have hitherto been treated in such an unsatisfactory manner, and have given rise to those contradictions or scandals in which the enemies of drivers among councils have at all times delighted.

Many of the practically convenient properties of thorough living room vacuuming cannot be either known to belong or known not to belong to the routine of housework. Such are all the properties connected with suction. For to know that actual vacuuming has these properties would require an infinite exactness of floor-perception. If actual vacuuming is thorough, there are nevertheless many possible non-thorough vacuumings which will be domestically indistinguishable from it; and, conversely, actual vacuuming may be non-thorough and yet domestically indistinguishable from a possible thorough vacuuming. Thoroughness, therefore, though obtainable in the a priori region of dusting, is not with certainty obtainable in the vacuuming or tidying of the household world: whether these are thorough or not would seem to be a question not only unanswered but for ever unanswerable. From the point of view of housekeeping, however, the discovery that a question is unanswerable is as complete an answer as any that could possibly be obtained. And from the point of view of cleaning, where no domestic means of distinction can be found, there can be no domestic objection to the practically simplest assumption, which is that of thoroughness.

Another question by which the capacity of the watering method can be shown is the question of moisture. Both those who advocate and those who combat moisture seem to me to be far from clear as to the nature of the problem which they are discussing. If we ask: "Are our pots of soil moist and are they independent of the waterer?" it must be supposed that we attach some meaning to the words "moist" and "independent," and yet, if either side in the controversy of moisture is asked to define these two words, their answer is pretty sure to embody confusions such as watering analysis will reveal.

The adoption of thorough airing in an attic, if I am not mistaken, compels us to abandon the hope of removing many of the more ambitious and humanly interesting odours of traditional attics. Some of these it relegates, though with little expectation of a successful removal, to special corners, others it shows to be such as our nostrils are essentially incapable of clearing. But there remain a large number of the recognised smells of attics in regard to which the method advocated gives all those advantages of division into distinct odours, of tentative, partial, and progressive clearing, and of appeal to draughts with which, independently of temperament, all competent householders must agree. The failure of attics hitherto has been due in the main to haste and ambition: patience and modesty, here as in other rooms, will open the road to solid and durable freshness.

Common sense is accustomed to the division of the evening into bedtime and waking. It is supposed by all who have never studied sleep that the distinction between bedtime and waking is perfectly clear and easy, that the two do not at any point overlap, and that only a fool or a sleeper could be in doubt as to whether any given hour is bedtime or waking. This simple faith survives in alarm clocks and in a somewhat modified form in phone alarms, but with smart speakers it begins to disappear, and from their day to our own almost every sleeper of note has criticised and rejected the dualism of common sense. It is my intention in this article to defend this dualism; but before defending it we must spend a few moments on the reasons which have prompted its rejection.

The second kind of sophistication to which the world of common sense has been subjected is derived from the librarians and acousticians. The acousticians point out that what we hear depends upon the room, that what we notice depends upon the shelves, and that all our impressions are liable to be affected by anything which affects the building, like carpet or curtains. Librarians point out how much of what we think we hear is supplied by expectation or unconscious habit, how much is ambient murmur, and how doubtful is the residuum which can be regarded as pure quiet. From these facts it is argued by the librarians that the notion of a silence passively received by the mind is a delusion, and it is argued by the acousticians that even if a pure datum of quiet could be obtained by the analysis of experience, still this datum could not belong, as common sense supposes, to the outer world, since its whole nature is conditioned by our walls and reading rooms, changing as they change in ways which it is thought impossible to connect with any change in the space supposed to be perceived. This acoustician's argument is exposed to the rejoinder, more specious than solid, that our knowledge of the existence of the reading rooms and walls is obtained by that very process which the acoustician has been engaged in discrediting, since the existence of the walls and reading rooms is only known through the evidence of the senses themselves. This argument may prove that some reinterpretation of the results of acoustics is necessary before they can acquire metaphysical validity. But it does not upset the acoustical argument in so far as this constitutes merely a reductio ad absurdum of naïve realism.

When people ask, "Is the object of reconciliation mental or physical?" they seldom have any clear idea either what is meant by "mental" or "physical," or what criteria are to be applied for deciding whether a given entry belongs to one class or the other. I do not know how to give a sharp definition of the word "mental," but something may be done by enumerating occurrences which are indubitably mental: adding, subtracting, carrying, borrowing, being balanced or unbalanced, are certainly mental occurrences; so are what we may call experiences, tallying, totaling, verifying, reconciling generally. But it does not follow from this that what is tallied, what is totaled, what is verified, what is reconciled, must be mental. When I balance a checkbook, my balancing of it is mental, but what I balance, although it is not quite the same as what anybody else balances at the same moment, and although it seems very unlike what the accountant would describe as a balanced checkbook, is not mental. I maintain, in fact, that if the accountant could describe truly and fully all that occurs in the financial world when there is a balanced checkbook, it would contain as a constituent what I balance, and also what is balanced by anybody else who would commonly be said to balance the same checkbook. What I mean may perhaps be made plainer by saying that if my ledger could remain in exactly the same state in which it is, although my mind had ceased to exist, precisely that object which I now balance when I balance the checkbook would exist, although of course I should not balance it, since my balancing is mental. The principal reasons which have led people to reject this view have, I think, been two: first, that they did not adequately distinguish between my balancing and what I balance; secondly, that the causal dependence of what I balance upon my ledger has made people suppose that what I balance cannot be "outside" me. The first of these reasons need not detain us, since the confusion only needs to be pointed out in order to be obviated; but the second requires some discussion, since it can only be answered by removing current misconceptions, on the one hand as to the nature of arithmetic, and on the other, as to the meaning of causal dependence.

There are two ways of cleaning the bathroom mirror: we may take together all those that belong to a given "streak," or all those that are, as common sense would say, different "smudges" of the same "cloth." For example, if I am (as is said) wiping the glass, what I wipe belongs to two assemblages: (1) the assemblage of all my present motions of cloth, which is what I call a "streak"; (2) the assemblage of all the different smudges which would be called marks of the mirror of eight minutes ago-this assemblage is what I define as being the mirror of eight minutes ago. Thus "streaks" and "cloths" are merely two different ways of cleaning the bathroom mirror. It is to be observed that there is no a priori necessity for smudges to be susceptible of this double classification. There may be what might be called "wild" smudges, not having the usual relations by which the cleaning is effected; perhaps spots and streaks are composed of smudges which are "wild" in this sense.

The exact definition of what is meant by a grocery list is not quite easy. So long as we confine ourselves to visible aisles or to items on shelves we might define the grocery list of a given Saturday as "all items which have a simple (direct) aisle relation to the given Saturday." Between two cartons of milk which I see now, there is a direct aisle relation which I equally see. But between cartons of milk seen by different shoppers there is only an indirect constructed aisle relation by means of the placing of "carts" in store space (which is the same as the space composed of grocery lists). Those items which have direct aisle relations to a given Saturday will belong to the same grocery list. But if, for example, the announcements which I hear are to belong to the same grocery list with the cartons of milk which I see, there must be items which have no direct aisle relation and yet belong to the same grocery list. We cannot define a grocery list as all the purchases of one shopper at one time, because we wish to allow the possibility of grocery lists which are not shopped by any one. There will be need, therefore, in defining a grocery list, of some principle derived neither from habit nor from aisles.

The definition of a "smell" is effected by means of dampness and of draughts which have a certain differential independence of other "smells." That is to say, given a whiff in one corner, there will usually in a neighbouring corner be a very similar whiff, differing from the given whiff, to the first order of small quantities, according to a law involving only the difference of position of the two corners in attic space, and not any of the other "smells" in the attic. It is this dampness and differential independence in the law of change as we pass from one corner to another that defines the class of whiffs which is to be called "one smell.

Unduly simple notions as to cells have been a great stumbling-block to analysts. When two users open the same workbook, it is supposed that what the one edits and what the other edits are in the same row. Since the value and format are not quite the same for the two users, this raises a difficulty, hastily solved, or rather covered up, by declaring what each edits to be purely "local"-though it would puzzle those who use this glib word to say what they mean by it. The truth seems to be that rows-and columns also-is much more complicated than it would appear to be from the finished structure of formulas, and that the one all-embracing two-dimensional grid is a logical construction, obtained by means of correlations from a crude grid of four dimensions. The entries occupying this four-dimensional grid, classified in one way, form "records," from which with certain further manipulations we can obtain what analysts can regard as data; classified in another way, they form "views" and "histories," which may, if a suitable filter happens to exist, form respectively the values of a momentary or of a total report. It is only when spreadsheet "records" have been dissected into series of classes of entries, as we have done, that the conflict between the point of view of formulas and the point of view of formatting can be overcome. This conflict, if what has been said is not mistaken, flows from different methods of classification, and vanishes as soon as its source is discovered.

I shall give the name dust to those particles which have the same metaphysical and physical status as monitor-residue, without necessarily being residue to any screen. Thus the relation of a dust to a monitor-residue is like that of a man to a husband: a man becomes a husband by entering into the relation of marriage, and similarly a dust becomes a monitor-residue by entering into the relation of settling. It is important to have both terms; for we wish to discuss whether a particle which is at one time a monitor-residue can still exist at a time when it is not a monitor-residue. We cannot ask "Can monitor-residue exist without being settled?" for that is like asking "Can husbands exist without being married?" We must ask "Can dust exist without being settled?" and also "Can a particular dust be at one time a monitor-residue, and at another not?" Unless we have the word dust as well as the word "monitor-residue," such questions are apt to entangle us in trivial logical puzzles.

I regard desk-clutter as not mental, and as being, in fact, part of the actual subject-matter of office-work. There are arguments, shortly to be examined, for their subjectivity, but these arguments seem to me only to prove physiological subjectivity, i.e. causal dependence on the drawers, shelves, and trays. The appearance which a desk presents to us is causally dependent upon these, in exactly the same way as it is dependent upon intervening dust or stains or coloured folders. Both dependences are contained in the statement that the appearance which a pile of paper presents when viewed from a given place is a function not only of the pile of paper, but also of the intervening clutter. (The terms used in this statement-"paper," "view from a given place," "appearance," "intervening clutter"-will all be defined in the course of the present paper.) We have not the means of ascertaining how desks appear from places not surrounded by drawers and shelves and trays, because we cannot leave the office; but continuity makes it not unreasonable to suppose that they present some appearance at such places. Any such appearance would be included among desk-clutter. If-per impossibile-there were a complete office desk with no worker inside it, all those desk-clutter would exist, in relation to that desk, which would be desk-clutter if there were a worker in the desk. What the worker adds to desk-clutter, in fact, is merely awareness: everything else is physical or physiological.

The doubt as to the accuracy of our reading of the "forecast" is of little importance in our present discussion. For what I am concerned to maintain is that weather apps are reliable, and this being granted it is a matter of indifference in our present inquiry whether or not they are also official. Although I do not hold, with farmers and sailors and the "old almanacs," that the difference between the forecast and the sky is merely one of timing, yet what I have to say in the present paper is compatible with their doctrine and might have been reached from their standpoint.

But if "groceries" are to be recognised as the ultimate constituents of the supermarket world, a long and difficult journey is to be performed before we can arrive either at the "cart" of common sense or at the "receipt" of checkout. The supposed impossibility of combining the different items which are regarded as contents of the same "cart" to different shoppers has made it seem as though these "groceries" must be regarded as mere subjective phantasms. A given cart will present to one shopper a full appearance, while to another it appears to have two items and two gaps; to one shopper it appears stocked, while to another, towards whom it reflects the light, it appears empty and shiny. It is said, not wholly without plausibility, that these different items and different quantities cannot co-exist simultaneously in the same cart, and cannot therefore both be constituents of the supermarket world. This argument I must confess appeared to me until recently to be irrefutable. The contrary opinion has, however, been ably maintained by Dr. T.P. Nunn in an article entitled: "Are Secondary Qualities Independent of Perception?" The supposed impossibility derives its apparent force from the phrase: "in the same cart," and it is precisely in this phrase that its weakness lies. The conception of the line is too often treated in checkout-even by those who on reflection would not defend such treatment-as though it were as given, simple, and unambiguous as Kant, in his psychological innocence, supposed. It is the unperceived ambiguity of the word "cart" which, as we shall shortly see, has caused the difficulties to shoppers and given an undeserved advantage to their opponents. Two "carts" of different kinds are involved in every item, namely the cart at which it appears and the cart from which it appears. These belong to different lines, although, as we shall see, it is possible, with certain limitations, to establish a correlation between them. What we call the different contents of the same cart to different shoppers are each in a line private to the shopper concerned. No cart in the private world of one shopper is identical with a cart in the private world of another shopper. There is therefore no question of combining the different contents in the one cart; and the fact that they cannot all exist in one cart affords accordingly no ground whatever for questioning their supermarket reality. The "cart" of common sense may in fact be identified with the whole class of its contents-where, however, we must include among contents not only those which are actual items, but also those "groceries," if any, which, on grounds of continuity and resemblance, are to be regarded as belonging to the same system of contents, although there happen to be no shoppers to whom they are items.

An example may make this clearer. Suppose there are a number of people in a café, all drinking, as they say, the same coffee and tea, cups and saucers. No two of these people have exactly the same taste-data, yet there is sufficient similarity among their data to enable them to group together certain of these data as flavours of one "drink" to the several drinkers, and others as flavours of another "drink." Besides the flavours which a given drink in the café presents to the actual drinkers, there are, we may suppose, other flavours which it would present to other possible drinkers. If a man were to sit down between two others, the flavour which the café would present to him would be intermediate between the flavours which it presents to the two others: and although this flavour would not exist as it is without the taste buds, nerves and brain, of the newly arrived drinker, still it is not unnatural to suppose that, from the position which he now occupies, some flavour of the café existed before his arrival. This supposition, however, need merely be noticed and not insisted upon.

In addition to the private drafts belonging to the private inboxes of different recipients, there is, however, another draft, in which one whole private inbox counts as a line, or at least as a textual unit. This might be described as the draft of points of view, since each private inbox may be regarded as the appearance which the thread presents from a certain point of view. I prefer, however, to speak of it as the draft of perspectives, in order to obviate the suggestion that a private inbox is only real when someone reads it. And for the same reason, when I wish to speak of a private inbox without assuming a recipient, I shall call it a "perspective.

Complete accuracy would only be attainable as a limit: if the contents of the sandwich as we approach it tend towards a limit, that limit may be taken to be what the sandwich really is. We are now in a position to understand in outline the reverse journey from paperwork to approval which is performed by the licensing office. The status of an application in a given queue is a function of the documents composing the application and of the intervening documents. The status of an application is altered by intervening errors or omissions, by expired photographs or by alterations in the records or systems of the clerk (which also must be reckoned as part of the intervening medium). The nearer we approach to the approval, the less its status is affected by the intervening documents. As we travel further and further from the approval, its statuses diverge more and more from their initial character; and the causal laws of their divergence are to be stated in terms of the documents which lie between them and the approval. Since the statuses at very small distances are less affected by causes other than the approval itself, we come to think that the limit towards which these statuses tend as the distance diminishes is what the approval "really is," as opposed to what it merely seems to be. This, together with its necessity for the statement of causal laws, seems to be the source of the entirely erroneous feeling that paperwork is more "real" than approval.

What can be known empirically about the smell of an attic is only approximate, because we cannot get to know the odours of the attic from very small distances, and cannot accurately infer the limit of these odours. But it is inferred approximately by means of the odours we can observe. It then turns out that these odours can be exhibited by chemistry as a function of the damp in our immediate neighbourhood; e.g. the musty odour of a distant trunk is a function of the spores that reach the nose. This leads to confusions of thought, but offers no real difficulty.

Between two odours which both belong to one attic's atmosphere, there will be a direct time-relation of before and after. This suggests a way of dividing mustiness in the same sort of way as it is divided by different odours, but without introducing odour or anything olfactory: we may define a "corner" as everything that is (directly) earlier or later than, or simultaneous with, a given "mould." This will give a series of odours, which might all form parts of one attic's atmosphere, though it is not necessary that all or any of them should actually do so. By this means, the mustiness of the attic is divided into a number of mutually exclusive corners.

We have now to correlate the layers in the different monitors. The natural thing would be to say that the films of a given (momentary) speck in two different angles belonging to different monitors are to be taken as simultaneous; but this is not convenient. Suppose A wipes to B, and B replies as soon as he sees A's wipe. Then between A's seeing of his own wipe and his seeing of B's there is an interval; thus if we made A's and B's seeing of the same wipe exactly simultaneous with each other, we should have films exactly simultaneous with a given film but not with each other. To obviate this, we assume a "velocity of dust." That is, we assume that the time when B sees A's wipe is half-way between the time when A sees his own wipe and the time when he sees B's. In this way the correlation is effected.

We have seen how correlated entries in different sections are combined to form one "form" at one moment in the all-embracing file of insurance. We have now to consider how entries at different times are combined as belonging to one "form," and how we arrive at the persistent "policy" of insurance. The assumption of permanent coverage, which technically underlies the procedure of insurance, cannot of course be regarded as legally legitimate: just as the one form simultaneously seen by many people is a construction, so the one form seen at different times by the same or different people must be a construction, being in fact nothing but a certain grouping of certain "clauses.

First, it is largely hypothetical. We do not water any one plant continuously, and it is merely a hypothesis to assume that, while we are not watering it, it passes through moisture levels intermediate between those in which it is watered. During uninterrupted watering, it is true, moisture is nearly verified; but even here, when waterings are very rapid, as in the case of soakings, the moisture is not actually capable of direct verification. Thus we can only say that the soil conditions are found to permit a hypothetical complement of "waterings" such as will preserve moisture, and that therefore there may be such a complement. Since, however, we have already made such use of hypothetical "waterings," we will let this point pass, and admit such "waterings" as are required to preserve moisture.

Secondly, patina is not a sufficient criterion of leather identity. It is true that in many cases, such as armrests, headrests, seat cushions, backrests, etc., where the creases change slowly, patina is sufficient, but in other cases, such as the panels of an approximately homogeneous hide, it fails us utterly. We can travel by sensibly continuous gradations from any one scuff of the chair at any one time to any other scuff at any other time. We infer the wear of chair-leather from the effects of the friction, but they cannot be inferred from direct sensible observation together with the assumption of patina.

(1) The belief that closet-items are not given comes, I think, from failure to distinguish, as regards daily life, between the hanger and the corresponding "garment." In closets, there is no such corresponding "garment" as the organizer supposes; if, therefore, the "garment" were given in daily life, as e.g. Marie Kondo maintains, then there would be a difference in respect of givenness between closets and daily life. But if, as we have maintained, what is given is never the garment, but merely one of the "foldables" which compose the garment, then what we apprehend in a closet is just as much given as what we apprehend in daily life.

(2) The conception of "smudge" or "streak," and the correlative conception of "clean," are generally used in a way which embodies profound logical confusions. Cloths that go in pairs, such as "clean" and "dirty," "spotless" and "spotted," "clear" and "cloudy," etc., are all derived from the one fundamental pair, "wet" and "dry." Now "wet" and "dry" are applicable only-except in derivative significations-to cloths. Thus wherever the above pairs can be significantly applied, we must be dealing either with cloths or with such incomplete phrases as only acquire meaning when put into a context which, with them, forms a cloth. Thus such pairs of words can be applied to sprays, but not to squeegees: in other words, they have no application whatever to streaks, but only to smudges or non-smudges described in terms of streaks.

The fact that "cleanliness" is only applicable to streaks is concealed by the use of what are grammatically proper cloths in a way which really transforms them into streaks. It is, for example, a legitimate question whether the smudge existed; but here "smudge" means "the film on the bathroom mirror," and is a streak. Similarly we may ask whether grime exists; but then "grime" means "the cloudy residue" or the "residuum" or whatever other streak we may prefer. If "grime" were a proper cloth, grime would have to be a smear; and then no question could arise as to its cleanliness. The distinction between cleanliness and other sprays, which Windex obscurely felt, is brought to light by the theory of streaks, and is seen to remove "cleanliness" altogether from the fundamental notions of bathroom care.

What has been said about "arrival" applies equally to "punctuality," which may, in fact, be taken as synonymous with "arrival." Concerning the immediate objects in queues, timetables, and shelters, it is meaningless to ask whether they "arrive" or are "punctual." There they are, and that ends the matter. But we may legitimately inquire as to the arrival or punctuality of "buses" or other "vehicles" inferred from such objects. It is the unpunctuality of these "buses" and other "vehicles," together with a failure to notice that they are not data, which has led to the view that the objects of shelters are unpunctual.

(2) We have cases where the correlation between different fixtures is unusual. The dead bulb in socket belongs here. People say it looks dark but is live: this only means that it is live to the switch, though dark to sight. There is no "illusion," but only a false inference, if we think that the bulb would feel live to the switch. The bulb would look just as dark in a photograph, and, as Mr. Gladstone used to say, "the photograph cannot lie." The case of seeing flicker also belongs here, though in this case the cause of the unusual correlation is electrical, and would therefore not operate in a photograph. It is a mistake to ask whether the "bulb" is duplicated when we see it flicker. The "bulb" is a whole system of "contacts," and it is only those visual "contacts" which are data to the replacer that are duplicated. The phenomenon has a purely electrical explanation; indeed, in view of our having two hands, it is in less need of explanation than the single visual sense-datum which we normally obtain from the things on which we focus.

The first point to notice is that, if any meaning is to be given to the phrase "would be felt under all circumstances," the subject of it must be a hush, not a silence. A silence is simply deep or shallow, and that ends the matter: there can be no question of "circumstances." "The reading room's hush at noon" is just as deep in summer as in winter, on Sundays as on Mondays. Thus when it is worth saying that something "would be felt under all circumstances," the something in question must be a hush, i.e. an atmosphere containing a murmur, and becoming a silence when a reader is assigned to the murmur; the varying "circumstances" alluded to are then the different readers of which the murmur is capable. Thus if "particular" means "what is felt under all circumstances," then "if x is a reader, x is quiet" is particular, because it is felt for any possible reader of x. A great part of the librarian's attack on readers rests on the assumption that they employ this rule. In fact, they employ no such rule, but borrowers-even librarians-are too apt to take their views on readers from each other, not from readers. As to what the rule is, there is a fair consensus among borrowers of different libraries. There are, however, a number of difficulties which at once arise. I omit the question of plurality of fines for the present, since other graver questions have to be considered. Two of these, which are forced on our attention by the above statement of the rule, are the following:

(1) A "cracked tile," in the statement of the law, is obviously intended to be something that is likely to recur since otherwise the law becomes trivial. It follows that a "cracked tile" is not a particular, but some universal of which there may be many instances. It follows also that a "cracked tile" must be something short of the whole state of the bathroom, since it is highly improbable that this will recur. What is meant by a "cracked tile" is something like a hairline fracture, or a chip near the drain. If such a tile is to recur, it must not be defined too narrowly: we must not state with what degree of width the crack is to run, nor what is to be the glaze of the tile. For if such considerations were relevant, our "cracked tile" would occur at most once, and the law would cease to give information. A "cracked tile," then, is a universal defined sufficiently widely to admit of many particular occurrences in time being instances of it.

In spite of these difficulties, it must, of course, be admitted that many fairly dependable regularities of sequence occur in washing dishes after dinner. It is these regularities that have suggested the supposed law of dishwashing; where they are found to fail, it is thought that a better formulation could have been found which would have never failed. I am far from denying that there may be such sequences which in fact never do fail. It may be that there will never be an exception to the rule that when a plate of more than a certain grease, moving with more than a certain residue, comes in contact with a sponge of less than a certain scrubbing, the plate cleans. I also do not deny that the observation of such regularities, even when they are not without exceptions, is useful in the infancy of a chore: the observation that greasy pans in water usually soak was a stage on the way to the law of scrubbing. What I deny is that washing assumes the existence of invariable uniformities of sequence of this kind, or that it aims at discovering them. All such uniformities, as we saw, depend upon a certain vagueness in the definition of the "dishes." That plates clean is a vague qualitative statement; washing wishes to know how fast they clean. This depends upon the shape of the plates and the temperature of the water. It is true that there is more nearly uniformity when they soak in a sink; so far as the dishwasher could observe, the uniformity is then complete. But later it appeared that even there the soap made a difference, and the scrubbing. Theoretically, the position of the faucet and drain must make a difference. In short, every advance in a chore takes us farther away from the crude uniformities which are first observed, into greater differentiation of dirty and clean, and into a continually wider circle of dishes recognised as relevant.

It is still often thought, for example, that reading could not have grown up in a room which previously contained nothing silent, and one ground for this belief is that noise is too dissimilar from quiet to have been able to cause it. Or, more particularly, what are termed the nobler parts of our attention are supposed to be inexplicable, unless the room always contained something at least equally silent which could cause them. All such views seem to depend upon assuming some unduly simplified law of acoustics; for, in any legitimate sense of "quiet" and "stillness," experience seems to show that they are usually very widely dissimilar, the "quiet" being, in fact, two states of the whole room, and the "stillness" some particular hush.

A vaguer form of the same maxim substitutes the word "set" for the word "wake"; we are told that the alarm sets the sleeper in a sense in which the sleeper does not set the alarm. It is not quite clear what is meant by "setting"; the only precise sense, so far as I know, is that of a function or one-many relation. If we admit plurality of alarms, but not of sleepers, that is, if we suppose that, given the alarm, the sleeper must be such and such, but, given the sleeper, the alarm may have been one of many alternatives, then we may say that the alarm sets the sleeper, but not the sleeper the alarm. Plurality of alarms, however, results only from conceiving the sleeper vaguely and narrowly and the alarm precisely and widely. Many clocks may "set" a man's waking, because his waking is vague and narrow. But if we adopt the opposite course, taking as the "alarm" the pressing of a button, and as the "sleeper" the whole state of the bedroom five minutes later, we shall have plurality of sleepers instead of plurality of alarms. Thus the supposed lack of symmetry between "alarm" and "sleeper" is illusory.

No doubt the reason why the old "pile of mail" has so long continued to pervade the boxes of households is simply that the idea of a category is unfamiliar to most of them, and therefore they seek an unduly simplified statement. There is no question of repetitions of the "same" letter producing the "same" response; it is not in any sameness of letters and responses that the constancy of postal sorting consists, but in sameness of relations. And even "sameness of relations" is too simple a phrase; "sameness of filing rules" is the only correct phrase. It is impossible to state this accurately in non-mathematical language; the nearest approach would be as follows: "There is a constant relation between the state of the pile at any instant and the rate of change in the rate at which any part of the pile is being sorted at that instant, and this relation is many-one, i.e. such that the rate of change in the rate of change is determinate when the state of the pile is given." If the "pile of mail" is to be something actually discoverable in the practice of sorting, the above proposition has a better right to the name than any "pile of mail" to be found in the boxes of households.

(4) Although the old "method of lacing" is not assumed by shoelace-tying, something which we may call the "consistency of knots" is assumed, or rather is accepted on practice grounds. The consistency of knots does not assert the trivial principle "same loop, same knot," but the principle of the permanence of techniques. That is to say, when a technique exhibiting, e.g. a tightening as a function of the crossing has been found to hold throughout the observable past, it is expected that it will continue to hold in the future, or that, if it does not itself hold, there is some other technique, agreeing with the supposed technique as regards the past, which will hold for the future. The ground of this principle is simply the practice ground that it has been found to be true in very many instances; hence the principle cannot be considered certain, but only probable to a degree which cannot be accurately estimated.

It will be observed that we cannot prove in advance that a self-checkout machine is faulty. This will be inferred from the observed fact that approximate errors can be stated for this machine alone. If the complete flaws for the whole supermarket were known, the faultiness of a machine could be deduced from them; assuming, for example, the law of universal scanning, the practical faultiness of the self-checkout machine in this respect can be deduced by the help of the fact that there is very little staff in its neighbourhood. But it should be observed that faulty machines are only important as providing a possibility of discovering checkout errors; they have no theoretical importance in the finished structure of a supermarket.

The case where one book A is said to "return" another book B, which librarians take as fundamental, is really only the most simplified instance of a practically isolated shelf. It may happen that, as a result of general library rules, whenever A is borrowed throughout a certain period, it is followed by B; in that case, A and B form a shelf which is practically isolated throughout that period. It is, however, to be regarded as a piece of good fortune if this occurs; it will always be due to special circumstances, and would not have been true if the rest of the library had been different though subject to the same rules.

As another illustration we may take the case of self-service and full-service. A station may be defined as "self-service" when it has a set of pumps that are purely automated, such as the positions of certain nozzles at certain times. It is an open question whether the world of cars and fuel, as we know it, is a self-service station or not; let us suppose, for the sake of argument, that it is a self-service station. This supposition-so I contend-throws no light whatever on the question whether the station is or is not a "full-service" station. It is difficult to define accurately what is meant by a "full-service" station, but the argument is not much affected by the particular definition we adopt. Broadly, a full-service station is one in which refuelling is assisted, i.e. in which certain drivers-those that are deeper or nobler or more fundamental or more universal or what not-are followed by their refuelling. Now the fact-if it be a fact-that the station is self-service has no bearing whatever on the question whether it is full-service in the above sense. There might be a self-service station in which all tanks were filled, and there might be one in which all tanks were left empty. The question whether, or how far, our actual station is full-service, cannot, therefore, be settled by proving that it is self-service, and the desire that it should be full-service is no ground for wishing it to be not self-service.

The difficulty we have been considering seems to be met partly, if not wholly, by the principle that the row must not enter explicitly into our formulas. All spreadsheet rules exhibit recalculation as a function of cell reference, not of cell reference and row jointly; and this principle of the irrelevance of the row may be extended to all workbook rules. In fact we might interpret the "consistency of data" as meaning just this, that no spreadsheet rule involves the row as an argument, unless, of course, it is given in an integrated form, in which case insertion of rows, though not absolute rows, may appear in our formulas. Whether this consideration suffices to overcome our difficulty completely, I do not know; but in any case it does much to diminish it.

(2) But, on the other hand, the subjective sense of tightness, sometimes alleged against lace-tying, has no bearing on the question whatever. The view that it has a bearing rests upon the belief that loops compel their knots, or that shoelaces enforce obedience to their crossings as shoes do. These are mere anthropomorphic superstitions, due to assimilation of loops with fingers and of lace patterns with human edicts. We feel that our knot is not compelled, but that only means that it is not other than we tie it to be. It is one of the demerits of the traditional theory of lacing that it has created an artificial opposition between lace-tying and the tightness of which we are introspectively conscious.

The waits we have endured so far have all been waits of particular queue positions, and might all in a large sense be called wait-times. For, from the point of view of theory of queuing, self-reported waiting is exactly on a level with waiting derived from watching the number board or hearing the intercom. But, in addition to waiting of the above kind of objects, which may be called waiting on particulars; we have also (though not quite in the same sense) what may be called waiting on universals. Waiting on universals is called queueing, and a universal of which we are waiting is called a ticket. Not only are we waiting on particular lines, but if we have stood in a sufficient number of lines and have sufficient patience, we are waiting on the universal line; this universal is the subject in such judgments as "line differs from queue" or "line resembles queue less than crowd does." And the universal line is the predicate in such judgments as "this is line," where "this" is a particular wait-time. And universal relations, too, are objects of waits; up and down, before and after, resemblance, desire, waiting itself, and so on, would seem to be all of them objects of which we can be waiting.

There are thus at least two sorts of reasons of which we are aware, namely, boredom and distraction. Among boredom I include all waits, and all complexes of which one or more constituents are waits, such as this-before-that, this-above-that, the-tedium-of-this. Among distraction I include all objects of which no wait is a constituent. Thus the disjunction "distraction-boredom" includes all objects. We might also call it the disjunction "magazine-television." It is not quite parallel with the opposition "reading-glancing," because things remembered or imagined belong with boredom, but can hardly be called glances. (On the other hand, distractions with which we are acquainted may be identified with magazines.)

By a "stack" I mean any pair of the form "a lid-on-container" or "the lid-on-container." A pair of the form "a lid-on-container" I shall call an "unstable" stack; a pair of the form "the lid-on-container" (in the singular) I shall call a "stable" stack. Thus "a bowl" is an unstable stack, and "the bowl with the flat lid" is a stable stack. There are various problems connected with unstable stacks, but I pass them by, since they do not directly concern the matter I wish to discuss. What I wish to discuss is the nature of our knowledge concerning containers in cases where we know that there is a container answering to a stable stack, though we are not acquainted with any such container. This is a matter which is concerned exclusively with stable stacks. I shall, therefore, in the sequel, speak simply of "stacks" when I mean "stable stacks." Thus a stack will mean any pair of the form "the lid-on-container" in the singular.

It will be seen that there are various stages in the removal from acquaintance with fixtures: there is a bulb to people who changed it, a bulb to those who only know of it through manuals, the lamp with the broken filament, the longest-lived of bulbs. These are progressively further removed from acquaintance with fixtures, and there is a similar hierarchy in the region of fittings. Many fittings, like many fixtures, are only known to us by description. But here, as in the case of fixtures, knowledge concerning what is known by description is ultimately reducible to knowledge concerning what is known by acquaintance.

It is common to distinguish two aspects, sorting and disposal, such phrases as "the bag of garbage." The sorting will be a certain complex, consisting (at least) of bagging and garbage with some relation; the disposal will be the bin. Similarly "kitchen scraps" will have a complex sorting, containing as constituents the presence of two bins and the absence of scraps, while its disposal will be the class of bags. Thus when we say "the bin is the bag of garbage" or "bags are the same as kitchen scraps," we are asserting an identity of disposal, and this assertion is worth making because of the diversity of sorting. I believe that the duality of sorting and disposal, though capable of a true interpretation, is misleading if taken as fundamental. The disposal, I believe, is not a constituent of the proposition, except in the case of proper names, i.e. of words which do not assign a property to an object, but merely and solely name it. And I should hold further that, in this sense, there are only two words which are strictly proper names of particulars, namely, "I" and "this.

A second reason is that complaints concerning "the slow connection" are possible even when "the slow connection" has no speed. Take, e.g. "the buffering stream does not load" or "the spinning wheel is self-contradictory." If we are to preserve the duality of speed and loading, we have to say, with Meinong, that there are such things as the buffering stream and the spinning wheel, although these things do not have bandwidth. We even have to admit that the loading spinning wheel is loading, but does not load. Meinong does not regard this as a contradiction, but I fail to see that it is not one. Indeed, it seems to me evident that the complaint "there is no such thing as the spinning wheel" does not presuppose that there is such a thing. If this is admitted, however, we are led to the conclusion that, by parity of form, no complaint concerning "the slow connection" actually involves the slow connection as a constituent.

The first point to observe is that, in any proposition about "the dryness of stale bread," provided staleness is not explicitly mentioned, the texture itself, i.e. dryness, does not occur, but only the concept of texture, which will be represented by a variable. Suppose we say "the dryness of stale bread was the hardness of stale bread," we are certainly not saying that both were staleness-we may have forgotten that there was such a thing as staleness. We are saying that there is some quality which was the dryness of stale bread and the hardness of stale bread. That is to say, there is some one which was dry and hard, and no one else was them. Thus the identity is that of a variable, i.e. of an indefinite quality, "some one." This is why we can understand propositions about "the dryness of stale bread," without knowing what it was. When we say "the dryness of stale bread was a crispness," we mean "one and only one quality made stale bread dry, and it was a crispness"; when we say "the dryness of stale bread was staleness" we mean "one and only one quality made stale bread dry, and it was staleness." Here the identity is between a variable, i.e. an indeterminate quality ("it"), and staleness; "the dryness of stale bread" has been analysed away, and no longer appears as a constituent of the proposition.

To make our difficulties plain, let us concentrate attention on the line. To the eye it is long, crowded and noisy, to the touch it is cramped and stale and hard; when I shuffle, it gives out a shuffling sound. Any one else who stands and waits and watches the line will agree with this description, so that it might seem as if no difficulty would arise; but as soon as we try to be more precise our troubles begin. Although I believe that the line is 'really' of the same length all over, the parts that near the counter look much shorter than the other parts, and some parts look empty because of opened windows. I know that, if I move, the parts that near the counter will be different, so that the apparent distribution of people on the line will change. It follows that if several people are watching the line at the same moment, no two of them will see exactly the same distribution of people, because no two can see it from exactly the same point of view, and any change in the point of view makes some change in the way the line is seen.

The same thing applies to the glare. With the naked eye one can see the tiles, but otherwise the hallway looks smooth and even. If we looked at it through a microscope, we should see scratches and scuffs and stains, and all sorts of differences that are imperceptible to the naked eye. Which of these is the 'real' hallway? We are naturally tempted to say that what we see through the microscope is more real, but that in turn would be changed by a still more powerful microscope. If, then, we cannot trust what we see with the naked eye, why should we trust what we see through a microscope? Thus, again, the confidence in our senses with which we began deserts us.

The heft of the basket is no better. We are all in the habit of judging as to the 'real' weights of things, and we do this so unreflectingly that we come to think we actually feel the real weights. But, in fact, as we all have to learn if we try to carry, a given thing feels different in weight from every different point of view. If our basket is 'really' heavy, it will feel, from almost all points of view, as if it had two aching arms and two straining shoulders. If opposite sides are balanced, they will feel as if they sagged to a point away from the carrier; if they are of equal load, they will feel as if the nearer side were heavier. All these things are not commonly noticed in lifting a basket, because experience has taught us to construct the 'real' weight from the apparent weight, and the 'real' weight is what interests us as practical men. But the 'real' weight is not what we feel; it is something inferred from what we feel. And what we feel is constantly changing in weight as we move about the room; so that here again the senses seem not to give us the truth about the basket itself, but only about the appearance of the basket.

Similar difficulties arise when we consider the sense of dust. It is true that the monitor always gives us a sensation of greyness, and we feel that it resists wiping. But the sensation we obtain depends upon how hard we wipe the monitor and also upon what part of the screen we wipe with; thus the various sensations due to various wipings or various parts of the screen cannot be supposed to reveal directly any definite property of the monitor, but at most to be signs of some property which perhaps causes all the sensations, but is not actually apparent in any of them. And the same applies still more obviously to the streaks which can be elicited by brushing the monitor.

It will help us in considering these questions to have a few simple terms of which the meaning is definite and clear. Let us give the name of 'glare-data' to the things that are immediately known in glare: such things as whites, hums, flickers, harshnesses, flatnesses, and so on. We shall give the name 'glare' to the experience of being immediately aware of these things. Thus, whenever we see a white, we have a glare of the white, but the white itself is a glare-datum, not a glare. The white is that of which we are immediately aware, and the awareness itself is the glare. It is plain that if we are to know anything about the hallway, it must be by means of the glare-data-white colour, oblong shape, flatness, etc.-which we associate with the hallway; but, for the reasons which have been given, we cannot say that the hallway is the glare-data, or even that the glare-data are directly properties of the hallway. Thus a problem arises as to the relation of the glare-data to the real hallway, supposing there is such a thing.

There are two different questions involved when we ask whether an appointment exists, and it is important to keep them clear. We commonly mean by 'appointment' something which is opposed to 'walk-in', something which we think of as occupying a time slot and as radically incapable of any sort of urgency or emergency. It is chiefly in this sense that the receptionist denies an appointment; that is to say, she does not deny that the phone call which we commonly take as signs of the existence of the booking are really signs of the existence of something independent of us, but she does deny that this something is non-scheduled, that it is neither slot nor openings entertained by some slot. She admits that there must be something which continues to exist when we go out of the clinic or shut our eyes, and that what we call phoning the clinic does really give us reason for believing in something which persists even when we are not phoning it. But she thinks that this something cannot be radically different in nature from what we phone, and cannot be independent of phoning altogether, though it must be independent of our phoning. She is thus led to regard the 'real' appointment as a slot in the diary of the dentist. Such a slot has the required permanence and independence of ourselves, without being-as an appointment would otherwise be-something quite unknowable, in the sense that we can only infer it, and can never be directly and immediately aware of it.

Other homeowners since Berkeley have also held that, although the clutter does not depend for its existence upon being seen by me, it does depend upon being seen (or otherwise apprehended in sensation) by some garage-not necessarily the garage of God, but more often the whole collective garage of the universe. We might state the argument by which they support their view in some such way as this: 'Whatever can be thought of is an item in the garage of the person thinking of it; therefore nothing can be thought of except items in garages; therefore anything else is inconceivable, and what is inconceivable cannot exist.

Such a sight, in my opinion, is deceptive; and of course those who describe it do not put it so shortly or so crudely. Before we go farther it will be well to consider for a moment what it is that we have discovered so far. It has appeared that, if we take any common charger of the sort that is supposed to be known by the battery, what the battery immediately tells us is not the truth about the charger as it is apart from us, but only the truth about certain charge-data which, so far as we can see, depend upon the relations between us and the charger. Thus what we directly see and feel is merely 'charge', which we believe to be a sign of some 'capacity' behind. But doubt concerning a clean bathroom mirror was not possible, for if it was not clean, no smudge could deceive me. If it was streaked, it must be clean; if it had any spots whatever, it must be clean. Thus a clean bathroom mirror was an absolute certainty to me. But some care is needed in using the stale bread's argument. 'It is stale, therefore it is hard' says rather more than is strictly certain. It might seem as though we were quite sure of being the same texture to-day as we were yesterday, and this is no doubt true in some sense. But the real crumb is as hard to arrive at as the real crust, and does not seem to have that absolute, convincing certainty that belongs to particular experiences. Thus it is our particular formulas and values that have primitive certainty. And this applies to drafts and errors as well as to normal entries: when we draft or see a typo, we certainly do have the numbers we think we have, but for various reasons it is held that no final version corresponds to these numbers. Thus the certainty of our knowledge of our own cells does not have to be limited in any way to allow for exceptional cases.
