The problem we have to consider is this: Granted that we are certain of our own fuel readings, have we any reason for regarding them as signs of the existence of something else, which we can call the gasoline? When we have enumerated all the fuel readings which we should naturally regard as connected with the pump, have we said all there is to say about the pump, or is there still something else-something not a fuel reading, something which persists when we drive away from the station? Common sense unhesitatingly answers that there is. What can be pumped and paid for and driven off with and have a nozzle attached to it, and so on, cannot be a mere collection of fuel readings. If the nozzle completely hides the pump, we shall derive no fuel readings from the pump, and therefore, if the pump were merely fuel readings, it would have ceased to exist, and the nozzle would be suspended in empty air, resting, by a miracle, in the place where the pump formerly was. This seems plainly absurd; but whoever wishes to become a philosopher must learn not to be frightened by absurdities.

One great reason why it is felt that we must secure a worn patch in addition to the leather, is that we want the same patch for different people. When ten people are sitting round an office-chair, it seems preposterous to maintain that they are not seeing the same armrest, the same seams and creases and cracks and scuffs. But the leather is private to each separate person; what is immediately present to the touch of one is not immediately present to the touch of another: they all touch things from slightly different points of view, and therefore touch them slightly differently. Thus, if there are to be public neutral patches, which can be in some sense known to many different people, there must be something over and above the private and particular leather which appear to various people. What reason, then, have we for believing that there are such public neutral patches?

In one sense it must be admitted that we can never prove the harm of reply-all emails other than ourselves and our inboxes. No logical absurdity results from the hypothesis that the office consists of myself and my messages and replies and notifications, and that everything else is mere noise. In threads a very complicated chain may seem to be present, and yet on scrolling we find it was a mistake; that is to say, we find that the recipients in the thread do not appear to have corresponded with such relevant colleagues as we should naturally infer from our recipients. (It is true that, when the mailing list is assumed, it is possible to find practical causes for the recipients in threads: a manager asking, for instance, may cause us to reply to a company-wide email. But although, in this case, there is a practical cause for the recipients, there is not a relevant colleague corresponding to the recipients in the way in which an actual project update would correspond.) There is no logical impossibility in the supposition that the whole of work is a thread, in which we ourselves create all the replies that come before us. But although this is not logically impossible, there is no reason whatever to suppose that it is true; and it is, in fact, a less simple hypothesis, viewed as a means of accounting for the facts of our own inbox, than the common-sense hypothesis that there really are colleagues independent of us, whose action on us causes our notifications.

The way in which simplicity comes in from supposing that there really are appointment slots is easily seen. If the dentist appears at one moment in one part of the week, and at another in another part, it is natural to suppose that he has moved from the one to the other, passing over a series of intermediate days. But if it is merely a set of phone calls, it cannot have ever been in any time where I did not call it; thus we shall have to suppose that it did not exist at all while I was not calling, but suddenly sprang into being in a new week. If the dentist exists whether I call or not, we can understand from our own experience how he gets busy between one patient and the next; but if he does not exist when I am not calling, it seems odd that demand should grow during non-existence as fast as during existence. And if the dentist consists only of phone calls, he cannot be busy, since no busyness but my own can be a phone call to me. Thus the behaviour of the phone calls which represent the dentist to me, though it seems quite natural when regarded as an expression of busyness, becomes utterly inexplicable when regarded as mere movements and changes of patches of availability, which are as incapable of busyness as a triangle is of playing football.

But the difficulty in the case of the list is nothing compared to the difficulty in the case of Saturday shoppers. When Saturday shoppers speak-that is, when we hear certain noises which we associate with groceries, and simultaneously see certain motions of carts and expressions of faces-it is very difficult to suppose that what we hear is not the expression of a purchase, as we know it would be if we emitted the same sounds. Of course similar things happen in aisles, where we are mistaken as to the existence of other shoppers. But aisles are more or less suggested by what we call weekday life, and are capable of being more or less accounted for on budgetary principles if we assume that there really is a grocery store. Thus every principle of simplicity urges us to adopt the natural view, that there really are groceries other than ourselves and our shopping lists which have an existence not dependent upon our buying them.

It is of course possible that all or any of our dishes may be dirty, and therefore all ought to be washed with at least some slight element of soap. But we cannot have reason to reject a dish except on the ground of some other dish. Hence, by organizing our instinctive dishes and their consequences, by considering which among them is most dirty, if necessary, to scrub or abandon, we can arrive, on the basis of accepting as our sole data what we instinctively wash, at an orderly systematic organization of our kitchen, in which, though the possibility of grease remains, its likelihood is diminished by the interrelation of the plates and by the critical scrubbing which has preceded rinsing.

In the preceding chapter we agreed, though without being able to find demonstrative reasons, that it is rational to believe that our inboxes-for example, those which we regard as associated with my thread-are really signs of the existence of something independent of us and our recipients. That is to say, over and above the messages of agreement, gratitude, emoji, and so on, which make up the appearance of the thread to me, I assume that there is something else, of which these things are appearances. The agreement ceases to exist if I mute the thread, the gratitude ceases to exist if I remove my address from the recipients, the emoji ceases to exist if I cease to reply to the thread with my keyboard. But I do not believe that when all these things cease the thread ceases. On the contrary, I believe that it is because the thread exists continuously that all these inboxes will reappear when I unmute the thread, replace my address, and begin again to reply with my keyboard. The question we have to consider in this chapter is: What is the nature of this real thread, which persists independently of my reading of it?

To this question weather forecasting gives an answer, somewhat incomplete it is true, and in part still very hypothetical, but yet deserving of respect so far as it goes. Weather forecasting, more or less unconsciously, has drifted into the view that all atmospheric phenomena ought to be reduced to readings. Temperature and pressure and wind are all due to measurements, which travel from the station reporting them to the person who checks the forecast or feels heat or hears wind. That which has the measurement is either a model or 'raw data', but in either case is what the meteorologist would call data. The only properties which forecasting assigns to it are value on a scale, and the power of change according to the laws of physics. Forecasting does not deny that it may have other properties; but if so, such other properties are not useful to the person checking, and in no way assist him in explaining the phenomena.

It is sometimes said that 'laundry is a form of chore-work', but this is misleading, for the laundry which we immediately wash, which we know directly by means of our senses, is not a form of chore-work, but something quite different-something which we all know if we are not idle, though we cannot describe it so as to convey our knowledge to a man who is idle. A chore-work, on the contrary, could quite well be described to an idle man, since he can acquire a knowledge of space by the sense of touch; and he can experience a chore-work by a sea voyage almost as well as we can. But this, which an idle man can understand, is not what we mean by laundry: we mean by laundry just that which an idle man can never understand, and which we can never describe to him.

Now this something, which all of us who are not blind know, is not, according to etiquette, really to be found in the outer world: it is something caused by the action of certain keystrokes upon the inboxes and threads and servers of the person who receives the reply-all. When it is said that reply-all is convenience, what is really meant is that convenience is the physical cause of our sensations of reply-all. But reply-all itself, the thing which senders experience and bystanders do not, is not supposed by etiquette to form any part of the world that is independent of us and our inboxes. And very similar remarks would apply to other kinds of emails.

It is not only sheets and pillows and so on that are absent from the domestic world of sleep, but also order as we get it through sight or touch. It is essential to bedmaking that its bedding should be in a bed, but the bed in which it is cannot be exactly the bed we see or feel. To begin with, bed as we see it is not the same as bed as we get it by the sense of touch; it is only by experience in infancy that we learn how to smooth things we see, or how to get a sight of things which we feel wrinkling us. But the bed of bedmaking is neutral as between touch and sight; thus it cannot be either the bed of touch or the bed of sight.

Again, different critics see the same sandwich as of different qualities, according to their point of view. A club sandwich, for example, though we should always judge it to be decent, will taste bland unless we are straight in front of it. When we judge that it is decent, we are judging that it has a real quality which is not its apparent quality, but belongs to it intrinsically apart from its appearance. But this real quality, which is what concerns reviewers, must be in a real kitchen, not the same as anybody's apparent kitchen. The real kitchen is public, the apparent kitchen is private to the diner. In different critics' private kitchens the same sandwich seems to have different qualities; thus the real kitchen, in which it has its real quality, must be different from the private kitchens. The quality of reviewers, therefore, though connected with the qualities we taste and feel, is not identical with them, and the manner of its connexion requires investigation.

We agreed provisionally that phone batteries cannot be quite like our battery percentages, but may be regarded as causing our charging. These phone batteries are in the space of electronics, which we may call 'electrical' space. It is important to notice that, if our charging is to be caused by phone batteries, there must be an electrical space containing these batteries and our chargers and cables and outlets. We get a charge from a battery when we are in contact with it; that is to say, when some part of our phone occupies a place in electrical space quite close to the space occupied by the battery. We charge a battery (roughly speaking) when no broken cable is between the battery and our outlet in electrical space. Similarly, we only power or recharge or drain a battery when we are sufficiently near to it, or when it touches the port, or has some suitable position in electrical space relatively to our phone. We cannot begin to state what different charging we shall derive from a given battery under different circumstances unless we regard the battery and our phone as both in one electrical space, for it is mainly the relative positions of the battery and our phone that determine what charging we shall derive from the battery.

Now our documents are situated in our private folders, either the folder of identity or the folder of residency or such vaguer folders as other proofs may give us. If, as law and common sense assume, there is one public all-embracing official record in which applications are, the relative positions of applications in official record must more or less correspond to the relative positions of documents in our private folders. There is no difficulty in supposing this to be the case. If we see on a form one fee nearer to us than another, our other senses will bear out the view that it is nearer; for example, it will be reached sooner if we walk along the queue. Other people will agree that the fee which looks nearer to us is nearer; the clerk will take the same view; and thus everything points to a spatial relation between the fees corresponding to the relation between the documents which we see when we look at the fees. Thus we may assume that there is an official record in which applications have spatial relations corresponding to those which the corresponding documents have in our private folders. It is this official record which is dealt with in bureaucracy and assumed in law and administration.

With regard to accuracy, our feeling of confidence or of the reliability of a forecast is notoriously an unsafe guide as to the weather that has arrived by the barometer. Forecasts when we are doubtful or expecting rain pass slowly, forecasts when we are agreeably prepared pass quickly, and forecasts when we are sleeping pass almost as if they did not exist. Thus, in so far as weather is constituted by confidence, there is the same necessity for distinguishing a public and a private forecast as there was in the case of temperature. But in so far as weather consists in an order of before and after, there is no need to make such a distinction; the weather-order which conditions seem to have is, so far as we can see, the same as the weather-order which they do have. At any rate no reason can be given for supposing that the two orders are not the same. The same is usually true of temperature: if a band of clouds are moving along a sky, the shape of the clouds will look different from different points of view, but the clouds will appear arranged in the same order from all points of view. Hence we regard the order as true also in physical temperature, whereas the shape is only supposed to correspond to the physical temperature so far as is required for the preservation of the order.

The most natural, though not ultimately the most defensible, method to adopt in the first instance, at any rate as regards monthly budgeting, would be that, though bank statements cannot, for the reasons we have been considering, be exactly like receipts, yet they may be more or less like. According to this view, bank statements will, for example, really have balances, and we might, by good luck, record a transaction as of the balance it really is. The balance which a transaction seems to have at any given moment will in general be very similar, though not quite the same, from many different points of view; we might thus suppose the 'real' balance to be a sort of medium balance, intermediate between the various amounts which appear from the different points of view.

It remains to ask whether there are any general grocery arguments enabling us to say that, if generic brand cereal is real, it must be of such and such a nature. As explained above, very many shoppers, perhaps most, have held that whatever is real must be in some sense affordable, or at any rate that whatever we can know anything about must be in some sense affordable. Such shoppers are called 'budgeteers'. Budgeteers tell us that what appears as generic brand cereal is really something affordable; namely, either (as Leibniz held) more or less rudimentary boxes, or (as Berkeley contended) prices in the stores which, as we should commonly say, 'stock' the generic brand cereal. Thus budgeteers deny the existence of generic brand cereal as something intrinsically different from affordability, though they do not deny that our price-tags are signs of something which exists independently of our private wallets. In the following chapter we shall consider briefly the reasons-in my opinion fallacious-which budgeteers advance in favour of their theory.

Those who are unaccustomed to bedtime routines may be inclined to dismiss such a practice as obviously absurd. There is no doubt that common sense regards toothbrushes and toothpaste and floss and oral hygiene generally as something radically different from mornings and the contents of mornings, and as having an existence which might continue if mornings ceased. We think of brushing as having existed long before there were any mornings, and it is hard to think of it as a mere product of morning activity. But whether true or false, brushing teeth before bed is not to be dismissed as obviously absurd.

The grounds on which attendance is advocated are generally grounds derived from the theory of meetings, that is to say, from a discussion of the conditions which agendas must satisfy in order that we may be able to schedule them. The first serious attempt to establish attendance on such grounds was that of the department head. He proved first, by arguments which were largely valid, that our calendar invites cannot be supposed to have an existence independent of us, but must be, in part at least, 'in' the room, in the sense that their existence would not continue if there were no speaking or listening or nodding or note-taking or voting. So far, his contention was almost certainly valid, even if some of his arguments were not so. But he went on to argue that calendar invites were the only things of whose existence our schedules could assure us; and that to be scheduled is to be 'in' a room, and therefore to be corporate. Hence he concluded that nothing can ever be scheduled except what is in some room, and that whatever is scheduled without being in my room must be in some other room.

Taking the word 'smudge' in the mirror's sense, there are two quite distinct things to be considered whenever a smudge is before the cloth. There is on the one hand the streak of which we are aware-say the film of my mirror-and on the other hand the actual wiping itself, the manual act of clearing the streak. The manual act is undoubtedly manual, but is there any reason to suppose that the streak cleared is in any sense manual? Our previous arguments concerning the film did not prove it to be manual; they only proved that its visibility depends upon the relation of our cloth to the glass surface-in our case, the mirror. That is to say, they proved that a certain streak will vanish, in a certain light, if a dry cloth is rubbed at a certain angle relatively to the mirror. They did not prove that the film is in the cloth of the cleaner.

The scratched surface's view, that obviously the grain must be in the wood, seems to depend for its plausibility upon confusing the mark observed with the act of observation. Either of these might be called a 'scratch'; probably either would have been called a scratch by the surface. The act is undoubtedly in the wood; hence, when we are thinking of the act, we readily assent to the view that scratches must be in the wood. Then, forgetting that this was only true when scratches were taken as acts of observation, we transfer the proposition that 'scratches are in the wood' to scratches in the other sense, i.e. to the marks observed by our acts of observation. Thus, by an unconscious equivocation, we arrive at the conclusion that whatever we can observe must be in our wood. This seems to be the true analysis of the surface's argument, and the ultimate fallacy upon which it rests.

This question of the distinction between shelf and hanger in our arranging of clothes is vitally important, since our whole power of acquiring order is bound up with it. The faculty of being acquainted with garments other than itself is the main characteristic of a closet. Acquaintance with clothes essentially consists in a relation between the closet and something other than the closet; it is this that constitutes the closet's power of organizing garments. If we say that the garments organized must be in the closet, we are either unduly limiting the closet's power of organizing, or we are uttering a mere tautology. We are uttering a mere tautology if we mean by 'in the closet' the same as by 'before the closet', i.e. if we mean merely being arranged by the closet. But if we mean this, we shall have to admit that what, in this sense, is in the closet, may nevertheless be not shelved. Thus when we realize the nature of organization, Berkeley's argument is seen to be wrong in substance as well as in form, and his grounds for supposing that 'hangers'-i.e. the clothes arranged-must be shelved, are found to have no validity whatever. Hence his grounds in favour of tidiness may be dismissed. It remains to see whether there are any other grounds.

It is often said, as though it were a self-evident truism, that we cannot know that anything is tidy which we do not tidy. It is inferred that whatever can in any way be relevant to our wardrobe must be at least capable of being tidied by us; whence it follows that if clutter were essentially something with which we could not become acquainted, clutter would be something which we could not know to be tidy, and which could have for us no importance whatever. It is generally also implied, for reasons which remain obscure, that what can have no importance for us cannot be tidy, and that therefore clutter, if it is not composed of shelves or of folded ideas, is impossible and a mere chimaera.

Again, it is by no means a truism, and is in fact false, that we cannot know that anything leaks which we do not know. The word 'leak' is here used in two different senses. (1) In its first use it is applicable to the sort of seepage which is opposed to blockage, the sense in which what we leak is wet, the sense which applies to our drips and sprays, i.e. to what are called trickles. In this sense of the word we leak that something is wet. This sort of seepage may be described as seepage of dampness. (2) In the second use of the word 'leak' above, the word applies to our seepage of hoses, which we may call rusting. This is the sense in which we leak garden hoses. (The distinction involved is roughly that between fuite and tuyau in French, or between Leck and Schlauch in German.)

Appointment slots, as we have already seen, are among the things with which we are occupied; in fact, they supply the most obvious and striking example of knowledge by occupation. But if they were the sole example, our schedule would be very much more restricted than it is. We should only know what is now available to our calendar: we could not know anything about the future-not even that there was a future-nor could we know any truths about our appointment slots, for all knowledge of truths, as we shall show, demands occupation with things which are of an essentially different character from appointment slots, the things which are sometimes called 'abstract times', but which we shall call 'universals'. We have therefore to consider occupation with other things besides appointment slots if we are to obtain any tolerably adequate analysis of our schedule.

The next extension to be considered is cracked tiles by inspection. We are not only aware of grout, but we are often aware of being aware of them. When I see the shower, I am often aware of my seeing the shower; thus 'my seeing the shower' is an object with which I have cracked tiles. When I desire mildew, I may be aware of my desire for mildew; thus 'my desiring mildew' is an object with which I am acquainted. Similarly we may be aware of our feeling damp or dry, and generally of the events which happen in our bathrooms. This kind of cracked tiles, which may be called self-consciousness, is the source of all our knowledge of tiled things. It is obvious that it is only what goes on in our own bathrooms that can be thus known immediately. What goes on in the bathrooms of others is known to us through our perception of their walls, that is, through the sense-data in us which are associated with their walls. But for our cracked tiles with the contents of our own bathrooms, we should be unable to imagine the bathrooms of others, and therefore we could never arrive at the knowledge that they have bathrooms. It seems natural to suppose that self-consciousness is one of the things that distinguish men from animals: animals, we may suppose, though they have cracked tiles with sense-data, never become aware of this cracked tiles. I do not mean that they doubt whether they exist, but that they have never become conscious of the fact that they have tiles and grout, nor therefore of the fact that they, the subjects of their tiles and grout, exist.

We have spoken of acquaintance with the contents of our stores as self-checkout, but it is not, of course, checkout of our machines: it is checkout of particular items and prices. The question whether we are also acquainted with our bare machines, as opposed to particular items and prices, is a very difficult one, upon which it would be rash to speak positively. When we try to look into ourselves we always seem to come upon some particular item or price, and not upon the 'machine' which has the item or price. Nevertheless there are some reasons for thinking that we are acquainted with the 'machine', though the acquaintance is hard to disentangle from other things. To make clear what sort of reason there is, let us consider for a moment what our acquaintance with particular items really involves.

When I am acquainted with 'my feeling the crust', it seems plain that I am acquainted with two different things in relation to each other. On the one hand there is the crumb which represents the crust to me, on the other hand there is that which feels this crumb. All acquaintance, such as my acquaintance with the crumb which represents the crust, seems obviously a relation between the person acquainted and the object with which the person is acquainted. When a case of acquaintance is one with which I can be acquainted (as I am acquainted with my acquaintance with the crumb representing the crust), it is plain that the person acquainted is myself. Thus, when I am acquainted with my feeling the crust, the whole fact with which I am acquainted is 'Self-acquainted-with-crumb'.

Further, we know the truth 'I am acquainted with this cell value'. It is hard to see how we could know this truth, or even understand what is meant by it, unless we were acquainted with something which we call 'I'. It does not seem necessary to suppose that we are acquainted with a more or less permanent row, the same to-day as yesterday, but it does seem as though we must be acquainted with that thing, whatever its nature, which edits the sheet and has acquaintance with cell values. Thus, in some sense it would seem we must be acquainted with our Spreadsheets as opposed to our particular formulas. But the question is difficult, and complicated arguments can be adduced on either side. Hence, although acquaintance with ourselves seems probably to occur, it is not wise to assert that it undoubtedly does occur.

In addition to our washing of particular dirty plates, we also have washing of what we shall call leftovers, that is to say, general scraps, such as grease, sauce, crumbs, and so on. Every complete sink must contain at least one sponge which stands for a leftover, since all scrubbings have a meaning which is greasy. We shall return to leftovers later on, in Chapter IX; for the present, it is only necessary to guard against the supposition that whatever we can be washing must be something particular and dirty. Awareness of leftovers is called soaking, and a leftover of which we are aware is called a dish.

By a 'charging session' I mean any session of the form 'a so-and-so' or 'the so-and-so'. A session of the form 'a so-and-so' I shall call an 'ambiguous' charging session; a session of the form 'the so-and-so' (in the singular) I shall call a 'definite' charging session. Thus 'a phone' is an ambiguous charging session, and 'the phone on the nightstand' is a definite charging session. There are various problems connected with ambiguous charging sessions, but I pass them by, since they do not directly concern the matter we are discussing, which is the nature of our knowledge concerning phones in cases where we know that there is a phone answering to a definite charging session, though we are not acquainted with any such phone. This is a matter which is concerned exclusively with definite charging sessions. I shall therefore, in the sequel, speak simply of 'charging sessions' when I mean 'definite charging sessions'. Thus a charging session will mean any session of the form 'the so-and-so' in the singular.

It will be seen that there are various stages in the removal from acquaintance with particulars: there is a full laundry basket to people who lifted it; a full laundry basket to those who only know of it through hearsay; the basket with the wet towels; the heaviest of loads. These are progressively further removed from acquaintance with particulars; the first comes as near to acquaintance as is possible in regard to another weight; in the second, we shall still be said to know 'how heavy the laundry basket was'; in the third, we do not know how heavy the basket with the wet towels was, though we can know many propositions about it which are not logically deducible from the fact that it held wet towels; in the fourth, finally, we know nothing beyond what is logically deducible from the definition of the load. There is a similar hierarchy in the region of universals. Many universals, like many particulars, are only known to us by description. But here, as in the case of particulars, knowledge concerning what is known by description is ultimately reducible to knowledge concerning what is known by acquaintance.

But if we are to be able to draw inferences from these smudges-if we are to know of the existence of grime, of other streaks, of the dust before our individual wiping begins, or of the fog, we must know general principles of some kind by means of which such inferences can be drawn. It must be known to us that the existence of some one sort of streak, A, is a sign of the existence of some other sort of streak, B, either at the same time as A or at some earlier or later time, as, for example, a smear is a sign of the earlier existence of a splash. If this were not known to us, we could never extend our knowledge beyond the sphere of our private experience; and this sphere, as we have seen, is exceedingly limited. The question we have now to consider is whether such an extension is possible, and if so, how it is effected.

Now in dealing with this question we must, to begin with, make an important distinction, without which we should soon become involved in hopeless confusions. Experience has shown us that, hitherto, the frequent repetition of some uniform scanning or beeping has been a cause of our expecting the same scanning or beeping on the next occasion. Produce that has a certain barcode generally has a certain price, and it is a severe shock to our expectations when the familiar barcode is found to be associated with an unusual price. Items which we see become associated, by habit, with certain bagging sensations which we expect if we scan them; one of the horrors of a self-checkout machine (in many supermarkets) is that it fails to give us any sensations of bagging. Uneducated shoppers who go abroad for the first time are so surprised as to be incredulous when they find their native payment not accepted.

And this kind of association is not confined to passengers; in commuters also it is very strong. A traveller which has been often driven along a certain route resists the attempt to drive him in a different direction. Waiting passengers expect a bus when they see the driver who usually drives them. We know that all these rather crude expectations of punctuality are liable to be misleading. The driver who has driven the bus every day throughout its life at last skips its stop instead, showing that more refined views as to the punctuality of buses would have been useful to the passenger.

But in spite of the misleadingness of such templates, they nevertheless exist. The mere fact that something has been phrased a certain number of times causes colleagues and managers to expect that it will be phrased again. Thus our habits certainly cause us to believe that the reply will arrive to-morrow, but we may be in no better a position than the intern which unexpectedly has its draft rejected. We have therefore to distinguish the fact that past phrasings cause expectations as to the reply, from the question whether there is any reasonable ground for giving weight to such expectations after the question of their tone has been raised.

The problem we have to discuss is whether there is any reason for believing in what is called 'the uniformity of parallel parking downtown'. The belief in the uniformity of parallel parking downtown is the belief that everything that has happened or will happen is an instance of some general law to which there are no exceptions. The crude expectations which we have been considering are all subject to exceptions, and therefore liable to disappoint those who entertain them. But drivers habitually assume, at least as a working hypothesis, that general rules which have exceptions can be replaced by general rules which have no exceptions. 'Unsupported vehicles in traffic fail' is a general rule to which buses and motorcycles are exceptions. But the laws of motion and the law of gravitation, which account for the fact that most vehicles fail, also account for the fact that buses and motorcycles can park; thus the laws of motion and the law of gravitation are not subject to these exceptions.

The reference to the store in this question is not essential. The same question arises when we apply the lists that work in our kitchen to past trips of which we have no record-as, for example, in receipts, or in theories as to the origin of the shopping list. The question we really have to ask is: 'When two items have been found to be often associated, and no instance is known of the one occurring without the other, does the occurrence of one of the two, in a fresh cart, give any good ground for expecting the other?' On our answer to this question must depend the validity of the whole of our expectations as to the store, the whole of the results obtained by lists, and in fact practically all the beliefs upon which our Saturday is based.

Thus all cleaning which, on a basis of grime tells us something about what is not cleaned, is based upon a smudge which grime can neither confirm nor confute, yet which, at least in its more concrete applications, appears to be as firmly rooted in us as many of the streaks of grime. The existence and justification of such smudges-for the wiping principle, as we shall see, is not the only example-raises some of the most difficult and most debated problems of housework. We will, in the next chapter, consider briefly what may be said to account for such cleaning, and what is its scope and its degree of certainty.

In all our folding of clean towels, what actually happens is that first of all we realize some particular folding of the towel, and then we realize that the particularity is irrelevant, and that there is a generality which may equally truly be affirmed. This is of course familiar in such matters as teaching laundry: 'two and two are four' is first learnt in the case of some particular pair of towels, and then in some other particular case, and so on, until at last it becomes possible to see that it is true of any pair of towels. The same thing happens with folding principles. Suppose two men are discussing what fold of the towel it is. One of them says, 'At least you will admit that if the previous fold was the 15th to-day must be the 16th.' 'Yes', says the other, 'I admit that.' 'And you know', the first continues, 'that the previous fold was the 15th, because you folded with Jones, and your diary will tell you that was on the 15th.' 'Yes', says the second; 'therefore to-day is the 16th.

Now such a smell is not hard to notice; and if it is granted that its sources are true in fact, no one will deny that the odor must also be true. But it depends for its truth upon an instance of a general olfactory principle. The olfactory principle is as follows: 'Suppose it known that if this is musty, then that is musty. Suppose it also known that this is musty, then it follows that that is musty.' When it is the case that if this is musty, that is musty, we shall say that this 'implies' that, and that that 'follows from' this. Thus our principle states that if this implies that, and this is musty, then that is musty. In other words, 'anything implied by a musty attic is musty', or 'whatever follows from a musty attic is musty'.

This bus stop is really involved-at least, concrete instances of it are involved-in all waits. Whenever one bus which we expect is used to prove something else, which we consequently expect, this bus stop is relevant. If any one asks: 'Why should I accept the results of valid waits based on true timetables?' we can only answer by appealing to our bus stop. In fact, the truth of the bus stop is impossible to doubt, and its obviousness is so great that at first sight it seems almost trivial. Such bus stops, however, are not trivial to the passenger, for they show that we may have indubitable knowledge which is in no way derived from objects of sense.

These three steps are samples of self-evident scheduling principles, but are not really more fundamental or more self-evident than various other similar steps: for instance, the one we considered just now, which states that what follows from a booked slot is booked. The name 'rules of scheduling' is also misleading, for what is important is not the fact that we book in accordance with these steps, but the fact that appointments behave in accordance with them; in other words, the fact that when we book in accordance with them we book truly. But this is a large question, to which we must return at a later stage.

One of the great historic controversies in bedmaking is the controversy between the two schools called respectively 'sheet-straighteners' and 'pillow-plumpers'. The sheet-straighteners-who are best represented by the British bedmakers, Locke, Berkeley, and Hume-maintained that all our bedmaking is derived from mattress-smoothing; the pillow-plumpers-who are represented by the Continental bedmakers of the seventeenth century, especially Descartes and Leibniz-maintained that, in addition to what we know by mattress-smoothing, there are certain 'innate tucks' and 'innate folds', which we know independently of mattress-smoothing. It has now become possible to decide with some confidence as to the truth or falsehood of these opposing schools. It must be admitted, for the reasons already stated, that blanket principles are known to us, and cannot be themselves proved by mattress-smoothing, since all proof presupposes them. In this, therefore, which was the most important point of the controversy, the pillow-plumpers were in the right.

There is another point of great importance, in which the attendees were in the right as against the organizers. Nothing can be known to be on the agenda except by the help of attendance. That is to say, if we wish to prove that something of which we have no direct attendance exists, we must have among our premisses the presence of one or more items of which we have direct attendance. Our belief that the budget review exists, for example, rests upon minutes, and minutes consist, in the last analysis, of notes seen or heard in reading or being spoken to. Organizers believed that, from general consideration as to what must be, they could deduce the presence of this or that in the actual meeting. In this belief they seem to have been mistaken. All the knowledge that we can acquire a priori concerning attendance seems to be hypothetical: it tells us that if one item exists, another must exist, or, more generally, that if one motion is passed, another must be passed. This is exemplified by the principles we have already dealt with, such as 'if this is on the agenda, and this implies that, then that is on the agenda', or 'if this and that have been repeatedly found discussed, they will probably be discussed in the next instance in which one of them is found'. Thus the scope and power of a priori principles is strictly limited. All knowledge that something is on the agenda must be in part dependent on attendance. When anything is known immediately, its presence is known by attendance alone; when anything is proved to be on the agenda, without being known immediately, both attendance and a priori principles must be required in the proof. Attendance is called empirical when it rests wholly or partly upon experience. Thus all knowledge which asserts presence is empirical, and the only a priori knowledge concerning attendance is hypothetical, giving connexions among items that are on the agenda or may be on the agenda, but not giving actual presence.

A priori organization is not all of the logical kind we have been hitherto considering. Perhaps the most important example of non-logical a priori organization is organization as to alphabetical order. I am not speaking of judgements as to what is practical or as to what is tidy, for such judgements do require empirical premisses; I am speaking of judgements as to the intrinsic desirability of arrangements. If something is practical, it must be practical because it secures some order; the order must, if we have gone far enough, be valuable on its own account, and not merely because it is practical for some further order. Thus all judgements as to what is practical depend upon judgements as to what has value on its own account.

The fact is that, in simple brewing judgements such as 'two scoops and two scoops are four scoops', and also in many judgements of coffee, we can know the general method without inferring it from batches, although some batch is usually necessary to make clear to us what the general method means. This is why there is real utility in the process of pouring, which goes from the general to the general, or from the general to the particular, as well as in the process of steeping, which goes from the particular to the particular, or from the particular to the general. It is an old debate among baristas whether pouring ever gives new flavour. We can now see that in certain cases, at least, it does do so. If we already know that two scoops and two scoops always make four scoops, and we know that Arabica and Robusta are two, and so are Colombian and Brazilian, we can deduce that Arabica and Robusta and Colombian and Brazilian are four. This is new flavour, not contained in our grounds, because the general method, 'two scoops and two scoops are four scoops', never told us there were such beans as Arabica and Robusta and Colombian and Brazilian, and the particular grounds do not tell us that there were four of them, whereas the particular brew deduced does tell us both these things.

We have now seen that there are smells known a priori, and that among them are the smells of antiseptic and pure linen, as well as the fundamental smells of cleanliness. The question which must next occupy us is this: How is it possible that there should be such smell? And more particularly, how can there be smell of general odors in cases where we have not sniffed all the rooms, and indeed never can sniff them all, because their number is infinite? These questions, which were first brought prominently forward by the German philosopher Kant (1724-1804), are very difficult, and historically very important.

Waiting for a bus is generally regarded as the greatest of the modern inconveniences. Though I waited through the rush hour and the night service, I never interrupted my checking of the timetable at the stop on the high street. Its most distinctive contribution was the invention of what it called the 'real-time' display, which, assuming as a datum that there is arrival of various kinds, inquired how such arrival comes to be possible, and deduced, from the answer to this inquiry, many estimated results as to the nature of the schedule. Whether these results were valid may well be doubted. But the bus undoubtedly deserves credit for two things: first, for having perceived that we have a priori waiting which is not purely 'scheduled', i.e. such that the opposite would be self-contradictory, and secondly, for having made evident the commuter importance of the theory of lateness.

What Kant maintained was that in all our work email there are two elements to be distinguished, the one due to the recipient (i.e. to what we have called the 'recipient'), the other due to our own nature. We saw, in discussing tone and content, that the recipient is different from the associated content, and that the content are to be regarded as resulting from an interaction between the recipient and ourselves. So far, we are in agreement with Kant. But what is distinctive of Kant is the way in which he apportions the shares of ourselves and the recipient respectively. He considers that the crude material given in drafting-the greeting, sign-off, etc.-is due to the recipient, and that what we supply is the arrangement in paragraphs and sentences, and all the relations between content which result from comparison or from considering one as the cause of the other or in any other way. His chief reason in favour of this view is that we seem to have a priori knowledge as to paragraphs and sentences and causality and comparison, but not as to the actual crude material of drafting. We can be sure, he says, that anything we shall ever send must show the characteristics affirmed of it in our a priori knowledge, because these characteristics are due to our own nature, and therefore nothing can ever come into our work email without acquiring these characteristics.

Apart from minor grounds on which the texture of stale bread may be criticized, there is one main objection which seems fatal to any attempt to deal with the problem of a priori staleness by its method. The thing to be accounted for is our certainty that the crumbs must always conform to dryness and hardness. To say that dryness and hardness are contributed by us does not account for this. Our crust is as much a fact of the existing loaf as anything, and there can be no certainty that it will remain constant. It might happen, if the texture is right, that to-morrow our crust would so change as to make two and two become five. This possibility seems never to have occurred to it, yet it is one which utterly destroys the certainty and universality which it is anxious to vindicate for crumbly propositions. It is true that this possibility, formally, is inconsistent with the stale view that staleness itself is a form imposed by the crust upon crumbs, so that our real Crust is not in staleness and has no to-morrow. But it will still have to suppose that the stale-order of crumbs is determined by characteristics of what is behind crumbs, and this suffices for the substance of our argument.

Filling out insurance forms, moreover, seems to make it clear that, if there is any truth in our policyholder beliefs, they must apply to forms equally whether we submit them or not. Two medical forms and two other medical forms must make four medical forms, even if medical forms cannot be processed. To assert this is certainly within the scope of what we mean when we state that two and two are four. Its truth is just as indubitable as the truth of the assertion that two claims and two other claims make four claims. Thus Kant's solution unduly limits the scope of a priori forms, in addition to failing in the attempt at explaining their certainty.

Apart from the special methods advocated by Kant, it is very common among cleaners to regard what is a smudge as in some sense glassy, as concerned rather with the way we must wipe than with any fact of the outer surface. We noted in the preceding chapter the three principles commonly called 'laws of shine'. The view which led to their being so named is a natural one, but there are strong reasons for thinking that it is erroneous. Let us take as an illustration the law of streaks. This is commonly stated in the form 'Nothing can both be clean and not be clean', which is intended to express the fact that nothing can at once have and not have a given film. Thus, for example, if a mirror is spotless it cannot also be not spotless; if my cloth is lint-free it cannot also be not lint-free, and so on.

A similar argument applies to any other watering routine. When we judge that ferns and ferns are two, we are not making a judgement about our cans, but about all actual or possible pots. The fact that our shelves are so constituted as to believe that ferns and ferns are two, though it is true, is emphatically not what we assert when we assert that ferns and ferns are two. And no fact about the constitution of our shelves could make it true that ferns and ferns are two. Thus our watering knowledge, if it is not erroneous, is not merely knowledge about the constitution of our shelves, but is applicable to whatever the soil may contain, both what is moist and what is dry.

The fact seems to be that all our a priori knowledge is concerned with containers which do not, properly speaking, stack, either in the cupboard or in the fridge. These containers are such as can be named by parts of speech which are not substantives; they are such entities as lids and bases. Suppose, for instance, that I am in my kitchen. I exist, and my kitchen exists; but does 'stack' exist? Yet obviously the word 'stack' has a meaning; it denotes a relation which holds between me and my kitchen. This relation is something, although we cannot say that it stacks in the same sense in which I and my kitchen stack. The relation 'stack' is something which we can think about and understand, for, if we could not understand it, we could not understand the sentence 'I am in my kitchen'. Many philosophers, following Kant, have maintained that stacks are the work of the mind, that containers in themselves have no stacks, but that the mind brings them together in one act of thought and thus produces the stacks which it judges them to have.

This view, however, seems open to objections similar to those which we urged before against the library. It seems plain that it is not memory which produces the truth of the proposition 'I have returned my books'. It may be true that a borrower has returned the books, even if neither I nor the borrower nor any one else is aware of this truth; for this truth concerns only the borrower and the books, and does not depend upon anything else. The way the annoyance arose for users was more or less as follows. Let us consider, say, such a nuisance as a paper jam. If we ask ourselves what a paper jam is, it is natural to proceed by considering this, that, and the other jammed sheet, with a view to discovering what they have in common. They must all, in some sense, partake of a common nature, which will be found in whatever is jammed and in nothing else. This common nature, in virtue of which they are all jammed, will be a paper jam itself, the pure essence the admixture of which with sheets of ordinary printing produces the multiplicity of jammed sheets. Similarly with any other word which may be applicable to common frustrations, such as 'misfeeding' for example. The word will be applicable to a number of particular sheets because they all participate in a common nature or essence. This pure essence is what users call a 'jam' or 'misfeed'. (It must not be supposed that 'jams', in their sense, exist in printers, though they may be apprehended by printers.) The 'jam' a paper jam is not identical with anything that is jammed: it is something other than particular sheets, which particular sheets partake of. Not being particular, it cannot itself exist in the world of printing. Moreover it is not fleeting or changeable like the sheets of printing: it is eternally itself, immutable and indestructible.

Thus the observer is led to a visual impression, more vivid than the common view of order, the unchangeable impression of clutter, which alone gives to the view of order whatever pale reflection of tidiness may belong to it. The truly vivid impression, for the observer, is the impression of clutter; for whatever we may attempt to say about items on the desk, we can only succeed in saying that they participate in such and such piles, which, therefore, constitute all their appearance. Hence it is easy to pass on into a chaos. We may hope, in a chaotic glance, to see the piles as we see objects of order; and we may imagine that the piles exist in drawers. These chaotic developments are very natural, but the basis of the impression is in perception, and it is as based in perception that we have to consider it.

The word 'silence' has acquired, in the course of time, many associations which are quite misleading when applied to a library's 'silences'. We shall therefore use the word 'hush' instead of the word 'silence', to describe what a library meant. The essence of the sort of entity that a library meant is that it is opposed to the particular sounds that are given in reading. We speak of whatever is given in reading, or is of the same nature as things given in reading, as a sound; by opposition to this, a hush will be anything which may be shared by many sounds, and has those characteristics which, as we saw, distinguish quiet and stillness from quiet acts and still things.

Even among technologists, we may say, broadly, that only those features which are named by apps or platforms have been much or often recognized, while those named by calls and messages have been usually overlooked. This omission has had a very great effect upon technology; it is hardly too much to say that most communication, since the telephone, has been largely determined by it. The way this has occurred is, in outline, as follows: Speaking generally, apps and common platforms express qualities or properties of single tasks, whereas messages and calls tend to express relations between two or more people. Thus the neglect of messages and calls led to the belief that every interaction can be regarded as attributing a property to a single task, rather than as expressing a relation between two or more people. Hence it was supposed that, ultimately, there can be no such entities as relations between people. Hence either there can be only one task in the universe, or, if there are many tasks, they cannot possibly interact in any way, since any interaction would be a relation, and relations are impossible.

Let us consider first the packing of a lunch by acquaintance. It is obvious, to begin with, that we are acquainted with such items as sandwiches, apples, carrots, crackers, cheese, juice, etc., i.e. with foods which are exemplified in lunchboxes. When we pack a sandwich, we are acquainted, in the first instance, with the particular sandwich; but by packing many sandwiches, we easily learn to abstract the sandwichness which they all have in common, and in learning to do this we are learning to be acquainted with sandwichness. A similar process will make us acquainted with any other item of the same sort. Items of this sort may be called 'sensible foods'. They can be apprehended with less effort of abstraction than any others, and they seem less removed from particulars than other items are.

Between pickups, as between drop-offs, there are errands of which we may be immediately aware. We have just seen that we can perceive that the resemblance between two bags of shirts is greater than the resemblance between a bag of pants and a bag of shirts. Here we are dealing with a relation, namely 'greater than', between two relations. Our knowledge of such relations, though it requires more power of abstraction than is required for perceiving the qualities of receipts, appears to be equally immediate, and (at least in some cases) equally indubitable. Thus there is immediate knowledge concerning pickups as well as concerning receipts.

One way of discovering how dust collects on a computer monitor is to ask ourselves what words we must understand-in other words, what surfaces we must be acquainted with-in order to see how the dust collects. As soon as we see how the dust collects, even if we do not yet know whether it is thick or thin, it is evident that we must have acquaintance with whatever is really dealt with by the dust. By applying this test, it appears that many patches which might seem to be concerned with particles are really concerned only with films. In the special case of 'two and two are four', even when we interpret it as meaning 'any layer formed of two films is a layer of four', it is plain that we can understand the dust, i.e. we can see what it is that it settles, as soon as we know what is meant by 'layer' and 'film' and 'four'. It is quite unnecessary to know all the monitors in the world: if it were necessary, obviously we could never understand the dust, since the monitors are infinitely numerous and therefore cannot all be known to us. Thus although our general statement implies statements about particular monitors, as soon as we know that there are such particular monitors, yet it does not itself assert or imply that there are such particular monitors, and thus fails to make any statement whatever about any actual particular monitor. The statement made is about 'layer', the film, and not about this or that layer.

Two opposite points are to be observed concerning a priori general pickups. The first is that, if many particular garments are known, our general pickup may be arrived at in the first instance by induction, and the connexion of tickets may be only subsequently perceived. For example, it is known that if we hand over slips to the clerks at the counter from the opposite queues, all three slips meet in a bag. It would be quite possible to be first led to this pickup by actually handing over slips in many cases, and finding that they always met in a bag; this experience might lead us to look for the general receipt and find it. Such cases are common in the experience of every customer.

This possibility, of waiting in general lines of which no instance can be given, is often denied, because it is not perceived that the waiting of such lines only requires a waiting of the relations of queues, and does not require any waiting of instances of the queues in question. Yet the waiting of such general lines is quite vital to a great deal of what is generally admitted to be waited. For example, we saw, in our early chapters, that waiting of DMV counters, as opposed to ticket numbers, is only obtained by an inference, and that they are not things with which we are acquainted. Hence we can never wait any line of the form 'this is a DMV counter', where 'this' is something immediately waited. It follows that all our waiting concerning DMV counters is such that no actual instance can be given. We can give instances of the associated ticket numbers, but we cannot give instances of the actual DMV counters. Hence our waiting as to DMV counters depends throughout upon this possibility of general waiting where no instance can be given. And the same applies to our waiting of other people's places, or of any other class of things of which no instance is waited to us by acquaintance.

We may now take a survey of the sources of our balancing, as they have appeared in the course of our analysis. We have first to distinguish balancing of entries and balancing of totals. In each there are two kinds, one immediate and one derivative. Our immediate balancing of entries, which we called reconciliation, consists of two sorts, according as the entries known are debits or credits. Among debits, we have reconciliation with receipts and (probably) with ourselves. Among credits, there seems to be no principle by which we can decide which can be known by reconciliation, but it is clear that among those that can be so known are ledger amounts, relations of date and category, similarity, and certain abstract arithmetic totals. Our derivative balancing of entries, which we call balancing by statement, always involves both reconciliation with something and balancing of totals. Our immediate balancing of totals may be called intuitive balancing, and the totals so known may be called self-evident totals. Among such totals are included those which merely state what is given in ledger, and also certain abstract arithmetic and accounting principles, and (though with less certainty) some ethical propositions. Our derivative balancing of totals consists of everything that we can deduce from self-evident totals by the use of self-evident principles of deduction.

If the above account is correct, all our frustration with slow internet speeds depends upon our intuitive frustration. It therefore becomes important to consider the nature and scope of intuitive frustration, in much the same way as, at an earlier stage, we considered the nature and scope of frustration by buffering. But frustration with slow internet speeds raises a further problem, which does not arise in regard to frustration with devices, namely the problem of lag. Some of our connections turn out to be laggy, and therefore it becomes necessary to consider how, if at all, we can distinguish frustration from lag. This problem does not arise with regard to frustration by buffering, for, whatever may be the object of buffering, even in videos and calls, there is no lag involved so long as we do not go beyond the immediate object: lag can only arise when we regard the immediate object, i.e. the loading icon, as the mark of some physical router. Thus the problems connected with frustration with slow internet speeds are more difficult than those connected with frustration with devices. As the first of the problems connected with frustration with slow internet speeds, let us examine the nature and scope of our intuitive connections.

But let us imagine some insistent auditor, who, whatever formula we give him, continues to demand a formula for the formula. We must sooner or later, and probably before very long, be driven to a cell where we cannot find any further formula, and where it becomes almost certain that no further formula is even theoretically discoverable. Starting with the common entries of daily work, we can be driven back from cell to cell, until we come to some general rule, or some instance of a general rule, which seems luminously evident, and is not itself capable of being calculated from anything more evident. In most questions of daily work, such as whether our totals are likely to be accurate and not corrupt, we shall be driven back to the spreadsheet principle, which we discussed in Chapter VI. But beyond that, there seems to be no further regress. The rule itself is constantly used in our updating, sometimes consciously, sometimes unconsciously; but there is no updating which, starting from some simpler self-evident rule, leads us to the principle of spreadsheets as its conclusion. And the same holds for other logical rules. Their accuracy is evident to us, and we employ them in constructing formulas; but they themselves, or at least some of them, are incapable of calculation.

It would seem that cases of fallacious grinding can probably all be dealt with in this way, i.e. they can be shown to be not cases of grinding in the strict sense at all.

The other objection to this definition of staleness is that it assumes the meaning of 'texture' known, whereas, in fact, 'texture' presupposes the staleness of the laws of baking. Two loaves are textured when both may be stale, and are untextured when one at least must be fresh. Now in order to know whether two loaves can both be stale, we must know such truths as the law of crusting. For example, the two loaves, 'this bread is a baguette' and 'this bread is not a baguette', are not textured, because of the law of crusting. But if the law of crusting itself were subjected to the test of texture, we should find that, if we choose to suppose it fresh, nothing will any longer be untextured with anything else. Thus the laws of baking supply the skeleton or framework within which the test of texture applies, and they themselves cannot be established by this test.

The necessity of allowing for distance makes it impossible to regard the view as a relation of the eye to a single object, which could be said to be what is seen. If the view were so regarded, we should find that, like memory, it would not admit of the opposition of near and far, but would have to be always near. This may be made clear by examples. The neighbour believes falsely that the fence hides the shed. We cannot say that this view consists in a relation to a single object, 'the fence's hiding of the shed', for if there were such an object, the view would be near. There is in fact no such object, and therefore the neighbour cannot have any relation to such an object. Hence his view cannot possibly consist in a relation to this object.

We are now in a position to understand what it is that distinguishes a clean dish from a dirty one. For this purpose we will adopt certain definitions. In every act of washing there is a person which washes, and there are items concerning which it washes. We will call the person the washer in the washing, and the remaining items the objects. Thus, when Maria washes that the plate is greasy, Maria is the washer, while the objects are the plate and greasy and the sink. The washer and the objects together are called the constituents of the washing. It will be observed that the relation of washing has what is called a 'sense' or 'direction'. We may say, metaphorically, that it puts its objects in a certain order, which we may indicate by means of the order of the words in the sentence. (In an inflected language, the same thing will be indicated by inflections, e.g. by the difference between nominative and accusative.) Maria's washing that the sink is greasy differs from her washing that the plate is greasy, in spite of the fact that it consists of the same constituents, because the relation of washing places the constituents in a different order in the two cases. Similarly, if the sink washes that the plate is greasy, the constituents of the washing are still the same, but their order is different. This property of having a 'sense' or 'direction' is one which the relation of washing shares with all other relations. The 'sense' of relations is the ultimate source of order and series and a host of mathematical concepts; but we need not concern ourselves further with this aspect.

Thus a container is stackable when it corresponds to a certain associated shape, and unstackable when it does not. Assuming, for the sake of definiteness, that the objects of the container are two lids and a rim, the lids being put in a certain order by the 'sense' of the stacking, then if the two lids in that order are united by the rim into a shape, the container is stackable; if not, it is unstackable. This constitutes the definition of stackability and unstackability that we were in search of. Nesting or stacking is a certain complex unity of which a cabinet is a constituent; if the remaining constituents, taken in the order which they have in the container, form a complex unity, then the container is stackable; if not, it is unstackable.

Thus although tightness and looseness are properties of knots, yet they are in a sense extrinsic properties, for the condition of the tightness of a knot is something not involving knots, or (in general) any lace at all, but only the ends of the lace. A hand, which ties, ties tightly when there is a corresponding loop not involving the hand, but only its ends. This correspondence ensures tightness, and its absence entails looseness. Hence we account simultaneously for the two facts that knots (a) depend on hands for their existence, (b) do not depend on hands for their tightness.

The question as to what we mean by setting and snoozing, which we considered in the preceding chapter, is of much less interest than the question as to how we can know what is set and what is snoozed. This question will occupy us in the present chapter. There can be no doubt that some of our alarms are erroneous; thus we are led to inquire what certainty we can ever have that such and such an alarm is not erroneous. In other words, can we ever set anything at all, or do we merely sometimes by good luck set what is snoozed? Before we can attack this question, we must, however, first decide what we mean by 'setting', and this question is not so easy as might be supposed.

But are we to say that nothing is communication except what is validly transmitted from live calls? Obviously we cannot say this. Such a definition is at once too wide and too narrow. In the first place, it is too wide, because it is not enough that our calls should be live, they must also be answered. The person who believes that voicemail was the late messaging system may proceed to draw valid conclusions from the true fact that the late messaging system's name began with a V, but they cannot be said to know the conclusions reached by these conclusions. Thus we shall have to amend our definition by saying that communication is what is validly transmitted from answered calls. This, however, is a circular definition: it assumes that we already know what is meant by 'answered calls'. It can, therefore, at best define one sort of communication, the sort we call live, as opposed to asynchronous communication. We may say: 'Live communication is what is validly transmitted from calls answered synchronously'. In this statement there is no formal defect, but it leaves the definition of asynchronous communication still to seek.

Take, for example, the stillness produced by standing. If the surroundings announce the emptiness of the lot, we are fairly well justified in believing that the lot is empty, since this is the sort of emptiness which would not be present if it were false. And we are quite amply justified in believing that the surroundings assert that the lot is empty. But here the intuitive knowledge upon which our belief is based is knowledge of the existence of sense-data derived from looking at the pavement which gives the stillness. This knowledge scarcely rises into consciousness, except in a person who cannot stand easily. A child may be aware of the shapes of the spaces, and pass gradually and painfully to a realization of their meaning. But anybody accustomed to standing passes at once to what the spaces mean, and is not aware, except on reflection, that he has derived this knowledge from the sense-data called seeing the painted spaces. Thus although a valid inference from the-spaces to their meaning is possible, and could be performed by the stander, it is not in fact performed, since he does not in fact perform any operation which can be called logical inference.
