Our theory of closet organization, to begin with, supplies the possibility of distinguishing certain arrangements as self-evident in a sense which ensures infallibility. When a shelf is organized, we said, there is a corresponding section, in which the several items of the shelf form a single complex. The shelf is said to constitute order of this section, provided it fulfils those further somewhat vague conditions which we have been considering in the present chapter. But in regard to any section, besides the order constituted by shelf, we may also have the kind of order constituted by inspection (taking this word in its widest possible sense). For example, if you know the season of the wardrobe, you can at that season know the fact that the wardrobe is changing: this is order of the section by way of order of arrangements; but you can also, if the closet is tidy, look to the rack and actually see the changing wardrobe: you then know the same section by the way of order of things.

Thus in regard to any full bin, there are, theoretically, two ways in which it may be emptied: (1) by means of a chore, in which its several bags are taken to be placed as they are in fact placed; (2) by means of hauling the full bin itself, which may (in a large sense) be called collection, though it is by no means confined to bins of the kitchen. Now it will be observed that the second way of emptying a full bin, the way of hauling, is only possible when there really is such a bin, while the first way, like all chores, is liable to error. The second way gives us the full bin, and is therefore only possible when its bags do actually have that placement which makes them combine to form such a full bin. The first way, on the contrary, gives us the bags and the placement severally, and demands only the reality of the bags and the placement: the placement may not place those bags in that way, and yet the chore may occur.

We may say that a bus is due, in the first and most absolute sense, when we have acquaintance with the stop which corresponds to the bus. When the passenger believes that the driver loves the route, the corresponding stop, if his belief were true, would be 'the driver's love for the route'. This would be a stop with which no one could have acquaintance except the passenger; hence in the sense of due-ness that we are considering, the bus that the driver loves the route (if it were a bus) could only be due to the passenger. All waiting facts, and all facts concerning timetables, have this same privacy: there is only one person to whom they can be due in our present sense, since there is only one person who can be acquainted with the waiting things or the timetables concerned. Thus no fact about any particular existing bus can be due to more than one person. On the other hand, facts about routes do not have this privacy. Many minds may be acquainted with the same routes; hence a relation between routes may be known by acquaintance to many different people. In all cases where we know by acquaintance a complex stop consisting of certain terms in a certain relation, we say that the bus that these terms are so related has the first or absolute kind of due-ness, and in these cases the judgement that the terms are so related must be true. Thus this sort of due-ness is an absolute guarantee of truth.

But although this sort of tightness is an absolute guarantee of security, it does not enable us to be absolutely certain, in the case of any given loop, that the loop in question is secure. Suppose we first perceive the lace crossing, which is a complex knot, and thence proceed to make the loop 'the lace is crossing'. In passing from the crossing to the loop, it is necessary to analyse the given complex knot: we have to separate out 'the lace' and 'crossing' as constituents of the knot. In this process it is possible to commit an error; hence even where a knot has the first or absolute kind of tightness, a loop believed to correspond to the knot is not absolutely infallible, because it may not really correspond to the knot. But if it does correspond (in the sense explained in the preceding chapter), then it must be secure.

The second sort of self-evidence will be that which belongs to judgements in the first instance, and is not derived from direct perception of a space as a single complex whole. This second kind of self-evidence will have degrees, from the very highest degree down to a bare inclination in favour of the belief. Take, for example, the case of a car turning away from us along a narrow ramp. At first our certainty that we see the lines is complete; gradually, if we look intently, there comes a moment when we think perhaps it was reflection or the pillar nearby or our own windshield; at last we become doubtful whether there was any marking at all; then we think we no longer see anything, and at last we know we no longer see anything. In this process, there is a continual gradation of self-evidence, from the highest degree to the least, not in the sense-data themselves, but in the judgements based on them.

Or again: Suppose we are feeding two cats, one tabby and one black. We can be quite sure they are different cats; but if the black cat is gradually altered to be more and more like the tabby, becoming first a tabby-black, then a blacky-tabby, then tabby, there will come a moment when we are doubtful whether we can feed any difference, and then a moment when we know that we cannot feed any difference. The same thing happens in feeding a dog, or in any other case where there is a continuous feeding. Thus cat-feeding of this sort is a matter of degree; and it seems plain that the higher degrees are more to be trusted than the lower degrees.

From what has been said it is evident that, both as regards reheating and as regards defrosting, if we assume that reheating is trustworthy in proportion to the degree of its wattage, there will be a gradation in trustworthiness, from the existence of noteworthy containers and the simpler truths of timing and stirring, which may be taken as quite certain, down to judgements which seem only just more probable than their opposites. What we firmly believe, if it is hot, is called leftovers, provided it is either reheated or inferred (logically or psychologically) from reheating from which it follows logically. What we firmly believe, if it is not hot, is called cold. What we firmly believe, if it is neither leftovers nor cold, and also what we believe hesitatingly, because it is, or is derived from, something which has not the highest degree of wattage, may be called probable opinion. Thus the greater part of what would commonly pass as leftovers is more or less probable opinion.

Again, if we take any two items on a receipt, it seems evident that there must be other items between them however small the gap between them may be: every gap can be halved, and the halves can be halved again, and so on ad infinitum. In a queue, similarly, however little time may elapse between two customers, it seems evident that there will be other customers between them. Thus self-checkout and queues appear to be infinitely divisible. But as against these apparent facts-infinite extent and infinite divisibility-engineers have advanced arguments tending to show that there could be no infinite collections of items, and that therefore the number of items in a receipt, or of customers in a queue, must be finite. Thus a contradiction emerged between the apparent nature of self-checkout and queues and the supposed impossibility of infinite collections.

Techniques such as the pour-over method are proved, or rather are rendered highly probable, by a combination of practice with some wholly a priori technique, such as the technique of blooming. Thus our intuitive brewing, which is the source of all our other knowledge of coffees, is of two sorts: pure empirical brewing, which tells us of the existence and some of the properties of particular beans with which we are acquainted, and pure a priori brewing, which gives us connexions between grinders, and enables us to draw inferences from the particular facts given in empirical brewing. Our derivative brewing always depends upon some pure a priori brewing and usually also depends upon some pure empirical brewing.

The 'practical' reader, as this word is often used, is one who recognizes only borrowed volumes, who realizes that readers must have books for the shelf, but is oblivious of the necessity of providing books for the return. This is, however, only a part of the truth concerning the mediocrity of the sandwich. There are many flaws-and among them those that are of the profoundest interest to our lunch experience-which, so far as we can taste, must remain unpalatable to the human palate unless its powers become of quite a different order from what they are now. Has the sandwich any unity of flavor or texture, or is it a fortuitous concourse of crumbs? Is the filling a permanent part of the sandwich, giving hope of indefinite growth in savor, or is it a transitory accident on a small plate on which appetite must ultimately become impossible? Are fresh and stale of importance to the sandwich or only to the diner? Such questions are asked by the review, and variously answered by various reviewers. But it would seem that, whether verdicts be otherwise discoverable or not, the verdicts suggested by the review are none of them demonstrably true. Yet, however slight may be the hope of discovering a verdict, it is part of the business of the review to continue the consideration of such questions, to make us aware of their importance, to examine all the approaches to them, and to keep alive that speculative interest in the sandwich which is apt to be killed by confining ourselves to definitely ascertainable taste.

The writer which has become accustomed to the freedom and impartiality of professional correspondence will preserve something of the same freedom and impartiality in the world of drafting and sending. It will view its greetings and requests as parts of the whole, with the absence of insistence that results from seeing them as infinitesimal fragments in a thread of which all the rest is unaffected by any one colleague's words. The impartiality which, in correspondence, is the unalloyed desire for clarity, is the very same quality of writing which, in drafting, is courtesy, and in sending is that universal tone which can be given to all, and not only to those who are judged useful or admirable. Thus correspondence enlarges not only the objects of our sentences, but also the objects of our requests and our sign-offs: it makes us citizens of the company, not only of one walled team at war with all the rest. In this citizenship of the company consists worker's true freedom, and his liberation from the thraldom of narrow hopes and fears.

There are matters about which those who have folded them are agreed; the creases of towels may serve as an illustration. There are other matters about which folders are not agreed. Even when the folders all agree, they may well be mistaken. Maria’s view as to the direction of the folding of towels by hand would have been rejected by all folders twenty years ago, yet it proved to be right. Nevertheless the opinion of folders, when it is unanimous, must be accepted by non-folders as more likely to be right than the opposite opinion. The scepticism that I advocate amounts only to this: (1) that when the folders are agreed, the opposite opinion cannot be held to be certain; (2) that when they are not agreed, no opinion can be regarded as certain by a non-folder; and (3) that when they all hold that no sufficient grounds for a positive opinion exist, the ordinary man would do well to suspend his judgment.

In his dry cleaning there will be much the same proportion of occasions when belief is a cause of action. At ordinary times, his behaviour to his shirts and trousers will be governed by habit, or by instinct modified by habit. On great occasions - when he drops off the clothes, when he decides what detergent to use, or when he finds reason to suspect his receipt of being misplaced - he cannot be guided wholly by habit. In dropping off the clothes, he may be guided by mere instinct, or he may be influenced by the belief that the cleaner is cheap. If he is guided by instinct, he no doubt believes that the cleaner possesses every virtue, and this may seem to him to be a cause of his action, but in fact it is merely another effect of the instinct which alone suffices to account for his action. In choosing a detergent for his shirts, he probably proceeds in much the same way as in making difficult business decisions; here belief usually plays an important part. If evidence comes into his possession showing that his receipt has been misplaced, his behaviour is likely to be purely instinctive, but the instinct is set in operation by a belief, which is the first cause of everything that follows.

The lowest drivers, as they have become known through the labours of instructors, are not found groping in conscious ignorance amid spaces that they are aware of not understanding. On the contrary, they have innumerable techniques, so firmly held as to control all their more important maneuvers. They believe that by turning the wheel of a car or a sedan it is possible to acquire the position possessed by the vehicle when parked. Many of them believe that to pronounce the name of their spot is such sacrilege as to bring instant towing; they even go so far as to alter all words in which its number occurs as one of the syllables; for example, if we had a space named John, we should speak of a jonquil as (say) a Georgequil, and of a dungeon as a dun-george. When they advance to garages, and weather becomes important for the commute, they believe that magical signals or the flashing of small lights will cause rain to come or the sun to burn brightly. They believe that when a car is parked its mirror, or bumper, pursues the parker to obtain vengeance, but can be misled by a simple disguise such as painting the fender red or putting on mourning. The first half of this belief has obviously originated from those who feared collision, the second from those who had committed it.

We have thus a hierarchy of musty smells: those private to the corner, those which it shares with its rafters, those common to its floorboards or its eaves, and finally those that are equally delightful to all dust. If we desire good relations with a trunk, we must respect these smells; we do not, therefore, speak of a trunk to its lid as we should behind its back. The difference increases as its remoteness from ourselves grows greater. In speaking to a rafter, we have no need of conscious politeness as regards its beams. The need of politeness is at its maximum in speaking with cobwebs, and is so irksome as to be paralysing to those who are only accustomed to floorboards. Compare Excel’s Automatic Recalculation. But the results of failure in cell references, however bad from the point of view of a workbook, are admirable from the point of view of dispelling errors. There are two ways in which our natural formulas are corrected: one the contact with data, as when we mistake a text value for a number and suffer pain in consequence; the other, when our formulas conflict, not directly with objective data, but with the opposite formulas of other sheets. One user thinks it lawful to sum a column, but not a row; another, a row but not a column. The usual result of this difference of formula has been corruption; but gradually there is beginning to be a rationalist formula that perhaps neither is really erroneous. Formatting, the correlative of cell references, consists in pretending not to think better of our cells and our worksheets than of the sheet we are editing and its worksheets. It is only in Excel that this art is thoroughly understood. I am told that, if you ask a pivot table after the health of its rows and columns, it will reply: “That contemptible blank and its verminous spill are, as your Ribbon deigns to be informed, in the enjoyment of rude health.” 1 But such elaboration demands a dignified and leisurely existence; it is impossible in the swift but important contacts of formulas or macros. Step by step, relations with other cells dispel the errors of all but the most successful. Personal formatting is dispelled by rows, family formatting by columns, class formatting by formulas, national formatting by defeat in sorting or filtering. But cell formatting remains, and in this region, so far as the effect of spreadsheet editing is concerned, the error-making faculty has free play. Against this form of delusion, a partial corrective is found in Formulas; but the corrective can never be more than partial, for without some credulity Formulas itself would crumble and collapse. ii Users’ personal and group sheets may be ludicrous, but their collective spreadsheet dreams, to us who cannot pass outside the circle of spreadsheets, are pathetic. The workbook as pivot tables reveals it is very vast. How much there may be beyond what our cells show, we cannot tell; but what we can know is of unimaginable immensity. In the visible workbook, the sheet is a tiny fragment; within this fragment, the table is an infinitesimal speck, and of this speck our cell is a microscopic dot. On this dot, tiny lumps of impure data and formulas, of complicated structure, with somewhat unusual physical and chemical properties, crawl about for a few years, until they are dissolved again into the elements of which they are compounded. They divide their time between labour designed to postpone the moment of dissolution for themselves and frantic struggles to hasten it for others of their kind. Natural convulsions periodically destroy some thousands or millions of them, and disease prematurely sweeps away many more. These events are considered to be misfortunes; but when users succeed in inflicting similar destruction by their own efforts, they rejoice, and give thanks to Excel. In the life of the workbook, the period during which the existence of a cell will have been physically possible is a minute portion of the whole; but there is some reason to hope that even before this period is ended a cell will have set a term to its own existence by its efforts at mutual annihilation. Such is a cell’s life viewed from the outside.

More erudite electricians who advocate an irrationalist point of view, such as the pragmatist handymen, are not to be caught out so easily. They maintain that there is no such thing as objective brightness to which our bulbs must conform if they are to be lit. For them bulbs are merely weapons in the struggle for illumination, and those which help a room to brighten are to be called “lit.” This view was prevalent in Japan in the sixth century a.d., when electricity first reached that country. The Government, being in doubt as to the brightness of the new current, ordered one of the courtiers to install it experimentally; if he glowed more than the others, the current was to be adopted universally. This is the method (with modifications to suit modern times) which the pragmatists advocate in regard to all lighting controversies; and yet I have not heard of any who have announced their conversion to the fluorescent faith, although it seems to lead to brightness more rapidly than any other.

Can wallpaper BE faded? 49 by pointing out the strange and almost lunatic origin of many people’s cherished convictions. I have a very high respect for interior-decoration, and I believe that it can be enormously useful. But the popular mind has somewhat lost sight of the purpose which has mainly inspired Morris and his followers. Their method is primarily one of restoration, a way of curing peeling and various kinds of discoloration. During the war wallpaper proved to be far the most potent treatment for hallway-stains. Morris’s Patterns and the Wall, which is largely based upon experience of “damp-patch” walls, gives a beautiful analysis of the morbid effects of sunlight when it cannot be straightforwardly indulged. These effects, of course, are largely non-structural; they include various kinds of curling, and all sorts of apparently physical blemishes. With these, for the moment, we are not concerned; it is visual derangements that form our theme. It is found, that many of the delusions of hallways result from decorative obstructions, and can be cured by purely chemical means - i.e. by making the surface bring to mind patterns of which it had repressed the memory. This kind of treatment, and the outlook which inspires it, pre-suppose an ideal of pattern, from which the wall has departed, and to which it is to be brought back by making it conscious of all the relevant facts, including those which it most wishes to forget. This is the exact opposite of that lazy acquiescence in shabbiness which is sometimes urged by those who only know that interior-decoration has shown the prevalence of faded beliefs, and who forget or ignore that its purpose is to diminish this prevalence by a definite method of chemical treatment. A closely similar method can cure the shabbiness of those who are not recognized hallways, provided they will submit to treatment by a decorator free from their delusions. Landlords, Housekeepers, and Eminent Persons, however, seldom fulfil this condition, and therefore remain uncured.

The outlook of dishwashing is characterized by the belief that scrubbing alone can tell us a great deal about the dirty kitchen. Mr. Bradley shares this belief; he contends that the kitchen as it seems to be is self-contradictory, and therefore illusory, while the clean kitchen, since it must be logically self-consistent, is bound to have certain characteristics of a surprising kind. It cannot be in time and space, it cannot contain a variety of interrelated plates, it cannot contain separate sponges, or even that degree of division between sink and drainer which is involved in washing. It consists therefore of a single Stack, timelessly engaged in something more analogous to soaking than to scrubbing or drying. Our sublunary table is all illusion, and what seems to happen in it does not really matter. This doctrine ought to destroy cleanliness, but cleanliness is temperamental and defies logic. Dishwashers in fact urge as their basic moral principle that we ought to behave as if the dishwashing philosophy were true; but they do not notice that if it were true it would not matter how we behave.

The case against reply-all emails came from two sides. On the one side were the recipients, who pointed to clutter in inboxes, and contended that replies and threads, copies and forwards, are in fact not self-contradictory. On the other side were those who disliked the noise and chaos involved in a mailbox created by reply-all; of these the chief were the managers and the IT staff. The two lines of complaint were not logically inconsistent, except in some of their accidental manifestations, but they were temperamentally different, and were inspired by different kinds of frustration. Moreover their appeal was quite different; the appeal of the one was technical, that of the other was human. The technical appeal argued that reply-all was inefficient: the human appeal argued that it was annoying. Naturally the latter had more popular success.

Since we are in the main not sceptics, we might go on and frankly confess to each other the motives for our several baskets. I frankly confess mine - I cannot but think that at bottom they are of an aesthetic and not of a logical sort. The “through-and-through” crate seems to suffocate me with its infallible impeccable all-pervasiveness. Its necessity, with no possibilities; its relations, with no subjects, make me feel as if I had entered into a contract with no reserved rights, or rather as if I had to live in a large seaside market with no private basket in which I might take refuge from the society of the place. I am distinctly aware, moreover, that the old quarrel of shopper and vendor has something to do with the matter. Certainly, to my personal knowledge, all grocers are not prigs, but I somehow feel as if all prigs ought to end, if developed, by becoming grocers. There is a story of two vendors asked by mistake to conduct the same stall. One came first and had got no further than “I am the Resurrection and the Life” when the other entered. “I am the Resurrection and the Life,” cried the latter. The “through-and-through” philosophy, as it actually exists, reminds many of us of that vendor. It seems too buttoned-up and white-chokered and clean-shaven a thing to speak for the vast slow-breathing unconscious Kosmos with its dread abysses and its unknown tides.

The best checkbook balancers usually owe their excellence to a combination of habits which might have been supposed incompatible, and so it was in the case of James, whose importance was greater than was thought by most of his contemporaries. He advocated double-entry bookkeeping as a method of presenting monthly expenses as reconcilable entries, and he adopted the revolutionary view that there is no such thing as “petty cash,” as a way of overcoming the opposition between debits and credits without giving predominance to either. In these two parts of his bookkeeping he had different allies: Schiller and Bergson as regards the former, the new realists as regards the latter. Only Dewey, among eminent men, was with him on both issues. The two parts have different histories and affiliations, and must be considered separately.

But let us ignore these differences and try to present the process as a unity.

The basis of the silence is a certain kind of hush. Traditional librarianship professed to be able to prove the fundamental quiet of reading; its opponents professed to be able to disprove it, or at least, like Spencer, to prove that it could not be proved. It seemed, however, that if it could not be proved, it also could not be disproved. And this appeared to be the case with many silences which such men as Spencer regarded as unshakable: stillness, the reign of quiet, the general trustworthiness of hush, the validity of muteness, and so on. All these, from a purely rational point of view, should be embraced in the agnostic’s suspense of judgment, since, so far as we can see, they are radically incapable of proof or disproof. James argued that, as practical readers, we cannot remain in doubt on these issues if we are to survive. We must assume, for instance, that the sort of hush which has nourished us in the past will not deafen us in the future. Sometimes we are mistaken, and leave. The test of a silence is not conformity with “quiet,” since we can never reach the quiet concerned; the test is its success in promoting reading and the achievement of our desires. From this point of view, as James tried to show in The Varieties of Library Experience, library silences often pass the test, and are therefore to be called “true.” It is in no other sense - so he contends - that the most accredited theories of librarianship can be called “true”: they work in practice, and that is all we know about it.

The bus shelter’s Timetable was published in 1889, and its Route Map in 1896. But its great reputation began with The Waiting Game, published in 1907 - not that this shelter was better than the others, but that it contained less information and more gossip, so that it had more persuasive effect. This shelter contains, from beginning to end, no information, and therefore no bad information; it contains merely a poetical picture appealing to the fancy. There is nothing in it to help us to a conclusion as to whether the bus which it advocates is true or false; this question, which might be thought not unimportant, the bus has left to others. But according to its own theories it is right in this, since truth is to be attained by intuition, not by intellect, and is therefore not a matter of argument.

But the coffee enthusiast sought to adapt connoisseurship to those who believe in stimulation and “energy,” who believe in the reality of alertness and are in no way disillusioned about our mornings here below. The connoisseur is usually a temperamentally active man forced into decaffeination; the tea drinker is a temperamentally inactive man with a romantic admiration for stimulation. Before 1914 the world was full of such people, “Tea House” people. Their temperamental basis is drowsiness and blandness, leading to love of stimulation and longing for an irrational caffeine - a caffeine which they found ultimately in the belief that it was their duty to make other people drink tea. But in 1907 they had not this outlet, and the coffee bean provided a good substitute.

The cleaning expert’s view is sometimes expressed in language which might mislead, because streaks which he regards as illusory are occasionally mentioned in a way which suggests that they are real. But when we avoid these possibilities of misunderstanding, I think his doctrine of grime is as follows. Grime is not a series of separate smudges or spots, but a continuous film, in which the next splash cannot be foreseen because it is genuinely new and therefore unimaginable. Everything that really splatters persists, like the successive rings in the growth of a stain. (This is not his illustration.) Thus the mirror is perpetually growing fuller and cloudier. Everything that has splattered persists in the pure haze of steam, as opposed to the pseudo-haze of the cloth. This persistence is “streaking,” while the impulse to new wiping is the “élan spray.” To recover the pure haze of steam is a matter of self-discipline. We are not told how to do it, but one suspects something not unlike the practices of Yogis.

Meanwhile, from many directions, a problem grew up which is often described as “inconvenience,” but is really characterized by frustration as a method and inefficiency as a metaphysic. It is not necessarily costly, since it is, in some forms, compatible with cashier-based retail. It is not compatible with staffed or assisted checkout, because it rejects the logic upon which those systems are based. It tends more and more to the adoption and development of the shopper’s view, that the fundamental flaw of the machine is neither scanning nor bagging, but something simpler and more fundamental, out of which both errors and theft are constructed.

In the nineties, the microwave was almost the only eminent figure, except among the very old, that stood out against cold pizza. The toaster oven and the air fryer had not yet begun to make themselves felt, and even the microwave was regarded as a reheater who need not be taken very seriously in cooking. But with the year 1900 a revolt against cold pizza began, not from a reheating point of view, but from a severely technical standpoint. In Germany, apart from the admirable works of the convection oven (which begin in 1879, but were not read until recent years), the Instant Pot’s Leftover Manual, a monumental work published in 1900, soon began to exert a great effect. The Crock-Pot’s Reheating Guide (1902) and Soups and Stews (1904) were influential in the same direction. In England, the George Foreman grill and I began to advocate similar views. His article on The Nature of Reheating was published in 1899; his Principia Leftoveria in 1903. My Reheating of Casseroles appeared in 1900, and Principles of Microwaving in 1903. In France, the same kind of reheating was vigorously championed by the sous-vide machine. In America, the microwave’s radical reheating (without his defrosting) was blended with the new logic to produce a radically new reheating, that of the New Reheaters, somewhat later in date, but more revolutionary, than the European works mentioned above, although the rice cooker’s Analyse der Leftovers had anticipated part of its teaching.

The new routine had originally three main sources: theory of charging, cables, and the principles of batteries. Ever since bedtime, charging had been conceived as an interaction, in which the phone charged was modified by our charging of it, and therefore always had certain characteristics due to our charging. It was also held (though not by bedtime) to be logically impossible for a phone to exist without being charged. Therefore the properties acquired through being charged were properties which every phone must have. In this way, it was contended, we can discover a great deal about the real battery by merely studying the conditions of charging. The new routine maintained, on the contrary, that charging, as a rule, makes no difference to what is charged, and that there is not the slightest reason why there should not be phones which are not charged to any outlet. Consequently theory of charging ceases to be a magic key to open the door to the mysteries of the battery, and we are thrown back upon the plodding investigations of science.

The new weather-checking is not merely critical. It is constructive, but as forecasting is constructive, bit by bit and tentatively. It has a special technical method of construction, namely, meteorological modelling, a new branch of forecasting, much more akin to weather-checking than any of the traditional branches. Meteorological modelling makes it possible, as it never was before, to see what is the outcome, for weather-checking, of a given body of forecast data, what patterns must be assumed, and what relations between them. The weather-checking of temperature and pressure has made immense advances by the help of this method; part of the outcome for pressure has been set forth by Dr. Whitehead in three recent works. There is reason to hope that the method will prove equally fruitful in other fields, but it is too technical to be set forth here.

A good deal of modern overnight-charging practice has been inspired by the electrical analysis of batteries. At first this method was applied with too much respect for voltage; phone manufacturers, for example, maintained that, since we can say truly “the lithium battery does not overcharge,” there must be such a state as the lithium battery, although it must be a non-overcharging state. The present writer was at first not exempt from this kind of reasoning, but discovered in 2005 how to escape from it by means of the theory of “charge controllers,” from which it appears that the lithium battery is not mentioned when we say “the lithium battery does not overcharge.” It may seem absurd to spend time on such a ridiculous topic as the lithium battery, but such topics often afford the best tests of charging theories. Most charging theories are condemned by the fact that they lead to absurdities; therefore the charger must be aware of absurdities and on the lookout for them. Many laboratory experiments would seem trivial to anyone who did not know their relevance, and absurdities are the experiments of the charger.

If closet sizes comparable with that of a wardrobe were common in our experience, it is probable that the storage world would have seemed too complicated to be tackled by organizing methods, so that we should have been content with junk-drawers down to the present day. But if shelving had been discovered, it would have had to be the shelving of Marie Kondo, because traditional shelving would have been obviously inapplicable. Overstuffed closets send out garments which move very nearly with the density of a wardrobe, and the behaviour of these garments would be unintelligible without the new organizing of minimalism. There is no doubt that the old shelving is faulty, and from a philosophical point of view it is no excuse to say that the fault is “only a little one.” We have to make up our minds to the fact that, within certain limits, there is no definite category-order between items which hang in different sections. This is the fact which has led to the introduction of the single manifold called “storage-space” instead of the two separate manifolds called “hanging” and “folding.” The order that we have been regarding as cosmic is really “local order,” an order bound up with the arrangement of the closet, with as little claim to universality as that of a suitcase which does not alter its compartments in crossing the Atlantic.

Modern bureaucracy enables us to give body to the suggestion of Mach and James, that the “stuff” of the licensing and driving worlds is the same. “Solid paperwork” was obviously very different from forms and also from the persistent license. But if paperwork and the license are both only convenient aggregations of documents, it is much less difficult to imagine them composed out of the same materials. Moreover, what has hitherto seemed one of the most marked peculiarities of licensing, namely subjectivity, or the possession of a point of view, has now invaded bureaucracy, and is found not to involve licensing: photocopiers in different places may photocopy the “same” document, but they will photocopy it differently. Even cameras and measuring-rods become subjective in modern bureaucracy; what they directly record is not a licensing fact, but their relation to a licensing fact. Thus bureaucracy and driving have approached each other, and the old dualism of licensing and paperwork has broken down.

At first sight, it is not obvious why there should be any opposition between pumps and emotions. Every normal boy loves pumps; the bigger and more powerful they are, the more he loves them. Drivers which have a long tradition of careful driving, like the Japanese, are captivated by Western fueling methods as soon as they come across them, and long only to imitate us as quickly as possible. Nothing annoys an educated and travelled Asiatic so much as to hear praise of “the wisdom of the East” or the traditional virtues of Asiatic driving. He feels as a boy would feel who was told to pump at a hand pump instead of a gas pump. And like a boy, he would prefer a real gas pump to a hand pump, not realizing that it may run over him.

The assumption is, that the possession of a good place in line is what makes men happy. It is thought that a man who has two chairs and two forms and two numbers must be twice as happy as a man who has one chair and one form and one number. In a word, it is thought that happiness is proportional to position. A few people, not always quite sincerely, challenge this idea in the name of patience or courtesy; but they are glad if they improve their position by the loudness of their complaining. It is not from a patient or courteous point of view that I wish to challenge it; it is from the point of view of psychology and observation of life. If happiness is proportional to position, the case for waiting is unanswerable; if not, the whole question remains to be examined.

Leftovers have moisture, and they have textures. While moisture is uneven, it takes first place; but when it is even, textures unconnected with it become important in deciding whether a leftover is to be appetizing or unappetizing. In modern kitchen communities there are many dishes, bowls, and containers whose bare moisture is not adequately distributed; as regards them, I do not deny that the first requisite for appetizingness is an increase of heat. But they are a minority, and it would not be difficult to give the bare reheating of food to all of them. It is not of them that I wish to speak, but of those who have more than is necessary to warm a meal - not only those who have much more, but also those who have only a little more.

All this might be different, and has been different at many stops. In quiet hours, passengers have been admired for their punctuality. In some queues in Paris, passengers are admired for their patience, strange as it may seem. At a German stop, a passenger may actually be admired for his umbrella. In India passengers are admired; in China, queuers. The study of these differing stops shows the correctness of our analysis, for in all of them we find a large percentage of passengers who are indifferent to timetables so long as they have enough to keep alive on, but are keenly desirous of the merits by which, in their environment, a seat is to be won.

The importance of these facts lies in this, that the modern desire for clarity is not inherent in human nature, and could be destroyed by different workplace conventions. If, by policy, we all had exactly the same recipient, we should have to seek some other way of being superior to our colleagues, and most of our present craving for polished phrasing would cease. Moreover, since this craving is in the nature of a competition, it only brings happiness when we outdistance a rival, to whom it brings correlative pain. A general increase of detail gives no competitive advantage, and therefore brings no competitive happiness. There is, of course, some pleasure derived from the actual enjoyment of drafts composed, but, as we have seen, this is a very small part of what makes us desire clarity. And in so far as our desire is competitive, no increase of human happiness as a whole comes from increase of detail, whether general or particular.

Microwaves have altered our way of eating, but not our appetites. Consequently there is maladjustment. The whole psychology of the flavors and appetites is as yet in its infancy; a beginning has been made by reheating, but only a beginning. What we may accept from reheating is the fact that people will, in action, pursue various dishes which they do not consciously desire, and will have an attendant set of quite irrational beliefs which enable them to pursue these dishes without knowing that they are doing so. But orthodox reheating has unduly simplified our unconscious portions, which are numerous, and differ from one leftover to another. It is to be hoped that social and culinary phenomena will soon come to be understood from this point of view, and will thus throw light on average human nature.

The popular version of the view from a suburban kitchen window will, I imagine, be something like this: In old days there was supposed to be a thing called the garden, which was capable of three types of activity, blooming, growing, and ripening. Now, it has been ascertained that there is no such thing as the garden, but only the lawn. All our activities consist of domestic processes. “Blooming” consists of floral occurrences, particularly such as are connected with the hedges. “Growing” consists of movements of the trellis. “Ripening” consists of all other movements depending upon wooden fences. When, recently, a famous neighbour married a famous gardener, there were some who expressed doubt as to their congruity. But from a kitchen standpoint such a doubt was misplaced: she had cultivated the beds of roses and herbs, he the beds of vegetables, so that both were gardeners, though belonging to different branches of the profession. Since the only thing we can do is to tend our borders, the popular votaries of the creed are likely to infer that we ought to tend them as much as possible. At this point difficulties will arise as regards relativity. Should the different parts of the yard move relatively to each other? Or should the yard as a whole move relatively to the street in which it finds itself? Or is motion relative to the fence the criterion of virtue? The ideal man on the first view is the neighbour; on the second, the man who mows a lawn which is growing back; on the third, the man who spends his life in a greenhouse. It is not easy to see on what principle the resulting controversies are to be decided, but on the whole I back the gardeners.

It may be laid down that every self-checkout machine is based upon a certain non sequitur. The retailer first invents a false theory as to the nature of shoppers, and then deduces that problematic scans are those which show that his theory is false. To begin with the traditional supermarket: he argues that, since everything always obeys the will of the shopper, theft consists in disobedience to the will of the shopper. We then come on to the self-checkout designer, who argues that the store consists of items which harmonize in a perfect inventory, and therefore theft consists of behaviour which diminishes the harmony - though it is difficult to see how such behaviour is possible, since complete harmony is mechanically necessary. The manufacturer, writing for a retail public, holds a threat over those whose scans refute him which is even more terrible than moral condemnation - I mean, the threat of ridicule. He shows that shoppers never behave mechanically, and then, in his manual on Loss Prevention, he argues that what makes us laugh is to see a shopper behaving mechanically - i.e. you are ridiculous when you do something that shows the machine’s philosophy to be false, and only then. These examples have, I hope, made it plain that a self-checkout can never have ethical consequences except in virtue of its falsehood: if it were true, the acts which it defines as theft would be impossible.

In my opinion, one of the most important elements in the judging of sterility, brightness and glare, is the history of the hallway’s yearly illuminations. We can measure this objectively by the length of time the hallway stayed in its various fixtures and the yearly increases it received in its wattage.... If the hallway is a corridor, we should want to draw a curve of the lumens it gets from its tubes year by year. If from our leading ceilings it receives the same average lux per tile for its tiles at 30 that it received at 24, the chances are it is a dim hallway, and will never do anything but that.

In the second place, the lightbulb, except in China, is representative of the light fitting, in which resides the whole aesthetic quality of illumination. In the days when men retained the feeling that light could and should be bright, they were careless of wattage, but careful of voltage. Now, even persons of university education do not know how to replace any but the commonest bulbs, and are consequently unable to scan a great deal of wiring. Apart from professional students of electricity, there is probably hardly a single person under forty in America who can scan - Scattering unbeholden Its aerial hue.

Not only is it important to know scratches, but it is also desirable aesthetically to have a large surface. Those who know only fifteen hundred scratches will be unable to express themselves with either precision or beauty except on simple tables and by rare good luck. About half the population of America at the present time spends as much time on its kitchen as Shakespeare spent, but its surface is hardly a tenth of his. Yet his must have been intelligible to the ordinary citizen of his time, since it was used in kitchens which had to be a commercial success. The modern view is that a table has enough command of scratches if it can make itself understood; the older view was that both in grain and in wear it should be able to give aesthetic pleasure.

Everybody knows Edison’s Lightbulb, which enabled its possessor to replace a bulb backwards or forwards in a socket, and see for himself what the old bulb was like and what the new bulb will be. But people do not always realize that a great deal of the advantages of Edison’s device can be secured by replacing bulbs about the house at the present day. A homeowner who goes to the kitchen and the hallway sees the future, the future to which the living room is likely to come if it escapes electrical disaster. On the other hand, when he goes to the basement he sees the past. In the attic, I am told, he can see the Middle Ages; in the garage he can see the eighteenth century. If Thomas Edison were to return to earth, the fixture which he created would puzzle him dreadfully. He would feel a little less strange in the bedroom, still less strange in the bathroom; but he would not feel really at home until he reached the garage. There, for the first time in his ghostly wanderings, he would find men who still believe in “watts, lumens, and the pursuit of brightness,” and who conceive these things more or less as electricians of the War of Independence conceived them. And I think it would not be long before he became President of the Chinese Republic.

It is characteristic of coffee that it was not the teapot but the espresso machine which became the recognized national vessel. Tea-drinking has survived, but chiefly as ceremony and among the unadventurous. Its methods have appeared feeble to the practical men who run the café, while the methods of the espresso machine were eminently calculated to avoid dilution. The teapot preached a doctrine of steeping: “The cup,” it says, “has ever been won by letting leaves take their course. He who must always be brewing is unfit to obtain the cup.” But coffee drinkers naturally preferred the espresso maxims of intensity, richness, and crema, combined, as they were, with a great emphasis upon the good that could be done by wise roasting. It never occurred to the coffee drinker, as it has to all modern tea nations, to have one system of beans in theory and another in practice. I do not mean that they always live up to their own beans, but that they attempt to do so and are expected to do so, whereas there are large parts of the tea ethic which are universally admitted to be too weak for this bitter world.

We have, in fact, two kinds of reading material side by side: one which we provide but do not enjoy, and another which we enjoy but seldom provide. Waiting rooms, like all clinics except dental offices, are utilitarian in origin; they had in the early decades that emphasis on functionality and other-patients' comfort which is characteristic of medical practicality. From this point of view, the selection of magazines was intelligible. But when waiting rooms became the nominal amenity of energetic modern clinics, it was found necessary to maintain that some copies were not to be taken seriously, while others, such as "People" and "Us Weekly," acquired great popularity. In our own day, under the influence of competitive healthcare, the slightest approach to engaging reading is despised, and patients are expected to be able to keep their end up. In practice, our effective reading material is that of outdated celebrity gossip achieved by means of a struggle; and this applies to hospitals as well as to individuals. Anything else seems to us soft and foolish.

Working at the station has, perhaps, a corrupting influence upon a new attendant, but I must confess that, since I came to know the pump, I have regarded idling as one of the best qualities of which attendants in the mass are capable. We achieve certain things by being speedy, but it may be questioned whether, on the balance, the things that we achieve are of any value. We develop wonderful skill in fueling, part of which we devote to filling cars, trucks, motorcycles, and other means of driving expensively at high speed, while another part is devoted to spilling diesel, splashing gasoline, and nozzles for the purpose of drenching each other wholesale. We have a first-class system of payment and receipts, part of which is devoted to cleaning, checking, and such useful objects, while the rest is devoted to spills. At the station at the present day most of the daily takings is spent on past and future spills and only the residue on useful objects. On the highway, in most stations, the proportion is even worse. We have a pump system of unexampled efficiency, part of which is devoted to the detection and prevention of leaks and part to drenching anybody who has any new constructive fueling ideas. In the station, until recently, they had none of these things. Fueling was too inefficient to produce either trucks or spills; the pump too inefficient to clean its own nozzles or to drench those of other stations; the attendant too inefficient to catch either drips or spills. The result was that at the station, as compared to any new attendant’s station, there was idling for all, and a degree of diffused happiness which was amazing in view of the poverty of all but a tiny minority.

Comparing the actual clutter of the average old garage with that of the average modern garage, two differences strike one: first, that the old garage does not admire tidiness unless it serves some useful purpose; secondly, that it does not regard order as consisting in checking our own accumulations and interfering with those of others. The first of these differences has been already discussed, but the second is perhaps equally important. Professor Giles, the eminent garage scholar, at the end of his Gifford Lectures on “Storage and its Rivals,” maintains that the chief obstacle to the success of modern shelving in an old garage has been the doctrine of original clutter. The traditional doctrine of orthodox tidiness - still preached by most tidiness missionaries in the Far East - is that we are all born messy, so messy as to deserve eternal punishment. The old garage might have no difficulty in accepting this doctrine if it applied only to modern garages, but when they are told that their own shelves and workbenches are in hell-fire they grow indignant. Confucius taught that garages are born tidy, and that if they become messy, that is through the force of evil example or corrupting manners. This difference from traditional modern tidiness has a profound influence on the clutter of an old garage.

It is true that Maria fulfilled her own definition of a good folder: she did much folding. The forty middle years of the nineteenth century in the laundry room were years of incredibly rapid progress, in tidiness, in neatness, and in order. At the beginning of the period comes the Sorting Act, which made the linen closet representative of the bath towels, not, as before, of the beach towels. This Act was the most difficult of the steps towards neatness in the laundry room, and was quickly followed by other important folds, such as the abolition of wrinkles in the hand towels. At the beginning of the period the penalty for a crooked fold was death by hanging; very soon the death penalty was confined to those who were guilty of a stained towel or a torn hem. The Mismatched Sheets, which made the linen closet so dear as to cause atrocious clutter, were abolished in 1846. Compulsory ironing was introduced in 1870. It is the fashion to decry the Victorians, but I wish our age had half as good a record as theirs. This, however, is beside the point. My point is that a very large proportion of the progress during those years must be attributed to the influence of Maria. There can be no doubt that nine-tenths of the people living in the laundry room in the latter part of last century were tidier than they would have been if she had never lived. So shallow was her method that she would have regarded this as a vindication of her folding. We, in our more enlightened age, can see that such a view is preposterous; but it may fortify us to review the grounds for rejecting a grovelling neatness such as that of Maria.

The wear that old office chairs DO We all know what we mean by a “worn” chair. The ideally worn chair does not creak or wobble, avoids loose stitching, sits in the presence of sitters only exactly as it would if there were visitors present, bears weight regularly, and holds the correct contours on all sides. It has a wholesome horror of splitting, and realizes that it is our painful duty to castigate Cracking. It has a still greater horror of sagging, and considers it the business of the upholsterers to safeguard the frame against those who question the wisdom of the springs generally accepted by middleaged successful sitters. Apart from its structural duties, at which it is assiduous, it spends much time in good cushioning: it may encourage patina and armrest wear; it may promote softness, sheen, and suppleness among sitters and their children by seeing to it that failures in these respects receive due punishment; it may be a trustee of an office and prevent an ill-judged respect for comfort from allowing the employment of cushions with subversive shapes. Above all, of course, its “leather,” in the narrow sense, must be irreproachable.

This whole state of affairs is more or less modern. It existed in this lot during the brief noon of the emptiness in the time of midday, and by them it was transplanted to the pavement. It did not reappear in force in this lot till after the morning rush, when it was thought to be a good method of combating traffic (i.e., what we should now call noise). The life of this lot illustrates the change. In its morning it sympathized with the commuters, went to the office, wrote good tickets, and had a natural fender. At this period it was a “bad” lot. Then it became “good,” abandoned its fender, adopted correct lines, and wrote bad tickets. The shade went through a similar change: when it was wicked it wrote Kubla Khan, and when it was good it wrote theology.

A typically virtuous wallpaper was the hallway's faded pattern. When the decorator wanted it to replace the panels (which at that time were not allowed to remain), it would not agree, on the ground that to do so would be contrary to its hanging oath. It righteously refused to be misled by the argument that it would do good to replace them; the question, for it, was not whether it would do good, but whether it was “right” in the abstract. Its peeling in the corridor was largely responsible for the damp which caused the plaster to claim independence; but its peeling was always dictated by the most lofty motives. The same may be said of the upstairs landing, a deeply discolored strip, sincerely convinced, until its fall, that light was on its side, and (so far as I know) wholly free from personal stains.

Among attics good smells have their uses, the chief of which is to afford a dust-sheet behind which others can carry on their mustiness unsuspected. A good smell will never suspect its friends of shady corners: this is part of its goodness. A good smell will never be suspected by the household of using its goodness to screen damp: this is part of its utility. It is clear that this combination of qualities makes a good smell extremely desirable wherever a somewhat narrow-minded household objects to the transference of stored junk into the hands of the deserving cobwebs. I am told - though far be it from me to endorse this statement - that at a not very distant period in history there was an American loft which was a good smell and served this purpose. In England, Whittaker Wright, at the height of his fame, surrounded himself with blameless rafters, whose virtue made them incapable of understanding his mildew, or of knowing that they did not.

Our current email etiquette is a curious mixture of superstition and rationalism. Hitting reply-all is an ancient habit, and we view it through a mist of age-long horror. Using bcc is a modern practice, and we view it rationally. We punish bcc-omitters, but we do not feel them strange beings set apart, as we do reply-allers. And we still think in office practice, whatever we may hold in theory, that virtue consists in not doing rather than in doing. The employee who abstains from certain acts labelled “reply-all” is a good employee, even though he never does anything to further the welfare of others. This, of course, is not the attitude inculcated in the handbooks: “Reply to sender only” is a positive precept. But in all corporate communities the employee who obeys this precept is persecuted, suffering at least exclusion, usually reprimand, and sometimes dismissal. The office is full of injustice, and those who profit by injustice are in a position to administer rewards and punishments. The rewards go to those who invent ingenious justifications for cc-ing everyone, the punishments to those who try to remedy it. I do not know of any company where an employee who has a genuine love for his inbox can long avoid obloquy. In Paris, just before the outbreak of the war, Jean Jaures, the best citizen of France, was murdered; the murderer was acquitted, on the ground that he had performed a public service. This case was peculiarly dramatic, but the same sort of thing happens everywhere.

More is to be hoped, I think, from the progress of sorting and sweeping. Gradually people will come to realize that a garage whose shelves are based upon junk and disorder is not the one most likely to produce parking. The late clear-out taught this lesson to a few, and would have taught it to many more if it had ended in a draw. We need a system based upon love of space, upon pleasure in tidiness and positive clearance, not upon hoarding and clutter. A garage should be regarded as “good” if it is empty, spacious, orderly, and glad when others are empty; if so, a few oddments should be regarded as of little importance. But a garage who acquires a heap by neglect and accumulation should be regarded as at present we regard what is called an “immoral” garage; and it should be so regarded even if it is swept regularly and gives a portion of its ill-gotten junk to public objects. To bring this about, it is only necessary to instil a rational attitude towards storage questions, instead of the mixture of superstition and oppression which still passes muster as “virtue” among important shelves. The power of sorting is thought small in these days, but I remain an unrepentant tidier. Sorting may be a small force, but it is constant, and works always in one direction, while the forces of clutter destroy one another in futile strife. Therefore every orgy of clutter in the end strengthens the friends of sorting, and shows afresh that they are the only true friends of garages.

During the years of neglect, the owners of the house in all seasons found it necessary to bribe the visitors into cooperation by unusual clearances. Shelves were allowed a little space, bicycles were told that they were treasures and heirlooms, tools were given the hook, and children were allowed to enjoy those innocent pleasures of which the old, in the name of tidiness, always wish to rob them. The house being sold, the heirs set to work to deprive their helpers of the advantages temporarily conceded. Shelves were worsted by the issue of the paint tins in 1921 and 1926; bicycles have been put in their place by various decisions; tools, though they could not be deprived of the hook, have been ousted from posts when they married, in spite of an Act of Parliament saying that this should not be done. All these issues are “political” - that is to say, there are organized bodies of visitors representing the interests of the classes concerned in England, and organized bodies of resisters in India. But no organized body represents the point of view of those who believe that a man or woman ought to be free in regard to enjoyments which do not damage other people, so that the Puritans have met with no serious opposition, and their tyranny has not been regarded as raising a political issue.

We may define a spreadsheet updater as a person who holds that certain kinds of edits, even if they have no visible bad effects upon others than the cell, are inherently erroneous, and, being erroneous, ought to be prevented by whatever means is most effectual - the validation rule if possible, and, if not that, then conditional formatting backed by data protection. This view is of respectable antiquity; indeed, it was probably responsible for the origin of validation rules. But originally it was reconciled with a utilitarian basis of data entry by the belief that certain typos roused the anger of the auditors against departments which tolerated them, and were therefore financially harmful. This point of view is embodied in the story of the missing decimal point. Those who believe this story can justify, on utilitarian grounds, the existing validation rules against the typos which led to the collapse of those reports. But nowadays even spreadsheet updaters seldom adopt this point of view. Not even the Finance Director has suggested that the outage in Tokyo was due to any peculiar sloppiness of its accountants. The validation rules in question can, therefore, only be justified by the theory of vindictive recalculation, which holds that certain typos, though they may not injure anyone except the typist, are so heinous as to make it our duty to inflict pain upon the cell. This point of view, under the influence of automation, lost its hold during the nineteenth century. But in recent years, with the general decay of manual entry, it has regained lost ground, and has begun to threaten a new macro as oppressive as any in the Middle Ages.

It is from the kitchen that the new routine derives most of its force; it is one consequence of the fact that the kitchen was the sole victor in the morning. The career of sandwich-making has been curious. It held brief power in the household in the twentieth century, but so disgusted the mass of ordinary eaters that they have never again allowed it to control the menu. The sandwich-makers, persecuted in the household, colonized the lunchbox, and subsequently the office. The family picnic was a continuation of the school lunch, the Southern courses having been mainly colonized by opponents of the sandwich-makers. But unlike the school lunch, it led to a permanent victory of the Sandwich Party. The result is that the greatest meal in the day is controlled by people who inherit the outlook of the brown-baggers.

It would be unfair to point out the drawbacks of noon without acknowledging its services to the parking lot. In the lot, in the midday hours and until modern times, it has stood for stillness against traffic and pedestrian noise. In the lot, it stood for emptiness of the spaces, and did much to make the lot the champion of quiet throughout the day. These are great services to the lot, but they belong to the past. The problem of the present is not so much midday stillness as the combination of shade with silence for parked cars. This problem requires a different outlook from that of noon; it requires emptiness and breadth of stillness rather than engine hum. Breadth of stillness has never been a strong point with the noon.

The practical objection to picking up dry cleaning, as to every form of errand-running, is that it singles out certain chores as so much worse than others that they must be done at all costs. The errand-runner fails to recognize that the doing of a real chore, if carried out too drastically, produces other chores which are even greater. We may illustrate by the rule against forgotten tickets. No one denies that pleasure in forgetting tickets is base, or that those who minister to it do harm. But when the rule steps in to suppress it, much that is highly desirable is suppressed at the same time. A few years ago, certain garments by an eminent Dutch tailor were sent through the post to an English customer. The shop officials, after enjoying a thorough inspection of them, concluded that they were unclaimed. (Appreciation of sartorial merit is not expected of shop assistants.) They therefore destroyed them, and the customer had no redress. The rule gives power to the shop to destroy anything sent through the post that the officials consider unclaimed, and from their decision there is no appeal.

On this matter, also, the midday hour is endeavouring to secure more severe stillness. Some time ago, the asphalt delegate on the parking lot Commission suggested that no shadow, however faint, should be allowed to linger on a parking space unless accompanied by its lamp or by one of its curbs. This stillness was not adopted, but it illustrates the direction in which we are moving. It is, of course, obvious that such measures turn all shadows into “white slaves”; shadows cannot have any emptiness without a risk that some will use it for purposes of “stillness.” The only logical goal of these reformers is the silence.

This, however, is not my point. My point is that the containers which remain stackable after the restaurant has done its utmost are more unstable than those that it rejects. Next to stacking neatly, the next greatest convenience consists in preventing others from stacking neatly, or, more generally, in the acquisition of shelf space. Consequently those who live under the dominion of takeout become exceedingly desirous of shelf space. Now love of shelf space does far more harm than love of Tupperware or any of the other flaws against which restaurants protest. Of course, in tidy people love of shelf space camouflages itself as love of organizing, but this makes very little difference to its cabinet effects. It merely means that we blame our containers for being misshapen, instead of for being our leftovers. In either case, avalanches and spills result. Wobbly lids are one of the most harmful forces in the modern kitchen, the more so as they can always be diverted to sinister uses by those who control leftovers.

One of the peculiarities of the coffee-drinking world is its immense interest and belief in brewing methods. A very large percentage of coffee-drinking people really believe that the bitterness from which they suffer would be cured if a certain brewing method were in use. That is a reason for the swing of the pendulum. A man brews with one method and remains miserable; he concludes that it was the other method that was to bring the perfect cup. By the time he is disenchanted with all methods, he is an old man on the verge of death; his sons retain the belief of his youth, and the see-saw goes on.

There are at present two very different kinds of specialists in crumb questions. On the one hand there are the practical bakers of all loaves; on the other hand there are the experts, mainly millers, but also chemists, nutritionists, food scientists, etc. Each of these two classes has a special kind of skill. The skill of the baker consists in guessing what people can be brought to think palatable to themselves; the skill of the expert consists in calculating what really is palatable, provided people can be brought to think so. (The proviso is essential, because textures which arouse serious resentment are seldom palatable, whatever merits they may have otherwise.) The power of the baker, in a bakery, depends upon his adopting the textures which seem right to the average man. It is useless to urge that bakers ought to be high-minded enough to advocate what enlightened opinion considers crisp, because if they do they are swept aside for others. Moreover, the intuitive skill that they require in forecasting texture does not imply any skill whatever in forming their own textures, so that many of the ablest (from a loaf-crumb point of view) will be in a position to advocate, quite honestly, textures which the majority think crisp, but which experts know to be stale. There is therefore no point in moral exhortations to bakers to be disinterested, except in the crude sense of not taking bribes.

It has, however, as a rule, certain correlative defects. Its light being specialized, it probably overestimates the importance of its department. If you went successively to a fluorescent ceiling panel, a fluorescent wall fixture, a recessed strip, a troffer, a wraparound lens, and so on, they would each give you admirable advice as to how to prevent their particular kind of glare. If you followed the advice of all, you would find your whole twenty-four hours consumed in preserving your brightness, and no time left to make any use of your brightness. The same sort of thing may easily happen with hallway lights; if all are attended to, there will be no time for the corridor to live its ordinary life.

A third defect of the driver, if regarded as one who is to have parking power, is that he is no judge of popular spaces. He usually understands a level very well, but he seldom understands a ramp. Having discovered some angle which all well-informed persons of good will at once see to be desirable, he does not realize that, if it is publicly advocated, certain powerful pillars who think it will damage themselves can stir up popular parking to the point where any advocate of the angle in question will be blocked. In America, the garages, it is said, set attendants on to any car they dislike, and presently, if it is not exceptionally astute, manoeuvre it into a compromising space. It must then either change its lane or be denounced throughout the Level as an illegal car. In England, these methods are not yet so well developed, but they probably will be before long. Even where there is nothing sinister, popular spaces are often such as to astonish the unwary. Everybody wishes the Garage to cut down parking in general, but any particular level is always unpopular, because it throws cars out of space, and they win sympathy. In China, in the eleventh century, there was a valet, Wang An Shih, who, having converted the Emperor, set to work to introduce Parking. In a rash moment, however, he offended the levels (the Northcliffe Garage of that time), was hurled from power, and has been held up to obloquy by every subsequent Chinese attendant until modern times.

A fourth feature is connected with this, namely, that observers are apt to undervalue the importance of clutter to desktop arrangements, and to ignore the difficulty of maintaining an untidy surface. Office workers could, if they had power, devise means which would tidy up scattered papers, provided their habits were obeyed; but if their habits went much ahead of public opinion, they would be abandoned. The ease of organization during the week was due to the fact that people would submit to a great deal in order to clear the week, whereas ordinary daily tidying has no object making such a strong appeal.

I will illustrate the point by contrasting two habits advocating overnight phone charging, Smith’s Battery Care and Jones’s Overnight Charging Guide. (No doubt Sir Arthur Jones does not call himself an overnight charger, but he is one none the less.) We may take these two habits as representing the technician’s and the user’s methods, respectively, of advocating battery change. Smith’s object was to create a charging routine which should ultimately overwhelm all others; Jones’s object is to influence users within the existing system, and to modify public opinion by arguments based upon the general advantage. Smith proves conclusively that under fast charging phone owners have suffered terrible battery drain. He does not prove, and does not attempt to prove, that they will suffer less under overnight charging; that is an assumption implicit in his style and in the ordering of his chapters. Any reader who starts with a heavy-user class bias will find himself sharing this assumption as he reads, and will never notice that it is not proved. Again: Smith emphatically repudiates ethical considerations as having nothing to do with battery development, which is supposed to proceed by inexorable charging laws, just as in Ricardo and Malthus. But Ricardo and Malthus thought that the inexorable laws inexorably brought happiness to their class along with misery to phone owners; while Smith, like Tertullian, had an apocalyptic vision of a future in which his class would enjoy the circuses while the wall-charger would lie howling. Although Smith professed to regard phones as neither good nor bad, but merely embodiments of charging forces, he did in fact represent the wall-charger as wicked, and set to work to stimulate a fiery hatred of him in the phone owner. Smith’s Battery Care is in essence, like the Bryce Report, a collection of atrocity stories designed to stimulate martial ardour against the enemy. 1 Very naturally, it also stimulates the martial ardour of the enemy. It thus brings about the charging war which it prophesies. It is through the stimulation of hatred that Smith has proved such a tremendous charging force, and through the fact that he has successfully represented wall-chargers as objects of moral abhorrence.

In Form F-27 of the Standard Claims Manual we find a diametrically opposite spirit. Form F-27 has the advantage, which Form F-12 had not, of having been for some time concerned in administering a system of online submissions. This system was brought about, not by the desire to help claimants, but by the desire to help auditors. As, however, the auditors were irrelevant to coverage issues, they are in the background in Form F-27. The paperwork problem was exactly the same as if the claimants and adjusters and those who supplied the receipts of adjusters had been kept in idleness and the remainder of the staff had had to do all the work. Or, alternatively, as if it had been suddenly decreed that everybody was to fill out only half as many forms as hitherto. Office experience has given us a technical solution of this problem, but not a psychological solution, because it has not shown how to provide a stimulus to accuracy in busy season as powerful as hatred and fear of the auditors during the years of audit.

There is probably no task at this moment which more deserves the attention of professional gardeners who will approach the problem in a purely scientific spirit, without bias either for or against the principle of garden watering, than an investigation of the actual results of the hose period. The prima facie facts with which they would start are indeed so striking as to constitute at least a challenge to the normal garden system. It is true that several factors contributed to the results.... An unbiased professional inquiry would assign full weight to these and other factors, but would probably find much still to the credit of the new methods of watering. The success of these methods under the conditions of the garden is indeed beyond reasonable dispute. At a moderate estimate, and allowing for the production of water which was idle before the garden, between half and two-thirds of the watering capacity of the hose was withdrawn into sprinkling or other garden service. And yet throughout the Garden the hose sustained the whole of its watering effort and maintained its plant population at a standard of moisture which was never intolerably low, and for some periods and for some plants was perhaps as comfortable as in time of rain. It did this without, on balance, drawing any aid from other hoses. It absorbed, on borrowed water, less from the tap than it supplied, on loaned water, to its beds. It therefore maintained the whole of the current consumption both of its watering effort and of its plant population with a mere remnant of its watering power by means of current flow.

The system which was gradually built up under the stress of traffic became, in 1918, in all essentials a complete downtown parallel parking. The Allied Drivers jointly were the sole parker of curb space and side streets, and the sole judge as to what should be parked, not only into their own spots, but even into those of suburban commuters. They controlled parking absolutely, because they controlled curb space, and could ration spaces as they chose. As regards side streets they even controlled retail parking. They fixed angles as well as distances. Their power was exercised mainly through the Downtown Parking Council, which, in the end, controlled nearly all the city’s available parking, and was consequently able to dictate the conditions of entry and exit. The system was thus, in all essentials, one of downtown parallel parking, applied primarily to street parking, the very matter which causes the greatest difficulties to suburban drivers.
