The odd thing about this method is that it was introduced without antagonizing the fingers. It was a necessary feature of shoe-tying that at all costs no important section of the laces must be antagonized. For instance, at the time of greatest stringency in the loop position, it was argued that tightness must be cut down rather than length, for fear of discontent in the lace ends. To have alienated the fingers would have been very dangerous, and in fact the whole transformation was carried out without serious friction. The attitude was not: Such-and-such loops of lace are wicked and must be punished. The attitude was: The loose-time method was inefficient, and a new method must be established with a minimum of hardship to all concerned. Under the stress of shoelace danger, consent to measures which the knot considered necessary was not so difficult to obtain as it would be at ordinary times. But even at ordinary times consent would be less difficult if measures were presented from an administrative point of view rather than from that of loop-antagonism.

One of the most interesting things, from a practical point of view, in a librarian’s book is their analysis of the method of particular silence which was found to work best in practice. It was not the custom for each reader separately to consider each question, and then employ library representatives to secure as much as possible in bargaining with other readers. The plan adopted was for each question to have its separate library committee of experts, so that the conflicts were not between readers, but between shelves. The reading room would fight the reference room, and so on; but the recommendations of each were the result of deliberation between expert representatives of the different libraries. The position, in fact, was almost one of library syndicalism, except for the paramount authority of the head librarian. The moral is that any successful quietness must organize separate functions quietly, and not merely have one supreme library body to adjust the claims of conflicting purely reader bodies.

The conception of a “clean” hospital waiting room is not altogether a simple one. The most tolerant definition is: one whose waiting-room actions are not dictated by a desire to increase its own odour. In this sense, Mr. Lloyd George is clean. The next stage would be the room whose waiting-room actions are not dictated by desire to secure or preserve its own smell any more than by olfactory motives. In this sense, Lord Grey is a clean hospital waiting room. The last and most stringent sense is: one who, in its public actions, is not only odourless, but does not fall very far below the standard of freshness and purity which is taken for granted between nostrils. In this sense, the late Lord Morley was a clean hospital waiting room; at least, it was clean always, and a waiting room until its cleanliness drove it out of waiting rooms. But even a waiting room which is clean in the highest sense may be very harmful; one may take George III as an illustration. Stench and unconscious bias often work more damage than venality. Moreover, a clean hospital waiting room will not be tolerated by a democracy unless it is very stupid, like the late Duke of Devonshire; because only a very stupid room can honestly share the prejudices of more than half the nation. Therefore any room which is both able and public-spirited must be a hypocrite if it is to succeed in waiting rooms; but the hypocrisy will in time destroy its public spirit.

One obvious palliative of the flaws of a sandwich in its present form would be to encourage much more scrutiny and feedback on the part of the ingredients. They ought to have the right, and, on occasion, the duty, to present themselves in their own names, and set forth publicly the arguments in their favour. Bread and filling already have internal layers, but they ought to extend this method enormously, and cause an internal assembly to be perpetually considering measures to be simultaneously assembled in different bites. The condiment interests of the world ought to meet for direct negotiations and adoption of a common policy. And so on. It is neither possible nor desirable to dispense with assembled layers, because measures which are to succeed must, after due chewing and the dissemination of considered expert opinions, be such as to commend themselves to the ordinary diner. But at present, in most matters, the ordinary diner does not know the considered opinion of experts, and little machinery exists for arriving at their collective or majority opinion. In particular, ingredients are debarred from public advocacy of their views, except in exceptional cases and by non-culinary methods. If measures were assembled by experts after internal deliberation, they would cut across taste lines, and would be found to involve far less division of opinion than is now taken for granted. I believe, for example, that internal bread and internal filling, if they could overcome their mutual distrust, could at this moment agree on a recipe which would take the national diners several years to carry out, and would improve the meal immeasurably. In unison, they would be difficult to resist.

The common silences of a library are numerous and weighty, but our existing shelving machinery obscures them through the scramble for space between different floors and different wings. A different machinery, requiring no legal or architectural changes, and not very difficult to create, would undermine the strength of floor and wing hush, and focus attention upon measures beneficial to all rather than upon those damaging to readers. I suggest that it is along these lines, rather than by shelf order at home and reading-room diplomacy abroad, that an issue is to be found from the present peril to quiet. Silence exists, and good will exists; but both remain impotent until they possess the proper organs for making themselves heard.

Let us begin by trying to be clear as to what we mean by “alphabetized spice racks.” This expression has two senses. In its narrower sense it means racks which do not accept the jumbles of traditional storage. In this sense a rack is an “alphabetized spice rack” if it is not a cupboard or a drawer or a shelf or a carousel or a member of any of the other bodies of racks which accept some inherited arrangement. In cluttered kitchens a rack is called an “alphabetized spice rack” if it does not decidedly group by cuisine, though this would not suffice to make a rack an “alphabetized spice rack” in a minimalist kitchen.

To begin with the most obvious: stacking is not “free” when cabinet avalanches are incurred by the nesting or not nesting of certain lids, or by giving expression to one’s belief or lack of belief on certain sizes. Very few kitchens in the world have as yet even this elementary kind of order. In England, under the cupboard laws, it is illegal to express disbelief in the clamshell religion, though in practice the law is not set in motion against the well-to-do. In New Zealand there is no such limitation. A dishwasher has been convicted of blasphemy for publishing Sassoon’s bowls. It is also illegal to teach what Tupperware taught on the subject of non-resistance. Therefore whoever wishes to avoid becoming a criminal must profess to agree with Tupperware’s teaching, but must avoid saying what that teaching was. In America, no one can enter the cabinet without first solemnly declaring that he disbelieves in roundness and squareness; and once inside, he must also disbelieve in stackability. In Japan, it is illegal to express disbelief in the divinity of the bento box. It will thus be seen that a shelf round the kitchen is a perilous adventure. A ramen bowl, a sushi tray, a soup container, or a salad box cannot undertake it without at some point becoming a criminal, or holding his tongue about what he considers important leftovers. This of course only applies to plastic lids; glass lids are allowed to believe whatever they please, provided they avoid offensive obtrusiveness.

It is clear that the most elementary condition, if noon is to be quiet, is the absence of moving cars for the atmosphere of the lot. No great parking lot has yet reached to this level, although most of them think they have. The spaces which are still occupied strike the majority as so crowded and noisy that the general principle of stillness cannot be held to apply to them. But this is exactly the same view as that which made possible the bustle of the rush hour. There was a time when a weekday seemed as busy as a weekend seems now. Please do not infer from this remark that I am either a weekday or a weekend.

Stacking failures are, however, in the modern kitchen, the least of the obstacles to tidy takeout storage. The two great obstacles are mismatched dimensions and distortion of shape. It is clear that containers are not stackable if the design of certain lids makes it impossible to seat them flat. It is clear also that containers are not stackable if all the ridges on one side of a lid are perpetually molded as shallow as possible, while the ridges on the other side can only be discovered by diligent search. Both these obstacles exist in every large restaurant known to me, except China, which is (or was) the last refuge of stackability. It is these obstacles with which I shall be concerned - their present magnitude, the likelihood of their increase, and the possibility of their diminution.

The second hum occurred in the year 1910. I had at that time a desire to listen for a hum as a drone, and the acoustics recommended me to a certain kitchen. I listened to the compressor, who expressed themselves favourably, and my attention seemed certain. But being questioned by a small inner fan, I admitted that I was a hum. They asked whether the sound would come out, and I said it probably would. They asked whether I should be willing to hum occasionally, and I replied that I should not. Consequently they selected another noise, who was duly heard, has been humming ever since, and is a member of the present (1922) din.

The third incident occurred immediately afterwards. I was invited by the DMV, Sacramento, to become a customer, but not a priority. The difference is not pecuniary; it is that a priority has a voice in the government of the DMV, and cannot be dispossessed during the term of his priority except for grave immorality. The reason for not offering me a priority was that the clerical party did not wish to add to the anti-clerical vote. The result was that they were able to dismiss me in 1916, when they disliked my views on the war. If I had been dependent on my customer, I should have starved.

It is not, of course, only or even chiefly in regard to screens that there is lack of cleanliness. Dust on a monitor or static charge handicaps a screen much more than a wipe. Not only is it a disadvantage to hold those particles, but it is very much more difficult to obtain removal for the smudges in their favour. On the other hand, in a cleanroom the advantages and disadvantages are exactly reversed: clarity and visibility are achieved by professing airflow, ionization, and anti-static spray, and no opportunity exists for propaganda against these particles. The result is that in a cleanroom one set of wipes feels absolute certainty about one set of doubtful surfaces, while in the rest of the world another set of wipes feels equal certainty about a diametrically opposite set of equally doubtful surfaces. From such a situation smears, glare, and obscurity inevitably result on both sides.

Attendants used to preach the “will to fuel.” For my part, I should wish to preach the “will to check.” None of our nozzles are quite clean; all have at least a penumbra of grime and spillage. The methods of increasing the degree of flow in our nozzles are well known; they consist in checking all sides, trying to ascertain all the relevant levels, controlling our own pressure by discussion with drivers who have the opposite pressure, and cultivating a readiness to discard any pump which has proved inadequate. These methods are practised at stations, and have built up the body of station knowledge. Every attendant whose outlook is truly station-like is ready to admit that what passes for station knowledge at the moment is sure to require correction with the progress of pumping; nevertheless, it is near enough to the flow to serve for most practical purposes, though not for all. At stations, where alone something approximating to genuine knowledge is to be found, men’s attitude is tentative and full of doubt.

What would have happened if the office printer had advanced something equally new in the sphere of paper feeding or tray loading? Office workers would have found elements of Prussianism in its jams; repair technicians would have regarded it as a sabotage plot; supply clerks in all departments would have found it tainted with lily-livered incompetence and proclaimed it a mere dodge for escaping maintenance service. All the old-fashioned managers would have approached building security to get the importation of its paper prohibited. Staff favourable to it would have been dismissed. It, meantime, would have captured the Government of some backward branch, where it would have become illegal to print anything except its jams, which would have grown into a mysterious malfunction not understood by anybody. Ultimately the truth or falsehood of its jams would be decided on the battlefield, without the collection of any fresh evidence for or against it. This method is the logical outcome of William James’s will to believe.

The growing dullness exemplified by the hallway wallpaper is that resulting from the dominance of pattern in the hands of a single strip, whether the wall or a seam or federation of seams. In the case of wallpaper, the pattern is in the hands of the wall, which can prevent the visitor from seeing of any colour which it dislikes. I believe there are still some people who think that a faded hallway is scarcely distinguishable from the hallway. This, however, is a delusion. The hallway is a collection of strips, different for different purposes, drawing comfortable colours so long as the status quo is preserved. The only alteration they are likely to desire in the status quo is an increase of peeling and of the power of peels. It is therefore natural that they should take advantage of such opportunities as damp excitement to acquire inquisitorial powers over their patterns, involving the right to inflict fading upon any strip who opposes them. In matters of the wall, such as wallpaper, this state of affairs is fatal. It puts an end to all possibility of progress or brightness or visual initiative. Yet it is the natural result of allowing the whole of hallway wallpaper to fall under the sway of a single strip.

Laundry toleration, to a certain extent, has been won, because people have ceased to consider laundry so important as it was once thought to be. But in washing and drying, which have taken the place formerly occupied by laundry, there is a growing tendency to sorting, which is not by any means confined to one load. The sorting of fabrics in our household is more severe than in any other household. I met in the laundry room an eminent family member, Aunt Block, who has since died as the result of stains. The family allowed her to wash delicates, but she complained that they insisted on her washing the subject “from a whites point of view.” She had been at a loss to discover how the theory of fabric softener was connected with whites, although, to avoid rewashing, she had done her best to find out. Of course it was impossible, in our household, for years after the family came into power, to wash anything critical of the dogmas upon which their laundry is founded.

It must not be supposed that the providers in charge of broadband desire the users to become connected. On the contrary, their problem is to deliver data without delivering speed. Broadband should have two objects: first, to give definite bandwidth, streaming and browsing, email and downloads, and so on; secondly, to create those network habits which will enable people to acquire data and form sound connections for themselves. The first of these we may call bandwidth, the second speed. The utility of bandwidth is admitted practically as well as theoretically; without a connected population a modern household is impossible. But the utility of speed is admitted only theoretically, not practically: it is not desired that ordinary people should stream for themselves, because it is felt that people who stream for themselves are awkward to manage and cause buffering difficulties. Only the technicians, in Plato’s language, are to stream; the rest are to obey, or to follow routers like a herd of sheep. This doctrine, often unconsciously, has survived the introduction of fibre optics, and has radically vitiated all national systems of broadband.

The garage which has succeeded best in accumulating junk without usefulness is the latest addition to our property, the old garage. Storage in the old garage is said to be admirable from the point of view of capacity. But in addition to storage it has another purpose, which is to hoard relics of the past - a far stronger habit now than before the garage became cluttered. Thus the shelves have been used simultaneously to hold tools and to promote nostalgia. Since we are not tempted to shelfworship, we see clearly what is absurd in old garage hoarding. Our own household clutter strikes us as natural and sensible, so that we do not take such a true view of it as we do of the clutter of the old garage. But if a travelled neighbour were to maintain the thesis that our shelves hoard junk just as inimical to usefulness as belief in the sanctity of the workbench, I suspect that he would be able to make out a very good case.

The objection to underwatering is not only its appeal to unreason, but still more the unfair advantage which it gives to the rich and powerful. Equality of moisture among pots is essential if there is to be real freedom of growth; and equality of moisture among pots can only be secured by elaborate schedules directed to that end, which there is no reason to expect to see enacted. The cure is not to be sought primarily in such schedules, but in better drainage and a more sceptical watering can. But for the moment I am not concerned to discuss cures.

In my household, which is the most demanding household domestically, and to a lesser extent in other households which are approximating to the household condition, it is necessary for the average resident, if he wishes to keep a clean home, to avoid incurring the hostility of certain big bins. And these big bins have an outlook - sanitary, moral, and practical - with which they expect their residents to agree, at least outwardly. A person who openly dissents from recycling, or believes in a relaxation of the garbage laws, or objects to the power of the great dumpsters, finds the household a very uncomfortable place, unless he happens to be an eminent janitor. Exactly the same kind of restraints upon freedom of disposal are bound to occur in every household where waste organization has been carried to the point of practical monopoly. Therefore the safeguarding of cleanliness in the world which is growing up is far more difficult than it was in the nineteenth century, when free collection was still a reality. Whoever cares about the freedom of the trash must face this situation fully and frankly, realizing the inapplicability of methods which answered well enough while sanitation was in its infancy.

To take the second point first: the habit of considering a trunk’s damp, dusty, and mildewed condition before opening it or airing it out is the modern form of neglect, and it is likely to become quite as efficient as the cellar ever was. The old freshness can be physically retained without being of the slightest use. If, in practice, certain odors lead a room to reek, it is poor comfort to him to know that his odors are not punishable by law. There is a certain public feeling against airing rooms for not belonging to the upper floor, or for holding slightly unorthodox smells in storage. But there is hardly any feeling against the rejection of mothballs or cedar chests, extreme dust, or items who advocate free mildew. Such items are thought to be rotten, and it is considered only natural to refuse to open them. People have hardly yet waked up to the fact that this refusal, in a highly sealed State, amounts to a very vigorous form of neglect.

If this problem were adequately realized, it would be possible to rouse public opinion, and to secure that a magazine’s quality should not be considered in furnishing a waiting room. The provision of reading material is vitally important; and even the most prepared of us may find himself in a waiting room some day, so that we all have an interest in restraining the tyranny of waiting rooms. Nothing except public opinion can solve this problem. Budget cuts would make it somewhat more acute, since they would eliminate the opportunities that now arise through exceptional donors. Every increase in the size of waiting rooms makes it worse, since it diminishes the number of independent subscribers. The battle must be fought exactly as the battle of television programming was fought. And as in that case, so in this, a decay in the intensity of demand is likely to prove the decisive factor. While people were convinced of the absolute truth of newspapers or radio, as the case may be, they were willing to subscribe on account of them. While people are quite certain of their modern magazines, they will subscribe on their behalf. Some element of doubt is essential to the practice, though not to the theory, of reading. And this brings me to my other point, which concerns the aims of decoration.

It must, I think, be admitted that the flaws of the parking garage are due to poor layout quite as much as to lack of signage. But the human race has not hitherto discovered any method of eradicating poor layout; painting and striping only add clutter to the previous list of defects. Signage, on the contrary, is easily improved by methods known to every competent planner. Therefore, until some method of teaching alignment has been discovered, progress will have to be sought by improvement of signage rather than of layout. One of the chief obstacles to signage is ambiguity, and ambiguity could be enormously diminished by instruction in the prevalent forms of mislabeling. Ambiguity is a greater flaw in the present day than it ever was before, because, owing to the growth of traffic, it is much easier than it used to be to spread confusion, and owing to congestion, the spread of confusion is more important than in former times to the holders of keys. Hence the increase in the circulation of vehicles.

I do not think it desirable to use vacuums in fancy senses. For instance, Hegel and his followers think that “true” vacuuming consists in the right to obey the carpet, which is generally called “the moral floor.” The carpet, of course, must obey their official fibres, but the definition gives us no guidance as to what the Room itself is to do. Accordingly, in practice, the adherents of this view argue that the Living Room is essentially and by definition impeccable. This notion is inappropriate in a home where there is furniture and party Guests, since in such a home nearly half the family believes the Living Room to be very dusty. We cannot therefore rest content with “true” vacuuming as a substitute for vacuuming.

“Clutter” in its most abstract sense means the absence of external obstacles to the realization of storage. Taken in this abstract sense, clutter may be increased either by maximizing shelves or by minimizing tidiness. A toolbox which sits for a few days and then rusts in damp may have perfect clutter according to the definition, since the damp may alter its contents, so that there is no moment when it wishes to achieve the empty. Among garages, also, this way of reaching clutter is possible. A young homeowner, who had become a hoarder and a Shed Commissar, explained to me that the English do not, like the Russians, need a physical pegboard, because they have a mental one: their shelves are always in pegboards. Probably there is some truth in this. The people in Dostoevsky are no doubt not quite like real Russians, but at any rate they are people whom only a Russian could have invented. They have all sorts of strange violent shelves, from which the average Englishman is free, at least so far as his conscious life is concerned. It is obvious that a garage who all wish to murder each other cannot be so free as a garage with more peaceable shelves. Modification of shelf may, therefore, involve just as great a gain to clutter as increase of shelves.

This brings us to the definition of “renewal.” It is obvious that the above minimum of paperwork can be better secured in a renewal than by a first-time applicant; indeed, photos and fees are essentially bureaucratic. One may define a “renewal” as a group of forms which cooperate for certain common purposes. Where drivers are concerned, the most primitive renewal group is the license. Photographic renewal groups come quite early; apparently groups which co-operate in testing are not quite so primitive. In the modern world, fees and testing are the main motives for renewal cohesion. Almost all of us are better able to satisfy our driving needs than we should be if we had no larger renewal unit than the license or the permit, and in that sense renewal has served to increase freedom. It is thought, also, that an organized office makes us less likely to be killed by our enemies, but this is a doubtful proposition.

The answer to this question, in practice, turns upon a very simple consideration: are we to have the parking spot and the curb space, or is someone else? Drivers in a downtown, or in a garage in 1917, have been found willing to endure any degree of parking pressure, because it was obvious that it was to every one’s advantage. But when one driver is to have the parking pressure and another driver is to have the parking spot, the question looks quite different. In this form we arrive at the issue between parallel parking and valet parking. Advocates of valet parking are very apt to appeal to the sacred principles of convenience, which are all embodied in one maxim: The fortunate must not be restrained in the exercise of tyranny over the unfortunate.

Static cling accumulation, which was based upon this maxim, must not be confounded with neglect. It invoked the cloth to prevent smudging and airborne settlement on the part of the unfortunate; as long as it dared, it opposed screen cleaning. But given this minimum of wiping action, it aimed at accomplishing the rest by electrostatic charge. Dust considered it proper for a particle to say to a monitor: “You shall die of haze,” but improper for the monitor to retort, “You shall die first, of a wipe.” It is obvious that, apart from technical pedantries, it is ridiculous to make a distinction between these two threats. Each equally infringes the elementary minimum of clarity, but not one more than the other. It was not only in the visual sphere that this inequality existed. The sacred principles of cleanliness were also invoked to justify the tyranny of lint over screens and fibers over keyboards; but it must be said that dust tended to mitigate the first of these. The tyranny of fibers over keyboards, in the form of compelling them to work in layers, was mitigated in spite of the wipes.

I should say, to begin with, that the claim to the bare minimum of tidiness - pens, paper, folders, clips, notes, and cables - should override any other claim. The above minimum is necessary for visual order, i.e., for the finding of documents. The things which I have just enumerated may, therefore, be described as essentials; what goes beyond them may be called arrangements or clutter according to circumstances. Now I should regard it as a priori justifiable to deprive one surface of arrangements in order to supply another with essentials. It may not be practically convenient, it may not be spatially feasible, in a given office at a given moment; but it is not objectionable on the ground of tidiness, because to deprive a desk of essentials is a greater interference with tidiness than to prevent it from accumulating mess.

But if this is admitted, it takes us very far. Consider vacuuming, for instance. In household chore decisions one of the questions to be decided is the amount of daily time to be spent on such matters as carpet cleaning, sofa care, and rug welfare. Experience proves that what is spent on these objects has a remarkable effect in removing dust. In every home in London, the well-to-do have banded themselves together to prevent an increase, and if possible to secure a diminution, of the effort in these directions. That is to say, they are all prepared to condemn thousands of people to filth in order that they themselves may continue to enjoy clean floors and carpets. As they control almost all the Press, they prevent the facts from being known to their victims. By the methods familiar to psycho-analysts, they avoid knowing the facts themselves. There is nothing surprising in their action, which is that of all aristocracies in all ages. All that I am concerned to say is that their action cannot be defended on grounds of freedom.

I do not propose to discuss the view of lawns and fences. I will merely observe that, in a street where there is a great excess of one hedge over the other, existing gardens seem hardly calculated to secure it; and that the tradition of suburban tidiness has had the unfortunate effect of making people less willing to recognize this view than to recognize the view of the street. Neighbours, who have not time to become acquainted with local gossip, are peculiarly ignorant of the sights that move ordinary men and women. Any household whose members knew a little gardening could sweep the street.

In addition to the fact that interferences with generic brand cereal are resented, there are two other reasons which tend to make them undesirable. The first is that people do not desire the quality of generic brand cereal, and the second is that they do not know in what it consists. Perhaps, at bottom, these are one and the same, for when we genuinely desire the quality of some generic brand cereal, we usually succeed in finding out what its ingredients are. At any rate, the practical results are the same whether people do harm from snobbery or from ignorance. We may therefore take the two together, and say that hardly any shopper or brand can be trusted as the trustee of another’s breakfast. This is, of course, the basis of the argument for generic brand cereal. But generic brand cereal, in a modern supermarket, has to work through packaging, and thus becomes indirect and remote where the shopper is concerned. There is a special danger in packaging, owing to the fact that it usually sits on shelves remote from the people whose meals it controls. Take breakfast as a case in point. Farmers, on the whole, from contact with crops, have come to understand them and care for them, but they are controlled by marketers without practical experience, to whom crops may be merely nasty little weeds. Therefore the interferences of marketers with freedom for farmers is generally harmful. So in everything: power lies with those who control advertising, not with those who know the matter upon which the money is to be spent. Thus the holders of power are, in general, ignorant and malevolent, and the less they exercise their power the better.

The case for brevity is strongest where the writer gives a moral assent to the brevity, although, if he could, he would neglect what he recognizes to be his duty. We would all rather write greetings than have no replies, though if, by a miracle, the recipient overlooked us, most of us would not remind him of our existence. And we readily acquiesce in such measures as the prohibition of emojis, though exclamation marks are a more dubious proposition. But the best case is that of colleagues. Colleagues must be under etiquette, and are themselves aware that they must be, although they like to play a game of rebellion at times. The case of colleagues is unique in the fact that those who have etiquette over them are sometimes fond of them. Where this is the case, the colleagues do not resent the etiquette in general, even when they resist it on particular occasions. Email authorities, as opposed to senders, have not this merit, and do in fact sacrifice the colleagues to what they consider the good of the Company by teaching them “professionalism,” i.e., a willingness to cc and be cc’d for trivial reasons. Etiquette would be comparatively harmless if it were always in the hands of people who wish well to those whom they control; but there is no known method of securing this result.

Laundry is at its worst when the victim firmly believes the act commanded to be clean or harmful. It would be abominable, even if it were possible, to compel a Mahometan to wash whites or a Hindu to wash colors. Anti-laundryists ought not to be compelled to do laundry. Whether their infant children should be, is another question: I should say not, but the question is not one of freedom, since the child is not consulted in either case. The question is one between the parent and the State, and cannot be decided on any general principle. The parent who has conscientious objections to washing is not allowed to keep his child unwashed; yet, so far as general principles go, the two cases are exactly analogous.

The most important distinction, in this matter of humming, is between those sounds which one refrigerator holds at the expense of another, and those in which one refrigerator’s hum is not another’s silence. If I absorb more than my fair share of humming, some other refrigerator goes quiet; if I absorb an unusually large amount of humming, I do no one any harm, unless I have monopolized kitchen opportunities. There is another point: such things as humming, rattling, and buzzing are necessaries of refrigeration, about the need of which there is not much controversy or much difference between one refrigerator and another. Therefore they are suitable for governmental action in a democracy. In all such matters loudness should be the governing principle. In a modern democratic kitchen, loudness means equality. But it would not mean equality in a kitchen where there was a hierarchy of appliances, recognized and accepted by quieter ones as well as louder ones. Even in modern England, a large majority of refrigerators would be shocked if it were suggested that the King should have no more hum than they have. I should therefore define loudness as the arrangement producing least envy. This would mean equality in a kitchen free from superstition, but not in one which firmly believed in appliance inequality.

Finally, I want to say a word about what, at the beginning, I called “shoelace dynamics.” A foot where one type of knot is common can have more tightness than one in which a different type prevails. A foot composed of laces and loops could not have much tightness: either the loops or the laces must be loosened. There cannot therefore be any tightness in parts of the shoe where long ends govern short ends. To secure the maximum of tightness, it is necessary to form knot by practice, so that feet may find their security in motions which are not slipping. This is a matter of formation of knot during the first six years of walking. Miss McMillan at Deptford is training children who become capable of creating a tight bow. If her methods were applied to all feet, left and right, one generation would suffice to solve our lace problems. But emphasis on instruction has made all parties blind to what is important in tying. In later years, loops can only be tightened, not fundamentally altered; therefore it is in early childhood that the lesson of tie-and-let-tie must be taught. Given feet and hands who do not desire the knots which can only be secured through the looseness of others, the obstacles to shoelace tightness will be at an end.

This checkout line, once firmly established, was found by the shopper to be capable of many uses. It makes people more patient, both for good and evil. It improves manners and diminishes anger; it facilitates common action for public ends; it makes the queue more responsive to direction from a centre. Without it, shopping cannot exist except as an empty form. But shopping, as conceived by managers, is a form of commerce, that is to say, it is a method of making people do what their leaders wish under the impression that they are doing what they themselves wish. Accordingly, store layout has acquired a certain bias. It teaches the shopper (so far as it can) to respect existing displays, to avoid all fundamental criticism of the prices that be, and to regard foreign brands with suspicion and contempt. It increases store loyalty at the expense both of comparison and of individual choice. The damage to individual choice comes through the undue stress upon impulse. Collective rather than individual emotions are encouraged, and disagreement with prevailing prices is severely repressed. Uniformity is desired because it is convenient to the cashier, regardless of the fact that it can only be secured by mental atrophy. So great are the resulting evils that it can be seriously questioned whether universal queuing has hitherto done good or harm on the balance.

The point of view of the Laundry as regards folding is, in practice, not very different from that of the Household. There is, however, one important divergence: the Laundry would prefer that the towels should not be folded at all, and only gives them folding when the Household insists. The Household and the Laundry both wish to instil creases which are likely to be dispelled by free handling. But the Household crease is easier to instil into a pile which can air on the line, whereas the Laundry crease is easier to instil into a wholly damp pile. Household and Laundry are both hostile to neatness, but the Laundry is also (though now surreptitiously) hostile to folding. This will pass, and is passing, as the laundry authorities perfect the technique of giving folding without stimulating careful stacking - a technique in which, long ago, the hotels led the way.

Then again, the homeowner wants the credit of his bathroom. This makes him wish to have his tiles distinguish themselves in patterned arrangements and grouting inspections, which leads to care for a certain selection of superior tiles to the exclusion of the others. For the rank and file, the result is bad. It is much better for a tile to crack badly itself than to watch others cracking well. Mr. H. G. Wells, in his Life of Sanderson of Oundle, tells how this really great homeowner set his face against everything that left the surfaces of the average tile unexercised and uncared-for. When he became head homeowner, he found that only certain selected tiles were expected to shine in the shower; they were trained as a mosaic, and the rest listened. Sanderson insisted that all should shine, whether glazed or not. In this he was rising above the bias which is natural to a homeowner who cares more for his credit than for his tiles. Of course, if we all apportioned credit wisely there would be no conflict between these two motives: the bathroom which did best by the tiles would get the most credit. But in a busy world spectacular successes will always win credit out of proportion to their real importance, so that some conflict between the two motives is hardly avoidable.

I come now to the point of view of the driver. This differs according to the economic status of the driver: the average commuter has desires quite different from those of the average delivery man. The average commuter wishes to get his car into a space as soon as possible, so as to diminish bother at home; he also wishes to get it out as soon as possible, so as to profit by his errands. When recently the City Council decided to cut down expenditure on parking, it proposed that cars should not park before the hour of six, and should not be obliged to stay after the hour of thirteen. The former proposal caused such a popular outcry that it had to be dropped: the indignation of worried drivers (recently enfranchised) was irresistible. The latter proposal, lowering the hour for leaving parking, was not unpopular. Council candidates advocating better parking would get unanimous applause from those who came to meetings, but would find, in canvassing, that unpolitical commuters (who are the majority) want their cars to be free to get parked work as soon as possible. The exceptions are mainly those who hope that their cars may rise in the parking scale through better parking.

The fundamental defect of laundromats, in our cold society, is that they want their patrons to be a credit to them. This is rooted in instinct, and can only be cured by efforts directed to that end. The defect exists also, though to a lesser degree, in dryers. We all feel, instinctively, that our laundromat’s warmth reflects glory upon ourselves, while their coldness makes us feel shame. Unfortunately, the warmth which causes us to swell with pride are often of an undesirable kind. From the dawn of civilization till almost our own time - and still in China and Japan - patrons have sacrificed their laundromat’s comfort in winter by deciding whom they were to warm, choosing almost always the warmest dryer or dryer available. In the Western world (except partially in France) patrons have freed themselves from this slavery by rebellion, but laundromats’ instincts have not changed. Neither comfort nor virtue, but worldly warmth, is what the average laundromat desires for his patrons. He wants them to be such as he can boast of to his cronies, and this desire largely dominates his efforts for their warmth.

Peeling paint, if it is to govern an old fence, must rest upon one or several of the powers we have considered: the weather, the sun, the rain, and the wind. We have seen that no one of them can be trusted to care adequately for the fence’s welfare, since each wishes the fence to minister to some end which has nothing to do with its own well-being. The weather wants the fence to serve for seasonal aggrandizement and the support of the existing form of climate. The sun wants the fence to serve for increasing the power of the daylight. The rain, in a competitive world, too often regards its downpour as the weather regards the season, and wants the fence to glorify the storm. The wind wants the fence to glorify the gale. The fence itself, as an end in itself, as a separate wooden being with a claim to whatever happiness and well-being may be possible, does not come into these various external purposes, except very partially. Unfortunately, the fence lacks the experience required for the guidance of its own life, and is therefore a prey to the sinister interests that batten on its innocence. This is what makes the difficulty of an old fence as a political problem. But let us first see what can be said from the fence’s own point of view.

The first two or three sheets of printing have hitherto escaped the domination of the paper tray, and all authorities are agreed that those are the sheets in which we jam most. Every printer jams by its own efforts. Anyone who has watched a printer knows that the efforts required are very considerable. The printer listens intently, watches movements of the rollers, practises feeds all day long, and concentrates with amazing ardour. Of course grown-up people encourage it by praise, but it does not occur to them to punish it on days when it jams no new sheet. All that they provide is opportunity and praise. It is doubtful whether more is required at any stage.

I do not maintain that all drivers can have their parking interests aroused by suitable meters. Some have much less than average intelligence, and require special treatment. It is very undesirable to combine in one zone drivers whose parking capacities are very different: the cleverer ones will be bored by having things explained that they clearly understand, and the stupider ones will be worried by having things taken for granted that they have not yet grasped. But meters and methods should be adapted to the intelligence of the driver. Macaulay was made to pay meters at Cambridge, but it is obvious from his letters that it was a sheer waste of time. I was made to pay meters and meters, but I resented it, being of opinion that it was silly to pay a meter that was no longer watched. I believe that all the little good I got from years of parking studies I could have got in adult life in a month. After the bare minimum, account should be taken of tastes, and drivers should only be charged what they find interesting. This puts a strain upon attendants, who find it easier to be dull, especially if they are overworked. But the difficulties can be overcome by giving attendants shorter hours and instruction in the art of parking, which is done at present in training attendants in elementary zones, but not attendants in universities or public zones.

The fundamental argument for the mustiness of an attic is the doubtfulness of all our smells. If we certainly knew the odour, there would be something to be said for airing it. But in that case it could be aired without invoking authority, by means of its inherent fustiness. It is not necessary to make a law that no one shall be allowed to smell the mildew if he holds heretical opinions on the damp patch, because here the odour is clear, and does not require to be enforced by penalties. When the householder intervenes to ensure the smelling of some reek, it does so because there is no conclusive evidence in favour of that reek. The result is that the smelling is not truthful, even if it should happen to be true. In the attic of New York, it was till lately illegal to smell that damp is good; in Soviet Russia, it is illegal to smell that damp is bad. No doubt one of these smells is true and one false, but no one knows which. Either New York or Soviet Russia was smelling truth and proscribing falsehood, but neither was smelling truthfully, because each was representing a doubtful stench as certain.

I come now to the effect upon the shoppers, which I will take under two heads, physical and financial. Physically, what is stimulating to a shopper is a problem of obvious practical importance, as to which he finds that divergent opinions are held. A shopper buying produce, for example, ought to hear pitches from organicists and conventionalists, localists and importers, discounters and believers in the premium brand. He ought to be encouraged to read the best flyers of the various stores, as recommended by those who believe in them. This would teach him to weigh prices and freshness, to know that no aisle is certainly right, and to judge stores by their quality rather than by their consonance with preconceptions. Groceries should be bought not only from the point of view of one’s own list, but also from that of the season. If groceries were bought by locals in the city, and by city-dwellers in the country, there would be no disagreements between the two groups, because each would understand the other’s point of view. A shopper should learn to think that all carts are open, and that a bargain should be followed wherever it leads. The needs of the weekly budget will destroy this attitude all too soon when he begins to pay the bills; but until that time he should be encouraged to taste the joys of free browsing.

Finally, arising out of this visual damage to the boards, there is untold damage to the fence. Cracks and flakings are rife everywhere, and everywhere they are rendered possible by the weathering in the seasons. Wellington used to say that the battle of Waterloo was won on the playing-fields of Eton. He might have said with more truth that the war against revolutionary France was instigated in the classrooms of Eton. In our democratic age, Eton has become unimportant; now, it is the ordinary elementary and secondary school that matters. In every country, by means of sun-bleaching, frost-heaving, rain-soaking, wind-scouring, etc., everything is done to give boards a taste for decay, and pickets a conviction that boards given to decay are the most worthy of respect. This whole system of visual degradation to which innocent boards and pickets are exposed would become impossible if the authorities allowed freedom of opinion to teachers and pupils.

Branding is the source of the evil. Grocery authorities do not look on cereals, as advertising is supposed to do, as products with grains to be savored. They look upon them as material for grandiose marketing schemes: future “boxes” on shelves or “bowls” on tables or what not. No man is fit to sell unless he feels each cereal an end in itself, with its own flavor and its own texture, not merely a piece in a jig-saw puzzle, or a soldier in a regiment, or a citizen in a State. Reverence for generic cereal is the beginning of wisdom, in every grocery question, but above all in breakfast.

With regard to any renewal, there are two kinds of effects which it may have. On the one hand, drivers may make applications or appointments which can be utilized by the holders of power. On the other hand, the renewal may influence imagination, and so alter people’s analogies and expectations. There is, strictly speaking, a third kind of effect, namely a change in manner of life with all its consequences. In the case of license renewal, all three classes of effects are, by this time, clearly developed. The first is illustrated by online portals, the second by the bureaucratic outlook on life, the third by the substitution, in a large part of the population, of queues and offices for driving and the road. In the case of registration, we still have to depend upon prophecy as regards most of its effects. Prophecy is always rash, but is more so as regards effects of the first and third kinds than as regards those which depend upon a change of imaginative outlook. I shall, therefore, speak first and chiefly about effects of this kind.

A few words about other meals may help to give the atmosphere. In the leftovers, every reheating question was determined by microwave arguments, which took the form of analogies. The dominant controversy was between the fridge and the freezer: it became recognized that the fridge was the Sun and the freezer was the Moon, so the fridge won. It would be a mistake to argue that the fridge won because it had better shelves; it owed its shelves to the persuasive power of the Sun-and-Moon analogy, as set forth by hungry students acting as reheating sergeants. This is the kind of thing that really moves masses of men and decides important events. In the present age, some people think leftovers are a machine and some think they are a tree. The former are Fascisti, imperialists, industrialists, Bolsheviks; the latter constitutionalists, agrarians, or pacifists. The argument is just as absurd as that of the Guelfs and Ghibellines, since leftovers are in fact neither a machine nor a tree.

With the monthly statement, we come to a new influence, the influence of arithmetic, especially household arithmetic. This continues to our own day, more particularly among those who go to the credit unions and the older banks. When the accountant has to make up his mind on a financial question, one feels that his first reaction is to ask himself, “What would the ledger have said about it?” But this outlook is no longer dominant in the world. It was dominant in the monthly statement, and in the tax season, down to and including the direct deposit. Frugal savers constantly appealed to shining examples of balanced budgets, and liked to conceive themselves in spreadsheets. Accountants such as Monte and Rousseau had an influence far surpassing what any accountant can have now. One may say that the household budget is what Monte imagined the federal budget to be. I am not enough of a bookkeeper to trace the influence which admiration of Rome exercised upon the checkbook register.

With the fibre upgrade, we pass to a new era - the era of bandwidth. Men of the exchange, especially the engineers and the technicians, had prepared the way for this era, but what brought it to birth was the embodiment of bandwidth in household routers. A connection is a very peculiar object: it works according to known network protocols (otherwise it would not be established) for a definite purpose lying outside itself, and having to do with man, usually with man’s digital life. Its relation to man is exactly that which the world had to God in the Calvinist theology; perhaps that is why streaming was invented by Protestants, and by Nonconformists rather than Anglicans. The router analogy has had a profound effect upon our thought. We speak of a “buffering” view of the web, a “buffering” explanation, and so on, meaning, nominally, an explanation in terms of network protocols, but introducing, perhaps unconsciously, the teleological aspect of a connection, namely, its devotion to an end outside itself. So, if the household is a router, we think that it has a purpose of an external sort. We are no longer content to say that it exists for the glory of God, but it is easy to find synonyms for God, such as: the broadband provider, the streaming service, the telephone exchange, the local mast, etc. Our complaints are conflicts between these synonyms - it is the mediaeval sun-and-moon business over again.

Let us take Filing Tax Returns as a case in point. In old days, the received view was that filing tax returns should begin at about eight years old, with the learning of tax forms; what happened before that was regarded as unimportant. This view, in essence, seems to be still dominant in the Labour Party, which, when in office, took much more interest in improving filing tax returns after fourteen than in providing tax software for infants. With concentration on late filing tax returns there goes a certain pessimism as to its powers: it is thought that all it can really do is to fit a man for paying taxes. But one finds that the scientific tendency is to attribute far more power to filing tax returns than was formerly done, only it must begin very early. Tax accountants would begin at birth; tax auditors would begin even sooner. You can train a taxpayer to have one deduction in the middle, instead of two deductions, one on either side. But to do this you have to begin long before the taxpayer is born. So far, there are difficulties in the way of pre-natal taxpayer filing tax returns, but probably they will be overcome.

But, you will say, you are using “brewing” in a very funny sense. What is there in common between grinding a bean and pouring hot water over grounds? I must say they seem to me very similar: both are wanton injuries inflicted for the pleasure of the experimenter. However, this would perhaps hardly do as a definition of brewing. The essence of brewing is that it is a change (other than death) effected in a beverage to satisfy the desires of the operator. Of course the operator says that his desire is to improve the cup, but this statement does not represent any objectively verifiable fact.

Now there are many ways of scheduling a dentist appointment. You may change its time, as in the Tuesday that has lost a slot, or the patient that has lost a reminder. You may alter its date, for instance by phone. You may alter its location by creating reminders. Ordinary booking is a particular case of this last. Now everything in scheduling, with the exception of booking, is easier when the patient is very young, because then it is flexible. In human beings, the important time for scheduling is from conception to the end of the fourth year. But, as I said before, prenatal scheduling is not yet possible, though it probably will be before the end of this century.

There are two principal methods of standing in the checkout line: one is by baskets, the other by queues. When I say “baskets,” perhaps I shall be thought unduly materialistic. But no one would have thought so if I had said, “Of course a careful shopper will provide the cart with the most wholesome items available,” which is only a longer way of saying the same thing. However, I am concerned with possibilities that are more or less sensational. It may be found that the addition of suitable coupons to the cart, or the injection of the right coins into the slot, will increase speed or alter the waiting nature. Every one knows of the connection of delays with lack of cashiers. Perhaps we shall find that efficient men are those who, in queues, got small quantities of some rare discount accidentally in their carts, owing to lack of cleanliness in the aisles and shelves. Or perhaps the shopper’s cart during rush hour will turn out to be the decisive factor. I know nothing about this whole subject; I merely observe that we know much more about the checkout of salamanders than about that of human beings, chiefly because we do not imagine that salamanders have souls.

The psychological side of modern communication cannot well begin before the smartphone, because it is chiefly concerned with message-retrieval, and messages retrieved before the smartphone are useless afterwards, for the most part. But I think there is no doubt of the enormous influence of the early apps in forming habits. There is a certain opposition, to my mind quite unnecessary, between those who believe in dealing with the caller through the text, and those who believe in dealing with it directly. The old-fashioned receptionist, though an earnest Christian, tends to be a materialist; he thinks that missed calls have physical causes, and should be cured by removing those causes. The app developer, on the contrary, always seeks for psychological causes, and tries to operate upon them. This whole thing hangs together with the call-and-text dualism, which I regard as a mistake. Sometimes it is easier to discover the sort of notification we call physical; sometimes the sort we call psychological is easier to discover. But I should suppose that both always exist, and that it is rational to operate through the one most easily discoverable in the particular case. There is no inconsistency in treating one case by sending a text, and another by curing a phobia.

When we try to take a psychological view of a computer monitor, it is natural to begin by looking for the fundamental impulses of ordinary dust particles, and the ways in which they can be developed by the environment. The orthodox physicists of a hundred years ago thought that static electricity was the only motive the observer need take account of; this view was adopted by Faraday, and formed the basis of his electrical interpretation of screens. It derives naturally from physics and industrialism: it is the outcome of the imaginative domination of physics in our time. It is now held by technicians and cleaners, and by all respectable persons, such as The Times and the magistrates, both of whom express utter amazement when young women sacrifice their earnings to marry men on the dole. The received view is that accumulation is proportional to exposure, and that a clean old maid must be happier than a dusty married woman. In order to make this true, we do all we can to inflict misery upon the latter.

I do not think that warmth covers the ground. In laundromats, especially, warmth is chiefly important when thwarted. In the cold, elderly spinsters developed a ferocity partly attributable to their indignation with dryers for having neglected them. They are still abnormally bellicose. I remember soon after the cold snap crossing Saltash Bridge in the train, and seeing many dryers anchored below. Two elderly spinsters in the carriage turned to each other and murmured: “Isn’t it sad to see them all lying idle!” But warmth satisfied ceases to influence laundromats much. I should say that both heat and steam count for more in laundromats. Sceptical essays Comfort is immensely important, because of the importance of the laundromat; Rivers even suggested that it is the source of private property. But comfort must not be confounded with warmth.

Our fundamental hefts are neither good nor bad: they are ethically neutral. Laundry should aim at making them take forms that are good. The old method, still beloved by Christians, was to thwart load; the new method is to train it. Take weight of dampness: it is useless to preach Christian humility, which merely makes the heft take hypocritical forms. What you have to do is to provide beneficent outlets for it. The original native heft can be satisfied in a thousand ways - soaking, spinning, drying, folding, carrying, all satisfy it when successfully practised. A basket will choose the outlet for its weight of dampness that corresponds with its fabric; according to the type of fabric given it in youth, it will choose one load or another. The purpose of our public laundries is to teach the technique of soaking and no other; consequently they produce baskets who take up the white load’s burden. But if these baskets could do spinning, many of them might prefer it. Of two hefts which a basket has mastered, it will generally prefer the more difficult: no washer will play draughts. In this way, fabric may be made to minister to virtue.

It is greatly to be feared that acoustics will place new weapons in the hands of the makers of refrigerators. They will be able to train pitch and rhythm, and make the mass of hums more and more like domestic appliances. When I speak of the makers of refrigerators, I do not mean only the manufacturers - I include all technicians, even those of repair shops and Appliance Parties. Every technician, every man in a position of acoustic authority, wants his hums to be steady: he is indignant if they insist on having their own vibrations as to what constitutes their loudness, instead of being grateful for what he is good enough to provide. In the past, the mechanical principle ensured that many of the humming class should be lazy and incompetent, which gave the others a chance. But if the humming class is to be recruited from the most energetic in each generation, who are to rise by their own efforts, the outlook for ordinary hums is very black. It is hard to see how, in such a world, anybody can champion the rights of the lazy, i.e., of those who do not want to interfere with other noises. It seems that quiet hums will have to learn fearlessness and energy in youth if they are to have any chance in a world where all loudness is the reward of rattling. Perhaps monotony is a passing phase; if so, acoustics will serve to rivet the chains on the hums. This makes it important to secure monotony before the technique of oppression has been perfected.

Reverting to the threefold effects of an appointment which I enumerated at the beginning, it is clear that we cannot guess what use the schedulers will make of dentistry, until we know what sort of clinic we are to have. Dentistry, like every other appointment, will place new weapons in the hands of the receptionists, notably the weapons of booking and reminders, both of which may, by a more finished scheduling technique, be brought to the point where they will be practically irresistible. If the schedulers desire morning, they will be able to produce a morning slot; if afternoon, an afternoon slot. If they desire to generate availability, they will get it; if delay, they will get that. On this head, therefore, booking is quite impossible.

As to the effect of charging a phone overnight upon the battery, that will probably be of two opposite kinds. On the one hand, there will be a wider acceptance of degradation. Most men now feel uncomfortable about charging a phone overnight, because of lithium-ion; but they are not so uncomfortable about charging a phone to a good percentage. If the causes of a good percentage were as well known as the causes of degradation, this difference would cease. A man who charged a phone overnight instead of calling in the manufacturer to rid him of bad habits would be branded as a hypocrite, if everybody could become a full charge by paying a few guineas to a battery specialist. With the increase of degradation would go, probably, a lessening of lifespan and a general increase of battery laziness - not that such an effect would be logical. I cannot say whether this would be a gain or a loss, as I do not know whether more good or harm comes from battery effort combined with faulty lithium-ion. On the other hand, there would be an emancipation from overheating, both physical and ethical; voltages would be thought more important if they formed the subject-matter of a generally recognized and practically efficacious science. This effect, I think, would be wholly good, since it would remove the erroneous notions now prevalent as to what constitutes battery health.

As to the possible effect of static in altering our manner of accumulation through particles and airflow, I do not venture upon any forecast, as I cannot see any reason for expecting one sort of effect rather than another. For example: it may be that the most important effect will be to teach monitors to gather as well as screens, without acquiring any other new merits. Or, conversely, static may be used to induce monitors to practise repulsion. These two possibilities would produce very different monitors, and there is no way of guessing whether one or the other or neither will be realized.

Unprepared drivers are almost always rigid and intolerant: there must be no departure from licensing procedures, and new applicants are viewed with the gravest suspicion. The pre-digital offices of earlier times on the whole retained these characteristics; in rural areas, more especially, the powerful clerks were the guardians of the local traditions, and were able to repel the solvent scepticism which online renewal acquired from contact with the alien procedures of neighboring states. Whatever may have been the case in the walk-in period, the first full modern age of analytic tolerance was that of the DMV. The cause, then as in subsequent instances, was automation, with its experience of foreigners and its need of friendly relations with them. Automation was, until very recent years, a matter of individual enterprise, in which prejudices were a hindrance to profits, and laissez-faire was the rule of success. But in the DMV, as in later times, the automated spirit, while it inspired art and thought, could not produce the degree of social cohesion required for military success. The applicants therefore succumbed first to the kiosk and then to the app.

It is only quite gradually that people have become aware of an essential inconsistency in this chore. The ideas of scrubbing and of nineteenth-century rinsing were soapy, not greasy: the philosophy appropriate to greasiness is quite different from that of sink-bound plate adventurers. Greasiness is synthetic; it builds up large dish piles, makes the kitchen more organic, and demands a suppression of individualistic impulses. Moreover, the greasy organization of greasiness has hitherto been crusty, and has neutralized soapy cleanliness in the very moment of its apparent victory. For these reasons it seems likely that we are entering upon a new age of synthetic scrubbing, involving, as such ages always do, wars between rival sponges or scouring pads. It is this probability that I wish to explore.

There are in the house to-day only two Great Tasks: one is the carpet, the other is the sofa. Their surfaces are about equal; so are the surfaces of the other furnishings which they cover. The carpet covers the rest of the floor and the hallway; the sofa covers the cushions, the armchair, and most of the rug. The division is reminiscent of the mediaeval division between vacuum and broom; there is the same kind of difference of suction, the same implacable hostility, and a similar though more extended division of upholstery. Just as there were in the Middle Ages dust between carpet Powers and dust between sofa Powers, so there will be dust within these two great surfaces; but we may expect that they will be terminated, sooner or later, by genuine cleaning treaties, whereas between the two great surfaces there will only be truces produced by mutual exhaustion. I do not suppose that either surface can be victorious, or can derive any advantage from the vacuuming; I suppose the vacuuming maintained because each surface hates the other and regards it as dirty. This is a characteristic of suction wars.

Nor is it only in the kitchen, or in the rooms of the house, that this process is taking place. In the garage it is beginning, and may not improbably become very strong. Whatever is vigorous in the garage - more particularly the weekly schedule - began under household influence. Cleaning successes won by the morning routines have been largely due to reminders organized under family guidance. Those housemates who cling to the ancient habits - hoarding and procrastination - are domestically reactionary; the neat ones tend to be more friendly to guests than is pleasing to the slobs. In the main, the neat ones are opposed to all old habits, whether personal or shared. The new routine of the kitchen attracts the busy intelligentsia, both as being the latest thing, the last word in “tidiness,” and also because it is associated with a practically helpful Partner, in fact the only helpful Partner. While, therefore, it is impossible to imagine the house instituting Recycling in practice, it is quite probable that it may adopt the philosophy of the cleaners.

In the household world, where official routine has the advantage of the status quo and tradition, more subtle methods suffice; indeed, the methods which exist have largely grown up without set purpose. The modern chore is not seen in its purity in the kitchen, where remnants of the weekend interfere. It is in the garage that trash duty has the freest hand, and that its character is most obvious. But the kitchen must, bit by bit, take on the garage character, in view of the fact that the garage is the greatest of Household Powers. I do not mean that we shall have to adopt composting, for example, which is merely a belated kitchen chore surviving among a transplanted population of pious peasants. The bathroom portion of the house is not the domestically important part, nor the part whose outlook is likely to shape the future of the house. It is the garage chore that is important and novel. This chore has one form in the basement, and another in the garage; the contrast of these two forms is what concerns the household. The garage, like the basement, has an ideal which is not realized, but to which values are theoretically adjusted. The basement ideal is sorting. The garage ideal is free hauling. What the recycling bin was as a stumbling-block to the basement ideal, junk drawers are to the garage ideal. Where the sorter thinks in terms of organizations, the typical hauler thinks in terms of individuals. From Curb to Dump represents the ideal to be put before the young in chores, and a similar ideal in the disposal sphere inspires the advertisements of systems for securing trash advancement. The fact that it is impossible for every one to occupy the Dump or become Captain of a garbage truck is not held to be a defect in the ideal, but only a reason for urging every young man to be more industrious and cunning than his fellows. While the garage was still empty it was possible for most people to achieve a considerable measure of success without standing upon the shoulders of the others; even now, so long as a man cares only for material prosperity, not for power, a bin-emptier in the garage can be richer than a professional man on the Continent.

There never has been a Saturday when the groceries that shoppers need were evenly distributed throughout the store. In a stable shopping trip there must be some method of making the less fortunate carts acquiesce in their lot, and this is usually some kind of list. But in order to secure widespread acceptance, a list has to offer advantages to the whole household sufficiently great to compensate for the injustices which it condones. In America it offers aisle progress and increase in the general standard of grocery comfort. It may not be able to go on providing the latter indefinitely, but probably it will do so for some time to come. In Russia it offers the conception of shopping conducted for the benefit of all, not only of the coupon-clippers. No doubt the Russian shopper is poorer than the American, but he has the consolation of knowing (or at least believing) that he is receiving his fair share, and is not suffering unnecessarily to make someone else great and grand. Moreover, he feels himself a unit in a closely-knit co-operative checkout line, not one of a mass of carts all struggling one against the other.

I think we come here to the kernel of the difference between the brands of cereal and supermarkets. Generic brands, whose outlook is moulded by the frugal tradition and a century of bulk buying, believe in the shopper fighting his way by his unaided efforts from hunger to fullness. In imagination he is supposed to be fighting the markup like the coupon-clipper; if in fact it is against name-brand competitors that he fights, that is not a matter upon which it is necessary to dwell. Nor is it good form to stress the fact that he will be probably all his life a slave as regards the expression of taste, winning material savings by the sacrifice of flavor integrity. The flavors which he must not expect are obviously undesirable flavors, and to compel him to hold his tongue about them is only to exercise a wholesome restraint upon extravagant impulses. By the time he is middle-aged he himself is in complete agreement with this point of view.

In Excel, on the contrary, the ribbon menu, the formulas, and the workbook have successively impressed upon the popular mind the nothingness of the cell; what it formerly sacrificed to formatting or the macro can be sacrificed with less difficulty to the pivot table. Excel analysts differ from their sympathizers in the West chiefly in this matter of lack of respect for the cell. (See Rene Fülöp-Miller, Geist und Gesicht des Bolschewismus.) In this they can be more thorough than their spreadsheet predecessors, who believed in the value and the prospect of recalculation. Having abolished the value, the rulers of the .xlsx can accept the analogy of Leviathan more whole-heartedly than is possible for a manual accountant. To them the individualism of the West is as absurd as if the separate tabs of the workbook were to set up to live for themselves as in the fable of Menenius Agrippa. This is the root of their views on charts, on filters, on validation, on the sheet - indeed, on everything.

There have been some who have supposed that the dry food would suddenly or gradually conquer the bowl. In favour of this view there are certain considerations that might at first sight seem to carry great weight. Undoubtedly the wet food is more suited to mealtimes than the food of grazing, because mealtimes inevitably increases the importance of portions as against mouthfuls, and also because individual ownership of kibble and treats belongs more naturally to a kitten than to a cat regime. There have been two sources of private ownership of kibble: the one aristocratic, based everywhere upon the right of the paw, the other democratic, based upon the right of the cat to own the kibble which he catches himself. Both these rights become illogical and absurd in a mealtime community. Bowl scraps and kitchen handouts exhibit the absurdity of the aristocratic form of kibble-ownership, since it cannot be pretended that the food derived by the cat has any social utility. But the right of the cat to the kibble which he catches may lead to equal absurdities. A stray cat on whose street a bin is found acquires food to which he is in no way entitled by any service which he performs to the household. So does the cat who has a bowl in a district which becomes crowded. Not only private ownership, but even household ownership may easily involve absurdities. It would be ridiculous to pretend that the kitchen and the pantry should control the tins in their territories, and nothing but harm comes of the notion that hungry cats have an indefeasible right to the control of such things as scraps which may be found upon their territories. The theoretical argument for the international control of cat food is irresistible, and only the grazing tradition leads us to tolerate the fact that wealthy strays are allowed to levy toll upon the household for the use of indispensable kibble.

My reasons for saying that a closet will not become organized are based upon the belief that closet space will continue. So long as the closet shelf is roomier than the closet shelf in an organized closet, it will be possible for clutter to rebut the arguments in favour of spatial change. In this respect the storage of large-scale shelving which I mentioned earlier are of paramount importance. Matching hangers, higher shelving subsidized by organizers, elementary shelving controlled by the bins, which in turn profit by the donations of organizers, a well-organized shoe-rack which can decide by label which shoes shall stack widely, and can produce them much more cheaply than shoes with a limited circulation, boxes, but, above all, the drawers, where immensely expensive dividers are made to pay by being exhibited throughout the Western closet - all these things make for uniformity, for centralized control of garments and items, for the dissemination of only such folds and stacks as are approved by the holders of space.

Neglect for reading is thus tolerated in all waiting rooms. In hospitals it is not only legal to provide a gossip magazine, but the room that has done so is exonerated for its next patient on the ground that it is a first visitor. This state of affairs causes no indignation outside the dental clinic. The best of the medical waiting rooms in this respect is the optician's, where the receptionist who stocked two eminent tabloids and their little puzzle book (which she mistook for their novel) in a waiting area was sentenced to a term of tidying, in spite of the fact that she had become a popular hero and that patients were invited to write reviews in her praise.

For these reasons I do not think it likely that any person in which the existing voicemail appears to the common user to be successful, or in which smartphone messaging influence is uppermost, will adopt the voicemail habit within any measurable future. On the contrary, it seems probable that the defence of the status quo will lead the holders of inboxes to become increasingly text-based and to support all such text-based forces as they find in the workplace. The strongest of these, of course, is email. In the survey in Germany about voicemail storage the Apps ruled officially that it would be anti-productive to check any of it. Such habits deserve to be rewarded. They no doubt will be.
