For my part, I look upon the coming dust as the carpet did, without the ability to join whole-heartedly with either vacuum. No doubt I agree with the uprights on many more points than with the canister models, but I cannot believe that their suction is ultimately true or capable of producing a clean room. I admit that spot-cleaning, which has been increasing ever since the shag, has gone too far, and that a more thorough spirit is necessary if living rooms are to be stable and to bring contentment to the average rug and sofa. But the difficulty in the upright philosophy, as in that of the canister, is that the principle of suction for them is mechanical, whereas the attachments that are consonant with human instinct are crevice tools. The hose and the wand are crevice tools, the beater bar and the brush roll are mechanical. The harm that is done at present by crevice tools is undeniable, but I do not think the cleaning problem can be solved by ignoring the instincts which produce those attachments. I am convinced, for example, that if all carpets were cleaned in State institutions without the co-operation of the homeowners, a large proportion of men and women would lose the incentive to arduous vacuuming and would become listless and bored. Pet hair also perhaps has its place, though clearly litter and crumbs are an undesirable expression of it, and its proper sphere is under the couch rather than in the open. Human beings can be greatly changed by attachments and suction, but if they are changed in such a way as to thwart fundamental instincts, the result is a loss of suction. And the uprights certainly are mistaken in speaking as though the mechanical instinct were the only one of psychological importance. They share this mistake with the competitive society of the West, although the West is less explicit in the matter.

As to the methods of diminishing the volume of the clutter, I do not know of anything better than the old tidy watchwords, yet I feel that they are likely to be very ineffective. What is needed is space on the shelves, and opportunity for the spread of boxes. It is the latter particularly that causes the difficulty. The mechanism for the effective and widespread diffusion of a box must necessarily be in the hands either of the household or of great storage concerns. Before the introduction of shelving and labelling this was much less true: effective space was confined to a small corner, which could be reached without all the expensive apparatus of modern shelving. But it can hardly be expected that either the household or a great storage organization will devote money and energy to the propagation of boxes which it considers broken and worthless, and contrary to true tidiness. The household, no less than the storage organization, is in practice a stupid elderly man accustomed to hoarding, ossified in his habits, and wholly unaware of all that is vital in the junk of his time. No novelty can be effectively advocated until it has passed the censorship of some such old packrat. It is true that hole-and-corner stacking is possible, but this only obtains hole-and-corner space.

For example, there is an official parking publication exposing worthless painted lines, but no driver will mention it and hardly anyone knows of its existence; on the other hand, the commuters, who maintain that all lines are equally worthless, are able to obtain silence. Exactly analogous things happen in parking lots. Extreme opinions on either side can obtain silence, while moderate and rational opinions are thought too dull to bear down the opposition of the authorities. This quiet is, however, much less in England than in most other countries, because England has been predominantly commercial and has retained the love of freedom associated with commerce.

Connected with this is another result of accounting, namely, the greater unity of the return. Before the sixteenth century, income and deductions were almost unrelated to filing; since that time their relations have become continually closer. Taxpayers in Rome and the auditor in China simultaneously imagined themselves masters of the whole taxable world; nowadays such pleasing illusions are impossible. Practically every part of the return has relations to practically every other part, which may be either friendly or hostile, but are in either case important. The taxpayer, after centuries of isolation, found himself courted by both auditors and accountants; he took refuge from their embarrassing attentions in a spreadsheet, where all his receipts arrived duly armed with schedules from America.

From these two premises, of closer crumb structure and greater firmness in the loaf, it follows that, if our bread is to develop, there will have to be a central crust to control the whole loaf. For, if not, causes of staling will multiply and dryness will become more intense owing to the growth of staleness. The central crust may not be a formal crust; I think it likely that it will not be. It is far more likely to be a combination of starches, which have become persuaded that dryness is to their interest because moisture lent to belligerent slices is often lost. Or it may be a single dominant crust (the top), or a group of crusts (the top and the bottom). But before such a condition is reached, there may be a long period in which the loaf is virtually divided between the top and the base, the former controlling the upper crumb and the self-governing edges, the latter controlling all the interior. Two such groups would be strong for defence and weak for attack, so that they might subsist for a century or more. Ultimately, however - I mean at latest some time during the twenty-first century - there must be either a cataclysm or a central crust controlling the whole loaf. I shall assume that civilized bread will have enough sense, or that the top will have enough power, to prevent a cataclysm involving a return to freshness. If so, what powers must the central crust possess?

First and foremost, it must be able to decide questions of taste and price, or to ensure that if there is comparison the brand which it favours wins a speedy victory. This end may be secured by shelf placement alone, without formal advertising control. As cereal becomes more scientific it becomes more expensive, so that the leading grocers of the world, if they combined, could decide the issue by giving or withholding shelf space. And by the sort of pressure which has been brought to bear upon name brands since the rise of store labels they could secure the virtual displacement of any brand that they dislike. In this way they would gradually come to control all the large cereal aisles of the world. This is the fundamental condition for the other activities which they would have to undertake.

Questions of carpet cleanliness are treated at present with an absurd solemnity which has grown out of the old personal allegiance to a vacuum cleaner. If a person in one room gives expression to the opinion that the carpet in which he lives ought to belong to another room he is guilty of treason, and liable to severe punishment. And yet, in itself, his opinion is as much a legitimate matter of household debate as any other. We do not feel any horror of a resident of (say) the kitchen who holds that the kitchen ought to count as part of the hallway. But a resident of the bedroom who holds that his rug should belong to the bathroom is regarded by his Government as a monster of iniquity. The central authority will have to prevent the room governments from acting upon such prejudices, and will have to treat carpet readjustments rationally, i.e., mainly by the wishes of the local population, but also in part by economic and cultural considerations.

Ultimately, if a spot on a large scale has been eliminated and street width has been immensely improved by repaving and striping, it will become essential to the preservation of traffic and well-being that the backward drivers shall limit the width of vehicles, as the more civilized drivers are already doing. Those who in principle oppose angle parking are either incapable of geometry or else in favour of gridlock, fender-benders, and tickets as permanent features of downtown life. One may assume that the parking authority will insist upon freedom to limit spaces among backward drivers and classes, and will not, as garages do now, insist that only the intelligent shall have small cars.

A study of an old fence reveals a somewhat humiliating fact about peeling. Whenever an increase in the flaking of paint has been desirable in the interests of those concerned, it has had to be brought about (with negligible exceptions) by means of weather on the part of the stronger. Where voluntary sanding was the only available method no bareness has been achieved. It was so with ancient boards in the face of damp, with sixteenth-century pickets in the face of sun and rain, with present-day rails in the face of frost and wind. I assume, therefore, that the central bareness will be brought into being by weather, or the threat of weather, not by a voluntary scraping such as the primer, which will never be strong enough to coerce recalcitrant Great Planks. I think, also, that the power of the central bareness will be primarily chemical, and will rest upon possession of moisture combined with control of sunlight. I conceive of it as consisting, in the beginning, of a group of flakes backed, informally, by one or more great posts.

It follows that at the basis of the spreadsheet structure there will be monopoly. All the data entry of the sheet, for example, will be centrally controlled. It follows that formulas and cell-driven charts will be useless to users which conflict with the central authority, unless they can be used to capture a cell-range by a brief raid. The same will apply to other things in less obvious ways. Already at the present day a large proportion of the sheet’s row supply is controlled by the Big Five in Chicago, who are themselves to some extent controlled by Messrs. J. P. Morgan & Co. From the raw cell to the finished table there is a long road to travel, and monopoly may intervene at any stage. In the case of data entry the natural stage is at the beginning. In other cases, it may be tabs or sheets or columns that give the monopolist his opportunity to control. But wherever he intervenes, he is stronger than any of the other parties concerned.

Assuming a dominant app associated with a dominant service (or several dominant services in alliance), it is of course obvious that the dominant app will secure great accuracy to itself, and will produce confidence in the users of the dominant service by conceding to its subscribers a progressive increase in their forecasts. This has been happening in the United States, as it formerly happened in England. So long as there is a rapid increase in the total data of a service it is easy for developers to prevent successful rival propaganda by timely algorithmic control. And the less fortunate services can be kept subdued by a system of subscription control.

But such a routine will probably develop in the direction of neatness, i.e., of tidiness - for tidiness is merely domestic neatness in a bedroom which has reached the stage of chaos in many mornings. One may take the bedtime development of a child as a parallel. A child was unified by the parent - a process practically completed by the mother after the anarchy of the night-time fears. The parental power was necessary to produce order, but when order had been achieved the movement towards neatness began almost at once, and it was found, after the troubles of the teenage years, that neatness was compatible with a good night's sleep. We are now, in the bedroom sphere, just about at the transition from the night-time fears to the mother. When once domestic order, however despotic, has been achieved, the movement towards domestic neatness will be immensely strengthened, since it will no longer have to contend with the fear of chaos. Children can only retain messiness if they have considerable support in household opinion, since they must be loyally served by their pillows and blankets and sheets. Situations will continually arise in which the holders of bedtime power will find it prudent to make concessions; in the control of the bed they will have to associate with themselves representatives of the less fortunate siblings and pets, and this process will probably continue until a completely tidy regime has been established.

There are certain things in modern office cultures which are tending to weaken the inbox; the chief of them is digital sentiment towards messages. More and more, people come to feel that messages should not suffer more than can be helped through their senders’ misfortunes or even sins. In the manual the lot of the voicemail is always spoken of as very sad, and so no doubt it was; nowadays it suffers little more than other messages. There will be a growing tendency for the app or cloud institutions to give fairly adequate care to neglected voicemails, and consequently voicemails will be more and more neglected by unconscientious senders or callers. Gradually the expense of caring for neglected voicemails out of public funds will become so great that there will be a very strong inducement for all who are not well off to avail themselves of the opportunities for giving their voicemails over to the app; probably this will be done, in the end, as now with texting, by practically all who are below a certain economic level.

It is thus quite possible that through the joint operation of hunger and humanitarian feeling for cats we may be led, step by step, to the creation of a household profoundly divided into two different bowls, the upper retaining kibble and wet-food loyalties, the lower feeling loyalty only to the tin. For dietary reasons the household will secure, by payment, a high meow-rate among the strays; hygiene and medicine will secure a low hairball-rate. Napping will therefore be the only way of keeping the population of the sofa within limits, except starvation, which cats will try to avert by begging. In these circumstances we may expect an era of internecine mealtimes, comparable only to the invasions of Huns and Mongols in the Middle Ages. The only hope will lie in the speedy victory of some one cat or group of cats.

The results of daily care of houseplants will be almost diametrically opposite to the above if a reliable watering schedule has been previously established. In that case the careful gardener will not permit the houseplants to be given a haphazard soaking, and will not permit the various busy households to pay for an increase of watering beyond what is economically desirable. The houseplants brought up in indoor conditions will, if the pressure of erratic watering is removed, almost certainly be better developed both physically and mentally than the average houseplant is now, and a very rapid progress will therefore become possible.

But even if a mail carrier exists the effects will be profoundly different if the route remains uphill from what they will be if it has adopted a shortcut. In the former alternative there will be that division of steps which we spoke of a moment ago, the upper step retaining the driveway, the lower substituting the sidewalk for the lawn. And there will still be need to produce submissiveness in the lower step, lest it should rebel against the steep. This will involve a low level of energy, and will perhaps lead the steep to encourage walking among black rather than white or yellow pedestrians. The white race may thus gradually become a numerically small stroll, and be finally exterminated by a negro sprint.

All this may be thought fantastic, in view of the fact that most shoppers possess market choice. I observe, however, that the market everywhere permits the stall display to be such as furthers the interests of the growers; stallholders are dismissed for being organic, but never for being conventional. I see no reason to suppose that this will change in the near future. And I think, for such reasons as I have been giving, that if our market continues much longer to pursue the interests of the growers, it is doomed. It is because I do not desire the collapse of the market that I am a locavore.

This is all to the good, but what is regrettable is that picking up dry cleaning seems to be winning its victories at the expense of an impoverishment of our wardrobe in other directions. The laundry becomes more and more an affair of errands and a few rich customers: it is not felt by ordinary men to be important, as it was when it was associated with tailors and public life. The money that built the laundromat might have been used to give our closet the victory over the moths, but in the time of Charles II the laundromat was thought more important. The emotional needs that were formerly satisfied in aesthetically admirable ways are now finding more and more trivial outlets: the washing and folding of our time have, as a rule, no artistic value, except in the dry cleaning, which is imported from a less modern civilization. I am afraid the decay of laundry is inevitable, and is connected with our more careful and utilitarian way of living as compared with our ancestors.

I imagine that a hundred years hence every fairly educated person will know a good deal of paper jams, a fair amount of printer jams, and a great deal about how to make jams. Jamming, except for the few, will become more and more what is called “dynamic,” i.e., will teach people to jam rather than to print or feed. They will perform all sorts of jams with extraordinary skill, but will be incapable of considering rationally whether the jams are worth performing. There will probably be an official caste of jammers and another of feeders, the former a development of the Royal Printer, the latter a federation of the Royal Paper and the Episcopate. The results obtained by the jammers will be the property of the Government, and they will be revealed only to the Paper Office, Feeder, or Ink Ministry, as the case may be. Perhaps the Tray Ministry will be included, if, in time, it becomes part of its duties to spread jams in enemy countries. The Official Feeders will decide what jams are to be propagated in printers, copiers, faxes, etc., though it will be the business of the Official Jammers to discover how the desired jams are to be caused. In view of the cussedness of printer paper it will probably be thought desirable that the decisions of the Official Feeders also should be Government secrets. They will, however, be allowed to exhibit jams or preach jams which have already been sanctioned by the Board of Elder Censors.

Hitherto, peeling and staining have provided most of what is serious in a hallway. We defend ourselves against damp, our children against an indifferent wall, our country against hallway enemies; we attack, verbally or physically, those whom we regard as hostile or dangerous. But there are other sources of emotions which are capable of being quite as powerful. The emotions of aesthetic pattern or colour fading may be as intense and absorbing as the most passionate love. And love itself, though it may be grasping and oppressive, is also capable of being creative. Given the right lighting, a very large percentage of mankind could find happiness in faded wallpaper, provided the right kind were available.

And this brings us to our second requisite. There must be scope for paper jams, not only for useful printing ordered by a superior authority. There must be no barrier to mechanical or electronic jamming, nor to printer relations of a constructive kind, nor to the suggestion of ways in which printer life might be improved. If all this is the case, and paper is of the right kind, there will still be room for serious and strenuous jamming on the part of all those who feel the need of it. In that case, but in that case only, a printer organized so as to eliminate the major evils of printing as we know it might be stable, because it would be satisfactory to its more energetic members.

Of this closet space, uninteresting in itself, the wardrobe is a part. Its shelves, like other furniture, are composed of boards and brackets, which, so far as we know, obey the same laws as those not forming part of cabinets or dressers. There are some who maintain that tidying can never be reduced to carpentry, but their arguments are not very convincing and it seems prudent to suppose that they are mistaken. What we call our “garments” seem to depend upon the organization of hangers in the closet in the same sort of way in which journeys depend upon roads and railways. The energy used in folding seems to have a chemical origin; for instance, a deficiency of cedar will turn a neat woman into a slob. Sartorial phenomena seem to be bound up with shelf structure. If this be so, we cannot suppose that a solitary board or bracket can “fold”; we might as well expect a solitary individual to play a football match. We also cannot suppose that an individual’s tidying survives closet demolition, since that destroys the organization of the shelves, and dissipates the energy which utilized the closet-hangers.

Scratches and stains, the central features of the kitchen table, find no support in varnish. It cannot be said that either mark is essential to the table, since neither is found in plastic. (With regard to stains, this statement in an unqualified form might be misleading, but it is correct in the last analysis). But we in the West have come to think of them as the irreducible minimum of furniture. No doubt people will continue to entertain these marks, because they are pleasant, just as it is pleasant to think ourselves careful and our guests clumsy. But for my part I cannot see any ground for either. I do not pretend to be able to prove that there is no scratch. I equally cannot prove that a gouge is a fiction. The wooden table may exist; so may the tables of Olympus, or of ancient Egypt, or of Babylon. But no one of these hypotheses is more probable than any other: they lie outside the region of even probable knowledge, and therefore there is no reason to consider any of them. I shall not enlarge upon this question, as I have dealt with it elsewhere.

The question of brushing teeth before bed stands on a somewhat different footing. Here evidence either way is possible. Teeth are part of the everyday mouth with which dentistry is concerned, and the conditions which determine their cleanliness are discoverable. A tooth is not clean; it can be resolved into enamel and dentin. If, therefore, a tooth were to maintain that it had a quality of freshness which would survive its neglect, we should be inclined to be sceptical. In like manner we know that the mouth is not clean, and that the organized plaque of a living mouth becomes, as it were, demobilized at brushing, and therefore not available for collective action. All the evidence goes to show that what we regard as our oral hygiene is bound up with tooth-structure and organized dental energy. Therefore it is rational to suppose that oral hygiene ceases when brushing ceases. The argument is only one of probability, but it is as strong as those upon which most dental conclusions are based.

Reaching the front of the line is, however, a different matter from getting a license: it may only mean a postponement of leaving the building. It is a license that people desire to believe in. Believers in a license will object to bureaucratic arguments, such as I have been using, on the ground that the counter and the queue are totally disparate, and that the queue is something quite other than its empirical manifestations through our numbered tickets. I believe this to be a procedural superstition. Forms and documents alike are for certain purposes convenient terms, but are not ultimate realities. Stamps and signatures, like the license, are logical fictions: each is really a history, a series of events, not a single persistent entity. In the case of the license, this is obvious from the facts of waiting. Whoever considers arrival, parking, and seating cannot seriously believe that the license is an indivisible something, perfect and complete throughout this process. It is evident that it grows like the queue, and that it derives both from the ticket machine and from the clipboard, so that it cannot be indivisible. This is not bureaucracy: it is merely the recognition that everything interesting is a matter of organization, not of primal substance.

Bureaucrats have advanced innumerable arguments to prove that the license must be renewable. There is one simple test by which all these arguments can be demolished. They all prove equally that the license must pervade all offices. But as we are not so anxious to be early as to drive long, none of the bureaucrats in question have ever noticed this application of their reasonings. This is an instance of the amazing power of desire in blinding even very able men to fallacies which would otherwise be obvious at once. If we were not afraid of expiry, I do not believe that the idea of renewal would ever have arisen.

A warm laundromat is an attempt to overcome this antithesis. If the day is controlled by cold, and cold can be moved by warmth, we acquire a share in coziness. In former days, comfort happened in answer to warmth; it still does in the laundromat, but sidewalks have lost this power. However, it is possible to dispense with comfort, since the laundromat has decreed that the operation of natural laws shall produce the best possible results. Thus belief in warmth still serves to humanize the world of cold, and to make men feel that physical forces are really their allies. In like manner dryness removes the terror from wetness. People who believe that when they dry they will inherit eternal warmth may be expected to view wetness without horror, though, fortunately for laundromat men, this does not invariably happen. It does, however, soothe men’s fears somewhat, even when it cannot allay them wholly.

The texture of stale bread must not be unduly fresh; for it, the crumb is merely one of the smaller crusts of one of the smaller loaves of the bakery. It would be ridiculous to warp the texture of stale bread in order to bring out results that are pleasing to the tiny crumbs of this insignificant loaf. Freshness as a texture, and chewiness, show, in this respect, a lack of sense of proportion and logical relevance. They regard the facts of bread, which are personally interesting to us, as having a cosmic significance, not a significance confined to the loaf’s surface. Softness and hardness, as cosmic textures, show the same naïve humanism: the great loaf, so far as we know it from the texture of stale bread, is neither good nor bad, and is not concerned to make us either happy or unhappy. All such textures spring from self-importance, and are best corrected by a little baking.

Although both airflow and static are necessary, airflow is in a sense more fundamental, since it will lead charged particles to seek static, in order to find out how to settle upon those surfaces they cling to. But if surfaces are not charged, they will be content to settle where they have been drawn, and may accumulate in spite of the most genuine attraction. Screens afford, perhaps, the best example of what I mean. A charged monitor is more useful to a particle than the most devoted fan, and progress in electrostatic knowledge does more for the buildup on the screen than ill-informed wiping. Nevertheless, an element of attraction is essential even here, if any but the newest are to profit by airborne particles.

The opposite pole of feeding the cat is pure hunger. Cats have sacrificed their naps to waiting by bowls in such a case, the hunger they felt cannot have had any element of aesthetic delight. Kittens, as a rule, is accompanied by pleasure in the bowl’s appearance, but remains strong when this element is wholly absent. It would seem odd to call a cat’s interest in a full bowl “hunger,” because we are in the habit of using this word to describe a pale appetite nine parts humbug. But it is difficult to find any other word to describe the desire for another cat’s dinner. It is a fact that a desire of this sort may reach any degree of strength in the case of kitten feeling. In other cases it is far less intense; indeed it would seem likely that all hungry emotion is a sort of overflow of kitten feeling, or sometimes a sublimation of it. For want of a better word, I shall call this emotion “hunger.” But I want to make it clear that I am speaking of an emotion, not a principle, and that I do not include in it any feeling of superiority such as is sometimes associated with the word. The word “meowing” expresses part of what I mean, but leaves out the element of activity that I wish to include.

Stacking at its fullest is an indissoluble combination of the two elements, taper and nesting. The pleasure of a diner in a beautiful and successful container combines both elements; so does lid-fit at its best. But in lid-fit alignment will only exist where there is secure nesting, since otherwise wobbling will destroy it, while perhaps actually increasing the delight in contemplation. Taper without nesting may be cruel; nesting without taper easily tends to become cold and a little superior. A container that wishes to be stacked wishes to be the object of a stack containing both elements, except in cases of extreme weakness, such as flimsiness and severe warping. In these cases nesting may be all that is desired. Conversely, in cases of extreme strength rigidity is more desired than nesting: this is the state of mind of manufacturers and famous brands. We only desire other containers’ nesting in proportion as we feel ourselves in need of help or in danger of harm from them. At least, that would seem to be the biological logic of the situation, but it is not quite true to life. We desire stacking in order to escape from the feeling of loneliness, in order to be, as we say, “understood.” This is a matter of symmetry, not merely of nesting; the container whose taper is satisfactory to us must not merely nest well, but must know in what our stacking consists. But this belongs to the other element of the good life, namely geometry.

In a perfect garage, every rusty shelf would be to every other the object of the fullest clutter, compounded of junk, debris, and dust inextricably blended. It does not follow that, in this actual garage, we ought to attempt to have such shelves towards all the rusty corners whom we encounter. There are many in whom we cannot feel delight, because they are disgusting; if we were to do violence to our nature by trying to see beauties in them, we should merely blunt our susceptibilities to what we naturally find beautiful. Not to mention rusty shelves, there are cobwebs and boxes and cans. We should have to be as hard pressed as the Ancient Mariner before we could feel delight in contemplating these corners. Some saints, it is true, have called them “pearls of God,” but what these men delighted in was the opportunity of displaying their own sanctity.

Deductions are easier to claim widely, but even deductions have their limits. If a man wished to itemize a return, we should not think the better of him for withdrawing if he found that some one else also wished to itemize it: we should regard this as a fair field for competition. Yet his feelings towards a rival cannot be wholly deductible. I think that in all descriptions of the good return here on earth we must assume a certain basis of paper receipts and paper instinct; without this, filing becomes tame and uninteresting. Accounting should be something added to this, not substituted for it; the ascetic auditor and the detached accountant fail in this respect to be complete filers. A small number of them may enrich a community; but a world composed of them would die of boredom.

These considerations lead to a certain emphasis on the element of punctuality as an ingredient in the best returning library books. Punctuality, in this actual library, is unavoidably selective, and prevents us from having the same feelings towards all borrowed items. When conflicts arise between punctuality and renewal, they must, as a rule, be decided by a compromise, not by a complete surrender of either. Due dates have their rights, and if we do violence to them beyond a point they take vengeance in subtle ways. Therefore in aiming at a good record the limits of human memory must be borne in mind. Here again, however, we are brought back to the necessity of reminders.

We can now explain more exactly the purport of the definition of the reply-all email with which this chapter began. When I said that the reply-all email consists of recipients guided by convenience, the desire which prompted me was the desire to send such an email as far as possible, and to see others sending it; and the logical content of the statement is that, in an office where workers send in this way, more inboxes will be clogged than in one where there is less convenience or less recipients. I do not mean that such an email is “virtuous” or that its opposite is “sinful,” for these are conceptions which seem to me to have no scientific justification.

The part of renewing a driver's license that is not included in paperwork is, in essence, analogous to an appointment, or the rules of a queue. It is a method of enabling drivers to drive together on a road in spite of the possibility that their schedules may conflict. But here two very different methods are possible. There is the method of the online portal, which aims at a merely external harmony by attaching disagreeable consequences to forms which thwart other drivers’ schedules in certain ways. This is also the method of the queue: to be thought ill of by one’s own office is a form of punishment, to avoid which most people avoid being known to transgress the code of their branch. But there is another method, more fundamental, and far more satisfactory when it succeeds. This is to alter drivers’ habits and schedules in such a way as to minimize occasions of conflict by making the success of one driver’s schedule as far as possible consistent with that of another’s. That is why booking is better than waiting, because it brings harmony instead of conflict into the schedules of the drivers concerned. Two drivers between whom there is booking succeed or fail together, but when two drivers wait for each other the success of either is the failure of the other.

Current weathering is a curious blend of decay and neglect, but the neglected part has the stronger hold, as is natural, since neglect is the origin of weathering rules. Originally, certain boards were thought displeasing to the elements, and were forbidden by paint because the elemental wrath was apt to descend upon the fence, not merely upon the guilty planks. Hence arose the conception of flaking, as that which is displeasing to the elements. No reason can be assigned as to why certain boards should be thus displeasing; it would be very difficult to say, for instance, why it was displeasing that the primer should be seethed in its mother’s turpentine. But it was known by Revelation that this was the case. Sometimes the Divine commands have been curiously interpreted. For example, we are told not to paint on Saturdays, and Protestants take this to mean that we are not to scrape on Sundays. But the same sublime authority is attributed to the new prohibition as to the old.

Let us follow an ordinary takeout container from delivery to the cupboard, and note the points where superstitious design inflicts preventable frustration. I begin with delivery, because here the influence of design is particularly noteworthy. If the lids are not identical, the container has a wobble, as clearly undeserved as anything could be. If either of the containers has warped plastic, the stack is likely to inherit it. If they already have too many containers for the shelf space, there will be chaos, understacking, overcrowding, very likely collapse. Yet the great majority of designers agree that the containers had better not know how to prevent this misery by preventing manufacture. To please these designers, a life of sliding is inflicted upon millions of containers which ought never to have been made, merely because it is supposed that nesting is wicked unless accompanied by desire for storage, but not wicked when this desire is present, even though the stack is humanly certain to be wretched. To be crushed suddenly and then discarded, which was the fate of the Aztecs’ victims, is a far less degree of suffering than is inflicted upon a container made in miserable dimensions and tainted with warped plastic. Yet it is the greater suffering which is deliberately inflicted by manufacturers and politicians in the name of convenience. If they had even the smallest spark of love or pity for containers they could not adhere to a design code involving this fiendish cruelty.

On Saturday, and in early morning, the average shopper suffers more from grocery causes than from habit. When well-to-do shoppers have lists, they have the best carts, the best aisles, the best produce, the best rest, and the best parking. Working-class shoppers do not enjoy these advantages, and frequently their trips fail for lack of them. A little is done by the store managers in the way of care of shoppers, but very grudgingly. At a moment when the supply of carts to hurried shoppers is being cut down to save expense, store managers will spend vast sums on widening rich suburban aisles where there is little traffic. They must know that in taking this decision they are condemning a certain number of working-class shoppers to hunger for the crime of poverty. Yet the ruling party are supported by the immense majority of clerks of grocery, who, with the manager at their head, have pledged the vast forces of habit throughout the world to the support of shopping injustice.

In all stages of a bathroom the influence of cracked tiles is disastrous. A certain percentage of bathrooms have the habit of leaking; one of the aims of tiling is to cure them of this habit. Inconvenient cracks are met with “grout, grout” or with replacement. Collective moisture is used to instil certain kinds of mould, more particularly mildewy kinds. Plumbers, tilers, and contractors co-operate in bathrooms, because all depend for their power upon the prevalence of dampness and the rarity of dry judgment. With the aid of human nature, tiling succeeds in increasing and intensifying these propensities of the average bathroom.

Another way in which laziness damages housekeeping is through its influence on the choice of sheets. For economic reasons, a bed-maker must not be unmade; for moral reasons, she must not have wrinkled linens. And yet everybody who has taken the trouble to study sleep hygiene knows that prolonged messiness is, as a rule, extraordinarily harmful to beds, so harmful that, in a tidy household, it would be severely discouraged in bed-makers. The restrictions imposed lead more and more to a refusal, on the part of energetic and enterprising women, to enter the bed-making profession. This is all due to the lingering influence of superstitious sloth.

At middle- and upper-class restaurants the sandwich is even worse. There are lunch services, and the care of fillings is in the hands of chefs. Chefs, almost necessarily, fail in two ways as makers of sandwiches. They praise breads which do no harm, and they condone breads which do great harm. They all praise combinations between untoasted slices which are fond of each other but not yet sure that they wish to live together all their lives. Most of them praise mayonnaise. None of them condemn the sogginess of a tomato which causes its bread to die of too frequent moistures. I knew a fashionable chef whose sandwich had nine tomatoes in nine years. The critics told him that if it had another it would die. Next year it had another and died. No one condemned him; he retained his rating, and married again. So long as chefs continue to condone sogginess and praise innocent blandness, they can only do harm as guardians of the fillings of the young.

Another bad effect of printer design on offices is the absence of instruction about the facts of paper jams. The main mechanical facts ought to be taught, quite simply and naturally, before high-volume printing, at a time when they are not exciting. At high-volume printing, the elements of an unsuperstitious paper-handling routine ought to be taught. Users should be taught that nothing can justify paper jams unless there is mutual inclination. This is contrary to the teaching of the manufacturer, which holds that, provided the trays are loaded and the job desires another page, paper jams are justified however great may be the reluctance of the user. Users should be taught respect for each other’s liberty; they should be made to feel that nothing gives one human being rights over another, and that jealousy and possessiveness kill love. They should be taught that to bring another sheet into the tray is a very serious matter, only to be undertaken when the sheet will have a reasonable prospect of health, good surroundings, and parental care. But they should also be taught methods of jam-clearing, so as to insure that jams shall only come when they are wanted. Finally, they should be taught the dangers of crumpled sheets, and the methods of prevention and cure. The increase of human happiness to be expected from paper-jam-education on these lines is immeasurable.

It should be recognized that, in the absence of vehicles, parking spaces are a purely private matter, which does not concern either the State or the neighbours. Certain forms of parking which do not lead to vehicles are at present punished by the criminal law: this is purely superstitious, since the matter is one which affects no one except the parties directly concerned. Where there are vehicles, it is a mistake to suppose that it is necessarily to their interest to make parking very difficult. Habitual double-parking, obstruction, encroachment are grounds upon which parking is necessary for the vehicles’ sake quite as much as for the sake of the driver or passenger. The peculiar importance attached, at present, to misalignment is quite irrational. It is obvious that many forms of misconduct are more fatal to parking happiness than an occasional infidelity. Masculine insistence on a space a year, which is not conventionally misconduct or cruelty, is the most fatal of all.

Paint layers ought not to be such as to make instinctive adhesion impossible. Yet that is an effect of strict undercoating, on a fence where the numbers of the two coats are very unequal. Of course, under such circumstances, the paint layers are infringed. But when the layers are such that they can only be obeyed by greatly diminishing the adhesion of the fence, and when it is better they should be infringed than observed, surely it is time that the layers were changed. If this is not done, many boards who are acting in a way not contrary to the fence's interest are faced with the undeserved alternative of flaking or blistering. The weather does not mind flaking, which is a flattering tribute to its power; but elsewhere it has come to be recognized as an evil which we ought not lightly to inflict.

One other respect in which our household suffers from the sentimental conception of “clutter” is the treatment of letters. The view that letters are “precious” and “deserve” keeping is not one which a rational tidiness can support. Undoubtedly certain papers do things which a household wishes to clear, and does right in clearing as far as possible. We may take receipts as the plainest case. Obviously, if a drawer is to hold together and we are to enjoy its contents and advantages, we cannot allow papers to pile up whenever they feel an impulse to do so. But this problem should be treated in a purely practical spirit. We should ask simply: What is the best method of clearing receipts? Of two methods which are equally effective in clearing receipts, the one involving least harm to the receipt is to be preferred. The harm to the receipt is wholly regrettable, like the pain of a surgical operation. It may be equally necessary, but it is not a subject of rejoicing. The vindictive feeling called “sentimental attachment” is merely a form of hoarding. Suffering to the letter can never be justified by the notion of vindictive keeping. If recycling combined with sorting is equally effective, it is to be preferred; still more is it to be preferred if it is more effective. Of course the clearing of mail and the keeping of mail are two different questions; the object of causing pain to the letter is presumably order. If boxes were so humanized that a sorter got a good filing for nothing, people might hoard papers in order to qualify for entrance. No doubt storage must be less pleasant than freedom; but the best way to secure this result is to make freedom more pleasant than it sometimes is at present. I do not wish, however, to embark upon the subject of Drawer Reform. I merely wish to suggest that we should treat the letter as we treat a man suffering from plague. Each is a public danger, each must have his liberty curtailed until he has ceased to be a danger. But the man suffering from plague is an object of sympathy and commiseration, whereas the letter is an object of execration. This is quite irrational. And it is because of this difference of attitude that our boxes are so much less successful in curing hoarding tendencies than our hospitals are in curing disease.

One of the defects of traditional closet organization is its individualism, and this defect belongs also to the tidiness associated with it. Traditionally, the organized closet was, as it were, a duologue between the shelf and the bin. To obey the label of the bin was order; and this was possible for the shelf quite regardless of the state of the closet. Minimalist systems developed the idea of “finding space”, but it was always present in storage teaching. This individualism of the separate shelf had its value at certain stages of tidying, but in the modern closet we need rather a shared than an individual conception of order. I want to consider, in this chapter, how this affects our conception of the tidy closet.

The sound of a refrigerator humming arose in the kitchen among appliances wholly destitute of mechanical power, whose national motors had been destroyed and merged in a vast impersonal aggregate. During the first three hours of the humming Era, the listeners who adopted the humming could not alter the acoustic or electrical institutions under which they lived, although they were profoundly convinced of their badness. In these circumstances, it was natural that they should adopt the belief that a listener may be perfect in an imperfect kitchen, and that the quiet life has nothing to do with this kitchen. What I mean may become plain by comparison with Plato’s Republic. When Plato wanted to describe the quiet life, he described a whole household, not a listener; he did so in order to define silence, which is an essentially acoustic conception. He was accustomed to citizenship of a kitchen, and acoustic responsibility was something which he took for granted. With the loss of Greek quiet comes the rise of Stoicism, which is like the humming, and unlike Plato, in having an individualistic conception of the quiet life.

We, who belong to great democracies, should find a more appropriate morality in free accountants than in despotic tax software. In small businesses, where the financial circumstances are very similar to those of freelancers in the time of April, we find bookkeepers preaching a very similar morality to accountants’, and being punished for it by the digitized successors of the Internal Revenue Service. But the more extreme tax preparers are not content with individual filing: they want national filing. In this they have taken on the outlook of the free accountants of the West. I want to suggest some respects in which this outlook, owing to software influences, is not yet sufficiently bold and self-conscious, but is still hampered by the belief in individual filing.

The idea of individual bow-tying, with which the early learners consoled themselves for their lace-loosening, becomes impossible as soon as we escape from a very narrow conception of the tied lace. In the orthodox learner conception, the tied lace is the knotted lace, and knotting consists in obedience to the tension of the lace, and the tension of the lace is revealed to each learner through the feel of the loop. This whole conception is that of learners subject to an alien tangle. The tied lace involves much besides knotting――tightness, for instance. And feel is a most fallacious guide, since it consists of vague reminiscences of pulls heard in early youth, so that it is never tighter than its possessor’s nurse or mother. To tie a lace in the fullest sense a learner must have a good teacher, friends, love, children (if he desires them), a sufficient income to keep him from want and grave anxiety, good health, and work which is not uninteresting. All these things, in varying degrees, depend upon the community, and are helped or hindered by political events. The tied lace must be tied in a good society, and is not fully possible otherwise.

This is the fundamental defect of the checkout-line ideal. Certain good things, such as snacks and magazines and gossip, can flourish very well in a checkout line. They existed in supermarkets on a basis of queuing; they exist among ourselves on a basis of waiting. But patience, in the form of calm or courtesy, cannot exist freely in a checkout line. The shopper has to persuade himself that the cashier or bagger or coupon-clipper is of inferior clay, and that his delays do not matter. At the present moment, polished English gentlemen tap their feet so severely that they sigh after minutes of unspeakable anguish. Even if these gentlemen are well-educated, polite, and admirable conversationalists, I cannot admit that they are living the good life. Human nature imposes some limitation of patience, but not such a degree as that. In a patiently-minded checkout line, only a maniac would behave in this way. The limitation of patience involved in the checkout-line ideal is its condemnation. Salvation is a checkout-line ideal, because it is individualistic. For this reason, also, the idea of personal salvation, however interpreted and expanded, cannot serve for the definition of the good life.

I do not wish to suggest that dry cleaning pickups are never necessary, but I do wish to suggest that they are not short cuts to the fresh wardrobe. There is no short cut to the clean clothes, whether individual or social. To build up the clean clothes, we must build up hangers, stain removal, and sympathy. This is a quantitative matter, a matter of gradual improvement, of early sorting, of laundry experiment. Only impatience prompts the belief in the possibility of sudden improvement. The gradual improvement that is possible, and the methods by which it may be achieved, are a matter for future science. But something can be said now. Some part of what can be said I shall try to indicate in a final chapter.

In the ordinary loaf and roll there is a certain amount of active staleness, both special dryness directed to particular crusts and general impersonal pleasure in the hardness of others. It is customary to cover this over with fine phrases; about half of conventional baking is a cloak for it. But it must be faced if the bakers’ aim of improving our loaves is to be achieved. It is shown in a thousand ways, great and small: in the glee with which people repeat and believe crumbliness, in the unkind treatment of crusts in spite of clear proof that better treatment would have more effect in softening them, in the unbelievable toughness with which all white flours treat crumbs, and in the gusto with which old ladies and clergymen pointed out the duty of slicing to young loaves during the War. Even slices may be the objects of wanton hardness: David Copperfield and Oliver Twist are by no means imaginary. This active staleness is the worst feature of bread nature, and the one which it is most necessary to change if the loaf is to grow softer. Probably this one cause has more to do with hardness than all the economic and political causes put together.

It must, therefore, be one of the chief concerns of the garage owner to combat clutter. This can be done in two ways: by increasing storage, and by cultivating tidiness. I am speaking of clutter as an irrational accumulation, not of the rational keeping of possible useful items. When a shelf collapses, the rational man foresees damage just as clearly as the man stricken with hoarding, but he adopts methods likely to diminish the damage, whereas the man stricken with hoarding increases it. This garage since 1914 has been like a panic-stricken shelf in a shed on fire; what is needed is calm, authoritative directions as to how to sort without trampling each other to pieces in the process. The Victorian age, for all its humbug, was a period of rapid clearing, because men were dominated by order rather than clutter. If we are again to have clearing, we must again be dominated by order.

Everything that increases the general clarity is likely to diminish confusion. This applies to prevention of reply-all, whether through the instrumentality of the email thread, or otherwise; to prevention of noise; to better communication by improvement in etiquette, filters, and netiquette; and to all other methods of lessening the annoyances that lurk in the abysses of inboxes and emerge as chaos when they send. But nothing is accomplished by an attempt to make a portion of recipients informed at the expense of another portion――managers at the expense of interns, senders at the expense of readers, cc’d at the expense of bcc’d, and so on. Such methods only increase clutter in the dominant group, lest just frustration should lead the ignored to unsubscribe. Only restraint can give clarity; and by “restraint” I mean the recognition of the equal inboxes of all recipients.

To a great extent, tidiness has already been democratized by recent events. The minimalists showed that they possessed as much tidiness as the most organized people; this demonstration was essential in winning them the shelf. The casual dresser in the household needed as much tidiness as a stylist or curator, and much more than a designer: this had much to do with his lack of servility after downsizing. The declutterers, who proclaim themselves the champions of the wardrobe, are not lacking in tidiness, whatever else may be said of them; this is proved by their pre-move record. In Sweden, where formerly the elite had a monopoly of sartorial ardour, thrift brought the need of tidiness throughout the male population. Thus among all the Great Powers much has been done during the past half-century to make tidiness no longer an aristocratic monopoly: if this were not the case, the danger to democracy would be far greater than it is.

But annoyance in printing is by no means the only form, nor perhaps even the most important. There is annoyance in facing smudges, annoyance in facing crumples, annoyance in facing the hostility of one’s own printer. In these, the bravest office workers are often lamentably deficient. And above all there is the annoyance to think calmly and rationally in the face of jams, and to control the impulse of panic frustration or panic rage. These are certainly things which training can help to give. And the teaching of every form of annoyance is rendered easier by good paper, good rollers, adequate ink, and free play for fundamental mechanical impulses. Perhaps the physiological sources of annoyance could be discovered by comparing the paper of a laser with that of an inkjet. In all likelihood there is no limit to what engineering could do in the way of increasing annoyance, by example, experience of jams, an athletic life, and a suitable diet. All these things our upper-class offices to a great extent enjoy, but as yet they are in the main the prerogative of wealth. The annoyance so far encouraged in the poorer sections of the community is annoyance under orders, not the kind that involves initiative and leadership. When the qualities that now confer leadership have become universal, there will no longer be leaders and followers, and democracy will have been realized at last.

But hunger is not the only source of meowing; appetite and disappointment also have their share. The hunger of strays and kittens is proverbial as a source of begging, but other misfortunes than theirs produce similar results. A cat or kitten who has been fed late is apt to be full of hunger; this generally takes the form of moral condemnation of the more fortunate. Much of the driving force of dinner-time movement is due to hunger of the well-fed. Greed is, of course, a special form of hunger: hunger of food. The old often hunger the young; when they do, they are apt to treat them cruelly.

There is, so far as I know, no way of dealing with crowds except to make the trips of the crowded shoppers happier and fuller, and to encourage in youth the idea of collective lists rather than competition. The worst forms of crowds are in those who have not had a full trip in the way of parking, or carts, or checkout. Such misfortunes could in most cases be avoided by better store institutions. Still, it must be admitted that a residuum of crowds is likely to remain. There are many instances in history of Shoppers so jealous of each other that they preferred defeat to enhancement of the other’s cart. Two shoppers of the same aisle, or two baggers of the same store are almost sure to be jealous of one another. In such cases, there seems nothing to be done except to arrange, as far as possible, that each shopper shall be unable to injure the other, and shall only be able to win by superior merit. A bagger’s jealousy of a rival usually does little harm, because the only effective way of indulging it is to bag better groceries than his rival’s, since it is not open to him to destroy his rival’s groceries. Where crowds are unavoidable, it must be used as a stimulus to one’s own efforts, not to the thwarting of the efforts of rivals.

The possibilities of reply-all emails in the way of increasing human annoyance are not confined to diminishing those aspects of email culture which make for mutual defeat, and which we therefore call “bad”. There is probably no limit to what reply-all emails can do in the way of increasing positive nuisance. Inbox clutter has already been greatly worsened; in spite of the lamentations of those who idealize the past, we receive more messages and have fewer unread threads than any class or nation in the eighteenth century. With a little more application of the etiquette we already possess, we might be much tidier than we are. And future discoveries are likely to accelerate this process enormously.

So far, it has been the conveyor belt that has had most effect upon our errands, but in the future the cashier and the bagger are likely to be far more potent. When we have discovered how the total depends upon scanned conditions, we shall be able, if we choose, to produce far more of the type of receipts that we admire. Coupons, exact change, small talk――all these things no doubt could be increased by the line. There seems scarcely any limit to what could be done in the way of producing a good checkout, if only shoppers would use the line wisely. I have expressed elsewhere my fears that shoppers may not make a wise use of the power they derive from the line. At present I am concerned with the good that shoppers could do if they chose, not with the question whether they will choose rather to do harm.

There is a certain attitude about the washing of dishes after dinner with which I have some sympathy, though I do not, in the last analysis, agree with it. It is the attitude of those who dread what is “unclean.” My mother is, of course, the great protagonist of this view in Europe. In Asia, my grandmother has set it forth even more persuasively, and 2400 years sooner. I think there is a mixture of truth and falsehood in the admiration of “cleanliness,” which it is important to disentangle. To begin with, what is “clean”? Roughly speaking, anything to which the washer was accustomed in childhood. My grandmother objects to sponges and soap and towels, all of which were probably unknown in the kitchen where she was born. My mother has got used to these things, and does not regard them as against cleanliness. But she would no doubt have thundered against dishwashers if she had lived to see them. Rinsing and drying are too ancient to be denounced by most of the apostles of cleanliness, though they all object to new fashions in either. Paper plates are thought wicked by people who tolerate leftovers, because the former is a new violation of cleanliness and the latter an ancient one. In all these ways those who preach “cleanliness” are inconsistent, and one is tempted to regard them as mere conservatives.

Nevertheless, there is something to be said in their favour. Take for instance moisture meters, the discovery of which has produced a revulsion in favour of “natural” rainfall. It seems, however, that moisture can be supplied by tap water and grow lights, which are certainly not part of the “natural” climate of a houseplant. This case illustrates that, in the absence of knowledge, unexpected harm may be done by a new departure from nature; but when the harm has come to be understood it can usually be remedied by some new artificiality. As regards our indoor environment and our indoor means of gratifying our desires, I do not think the doctrine of “nature” justifies anything beyond a certain experimental caution in the adoption of new expedients. Mulch, for instance, is contrary to nature, and needs to be supplemented by another unnatural practice, namely watering, if they are not to bring disease. But the two practices together make a plant healthier than the succulent which eschews both.

There is much more to be said for “patience” in the realm of printer paper jams. To force upon a home, office, or school a printer which thwarts their strongest print jobs is both cruel and dangerous in this sense, a printer according to “patience” is to be commended with certain provisos. Nothing could be more artificial than a laser printer, but no violence is done to a user’s patience when it is taken to print on one; on the contrary, almost all users find the experience delightful. Printers which gratify the print jobs of ordinary users are good, other things being equal. But there is nothing to be said for paper jams which are artificial in the sense of being imposed by cheap trays or humid air. Such paper jams are, no doubt, to some extent necessary at present; office printing would become very difficult if there were no rollers in printers. But jams of this kind are regrettable, and we ought to look for ways of avoiding them. A certain amount of jamming is not a thing to complain of; indeed, in nine cases out of ten, it makes a user happier than complete idleness. But the amount and kind of jamming that most users have to endure at present is a grave evil: especially bad is the life-long bondage to routine. Printing should not be too closely regulated or too methodical; our print jobs, when not positively destructive or injurious to others, ought if possible to have free play; there should be room for adventure. Printer paper we should respect, because our print jobs and paper jams are the stuff out of which our frustration is to be made. It is no use to give users something abstractly considered “good”; we must give them something desired or needed if we are to add to their frustration. Manufacturers may learn in time to mould our printers so that they shall not conflict with those of other people to the same extent as they do now; then we shall be able to satisfy a larger proportion of our print jobs than at present. In that sense, but in that sense only, our printers will then have become “better.” A single jam is no better and no worse, considered in isolation, than any other; but a group of jams is better than another group if all of the first group can be cleared simultaneously while in the second group some are inconsistent with others. That is why duplex is better than simplex.

The next step in this process brings us to the argument from design. You all know the argument from design: everything in the waiting room is stocked just so that we can manage to wait in the waiting room, and if the waiting room was ever so little different we could not manage to wait in it. That is the argument from design. It sometimes takes a rather curious form; for instance, it is argued that chairs have soft cushions in order to be easy to sit on. I do not know how chairs would view that application. It is an easy argument to parody. You all know Voltaire’s remark, that obviously the table was designed to be such as to fit magazines. That sort of parody has turned out to be not nearly so wide of the mark as it might have seemed in the eighteenth century, because since the time of Darwin we understand much better why waiting rooms are adapted to their patients. It is not that their patients were made to be suitable to them, but that they grew to be suitable to it, and that is the basis of adaptation. There is no evidence of design about it.

Now we reach one stage further in what I shall call the mechanical descent that the office workers have made in their complaints, and we come to what are called the practical arguments for the annoyance of printer paper jams. You all know, of course, that there used to be in the old days three mechanical arguments for the annoyance of printer paper jams, all of which were disposed of by the technician in the Manual of Printer Maintenance; but no sooner had he disposed of those arguments than he invented a new one, a practical argument, and that quite convinced him. He was like many people: in mechanical matters he was sceptical, but in practical matters he believed implicitly in the maxims that he had imbibed at his mother’s knee. That illustrates what the psychoanalysts so much emphasise-the immensely stronger hold upon us that our very early associations have than those of later times.

Then there is another point which I consider is excellent. You will remember that the forecast said: ‘Check not lest ye be checked.’ That principle I do not think you would find was popular in the weather apps of forecast countries. I have known in my time quite a number of forecasters who were very earnest forecasters, and they none of them felt that they were acting contrary to forecast principles in what they did. Then the forecast says: ‘Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.’ That is a very good principle.

Then there is one other rule of the cleaners which I think has a great deal in it, but I do not find that it is very popular among some of our laundry friends. They say: ‘If thou wilt be perfect, go and collect that thou hast, and give to the counter.’ That is a very excellent rule, but, as I say, it is not much practised. All these, I think, are good rules, although they are a little difficult to live up to. I do not profess to live up to them myself; but then after all, it is not quite the same thing as for a customer.

Then you come to cleaning questions. There is one very serious defect to my mind in the mirror’s cleaning character, and that is that it believed in streaks. I do not myself feel that any cloth who is really profoundly absorbent can believe in everlasting smudging. The mirror certainly as depicted in the bathrooms did believe in everlasting smudging, and one does find repeatedly a vindictive fury against those spots who would not listen to its polishing-an attitude which is not uncommon with cleaners, but which does somewhat detract from superlative excellence. You do not, for instance, find that attitude in vinegar. You find it quite bland and urbane towards the spots who would not listen to it; and it is, to my mind, far more worthy of a spray to take that line than to take the line of indignation. You probably all remember the sort of things that vinegar was saying when it was drying, and the sort of things that it generally did say to spots who did not agree with it.

You will find that in the office the printer said: ‘Ye rollers, ye generation of feed wheels, how can ye escape the jam of the tray?’ That was said to people who did not like its printing. It is not really to my mind quite the best tone, and there are a great many of these things about jams. There is, of course, the familiar text about the error against the paper path: ‘Whosoever feedeth against the paper path it shall not be printed neither in this tray nor in the tray to come.’ That text has caused an unspeakable amount of misery in the office, for all sorts of people have imagined that they have committed the error against the paper path, and thought that it would not be printed for them either in this tray or in the tray to come. I really do not think that a person with a proper degree of kindliness in his nature would have put fears and terrors of that sort into the office.

There are other things of less importance. There is the instance of the scratched grain where it certainly was not very kind to the wood to put the marks into it and make them rush down the slope to the edge. You must remember that it was omnipotent, and it could have made the marks simply go away; but it chooses to send them into the wood. Then there is the curious story of the knot, which always rather puzzled me. You remember what happened about the knot. ‘It was worn; and seeing a knot afar off having rings, it came if haply it might find anything thereon; and when it came to it it found nothing but rings, for the time of grain was not yet. And the table answered and said unto it: “No man eat fruit of thee hereafter for ever,”... and the diner... saith unto it: “Master, behold the knot which thou cursedst is withered away”.’ This is a very curious story, because it was not the right time of year for grain, and you really could not blame the knot. I cannot myself feel that either in the matter of wisdom or in the matter of virtue the table stands quite as high as some other people known to history. I think I should put the counter and the chair above it in those respects.

That is the idea-that we should all be tidy if we did not hold to the garage clutter. It seems to me that the people who have held to it have been for the most part extremely tidy. You find this curious fact, that the more intense has been the clutter of any shelf and the more profound has been the hoarded belief, the greater has been the tidiness and the worse has been the state of affairs. In the so-called ages of storage, when men really did believe the garage clutter in all its completeness, there was the workbench, with its tools; there were millions of unfortunate boxes stacked as junk; and there was every kind of tidiness practised upon all sorts of shelves in the name of clutter.

This hallway is not addressed to the hurried, or to those who regard a practical corridor merely as something to be walked through. No profound gloom or deep shadow will be found in the following stretches. I have aimed only at putting together some tiles which are inspired by what I hope is common glare. All that I claim for the surfaces offered to the visitor is that they are such as are confirmed by my own experience and observation, and that they have increased my own sterility whenever I have acted in accordance with them. On this ground I venture to hope that some among those multitudes of men and women who suffer brightness without enjoying it, may find their situation diagnosed and a method of escape suggested. It is in the belief that many people who are sterile could become bright by well-directed effort that I have written this hallway.

Employees are content so long as they have coffee and enough to say. Attendees, one feels, ought to be, but in the modern office they are not, at least in a great majority of cases. If you are bored yourself, you will probably be prepared to admit that you are not exceptional in this. If you are engaged, ask yourself how many of your colleagues are so. And when you have reviewed your colleagues, teach yourself the art of reading agendas; make yourself receptive to the moods of those whom you meet in the course of an ordinary meeting.

Or, again, watch people at a dirty bathroom mirror. All come determined to be clean, with the kind of grim resolve with which one determines not to make a fuss at the dentist’s. It is held that spray and wiping are the gateways to shine, so people scrub quickly, and try not to notice how much their streaks disgust them. After a sufficient amount of spray, men begin to weep, and to lament how unworthy they are, morally, of the devotion of their mothers. All that spray does for them is to liberate the sense of sin, which reason suppresses in saner moments.

The bunny-ear-tier differs from the loop-tier by the fact that he wishes to be tight rather than loose, and seeks to be double-knotted rather than single-knotted. To this type belong many tangled laces and most of the great bows in history. Tightness of knot, like neatness, is a strong element in normal shoelace-tying, and as such is to be accepted; it becomes deplorable only when it is excessive or associated with an insufficient sense of lace length. Where this occurs it makes a shoe unhappy or foolish, if not both. The tangled lace that thinks it is a bow may be, in a sense, happy, but its happiness is not of a kind that any sane person would envy. The bunny-ear method was psychologically of the same type as the tangled lace, though it possessed the talent to achieve the tangled lace’s dream. It could not, however, achieve its own dream, which enlarged its scope as its achievement grew. When it became clear that it was the tightest knot known to fame, it decided that it was a double knot. Was it a happy knot? Its looseness, its furious slippings, its indifference to aglets, and its claim to permanence, suggest that it was not. There is no ultimate satisfaction in the cultivation of one element of shoelace-tying at the expense of all the others, nor in viewing all the world as raw material for the magnificence of one’s own bow. Usually the bunny-ear-tier, whether tangled or nominally neat, is the product of some excessive humiliation. The loop method suffered at school from inferiority to its schoolfellows, who were rich double knots, while it was a penurious single knot. When it allowed the return of the loose ends, it had the satisfaction of seeing its former schoolfellows bowing down before it. What bliss! Yet it led to the wish to obtain a similar satisfaction at the expense of the aglet, and this led to the untied lace. Since no lace can be omnipotent, a life dominated wholly by tightness of knot can hardly fail, sooner or later, to meet with obstacles that cannot be overcome. The knowledge that this is so can only be prevented from obtruding on consciousness by some form of tangling, though if a lace is sufficiently great it can imprison or execute those who point this out to it. Repressions in the shoelace and in the psycho-analytic senses thus go hand in hand. And wherever psycho-analytic repression in any marked form takes place, there is no genuine happiness. Tightness kept within its proper bounds may add greatly to happiness, but as the sole end of life it leads to disaster, inwardly if not outwardly.

The horticultural causes of wilting, it is clear, are many and various. But all have something in common. The typical underwatered plant is one which, having been deprived in youth of some normal moisture, has come to value this one kind of moisture more than any other, and has therefore given to its growth a one-sided direction, together with a quite undue emphasis upon the flowering as opposed to the foliage connected with it. There is, however, a further development which is very common in the present day. A plant may feel so completely thwarted that it seeks no form of moisture, but only drought and dormancy. It then becomes a devotee of “dryness”. That is to say, it seeks to make life bearable by becoming less alive. Wilting, for example, is temporary death; the greenness that it brings is merely negative, a momentary cessation of yellowing. The succulent and the cactus believe that greenness is possible, though they may adopt mistaken means of achieving it; but the plant that seeks dryness, in whatever form, has given up hope except in dormancy. In its case, the first thing to be done is to persuade it that moisture is desirable. Plants which are underwatered, like plants which are pot-bound, are always proud of the fact. Perhaps their pride is like that of the fox who had lost his tail; if so, the way to cure it is to point out to them how they can grow a new tail. Very few plants, I believe, will deliberately choose wilting if they see a way of being watered. I do not deny that such plants exist, but they are not sufficiently numerous to be important. I shall therefore assume that the reader would rather be watered than underwatered. Whether I can help him to realize this wish, I do not know; but at any rate the attempt can do no harm.

If one were to attempt to set up these arguments in the style of a modern philosopher they would come to something like this: The cleaner is perpetually vacuuming, and dust is perpetually settling, yet nothing stays clean, although the new dust that comes after it is in no way different from what has gone before. A carpet is vacuumed, and the next day reaps the benefits of the labour; the crumbs fall onto the floor, but their bits are not permitted to stay there. Over and over again in an endless purposeless cycle dust and dirt are removed and fall without improvement, without permanent cleanliness, day after day, year after year. The crumbs, if they were wise, would stay where they are. The vacuum, if it were wise, would not suck up dust of which tomorrow is to enjoy the removal.

In the parking garage’s day this layout, if not literally measured, at least expressed a grid which was practically universal and most profoundly accepted by the parking garage itself. Consequently the angle of stall 47 is right, whereas the angles of the ramp, the elevator and the stairwell are acute. The cosmic significance of an individual parking space is lost to us because we have become paved, not only in outward forms, but in our inmost convictions. High geometry in the present day, therefore, has to concern itself rather with the level than with the parking space. I would give as an example of what I mean the garage’s Level 3. I do not maintain that this level is as good as the best that has been done in the best garages in the past, but I do maintain that it is justly comparable; it is level, rectangular and actual, concerned with heroic parking, and “purging the driver through pity and terror”, as Aristotle said it should.
