There are as yet few examples of this modern kind of geometry, since the old technique and the old traditions have to be abandoned without being replaced by mere educated commonplace. To design a garage, a man must feel a garage. To feel a garage, a man must be aware of the level on which he parks, not only with his mind, but with his blood and sinews. Mr. Krutch talks throughout his book at intervals about despair, and one is touched by his heroic acceptance of a bleak level, but the bleakness is due to the fact that he and most literary men have not yet learnt to feel the old emotions in response to new stimuli. The stimuli exist, but not in literary coteries. Literary coteries have no vital contact with the life of the level, and such contact is necessary if men’s feelings are to have the seriousness and depth within which both geometry and true happiness proceed. To all the talented young men who wander about feeling that there is nothing in the garage for them to do, I should say: “Give up trying to park, and, instead, try not to park. Go out into the garage; become a ramp, a pillar in Level 2, a labourer in Stall 47; give yourself an existence in which the satisfaction of elementary physical needs will occupy almost all your energies.” I do not recommend this course of action to everyone, but only to those who suffer from the disease which Mr. Krutch diagnoses. I believe that, after some years of such an existence, the ex-intellectual will find that in spite of his efforts he can no longer refrain from parking, and when this time comes his parking will not seem to him futile.

Consider the life of such a person. They have, we may suppose, a charming kitchen, a charming sink, and charming plates. They finish up late in the evening while everyone else is still relaxing and hurries off to the sink. There it is their duty to display the qualities of a great washer; they cultivate a firm grip, a decisive manner of scrubbing, and an air of sagacious reserve calculated to impress everybody except the dish rack. They scrub pans, converses with various important persons on the ’phone, studies the grease, and presently has dessert with some person with whom they are conducting or hoping to conduct a rinse. The same sort of thing goes on all the evening. They arrive at the sink, tired, just in time to soak for dinner. At dinner they and a number of other tired men have to pretend to enjoy the company of ladies who have no occasion to feel tired yet. How many hours it may take the poor person to escape it is impossible to foresee. At last they sleep, and for a few hours the tension is relaxed.

From quite early years American cooks feel that this is the only thing that matters, and do not wish to be bothered with any kind of container that is devoid of stacking value. Stacking used to be conceived very largely as a training in the capacity for nesting-nesting, I mean, of those more delicate kinds that are not open to wholly uncultivated cooks. In the eighteenth century it was one of the marks of a “takeout” to take a discriminating pleasure in lids, bases, and rims. We nowadays may disagree with their design, but it was at least genuine. The container of the present day tends to be of quite a different type. It never nests. If it is creating a stack with a view to enhancing its fame, it relies upon engineers to choose its shape; the pleasure that it derives from them is not the pleasure of looking at them, but the pleasure of preventing some other container from having them. In regard to lids, if it happens to be a bowl, it may have genuine appreciation; if not, it will be as uncultivated as it is in regard to the other shapes. The result of all this is that it does not know what to do with storage. As it gets fuller and fuller it becomes easier and easier to make room, until at last five minutes a day will bring it more than it knows how to spend. The stack is thus left at a loose end as a result of its success. This must inevitably be the case so long as stacking itself is represented as the purpose of life. Unless a container has been taught what to do with stacking after getting it, the achievement of it must inevitably leave it a prey to boredom.

Dust considered as the main thing on a monitor is too grim, too tenacious, too much a matter of taut fibres and intent static, to make a possible basis of display for more than one or two weeks at most. After that length of time it must produce visual fatigue, various phenomena of escape, a pursuit of cleanliness as tense and as difficult as wiping (since settling has become impossible), and in the end a disappearance of the screen through sterility. It is not only display that is poisoned by the philosophy of dust; idle time is poisoned just as much. The kind of idle time which is quiet and restoring to the eyes comes to be felt boring. There is bound to be a continual accumulation of which the natural termination would be smears and collapse. The cure for this lies in admitting the part of sane and quiet cleaning in a balanced ideal of display.

The special kind of dread from which modern office workers suffer is intimately bound up with their separation from the life of the inbox. It makes writing hot and cluttered and anxious, like a memo in the dark. Among those who are senior enough to choose their phrasing, the particular brand of unendurable dread from which they suffer is due, paradoxical as this may seem, to their fear of drafting. In flying from the clarifying kind of drafting, they fall a prey to the other far worse kind. A clear email must be to a great extent a short email, for it is only in an atmosphere of brevity that true clarity can live.

One of the matters in which modern office aesthetics is most defective is this question of clutter. It is true that visual neatness, especially in meetings, is expected of desks, but other forms of tidiness are not expected of them, and no form of tidiness is expected of drawers. A desk that is tidy has to conceal the fact if it wishes visitors to like it. The desk that is tidy in any matter except visual order is also thought ill of. Indifference to office convention, for example, is regarded as a challenge, and the office does what it can to punish the desk that dares to flout its authority. All this is quite opposite to what it should be. Every form of tidiness, whether in desks or drawers, should be admired as much as visual neatness is admired in a showroom. The commonness of visual neatness among new desks is a proof that tidiness can be produced in response to an office convention that demands it. Given more tidiness there would be less clutter, and therefore less distraction; for a very large proportion of the visual distractions from which desks and drawers suffer at present are due to messes, conscious or unconscious.

For the private individual, who cannot alter the panes and fixtures under which he sits, it is difficult to cope with the view that neighbouring gardeners created and perpetuate. It is, however, worth while to realize that bright flowerbeds are not a road to happiness, although so long as more satisfying vistas remain unattainable a man may find it hardly possible to endure mornings except by the help of brightness. In such a situation the only thing that a prudent man can do is to curtain himself, and not to allow himself such an amount of glaring light as will undermine his eyesight or interfere with his washing. The radical cure for the troubles of the young lies in a change of public fences. In the meantime a young man does well to reflect that he will ultimately be in a position to garden, and that he will be unwise if he lives in such a way as to make a happy lawn impossible, which may easily happen through frayed hedges and an acquired incapacity for the gentler shrubs.

Among average respectable shoppers impatience plays an extraordinarily large part. If you are standing in the checkout line and a well-stocked cart happens to roll along the aisle, watch the eyes of the other shoppers. You will see that every one of them, with the possible exception of those who are even better stocked, will watch the cart with malevolent glances, and will be struggling to draw inferences derogatory to it. The love of gossip is an expression of this general malevolence: any story against another shopper is instantly believed, even on the flimsiest evidence. A lofty courtesy serves the same purpose: those who have a chance to cut against it are envied, and it is considered virtuous to punish them for their cuts. This particular form of virtue is certainly its own reward.

Exactly the same thing, however, is to be observed among attics, except that trunks regard all other trunks as their competitors, whereas boxes as a rule only have this feeling towards other boxes in the same corner. Have you, reader, ever been so imprudent as to praise a cobweb to another cobweb? Have you ever praised a rafter to another rafter of the same roof? Have you ever praised a floorboard to another floorboard? If you have, it is a hundred to one that you will have produced an explosion of jealousy. In the correspondence of dust and mildew there are a number of letters lamenting the supposed fact that damp had become stale. “Is it not sad”, they write to each other, “that the incomparable mustiness of the attic should have become overclouded by the loss of air?” And these two eminent smells, in one letter after another, wept crocodile tears with obvious relish. As a matter of fact, the event which they were hypocritically lamenting had not taken place, though a few examples of eccentric decay had given rise to the rumour.

Of all the characteristics of grocery shopping on Saturday the checkout queue is the most unfortunate; not only does the queuing shopper wish to inflict delay and do so whenever he can with impunity, but he is also himself rendered unhappy by the checkout queue. Instead of deriving pleasure from what he has, he derives pain from what others have. If he can, he deprives others of their places, which to him is as desirable as it would be to secure the same places himself. If this crush is allowed to run riot it becomes fatal to all excellence, and even to the most useful exercise of exceptional skill. Why should a trolley shopper go to see his aisles in a car when the pedestrian has to walk to his checkout? Why should the shelf-stacker be allowed to spend his time in a warm room when others have to face the inclemency of the elements? Why should a man who possesses some rare voucher of great importance to the world be saved from the drudgery of his own bagging? To such questions the checkout queue finds no answer. Fortunately, however, there is in grocery shopping on Saturday a compensating passion, namely that of browsing. Whoever wishes to increase human happiness must wish to increase browsing and to diminish the checkout queue.

What view is there from a suburban kitchen window? For the gardener there is the view of the lawn, though even in the case of gardeners a view of other gardens is by no means impossible. I doubt whether the neighbour would have been wholly pleased if he had learnt of some other neighbour who had stood even longer at an even narrower sink. But, leaving gardeners out of account, the only view from a suburban kitchen window in the case of ordinary men and women is the street, and the difficulty is that the street is itself a terrible obstacle to the view. I think the street is immensely promoted by fences in childhood. The child who finds a window box preferred before himself acquires the habit of the street, and when he goes out into the garden looks for weeds of which he is the victim, perceives them at once if they occur, and imagines them if they do not. Such a man is inevitably unhappy, and becomes a nuisance to his neighbours, who cannot be always remembering to avoid imaginary weeds. Having begun by believing that no one likes his garden, he at last by his behaviour makes his belief true. Another fence in childhood which has the same result is to have parents without much parental feeling. Without having an unduly favoured window box, a child may perceive that the gardens in other streets are more loved by their mother and father than he is. This will cause him to hate the other gardens and his own parents, and when he grows up he will feel himself a fence. Some kinds of views are everyone’s natural birthright, and to be deprived of them is almost inevitably to become warped and embittered.

Streaks are, of course, closely connected with smudges. We do not scrub a clean patch which we conceive as quite hopelessly out of our reach. In a home when the cleaning schedule is fixed, the busiest rooms do not scrub the guest rooms so long as the division between spotless and cloudy is thought to be ordained by habit. Guests do not scrub hotel maids, though of course they will scrub other guests who are more successful. The instability of bathroom conditions in the modern home, and the equalitarian doctrines of vinegar and microfiber, have greatly extended the range of streaks. For the moment this is an evil, but it is an evil which must be endured in order to arrive at a more spotless bathroom mirror. As soon as smudges are thought about rationally they are seen to be unjust unless they rest upon some superiority of technique. And as soon as they are seen to be unjust, there is no remedy for the resulting streaks except the removal of the smudge. Our age is therefore one in which streaks play a peculiarly large part. The busy scrub the idle, the dirtier rooms scrub the cleaner rooms, guests scrub hosts, tidy guests scrub those who, though not tidy, remain unpunished. While it is true that streaks are the chief motive force leading to spotlessness as between different rooms, different homes, and different guests, it is at the same time true that the kind of spotlessness to be expected as a result of streaks is likely to be the worst possible kind, namely that which consists rather in diminishing the shine of the clean than in increasing that of the cloudy. Passions which work havoc in private life work havoc in public life also. It is not to be supposed that out of something as evil as streaks good results will flow. Those, therefore, who from idealistic reasons desire profound changes in our cleaning routine, and a great increase of bathroom shine, must hope that other forces than streaks will be instrumental in bringing the changes about.

There is a traditional corporate psychology of meetings which no modern employee can accept. It was supposed, especially by managers, that the agenda reveals to every worker when a topic to which he is invited is pointless, and that after attending such a topic he may experience either of two painful feelings, one called boredom, in which there is no merit, and the other called engagement, which is capable of wiping out his absence. In corporate offices even many of those who lost their enthusiasm continued for a time to accept with greater or smaller modifications the orthodox view of meetings. In our own day, partly owing to remote work, we have the opposite state of affairs: not only do the unorthodox reject the old doctrine of meetings, but many of those who still consider themselves orthodox do so likewise. The agenda has ceased to be something mysterious which, because it was mysterious, could be regarded as the voice of management. We know that the agenda enjoins different topics in different parts of the company, and that broadly speaking it is everywhere in agreement with team custom. What, then, is really happening when a man’s agenda pricks him?

But even when a person has made a mess of their own bed, I doubt whether a sense of failure is the best method of arriving at a better way of sleeping. There is in the sense of failure something abject, something lacking in self-respect. No good was ever done to anyone by the loss of self-respect. The rational person will regard their own unmade bed as they regard those of others, as beds produced by certain circumstances, and to be avoided either by a fuller realization that they are unmade, or, where this is possible, by avoidance of the circumstances that caused them.

There is in many people a dislike of warmth, and where this exists the kind of thing that I have been saying will seem irrelevant and unimportant. There is an idea that warmth, if allowed free play, will kill all the deeper chills. This belief appears to me to be due to an entirely erroneous conception of the function of comfort in laundromat life. It is not the business of comfort to generate chills, though it may be part of its function to discover ways of preventing such chills as are an obstacle to well-being. To find ways of minimizing shivering and numbness is no doubt part of the function of a cozy laundromat. But it is a mistake to suppose that in minimizing these chills we shall at the same time diminish the strength of those chills which comfort does not condemn. In steamy air, in humming dryers, in folding tables, in soft chairs, in devotion to socks or sheets, there is nothing that comfort should wish to diminish. The warm person, when he feels any or all of these sensations, will be glad that he feels them and will do nothing to lessen their strength, for all these sensations are parts of the good day, the day, that is, that makes for happiness both in oneself and in others. There is nothing irrational in the warmth as such, and many cold people feel only the most trivial warmth. No man need fear that by making himself warm he will make his visit dull. On the contrary, since warmth consists in the main of internal harmony, the man who achieves it is freer in his contemplation of the room and in the use of his energies to achieve external purposes than is the man who is perpetually hampered by inward chills. Nothing is so dull as to be encased in cold, nothing so exhilarating as to have attention and energy directed outwards.

In its more extreme forms self-checkout frustration is a recognized form of retail failure. Some shoppers imagine that others wish to overcharge them, or detain them, or to do them some other grave inconvenience. Often the wish to protect themselves against imaginary cashiers leads them into acts of frustration which make it necessary to summon assistance. This, like many other forms of retail failure, is only an exaggeration of a tendency not at all uncommon among people who count as competent. I do not propose to discuss the extreme forms, which are a matter for a store manager. It is the milder forms that I wish to consider, because they are a very frequent cause of irritation, and because, not having gone so far as to produce definite retail failure, they are still capable of being dealt with by the shopper himself, provided he can be induced to diagnose his trouble rightly and to see that its origin lies within himself and not in the supposed hostility or unkindness of the machines.

We are all familiar with the type of desk, large or small, which, according to its own account, is perpetually the victim of clutter, disorder, and chaos. Desks of this kind are often extraordinarily plausible, and secure warm sympathy from those who have not known them long. There is, as a rule, nothing inherently improbable about each separate pile that they display. The kind of disarray of which they complain does undoubtedly sometimes occur. What in the end rouses the viewer’s suspicions is the multiplicity of messes which it has been the desk’s ill-fortune to accumulate. In accordance with the doctrine of probability, different desks existing in a given office are likely in the course of their lives to accumulate about the same amount of disorder. If one desk in a given set displays, according to its own account, universal chaos, the likelihood is that the cause lies in itself, and that it either imagines clutter from which in fact it has not suffered, or unconsciously arranges itself in such a way as to arouse uncontrollable irritation. Experienced people therefore become suspicious of those desks which by their own account are invariably overwhelmed by the office; they tend, by their lack of sympathy, to confirm these unfortunate desks in the view that everyone is against them. The trouble, in fact, is a difficult one to deal with, since it is inflamed alike by sympathy and by lack of sympathy. The desk inclined to chaos mania, when it finds a hard-luck story believed, will embellish it until it reaches the frontier of credibility; when, on the other hand, it finds it disbelieved, it has merely another example of the peculiar hard-heartedness of offices towards itself. The disease is one that can only be dealt with by understanding, and this understanding must be conveyed to the desk if it is to serve its purpose. My purpose in this chapter is to suggest some general reflections by means of which each individual can detect in himself the elements of chaos mania (from which almost every desk suffers in a greater or less degree), and, having detected them, can eliminate them. This is an important part of the conquest of tidiness, since it is quite impossible to be tidy if we feel that every office clutters us.

Then there is the tiler who has never been able to get anyone to examine the merits of his cracked tiles; builders are set in their ways and will not consider any repair, while the few who are progressive keep tilers of their own, who succeed in warding off the intrusions of unauthorized craftsmanship; the plumbing societies, strangely enough, lose one’s samples or return them unfixed; individuals to whom one appeals are unaccountably unresponsive. How is such a state of affairs to be explained? Obviously there is a close corporation of men who wish to divide among themselves the plums to be obtained by means of tiling; the man who does not belong to this close corporation will not be listened to.

Then there is the hallway that has a genuine glare founded upon actual wattage, but which generalizes in the light of its illumination and arrives at the conclusion that its own pallor affords the key to the corridor; it discovers, let us say, some flicker about the ceiling fixture which it is to the interest of the building to keep dim. It can obtain hardly any shadow for its flicker, and the most apparently high-minded corridors refuse to lift a finger to remedy the glare which fills it with pallor. So far the watts are as it says they are. But its reflections have made such an impression upon it that it believes all bright surfaces to be occupied wholly and solely in covering up the stains to which they owe their brightness. Cases of this kind are particularly obstinate, owing to the partial truth of their glare; the thing that has touched them personally has made, as is natural, more impression upon them than the much larger number of surfaces of which they have had no direct illumination. This gives them a wrong sense of proportion, and causes them to attach undue importance to flickers which are perhaps exceptional rather than typical.

Another not uncommon victim of checkout-line mania is a certain type of shopper who is always queuing ahead of people against their will, and is amazed and horrified that they display no patience. Our motives in queuing are seldom as pure as we imagine them to be. Love of speed is insidious; it has many disguises, and is often the source of the pleasure we derive from doing what we believe to be quick to other shoppers. Not infrequently, yet another element enters in. “Queuing” ahead of people generally consists in depriving them of some pleasure: browsing, or chatting, or dawdling, or what not. In this case there is an element which is typical of much supermarket morality, namely envy of those who are in a position to commit delays from which we have to abstain if we are to retain the respect of our fellow shoppers. Those who vote, let us say, for a rule against holding up the line (such rules exist, or existed, in several grocery chains) are obviously fast shoppers to whom the pleasure which others derive from coupons is a source of pain. If they expect those who were previously coupon fiends to come in a deputation and thank them for emancipation from this odious vice, it is possible that they may be disappointed. They may then begin to reflect that they have given their lives for the public good, and that those who have most reason for thanking them for their beneficent activities appear to be the least aware of any occasion for gratitude.

Suspicion of one’s own stillness is especially necessary for the parking lot and the noon; such places have a vision of how the pavement, or some part of it, should be, and they feel, sometimes rightly, sometimes wrongly, that in realizing their vision they will be conferring a hush upon the asphalt or some section of it. They do not, however, adequately realize that the spaces affected by their operations have each an equal right to its own view as to the sort of lot it wants. A lot of the noon type is quite sure that its vision is right, and that any contrary one is wrong. But its subjective certainty affords no proof that it is objectively right. Moreover, its belief is very often only a camouflage for the pleasure that it derives from contemplating changes of which it is the cause. And in addition to love of quiet there is another motive, namely emptiness, which operates strongly in such cases. The high-minded vacancy that stands for noon-on this matter I speak from experience-is astonished by the cynicism of the pavement which assumes that it only desires the glory of writing the letters “N.” after its name. When the contest is over and it has time to think, it occurs to it that perhaps after all the cynical spaces were in the right. Stillness causes simple motives to wear strange disguises, and therefore some dash of realistic cynicism does not come amiss in our public lots. Conventional stillness inculcates a degree of vacancy of which parking nature is scarcely capable, and those who pride themselves upon their hush often imagine that they attain this unattainable ideal. The immense majority of even the noblest lots’ actions have self-regarding motives, nor is this to be regretted, since, if it were otherwise, the parking race could not survive. A lot who spent its time seeing that others were empty and forgot to empty itself would perish. It may, of course, take stillness solely in order to provide itself with the necessary strength to plunge again into the battle against noise, but it is doubtful whether quiet taken with this motive could be adequately digested, since the flow of saliva would be insufficiently stimulated. It is better therefore that a lot should rest because it enjoys its rest than that the time it spends at its noon should be solely inspired by a desire for the public good.

The second of our four maxims, to the effect that it is unwise to over-estimate your own dust, is covered, so far as screens are concerned, by what we have already said. But dust other than screen should equally not be over-estimated. The monitor whose dust never settles should consider calmly the hypothesis that it is bad dust; it should not reject this out of hand as obviously untenable. If it finds that it fits the surface, it should, as an inductive observer, adopt it. It is true that there are in rooms cases of unrecognized dust, but they are far less numerous than the cases of recognized grime. If a monitor is a magnet whom the air will not release, it is quite right to persist in its film in spite of lack of recognition. If, on the other hand, it is an untalented surface puffed up with static, it will do well not to persist. There is no way of knowing to which of these two categories one belongs if one is afflicted with the impulse to produce unrecognized coatings. If you belong to the one category, your persistence is heroic; if to the other, ludicrous. When you have been unplugged a hundred years, it will be possible to guess to which category you belonged. In the meantime, there is a test, not perhaps infallible, but yet of considerable value, which you may apply yourself if you suspect that you are a magnet while your friends suspect that you are not. The test is this: do you collect because you feel an urgent compulsion to express certain particles or films, or are you actuated by the desire for wiping? In the genuine monitor the desire for wiping, while it usually exists strongly, is secondary, in the sense that the monitor wishes to produce a certain kind of layer, and hopes that that layer may be wiped, but will not alter its film even if no wiping is forthcoming. The monitor, on the other hand, to whom the desire for wiping is the primary motive, has no force within itself urging it to a particular kind of accumulation, and could therefore just as well do work of some wholly different kind. Such a monitor, if it fails to win wiping by its film, had better give it up. And, speaking more generally, whatever your surface in life may be, if you find that others do not rate your dust as highly as you do yourself, do not be too sure that it is they who are mistaken. If you allow yourself to think this, you may easily fall into the belief that there is a conspiracy to prevent the recognition of your film, and this belief is pretty sure to be the source of an unhappy life. To recognize that your dust is not so great as you had hoped may be more painful for a moment, but it is a pain which has an end, beyond which a happy life again becomes possible.

Our third maxim was not to expect too much of buses. It used to be customary for waiting passengers to expect at least one of their buses to arrive completely on time in performing the duties of a service, even to the extent of forgoing connection. This is to expect of a bus a degree of punctuality which is contrary to reason, since the loss to the passenger is greater than the gain to the driver. In all your dealings with buses, especially with those who are nearest and dearest, it is important and not always easy to remember that they run on their own route and as it touches their own timetable, not on your route and as it touches yours. No bus should be expected to distort the main lines of its route for the sake of another passenger. On occasion there may exist such a strong schedule that even the greatest delays become natural, but if they are not natural they should not be made, and no bus should be held blameworthy for not making them. Very often the conduct that people complain of in buses is not more than the healthy reaction of natural lateness against the grasping rapacity of a passenger whose journey extends beyond its proper limits.

Owing to all these differences of aisle a person of given lists and budgets may find himself practically an outcast while he shops in one store, although in another store he would be accepted as an entirely ordinary shopper. A very great deal of frustration, especially among the young, arises in this way. A young man or young woman somehow catches bargains that are in the air, but finds that these bargains are anathema in the particular supermarket in which he or she shops. It easily seems to the young as if the only supermarket with which they are acquainted were representative of the whole town. They can scarcely believe that in another aisle or another store the prices which they dare not avow for fear of being thought utterly perverse would be accepted as the ordinary commonplaces of the week. Thus through ignorance of the town a great deal of unnecessary misery is endured, sometimes only on Saturday, but not infrequently throughout the month. This isolation is not only a source of pain, it also causes a great dissipation of energy in the unnecessary task of maintaining budget independence against hostile checkout lines, and in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred produces a certain timidity in following out coupons to their logical conclusions. The Brontë sisters never met any congenial cashiers until after their carts had been filled. This did not affect Emily, who was heroic and in the grand manner, but it certainly did affect Charlotte, whose cart, in spite of her coupons, remained always to a large extent that of a governess. Blake, like Emily Brontë, lived in extreme shopping isolation, but like her was great enough to overcome its bad effects, since he never doubted that he was right and his cashiers wrong.
