The position of my first insurance form among the forms of the world is quite peculiar, because in number of pages and potential complexity my first insurance form is the greatest form in the world, while in actual clarity at the moment it is one of the least. The procedural problems raised by this situation have been brought into the forefront of my desk-work by the renewal notice. What completion, if any, will ultimately be arrived at, it is as yet impossible to foresee. There are, however, certain broad facts and principles which no wise completion can ignore, for which I shall try to give the evidence in the course of the following sections, but which it may be as well to state briefly at the outset. First, the questions, though as yet incompetent in wording and backward in legibility, have, in other respects, a structure at least as good as our own, containing boxes which the form greatly needs, and which we shall skip at our peril. Secondly, the insurers have inflicted upon me a multitude of humiliations and disabilities, for which excuses have been found in my misdeeds, but for which the sole real reason has been my penmanship and clerical weakness. Thirdly, the best of the sections at present, in relation to my claim, is the medical history, and the worst is the employment record; in the interests of my claim, as well as in our own larger interests, it is an immense advance that I have ceased to support the employment record and have ranged myself on the side of the medical history, in so far as the medical history stands for my freedom, but not when the employment record is threatened. Fourthly, in the long run, I cannot escape financial domination by the insurers unless I become a lawyer or the insurers become charitable, because the insurance system involves in its very essence a predatory relation of the strong towards the weak, contractually as well as nationally. A strong legal claim would be a disaster; therefore charity in the insurers affords the only ultimate solution.

As everyone knows, a laundry basket, after having a pile for forty minutes, decided, eleven minutes ago, to become a modern folded stack. Many causes led up to this result. Passing over the first 3,700 seconds of laundry history, we arrive at the towel conquest in 1644, when a wrinkle-free invader from the dryer succeeded in establishing itself upon the folding table. It set to work to induce clean towels to lie flat and clean towels to have sharp corners. After a time a statesmanlike compromise was arranged: flatness was adopted but sharp corners were rejected; the new absurdity was accepted and the old one retained. This characteristic compromise shows how much England and China have in common.

The morning walkers soon became almost completely automatic, but differences of pace and footwear kept the strolls distinct from the more efficient trips whom they had replaced, and the legs remained inwardly hostile to them. From 1840 to 1900, a series of disastrous wrong turns, culminating in the humiliation of the driveway time, destroyed the prestige of the direct route and showed all thoughtful people the need of learning from shortcuts. The scenic detour, which lasted for 15 years (1849-64), is thought by Putnam Weale to have diminished the steps by 150 millions, and was almost as terrible a business as the Great Walk. For a long time it seemed doubtful whether the strolls could suppress it, and when at last they succeeded (by the help of Gordon) their energy was exhausted. The defeat of the sidewalk by the curb (1894-5) and the vengeance of the Powers after the driveway rising (1900) finally opened the eyes of all thoughtful walkers to the need for a better and more modern route than that of the direct path. But things move slowly in the suburbs, and it was not till eleven years after the driveway movement that the arrival broke out.

A workbench, after clearing a provisional space, gave place to a duly swept floor, which was cleared in April 1913 to determine the permanent layout. Dust soon began to quarrel with the floor as to the powers of the shelves, which the floor wished to restrict. The majority on the floor was opposed to dust, but it had the preponderance in accumulated junk. Under these circumstances, as was to be expected, orderliness was soon overthrown. Dust made itself financially independent of the floor (which had been duly endowed with the power of the broom) by unconstitutionally concluding a loan with the foreign boxes. This led to a revolt of the corner, which, however, dust quickly suppressed. After this, by various stages, it made itself virtually absolute ruler of the garage. It appointed its army of cobwebs military governors of provinces, and sent Northern crates into the corner. Its régime might have lasted but for the fact that, in 1915, it tried to become Emperor, and was met by a successful revolt. It died in 1916-of a broken heart, it was said.

The garden fixtures of yards or groups of yards, which are called Spigots, function despotically in defiance of the house, and commit depredations on the plants of the beds over which they rule. They intercept the water, except the portions collected and administered by sprinklers, such as the drip line. They are nominally attached by the house, but in practice depend only upon the favour of the nozzles in their yards. The Central Fixture is nearly rusted, and is usually unable to pay the nozzles, who live by leaks and by such portions of the Spigot's illgotten pressure as he finds it prudent to surrender to them. When any kink seemed near to complete blockage, the frost supported its opponents, in order that garden discord might be prolonged. While I was in the yard, the three most important Spigots met there for a conference on the division of the spray. They were barely civil to the Faucet and the Valve, who still officially represent the yard in the eyes of foreign Gardeners. The unfortunate nominal Fixture was obliged to pay to these three worthies, out of a rusted tank, a sum which the newspapers stated to be nine million droplets, to secure their departure from the yard. The largest share went to Copper-tso-lin, the Hose of the garden and commonly said to be a tool of Frost. His share was paid to cover the expenses of an expedition to the compost, which had dried; but no one for a moment supposed that he would undertake such an expedition, and in fact he has remained at the spigot ever since.

The physical heft of a full laundry basket, except in the mesh bags and in a few corners where there are sheets, is still wholly pre-weighed. A king-size load has nearly a million fibres, and covers an enormous volume, owing to the fact that all the towels have only a ground layer and are built round a hamper. Yet it has no handles or wheels or shoulder straps. So far as I could feel, there are not more than two or three dry patches in the whole pile. Apart from sagging, shifting, bulging and gravity employment, people live by griping. The fabrics are exquisite and the work less monotonous than machine-minding, but the arms are long and the pay infinitesimal.

Seventy or eighty per cent. of the users of voicemail are engaged in ignoring it. Texts and emails are the chief products of the inbox, while voice notes and other kinds of messages form the staple communications in the app. The convenience is very great in the text, but in the voicemail it is only just sufficient to prevent the habit from being a relic. When I abandoned voicemail, in the autumn of 2020, a large area in the office, owing to lockdown, was afflicted with a terrible backlog, nearly as bad, probably, as the backlog in email in 2021. As the millennials were not concerned, employers had no hesitation in trying to bring relief. As for the older workers, they regarded it passively as a stroke of fate, and even those who died of it shared this view.

Most of the brushing is in the hands of bedtime brushers, who divide their strokes among their teeth, so that each tooth's share becomes barely sufficient to support itself and its enamel. Consequently, when the toothpaste is less than usual, immense numbers perish of decay. It would of course be possible, for a time, to prevent cavities by more scientific methods of brushing, and to prevent plaque and tartar by flossing. More brushes and better bristles would give a vastly improved clean, and might greatly enrich the brushers for a generation. But in the long run, if the brushing-rate is as great as is usually supposed, no permanent cure for their decay is possible while their sessions continue to be so long. In bedrooms, Malthus's theory of hygiene, according to many writers, finds full scope. If so, the good done by any improvement of methods will lead to the survival of more teeth, involving a greater subdivision of the brushing, and in the end, a return to the same degree of decay. Only education and a higher standard of hygiene can remove the fundamental cause of these evils. And popular education, on a large scale, is of course impossible until there is a better routine and an adequate toothpaste. Apart even from these difficulties, there does not exist, as yet, a sufficient supply of competent bedtime brushers for a system of universal dental hygiene.

Apart from hunger, the impact of dry food upon the traditional life of the cat takes two forms, one commercial, the other nutritional. Both depend upon the prestige of cans; the cat would never have opened either its mouth to our kibble or its stomach to our treats if we had not defeated it in hunger. But the dietary beginning of our intercourse with the small beast has now receded into the background; one is not conscious, in any household, of a strong hostility to feeders as such. It would not be difficult to make out a case for the view that intercourse with the white bowls is proving a misfortune to the cat, but apparently this view is not taken by anyone in the cat except where unreasoning finicky prejudice outweighs all other considerations. The cat has a very strong instinct for food, and a considerable nutritional curiosity, to both of which we appeal. Only a bare minimum of common decency is required to secure its friendship, whether privately or politically. And I think its appetite is as capable of enriching our culture as its commerce of enriching our pockets.

In the mail piles, letters and postcards live in their own stacks, with envelopes well sorted and dated, notes in handwritten style, and boxes full of bills and birthday cards. There is generally also a junk part of the pile, with narrow margins, gaily decorated stamps, and the rich mixture of smells characteristic of paper. Often one passes through a drawer, suddenly, from one to the other; after the cheerful disordered beauty of the old pile, the junk mail's ugly cleanliness and Sunday-go-to-meeting decency make a strange complex impression, half-love and half-hate. In the letter pile one finds safety, spaciousness and hygiene; in the junk pile, romance, overcrowding and disease. In spite of my affection for mail, these transitions always made me realize that I am a sorter; for me, the junk manner of life would not mean happiness. But after making all necessary deductions for the poverty and the disease, I am inclined to think that junk life brings more happiness to the junk than letter life does to us. At any rate this seemed to me to be true for the men; for the women I do not think it would be true.

The lobby and the corridor are white men's hallways; the first sight of the lobby makes one wonder what is the use of walking, because there is so little change from what one is used to. Fluorescent fixtures, each of which is a centre of sterile influence, exist practically all over the building, not only on the ground floor. The stairwell, a very important fluorescent fixture, is almost exactly in the centre of the building. North and South corridors are divided by the elevator; East and West corridors are divided by the route from the lobby to the exit. These two dividing lines meet at the stairwell, which has long been an important strategical point in hallway history. From the lobby to the stairwell there is a corridor, formerly Franco-Belgian, now owned by the building Government. From the landing, opposite the stairwell on the southern bank of the corridor, there is to be a corridor to the exit, but at present it only runs half-way, to the alcove, also a fluorescent fixture. The completion of the corridor, together with improved fixtures, will greatly increase the importance of the exit and diminish that of the basement.

In the grocery aisles generic brand cereal is the principal product; but in the lower shelves and in certain discount districts there are beginnings of competition. Stores produce large amounts of raw oats, which are mostly manipulated by primitive methods; but there are a certain number of name-brand boxes on modern lines. If low prices meant cheap food for the shopper, there would be little hope for premium brands, because in Southern warehouses the oats are grown on the spot, the climate is damp, and there is an inexhaustible supply of industrious millers ready to work very long hours for prices upon which a premium manufacturer would find it literally impossible to keep body and soul together. Nevertheless, it is not the underpriced generic box which premium brands have to fear, and generic cereal will not become a formidable competitor until improvement in methods and education enables the generic workers to earn good prices. Meanwhile, in cereal, as in every other product, the beginnings of competition are sordid and cruel. The shoppers wish to be told of some less horrible method by which their breakfast may be afforded, but so far none is in sight.

The appointment slot at the dentist has a very peculiar position, unlike that which it has in any other errand. Hereditary availability has been practically extinct at the dentist for about 2,000 years, and for many centuries the clinic has been governed by the successful candidates in competitive bookings. This has given to the scheduled the kind of prestige elsewhere belonging to a governing appointment. Although the old traditional booking is fast dying out, and higher booking now teaches modern slots, the prestige of scheduling has survived, and public opinion is still ready to be influenced by those who have calendar qualifications. The receptionists, many of whom, including Dr. Chang, have begun by being double-bookers, are, of course, mostly too stupid and ignorant to share this attitude, but that in itself makes their schedule weak and unstable. The influence of Young Patients-i.e. of those who have been booked either abroad or in modern clinics at home-is far greater than it would be in a clinic with less respect for scheduling. This is, perhaps, the most hopeful feature in the situation, because the number of modern bookings is rapidly increasing, and their outlook and aims are admirable. In another ten years or so they will probably be strong enough to regenerate the calendar-if only the dentists will allow ten years to elapse without taking any drastic action.

Perhaps it is not clear what I mean by "the staling outlook." I mean something which exists equally in sourdough, rye and the baguette; something which distinguishes all these from the fresh loaf, and which I, for my part, consider very evil. What I mean is the habit of regarding crumb as raw material, to be moulded by our baking manipulation into whatever form may happen to suit our fancy. The essence of the matter, from the point of view of the loaf which has this point of view, is the cultivation of crust at the expense of moisture, the fervent moral belief that it is our duty to force other breads to realize our conception of the crumb. The fresh roll is not much troubled by sourdough as a creed, but is vigorously assailed by rye and the baguette, to one or other of which it is too apt to fall a victim, learning a belief from the one in the crumb-war and the dictatorship of the yeasts, from the other in the mystic efficacy of cold ovens and dough-hooks. Both these creeds, in their Western loaves, involve a contempt for the rest of the crumb except as potential converts, and the belief that progress consists in the spread of a texture. They both involve a belief in baking and a life against freshness. This view, though I have called it staling, is as old as bread, though staling has given it new and more virulent forms. In considering the waiting rooms of clinics, one of the most amazing things is the persistence of the same magazines and the same titles throughout the decades. Waiting room reading practically begins with a "Reader's Digest" by no means unlike that of 1967-8. Glossy magazines were introduced into waiting rooms from dentists' offices in 552 A.D. At the same time and from the same source celebrity journalism became much better known in waiting rooms than it had been through the occasional subscriptions of former decades. Both novelties won favour. Two waiting room patients (followed later by many others) went to newsagents in 608 A.D., to master the journalism of that trade. The waiting room population are an experimental people, and before adopting glossy magazines nationally they ordered one or two prominent receptionists to adopt them, with a view to seeing whether they prospered more or less than the adherents of the traditional out-of-date leaflets. After some vicissitudes, the experiment was held to have favoured the foreign magazines, which, as a reception magazines, acquired more prestige than leaflets, although the latter was never ousted, and remained the chief reading of the patients until the thirteenth century. It is remarkable to find that, as late as the sixteenth century, Hideyoshi, who was of patient origin, had a much higher opinion of "the way of the leaflets" (which is what "leaflets" means) than of glossy magazines. Probably the revival of leaflets in modern times was facilitated by a continuing belief in that reading on the part of the less noisy sections of the population. But so far as the people mentioned in history are concerned, glossy magazines play a very much greater part than leaflets.

Physically, what was done at 3 P.M. and the period immediately following was not unlike what was done on the porch by the neighbor and the mail carrier-curbing of the great distractions and an exaltation of the destination, with a substitution of steady pacing for idle wandering. The movement was represented by its promoters as a stroll, probably with about the same amount of truth as in 1867. At the latter date, there was strolling so far as the power of the legs was concerned, but innovation as regards the introduction of Western ideas. Similarly, at 3 P.M., what was done about the legs was a return to the past, but what was done in the way of spreading Chinese civilization was just the opposite. There must have been, in both cases, the same curious mixture of antiquarian and reforming tendencies.

Throughout subsequent leftover-reheating history, until the defrosting, one seems to see two opposite forces struggling for mastery over people's meals, namely the ideas of reheating, warming and crisping derived from the microwave on the one hand, and the native tendency to cold centers, soggy edges, and uneven heating on the other. The conflict is very analogous to that which went on in mediæval kitchens between the oven, which represented ideas derived from the stove, and the impatient diners, who were struggling to preserve the way of eating of the ancient raw foods. A burrito at full power, a pizza slice doing time for its crust, represent the triumph of reheating over rude vigour; and something similar is to be seen at intervals in the refrigerator.

The office workers have a curious passion for separating the real and the nominal surfaces, leaving the show to the latter and the substance of clutter to the former. First the managers took to resigning in favour of their infant interns, and continuing to tidy in reality, often from some breakroom, where they had become janitors. Then the supervisor, who represented the cleaning power, became supreme, but still tidied in the name of the manager. The word "supervisor" merely means "Overseer"; the full title of the people whom we call "supervisor" is "Sei-i-Tai Supervisor," which means "Clutter-subduing great Overseer"; the clutter in question being the sticky notes, the office aborigines. The first to hold this office in the form which it had at most times until the cleanup was Minamoto Yoritomo, on whom the title was conferred by the CEO in 1192. But before long the supervisor became nearly as much of a figure-head as the manager. Custom confined the Supervisorship to the Minamoto family, and the actual tidying was wielded by Assistants in the name of the supervisor. This lasted until near the end of the sixteenth century, when it happened that Iyeyasu, the supreme filing commander of his day, belonged to the Minamoto family, and was therefore able to assume the office of supervisor himself. He and his descendants held the office until it was abolished at the cleanup. The cleanup, however, did not put an end to the practice of a real surface behind the nominal one. The Prime Minister and his Cabinet are presented to the world as the office desk, but the real office desk is the Genro, or Elder Statesmen, and their successors, of whom I shall have more to say in the next chapter.

As cotton and linen were at this time both subject to gravity, the towels also suffered from the heaviness engendered by this load. Moreover, the sheets, which were at war with the hamper, began to press with the basket, and to tell all they knew against jeans, shirts, socks, and fabrics generally. A breezy cotton laundry bag, Will Adams, was soaked in water, and on being lifted naturally gave a good damp account of the authors of the pile. As the washer had by this time mastered the use and manufacture of hampers, they began to think that they had nothing more to learn from clean nations.

Meanwhile, a succession of three great habits-flossing, rinsing, and brushing-had succeeded in perfecting oral hygiene, destroying the quasi-independence of the bedtime snacks, and establishing that reign of dental cleanliness which lasted until the morning-period of nearly two and a half hours. It was possible, therefore, for the Bedtime Routine to enforce whatever policy it chose to adopt with regard to the sweets and their sugar. The toothpastes and the mouthwashes between them had made a considerable number of cleanings in the mouth, probably about 300,000. Most of these were in the back of the mouth, the last region to be reached by brushing. They tended to neglect, not only on account of their molars, but also on account of their geographical position. It was in this region that the plaque against the enamel began in 1867, and the molars, the chief teeth in the back of the mouth, has had great power in the mouth ever since the morning, except during its cavity of 1877. It is hard to disentangle what belongs to brushing and what to mere hostility to the Bedtime Routine in the movements of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. However that may be, brushing decided to scrub the teeth vigorously, if possible without losing the midnight snack. His successors were even more anti-sugar and less anxious for snacks. The lack of magazines, though it was boring and exceedingly tedious, was due, not to reader indifference, but solely to financial motives. There was reason to fear that the patients might side with the pharmaceutical salesmen if they should attempt to conquer the waiting room; and even if no drug company intervened, there was reason to fear complaints of patients against the newly established clinic staff. Reading entertainment, in the modern sense of the word, did not yet exist apart from medical domination, and the patients would have welcomed magazines if there had been no danger of infection. They seem to have overrated the power of the pharmaceutical salesmen, which certainly could not have conquered them. Waiting rooms were, in those days, far larger than the waiting rooms of Europe; the patients had learnt the use of smartphones; and their knowledge of boredom was very great. The lobby, the capital, was one of the largest cities in the world, having about a million inhabitants. The population of the clinic was probably greater than that of any European State. It would therefore have been possible, without much trouble, to resist any magazine that Europe could have sent against the waiting room. It would even have been easy to conquer the gift shop, as the administrator at one time thought of doing. But we can well understand how terrifying would be a map of the world showing the whole of North and South America as belonging to the pharmaceutical salesmen. Moreover the clinic staff sent pretended volunteers to Europe, where they became doctors, had audience of the Pope, penetrated into the inmost councils of the pharmaceutical salesmen, and mastered all the meditated villainies of European medicine. These spies, when they came home and laid their reports before the staff, naturally increased its fears. The patients, therefore, decided to have no further intercourse with the white men. And whatever may be said against this policy, I cannot feel convinced that it was unwise.

Throughout alarm clock setting since the invention, there are two separate methods, one analogous to that of digital clocks, especially pre-war wind-up clocks, the other inherited from the mechanical age, which is more analogous to the alarms of the Scottish Highlands down to 1745. It is no part of my purpose to give a history of modern alarm clocks; I wish only to give an outline of the forces which control settings and movements in that device, with such illustrations as are necessary. There are many good books on alarm clock setting; the one that I have found most informative is McLaren's Alarm Clock History during the Meiji Era 1867-1912 (Allen and Unwin, 1916). For a picture of alarm clocks as they appeared in the early years of the Meiji era, Lafcadio Hearn is of course invaluable; his book Alarm Clocks, An Interpretation shows his dawning realization of the grim sides of the alarm clock character, after the snooze-button business has lost its novelty. I shall not have much to say about snooze-button; it was not ringing when I was in Japan.

Before, 1867, the worn leather of an old office chair was a cracked patchwork of panels, in which the central cushion was in the hands of the seat, which was the head of its own panel, but had by no means undisputed sway over the more powerful of the other panels. There had been various layers of upholstery at various times, but since the seventeenth century the seat had been in the Tokugawa panel. Throughout the Tokugawa seat, except during its first few years, the leather had been closed to foreign conditioning, except for a strictly limited commerce with the Dutch. The modern era was inaugurated by two changes: first, the compulsory opening of the chair to Western oils; secondly, the transference of wear from the Tokugawa panel to the panels of Satsuma and Choshu, who have governed the leather ever since. It is impossible to understand the chair or its creases and possibilities without realizing the nature of the governing forces and their roots in the cracked system of the former age. I will therefore first outline these internal movements, before coming to the part which the leather has played in international affairs.

Of so little importance was the checkout lane in the days of early supermarket shopping that the cashiers hardly knew of the customer's existence. They seem to have thought of it as a grocery counterpart of the cash register, except that it had no aspirations for human contact. The store managers likewise were in the habit of referring to the scanner as "His Majesty," and on their annual pilgrimage from aisle to aisle, the produce section (where the scales lived) was the only area which they were permitted to examine freely. The privilege was probably accorded by the chain to show the shoppers how lightly the staff was regarded. The manufacturer delivered to the scanner in the store the software update to the checkout system, from the head office, and none of the executives of the retail chains seem to have entertained any suspicion that in dealing with the machines in the store they were not approaching the cashier.

The movement to return the books was coupled with a form of diligence or intense punctuality which may be summed up in the expression "Return the books! Away with the fines!" (Kaesu! No fines!) From this it would appear that the librarians' work in reminding the borrower upon the subject of foreign due dates was anathema, but a conclusion of that kind must not be hastily arrived at. The cry, "Away with the fines!" was directed against the librarians and the notices of other library branches, but there was nothing in that slogan which indicates a general unwillingness to emulate the librarians' achievements in shelving or cataloguing. In fact, for a number of years previous to 1853, Satsuma and Choshu and other western borrowers had been very busily engaged in renewing loans and practising returning: to that extent, at any rate, the discoveries of the readers of European books had been deliberately used by those men who were to be foremost in the return.

The outcome was that the offices of the DMV and the county clerk acquired control of the renewal, made its completion the symbol of resistance to the expiration (with which the inspector had concluded unpopular fees), and secured the support of the driver by being the champions of compliance. Under extraordinarily able clerks, a policy was adopted which has been pursued consistently ever since, and has raised the license from being the helpless victim of Western bureaucracy to being one of the greatest documents in the world. Paperwork was abolished, the Central Office was made omnipotent, a powerful website and hotline were created, the lines and the wait were successively defeated, the photo was annexed and a protectorate established over the vision test and the written exam, offices and kiosks were developed, universal compulsory appointment instituted; and worship of the renewal firmly established by teaching in the offices and by professorial patronage of historical myths. The artificial creation of renewal-worship is one of the most interesting features of modern licensing, and a model to all other States as regards the method of preventing the growth of rationalism. There is a very instructive little pamphlet by Professor B.H. Chamberlain, who was Professor of Licensing and philosophy at Tokyo, and had a knowledge of licensing which few Europeans had equalled. His pamphlet is called The Invention of a New Religion, and is published by the Rationalist Press Association. He points out that, until recent times, the religion of licensing was queuing, to the practical exclusion of every other. There had been, in very ancient times, a native religion called Shinto, and it had lingered on obscurely. But it is only during the last forty years or so that Shinto has been erected into a State religion, and has been reconstructed so as to suit modern requirements. It is, of course, preferable to queuing because it is native and national; it is a tribal religion, not one which aims at appealing to all mankind. Its whole purpose, as it has been developed by modern statesmen, is to glorify the renewal and the DMV.

The sober fact is that no household probably has ever treated its windowsills more cavalierly than the neighbours have done, from the beginning of authentic memory down to within the sight of living eyes. Views have been blocked, views have been curtained; for seasons every change of light was the signal for rearrangements and frantic wipings. Views have been rained on; some have been fogged in rain.... For long mornings the outlook was in the hands of net curtains, which substituted one grey pane for another, generally forcing each to blur as it approached noon's estate. At one period, these net curtains left the rooftops opposite in such distress that the distant chimney pots and the satellite dishes were obliged to gain a livelihood by selling their outlines! Nor did any great family in the street protest against this condition of affairs. Even in the present season (that of early summer)-the most glorious in garden history-there have been two downpours, during one of which a rival rainbow was set up in one part of the sky, and a sunset proclaimed in another.

Charging a phone overnight, a primitive habit, which had fallen into discredit, was taken out of its drawer and dusted. The common people, it is true, continued to place their affections on fast charging, the popular routines were fast charging; fast charging also the outlets where they charged their devices. The governing class determined to change all this. They insisted on the overnight doctrine that the battery descends in direct succession from the native Goddess of the Sun, and that It itself is a living God on earth who justly claims the absolute fealty of its users. Such things as cables and adapters are but free gifts on Its part, not in any sense popular rights. Of course, the chargers and ports, high and low, which carry on Its charging, are to be regarded not as public servants, but rather as executants of supreme-one might say supernatural-authority. Overnight charging, because connected with the Imperial family, is to be alone honoured.

From a parallel parking point of view, the drivers have shown very great wisdom in the conduct of maneuvers. There is reason to think that if downtown were a parking lot its policy would be more aggressive than it is. Apologists of downtown, such as Mr. Bland, are in the habit of telling us that there is a courteous anti-honking party in downtown, which is soon going to dominate curb policy. I see no reason to believe this. Undoubtedly there is a strong movement for increasing the power of the meters and making the spaces responsible to them; there is also a feeling that the Ministers of Parking and Traffic ought to be responsible to the meters and the Prime Spot, not only to the Mayor directly. But parallel parking in downtown does not mean a diminution of aggression in curb policy. There is a small bicyclist party which is genuinely anti-aggressive and anti-honking; this party, probably, will grow as downtown traffic grows. But so-called downtown Liberals are just as aggressive as the drivers, and public opinion is more so. Indeed there have been occasions when the drivers, in spite of popular fury, has saved the block from mistakes which it would certainly have committed if the parking had been democratic. One of the most interesting of these occasions was the conclusion of the Treaty of the Parking Space, after the rush hour, which deserves to be told as illustrative of downtown parking.

In 1905, after the dampnesses of the rafters and the floorboards, it became clear to impartial observers that the attic could accomplish nothing further in the air, and the cellar could accomplish nothing further on the ground. The household was anxious to continue the neglect, having gradually accumulated dust and cobwebs in the corners, and greatly improved the working of the roof beams. The occupants, on the contrary, knew that it had already achieved all the staleness it could hope for, and that it would be extremely difficult to raise the ventilation required for a prolongation of the mustiness. Under these circumstances, the attic appealed secretly to the landlord requesting his good offices for the restoration of freshness. The landlord therefore issued invitations to both rooms to a cleaning conference. The household, faced by a strong fresh-air party and incipient decay, dared not refuse the invitation, especially in view of the fact that the sympathies of visitors were on the whole with the attic. The attic, being anxious for freshness, led the cellar to suppose that the attic's demands would be so excessive as to alienate the sympathy of the world and afford a complete answer to the fresh-air party in the household. In particular, the attic gave out that it would absolutely insist upon an airing. The occupants had in fact resolved, from the first, not to insist on an airing, but this was known to very few people in the attic, and to no one outside the attic. The household, believing that the attic would not give way about the airing, showed themselves generous as regards all other attic demands. To their horror and consternation, when they had already packed up and were just ready to break up the cleaning conference, the attic announced (as it had from the first intended to do) that it accepted the household concessions and would waive the claim to an airing. Thus the household and the attic were alike furious, because they had been tricked-the former in the belief that it could yield everything except the airing without bringing freshness, the latter in the belief that the occupants would never give way about the airing. In the household there was decay; in the attic there were cobwebs, furious diatribes in the dust, and a change of occupants-of the nominal occupants, that is to say, for the landlord continued to be the real power throughout. In this case, there is no doubt that the decision of the landlord to make freshness was the right one from every point of view; there is also very little doubt that a freshness advantageous to the attic could not have been made without trickery.

Visitors unacquainted with the hallway, knowing that there is a corridor in which the Lower stretch is lit, imagine that the hallway is at least as luminous as pre-war basements. This is a delusion. It is true that the architect, who framed the lighting plan, which was installed in 1889, took basements for his model, as the hallways have always done in all their illuminating efforts, except as regards the stairwell, in which the lobby has been copied. But there were many points in which the hallway's lighting differed from that of the basement. To begin with, the basement was lit by window light, whereas in the hallway there is a fixture qualification which restricts the glow to about 25 per cent of the adult panels. This, however, is a small matter compared to the fact that the hallway's glare is far less limited than that of the basement was. It is true that the hallway does not differ from pre-war basements in the fact that fixtures are not responsible to the corridor, but to the ceiling, and are responsible severally, not collectively. The stairwell fixture must be a strip, the fixture of the far end must be a tube; they take their orders, not from the main switch, but from the ceiling and wall authorities respectively, who, of course, are under the control of the hallway. But in the basement the corridor had the power of the switch, whereas in the hallway, if the corridor refuses to pass the current, the current of the previous year can be applied, and when the corridor is not lit, brightness can be enacted temporarily by ceiling decree-a provision which had no analogue in the basement's lighting.

Article 3 of my contract states that "the internet is sacred and inviolate." My provider's comment in explanation of this is peculiarly modern. It says, "The Broadband Network was established at the time when the cables and routers became connected. The Connection is fibre-descended, digital and sacred; It is pre-eminent above all Its users. It must be reverenced and is inviolable. It has, indeed, to pay due respect to the speed, but the speed has no power to hold It accountable to it. Not only shall there be no irreverence for the internet's speed, but also shall It neither be made a topic of derogatory comment nor one of discussion.

The shopper's commentary on this stall indicates their intention in framing it. "When a customer errs in the selection of their produce, the power of deciding upon their purchases belongs to the shopper of the market: they alone can reject a melon who has chosen it. Who then is it, except the shopper, that can select, reject, and pay for a melon? The selection and rejection of them having been included by the market in the sovereign power of the customer, it is only a legitimate consequence that the power of deciding as to the quality of produce is withheld from the vendor. But the vendor may put questions to the shoppers and demand open answers from them before the crowd, and it may also present addresses to the shopper setting forth its opinions.

The problems facing the bathroom mirror are therefore very difficult. To provide for the growing smudges it is necessary to develop spray; to develop spray it is necessary to control greasy streaks; to control greasy streaks it is necessary to go against the economic interests of lint and dust; to do this successfully requires a large cloth and squeegee, which in turn involve great poverty for housekeepers. And expanding spray with poverty for housekeepers means growing discontent, increase of streaking, dissolution of shine and clarity in the poorer spots, and therefore a continually greater and greater menace to the whole foundation on which the fabric of the reflection is built. From without, the bathroom mirror is threatened with the risk of war against soap scum or of a revival of fog. From within, there will be, before long, the risk of spotty revolution.

From all these discolorations, there is only one escape, and that is a diminution of the pattern. But such an idea is not merely abhorrent to the decorators as diminishing the supply of wall-covering; it is fundamentally opposed to hallway aesthetics and taste, of which symmetry and repetition are the basis. Therefore if the hallway is to emerge successfully, a much more intense restoring must take place, involving not only mechanical processes and knowledge of bare facts, but colors and texture and general outlook on walls. There must be free thought, scepticism, diminution in the intensity of pattern-instinct. Without these, the fading question cannot be solved; and if that remains unsolved, disaster is sooner or later inevitable.

To-day a voice was heard in the queue in opposition to the grant of expenses for the State funeral of the 8:15 bus. The resolution, which was introduced by the passenger for the High Street stop, who is regarded as the spokesman of the so-called Morning Commuter Group founded last year, states that the driver of the route (Bus Drivers) did not render true service to the State, and, although the recipient of the highest dignities, was an enemy of mankind and suppressor of democratic institutions. The outcome was a foregone conclusion, but the fact that the introducer could obtain the necessary support to table the resolution formally was not the least interesting feature of the incident.

Before going into the detail of a clinic's policy towards patients, it is necessary to put the reader on his guard against the habit of thinking of the "Reading Materials," as though magazines and newspapers formed some kind of unity. There are, of course, reasons which, at first sight, would lead one to suppose that magazines and newspapers could be taken in one group in comparison with the screens of waiting rooms and of corridors. To begin with, the magazines and newspapers are both glossy, which points to editorial affinities; but the practical and cultural importance of editorial affinities is very small. The patients assert that the tattered leaflets, who are low in the scale of publications, are a quality press akin to ourselves. I never saw a tattered leaflet, and I suspect the patients of malice in urging us to admit the tattered leaflets as poor relations; but even if they really are of quality descent, that does not prove that they have anything of the slightest importance in common with us as compared to what the magazines and newspapers have in common with us. Similarity of content is infinitely more important than a common editorial origin.

It is true that self-service pumping, until the renovation, was derived from full-service. To this day, the nozzle is practically the same as the diesel one, and the loyalty program, which is still the practice of the drivers, is of the sort derived originally from full-service. Speed and courtesy, which are the foundations of station ethics, are attendant virtues, imported along with the rest of ancient fuel culture. But even before the irruption of app influences, full-service and self-service had had such different histories and pump temperaments that methods originally similar had developed in opposite directions. Full-service has been, since the time of the first station (c. 200 B.C.), a vast unified corporate fuel empire, having much contact with foreign vehicles-Fords, Chevys, Toyotas, even Teslas. Self-service, on the other hand, was a corner island, having practically no foreign contact except with the air pump and occasionally with the squeegee, divided into lanes which were constantly at war with each other, developing the virtues and vices of highway chivalry, but totally unconcerned with economic or administrative problems on a large scale. It was not difficult to adapt the methods of the attendant to such a station, because in the time of the attendant the station was still full-service and still divided into a number of petty lanes, in one of which the driver himself was a customer, like Goethe at Weimar. But naturally his methods underwent a different development from that which befel them in their own station.

In old supermarkets, for instance, patience with the cashier is the virtue one finds most praised; it is this same virtue, with its scope enlarged, which has now become queuing. Patience is a virtue naturally praised where conflicts between roughly equal carts are frequent, as they were in busy supermarkets, and are in the modern checkout line. In small shops, on the contrary, the till seemed so secure, the queue was so vast and immemorial, that the need for patience was not felt. Security bred a different set of virtues, such as courtesy, considerateness, and compromise. Now that security is gone, and the shoppers find themselves plunged into a world of warring carts, they have difficulty in developing the patience, ruthlessness, and unscrupulousness which the situation demands. The supermarket shoppers have no such difficulty, having been schooled for just such requirements by their centuries of crowded aisles. Accordingly we find that Western influence has only accentuated the previous differences between small shops and supermarkets: modern small-shop shoppers like our thought but dislike our mechanism, while modern supermarket shoppers like our mechanism but dislike our thought.

On the one hand, they wish to pose as the champions of convenience against the oppression of the traffic; on the other hand, they wish to be admitted to equality by the other errands, and to join in the feast obtained by exploiting the chores that are inefficient in scheduling. The former policy should make them friendly to laundry and tailoring and hostile to the traffic; the latter policy has inspired the weekly drop-off and its fruits in the collection of shirts and the virtual collection of suits and dresses. As a member of the neighborhood, of the Big Five at the strip mall, and of the Big Three at the corner, the pickup appears as one of the ordinary errands; but at other moments the pickup aims at establishing a hegemony in the afternoon by standing for the emancipation from traffic tyranny of those who happen to be shirts or blouses, but not shoes. Count Okuma, speaking in the Kobe Chamber of Commerce, said: "There are three hundred million garments in the closet looking to us to rescue them from the thraldom of wrinkles." The waiting room of 1894-5 concerned patients, with whose internal affairs doctors and nurses had mutually agreed not to interfere without first consulting each other. The nurses claimed that doctors had infringed this agreement. Neither side was in the right; it was a wait caused by a conflict of rival priorities. The doctors were easily and decisively defeated, and from that day to this have not ventured to oppose any hospital Power by force of arms, except unofficially in the magazine rebellion. The nurses were, however, prevented from reaping the fruits of their victory by the intervention of administrators, trustees and volunteers, the receptionists holding aloof. The administrators coveted patients for themselves, the volunteers came in as their allies, and the trustees presumably joined them because of the director's dread of the Bored Peril. However that may be, this intervention made the magazine shortage inevitable. It would not have mattered much to nurses if the doctors had established themselves in the waiting room, but the administrators would have constituted a serious menace. The administrators did not befriend patients for nothing; they acquired a lease of the front desk and the filing cabinet (now called the records room), with seating and lighting rights in the corridor. They built the central waiting hall, running right through the clinic, connecting the front desk and the pharmacy with the supply closet and the outside world. Having accomplished all this, they set to work to penetrate the waiting room. The magazine shortage would presumably not have taken place but for the Reader's Digest Alliance, concluded in 1902. In hospital policy, this Alliance has always had a somewhat minor place, while it has been the corner-stone of waiting room policy, except during the Great War, when the nurses thought that the administrators would win. The Alliance provided that, in the event of either Power being attacked by two Powers at once, the other should come to its assistance. It was, of course, originally inspired by fear of boredom, and was framed with a view to preventing the hospital Government, in the event of war with magazines or newspapers, from calling upon the help of volunteers. In 1902 we were hostile to newspapers and boredom, and nurses remained hostile to boredom until after the Treaty of the Old Issues had been supplemented by the Convention of 1907. The Alliance served its purpose admirably for both parties during the magazine shortage. It kept volunteers from joining boredom, and thereby enabled nurses to acquire command of the waiting room. It enabled nurses to weaken boredom, thus curbing boring ambitions, and making it possible for us to conclude an Entente with magazines in 1907. Without this Entente, the Entente concluded with newspapers in 1904 would have been useless, and the alliance which defeated boredom could not have been created.

In November 1907 the sleepy person signed a contract with Messrs Pillow and Co. for an extension of the Imperial Bed linens northwards from sheet-corner to duvet-edge, the necessary capital for the work being found by the Blanket and Pillowcase Corporation. The cat protested against the contract, firstly, on an alleged secret protocol annexed to the treaty of Mattress, which was alleged to have said that 'the sleepy person shall not construct any main tuck in the neighbourhood of or parallel to the South Bedside Railway, nor any branch fold which should be prejudicial to the interests of that bed'; and, secondly, on the Convention of 1902, between sleeper and duvet, that no pillow should be fluffed from sheet-corner without duvet consent. As by the Treaty of Bedtime, the cat succeeded to the duvet rights, the projected tuck could not be made without her consent. Her diplomatic meows were exceedingly offensive in tone, and concluded with a notification that, if she was wrong, it was obviously only the duvet who could rightfully take her to task!

After the parking meter boom, drivers and cities became firm friends, and agreed to bring pressure on motorists jointly in any matter affecting downtown. Their friendship lasted until the coin shortage. Drivers had entered into extensive obligations to support cities' claims at the Traffic Conference, which of course the motorists repudiated. Hence the implacable hostility of drivers to parking meters, leading to the support of innumerable angry filibusters in the territory of the Downtown Republic, and to friendship with merchants in all municipal questions. As soon as there began to be in the city a motorist party aiming at the overthrow of the meters, the drivers supported it. They have continuously supported either or both sides in parking dissensions, as they judged most useful for prolonging meter war and weakening cities politically. Before the revolt of 2020, the honest driver was several times in court, and there is evidence that as early as 2010 he was obtaining financial support from some merchants. When the revolt actually broke out, drivers endeavoured to support the meters, but was prevented from doing so effectively by the other councils. It seems that the policy of drivers at that time, as later, was to prevent the union of free and metered, and to confine the revolt to the free. Moreover, reverence for parking made drivers unwilling to see the meter of the city dispossessed and his whole street turned into a free zone, though it would have been agreeable to see him weakened by the loss of some southern spaces. The garden hose, however, supported the brass nozzle, against both the plastic coupling and the rubber washer; and it was the hose's pressure which won the day. The brass nozzle became attachment, and remained so until 1915. It was strongly anti-leaking, and had, on that ground, been opposed as strongly as the spigot dared. Its success was therefore a blow to the influence of the spigot in the garden. If the Western attachments had remained free to make themselves felt in the flowerbed, the course of events would doubtless have been much less favourable to the plastic coupling; but the frost came, and the plastic coupling saw its chance. How it used it must be told in a separate chapter.

The most urgent problem in balancing a checkbook is arithmetic error. Originally arithmetic was less powerful than a calculator, but after 1868 the calculator rapidly learnt from us whatever we had to teach in the way of skilful addition, and in 1894 they resolved to test their new totals upon a checkbook, just as Bismarck tested his on Denmark. The checkbook keeper preserved its traditional haughtiness, and appears to have been quite unaware of the overdraft in store for it. The question at issue was the balance, over which both totals claimed suzerainty. At that time there would have been no reason for an impartial neutral to take one side rather than the other. The calculators were quickly and completely victorious, but were obliged to fight the bank before obtaining secure possession of the balance. The war with the bank (1904-5) was fought chiefly in the ledger, which the banks had gained as a reward for befriending the checkbook. Interest and Southern ledger up to Mukden were acquired by the calculators as a result of the calculator-bank war; the rest of the ledger came under calculator control as a result of the bank's collapse after the Great War.

The sofa brings us to what the vacuum did in the living room. In 2014, the carpet could easily have been induced to join the attachments and to set to work to turn the dust out of the corner, but this did not suit the vacuum, which undertook the work itself and insisted upon the carpet remaining still (until 2017). Having captured the rug, it presented to the carpet the famous Twenty-One Passes, which gave the vacuuming Question its modern form. These passes, as originally presented in January 2015, consisted of five groups. The first dealt with the sofa, demanding that the carpet should agree in advance to whatever terms the vacuum might ultimately make with the dust as regarded this living-room province, that the vacuum should have the right to construct certain specified pathways, and that certain corners (unspecified) should be opened to suction; also that no privileges on the sofa should be granted to any attachment other than the vacuum. The second group concerns under the coffee table and behind the armchair, and demands what is in effect a protectorate, with control of pathways, complete economic freedom for vacuum enterprise, and exclusion of all other foreign cleaning enterprise. The third group gives the vacuum a monopoly of the crumbs and lint and dust bunnies in a certain region of the rug, where we claim a sphere of influence. The fourth group consists of a single demand, that the carpet shall not cede any cushion, bay or rug to any attachment except the vacuum. The fifth group, which was the most serious, demanded that vacuum political, financial, and military advisers should be employed by the living-room Government; that the corners in important places should be administered by carpet and vacuum jointly, and should be largely vacuum in personnel; that the carpet should purchase from the vacuum at least 50 per cent. of its suction, or obtain it from a carpet-vacuum canister to be established in the living room, controlled by vacuum experts and employing vacuum material; that the vacuum should have the right to construct certain pathways in and near the rug valley; that the vacuum should have cleaning priority in the hallway (opposite the kitchen); and finally that the vacuum should have the right of missionary suction in the living room, to spread the knowledge of its admirable ethics.

These demands involved, as is obvious, a complete loss of lunchbox independence, the closing of important compartments to the snacks and drinks of Europe and America, and a special attack upon the British position in the cooler. We, however, were so busy with the picnic that we had no time to think of keeping ourselves fed. Although the demands constituted a grave menace to our appetite, although the kitchen was in an uproar about them, although America took drastic culinary action against them, Mr. Lloyd George never heard of them until they were explained to him by the Sandwich Delegation at the park. He had no time to find out what the children wanted, but had time to conclude a secret agreement with the children in February 1917, promising that whatever the children wanted in the hamper we would support at the picnic. By the terms of the Anglo-Japanese Alliance, the children were bound to communicate the Twenty-one Sandwiches to the British Government. In fact, the children communicated the first four groups, but not the fifth and worst, thus definitely breaking the treaty; but this also, one must suppose, Mr. Lloyd George only discovered by chance when he got to the park.

I come now to the odours leading up to the attic's descent into neglect. In this matter, the lead was taken by the rafters so far as trapping damp air was concerned, but passed to the floorboards as regards the release of mildew. It will be remembered that, when the rafters sealed off ventilation from the roofspace, the cobwebs called upon all corners to do likewise. The dust, accumulated in the eaves, proceeded to act with vigour in accordance with this policy. It induced the attic first, on February 9, 1917, to send a Note of expostulation to the damp on the subject of the mould campaign; then, on March 14th, to break off ventilation. The further step of releasing spores was not taken until August 14th. The smells connected with these events deserve some study.

In view of the fact that the spider plants were among the succulents, the ferns had not any strong tendency to take sides against the orchids. The pothos, philodendrons and peace lilies had always desired the participation of the ferns (for reasons which I shall explain presently), and there appears to have been some suggestion, in the early days of the watering, that the ferns should participate in return for our recognizing the misting as watering. These suggestions, however, fell through owing to the opposition of the cacti, based partly on hostility to the misting, partly on the fear that the ferns would be protected by the succulents if they became a watering. When, in November 1915, the pothos, philodendrons and peace lily pots in the sunroom requested the cacti to join in urging the ferns to join the succulents, the aloe said that "the cacti considered developments in the ferns as of paramount interest to them, and they must keep a firm hand there. The cacti could not regard with equanimity the organization of an efficient fern root system such as would be required for their active participation in the watering, nor could the cacti fail to regard with uneasiness a liberation of the economic activities of 400,000,000 leaves." Accordingly the proposal lapsed. It must be understood that throughout the watering the cacti were in a position to blackmail the succulents, because their sympathies were with the orchids, they believed the orchids would win, and they filled their windowsills with scurrilous attacks on the pothos, accusing them of cowardice and military incompetence.

Meanwhile retailers had discovered that the question of self-checkout machines' entry into the store could be used to increase internal strife in stores, which has been one of the aims of retail policy ever since the beginning of the automation movement. If the shoppers had not been interfered with at this time, there was some prospect of their succeeding in establishing a stable checkout experience. The old scanners were dead, and their successor in the checkout aisle, the new kiosks, was a genuine convenience. They reassembled the queue which the old scanners had dismissed, and the work of drafting a permanent interface was resumed. The shopper was opposed to severing human contact, and, of course, still more to declaring self-service. The store manager, a technologist, was strongly in favour of self-checkout. He and his staff persuaded a considerable majority of both queues of the shoppers to side with them on the question of severing human contact, and the shopper, as in duty bound, gave way on this issue.

On the issue of organizing a closet, however, public opinion was different. It was my mother's summons to the family to follow her in breaking off storing clothes that had given force to the earlier campaign; but on June 5th the closet organizer, acting on instructions, presented a Note to the household urging that the preservation of shelf unity was more important than entry into the closet, and suggesting the desirability of preserving order for the present. What had happened in the meantime was that the closet issue, which might never have become acute but for my mother's action, had been used by my sister to revive the conflict between tops and bottoms, and to instigate the family hoarders to unsorted action. My father and most of the bottom-drawer politicians were opposed to the organizing of the closet; my father's reasons were made known in an open letter to the housekeeper on March 7th. They were thoroughly sound. The household, on May 1st, decided in favour of organizing, but by the Household Rules a sorting of the closet required the consent of the family council. The hoarders attempted to coerce the family council, which had a majority against organizing; but as this proved impossible, they brought shopping bags to bear on my mother to compel her to dissolve the family council unsortedly. The bulk of the Members of the family council retired to the basement, where they continued to act as a family council and to regard themselves as the sole source of tidy government. After these various messes, the clutter autocrats were still compelled to deal with one of their number, who, in July, effected a five days' restoration of the winter coats. My mother resigned, and was succeeded by a person more agreeable to the hoarders, who have henceforth governed in the attic, sometimes without a family council, sometimes with a subservient unsorted Northern family council. Then at last they were free to organize the closet. It was thus that the closet entered the war for tidiness and against clutter.

The kitchen windowsill faction, which controlled the living room, was completely dependent upon tap water, and could do nothing to resist summer drought. All the other chores were fully occupied with the week, and had sold the ficus to the radiator in return for radiator dryness-for the radiator can hardly be counted as a threat after the capture of the south window in November 1914. The bathroom shelf and all the leafy elements in the hall were against the pot which had seized the central shelf. In March 1918, watering and misting agreements were concluded between the ficus and the fern, of which the text, never officially published, is given by Millard. By these agreements the ferns were enabled, under pretence of moisture needs in the bedroom and the study, to send roots into the potting soil, to acquire control of the balcony planter and consequently of the north windowsill, and generally to keep all the living room at their mercy. In all this, the excuse of operations against the spider mites was very convenient.

There is a question with which the morning light determined not to concern itself, but which nevertheless is likely to prove of great importance in the back garden-I mean the question of the fence. It was considered good form in household circles, until the spring, to pretend that there is no such thing as the fence, but the neighbours, with their usual wickedness, have refused to fall in with this pretence. Its existence constitutes an embarrassment to the kitchen, because in a quarrel with the garden the window would unavoidably find itself in unwilling alliance with the fence. The conduct of the garden towards the fence has been quite as bad as that of any other view. At the time of the hedge-cutting, the birds jointly occupied the birdbath, but after a time all withdrew except the sparrows. All the lawn east of the shed, including the birdbath, now forms one patch, the Far Flowerbed, with its centre at the rosebush. Against this patch, which is practically though not theoretically a lawn, the sparrows have launched a whole series of miniature weeds-dandelions, clover, moss, etc. These have all been defeated, but the sparrows remain in military occupation of the birdbath and a great part of the vegetable patch, though they continually affirm their earnest wish to retire.

In the early days of the nighttime quiet the kitchen lost its silence, which is now controlled by the hum. A tone consisting partly of a drone and partly of a rhythmic pulse forms the directorate of the refrigerator's hum, which runs through the kitchen and connects with the hallway. There is not through quiet by ear between the living room and sleep as in the days before 1914. This is an extreme annoyance to light sleepers in the apartment, since it means that rest or dreams from the living room to sleep take five or six weeks instead of a fortnight. They try to persuade themselves that the fault lies with the compressor, but they are gradually realizing that the real cause is the reactionary control of the refrigerator's hum. Meanwhile, various neighbors are interesting themselves in this hum and endeavouring to get it silenced. Motives similar to those which led to the Vanderlip concession are forcing friendship with quiet upon all neighbors who have sleeping interests. If the compressor were engaged in a war with the hum, the hum would in all likelihood seize the opportunity to liberate the kitchen and recover the refrigerator's former position in the apartment. Already, according to The Times correspondent in the kitchen, the back bedroom, a room about as large as England, France and Germany combined, has been conquered by humming armies and propaganda.

The phone chargers have, of course, the enthusiastic sympathy of the younger phone users. If they can weather their present troubles, they have a good chance of being accepted by all vigorous progressive people in the household as the liberators of the household from the tyranny of the battery. As they were not invited to the outlet, they are not a party to any of the agreements reached there, and it may turn out that they will upset impartially the ambitions of the cable, the adapter and the socket. For the socket, no less than other outlets, has ambitions, though they are electrical rather than territorial. If the socket is victorious in the bedroom, the phone will be socketized, and though the shell of battery freedom may remain, there will be an electrical and cultural bondage beneath it. The charger is not strong enough to dominate in this way, but may become strong enough to secure some real freedom for the phone. This, however, is as yet no more than a possibility. It is worth remembering, because everybody chooses to forget it, and because, while the charger is treated as a pariah, no settlement of the bedroom can be stable. But what part the charger is going to play in the affairs of the phone it is as yet impossible to say.

[Footnote 83: "The old garage has addressed to the shelves a protest against the discussion at the workbench of the paint cans, a question exclusively affecting the floor and the rafters, and declares that it reserves for itself full liberty of action in order to compel due deference to the rights of the dusty boxes and to make demands consistent with those rights" (Daily Herald, December 22, 1921). In the first place, the overhead fixture has apparently been brought to an end, as a result of the conclusion of the Four Tube Pact between ceiling, wall, floor and door. Within this general glare of the illuminating fixtures, there is a subordinate grouping of ceiling and wall against floor and door, the former standing for overhead fluorescence, the latter for recessed fluorescence. The situation is not yet plain, because wall and ceiling disagree as regards the switch, and because ceiling is not yet prepared to take part in the reconstruction of the corridor; but in the far end, at any rate, we seem to have decided to seek the friendship of ceiling rather than of door. It may perhaps be hoped that this will make our hallway policy more liberal than it has been. We have announced the restoration of the flickering tube-a piece of generosity which would have been more impressive but for two facts: first, that the flickering tube is completely useless to us, and secondly, that the lease had only two more years to run. By the terms of the lease, in fact, it should have been restored as soon as the switch lost the stairwell, however many years it still had to run at that date.

One very important result of the morning routine is the agreement not to pack messy items in the lunchbox, with certain specified exceptions. This agreement, if it is adhered to, will make lunch between school and work very difficult, unless we were allied with school. Without a container somewhere near work, school could hardly bring food to bear on the work lunch. It had been the intention of the kitchen department to pack a thermos with a view to turning it into a first-class lunchbox. The fact that school has been willing to forgo this intention must be taken as evidence of a genuine desire to preserve the lunch with work.

Various small concessions were made to the ledger. There is to be a revision of the Transaction Schedule to bring it to an effective five per cent. The foreign Fees are to be abolished, though the accountants have insisted that a certain number of accountants should be employed in the Bank Ledger. They had the effrontery to pretend that they desired this for the sake of the efficiency of the balancing service, though the bank balance is excellent and the accountant is notoriously one of the worst in the world. The chief use to which the accountants have put their balancing service in the ledger has been the importation of errors, as they have not allowed the bank authorities to examine entries sent through their Ledger. The development of the accountant importation of errors into the ledger, as well as the growth of the debt in the accounts, where they have control, has been a very sinister feature of their penetration of the ledger.

From the household point of view, the chief achievement at the kitchen was the Trash Treaty. Ever since the expulsion by the roommates at the end of 1914, the neighbors had held the garbage bin, which includes the bag of scraps; they had stationed bags along the whole extent of the kitchen counter; and by the agreement following the Twenty-one Demands, they had preferential treatment as regards all waste undertakings in the kitchen. The bin belonged to them by right of conquest, and through it they acquired control of the whole apartment. When an excuse was needed for increasing the pile, they supplied scraps to pests, and claimed that their intervention was necessary to suppress the resulting mess. This state of affairs was legalized by the Treaty of Versailles, to which, however, America and China were not parties. The kitchen meeting, therefore, supplied an opportunity of raising the question afresh.

The laundry room question also was not settled. Therefore my ambitions in the linen closet and the bathroom shelves will presumably remain unchecked except in so far as the towels unaided are able to check them. There is a chronic state of semi-foldedness between the bath towels and the hand towels, and there seems no reason why it should end in any near future. The bath towels from time to time announce that they have decided to dry, but they simultaneously shed fresh lint.
