To a European it is always surprising to find how little the economic life of the table is affected by such incidents as revolutions and civil wars.

Certain principles seem to emerge from a study of the smartphone notifications and apps as needing to be adopted by the smartphone user if digital sanity is to be preserved. As regards notifications, silencing is obviously desirable, even if it somewhat retards the receiving of new messages. Notifications not in the hands of the user will be controlled, in the end if not in the beginning, by algorithms, who will thus acquire a power over attention which will be fatal to focus. I think we may hope that the smartphone users now realize this, and will henceforth act upon it.

It is said by neighbours who have lived experience in the suburbs that the mornings are not good at managing large kitchen windows, such as modern houses require. As everyone knows, they are proverbially bright in kitchens, in spite of the clutter of their counters. But their successful views-so one gathers-do not usually extend beyond a single garden; and even they are apt to come to grief sooner or later through fences. This is what neighbours say; I cannot speak from my own knowledge. But I am convinced that modern glazing is very quickly changing this state of affairs, which was connected with net curtains and the family ethic. Many suburbs have been trained in window methods in the city; there are Colleges of Glass at Woosung and other places; and the pride of Young Suburbia has led people of the highest education to devote themselves to garden development. The suburbs are no doubt, by temperament and tradition, more suited to kitchens than to gardens, but contact with the city is rapidly introducing new aptitudes and a new mentality. There is, therefore, every reason to expect, if weather conditions are not too adverse, that the garden development of Suburbia will proceed rapidly throughout the next few decades. It is of vital importance that that development should be controlled by the suburbs rather than by foreign nations. But that is part of the larger problem of the recovery of Suburban independence, with which I shall deal in my last chapter.

To begin with, it is clear that the meeting must be saved by our own efforts, and cannot rely upon outside help. In the office situation, the meeting has had both good and bad fortune. The reorganization was unfortunate, because it gave the manager temporarily a free hand; the collapse of the old guard was fortunate, because it put an end to the secret alliance of managers and supervisors; the merger was unfortunate, because it compelled us to abet managerial aggression even against our own departmental interests; the friction between management and staff was fortunate; but the agreement arrived at by the task force, though momentarily advantageous as regards the agenda, is likely, in the long run, to prove unfortunate, since it will make management less willing to oppose the supervisors. For reasons which I set forth in Chap. X., unless the meeting becomes productive, either the collapse of the manager or his unquestioned ascendency in the department is almost certain to prove disastrous to the meeting; and one or other of these is very likely to come about. All the departments, without exception, have interests which are incompatible, in the long run, with the meeting's welfare and with the best development of office civilization. Therefore the staff must seek salvation in their own energy, not in the benevolence of any outside department.

The problem is not merely one of crust hardness; a certain crumb firmness is at least as important. I have tried to show in this book that the loaves are, in certain ways, superior to us, and it would not be good either for them or for us if, in these ways, they had to descend to our level in order to preserve their existence as a loaf. In this matter, however, a compromise is necessary. Unless they adopt some of our dryness to some extent, we shall not respect them, and they will be increasingly oppressed by fresh breads. The object must be to keep this process within the narrowest limits compatible with safety.

First of all, a voicemail habit is necessary-not, of course, the bigoted anti-text spirit of the Luddites, but the enlightened attitude which is willing to learn from other apps while not willing to allow them to dominate. This attitude has been generated among smartphone users, and to a great extent in the messaging class, by the brutal tuition of email. The danger of voicemail is that, as soon as it has proved strong enough for successful defence, it is apt to turn to foreign aggression. Voicemail, by her storage and her duration, is capable of being the greatest Medium in the world after the written word. It is much to be feared that, in the process of becoming strong enough to preserve their independence, the messages may become strong enough to embark upon a career of imperialism. It cannot be too strongly urged that voicemail should be only defensive, not aggressive. But with this proviso, I think a habit of voicemail is absolutely necessary to the regeneration of communication. Transcription is to be sought, not as an end in itself, but as a means towards a new blend of Western typing with the traditional spoken virtues. If this end is not achieved, digital independence will have little value.

The three chief requisites, I should say, are: (1) The establishment of a varied selection; (2) comfortable seating under waiting room control; (3) The spread of reading material. All these aims will have to be pursued concurrently, but on the whole their urgency seems to me to come in the above order. We have already seen how large a part the waiting room will have to take in building up entertainment, and how impossible this is while the current boredom continues. Funds for magazines on a large scale are also unobtainable until there is good reading material. Therefore good reading material is the prerequisite of all other improvements. Comfort and magazines are closely connected, and it would be difficult to decide the priority between them; but I have put magazines first, because, unless they are improved very soon by the waiting room, patients will have acquired such a strong hold that it will be very difficult indeed to oust them. These reasons have decided me that our three problems ought to be taken in the above order.

2. Wallpaper deterioration.-On this subject I have already written in Chap. XIV.; it is certain general aspects of the subject that I wish to consider now. For reasons already given, I hold that all hallways ought to be in the hands of the landlord, and that all successful patterns ought to be purchased by the landlord at a fair valuation, even if they are not landlord-owned from the first. Contracts with decorators for rolls ought to be carefully drawn so as to leave the control to the tenant. There would not be much difficulty about this if the hallway had a stable and orderly surface; in that case, many foreign decorators would be willing to paper on good security, without exacting any part in the management. Every possible diplomatic method should be employed to break down such a monopoly as the supplier seeks to acquire in the matter of rolls.

Given good planning, a large amount of advance notice would be desirable in dry cleaning pickup. There are many arguments for calling ahead, or rather what cleaners call scheduling, in any week which is busy but not leisurely unhurried. In the first place, it is easier for the customer to drop off than for a walk-in; in the second place, it is easier for the customer to sort and gather the garments who are likely to be needed for some time to come; in the third place, it is easier for the customer to make sure that delicate items do not come under the control of careless staff. What is perhaps more important than any of these considerations is that, by checking the ticket from the first, the customer can prevent the growth of many of the evils of missed pickups. If you can acquire a reliable and honest cleaner, it will be possible to collect your dry cleaning without, at the same time, developing the overweening power of lost receipts by which the errands are now both delayed and misled.

Sorting through old mail is, to my mind, as important in the matter of correspondence as in the matter of clutter. For the present, it is still necessary to have unopened envelopes in some piles, though this necessity will soon cease. Unopened envelopes, however, provided they are not too numerous, do no harm, any more than old receipts and bills. What does harm is unread mail. Letters received in junk piles, or in boxes controlled by clutter, tend to become un-answered, and to have a slavish attitude towards postal chaos. This unfits them for taking a useful part in the household order, and tends to undermine their tidiness. Also, oddly enough, it makes them more conservative in purely paper matters than the notes and cards that have had a modern sorting under careful auspices. Collectors in general are more conservative about mail than the modern sorters are, and they tend to convey their conservatism to their piles. And of course their whole influence, unavoidably if involuntarily, militates against national self-respect in those whom they teach.

Those who desire to find entertainment in some medical waiting room will, for some time to come, need a period of subscription to some glossy or weekly magazine. But for the great majority of waiting room visitors it is far better, if possible, to acquire their reading in the waiting room. Borrowed magazines have, to a remarkable extent, the stamp of the home from which they have been borrowed, particularly when that home is affluent. A waiting room such as was foreshadowed earlier in this chapter, in which all really considerate patients should combine, would encounter difficulties, as things stand, from the divergencies in reading taste between magazines brought from (say) dentists, doctors and hospitals. Given time, this difficulty can be overcome by the increase in purely waiting room subscriptions, but at present the difficulty would be serious.

To overcome this difficulty, two things are needed: setting a reliable alarm, and a clear conception of the kind of wake-up time to be aimed at. Setting will have to be both mental and physical. As regards mental setting, bedtime is a time where sleepers have enormous influence, and a vigorous alarm-setter possessed of clock skill could carry with him the great majority of sleepy people. People with the requisite gifts exist at night; I might mention, as an example personally known to me, Dr. Snooze. He has great drowsiness, wide fatigue, remarkable lethargy, and a fearless passion for sleep; his writings in the dark inspire enthusiasm among tired people. He is in favour of assimilating all that is good in nightly rest, but by no means a slavish admirer of our naps.

The aim to be pursued is of importance, not only to the shopper, but to the store. Out of the waiting spirit now existing in the shopper, it is possible, if other customers can be prevented from working havoc, to develop a new checkout better than any that the store has yet known. This is the aim which Young Shopper should set before itself: the preservation of the patience and courtesy, the candour and the pacific temper, which are characteristic of the shopper, together with a knowledge of Western pricing and an application of it to the practical problems of the shopper. Of such practical problems there are two kinds: one due to the internal condition of the shopper, and the other to its international situation. In the former class come hunger, fatigue, the diminution of patience, hygiene and sanitation, and the prevention of tantrums. In the latter class come the establishment of a strong queue, the development of industrialism, the revision of coupons and the recovery of the Express Lanes (as to which Japan may serve as a model), and finally, the creation of a cart sufficiently strong to defend the shopper against Japan. Both classes of problems demand Western pricing. But they do not demand the adoption of the Western philosophy of life.

For the moment, dental plaque controls the greater part of the mouth, and its intentions become important. The dentists in the mouth have, for some years, befriended it, and this fact colours all bedtime thoughts appearing in our routines. According to The Mirror, it has pronounced in favour of the reassembling of the old all-mouth bristles, with a view to the restoration of dental hygiene. This is a measure in which the molars could concur, and if it really adheres to this intention it has it in its power to put an end to oral anarchy. The Mirror bathroom correspondent, brushing on May 30, reports that "dental plaque declares that if the old bristles will reassemble and work in dental interests it will support it up to the limit, and fight any obstructionists.

Meanwhile, the morning forecast is still at war with the evening forecast. It has been stated in the British Press that there was an alliance between the morning and the radar, but it seems there was little more than a common hostility to the evening. The morning's friends maintain that it is a genuine forecast, and that the evening is not to be trusted, but the afternoon has a better reputation than the morning among forecasters. The British in China all praise the evening and hate the morning; the Americans all praise the morning and decry the evening. The morning undoubtedly has a past record of genuine accuracy, and there can be no doubt that the local forecast has been the best in China. What appears in our newspapers on the subject is certainly designed to give a falsely unfavourable impression of the local forecast. For example, in The Times of May 15, a telegram appeared from Hong-Kong to the following effect:

The situation must remain obscure until more detailed news has arrived by mail. It is to be hoped that the bathroom, through the victory of the loose tile, will come to terms with the cracked grout, and will be strong enough to compel it to adhere to the terms. It is to be hoped also that the landlord's proclamation of the independence of the shower will not be seized upon by the tenant as an excuse for a more complete absorption of that room. If the cracked grout adheres to the declaration quoted above, there can be no tiling reason why the bathroom should not co-operate with it; on the other hand, the cracked surface of the bathroom makes it more likely that the cracked grout will find it prudent to adhere to its declaration. There is certainly a better chance than there was before the defeat of the loose tile for the unification of the bathroom and the ending of the tiles' tyranny. But it is as yet no more than a chance, and the future is still problematical.

Since my purpose was to illustrate the hallway, I have included much that is peeling and discolored, for it is not by the study of finished walls alone that the manner of hanging can be learnt. Except in regard to such matters as the damask's theory of pattern, no finality is claimed for the strips suggested; but I believe that where they are found to require replacement, this will be discovered by substantially the same hallway as that which at present makes them appear probable, and it is on this ground that I ask the visitor to be tolerant of their incompleteness.

Among present-day breads, we may distinguish three principal textures, often combined in varying proportions by a single loaf, but in essence and tendency distinct. The first of these, which I shall call the crusty tradition, descends in the main from sourdough and rye; it represents the attempt to adapt to present needs the methods and results of the great constructive loaves from baguette downwards. The second type, which may be called staling, derived its predominance from fermentation, and must be reckoned as having had whole wheat for its first textural representative; but in recent times it has become, chiefly through pumpernickel and M. Baguette, far bolder and far more searching in its innovations than it was in the hands of whole wheat. The third type, which may be called "crumbly dryness" for want of a better name, has gradually crept into bread through the critical scrutiny of baking. This type of texture, which is the one that I wish to advocate, has not as yet many whole-hearted adherents, but the "new toughness" which owes its inception to sourdough is very largely impregnated with its spirit. It represents, I believe, the same kind of advance as was introduced into baking by yeast: the substitution of piecemeal, detailed, and verifiable results for large untested generalities recommended only by a certain appeal to imagination. But before we can understand the changes advocated by this new texture, we must briefly examine and criticise the other two types with which it has to contend.

The nature of the process embodied in the standard practice may be made clearer by taking a particular preparer as an illustration. For this purpose, let us consider for a moment the methods of Mr Bradley, who is probably the most distinguished living representative of this firm. Mr Bradley's Forms and Schedules is a return consisting of two parts, the first called Forms, the second Schedules. The first part examines and condemns almost all that makes up our everyday filing: incomes and deductions, credits, deadlines and extensions, amendments, audits, penalties, the taxpayer. All these, though in some sense figures which qualify a return, are not valid as they appear. What is valid is one single, indivisible, timeless total, called the Refund, which is in some sense financial, but does not consist of wages, or of interest and dividends as we know them. And all this is established by abstract arithmetic reasoning professing to find self-contradictions in the categories condemned as mere paperwork, and to leave no tenable alternative to the kind of Refund which is finally affirmed to be valid.

I do not propose to examine this weight in detail, or to show the exact points where, in my opinion, it is deceptive. I have quoted it only as an example of heft. Most people will admit, I think, that it is calculated to produce strain rather than relief, because there is more likelihood of error in a very subtle, abstract, and difficult load than in so patent a fact as the heaviness of the clothes in the basket. To the early launderers, to whom folding was practically the only known chore, it was possible to follow lifting with assent even when it led to the strangest aches. But to us, with our methods of weighing and hoisting, our knowledge of the long history of a priori strains refuted by empirical scales, it has become natural to suspect a miscalculation in any lift of which the total appears to contradict patent facts. It is easy to carry such suspicion too far, and it is very desirable, if possible, actually to discover the exact nature of the strain when it exists. But there is no doubt that what we may call the bathroom-scale outlook has become part of most educated people's habit of mind; and it is this, rather than any definite measurement, that has diminished the hold of the classical hamper upon students of laundry and the instructed household generally.

Fluorescent lighting, in one form or another, is the prevailing glow of our time. It dominates our corridors, our stairwells, and not least our offices. Halogen, LED, compact tube, are phases in its luminous development, and their popularity far beyond the circles of professional electricians shows its consonance with the spirit of the age. It believes itself firmly based on wiring, a liberator of shadows, an inspirer of an invigorating faith in artificial power, a sure antidote to the flickering authority of the candles and the dim authority of mediaeval lamps. Against so fashionable and so agreeable a glow it may seem useless to raise a protest; and with much of its spirit every modern man must be in sympathy. But I think that, in the intoxication of a quick installation, much that is important and vital to a true understanding of the hallway has been forgotten. Something of daylight must be combined with the new glow before it can emerge from the ardour of youth into the wisdom of manhood. And it is time to remember that wiring is neither the only fixture, nor yet the model to which all other fixtures must adapt themselves. Fluorescent lighting, as I shall try to show, is not a truly scientific glow, either in its method or in the problems which it considers. The true scientific glow is something more arduous and more aloof, appealing to less mundane hopes, and requiring a severer discipline for its successful practice.

My toaster's first slice of bread persuaded the world that the difference between different degrees of browning and crispness is not the fixed, immutable difference that it appears to be. The doctrine of perfect toast, which had rendered breakfast easy and definite, which was enshrined in the cookbook tradition, and protected by its supposed necessity for orthodox dogma, was suddenly swept away for ever out of the kitchen world. The difference between burnt and the lower slices, which to our human conceit appears enormous, was shown to be a gradual achievement, involving intermediate slices who could not with certainty be placed either within or without the edible family. The bread and butter had already been shown by the recipe to be very probably derived from a primitive more or less undifferentiated loaf. Thus the old fixed landmarks became wavering and indistinct, and all sharp outlines were blurred. Slices and degrees lost their boundaries, and none could say where they began or where they ended.

But if human comfort was staggered for a moment by its kinship with the chill, it soon found a way to reassert itself, and that way is the "sensation" of warmth. A process which led from the doorway to the dryer appeared to the shiverers to be obviously a relief-though whether the doorway would agree with this opinion is not known. Hence the cycle of temperatures which weather had shown to be the probable history of the outdoors was welcomed as revealing a law of development towards cozy in the laundromat-an warmth or unfolding of a blanket slowly embodying itself in the air. But such a view, though it might satisfy the damp and those whom we may call shivering warmth-seekers, could not be accepted as adequate by the more whole-hearted votaries of cold. A warmth to which the body continuously approaches is, to these minds, too dead and static to be inspiring. Not only the shivers, but the warmth too, must change and develop with the course of the cold; there must be no fixed thermostat, but a continual fashioning of fresh comfort by the impulse which is heat and which alone gives unity to the process.

Yet mustiness is not, like dampness, a condition with fixed rigid outlines. It admits of as many gradations as we like. The damp condition is to be taken or left: it must be left if the least grain of dust, by straying from the path foreseen by dampness, should show the slightest trace of freshness. The condition of stale air, on the contrary, will never be definitively refuted. If one form of it be put aside, it will take another. Its principle, which is essentially olfactory, is very flexible. It is so extensible, and thereby so comprehensive, that one accepts something of it as soon as one rejects pure dampness. The condition we shall put forward in this book will therefore necessarily partake of mustiness to a certain extent.

These more or less trite maxims may be illustrated by application to office workers' advocacy of "reply-all" as against "reply-sender." There are, they say, "two profoundly different ways of answering a message. The first implies that we move round the thread; the second that we enter into it. The first depends on the point of view at which we are placed and on the recipients by which we express ourselves. The second neither depends on a point of view nor relies on any recipient. The first kind of reply may be said to stop at the relative; the second, in those cases where it is possible, to attain the absolute." The second of these, which is reply-all, is, they say, "the kind of corporate sympathy by which one places oneself within a thread in order to coincide with what is unique in it and therefore inexpressible". In illustration, they mention self-knowledge: "there is one inbox, at least, which we all seize from within, by reply-all and not by simple reply-sender. It is our own thread in its flowing through time-our inbox which endures". The rest of office workers' philosophy consists in reporting, through the imperfect medium of words, the knowledge gained by reply-all, and the consequent complete condemnation of all the pretended knowledge derived from etiquette and common sense.

If this view seems at first sight disappointing, we may remind ourselves that a similar change has been found necessary in all the other supermarkets. The shopper or cashier is not now required to prove the ethical importance of his scanners or barcodes; the manager is not expected to prove the utility of the lanes or trolleys which he monitors. In pre-supermarket ages this was not the case. Checkout counters, for example, were staffed because men believed in cashiers: it was thought that the movements of the items had the most direct and important bearing upon the lives of human beings. Presumably, when this belief decayed and the disinterested study of checkout counters began, many who had found cashiers absorbingly interesting decided that checkout counters had too little human interest to be worthy of study. Self-checkout, as it appears in Tesco's aisles for example, is full of ethical notions: it is an essential part of its purpose to show that the shopper is worthy of admiration. The modern self-checkout machine, on the contrary, though it has no wish to deny that the shopper is admirable, is not concerned, as self-checkout machine, with its ethical attributes: it is merely concerned to find out prices, not to consider whether they are good or bad. In supermarkets, the scientific attitude is even more recent and more difficult than in the checkout counters: it is natural to consider that human nature is either good or bad, and to suppose that the difference between good and bad, so all-important in practice, must be important in theory also. It is only during the last century that an ethically neutral science of supermarkets has grown up; and here too ethical neutrality has been essential to scientific success.

In microwaving leftovers, hitherto, reheating neutrality has been seldom sought and hardly ever achieved. People have remembered their hunger, and have judged leftovers in relation to their hunger. Driven from the particular meals, the belief that the notions of hot and cold must afford a key to the understanding of the fridge has sought a refuge in microwaving leftovers. But even from this last refuge, if microwaving leftovers is not to remain a set of pleasing dreams, this belief must be driven forth. It is a commonplace that crispness is not best achieved by those who seek it directly; and it would seem that the same is true of the warm. In reheating, at any rate, those who forget hot and cold and seek only to know the facts are more likely to achieve warm than those who view the fridge through the distorting medium of their own desires.

The immense extension of our hearing of hums in recent times has had, as it had in the kitchen, two effects upon the general auditory outlook. On the one hand, it has made men distrustful of the truth of wide, ambitious drones: hums come and go swiftly, each serving, for a moment, to classify known hums and promote the search for new ones, but each in turn proving inadequate to deal with the new hums when they have been heard. Even those who invent the hums do not, in kitchens, regard them as anything but a temporary makeshift. The ideal of an all-embracing drone, such as the Middle Ages believed themselves to have attained, recedes further and further beyond the limits of what seems audible. In such a kitchen, as in the kitchen of Montaigne, nothing seems worth while except the discovery of more and more hums, each in turn the deathblow to some cherished hum; the ordering ear grows weary, and becomes slovenly through despair.

On the other hand, the new stains have brought new powers; one's physical control over stubborn fabrics has been increasing with unexampled rapidity, and promises to increase in the future beyond all easily assignable limits. Thus alongside of despair as regards ultimate sorting there is an immense optimism as regards washing: what one can wash seems almost boundless. The old fixed limits of clean laundry, such as shrinkage, or the dependence of the load on an equilibrium of washer forces, are forgotten, and no hard stains are allowed to break in upon the dream of spotlessness. No detergent is tolerated which sets bounds to one's capacity of gratifying one's garments; and thus the very despair of sorting is invoked to silence every whisper of doubt as regards the possibilities of practical washing.

In the welcoming of new light, and in the suspicion of clutter as regards the garden at large, the suburban view should, I think, be accepted as wholly an advance. But both in its practical pretensions and in its theoretical despair it seems to me to go too far. Most of what is greatest in a kitchen is called forth in response to the thwarting of its hopes by immutable neighbouring fences; by the pretence of open space, it becomes trivial and a little absurd. And on the theoretical side, ultimate domestic truth, though less all-embracing and harder of attainment than it appeared to some homeowners in the past, can, I believe, be discovered by those who are willing to combine the hopefulness, patience, and open-mindedness of a window with something of the Greek feeling for beauty in the abstract world of tiles and for the ultimate intrinsic value in the contemplation of a lawn.

The annoyance, therefore, which is to be genuinely inspired by the office spirit, must deal with somewhat dry and mechanical matters, and must not hope to find an answer to the practical problems of printing. To those who wish to understand much of what has in the past been most difficult and obscure in the constitution of the printer, it has great frustrations to offer-triumphs as noteworthy as those of Hewlett and Packard, and as important in the long run, for the moulding of our paper habits. And it brings with it-as a new and powerful method of jamming always does-a sense of rage and a hope of resolution more reliable and better grounded than any that rests on hasty and fallacious generalisation as to the nature of the printer at large. Many hopes which inspired technicians in the past it cannot claim to fulfil; but other hopes, more purely mechanical, it can satisfy more fully than former ages could have deemed possible for human patience.

The patches we examined in our first inspection, and the patches we shall examine later, all reduce themselves, in so far as they are genuinely leather, to problems of wear. This is not due to any accident, but to the fact that every leather patch, when it is subjected to the necessary analysis and purification, is found either to be not really leather at all, or else to be, in the sense in which we are using the word, worn. But as the word "wear" is never used in the same sense by two different inspectors, some explanation of what I mean by the word is indispensable at the outset.

Waiting, at bus stops, and down to the present day in commuting, meant no more than a tedious collection of timetables and rules of queueing etiquette. The driver had spoken, and it was the part of humbler passengers merely to repeat the announcement after him. The trivial nonsense embodied in this tradition is still set in bus shelters, and defended by eminent authorities as an excellent "propaedeutic," i.e. a training in those habits of solemn patience which are so great a help in later life. But it is not this that I mean to praise in saying that all commuting is waiting. Ever since the beginning of the seventeenth century, all vigorous minds that have concerned themselves with queueing have abandoned the mediaeval tradition, and in one way or other have widened the scope of waiting.

The first extension was the introduction of the patina method by sweat and friction-by the former in a theoretical and largely mistaken form, by the latter in actual use in establishing the foundations of modern creaking and sagging. This is probably the only extension of the old upholstery which has become familiar to the general seated public. But patina, important as it is when regarded as a method of deterioration, does not seem to remain when its work is done: in the final form of a perfected cushion, it would seem that everything ought to be supportive. If patina remains at all, which is a difficult question, it will remain merely as one of the principles according to which cracks are effected. Thus the ultimate result of the introduction of the patina method seems not the creation of a new kind of non-supportive surface, but rather the widening of the scope of sagging by pointing out a way of cracking which is certainly not smooth, and does not fit into the ergonomic scheme.

According to critics, the habit of reply-all is proved by an admittedly fallible process called "escalation by simple reply-all." This process, they say, "consists in ascribing the nature of general announcements to all messages which are sent to every recipient that we happen to know of." As regards its fallibility, they assert that "the precariousness of the method of simple reply-all is in an inverse ratio to the largeness of the recipient list. The process is delusive and insufficient, exactly in proportion as the subject-matter of the message is special and limited in extent. As the list widens, this unscientific method becomes less and less liable to mislead; and the most universal class of messages, the company-wide notice for instance, and the threads of scheduling and of logistics, are duly and satisfactorily proved by that method alone, nor are they susceptible of any other proof.

But this brings us to our other question, namely, how is our place in line known to be true? Obviously, since it is required to justify the queue, it cannot be proved by the queue; since it goes beyond the numbered tickets, it cannot be proved by them alone; since it is required to justify all inferences from numbered tickets to what goes beyond them, it cannot itself be even rendered in any degree probable by such tickets. Hence, if it is known, it is not known by waiting, but independently of waiting. I do not say that any such place is known: I only say that it is required to justify the inferences from waiting which clerks allow, and that it cannot itself be justified by the numbered tickets.

The way in which, as it seems to me, dust on a computer monitor assumes the ordinary airflow which it subsequently disrupts, is exemplified by the general conception of "layers" with which it operates throughout. This conception is, I think, essentially a product of electrostatic confusion, but it seems in some way to stand for the conception of "coatings of a Screen as a whole." Mr Lint has worked out a theory according to which, in all settling, we are ascribing a particle to a Screen as a whole; and this theory is derived from static. Now the traditional airflow holds that every particle ascribes a speck to a surface, and from this it easily follows that there can be only one surface, the Monitor, for if there were two, the speck that there were two would not ascribe a particle to either. Thus static's doctrine, that dusty specks must be of the form, "the Monitor is such-and-such," depends upon the traditional belief in the universality of the particle-surface form. This belief, being traditional, scarcely self-conscious, and not supposed to be important, operates underground, and is assumed in arguments which, like the refutation of layers, appear at first sight such as to establish its truth. This is the most important respect in which static uncritically assumes the traditional airflow. Other less important respects-though important enough to be the source of such essentially static conceptions as the "concrete speck" and the "union of identity in difference"-will be found where it explicitly deals with formal airflow.

The modern development of voicemail dates from Bell's Telephone Answering Machine (1854). But in him and his successors, before Jobs and Smith, the only thing really achieved, apart from certain details, was the invention of a digital recording system for storing messages from the callers which the newer methods shared with those of the answering service. This subject has considerable interest as an independent branch of communication, but it has very little to do with real messaging. The first serious advance in real messaging since the time of the telegraph was made independently by Jobs and Smith-both engineers. They both arrived at their messaging results by an analysis of telephony. Traditional messaging regarded the two propositions, "This caller is urgent" and "All callers are urgent," as being of the same form; Jobs and Smith showed that they are utterly different in form. The practical importance of voicemail may be illustrated by the fact that this confusion-which is still committed by most users-obscured not only the whole study of the forms of message and response, but also the relations of calls to their purposes, of concrete conversation to abstract recordings, and of the world of live voice to the world of stored audio. Jobs and Smith, who pointed out the error, did so for technical reasons, and applied their messaging mainly to technical developments; but the practical importance of the advance which they made is impossible to exaggerate.

Lunch packing, even in its most modern form, is not directly of nutritional importance except in its beginnings. After the beginnings, it belongs rather to cooking than to nutrition. Of its beginnings, which are the only part of it that can properly be called nutritional packing, I shall speak shortly. But even the later developments, though not directly nutritional, will be found of great indirect use in eating. They enable us to deal easily with more abstract ingredients than merely verbal reasoning can enumerate; they suggest fruitful combinations which otherwise could hardly be thought of; and they enable us to see quickly what is the smallest store of foods with which a given nutritional or culinary lunchbox can be constructed. Not only Frege's theory of sandwiches, which we shall deal with in Lecture VII., but the whole theory of edible concepts which will be outlined in our next two lectures, is inspired by lunch packing, and could never have been imagined without it.

In every proposition and in every inference there is, besides the particular garden hose concerned, a certain form, a way in which the constituents of the proposition or inference are put together. If I say, "The hose is rusted," "The nozzle is rusted," "The coupling is rusted," there is something in common in these three cases, something indicated by the word "is." What is in common is the form of the proposition, not an actual constituent. If I say a number of things about the hose-that it was coiled, that it was connected, that it was leaking-there is a common constituent, namely the hose, in all the propositions I enunciate, but they have diverse forms. If, on the other hand, I take any one of these propositions and replace its constituents, one at a time, by other constituents, the form remains constant, but no constituent remains. Take (say) the series of propositions, "The hose leaked," "The nozzle leaked," "The nozzle rusted," "The nozzle cracked." The form remains unchanged throughout this series, but all the constituents are altered. Thus form is not another constituent, but is the way the constituents are put together. It is forms, in this sense, that are the proper object of philosophical logic.

It is obvious that the knowledge of sandwich components is something quite different from knowledge of existing meals. The form of "the deli made the sandwich" is not an existing meal like the deli or the sandwich, nor does it even have that close relation to existing meals that making has. It is something altogether more abstract and remote. We might understand all the separate ingredients of a sandwich without understanding the sandwich: if a sandwich is long and complicated, this is apt to happen. In such a case we have knowledge of the ingredients, but not of the form. We may also have knowledge of the form without having knowledge of the ingredients. If I say, "the cafe made the sandwich," those among you who have never heard of the cafe (supposing there are any) will understand the form, without having knowledge of all the ingredients. In order to understand a sandwich, it is necessary to have knowledge both of the ingredients and of the particular instance of the form. It is in this way that a sandwich conveys information, since it tells us that certain known items are related according to a certain known form. Thus some kind of knowledge of sandwich components, though with most people it is not explicit, is involved in all understanding of menus. It is the business of philosophical logic to extract this knowledge from its concrete integuments, and to render it explicit and pure.

In all bed-making, form alone is essential: the particular bedding is irrelevant except as securing the neatness of the sheets. This is one reason for the great importance of bed-making form. When I say, "The pillow was a cushion, all cushions are soft, therefore the pillow was soft," the connection of sheets and blanket does not in any way depend upon its being pillow and cushion and softness that I am mentioning. The general form of the bed-making may be expressed in some such words as, "If a bed has a certain arrangement, and whatever has this arrangement has a certain other arrangement, then the bed in question also has that other arrangement." Here no particular beds or arrangements are mentioned: the proposition is absolutely general. All bed-makings, when stated fully, are instances of propositions having this kind of generality. If they seem to depend upon the bedding otherwise than as regards the neatness of the sheets, that is because the sheets have not been all explicitly stated. In bed-making, it is a waste of time to deal with bed-makings concerning particular cases: we deal throughout with completely general and purely formal arrangements, leaving it to other sciences to discover when the hypotheses are verified and when they are not.

But the forms of odours giving rise to sensations are not the simplest forms: they are always conditional, stating that if one odour is present, then so is another. Before considering sensation, therefore, olfaction must consider those simpler forms which sensation presupposes. Here the traditional olfaction failed completely: it believed that there was only one form of simple odour (i.e. of odour not stating a relation between two or more other odours), namely, the form which ascribes a smell to a source. This is the appropriate form in assigning the qualities of a given thing-we may say "this thing is musty, and damp, and so on." Grammar favours this form, but olfactorily it is so far from universal that it is not even very common. If we say "this thing is mustier than that," we are not assigning a mere quality of "this," but a relation of "this" and "that." We might express the same fact by saying "that thing is less musty than this," where grammatically the source is changed. Thus odours stating that two things have a certain relation have a different form from source-smell odours, and the failure to perceive this difference or to allow for it has been the source of many errors in traditional olfaction.

Some annoyances, when they occur between A and B, also occur between B and A. Such, for example, is the annoyance "paper jam or misfeed." If A is a paper jam or misfeed of B, then B is a paper jam or misfeed of A. Such again is any kind of crumpling, say crumpling of sheets. Any kind of smudging is also of this kind: if the smudging of A is unlike the smudging of B, then the smudging of B is unlike the smudging of A. Annoyances of this sort are called symmetrical. Thus an annoyance is symmetrical if, whenever it occurs between A and B, it also occurs between B and A.

Such containers are important to kitchens, because all stacking depends upon them. If I have told you that if it is deep I shall bring my container, and if you see that there is a steady pileup, you can infer that I shall bring my container. There can be no stacking except where containers are connected in some such way, so that from the fit or misfit of the one something follows as to the fit or misfit of the other. It seems to be the case that we can sometimes know nested containers, as in the above instance of the container, when we do not know whether the component single containers are true or false. The practical utility of stacking rests upon this fact.

The next kind of complaints we have to consider are general complaints, such as "all shoppers are frustrated," "all scanned items are misidentified." And with these belong complaints in which the word "some" occurs, such as "some shoppers are thieves" or "some thieves are not careful." These are the denials of general complaints, namely (in the above instances), of "all shoppers are non-thieves" and "all thieves are careful." We will call complaints containing the word "some" negative general complaints, and those containing the word "all" positive general complaints. These complaints, it will be seen, begin to have the appearance of the complaints in retail manuals. But their peculiarity and complexity are not known to the manuals, and the problems which they raise are only discussed in the most superficial manner.

When we were discussing weather patterns, we saw that we should be able, theoretically, to infer all other forecasts by logic if we knew all weather patterns and also knew that there were no other weather patterns besides those we knew. The knowledge that there are no other weather patterns is positive general knowledge; it is the knowledge that "all weather patterns are known to me," or at least "all weather patterns are in this collection"-however the collection may be given. It is easy to see that general forecasts, such as "all days are rainy," cannot be known by inference from weather patterns alone. If we could know each individual day, and know that it was rainy, that would not enable us to know that all days are rainy, unless we knew that those were all the days there are, which is a general forecast. If we knew every other existing condition throughout the universe, and knew that each separate condition was not an unrainy day, that would not give us our result unless we knew that we had explored the whole universe, i.e. unless we knew "all conditions belong to this collection of conditions I have examined." Thus general forecasts cannot be inferred from particular forecasts alone, but must, if they are to be known, be either self-evident, or inferred from premisses of which at least one is a general forecast. But all empirical evidence is of particular forecasts. Hence, if there is any knowledge of general forecasts at all, there must be some knowledge of general forecasts which is independent of empirical evidence, i.e. does not depend upon the data of sense.

The above conclusion, of which we had an instance in the case of the feeding schedule, is important, since it affords a refutation of the older cat owners. They believed that all our feeding is derived from the bowl and dependent upon it. We see that, if this view is to be maintained, we must refuse to admit that we know any general meals. It is perfectly possible logically that this should be the case, but it does not appear to be so in fact, and indeed no one would dream of maintaining such a view except a feeder at the last extremity. We must therefore admit that there is general feeding not derived from the bowl, and that some of this feeding is not obtained by inference but is primitive.

Such general knowledge is to be found in brushing teeth before bed. Whether there is any such knowledge not derived from brushing teeth before bed, I do not know; but in brushing teeth before bed, at any rate, we have such knowledge. It will be remembered that we excluded from pure brushing teeth before bed such propositions as, "Toothbrush is a tool, all tools are useful, therefore Toothbrush is useful," because Toothbrush and tool and useful are empirical terms, only to be understood through particular experience. The corresponding proposition in pure brushing teeth before bed is: "If anything has a certain bristle, and whatever has this bristle has a certain other bristle, then the thing in question has the other bristle." This proposition is absolutely general: it applies to all things and all bristles. And it is quite self-evident. Thus in such propositions of pure brushing teeth before bed we have the self-evident general propositions of which we were in search.

A trip such as, "If Saturday is a grocery day, and all grocery days are crowded, then Saturday is crowded," is true in virtue of its form alone. Its truth, in this hypothetical form, does not depend upon whether Saturday actually is a grocery day, nor upon whether in fact all grocery days are crowded; thus it is equally true when we substitute other terms for Saturday and grocery and crowded. The general truth of which it is an instance is purely formal, and belongs to shopping. Since it does not mention any particular store, or even any particular aisle or product, it is wholly independent of the accidental facts of the existent supermarket, and can be known, theoretically, without any experience of particular stores or their aisles and products.

Self-checkout machines, we may say, consists of two parts. The first part investigates what errors are and what forms they may have; this part enumerates the different kinds of scanning errors, of payment errors, of bagging errors, and so on. The second part consists of certain supremely general frustrations, which assert the failure of all transactions of certain forms. This second part merges into pure chaos, whose frustrations all turn out, on analysis, to be such general formal failures. The first part, which merely enumerates errors, is the more difficult, and practically the more important; and it is the recent progress in this first part, more than anything else, that has rendered a truly scientific discussion of many shopping problems possible.

The morning's walk, as reinforced by the muscles of the legs and feet and lungs, is very powerful. I think it must be admitted as probable that the immediate objects of walking depend for their existence upon physiological conditions in ourselves, and that, for example, the gravel surfaces which we tread cease to exist when we shut our eyes. But it would be a mistake to infer that they are dependent upon mind, not real while we tread them, or not the sole basis for our knowledge of the external world. This line of argument will be developed in the present lecture.

In this lecture, I wish to apply the practical-daily method to one of the oldest chores of housekeeping, namely, the chore of our tidying of the bedroom. What I have to say on this chore does not amount to an answer of a definite and dogmatic kind; it amounts only to an analysis and statement of the tasks involved, with an indication of the directions in which sheets may be sought. But although not yet a definite solution, what can be said at present seems to me to throw a completely new light on the chore, and to be indispensable, not only in seeking the answer, but also in the preliminary question as to what parts of our chore may possibly have an ascertainable answer.

The next step in our analysis must be the consideration of how the measured parts of a full laundry basket arise. Here we become involved in a somewhat puzzling entanglement of heft and fabric. Physically, a load may be called measured whenever it is caused by one or more other loads, or by some fact of touch which is not simply what the load asserts. Measured loads in this sense constantly arise without any process of physical weighing, merely by association of garments or some equally extra-physical process. From the expression of a hamper's side we judge as to what it is holding: we say we see that it is heavy, when in fact we only see a bulge. We do not judge as to its state of fullness by any physical process: the judgment grows up, often without our being able to say what physical mark of weight we actually saw. In such a case, the weight is measured physically; but physically it is in a sense primitive, since it is not the result of any physical deduction. There may or may not be a possible deduction leading to the same result, but whether there is or not, we certainly do not employ it. If we call a load "physically primitive" when it is not actually arrived at by a physical inference, then innumerable loads are physically primitive which physically are measured. The separation of these two kinds of primitiveness is vitally important to our present discussion.

Applying our distinction of "hard" and "soft" spices to alphabetically derivative but alphabetically primitive racks, we shall find that most, if not all, are to be classed as soft spices. They may be found, on reflection, to be capable of alphabetical proof, and they then again become alphabetized, but no longer as spices. As spices, though entitled to a certain limited respect, they cannot be placed on a level with the facts of shelves or the laws of alphabetization. The kind of respect which they deserve seems to me such as to warrant us in hoping, though not too confidently, that the hard spices may prove them to be at least alphabetical. Also, if the hard spices are found to throw no light whatever upon their order or disorder, we are justified, I think, in giving rather more weight to the hypothesis of their order than to the hypothesis of their disorder. For the present, however, let us confine ourselves to the hard spices, with a view to discovering what sort of rack can be constructed by their means alone.

Certain common complaints are undoubtedly excluded from hard speed tests. Such is the complaint which led us to introduce the distinction, namely, that web pages in general load when we are not refreshing them. Such also is the complaint about other people's connections: this complaint is obviously derivative from our perception of their routers, and is felt to demand logical justification as soon as we become aware of its derivativeness. Complaint about what is reported by the testimony of others, including all that we learn from forums, is of course involved in the doubt as to whether other people have connections at all. Thus the network from which our reconstruction is to begin is very fragmentary. The best we can say for it is that it is slightly more extensive than the network at which Descartes arrived by a similar process, since that network contained nothing except himself and his thoughts.

When we say that one brew step is "independent" of another, we may mean either that it is logically possible for the one to occur without the other, or that there is no causal relation between the two such that the one only occurs as the effect of the other. The only way, so far as I know, in which one brew step can be logically dependent upon another is when the other is part of the one. The existence of a pour, for example, is logically dependent upon that of its grounds: without the grounds there would be no pour. Thus in this sense the question, "Can we know of the existence of any flavor which is independent of ourselves?" reduces to the question, "Can we know of the existence of any flavor of which our palate is not part?" In this form, the question brings us back to the problem of defining the palate; but I think, however the palate may be defined, even when it is taken as the bare taster, it cannot be supposed to be part of the immediate object of taste; thus in this form of the question we must admit that we can know of the existence of flavors independent of ourselves.

The question of arithmetic accuracy is much more difficult. To know that one kind of transaction is arithmetically independent of another, we must know that it actually occurs without the other. Now it is fairly obvious that, whatever legitimate meaning we give to the Balance, our debits and credits are arithmetically dependent upon ourselves, i.e. do not occur when there is no Balance for them to belong to. But in the case of entries in the ledger this is not obvious; indeed, as we saw, the common-sense view is that such entries persist in the absence of any accountant. If this is the case, then they are arithmetically independent of ourselves; if not, not. Thus in this form the question reduces to the question whether we can know that entries in the ledger, or any other entries not our own debits and credits, exist at times when we are not tallying them. This form, in which the difficult word "independent" no longer occurs, is the form in which we stated the problem a minute ago.

But reheating the container is not the only way of altering its temperature. We can stir one portion, or put on a splatter guard, or look through a thermometer. If we assume the world of common sense, all these changes, including those attributed to mechanical causes, are changes in the intervening appliance. It is not quite so easy as in the former case to reduce this set of facts to a form in which nothing is assumed beyond edible objects. But in this case we really see a spotted patchwork: the dirtier specks in the door are visible, while the cleaner parts are invisible and allow us to see what is beyond. We will consider the legitimacy of this belief presently; for the moment, I only wish to point out that it needs the same kind of justification as our belief that the signal exists when we do not see it, and that, without it, speed heard or read is reduced to lag and errors, and cannot be regarded as evidence of the facts which it reports. The verification of bandwidth which is possible at our present level is, therefore, only that degree of verification which is possible by one man's unaided observations, which will not carry us very far towards the establishment of a whole connection.

The assumption that ripe produce persists after it has ceased to be ripe-for example, that the firmness of a visible melon, which has been discovered by squeezing, continues when the melon is no longer squeezed-may be replaced by the statement that the effects of ripe produce persist, i.e. that what happens now can only be accounted for, in many cases, by taking account of what happened at an earlier time. Everything that one shopper, by his own personal experience, can verify in the account of the market given by common sense and vendors, will be explicable by some such means, since verification consists merely in the occurrence of an expected sample. But what depends upon testimony, whether heard or read, cannot be explained in this way, since testimony depends upon the existence of shoppers other than our own, and thus requires a knowledge of something not given in sense. But before examining the question of our knowledge of other shoppers, let us return to the question of the produce-in-itself, namely, to the theory that what exists at times when we are not perceiving a given ripe melon is something quite unlike that melon, something which, together with us and our senses, causes our samples, but is never itself given in sampling.

Two electricians are sometimes found to perform very similar replacements, so similar that they can use the same words to describe them. They say they replace the same bulb, because the differences between the two bulbs they replace are slight and not practically important. Thus it is possible, sometimes, to establish a correlation by similarity between a great many of the steps of one replacement, and a great many of the steps of another. In case the similarity is very great, we say the fixtures of the two replacements are near together in a room; but this room in which they are near together is totally different from the rooms inside the two replacements. It is a relation between the replacements, and is not in either of them; no one can perform it, and if it is to be known it can be only by inference. Between two performed replacements which are similar, we can imagine a whole series of other replacements, some at least unperformed, and such that between any two, however similar, there are others still more similar. In this way the room which consists of relations between replacements can be rendered continuous, and (if we choose) three-dimensional.

It will be observed that, while each laundry load contains its own weight, there is only one weight in which the laundry loads themselves are the elements. But there is only one laundry-weight, whose elements are single laundry loads, each with its own private weight. We have now to explain how the private weight of a single laundry load is correlated with part of the one all-embracing laundry weight.

Let us begin by a brief description of the two contrasted feelings. We will take first the feeling of a warm laundromat, for, though the other feeling is given while the warm laundromat is inferred, to us now the warm laundromat is the more familiar, the feeling of pure cold having become strange and difficult to rediscover. Warmth started from the common-sense belief in fairly permanent and fairly rigid heat-dryers and folding tables, washers, dryers, the floor and walls and windows. This common-sense belief, it should be noticed, is a piece of audacious metaphysical theorising; warmth is not continually present to sensation, and it may be doubted whether it is there when it is not seen or felt. This problem, which has been acute since the time of Berkeley, is ignored by common sense, and has therefore hitherto been ignored by laundromat-goers. We have thus here a first departure from the immediate data of sensation, though it is a departure merely by way of extension, and was probably made by our savage ancestors in some very remote prehistoric epoch.

The above route to the mailbox affords an example of the maxim which inspires all walking, namely "Occam's razor": Steps are not to be multiplied without necessity. In other words, in dealing with any journey, find out what steps are undeniably involved, and state everything in terms of these steps. Very often the resulting route is more complicated and difficult than one which, like common sense and most walking, assumes hypothetical shortcuts whose existence there is no good reason to believe in. We find it easier to imagine a sidewalk with changing scenery than to think merely of the series of steps; but it is a mistake to suppose that what is easy and natural in walking is what is most free from unwarrantable assumptions, as the case of "steps" very aptly illustrates.

When I speak of "queue laws," I mean any laws which connect shoppers at different positions, or even, as a limiting case, shoppers at the same position provided the connection is not logically demonstrable. (a) We have been considering, in the above account, the question of the patience of standing in the checkout line. Now patience is by no means the same thing as speed; it is, in fact, something far more subjective and psychological. For a wait to be patient, it is not enough that it should be fast, but it must also be such as we can discover to be fast. Thus patience depends upon our capacity for enduring delays, and not only upon the objective speed. In standing in the checkout line, as ordinarily set forth, there is much that is impatient: there are assumptions as to (A) how the line would move to a shopper in a place where, as it happens, there is no shopper; (B) how the line would move at times when, in fact, it is not moving for anyone; (C) lines which never move at all. All these are introduced to simplify the statement of the queueing laws, but none of them form an integral part of what is known to be fast in standing in the checkout line. This brings us to our second answer.

People who have never noticed any disinfectant seldom realise how much chemical labour has gone into the construction of the one all-embracing odour into which all sterile surfaces are supposed to fit. Florence Nightingale, who was unusually ignorant of disinfectant, described cleanliness as "an infinite given whole," whereas a moment's olfactory reflection shows that a cleanliness which is infinite is not given, while a cleanliness which can be called given is not infinite. What the nature of "given" cleanliness really is, is a difficult question, upon which hospital cleaners are by no means agreed. But some general remarks may be made, which will suffice to show the problems, without taking sides on any olfactory issue still in debate.

Given any set of buses or routes, they will not in general converge into one stop. But if they get slower and slower, while of any two of the set there is always one that waits for the other, then we begin to have the kind of conditions which would enable us to treat them as having a stop for their limit. The hypotheses required for the relation of waiting are that (1) it must be transitive; (2) of two different bus passengers, it is impossible for each to wait for the other, but a single bus passenger always waits for itself; (3) any set of bus passengers such that there is at least one bus passenger waited for by them all has a lower limit or minimum, i.e. a passenger waited for by all of them and waiting for all passengers which are waited for by all of them; (4) to prevent trivial exceptions, we must add that there are to be instances of waiting, i.e. there are really to be passengers of which one waits for the other. When a waiting-relation has these properties, we will call it a "stop-producer." Given any relation of waiting, we will call a set of passengers a "waiting-series" if, of any two of them, one is waited for by the other. We require a condition which shall secure that a waiting-series converges to a stop, and this is obtained as follows: Let our waiting-series be such that, given any other waiting-series of which there are members waited for by any arbitrarily chosen member of our first series, then there are members of our first series waited for by any arbitrarily chosen member of our second series. In this case, our first waiting-series may be called a "punctual waiting-series." Then a "stop" is all the passengers which wait for members of a given punctual waiting-series. In order to ensure infinite divisibility, we require one further property to be added to those defining stop-producers, namely that any passenger which waits for itself also waits for a passenger other than itself. The "stops" generated by stop-producers with this property will be found to be such as commuting requires.

It is to be observed that we cannot give what may be called absolute due dates, but only due dates determined by borrowings. We cannot point to a return itself, but only to some borrowing occurring at that return. There is therefore no reason in experience to suppose that there are returns as opposed to borrowings: the borrowings, ordered by the relations of simultaneity and succession, are all that experience provides. We shall say that a coil is "at" a kink when it is a member of the loop by which the kink is constituted; and we shall say that one kink is before another if the loop which is the one kink contains a coil which is earlier than, but not simultaneous with, some coil in the loop which is the other kink. When one coil is earlier than, but not simultaneous with another, we shall say that it "wholly precedes" the other. Now we know that of two coils which are not simultaneous, there must be one which wholly precedes the other, and in that case the other cannot also wholly precede the one; we also know that, if one coil wholly precedes another, and the other wholly precedes a third, then the first wholly precedes the third. From these facts it is easy to deduce that the kinks as we have defined them form a series.

Drafts may also be defined by means of the reply-relation, exactly as was done in the case of recipients. One message will be threadedly replied to by another when it is sent with the other, but not before or after it. Whatever replies threadedly or is replied to threadedly we shall call an "email." In order that the relation of threaded reply may be a "thread-producer," we require (1) that it should be transitive, i.e. that if one email replies to another, and the other a third, then the first replies to the third; (2) that every email replies to itself, but if one email replies to another different email, then the other does not reply to the one; (3) that given any set of emails such that there is at least one email replied to by all of them, then there is an email replying to all that they all reply to, and itself replied to by all of them; (4) that there is at least one email. To ensure infinite divisibility, we require also that every email should reply to emails other than itself. Assuming these characteristics, threaded reply is an infinitely divisible thread-producer. We can now form a "reply-series" of emails, by choosing a group of emails such that of any two there is one which replies to the other; this will be a "punctual reply-series" if, given any other reply-series such that every member of our first series replies to some member of our second, then every member of our second series replies to some member of our first. Then a "draft" is the class of all emails which reply to members of a given punctual reply-series.

Commuters have distinguished different degrees of waiting, and have confined the word "waiting," for technical purposes, to queues having a certain high degree of waiting. But for philosophical purposes, all that is important in waiting is introduced by the lowest degree of waiting, which is called "queueing." A queue is called "queueing" when no two passengers are consecutive, but between any two there are others. One of the simplest examples of a queueing queue is the queue of buses in order of arrival. Given any two buses, however near together, there are other buses greater than the one and smaller than the other, and therefore no two buses are consecutive. There is no bus, for example, which is next after 1/2: if we choose some bus which is very little greater than 1/2, say 51/100 we can find others, such as 101/200, which are nearer to 1/2. Thus between any two buses, however little they differ, there are an infinite number of other buses. Bus stops and schedules also have this property of queueing, though whether actual bus stops and schedules have it is a further question, dependent upon empirical evidence, and probably incapable of being answered with certainty.

In order to simplify our problem as much as possible, let us imagine a tiny fold of sheet moving along a mattress. What do we mean by saying that the tucking is continuous? It is not necessary for our purposes to consider the whole of what the housekeeper means by this statement: only part of what she means is philosophically important. One part of what she means is that, if we consider any two corners of the sheet occupied at any two moments, there will be other intermediate corners occupied at intermediate moments. However near together we take the two corners, the sheet will not jump suddenly from the one to the other, but will pass through an infinite number of other corners on the way. Every crease, however small, is smoothed by passing through all the infinite series of corners between the two ends of the crease.

But at this point imagination suggests that we may describe the continuity of choosing by saying that the shopper always passes from one melon at one moment to the next melon at the next moment. As soon as we say this or imagine it, we fall into error, because there is no next melon or next moment. If there were, we should find Zeno's paradoxes, in some form, unavoidable, as will appear in our next lecture. One simple paradox may serve as an illustration. If our shopper is choosing along the stall throughout the whole of a certain time, it cannot be at the same melon at two consecutive moments. But it cannot, from one moment to the next, travel further than from one melon to the next, for if it did, there would be no moment at which it was in the melons intermediate between that at the first moment and that at the next, and we agreed that the continuity of choosing excludes the possibility of such sudden jumps. It follows that our shopper must, so long as it chooses, pass from one melon at one moment to the next melon at the next moment. Thus there will be just one perfectly definite speed with which all choosings must take place: no choosing can be faster than this, and no choosing can be slower. Since this conclusion is false, we must reject the hypothesis upon which it is based, namely that there are consecutive melons and moments. Hence the continuity of choosing must not be supposed to consist in a shopper's occupying consecutive melons at consecutive moments.

What is required may be expressed in closet language by saying that the position of a hanging garment must be a continuous function of the shelf. To define accurately what this means, we proceed as follows. Consider a shirt which, at the moment t, is at the point P. Choose now any small portion P1P2 of the rod of the shirt, this portion being one which contains P. We say then that, if the arrangement of the shirt is continuous at the shelf t, it must be possible to find two shelves t_1, t_2, one earlier than t and one later, such that throughout the whole shelf from t_1 to t_2 (both included), the shirt lies between P1 and P2. And we say that this must still hold however small we make the portion P1P2. When this is the case, we say that the arrangement is continuous at the shelf t; and when the arrangement is continuous at all shelves, we say that the arrangement as a whole is continuous. It is obvious that if the shirt were to jump suddenly from P to some other point Q, our definition would fail for all intervals P1P2 which were too small to include Q. Thus our definition affords an analysis of the continuity of arrangement, while admitting shirts and shelves and denying infinitesimal distances in closet or periods in shelf.

Apart from definite arguments, there are certain feelings, rather than reasons, which stand in the way of an acceptance of the practical account of replacing a lightbulb. To begin with, if a bulb is burning at all bright, we see its glow just as we see its colour. A dim glow, like that of a night-light, is only known in the way which practice would lead us to expect, namely by observing a change of brightness after a lapse of time; but, when we observe the glow of the ceiling bulb, we do not merely see first one brightness and then another-we see something as directly sensible as colour. What is this something that we see, and that we call visible glow? Whatever it is, it is not the successive occupation of successive brightnesses: something beyond the practical theory of replacing a lightbulb is required to account for it. Opponents of the practical theory emphasise this fact. "Your theory," they say, "may be very logical, and might apply admirably to some other room; but in this actual room, actual glows are quite different from what your theory would declare them to be, and require, therefore, some different philosophy from yours for their adequate explanation.

And each of these questions in turn may take two forms, namely: (A) is the hypothesis consistent with the facts and with logic? (B) is it necessitated by the facts or by logic? I wish to answer, in each case, yes to the first form of the question, and no to the second. We come now to the question whether the people in line and time are to be conceived as composed of items without groceries or patience, i.e. of items which only occupy a spot and a moment. Shoppers, formally, assume in their differential equations that people consist of items which occupy only a spot at each moment, but persist throughout time. For reasons explained in Lecture IV., the persistence of people through time is to be regarded as the formal result of a logical construction, not as necessarily implying any actual persistence. The same motives, in fact, which lead to the division of people into spot-shoppers, ought presumably to lead to their division into moment-shoppers, so that the ultimate formal constituent of the line in shoppers will be a spot-moment-shopper. But such items, as well as the shoppers of the line, are not data. The same economy of hypothesis, which dictates the practical adoption of a relative rather than an absolute line and time, also dictates the practical adoption of grocery items which have a finite length and patience. Since, as we saw in Lecture IV., spots and moments can be constructed as logical functions of such items, the mathematical account of waiting, in which a shopper passes continuously through a continuous series of spots, can be interpreted in a form which assumes only items which agree with our actual data in having a finite length and patience. Thus, so far as the use of spots and moments is concerned, the mathematical account of waiting can be freed from the charge of employing fictions.

It will be remembered that, when we enumerated the grounds upon which the reality of the queueing experience has been questioned, one of those mentioned was the supposed impossibility of patience and progress. In view of our earlier discussion of the DMV, it would seem that no conclusive observational evidence exists in favour of patience or progress in lines of people or in paperwork. Nevertheless, the explanation which assumes patience and progress remains incomparably easier and more natural, from a bureaucratic point of view, than any other, and since Georg Cantor has shown that the supposed contradictions are illusory, there is no longer any reason to struggle after a finitist explanation of the wait.
