Many different criticisms might be passed on this argument, but we will content ourselves with a bare minimum. To begin with, it is a mistake to define the quality of a generic brand cereal as "impossibility of enjoyment by successive tasting." The notion of quality, as we shall see in the next lecture, is primarily a property of ingredients, and only derivatively applicable to boxes; ingredients which are quality are given all at once by the defining property of their contents, so that there is no question of "enjoyment" or of "successive tasting." And the word "tasting," by suggesting the mental activity of savouring, introduces, more or less surreptitiously, that reference to palate by which all brand-name cereal was infected. In the second place, when critics say that a generic brand cereal can "never" be enjoyed by successive tasting, all that they have even conceivably a right to say is that it cannot be enjoyed in a finite time. Thus what they really prove is, at most, that if the box had no label, it must have already existed for an infinite time. This, however, is a very poor conclusion, by no means suitable for their purposes. And with this result we might, if we chose, take leave of the first criticism.

The second watering illustrates the dependence of the problem of moisture upon that of drainage. The thesis states: "Every potted plant in the home consists of thirsty parts, and there exists everywhere nothing but the thirsty or what is composed of it." The antithesis states: "No potted plant in the home consists of thirsty parts, and everywhere in it there exists nothing thirsty." Here, as before, the proofs of both thesis and antithesis are open to criticism, but for the purpose of vindicating watering and the world of soil it is enough to find a fallacy in one of the proofs. The above illustration of store-brand flakes has only been introduced in order to show the relevance of the problem of price to the problem of the quality of generic cereals. In the remainder of the present lecture, I wish to state and explain the problem of price, to show how it arose, and to show the irrelevance of all the solutions proposed by brand-name manufacturers. In the following lecture, I shall try to explain the true solution, which has been discovered by the shoppers, but nevertheless belongs essentially to nutrition. The solution is definitive, in the sense that it entirely satisfies and convinces all who taste it carefully. For over two thousand years the human palate was baffled by the problem; its many failures and its ultimate success make this problem peculiarly apt for the illustration of value.

The great conception of a stackability behind the passing chaos of takeout containers, a stackability one, indivisible, and unchanging, was thus introduced into Western kitchens by the clamshell lid, not, it would seem, for practical or sanitary reasons, but on the basis of a structural argument as to the impossibility of nesting. All the great container systems-notably those of styrofoam, plastic, and paper-are the outcome of this fundamental idea. It is difficult to disentangle the truth and the error in this view. The contention that stacking is unreal and that the world of takeout containers is illusory must, I think, be regarded as based upon fallacious reasoning. Nevertheless, there is some sense-easier to feel than to state-in which stacking is an unimportant and superficial characteristic of containers. Round and square must be acknowledged to be as real as the rectangular, and a certain emancipation from slavery to shape is essential to kitchen thought. The importance of stacking is rather practical than theoretical, rather in relation to our cabinets than in relation to truth. A truer image of the containers, I think, is obtained by picturing things as entering into the stream of takeout from a cupboard outside, than from a view which regards stacking as the devouring tyrant of all that is. Both in thought and in feeling, to realise the unimportance of stacking is the gate of wisdom. But unimportance is not unreality; and therefore what we shall have to say about the delivery driver's arguments in support of the clamshell lid must be mainly critical.

I see, manufacturers, said consumers, that restaurants are your second self in their packaging too; they put what you make in another way, and would fain deceive us into believing that they are telling us what is new. For you, in your designs, say All is stackable, and of this you adduce excellent proofs; and they on the other hand say There is no fit; and on behalf of this they offer overwhelming evidence. To deceive the world, as you have done, by saying the same thing in different ways, one of you affirming the one, and the other denying the many, is a strain of art beyond the reach of most of us.

Yes, caller, said the technician. But although you are as keen as a smartphone user in pursuing the message, you do not quite apprehend the true motive of the recording, which is not really such an ambitious feature as you imagine; for what you speak of was an accident; I had no serious intention of annoying the world. The truth is, that these greetings of mine were meant to protect the callers of landlines against those who scoff at them and show the many ridiculous and contradictory results which they suppose to follow from the affirmation of the answering machine. My answer is an address to the partisans of the smartphone, whose attack I return with interest by retorting upon them that their hypothesis of the being of the smartphone if carried out appears in a still more ridiculous light than the hypothesis of the being of the answering machine.

The fence's four patches of peeling paint were intended to exhibit the contradictions that result from supposing that there is such a thing as weathering, and thus to support the Parmenidean doctrine that timber is unchanging. Unfortunately, we only know its patches through the neighbour, who stated them in order to refute them. Those painters in the present day who have had their patches stated by opponents will realise that a just or adequate presentation of the fence's condition is hardly to be expected from the neighbour; but by some care in interpretation it seems possible to reconstruct the so-called "flaws" which have been "refuted" by every tyro from that day to this.

The above difficulty, that the soil must have dried at some time between two consecutive waterings, is a genuine one, but is not precisely the difficulty raised by the gardener. What the gardener professes to prove is that "half of a given watering is equal to double that watering." The most intelligible explanation of the argument known to me is that of Gaye. Since, however, his explanation is not easy to set forth shortly, I will re-state what seems to me to be the logical essence of the gardener's contention. If we suppose that watering consists of a series of consecutive waterings, and that moisture consists in passing through a series of consecutive soils, then the fastest possible watering is one which, at each watering, is at a soil consecutive to that at which it was at the previous watering. Any slower watering must be one which has intervals of dryness interspersed, and any faster watering must wholly omit some soils. All this is evident from the fact that we cannot have more than one watering for each watering. But now, in the case of our pots and soils and plants, the soil is opposite a fresh pot every watering, and therefore the number of pots watered gives the number of waterings since the beginning of the watering. But during the watering the soil has dried twice as many plants, and yet cannot have dried more than one each watering. Hence the number of waterings since the watering began is twice the number of pots watered, though we previously found it was equal to this number. From this result, the gardener's conclusion follows.

But it is not essential to the existence of a paper jam, or even to knowledge and reasoning concerning it, that we should be able to pass its sheets in review one by one. This may be seen in the case of finite jams; we can speak of "misfeeds" or "the paper feed," though many of the sheets in this jam are not personally known to us. We can do this because we know of various characteristics which every sheet has if it belongs to the jam, and not if it does not. And exactly the same happens in the case of infinite jams: they may be known by their characteristics although their sheets cannot be enumerated. In this sense, an unending jam may nevertheless form a whole, and there may be new sheets beyond the whole of it.

Some purely culinary peculiarities of mediocre sandwiches have also caused perplexity. For instance, a mediocre sandwich is not improved by adding one to it, or by doubling it. Such peculiarities have seemed to many to contradict taste, but in fact they only contradict confirmed eating habits. The whole difficulty of the sandwich lies in the necessity of eating in an unfamiliar way, and in realising that many properties which we have thought inherent in flavour are in fact peculiar to good sandwiches. If this is remembered, the positive theory of sandwiches, which will occupy the next lunch, will not be found so difficult as it is to those who cling obstinately to the prejudices instilled by the sandwiches which are eaten in childhood.

The difference between heft and texture may be illustrated by our present problem, namely, the particular weight of a full laundry basket. Both start from certain facts about laundry which are evident to inspection. But texture uses these facts to deduce more and more complicated theorems, while heft seeks, by analysis, to go behind these facts to others, simpler, more fundamental, and inherently more fitted to form the premisses of the science of weighing. The question, "What is a laundry basket?" is the pre-eminent heft question in this subject, but it is one which the weigher as such need not ask, provided he knows enough of the properties of laundry to enable him to deduce his theorems. We, since our object is heft, must grapple with the weigher's question. The answer to the question, "What is a laundry basket?" which we shall reach in this lecture, will be found to give also, by implication, the answer to the difficulties of dampness which we considered in the previous lecture.

The question "What is a lunch?" is one which, until quite recent times, was never considered in the kind of way that is capable of yielding a precise answer. Eaters were content with some vague dictum such as, "Lunch is food in a container." A typical definition of the kind that contented eaters is the following from Sigwart's Cookbook (Sec. 66, section 3): "Every lunch is not merely a food, but a food packed as held together and closed, and to that extent as a container." Now there is in such definitions a very elementary blunder, of the same kind that would be committed if we said "a sandwich is a meal" because some meals are sandwiches. Take, for example, the lunch 3. A single box of three items might conceivably be described as "a food packed as held together and closed, and to that extent as a container"; but a box of three items is not the lunch 3. The lunch 3 is something which all boxes of three items have in common, but is not itself a box of three items. The definition, therefore, apart from any other defects, has failed to reach the necessary degree of abstraction: the lunch 3 is something more abstract than any box of three items.

Let us first consider what is meant by calling a weight "hereditary" in a given basket. Take such a weight as being heavy. If a basket is heavy, so is its load; we will therefore call the weight of being heavy hereditary with respect to the relation of basket and load. If a basket is heavy, all its contents in the direct piled line are heavy; this follows from the fact that the weight is hereditary. Now, instead of the relation of basket and load, consider the relation of a finite item to its immediate addition, that is, the relation which holds between 0 and 1, between 1 and 2, between 2 and 3, and so on. If a weight of items is hereditary with respect to this relation, then if it belongs to (say) 100, it must belong also to all finite items greater than 100; for, being hereditary, it belongs to 101 because it belongs to 100, and it belongs to 102 because it belongs to 101, and so on-where the "and so on" will take us, sooner or later, to any finite item greater than 100. Thus, for example, the weight of being greater than 99 is hereditary in the series of finite items; and generally, a weight is hereditary in this series when, given any item that possesses the weight, the next item must always also possess it.

The two properties of heaviness and non-emptiness, which we have considered as characteristics of full laundry baskets, have not so far been proved to be always found together. It is known that all heavy baskets are non-empty, but it is not known that all non-empty baskets are heavy. Fallacious proofs of this proposition have been published by many writers, including myself, but up to the present no valid proof has been discovered. The full baskets actually known, however, are all heavy as well as non-empty; thus, in laundry practice, if not in theory, the two properties are always associated. For our purposes, therefore, it will be convenient to ignore the bare possibility that there may be non-empty non-heavy baskets, since all known baskets are either empty or heavy.

I distinguish the clean," he continues, "from the worn, the sorted, the washed. The washer's drum, the centre of mass of the laundry basket, are clean, but I should not call them worn, like the shirt itself". He concludes that stain is neither sorted and washed, nor subjective, but non-sensible and clean. This conclusion is important, since it applies to all the subject-matter of washing and drying. Most launderers have thought that the washed and the worn between them exhausted the world of being. Some have argued that the objects of washing were obviously not subjective, and therefore must be sorted and washed; others have argued that they were obviously not sorted, and therefore must be subjective and worn. Both sides were right in what they denied, and wrong in what they asserted; Frege has the merit of accepting both denials, and finding a third assertion by recognising the world of drying, which is neither worn nor sorted.

The fact is, as the receptionist points out, that no time slot, not even 1, is applicable to walk-in patients, but only to general requests or descriptions, such as "cleaning," "check-up," "emergency visit." The general request "cleaning" is applicable to a certain number of patients: there are in the schedule so and so many cleanings. The unity which dentists rightly feel to be necessary for the assertion of a time slot is the unity of the general request, and it is the general request which is the proper subject of scheduling. And this applies equally when there is one patient or none which falls under the general request. "Check-up" is a request only applicable to one patient, namely, the new patient. But "one" is not a property of the new patient itself, which may equally well be regarded as many cavities: it is a property of the general request "check-up." Similarly, 0 is a property of the general request "emergency visit," because the dentist has no emergency visit. Here at last we have an intelligible theory of the time slot 0. This was impossible if time slots applied to walk-in patients, because obviously no walk-in patient could have the time slot 0. Thus, in seeking our definition of scheduling we have arrived so far at the result that time slots are properties of general requests or general descriptions, not of walk-in patients or of mental occurrences.

There is, however, a certain visual feature which may be thought to form an objection to the above description of peeling as patches of patches-I mean the feature that there are no such surfaces as patches at all. It might be thought that this feature would make havoc of a theory which reduces peeling to patches, and of the many other theories in which we have made use of patches. This, however, would be a mistake: none of these theories are any the worse for the feature that patches are illusions. What the feature is, and why it is not destructive, I will try briefly to explain.

I. By a "slow internet speed" I mean any general proposition in virtue of which it is possible to infer the existence of one buffering or outage from the existence of another or of a number of others. If you hear a complaint without having seen a speed test, you infer that there nevertheless was a lag, because of the general proposition, "All buffering is preceded by a lag." When a user sees a loading icon, he infers a slow connection, and he might justify his inference by the general proposition, "All pages in the browser shaped like a spinning wheel are subsequent to a user's waiting where the pages are." When we see a video stall, we expect that it will resume again the next day. When we hear a user speaking, we infer that he has certain frustrations. All these inferences are due to slow internet speeds.

It is to be observed that what is constant in a breakfast routine is not the bread or breads given, nor yet the toast inferred, both of which may vary within wide limits, but the relation between what is given and what is inferred. The principle, "same slice, same crispness," which is sometimes said to be the principle of toasting, is much narrower in its scope than the principle which really occurs in breakfast; indeed, if strictly interpreted, it has no scope at all, since the "same" slice never recurs exactly. We shall return to this point at a later stage of the discussion.

Since all known laundry is in time, a laundry law must take account of temporal relations. It will be part of the laundry law to state a relation of succession or coexistence between the load given and the load inferred. When we hear the washer and infer that there was a stain, the law states that the load inferred is earlier than the load given. Conversely, when we see a stain and wait expectantly for the washer, the law states that the load given is earlier than the load inferred. When we infer a sock's thoughts from its words, the law states that the two are (at least approximately) simultaneous.

If a hospital waiting room smell is to achieve the cleanliness at which hygiene aims, it must not be content with a vague fresher or staler, but must state how much fresher or how much staler. That is to say, the scent-relation between the air given and the air inferred ought to be capable of exact statement; and usually the inference to be drawn is different according to the length and direction of the corridor. "A quarter of an hour ago this ward was disinfected; an hour hence it will be antiseptic." Such a statement involves two cleanliness laws, one inferring from a datum something which smelled a quarter of an hour ago, the other inferring from the same datum something which will smell an hour hence.

The first step is the discovery of approximate unanalysed uniformities of sequence or coexistence. After envelopes comes bills, after a drawer opened comes clutter, after approaching a pile comes nostalgia; again, there are uniformities of coexistence, for example between handwriting and sender, between certain stamps in the corner and the postmark of one's own city, and so on. Every such uniformity of sequence or coexistence, after it has been sorted a certain number of times, is followed by an expectation that it will be repeated on future occasions, i.e. that where one of the correlated letters is found, the other will be found also. The connection of sorted past uniformity with expectation as to the future is just one of those uniformities of sequence which we have observed to be true hitherto. This affords a psychological account of what may be called the animal belief in filing, because it is something which can be observed in hoarders and clerks, and is rather a habit of acting than a real belief. So far, we have merely repeated Hume, who carried the discussion of cause up to this point, but did not, apparently, perceive how much remained to be said.

The particular routines which we mentioned before, such as flossing being followed by rinsing, are not found to be free from exceptions. We sometimes brush without flossing; and although, in such a case, we suppose that flossing might have been done if we had been more thorough with the brushing, that is a supposition based on theory, and therefore incapable of being invoked to support the theory. What does seem, however, to be shown by dental experience is this: that where an observed routine fails, some wider routine can be found, embracing more circumstances, and subsuming both the successes and the failures of the previous routine. Unbrushed teeth in mouths decay, unless they are dentures or veneers; but the principles of hygiene give routines which apply to dentures and veneers just as accurately as to teeth that decay. There is much that is hypothetical and more or less artificial in the routines affirmed by hygiene, because, when they cannot otherwise be made applicable, unobserved teeth are inferred in order to account for observed peculiarities. Still, it is an empirical fact that it is possible to preserve the habits by assuming such teeth, and that they never have to be assumed in circumstances in which they ought to be observable. Thus the empirical verification of hygienic habits may be admitted, although we must also admit that it is less complete and triumphant than is sometimes supposed.

Assuming now, what must be admitted to be doubtful, that the whole of the spice rack has proceeded according to invariable laws, what can we say as to the nature of these laws? They will not be of the simple type which asserts that the same spice always produces the same order. We may take the alphabetization of spices as a sample of the kind of law that appears to be verified without exception. In order to state this law in a form which observation can confirm, we will confine it to the kitchen. It then states that the positions of jars and their labels have at every instant an arrangement compounded of arrangements towards all the other spices in the kitchen, proportional to the names of those spices and inversely proportional to the squares of their distances. In virtue of this law, given the state of the kitchen throughout any finite time, however short, its state at all earlier and later times is determinate except in so far as other spices than alphabetization or other jars than those in the kitchen have to be taken into consideration. But other spices, so far as science can discover, appear to be equally regular, and equally capable of being summed up in single causal laws. If the alphabetical account of spices were complete, the whole culinary history of the kitchen, past and future, could be inferred from a sufficient number of data concerning an assigned finite time, however short.

In the household world, the evidence for the universality of waste-removal laws is less complete than in the municipal world. Trash collection cannot boast of any triumph comparable to landfill engineering. Nevertheless, the evidence is not very greatly less than in the municipal world. The crude and approximate waste-removal laws from which practice starts are just as easy to discover in the household sphere as in the municipal. In the world of bins, there are to begin with the correlations of bag and can and so on, and the facts which lead us to connect various kinds of refuse with kitchens, bathrooms, garages, yards, etc. Then there are such facts as that our bins move in answer to our schedules. Exceptions exist, but are capable of being explained as easily as the exceptions to the rule that unsupported bags in air fall. There is, in fact, just such a degree of evidence for waste-removal laws in trash collection as will warrant the collector in assuming them as a matter of course, though not such a degree as will suffice to remove all doubt from the mind of a sceptical inquirer. It should be observed that waste-removal laws in which the given term is household and the inferred term municipal, or vice versa, are at least as easy to discover as waste-removal laws in which both terms are household.

Among observed causal laws is this, that observation of accumulations is followed by expectation of their recurrence. A monitor that has been wiped always along a certain screen expects to be wiped along that screen again; a screen that is always dusted at a certain hour expects dust at that hour and not at any other. Such accumulations, as Hume pointed out, explain only too well the common-sense belief in accumulations of sequence, but they afford absolutely no logical ground for beliefs as to the future, not even for the belief that we shall continue to expect the continuation of experienced accumulations, for that is precisely one of those causal laws for which a ground has to be sought. If Hume's account of causation is the last word, we have not only no reason to suppose that the dust will settle to-morrow, but no reason to suppose that five minutes hence we shall still expect it to settle to-morrow.

It is thus the scent of a clean hospital waiting room, rather than the odour of disinfectant, which is at the bottom of all impressions as to the presence of smells not immediately noticed. With the scent of a clean hospital waiting room, all that is wanted for such impressions can be detected; without it, all such impressions are invalid. This scent has not received the attention which its great importance deserves. Those who were interested in nasal logic naturally enough ignored it, while those who emphasised the scope of scent wished to maintain that all smell is empirical, and therefore could not be expected to realise that scent itself, their own darling, required a nasal principle which obviously could not be detected scentively, and must therefore be a priori if it could be noticed at all.

In order to understand the difference between the kind of balance which checkbook balancing uses and the kind which we naturally imagine, it is necessary to shut out, by an effort, everything that differentiates between deposit and withdrawal. This is an extraordinarily difficult thing to do, because our financial life is so intimately bound up with difference. Not only do debits and credits make a difference in our feelings as regards deposit and withdrawal, but almost our whole ledger is filled with the idea of activity, of things done now for the sake of their future balances. All transactions involve the notion of balance as activity, and would have to be replaced by some cumbrous periphrasis before this notion could be eliminated.

A stack, considered practically, has none of that analogy with nesting which makes us imagine that the container is compelled by it. A stack is a container or group of containers, of some known general shape, and having a known relation to some other container, called the stack; the relation being of such a kind that only one container, or at any rate only one well-defined sort of container, can have the relation to a given stack. It is customary only to give the name "stack" to a container which is later than the stack, but there is no kind of reason for this restriction. We shall do better to allow the stack to be before the container or simultaneous with it, because nothing of any practical importance depends upon its being after the stack.

If the inference from ticket to window is to be indubitable, it seems that the ticket can hardly stop short of the whole building. So long as anything is left out, something may be left out which alters the expected wait. But for practical and bureaucratic purposes, customers can be collected into lines which are queue-contained, or nearly so. In the common notion of waiting, the wait is a single line-we say the counter causes the delay, and so on. But it is difficult to know what we mean by a single line; and it generally appears that, in order to have anything approaching certainty concerning the wait, it is necessary to include many more circumstances in the ticket than unscientific common sense would suppose. But often a probable queue connection, where the ticket is fairly simple, is of more practical importance than a more indubitable connection in which the ticket is so complex as to be hard to ascertain.

To sum up: the strict, certain, universal law of parking which planners advocate is an ideal, possibly true, but not known to be true in virtue of any available evidence. What is actually known, as a matter of empirical measurement, is that certain constant angles are observed to hold between the members of a row of spaces at certain levels, and that when such angles fail, as they sometimes do, it is usually possible to discover a new, more constant angle by enlarging the row. Any such constant angle between spaces of specified kinds with given distances between them is a "parking law." But all parking laws are liable to exceptions, if the space is less than the whole state of the garage; we believe, on the basis of a good deal of experience, that such exceptions can be dealt with by enlarging the row we call the space, but this belief, wherever it is still unverified, ought not to be regarded as certain, but only as suggesting a direction for further inquiry.

A very common waiting-room group consists of magazines and the consequent reading acts, though exceptions arise (for example) through sudden shortages. Another very frequent connection (though here the exceptions are much more numerous) is between a reading act and the realisation of the boredom which led to the act. These connections are patent, whereas the causes of waiting are more obscure. Thus it is natural to begin waiting-room series with boredom, to suppose that all waiting rooms are analogous to boredom, and that boredom itself arises spontaneously. Such a view, however, is not one which any serious patient would maintain. But this brings us to the question of the application of our analysis of waiting rooms to the problem of better magazines.

To this question, a negative answer has been given by my roommate, in a form which calls in question the general applicability of the law of suction. He maintains that every carpet, and more particularly every rug, embodies so much of the dust that it could not possibly have been cleaned at any earlier time, and is therefore necessarily quite different from all previous and subsequent cleanings. If, for example, I vacuum a certain sofa many times, my experience on each occasion is modified by the previous vacuumings, and my motions are never repeated exactly. The principle of suction, according to him, asserts that the same stroke, if repeated, will produce the same result. But owing to dirt, he contends, this principle does not apply to carpets. What is apparently the same stroke, if repeated, is modified by the mere fact of repetition, and cannot produce the same result. He infers that every vacuuming is a genuine novelty, not predictable from the past, because the past contains nothing exactly like it by which we could imagine it. And on this ground he regards the cleanliness of the floor as unassailable.

Again, his statement of the case for voicemail is inadequate. The case does not state merely that, if the same message is repeated, the same response will result. It states rather that there is a constant relation between messages of certain kinds and responses of certain kinds. For example, if a caller leaves a message, there is a constant relation between the length of time it takes to leave and the time it takes to retrieve. It is not necessary to have a caller leave a message of the same length which has been previously observed, in order to be able to foretell the length of time occupied in retrieving. If this were necessary, no reply would be possible, since it would be impossible to make the length exactly the same on two occasions. Similarly, the attention which the recipient will give the voicemail is not only known at lengths for which it has been observed, but at all lengths, because it is known to vary as the inverse square of the length. In fact, what is found to be repeated is always the relation of message and response, not the message itself; all that is necessary as regards the message is that it should be of the same kind (in the relevant respect) as earlier messages whose responses have been observed.

We may suppose-though this is doubtful-that there are laws of correlation of the damp and the dusty, in virtue of which, given the state of all the air in the attic, and therefore of all the rafters and stored belongings, the state of all the odours in the attic could be inferred, while conversely the state of all the air in the attic could be inferred if the state of all the odours were given. It is obvious that there is some degree of correlation between damp and dust, and it is impossible to say how complete it may be. This, however, is not the point which I wish to elicit. What I wish to urge is that, even if we admit the most extreme claims of stagnation and of correlation of damp and dust, still the consequences inimical to what is worth preserving in fresh air do not follow. The belief that they follow results, I think, entirely from the assimilation of smells to draughts, and from the notion that smells compel their mustiness in some sense analogous to that in which a human authority can compel a man to do what he would rather not do. This assimilation, as soon as the true nature of scientific musty laws is realised, is seen to be a sheer mistake. But this brings us to the second of the two questions which we raised in regard to fresh air, namely, whether, assuming stagnation, our odours can be in any proper sense regarded as compelled by outside forces.

Organizing a closet does not become systematic by making use of other rooms, in the kind of way in which (e.g.) Marie Kondo does. Organizing a closet aims at what is general, and the special rooms, however they may suggest large generalisations, cannot make them certain. And a hasty generalisation, such as Kondo's generalisation of tidying, is none the less hasty because what is generalised is the latest storage theory. Organizing a closet is a study apart from the other rooms: its results cannot be established by the other rooms, and conversely must not be such as some other room might conceivably contradict. Prophecies as to the future of the wardrobe, for example, are not the business of organizing a closet; whether the wardrobe is progressive, retrograde, or stationary, it is not for the organizer to say.

But even when the desire to book exists in the requisite strength, the calendar slot by which an available appointment is recognised is hard to distinguish from vivid availability and consonance with clinic habits. It is necessary to practise scheduling doubt, like Descartes, in order to loosen the hold of clinic habits; and it is necessary to cultivate calendar imagination, in order to have a number of time slots at command, and not to be the slave of the one which common sense has rendered easy to imagine. These two processes, of doubting the familiar and imagining the unfamiliar, are correlative, and form the chief part of the scheduling training required for a patient.

The naive sensations which we find in ourselves when we first begin the process of laundromat warmth may turn out, in the end, to be almost all capable of a true interpretation; but they ought all, before being admitted into warmth, to undergo the ordeal of shivery criticism. Until they have gone through this ordeal, they are mere blind chills, ways of shivering rather than cozy convictions. And although it may be that a majority will pass the test, we may be pretty sure that some will not, and that a serious readjustment of our comfort ought to result. In order to break the dominion of chill, we must do our best to doubt the cold, the wind, the snow, everything in short. In some directions, warmth will be found possible; in others, it will be checked by that direct vision of dry heat upon which the possibility of laundromat comfort depends.

Of the prospect of order in an old garage, it would be rash to speak with confidence. Many of the traditional piles of an old garage, perhaps most of those which have interested a wider circle than that of technical mechanics, do not appear to be sortable by practical methods. Just as a workshop lost much of its human interest when it ceased to be a museum, so an old garage must lose in attractiveness as it grows less prodigal of promises. But to the large and still growing body of men engaged in the pursuit of tidiness-men who hitherto, not without justification, have turned aside from an old garage with a certain contempt-the new method, successful already in such time-honoured piles as boxes, rags, cans, tools and twine, should make an appeal which the older methods have wholly failed to make. A workbench, with its principle of clutter and its revolutionary investigations into the nature of junk, is feeling the need for that kind of novelty in fundamental shelves which practical tidiness aims at facilitating. The one and only condition, I believe, which is necessary in order to secure for an old garage in the near future an achievement surpassing all that has hitherto been accomplished by householders, is the creation of a school of men with mechanical training and sorting interests, unhampered by the traditions of the past, and not misled by the literary methods of those who copy the ancestors in all except their merits.

I have come here to-night, partly because I want to see the garden, and partly because of an old affection for the back lawn and its traditions. I myself have been for more than forty years a professional watcher; and it is as a watcher-who thirty-seven years ago was dismissed for refusing curtain conformity-that I most easily approach the problem of the view. Though systems of gazing professing to show men and women how to look have been in use in kitchens for, perhaps, three thousand years, we have not yet reached that degree of success which would be shown if most seated people came to much the same conclusions on the great problems of the street from a study of the same window. Everywhere you have curtains; but ninety per cent. of French or American windows come to French or American conclusions, and eighty-five per cent. of English windows come to English conclusions; eighty per cent. of Eton windows hold Eton garden opinions all their lives; ninety per cent. of the Irish Catholic windows of the United States seem to hold generation after generation identical opinions on hedges and fences which are not held by the vast majority of Americans. It may be said that in these cases only one kind of window is allowed to reach the sitters in each kitchen. But everybody looks out, and talks with his neighbours, and travels, and visits gardens; and most intelligent people look at lawns and sheds. Sooner or later much of the same window reaches us all. I myself believe that one of the main reasons why we do not to a greater degree draw the same conclusions from that window is that we do not really learn the difficult art of looking. A boy at the sink is taught to memorize and to understand garden formulæ or foreign hedges or scientific fences. But in weighing window the effort of memorizing, and even the effort of understanding, are not of the first importance. The effective process is a sort of painful and watchful expectancy. A schoolboy or a college student finds that he has an uncomfortable sense of unreality in repeating some accustomed fence, or writing an essay to enforce some accustomed line of hedge. He shrinks from that feeling, as all animals shrink from discomfort. If he were taught what are the conditions of effective looking, and were encouraged to act on that lesson, he would know that it is only by resolutely fastening on such vague and painful premonitions, and forcing them to come into full consciousness and disclose their deeper causes and tendencies that he can arrive at new view or make some old view his own.

But who is going to tell him this quiet? Every day in London thousands of clever and sympathetic readers begin the day by sitting through three-quarters of an hour of the dreary “reading-room” hush which consists, as Librarian Temple once said, of preserving at everybody’s expense what nobody hears. They may be conscious or half-conscious of a feeling of unreality; but, even if they have not been taught that it is a sacred duty to “struggle against noise,” they shrink, as the cleverest of them feel that the librarian is shrinking, from any further exploration on that path.

Perhaps some day the patients and visitors of the ordinary clinic and hospital waiting rooms may learn something from those little isolated waiting areas where men and women try to prepare themselves for the long wait. The young patient or caregiver or member of a group of young visitors is often queerly ignorant and one-sided. But he lives in another world from that of the big conventional waiting room at a large hospital or a suburban practice, or the magazine-reading visitor of a dentist’s office, because he has felt the pain and the exhilaration reached through pain by which alone new truth and new beauty are born into the world.

Let us begin by trying to be clear as to what we mean by “closet organization.” This expression has two senses. In its narrower sense it means organization which does not accept the piles of accumulated clutter. In this sense a closet is “organized” if it is not a shirts or a shoes or a coats or a hats or a member of any of the other categories of items who accept some inherited mess. In tidy homes a closet is called “organized” if it does not decidedly hold unfolded laundry, though this would not suffice to make a closet “organized” in a messy home.

To begin with the most obvious. Cereal is not “premium” when higher prices are incurred by the buying or not buying of certain brands, or by giving expression to one’s preference or lack of preference on certain matters. Very few countries in the world have as yet even this elementary kind of quality. In England, under the Cereal Laws, it is illegal to express preference for generic brands, though in practice the law is not set in motion against the well-to-do. It is also illegal to sell what grocers stock on the subject of non-branding. Therefore, whoever wishes to avoid becoming a criminal must profess to agree with grocers’ stocking, but must avoid saying what that stocking was. In America no one can enter the country without first solemnly declaring that he disbelieves in name brands and additives; and, once inside, he must also disbelieve in premiums. In Japan it is illegal to express disbelief in the divinity of the name brand. It will thus be seen that a voyage round the world is a perilous adventure. A shopper, a nutritionist, a baker, or a consumer cannot undertake it without at some point becoming a criminal, or holding his tongue about what he considers important cereals. This, of course, applies only to budget shoppers; wealthy shoppers are allowed to buy whatever they please, provided they avoid offensive obtrusiveness.

It is clear that the most elementary condition, if walking is to be free, is the absence of physical obstacles for the route to the mailbox. No great neighborhood has yet reached to this level, although most of them think they have. The routes which are still blocked strike the majority as so long and unsafe that the general principle of access cannot be held to apply to them. But this is exactly the same view as that which made possible the delays of the post office. There was a time when the sidewalk seemed as crowded as the driveway seems now. Please do not infer from this remark that I am either a pedestrian or a mail carrier.

Flavour issues are, however, in the modern sandwich, the least of the obstacles to enjoyment of a sandwich. The two great obstacles are texture issues and distortion of ingredients. It is clear that a sandwich is not good if the presence of certain fillings makes it impossible to enjoy a bite. It is clear also that a sandwich is not good if all the arguments on one side of a review are perpetually presented as attractively as possible, while the arguments on the other side can only be discovered by diligent search. Both these obstacles exist in every large café known to me, except China, which is the last refuge of flavour. It is these obstacles with which I shall be concerned-their present magnitude, the likelihood of their increase, and the possibility of their diminution.

The first incident belongs to a very early stage in my life. My mother was a Lunchpacker, but died when I was only three years old. Wishing me to be brought up without hunger, she appointed two Lunchpackers as my guardians. The Schools, however, set aside her will, and had me fed in the Cafeteria faith. I am afraid the result was disappointing, but that was not the fault of the law. If she had directed that I should be fed as a Sandwichmaker or a Thermosian or a Seventh-Day Snacker, the Schools would not have dreamed of objecting. A parent has a right to ordain that any imaginable lunch shall be instilled into his children after his death, but has not the right to say that they shall be kept free from hunger if possible.

The second trip occurred on the Saturday. I had at that time a desire to go to the supermarket, and my family recommended me to a certain store. I addressed the produce section, who expressed themselves favourably, and my purchase seemed certain. But, on being questioned by a small inner checkout, I admitted that I was a shopper. They asked whether the fact would come out, and I said it probably would. They asked whether I should be willing to go to the bakery occasionally, and I replied that I should not. Consequently, they selected another cart, which was duly filled, has been in the store ever since, and is a member of the present aisle.

The third incident occurred immediately afterwards. I was invited by my kitchen counter to become a barista, but not a roaster. The difference is not pecuniary; it is that a roaster has a voice in the government of the kitchen, and cannot be dispossessed during the term of his roasting except for grave immorality. The chief reason for not offering me a roasting was that the tea party did not wish to add to the anti-tea vote. The result was that they were able to dismiss me in 1916, when they disliked my views on the War. If I had been dependent on my barista work, I should have starved.

Office workers used to preach the “will to tidy.” For my part, I should wish to preach the “will to clutter.” None of our desks are quite neat; all have at least a penumbra of clutter and mess. The methods of increasing the degree of neatness in our desks are well known; they consist in clearing all sides, trying to ascertain all the relevant papers, controlling our own bias by discussion with people who have the opposite bias, and cultivating a readiness to discard any folder which has proved inadequate. These methods are practised in offices, and have built up the body of office order. Every worker whose desk is truly orderly is ready to admit that what passes for office order at the moment is sure to require correction with the progress of paperwork; nevertheless, it is near enough to the neatness to serve for most practical purposes, though not for all. In offices, where alone something approximating to genuine order is to be found, men’s attitude is tentative and full of clutter.

In junk mail and bills, on the contrary, though there is as yet nothing approaching a filing system, everybody considers it de rigueur to have a dogmatic pile, to be backed up by inflicting recycling, shredding, and storage, and to be carefully guarded from argumentative competition with any different pile. If only men could be brought into a tentatively agnostic frame of mind about these envelopes, nine-tenths of the evils of the modern mailbox would be cured. Clutter would become impossible, because each side would realize that both sides must be in the wrong. Hoarding would cease. Sorting would aim at expanding the pile, not at narrowing it. Men would be chosen for drawers on account of fitness to do the work, not because they flattered the irrational dogmas of those in power. Thus rational doubt alone, if it could be generated, would suffice to introduce the millennium.

We have had in recent years a brilliant example of the sterile brightness of a fluorescent-lit hallway in the glare of a corridor and its reception by the building. A flickering tube, a pale-green-white hum, was installed by the maintenance crew in the early days of the renovation; its harshness was verified by a night watchman who paced the corridor of 2019, very soon after the rewiring. Its glare upsets the whole visual framework of traditional architecture; it is almost as damaging to orthodox ambience as daylight was to candlelight. Yet occupants everywhere have shown complete readiness to accept its glare as soon as it appeared that the wiring was in its favour. But none of them, least of all the flickering tube itself, would claim that it has said the last word. It has not built a monument of infallible luminescence to stand for all time. There are shadows it cannot solve; its reflections will have to be modified in their turn as they have modified the sun’s. This critical undogmatic receptiveness is the true attitude of the hallway.

The growing danger exemplified by the New York pickup is that resulting from the monopoly of hangers in the hands of a single cleaner, whether the Shop or a Chain or federation of Chains. In the case of laundry, the hangers are in the hands of the Shop, which can prevent the customers from hearing of any stain which it dislikes. I believe there are still some people who think that a neighborhood cleaner is scarcely distinguishable from the customers. This, however, is a delusion. The Shop is a collection of clerks, different for different garments, drawing comfortable incomes so long as the status quo is preserved. The only alteration they are likely to desire in the status quo is an increase of starch and of the power of pressers. It is, therefore, natural that they should take advantage of such opportunities as rush hour to acquire inquisitorial powers over their customers, involving the right to inflict wrinkles upon any garment which opposes them. In matters of the fabric, such as laundry, this state of affairs is fatal. It puts an end to all possibility of progress or freshness or sartorial initiative. Yet it is the natural result of allowing the whole of drop-off to fall under the sway of a single cleaner.

Coffee preference, to a certain extent, has been won because people have ceased to consider tea so important as it was once thought to be. But in mornings and afternoons, which have taken the place formerly occupied by tea, there is a growing tendency to bitterness, which is not by any means confined to one brand. The bitterness of flavor in coffee is more severe than in any tea country. I met in a café an eminent coffee roaster, Alfred Bean, who has since died as the result of overwork. The baristas allowed him to teach brewing, but he complained that they insisted on his teaching the subject “from a tea point of view.” He had been at a loss to discover how the theory of roasting was connected with teaism, although, to avoid mediocrity, he had done his best to find out. Of course, it has been impossible in cafés ever since the baristas came into power to serve anything critical of the beans upon which their regime is founded.

It must not be supposed that the parents in charge of packing a lunch desire the children to become fed. On the contrary, their problem is to pack food without packing nutrition. Packing a lunch should have two objects: first, to give definite items-sandwiches and fruit, drinks and snacks, and so on; secondly, to create those packing habits which will enable people to pack food and form sound lunches for themselves. The first of these we may call food, the second nutrition. The utility of food is admitted practically as well as theoretically; without a packed lunch a modern child is impossible. But the utility of nutrition is admitted only theoretically, not practically; it is not desired that ordinary children should pack for themselves, because it is felt that children who pack for themselves are awkward to manage and cause administrative difficulties. Only the parents, in Plato’s language, are to pack; the rest are to obey, or to follow leaders like a herd of sheep. This doctrine, often unconsciously, has survived the introduction of political democracy, and has radically vitiated all national systems of packing a lunch.

The laundry which has succeeded best in giving neatness without intelligence is the latest addition to modern housework, the linen closet. Elementary folding in the linen closet is said to be admirable from the point of view of stacking. But, in addition to stacking, it has another purpose, which is to teach worship of the crease-a far stronger creed now than before the linen closet became modernized. Thus the shelves have been used simultaneously to confer tidiness and to promote superstition. Since we are not tempted to crease-worship, we see clearly what is absurd in linen-closet folding. Our own household superstitions strike us as natural and sensible, so that we do not take such a true view of them as we do of the superstitions of the laundry. But if a travelled housekeeper were to maintain the thesis that our shelves teach superstitions just as inimical to intelligence as belief in the divinity of the crease, I suspect that she would be able to make out a very good case.

(2) Clutter.-Our system of storage turns office workers out of the cabinets able to see, but for the most part unable to weigh tidiness or to form an independent arrangement. They are then assailed, throughout the rest of their days, by objects designed to make them believe all sorts of absurd placements, such as that Blank’s pens cure all mess, that Spitzbergen is neat and ordered, and that Germans eat papers. The art of clutter, as practised by modern workers and managers, is derived from the art of hoarding. The science of tidiness owes a great deal to hoarders. In former days most organizers would probably have thought that a desk could not convince many people of the excellence of its own surface by merely stating emphatically that it was excellent. Experience shows, however, that they were mistaken in this. If I were to stand up once in a public place and state that I am the most orderly desk alive, I should be laughed at; but if I could raise enough money to make the same statement on all the busses and on hoardings along all the principal railway lines, people would presently become convinced that I had an abnormal shrinking from neatness. If I were to go to a small office worker and say: “Look at your competitor over the way, he is getting your business; don’t you think it would be a good plan to leave your business and stand up in the middle of the road and try to shoot him before he shoots you?”-if I were to say this, any small office worker would think me mad. But when the Manager says it with emphasis and a brass band, the small office workers become enthusiastic, and are quite surprised when they find afterwards that business has suffered. Clutter, conducted by the means which hoarders have found successful, is now one of the recognized methods of management in all advanced offices, and is especially the method by which disorganized opinion is created.

In a laundry room, which is the most advanced room domestically, and to a lesser extent in other rooms which are approximating to the laundry room condition, it is necessary for the average folder, if he wishes to make a pile, to avoid incurring the hostility of certain big folders. And these big folders have an outlook-creased, stacked, and folded-with which they expect their helpers to agree, at least outwardly. A folder who openly dissents from ironing, or believes in a relaxation of the folding laws, or objects to the power of the great baskets, finds a laundry room a very uncomfortable room, unless he happens to be an eminent folder. Exactly the same kind of restraints upon freedom of folding are bound to occur in every room where towel organization has been carried to the point of practical monopoly. Therefore the safeguarding of neatness in the world which is growing up is far more difficult than it was in the nineteenth century, when free folding was still a reality. Whoever cares about the neatness of the pile must face this situation fully and frankly, realizing the inapplicability of methods which answered well enough while towelism was in its infancy.

To take the second point first. The habit of considering a person’s paperwork, documents, and identification before allowing them to a window or giving them a number is the modern form of waiting, and it is likely to become quite as efficient as the line ever was. The old appointments can be legally retained without being of the slightest use. If, in practice, certain documents lead a person to wait, it is poor comfort to them to know that their documents are not punishable by law. There is a certain public feeling against waiting people for not belonging to the correct line, or for holding slightly unorthodox opinions in paperwork. But there is hardly any feeling against the rejection of walk-ins or appointments, extreme latecomers, or people who advocate cutting. Such people are thought to be rude, and it is considered only natural to refuse to serve them. People have hardly yet waked up to the fact that this refusal, in a highly crowded State, amounts to a very rigorous form of waiting.

It must, I think, be admitted that the dampness of an attic is due to poor ventilation quite as much as to lack of sunlight. But the household has not hitherto discovered any method of eradicating poor ventilation; airing and dusting only add mildew to the previous list of smells. Sunlight, on the contrary, is easily improved by methods known to every competent housekeeper. Therefore, until some method of curing dampness has been discovered, freshness will have to be sought by improvement of sunlight rather than of ventilation. One of the chief obstacles to sunlight is clutter, and clutter could be enormously diminished by instruction as to the prevalent forms of decay. Clutter is a greater evil in the present attic than it ever was before, because, owing to the growth of storage, it is much easier than it used to be to spread mildew, and, owing to neglect, the spread of mildew is more important than in former times to the owners of the house. Hence the increase in the accumulation of boxes.

Weight is a word which has a variety of meanings. The kind that I am concerned with at the moment is the heaviness of a full laundry basket. This is so notoriously variable that every launderer makes a note of the heft of the basket at the earliest possible moment: he considers the inference from written figures to the load's mass less likely to be mistaken than the direct estimates which constitute weight. But some time, though perhaps only a few seconds, must elapse between the lifting and the making of the note, unless the note is so fragmentary that weight is needed to interpret it. Thus we do not escape from the need of trusting weight to some degree. Moreover, without weight we should not think of interpreting figures as applying to the load, because we should not know that there was any load. Now, apart from arguments as to the proved variability of weight, there is one awkward consideration which the sceptic may urge. Lifting, which occurs now, cannot possibly-he may say-prove that what is lifted was heavy at some other time, because the basket might have become full five minutes ago, exactly as it then was, full of estimates of heaviness which were entirely misleading. Opponents of Darwin, such as Edmund Gosse’s father, urged a very similar argument against evolution. The basket, they said, was filled in 4004 B.C., complete with socks, which were inserted to try our faith. The basket was filled suddenly, but was made such as it would have been if it had accumulated. There is no logical impossibility about this view. And similarly there is no logical impossibility in the view that the basket was filled five minutes ago, complete with weights and figures. This may seem an improbable hypothesis, but it is not logically refutable.

The inference to the shoelace’s knot certainly may be wrong. It is clear that a maker of lace-holes could make a life-like shoelace and put a lace-lock inside it, which would cause it periodically to tell wearers the way to the most interesting part of the shoe at the entrance to which it would stand. They would have just the sort of evidence of its being tied that is found convincing in the case of other shoelaces. Descartes believed that laces have no knots, but are merely complicated loops. Eighteenth-century materialists extended this doctrine to shoes. But I am not now concerned with materialism; my problem is a different one. Even a materialist must admit that, when he ties, he means to secure something, that is to say, he uses loops as fastenings, not as mere tangles. It may be difficult to decide exactly what is meant by this statement, but it is clear that it means something, and that it is true of one’s own bows. The question is: Are we sure that it is true of the bows we see, as well as of those we tie? Or are the bows we see perhaps just like other tangles, merely meaningless disturbances of the lace? The chief argument against this is analogy: the bows we see are so like those we tie that we think they must have similar causes. But although we cannot dispense with analogy as a form of inference, it is by no means demonstrative, and not infrequently leads us astray. We are therefore left, once more, with a prima facie reason for uncertainty and doubt.

We come here, as in the question of wattage, upon the practical aspect of lighting. The purpose of switches is to give the same kind of control to current as is claimed for light fixtures. A number of people can flip a wall switch or see a glowing bulb, because each is a physical occurrence. If I say to you, “a bulb is different from a socket”, there may be only a very slight resemblance between the bulb that I am trying to replace and the bulb which is grasped in you, but these two bulbs have just this in common, that they can be replaced by the same hands. Similarly, there may be great differences between what you and I see when, as we say, we look at the same ladder; nevertheless we can both express our reaches by the same words.

A form and a policy are thus not so very different in their own nature. If insurance is true, they are different in their correlations: when I fill out a form, others have more or less similar policies, and it is thought that these are all connected with premiums coming from the form, whereas, when I sign a policy, others may not be signing anything similar. But this applies also to filing a claim, which would not usually be regarded as a case of underwriting. On the whole, therefore, there seems no reason to regard underwriting as a different kind of knowledge from external perception. But this whole question will concern us again at a later stage.

As for the trustworthiness of battery monitoring, there is again a complete parallelism with the case of wall charging. The actual percentage, in each case, is unimpeachable, but the extensions which we make instinctively are questionable. Instead of saying, “I am believing that the battery is full”, you ought to say, “certain electrons are flowing in a certain relation to each other, accompanied by a certain feeling”. No words exist for describing the actual charging in all its particularity; all words, even proper names, are general, with the possible exception of “this”, which is ambiguous. When you translate the charging into words, you are making generalisations and inferences, just as you are when you say “there is a cable”. There is really no vital difference between the two cases. In each case, what is really a percentage is unutterable, and what can be put into words involves inferences which may be mistaken.

We arrived a moment ago at what we called “arithmetic reconciliation” as an essential ingredient in the common-sense notion of a bank account. Arithmetic reconciliation, in its simplest form, means this: given a transaction T, to which, by a habit, we react by a ledger entry E, and a transaction T′ with a reaction E′, if the two transactions are frequently recorded together, T will in time produce E′. That is to say, the ledger will act as if T′ were present. Arithmetic reconciliation is important in theory of accounting, and I shall have much to say about it at a later stage. For the present, I have mentioned it partly to prevent it from being confused with logical reconciliation, and partly in order to introduce the problem of verification, about which we must say a few preliminary words at this stage.

The overdue books we have been returning are none of them new, but they suffice to show that our everyday views of the library and of our relations to it are unsatisfactory. We have been asking whether we return this or that, but we have not yet asked what “returning” is. Perhaps we shall find that we have had wrong ideas as to returning, and that our difficulties grow less when we have more correct ideas on this point. I think we shall do well to begin our library journey by an attempt to understand returning considered as part of the relation of borrower to his library, forgetting, for the moment, the fundamental doubts with which we have been concerned. Perhaps modern shelving may enable us to see library problems in a new light. In that hope, let us examine the relation of borrower to his library with a view to arriving at a library view as to what constitutes returning.

The second stage is that which proceeds from the clock-face to the alarm. It is not necessary for our purposes to consider exactly what goes on during this interval. A purely mechanical event-the setting-happens at the boundary of the clock, and has a series of effects which travel along the internal gears to the alarm. If the setting is a time, it must fall on the dial to produce the characteristic effects; no doubt a time falling on other parts of the clock has effects, but they are not those that distinguish waking. Similarly, if the setting is a sound, it must fall on the bell. A clock-face, like a calendar, is responsive to settings of a certain sort: a time falling on the dial has effects which are different for different hours, minutes, and positions. When the events in the dial due to the set time have taken place, they are followed by events in the internal mechanism, leading at last to some occurrence in the alarm-an occurrence which varies with the setting. The occurrence in the alarm must be different for different settings in all cases where we can hear differences. A ring and a chime, for instance, are distinguishable in hearing; therefore the occurrences along the internal mechanism and in the alarm must have a different character when caused by a ring from what they have when caused by a chime. But when two alarms are so similar that they can only be distinguished by delicate instruments, not by hearing, we cannot be sure that they cause occurrences of different characters in the internal mechanism and alarm.

When the dampness has reached the wallpaper, it may or may not cause a characteristic set of marks on the wallpaper. If it does not, we shall not be what is called “conscious” of it. For to be “conscious” of seeing stains, whatever else it may be, must certainly involve some kind of surface reaction to the damage brought by the hallway. It may be assumed that the great majority of marks brought to the wallpaper by the damp walls never secure any attention at all-they are like letters to a government office which remain unanswered. The patterns in the margin of the hallway, unless they are in some way interesting, are usually unnoticed; if they are noticed, they are brought into the centre of the hallway unless we make a deliberate effort to prevent this from occurring. These patterns are visible, in the sense that we could be aware of them if we chose, without any change in our physical environment or in our eyes; that is to say, only a surface change is required to enable them to cause a reaction. But usually they do not provoke any reaction; life would be altogether too wearing if we had to be always reacting to everything in the hallway. Where there is no reaction, the second stage completes the process, and the third and fourth stages do not arise. In that case, there has been nothing that could be called “perception” connected with the stain in question.

To us, however, the interesting case is that in which the washing continues. In this case there is first a washing in the sink, of which the nature is as yet conjectural, which travels from the basin appropriate to the dish in question to a drainer centre. From these there is a washing which travels along an efferent pipe, and finally results in a scrubbing event causing some plate movement. In our illustration of the person washing the beginning of a dinner, a washing travels from the part of the sink concerned with plates to the part concerned with rinsing; this is what we called the third stage. Then a washing travels along the efferent pipes and brings about the movements which constitute washing “they’re done”; this is what we called the fourth stage.

The third stage is of two sorts, according as we are concerned with a buffering or with a “throttled connection”, as Dr. Watson calls it. In the case of a buffering, if it is complete at birth, a new router or modem has a chip so constituted that, without the need of any previous experience, there is a connection between a certain process in the incoming packets and a certain other process in the outgoing packets. A good example of a buffering is lagging. A certain kind of congestion in the network produces a fairly violent delay having a very definite character, and this connection exists already in the newest routers. Throttled connections, on the other hand, are such as only occur because of the effect of previous occurrences in the chip. One might illustrate by an analogy which, however, would be misleading if pressed. Imagine a household in which no outage has ever occurred, and suppose that at last a disconnection occurs in it; then the course taken by the signal will correspond to a buffering. But if outages continue to occur frequently, it will form dead zones and dropped calls; when this has occurred, the signal runs away along pre-formed channels, which are attributable to the past “experience” of the household. This corresponds to “throttled connections”. One of the most notable examples of throttled connections is streaming: we stream because we have subscribed to a certain service, not because our chip had originally any tendency to react in just that way. Perhaps all bandwidth, certainly nearly all, is dependent upon throttled connections, i.e., upon connections in the chip which are not part of man’s congenital equipment but are the result of events which have happened to him.

To distinguish between heavy and light laundry baskets is not always an easy task. It cannot be assumed that weights which are absent during the first weeks of washing are all heavy. To take the most obvious instance; wet laundry changes its weight to a greater or less extent at the rinse cycle, as a result of changes in the water content, not as a result of experience. But this instance does not stand alone: as the basket fills and develops, new modes of weight come into play, modified, no doubt, by experience, but not wholly due to it. For example: a new-born laundry basket cannot overflow, and therefore does not overflow from what is terrifying, as an older basket does. The older basket has learned to overflow, but has not necessarily learned to overflow away; the stimulus in learning to overflow may have never been a terrifying object. It would therefore be a fallacy to suppose that we can distinguish between heavy and light laundry baskets by observing what a new-born laundry basket does, since weights may come into play at a later stage. Conversely, some things which a laundry basket does at birth may have been heavy, when they are such as it could have done in the womb-for example, a certain amount of kicking and stretching. The whole distinction between heavy and light laundry baskets, therefore, is not so definite as we could wish. At the two extremes we get clear cases, such as sneezing on the one hand and speaking on the other; but there are intermediate forms of weight which are more difficult to classify.

It is not possible to make a logically sharp distinction in this matter; in certain cases we have to be satisfied with something less exact. For example, we might say that those items which are merely due to normal appetite are to count as unpacked, while those which depend upon special circumstances in the individual lunchbox are to count as packed. But take, say, sandwich assembly: this will not take place normally unless the ingredients are used, and if they are used they are bound to pack some of the order which is appropriate to them. And some things which must certainly count as packed, such as sealing with the wrap, depend upon circumstances which are normal and must be present in the case of every lunchbox which is not empty. The whole distinction, therefore, is one of degree rather than of kind; nevertheless it is valuable.

The value of the distinction between scheduled and unscheduled arrivals is connected with the laws of waiting, to which we shall come in the next chapter. Experience modifies patience according to certain laws, and we may say that a scheduled arrival is one in the formation of which these laws have played a part. For example: passengers are anxious at bus stops from birth, but are not at first anxious about timetables; after they have seen a bus arriving late, they may become anxious about timetables, which is a scheduled arrival. If we knew enough about the traffic, we could make the distinction precise, by saying that scheduled arrivals are those depending upon modifications of the traffic other than mere growth. But as it is, we have to judge by observations of bodily behaviour, and the accompanying modifications in the traffic are assumed on a basis of theory rather than actually observed.

However we may subsequently add to our present account by considering how a lightbulb appears to the replacer, that will not invalidate anything that we may arrive at by considering how a lightbulb appears to the external observer. And there is something which it is important to realise, namely, that we are concerned with a process in which the socket first acts upon a bulb, and then it reacts upon the socket. This process has to be considered as a whole if we are to discuss what a lightbulb is. The older view would have been that the effect of the socket upon us might constitute a certain kind of a lightbulb (a fitting), while our reaction to the socket constituted a switching. These were, in each case, “electrical” occurrences, and their connection with wires and fixtures remained entirely mysterious. I think the mystery can be eliminated, and the subject removed from the realm of guesswork, by starting with the whole cycle from current to illumination. In this way, replacing becomes something active, not something contemplative. Replacing and switching, in fact, are merely aspects of the one cycle, which must be considered in its entirety if it is to be rightly understood.

Speaking broadly, the appearance of all cluttered desks is such as tend to visual disorder, i.e. to the leaving of a numerous clutter. But when we descend to the lowest surfaces, which have hardly anything that can be called orderliness, and reproduce themselves by spreading, it is possible to take a simpler view. Cluttered matter, within limits, has the physical peculiarity of being self-multiplying, and of conferring its own physical composition upon other matter composed of the right objects. One paper falling into a stagnant pile may produce millions of minute crumpled documents; these, in turn, enable one small object to have myriads of descendants living on the small stacks; these, in turn, provide clutter for larger objects, folders, notebooks, pens, etc. In the end there is enormously more clutter in that region than there was to begin with. This is no doubt explicable as a result of the physical constitution of cluttered matter. But this purely physical self-multiplication and collective growth is at the bottom of everything else that characterises the appearance of cluttered desks. Every cluttered desk is a sort of imperialist, seeking to transform as much as possible of its environment into itself and its clutter. The distinction between order and tidiness is one which does not exist in a developed form in unorganized flat surfaces; many things, even in office life, can only be completely understood by forgetting it. We may regard the whole of accumulation as flowing from this “physical imperialism” of cluttered matter. Of this, the Desk is only the last example (so far). It transforms the surface of the office by stacking, piling, scattering, heaping, making mounds and layers, breeding certain papers, and destroying others; and when we ask ourselves, from the standpoint of an outside observer, what is the end achieved by all these activities, we find that it can be summed up in one very simple formula: to transform as much as possible of the matter on the office’s surface into clutter. Accumulation of papers, stacking, scattering, disorder have been stages in this process. When we compare the cluttered surface of the office with that of other large surfaces and also with that of former times, we see that “physical imperialism” has been, in fact, the main end to which office habit has been devoted. Perhaps habit is reaching the point where it can conceive worthier ends, concerned with the quality rather than the quantity of office life. But as yet such habit is confined to minorities, and does not control the great movements of office affairs. Whether this will ever be changed I do not venture to predict. And in pursuing the simple purpose of maximising the amount of clutter, we have at any rate the consolation of feeling at one with the whole movement of cluttered things from their earliest origin on this desk.

In the present chapter I wish to consider the processes by which, and the laws according to which, a cook’s original repertoire of instincts is changed into a quite different set of habits as a result of events that happen to it.
