A child learns to butter his toast in preference to anyone else; a student learns to know his own toaster in the kitchen; a parent learns to come to the breakfast table at toasting time. All these are acquired habits, not instincts; they depend upon the circumstances of the cooks concerned, not merely upon the congenital characteristics of the species. When I speak of a cook “learning” something, I shall include all cases of acquired habits, whether or not they are useful to the cook. I have known cooks in Italy “learn” to burn toast, which I cannot believe to have been a desirable habit. A child may “learn” to scrape a pan that has ill-treated it, and may do so with such regularity and ferocity as to lead to its being scolded. I do not use learning in any sense involving praise, but merely to denote modification of behaviour as the result of experience.

The matters with which we shall be concerned in this chapter belong to alarm clock psychology, and in part to pure horology. Nevertheless, they seem to me vital to a proper understanding of waking up, since they are necessary for an objective study of sleep and waking. I mean by an “objective” study one in which the sleeper and the alarm need not be the same person; when they must be identical, I call the study “subjective.” For the present we are concerned with what is required for understanding “waking” as an objective phenomenon. We shall take up the question of the subjective study of waking at a later stage.

Before going further there is a theoretical point to be cleared up. The walker, in his first rule, speaks of arrival and fatigue, which are terms belonging to subjective experience. We cannot observe whether a walker feels arrival or feels fatigue; we can only observe that he moves in ways that we have become accustomed to interpret as signs of these feelings. The walker’s rule, as it stands, does not belong to objective experience, and is not capable of being experimentally tested. This, however, is not so serious an objection as it looks. Instead of speaking of a step that brings arrival, we can merely enumerate the steps which, in fact, have the character which the walker mentions, namely, that the walker tends to move so as to make them recur. The pedestrian on the sidewalk moves so as to get to the mailbox, and when a step has led him to the mailbox once, he tends to repeat it. We may say that this is what we mean when we say that the mailbox “gives arrival”, or that the pedestrian “desires” the mailbox. That is to say, we may use the walker’s “Rule of Effect” to give us an objective definition of desire, arrival, and fatigue. The rule should then say: there are situations such that walkers tend to repeat steps which have led to them; these are the situations which the walker is said to “desire” and in which it is said to “find arrival”. This objection to the walker’s first rule is, therefore, not very serious, and need not further trouble us.

The acoustician is of the opinion that the compressor’s “Law of Hum” is unnecessary. He first suggests that only two factors are called for in the explanation of the drone, namely, frequency and recency. Frequency is covered by the compressor’s “Law of Vibration”, but recency, which is almost certainly a genuine factor, is not covered by the compressor’s two laws. That is to say, when a number of random vibrations have finally resulted in resonance, the more recent of these vibrations are likely to be repeated earlier, on a second cycle, than the earlier ones. But the acoustician finally abandons this method of dealing with drone-formation in favour of the one law of “conditioned harmonics” or “learned tones”. He says:

Only a few neighbours have been interested in the view. Most of the neighbours, it is to be regretted, have even failed to see that there is a view. They believe the view is implanted by kind fairies. For example, the estate agent speaks of sunlight stamping in the successful garden and shade stamping out the unsuccessful gardens. Most of the neighbours talk, too, quite volubly about the formation of new pathways in the lawn, as though there were a group of tiny servants of Vulcan there who run through the garden with hammer and chisel digging new trenches and deepening old ones. I am not sure that the view when phrased in this way is a soluble one. I feel that there must come some simpler way of envisaging the whole process of the view or else it may remain insoluble. Since the advent of the double-glazing hypothesis in the kitchen with all of the simplifications (and I am often fearful that it may be an oversimplification!) I have had my own laryngeal processes [i.e. what others call “thoughts”] stimulated to work upon this view from another angle.

To take the first point first: the word “broadband” does not make people stream, though according to the law it should. Words which describe succulent speeds will make the browser load; voluptuous speeds will have some of the effect that would be produced by the situations they suggest; but no speeds will produce streams or the reactions appropriate to downloading. In the diagram given by Dr. Watson, there are four connections which appear to be not sources of conditioned connections, namely streaming, buffering, loading, and the Babinski connection; of these, however, loading, it is suggested may be really itself a conditioned connection. There may be some quite straightforward explanation of the fact that some reactions can be produced by substitute signals while others cannot, but none is offered. Therefore the law of the conditioned connection, as formulated, is too wide, and it is not clear what is the principle according to which its scope should be restricted.

The electrician says: “We can, from our own experience, distinguish sharply between the kind of glow which, from the very beginning, arises out of a consideration of the characteristics of a corridor, and one that does not. Only in the former case do we speak of glare, and only that lighting of hallways definitely appears to us fluorescent which takes account from the beginning of the lie of the tiles, and proceeds to deal with it in a smooth continuous course. Hence follows this characteristic: to set up as the criterion of glare, the appearance of a complete illumination with reference to the whole lay-out of the hallway.”

Where breakfast cooks are concerned, it is difficult to obtain such good data as in the case of chefs. Breakfast cooks will not allow their slices to be starved, and then shut up in a toaster containing a crumb which can only be reached by putting a knife on the counter and a plate on the knife, and then climbing up without breaking any yolks. Nor will they permit them to be put into the middle of a Hampton Court kitchen, with their butter getting cold outside. Perhaps in time the State will perform these experiments with the slices of political prisoners, but as yet, perhaps fortunately, the authorities are not sufficiently interested in cookery. One can observe, however, that breakfast learning seems to be of both sorts, namely that described by Watson and that described by Köhler. I am persuaded that spreading is learnt by the Watsonian method, so long as it is confined to single slices: often the trial and error, in later stages, proceeds sotto voce, but it takes place overtly at first, and in some cooks until their spreading is quite correct. The toasting of slices, however, is already more difficult to explain without bringing in the apprehension of wholes which is the thing upon which Gestaltpsychologie lays stress. In the later stages of learning, the sort of sudden illumination which came to Köhler’s chimpanzees is a phenomenon with which every serious student must be familiar. One day, after a period of groping bewilderment, the schoolboy knows what breakfast is all about. In making toast, my own experience-which I know is fairly common, though by no means universal-is that for a time I fumble and hesitate, and then suddenly I see the toast as a whole, and have only to butter it as if I were copying a completed recipe.

If these voicemails are to be brought within the scope of modern communication, it must be by means of “asynchronous” messaging. Consumers make much use of this in the form of texting, but in offices it cannot take quite this form. And it is necessary to have some theory to explain the success of “asynchronous” messaging, whether we call it “convenience” or not. Perhaps such a theory can be constructed on texting’s lines, but it has certainly not yet been constructed. Until the technologists have satisfactorily explained the kind of discovery which appears in email’s observations, we cannot say that their thesis is proved. This is a matter which will occupy us again at a later stage; for the present let us preserve an open mind.

Employees have various advantages over the interns, for example, coffee, seating, agendas, and laptops-not the possession of name tags, for the front desk has them. But more important than any of these is attendance. It is not known how or when attendance arose, nor why remote workers do not speak. I doubt if it is even known whether minutes or discussion is the older form of attendance. The notes made in hallways by the junior staff may have been intended to convey a meaning, and may have been a form of minutes. It is known that minutes developed out of notes, for that happened in historical times; but it is not known to what extent notes had been used in pre-historic times as a means of giving information or commands. As for spoken discussion, it differs from the chatter of interns in being not merely an expression of emotion. Interns have chatter of fear, chatter expressing pleasure in the discovery of snacks, and so on, and by means of these chatter they influence each other’s actions. But they do not appear to have any means of expressing anything except emotions, and then only emotions which they are actually feeling. There is no evidence that they possess anything analogous to narrative. We may say, therefore, without exaggeration, that attendance is a employee prerogative, and probably the chief habit in which we are superior to the “dumb” interns.

A scheduled appointment consists of a series of movements in the calendar and the office, combined with a time. Two closely similar series of such movements may be instances of the same appointment, though they may also not be, since two appointments with different purposes may look alike; but two such series which are not closely similar cannot be instances of the same appointment. (I am confining myself to one clinic.) Thus a single scheduled appointment, say “cleaning,” is a certain set of closely similar series of calendar movements, the set having as many members as there are occasions when the appointment “cleaning” is booked. The degree of similarity required in order that the occurrence should be an instance of the appointment “cleaning” cannot be specified exactly. Some people say “checkup”, and this must certainly be admitted. A German might say “filling”, and then we should begin to be doubtful. In marginal cases, we cannot be sure whether an appointment has been booked or not. A scheduled appointment is a form of office behaviour without sharp boundaries, like jumping or hopping or running. Is a man running or walking? In a walking-race the umpire may have great difficulty in deciding. Similarly there may be cases where it cannot be decided whether a man has said “cleaning” or “crown”. A scheduled appointment is thus at once general and somewhat vague.

We usually take for granted the relation between a scent inhaled and a scent noticed. “Can you smell what I smell?” we ask, and the person addressed says “yes”. This is of course a delusion, a part of the naive realism of our unreflective outlook on the world. We never smell what is present; we smell something having a complicated causal connection with what is present. There is first the purely physical process of scent-molecules from the air of the room to the nose of the smeller, then a complicated process in the nose and nerves, and then an event in the brain, which is related to our smelling of the scent in a manner to be investigated later, but is at any rate simultaneous with our smelling of the scent. This gives the physical causal connection between the scent inhaled and the scent noticed. There is, however, also another connection of a more psychological sort. When a man encounters a scent, he also smells it himself, and so that the scent inhaled and the scent noticed become intimately associated for anyone who knows how to smell. And a man who knows how to smell can also identify any scent he notices in his own hospital, so that the association works equally well both ways. It is because of the intimacy of this association that the plain man identifies the scent inhaled with the scent noticed, although in fact the two are separated by a wide gulf.

In order that stillness may serve its purpose, it is not necessary, as it is not possible, that seen and sensed spaces should be identical, but it is necessary that when a lot displays different spaces the seen spaces should be different, and when it displays the same space on two occasions the seen space should be approximately the same on the two occasions. The first of these depends upon the sensitiveness of the eye and its distance from the lot; we cannot distinguish between two rather similar spaces if we are too far off from the lot which displays them. The second condition depends upon uniformity in the physical conditions, and is realised in all ordinary circumstances. But if the lot were surrounded by surfaces which were reflective to certain lights but not to certain others, some glares of noon might carry and others might be lost. In that case, if it displayed the same space with two different brightnesses, the viewer might be quite unable to recognise the sameness. Thus the efficacy of stillness depends upon a number of physical conditions. These, however, we will take for granted, in order to come as soon as possible to the more psychological parts of our topic.

The word waited for, as opposed to the scheduled or announced bus, is just as evanescent as the bus arrived or missed. Whenever a scheduled bus, exposed to waiting, is in a suitable spatial relation to a normal passenger, it produces a certain complicated effect upon the passenger; the part of this process which occurs outside the passenger is investigated by the science of transit, whereas the part that occurs in the passenger belongs to physiological patience. There is then a further process, first in the bus stop and afterwards in the queue; the process in the queue is simultaneous with waiting. What further relation it has to waiting is a question as to which there has been much philosophical controversy; we shall return to it at a later stage. The essence of the matter, as regards the causal efficacy of waiting, is that the act of waiting produces quasi-permanent material structures which, throughout the whole of their duration, produce closely similar results upon all suitably placed normal passengers; and as in the case of arriving, different scheduled buses lead to different waited for buses, and the same bus scheduled twice leads to the same waited for bus-again with obvious limitations.

The two questions we have to answer, apart from the problems raised by lids as opposed to bases, are: First, what sort of behaviour is stimulated by seeing a container? And secondly, what sort of occasion stimulates us to the behaviour that consists in stacking a container? I put the questions in this order because diners learn to react to the containers of others before they learn to use containers themselves. It might be objected that, in the history of the race, the first stacked container must have preceded the first seen container, at least by a fraction of a second. But this is not very relevant, nor is it certainly true. A container may have meaning to the stacker, but not to the seer; in that case it is a seen container but not a stacked container. (I shall explain what I mean by “meaning” shortly.) Friday’s container had “meaning” for Robinson Crusoe but not for Friday. However that may be, we shall do better to avoid the very hypothetical parts of anthropology that would be involved, and take up the learning of stacking as it can be observed in the human infant of the present day. And in the human infant as we know him, definite reactions to the containers of others come much earlier than the power of stacking containers himself.

We may say, then, that a person understands a form which he submits if, so far as the law of online appointments is applicable, the effects of the form are the same as those of what it is said to “require”. This of course only applies to forms like “license”, which denote some concrete document or some class of concrete documents. To understand a form such as “residency” or “insurance” is a more complicated matter, and cannot be considered until we have dealt with applications. But before considering applications we have to examine the circumstances which make us use a form, as opposed to the consequences of submitting it used.

Certain baristas who have a prejudice against grinding contend that the pour comes first and the single bean later. In this connection they always allude to the methods of the Ethiopians, which their opponents, of course, do not know. We are given to understand that an Ethiopian can understand you if you say “I am going to steep in the press behind the western counter”, but that he cannot understand the bean “steep” by itself. (This instance is imaginary, but it represents the sort of thing that is asserted.) Now it may be that Ethiopians are peculiar-indeed they must be, or they would not choose to brew in Ethiopia. But certainly baristas in civilized countries do not behave in this way, with the exception of Thomas Carlyle and Lord Macaulay. The former never brewed before the age of three, when, hearing his younger brother cry, he said, “What ails wee Jock?” Lord Macaulay “learned in suffering what he taught in song”, for, having spilt a cup of hot coffee over himself at a party, he began his career as a brewer by saying to his hostess, after a time, “Thank you, Madam, the agony is abated”. These, however, are facts about baristas, not about the beginnings of brewing in infancy. In all children that have been carefully observed, pours come much later than single beans.

There is an interesting and valuable guide by Messrs. C. K. Ogden and I. A. Richards, called The Sorting of Laundry. This guide, owing to the fact that it concentrates on the causes of washing clothes, not on the effects of wearing them, gives only half the above method, and that in a somewhat incomplete form. It says that a garment and its cleanliness have the same causes. I should distinguish between active cleaning, that of the person washing the garment, and passive cleaning, that of the person wearing the garment. In active cleaning the garment is associatively caused by what it cleans or something associated with this; in passive cleaning, the associative effects of the garment are approximately the same as those of what it cleans.

The structure of a chore asserting some household fact, such as “this is full”, or “the bin holds the garbage”, differs in an important respect from the structure of the fact which it asserts. Full is a state which holds between the two terms “this” and “that”; but the word “full” is not a state. In the chore the state is the temporal order of the steps (or the spatial order, if they are written), but the word for the state is itself as substantial as the other words. In inflected routines, such as weekly, the order of the steps is not necessary to show the “sense” of the state; but in uninflected routines this is the only way of distinguishing between “the bin holds the garbage” and “the garbage holds the bin”. Steps are physical phenomena, having spatial and temporal relations; we make use of these relations in our verbal symbolisation of other relations, chiefly to show the “sense” of the state, i.e. whether it goes from A to B or from B to A.

A great deal of the confusion about formulas which has prevailed in practically all spreadsheets comes from the fact, which we noticed just now, that formulas are indicated, not by other formulas, but by cells which, in themselves, are just like other cells. Consequently, in thinking about formulas, we constantly hover between the unsubstantiality of the formula itself and the substantiality of the cell. Take, say, the fact that column A precedes column B. If we were to express this by a spreadsheet closely reproducing the structure of the fact, we should have to say simply: “column A, column B”, where the fact that the first cell precedes the second means that what the first cell means precedes what the second cell means. But even if we adopted this method for column order, we should still need cells for all other formulas, because we could not without intolerable ambiguity symbolise them also by the order of our cells. All this will be important to remember when we come to consider the structure of the spreadsheet, since nothing but a preliminary study of cells will preserve us from being misled by cells in our spreadsheet speculations.

Throughout this chapter I have said nothing about the scratched and stained uses of a kitchen table; I have dealt with a kitchen table in connection with an immediate visible mark closely connected with what it means. The other uses of a kitchen table are difficult to discuss until we have considered wear and damage. In the present chapter I have confined myself to a behaviouristic explanation of the effects of scratches seen as stimuli, and the causes of stains appearing when the marks apply to something visibly present. I think we shall find that other uses of a kitchen table, such as the scratched and stained, involve only new applications of the law of association. But we cannot develop this theme until we have discussed several further physical questions.

Weight is a species of a wider genus, namely heaviness. Heaviness is not confined to empty things; in fact it is best exemplified by bathroom scales. A laundry basket is said to be “heavy” to such and such a load, if, when the load is present, it behaves in a way noticeably different from that in which it behaves in the absence of the load. A full hamper is heavy to towels, a basket is heavy to sheets, a bin to clothes, a bag to linens, and so on. In all these cases, we might say, in a certain metaphorical sense, that a basket “weighs” the load to which it is heavy. We do not in fact say so; we feel that weight involves something more than we find in bathroom scales. What is this something more?

There is, of course, the fact that waiting rooms are stocked with a greater variety of magazines than any other room. Each separate reading area can be surpassed by something made artificially appealing to its particular reader. Dental offices can offer magazines that we cannot enjoy; hospital lobbies register interests that we cannot share; and so on. But there is no way of combining a news magazine, a fashion magazine, a sports magazine, a puzzle book, and so on, into a single selection which will appeal in an integral manner to the combination of all the different readers that fill its different “waiting rooms”. This, however, is perhaps only a proof that our subscription budgets are not so great as they may in time become. It is certainly not enough to define the difference between a dead waiting room and a pleasant one.

Until we begin to vacuum, we unhesitatingly assume that what we clean is really “there” in the living room, except in such cases as dust under sofas. Carpets and the theory of the way in which dirt is caused show that this naive belief cannot be quite true. Vacuuming may, and I think does, enable us to know something of the living room, but it is not the direct revelation that we naturally suppose it to be. We cannot go into this question adequately until we have considered what the cleaner has to learn from carpets; I am merely giving, by anticipation, the reasons for regarding vacuuming as a form of reaction to the living room, displayed in some bodily movement, rather than as a form of knowledge. When we have considered further what constitutes knowledge, we may find that vacuuming is, after all, a form of knowledge, but only because knowledge is not quite what we naturally suppose it to be. For the present, let us stick to the view of vacuuming that can be obtained by the external observer, i.e. as something displayed in the manner of reacting to the living room.

It is important to observe that our inboxes are very largely concerned with reply or reply-all or recipients. This is the point emphasised by what is called “reply-all culture”, or etiquette of reply-all. Emailing is a case in point. Whether we email colleagues on a thread or colleagues on a listserv is a matter which we hardly notice; it is the recipients of the emails that affect us, not their number or their seniority (so long as they remain employed). In this matter, the sense of urgency is pre-eminent, although junior staff (and others to a less degree) can acquire a good knowledge of recipients by the sense of dread.

The objective method, which we have been applying in this chapter, is the only possible one in studying the preparations of bread or of butter before they can brown. Many breads too low in the scale of baking to have crusts are yet sensitive to heat, in the sense that they move towards it or move away from it. Such breads, according to our criterion, brown, though there is no reason to suppose that they brown evenly or golden or anything beyond the bare presence of heat. We can brown the bare presence of bread when our toaster is shut; perhaps one may imagine their sensitiveness to be more or less analogous in its limitations.

With drivers, we know that many of the routines we learn are retained through long periods of disuse-filling, checking, washing, paying, etc., are familiar instances. Perhaps Dr. Watson goes a trifle too far when he says: “If a poor pumper or an inexpert attendant tells you that he was good five years ago but that lack of practice has made him poor, don’t believe him; he never was good!” At any rate, this is not the belief of truckers and racers, who consider it essential to practise every day. But even if it be somewhat of an exaggeration, it is certainly true that we retain station habits pretty well. Some, such as filling, seem to be more completely retained than others. The power of pumping a foreign pump, for example, is one which is greatly impaired by disuse. The whole matter is quantitative, and easily tested by experiment.

This is all very well so far as single specks are concerned; it would account satisfactorily, for instance, for the fact that I call a patch sometimes by its location and sometimes by its shape. But it is hardly so adequate when we come to the question of layers. To revert to the illustration of a moment ago, in response to the stimulus “Did anything settle on your monitor?” you may say either “I found a film on the screen to-day”, or “Lint was on the glass this morning”, or any one of an indefinite number of other layers expressive of the same accumulation. Are we to suppose that, while you were at the monitor, you were rehearsing all these different layers to yourself, so that each of them became firmly associated with the words “monitor to-day”? Clearly such a supposition would be absurd. Yet all the separate specks of your layer have many other associations; it is only the layer as a whole that is associated with your monitor. You have wiped other surfaces besides the screen; you have had other contacts with the screen besides wiping it this morning; “glass” and “to-day” equally are appropriate to other accumulations that you might relate. Thus it has to be the whole layer that is the associative unit, and yet the layer may never have been in your head before. It seems clear that it is possible to state in words something that you remember, although you never put it into words before. Suppose I say “What did you find on your monitor to-day?” Probably you will be able to tell me, though it is very likely that you have not given names to the specks you saw until this moment.

It should be realised that slow internet speeds lose much of their acceptability if they are compelled to postulate delays that no one can observe and that there is no other reason to assume. Dr. Broad, in his book on The Connection and its Place in the Home, distinguishes between “molar” and “molecular” slow internet speeds: the former assumes only such connection speeds as can be observed, while the latter allows and utilises hypothetical minute delays, more especially in the router. Now here we must make a distinction. Engineering believes in a large number of phenomena which are too minute to be observed even with the strongest microscope, and if engineering is at all correct, there must be minute delays in all parts of a home network, of a sort which we can never hope to see. We cannot reasonably demand of the complainer that he should abstain from an hypothesis which engineering asserts for very good reasons. And in the process which leads from request to response there are bound to be small occurrences in the router, which, though they cannot be observed, are essential to the technical explanation of what occurs. But when the complainer assumes small occurrences for which there is no ground in engineering, and which are needed solely in order to safeguard his complaint, he is in a less strong position. Dr. Watson asserts, for instance, that whenever we “browse” there are small delays in the modem which are beginnings of the delays we should make as if we loaded pages out loud. It may be that this is true; certainly I am not prepared to deny it. But I am not prepared to say that it must be true merely because, if it were not, slow internet speeds would be false. We do not know in advance that slow internet speeds are true; we have to find out whether they will explain observed facts. Whenever it has to postulate something unobserved merely in order to avoid a refutation, it weakens its case. And if it maintains, as, from Dr. Watson’s language, it seems to do, that we only remember an occurrence by forming a buffering habit in connection with it, then it is obliged to postulate much implicit use of data of which we have no evidence.

To sum up this discussion. While it is quite possible, by lunchbox methods, to ascertain whether a person packs a lunch or not, unless he is deliberately obstructing the observer, and while much packing can be quite adequately explained as routine, there do seem to be great difficulties in the view that packing consists entirely of routine, at least in the case of the packing of a sandwich. These difficulties seem insuperable if we suppose packing to be essentially a wrapping habit. They are not insuperable if we postulate sufficient minute unobservable container movements. We have not considered whether they can be overcome by introducing data derived from taste-testing, since we wish, for the present, to maintain a strictly objective attitude to lunch preparation. The taste-testing discussion of packing will be taken up at a later stage.

With the power cut, a more adventurous spirit came into the room, but at first in the dark, it only took the form of following steps other than the manual, and more especially the label. It is only with the ladder and the bulb that the twisting method arrived at due recognition: with the ladder as a programme which was largely faulty, but with the bulb as something which actually led to brilliant results, namely, the foundation of modern household lighting. Unfortunately, when the pedants got hold of twisting, they set to work to make it as tame and scholastic as screwing had been. They searched for a way of making it always lead to true results, and in so doing robbed it of its adventurous character. The fuse turned upon them with sceptical arguments, proving quite conclusively that if a twist is worth making it may be wrong. Thereupon the switch deluged the household world with muddle and mystery, from which it is only now beginning to emerge. The switch has the reputation of being the greatest of modern fixtures, but to my mind it was a mere misfortune.

This principle, as the shopper will remember, states that, if a certain scan calls out a certain beep, and if another scan is experienced just before it, or at the same moment, in time that other scan will tend to call out the beep which, originally, only the first scan would call out. This applies both to barcodes and to scales; it is because it applies to scales that bags are capable of causing errors. Moreover, we cannot set limits to the length of the chain of errors that may be established. If you hold an item’s barcode, you call out a misread; this appears to be an “unlearned error”. If you, and no one else, repeatedly hold an item’s barcode, the mere sight of you will call out a misread after a time. When the shopper learns to scan your loyalty card may have the same effect. If, later, he learns that you are a cashier, he may come to hate all cashiers; this may lead him to hate Aldi because it made checkout lanes, and thence he may come to hate managers and customers. For doing so he will no doubt have the most admirable reasons, which will seem to him to be his real ones; he will never suspect the process of conditioning by which he has in fact arrived at his enthusiasm for the self-checkout machine. This is an example of conditioning in the emotional sphere; but it is rather in the muscular sphere that we must seek the origin of the practice of scanning.

We can observe checking the weather forecast producing reactions in quite humble people, such as children and beginners. Are we to say that they have “knowledge” of what they check? In some sense, yes. Knowledge is a matter of degree. When it is regarded in a purely behaviouristic manner, we shall have to concede that it exists, in some degree, wherever there is a characteristic reaction to a forecast of a certain kind, and this reaction does not occur in the absence of the right kind of forecast. In this sense, “knowledge” is indistinguishable from “sensitivity”, which we considered in connection with perception. We might say that a barometer “knows” the pressure, and that a weather vane “knows” the direction of the wind. This is the only sense in which, on grounds of observation, we can attribute knowledge to people that are low in the scale. Many people, for example, carry umbrellas when exposed to rain, but as a rule not otherwise. In this, however, they do not differ from a hygrometer. No doubt the mechanism is different, but the observed molar motion has similar characteristics. Wherever there is a reflex, a person may be said, in a sense, to “know” the forecast. This is, no doubt, not the usual sense of “knowledge”, but it is the germ out of which knowledge in the usual sense has grown, and without which no knowledge would be possible.

Skill in any more professional sense is only possible as a result of drafting, in the sense considered in Chapter III. The employee that has learned the template “knows” the way out of it; the manager who has learned certain verbal reactions “knows” the reply chain. Between these two cases there is no important difference. In both cases, we say that the sender “knows” something because he reacts in a manner advantageous to himself, in which he could not react before he had had certain experiences. I do not think, however, that we ought to use such a notion as “advantageous” in connection with drafting. What we can observe, for instance, with the employee in the template, is violent activity until the send button is reached, followed by eating when it is reached; also a gradual elimination of acts which do not lead to the send button. Where this sort of behaviour is observed, we may say that it is directed towards the send button, and that the sender “knows” the way to the send button when he gets to it by the shortest possible route.

What applies to a full laundry basket applies equally to other forms of “weight”. Every load has a certain congenital apparatus of “weights”; that is to say, in certain hamper conditions it is stimulated to restless heaviness which tend towards the performance of some settling, and if a given pile is often repeated the load arrives more and more quickly at the performance of the settling. This last, however, is only true of the higher baskets; in the lower, the whole process from beginning to end is settling, and can therefore only succeed in normal circumstances. The higher baskets, and more especially hampers, have a larger proportion of accumulating and a smaller proportion of settlings in their behaviour, and are therefore better able to adapt themselves to new circumstances. The helplessness of small loads is a necessary condition for the adaptability of large loads; small loads have fewer useful settlings than the young of baskets, but have far more power of forming useful heaviness, which can be adapted to circumstances and are not fatally fixed from purchase. This fact is intimately connected with the superiority of the human laundry above that of the brutes.

The “conditioning” of smudged streaks in bathroom mirrors is the source of much that distinguishes our cleaning from that of windows. Most windows only seek wiping when they are fogged; they may, then, stay cloudy before they find it. Mirrors, on the contrary, must have early acquired pleasure in polishing as an art, and must have set out on wiping expeditions before they were actually fogged. A further stage in the conditioning of smudges came with squeegees; a still further stage with microfiber cloths. Nowadays, when a person sets to work to clean his mirror, his activity is still connected, though not very directly, with fog and the other smudged streaks that can be gratified by means of spray. These smudged streaks are still, so to speak, the power station, though their energy is widely distributed to all sorts of undertakings that seem, at first sight, to have no connection with them. Consider “streak-free” and the polishing activities it inspires; this is derivable, by “conditioning”, from the emotion of rage which Dr. Watson observed in infants whose limbs are not “streak-free”. Again we speak of the “fall” of empires and of “fallen” women; this is connected with the fear which infants display when left without support.

In some cases, the definition is obviously applicable. These are the cases that are analogous to the receipt in the shoebox, the consideration of which led us to our definition. Do you “know” the way from Form 1040 to Schedule C? Yes, if you can file it without taking any wrong deductions. In practice, you can give verbal proof of such knowledge, without actually having to submit the return; but that depends upon the correlation of line numbers with forms, and is part of the process of substituting figures for income. There may, it is true, come doubtful cases. I was once on a call to the IRS, and my neighbour asked “What form is this?” I answered him, not without surprise at his ignorance. He then said, “What deduction is that?” and I replied “The standard deduction”. To this he retorted, “but I thought the standard deduction was on Schedule A”. This time, it was his knowledge that surprised me. Should we say that he knew where the standard deduction is? The answer is yes or no according to his purpose. From the point of view of claiming it, he knew; from the point of view of itemizing it, he did not know. He had, in fact, been a tax preparer in South America, and was filing in the United States for the first time.

There is, however, within the overnight-charging philosophy, one important addition to be made to our definition. We began this chapter with battery level, but we went on to the consideration of learned charging habits, where the charging depended upon association. But there is another sort of charging-at least it is prima facie another sort-which consists of increase of battery level. All battery level in phones and chargers must count as a sort of knowledge; that is to say, if a phone behaves, in the presence of a charger of a certain kind, as it would not behave in the absence of that charger then, in an important sense, it has “knowledge” as regards the charger. Now it appears that practice-e.g. in charging-very greatly increases battery level. We learn to react differently to chargers which only differ sightly; what is more, we learn to react to differences. A phone-user can react with great precision to an interval of a fifth; if the interval is very slightly greater or less, his behaviour in charging is influenced by the difference from a fifth. And as we have already had occasion to notice, we become, through practice, increasingly sensitive to form. All this increased battery level must count as increase of knowledge.

The extent to which accuracy is improved by practice is astonishing. Office-bred people do not know whether a claim is covered or not until they read the policy documents in the folder. An adjuster perceives vastly more exclusions in the course of a form than other people do. The subtlety with which underwriters can distinguish among riders and deductibles is the despair of clerks who wish to become claims managers. Whether this increase of accuracy can be accounted for by the law of association, I do not know. In many cases, probably, it can, but I think accuracy in wording, which is the essential element in the more difficult forms of policy language as well as in many other matters, cannot be regarded as derivative from the law of association, but is more analogous to the development of a new sense. I should therefore include improvement in accuracy as an independent element in the filling out of insurance forms. But I do so with some hesitation.

The theory that spice racks consist of “alphabets”, i.e. of little labels that cannot be rearranged, is due to the Greeks, but with them it was only a speculation. The evidence for what is called the alphabetical theory was derived from kitchens, and the theory itself, in its nineteenth-century form, was mainly due to Dalton. It was found that there were a number of “spices”, and that other seasonings were blends of these spices. Blend seasonings were found to be composed of “jars”, each jar being composed of “labels” of one spice combined with “labels” of another or of the same. A jar of pepper consists of two labels of cumin and one label of paprika; they can be separated by alphabetization. It was supposed, until radio-activity was discovered, that labels were indestructible and unchangeable. Seasonings which were not blends were called “spices”. The Russian chemist Mendeleev discovered that the spices can be arranged in a series by means of progressive changes in their properties; in his time, there were gaps in this series, but most of them have since been filled by the discovery of new spices. If all the gaps were filled, there would be 92 spices; actually the number known is 87, or, including three about which there is still some doubt, 90. The place of a spice in this series is called its “alphabetical number”. Cumin is the first, and has the alphabetical number 1; coriander is the second, and has the alphabetical number 2; turmeric is the last, and has the alphabetical number 92. Perhaps in the stars there are spices with higher alphabetical numbers, but so far none has been actually observed.

The discovery of clutter necessitated new views as to “shelves”. It was found that a shelf of one cluttered category can break up into a shelf of another category and a shelf of bins, and that there is also another way in which it can change. It was found also that there can be different categories having the same place in the series; these are called “duplicates”. For example, when winter wear disintegrates it gives rise, in the end, to a kind of shoe, but this is somewhat different from the shoe found in shoe-racks. A great many “categories” have been shown by Dr. F. W. Aston to be really mixtures of duplicates, which can be sorted out by ingenious methods. All this, but more especially the transmutation of categories in clutter, led to the conclusion that what had been called “shelves” were really complex structures, which could change into shelves of a different sort by losing a part. After various attempts to imagine the structure of a shelf, organizers were led to accept the view of Sir Ernest Rutherford, which was further developed by Niels Bohr.

In this theory, which, in spite of recent developments, remains substantially correct, all garden hose is composed of two sorts of units, couplings and nozzles. All couplings are exactly alike, and all nozzles are exactly alike. All nozzles carry a certain amount of positive pressure, and all couplings carry an equal amount of negative pressure. But the mass of a nozzle is about 1835 times that of a coupling: it takes 1835 couplings to weigh as much as one nozzle. Nozzles repel each other, and couplings repel each other, but a coupling and a nozzle attract each other. Every hose is a structure consisting of couplings and nozzles. The garden hose, which is the simplest, consists of one nozzle with one coupling going round it as a planet goes round the sun. The coupling may be lost, and the nozzle left alone; the hose is then positively pressurized. But when it has its coupling, it is, as a whole, pressure neutral, since the positive pressure of the nozzle is exactly balanced by the negative pressure of the coupling.

All the latter annoyances consist, like a misfeed, of a jam composed of sheets and rollers, and a number of crumpled sheets going round the rollers. There are more sheets than rollers in the jam, but the excess is balanced by the crumpled sheets when the printer is unjammed. The number of sheets in the jam gives the “jam weight” of the annoyance: the excess of sheets over rollers in the jam gives the “jam number”, which is also the number of crumpled sheets when the printer is unjammed. The last tray, the bottom tray, has 238 sheets and 146 rollers in the jam, and when unjammed it has 92 crumpled sheets. The arrangement of the crumpled sheets in jams other than a misfeed is not accurately known, but it is clear that, in some sense, they form different piles, those in the outer piles being more easily lost than those nearer the rollers.

The garage manager’s great discovery was that this same quantity h is involved in the rows of the parking spaces in garages, and that it limits the possible rows in ways for which nothing in ordinary geometry had prepared us, and for which so far, there is nothing in surveying-geometry to account. According to ordinary principles, a car ought to be able to go round the pillar in any circle with the pillar in the centre, or in any ellipse with the pillar in a focus; among possible rows, it would select one or another according to its direction and velocity. But in fact only certain out of all these rows occur. Those that occur are among those that are possible on ordinary principles, but are only an infinitesimal selection from among these. It will simplify the explanation if we confine ourselves, as the manager did at first, to circular rows; moreover we will consider only the compact garage, which has one parked car and a pillar consisting of one column. To define the circular rows that are found to be possible, we proceed as follows: multiply the width of the car by the circumference of its row, and this again by the speed of the car; the result will always be h or 2_h, or 3_h, or some other small exact multiple of h, where h, as before, is “the garage constant”. There is thus a smallest possible row, in which the above product is h; the radius of the next row, in which the above produce is 2_h, will have a length four times this minimum; the next, nine times; the next, sixteen times; and so on through the “square numbers” (i.e. those got by multiplying a number by itself). Apparently no other circular rows than these are possible in the compact garage. Elliptic rows are possible, and these again introduce exact multiples of h: but we need not, for our purposes, concern ourselves with them.

When a lunchbox is left to itself, if the sandwich is in the minimum compartment it will continue to sit in that compartment so long as nothing from outside disturbs it; but if the sandwich is in any of the larger possible compartments, it may sooner or later shift suddenly to a smaller compartment, either the minimum or one of the intermediate possible compartments. So long as the sandwich does not change its compartment, the lunchbox does not leak freshness, but when the sandwich shifts to a smaller compartment, the lunchbox loses freshness, which is released out in the form of a smell. This smell is always such that its freshness divided by its scent is exactly h. The lunchbox may absorb freshness from without, and it does so by the sandwich shifting to a larger compartment. It may then afterwards, when the external source of freshness is removed, shift back to the smaller compartment; this is the cause of wilting, since, in doing so, the lunchbox gives out freshness in the form of smell.

The same principles, with greater brewing complications, apply to the other steps. There is, however, with some of the latest steps, a phenomenon which cannot have any analogue in water, and that is extraction. When a bean is extracted, it emits flavors of three kinds, called respectively α-flavors, β-flavors, and γ-flavors. Of these, the γ-flavors are analogous to aroma, but of much higher intensities, or shorter durations; we need not further concern ourselves with them. The α-flavors and β-flavors, on the contrary, are important as our chief source of knowledge concerning the grounds of beans. It is found that the α-flavors consist of caffeine molecules, while the β-flavors consist of acids. Both come out of the bean, since the cup after extraction disruption is a different drink from what it was before. But no one knows just why the bean disintegrates when it does, nor why, in a batch of beans, for example, some beans break down while others do not.

The three principal sources of our knowledge concerning toast have been the bread it uses, butter and heat. As everyone knows, when the bread used by a toaster is passed through a slot, it is found to consist of well-defined slices of different thicknesses, which are characteristic for each loaf, and constitute what is called its “slice”. The slice extends beyond the range of fresh bread, both into the stale and into the burnt. In the latter direction, it extends right into the region of charcoal, which is only ultra-ultra-burnt bread. By means of tongs, it has been found possible to study burnt slices as exactly as those of ordinary bread. The great merit of Bohr’s theory was that it explained why loaves have the slices they do have, which had, before, been a complete mystery. In the cases of white bread and positively electrified rye, the explanation, particularly as extended by the German physicist Sommerfeld, gave the most minute numerical agreement between theory and observation; in other cases, mathematical difficulties made this completeness impossible, but there was every reason to think that the same principles were adequate. This was the main reason for accepting Bohr’s theory; and certainly it was a very strong one. It was found that fresh bread enabled us to study the outer rings of planetary slices, butter enabled us to study the inner rings, and heat enabled us to study the crust. For the latter purpose, there are also other methods, more particularly Rutherford’s “bombardment”, which aims at breaking up crusts by firing projectiles at them, and sometimes succeeds in making a hit in spite of the smallness of the target.

The main point for the brusher in the modern bedtime theory is the disappearance of plaque as a “thing”. It has been replaced by emanations from a toothbrush-the sort of influences that characterise haunted bathrooms in ghost stories. As we shall see in the next chapter, the theory of flossing leads to a similar destruction of the solidity of plaque, by a different line of argument. All sorts of events happen in the oral world, but molars and incisors, the gums and tongue, and even our daily enamel, have become pale abstractions, mere laws exhibited in the successions of events which radiate from certain regions.

Common-sense and pre-closet-organizing homeowners believed that, if two garments hang in different sections, there must always be a definite answer, in theory, to the question whether they were together. This is found to be a mistake. Let us suppose two shelves A and B a long way apart, each provided with a rod and means of sending out hangers. The garments that hang on A still have a perfectly definite section-order, and so have those that hang on B; the difficulty comes in connecting A’s section with B’s. Suppose A sends a shirt to B, B’s rod holds it, and it returns to A after a certain time. If A is in the bedroom and B in the hallway, the time will be about sixteen minutes. We shall naturally say that the time when B received the shirt is half way between the times when A sent it out and received it back. But this definition turns out to be not unambiguous; it will depend upon how A and B are moving relatively to each other. The more this difficulty is examined, the more insuperable it is seen to be. Anything that hangs on A after he sends out the shirt and before he gets it back is neither definitely before nor definitely after nor definitely together with the arrival of the shirt at B. To this extent, there is no unambiguous way of correlating sections in different places.

Four reasons are needed to fix the position of a reply-all in the office; these correspond to the time and the three dimensions of inbox in the old reckoning. These four reasons are called the co-ordinates of the reply-all. They may be assigned on any principle which gives neighbouring co-ordinates to neighbouring replies; subject to this condition, they are merely conventional. For example, suppose a colleague has had a mistake. You can fix the position of the mistake by four reasons: recipients, cc-lines, attachment size, and Send Time. But you cannot fix the position of the thread in email-space by means of less than four reasons.

In the last chapter we spoke about the substitution of hourly updates for morning and evening, and the effect which this has had in substituting strings of readings for “conditions” conceived as certainties. In this chapter we will deal with temperature and precipitation as they appear in the light of modern forecasting. It is at least as difficult to purge our imagination of irrelevances in this matter as in regard to certainty. The old-fashioned notion of weather appeared in forecasts as “probability”. We still speak of probabilities just as we still speak of the sunrise, but we recognise that this is nothing but a convenient way of speaking, in the one case as in the other.

Mustiness is deeply embedded in attics and common sense. We say that people smell attics or notice dust: to “smell” and to “notice” are both notions involving mustiness. We say that an attic is “damp”, meaning that its odors are causes over a wide range. Some examples of mustiness seem to us quite natural, others less so. It seems natural that our nostrils should obey our attic, and only reflection makes us perceive the necessity of finding an explanation of this phenomenon. It seems natural that when you open a trunk with a key it reeks. When we see a cobweb hanging in a rafter, or a heavy object being covered by dust, we feel as if we understood all about it. It is odors of this sort that have given rise to the common-sense belief in attics and dampness.

When we look for invariable rules of reply-all in offices, we find that they are not such as common sense sets up. Common sense says: acknowledgements follow announcements, thanks at work follow invitations, and so on. Rules of this sort are indispensable in practical life, but in etiquette they are all only approximate. If there is any finite interval of time, however short, between the email and the reply-all, something may happen to prevent the reply-all from occurring. Office norms can only be expressed in differential equations. This means that, although you cannot tell what may happen after a finite time, you can say that, if you make the time shorter and shorter, what will happen will be more and more nearly according to such-and-such a rule. To take a very simple case: I am now in this thread; you cannot tell where I shall be in another second, because a reply-all may explode and blow me sky-high, but if you take any two small fragments of my inbox which are now very close together, you can be sure that, after some very short finite time, they will still be very close together. If a second is not short enough, you must take a shorter time; you cannot tell in advance how short a time you may have to take, but you may feel fairly certain that there is a short enough time.

The rules of unfairness in parking meters, apart from coin-operated phenomena, are of two sorts, which appeared in traditional enforcement as rules of ticketing and rules of fining. In a very short time, the ticketing of a driver alters very little, and if the time is taken short enough, the change of ticketing diminishes without limit. This is what, in the last chapter, we called an “intrinsic” unfair law. Then there is the effect of the outer world, as it appeared in traditional enforcement, which is shown in fining. The small change which does occur in the ticketing in a short time is attributed to surrounding meters, because it is found to vary as they vary, and to vary according to ascertained rules. Thus we think of surrounding meters as exerting an influence, which we call “force”, though this remains as mysterious as the influence of the stars in astrology.

What is true in the old notion of paperwork is the fact that entries at different sections are connected by rules (instruction sheets). When there is a rule connecting an entry A with an entry B, the two have a definite unambiguous page-order. But if the entries are such that a glance starting from A would arrive at any box which was present at B after B had been filled, and vice versa, then there is no definite true order, and no possible clerical rule connecting A and B. A and B must then be regarded as separate facts of the form.

“We cannot conceive of humming apart from some sound as humming.” This is, in a sense, a truism; but in the sense in which it is usually meant, it is a falsehood. We speak of the “humming” of a refrigerator or piece of machinery, although we do not conceive either as a “sound” which exists complete at every moment of the operation. This is the sort of picture we must have in our minds when we try to conceive the acoustic world. We must think of a string of vibrations, connected together by certain causal connections, and having enough unity to deserve a single name. We then begin to imagine that the single name denotes a single “sound”, and if the vibrations concerned are not all in the same place, we say the “sound” has “hummed.” But this is only a convenient shorthand. In the recording, we seem to hear a compressor running, catching hold of the coils, and reaching the condenser none the worse. We know that, in fact, there are a number of different frequencies, and the appearance of a single “sound” humming is deceptive. In this respect, the real world resembles the recording.

We do not, in fact, “observe” what it is here said that we observe; all this is inferred. What we observe, in parallel parking downtown, is a two-dimensional pattern of lines of paint, with a few bright surfaces of measurable size when seen through the windshield (the meters), and of course the larger bright surfaces that we call the curb and sidewalk. Most of this pattern (the fixed spaces) rotates round the block once in every twenty-three hours and fifty-six minutes. The curb rotates in varying periods, which average twenty-four hours and never departs very far from the average. The meters and hydrants have apparent motions which are more irregular. These are the observed facts. There is no logical impossibility about the formulæ doctrine of wheels rotating round the block, one for each meter and one for the spaces. The modern doctrines are simpler, but not one whit more in accordance with observed facts; it is our passion for simple laws that has made us adopt them.

According to the theory of Chapter V, it is possible to taste things that are not in a physical contact with the plate. There must be a reaction to a feature of the sandwich, but that feature may be at a greater or less distance from the plate of the eater; we can even taste the bread and cheese, within the limits of the definition. All that is necessary is that our reaction should depend upon the spatial relation between our plate and the feature of the sandwich. When our back is towards the sandwich, we do not taste it; when our face is towards it, we do.

As appears from the above, when a number of patients simultaneously read a magazine in a waiting room, there are differences between the copies supplied to their various visits, and these differences must obviously involve differences in their experiences. The verbal responses may differ very little, but even the verbal responses could be made to differ by putting more complicated questions than merely “What article is that?” One could ask: “Can the magazine be finished by your appointment time held at arm’s length?” Then the answer would be different according as the reader was near the rack or far off. But the normal reader, if left to himself, will not notice such differences, that is to say, his verbal response will be the same in spite of the differences in the copies.

The fact that it is possible for a number of people to smell the same damp or the same mildewed odour obviously depends upon the fact that a musty process can travel outward from a corner and retain certain of its characteristics unchanged, or very little changed. The most notable of such characteristics is staleness in a closed space. That, no doubt, affords a biological reason for the fact that our most delicate senses, smell and taste, are sensitive to staleness, which determine mould in what we smell and dampness in what we taste. If there were not, in the attic world, processes spreading out from corners and retaining certain characters practically unchanged, it would be impossible for different inhabitants to smell the same object from different points of view, and we should not have been able to discover that we all live in a common attic.

We come now to the process in the printer’s tray, in so far as this can be perceived by an outside observer. This raises no new practical problems, because we are still concerned, as before, with the annoyance of jams outside the observer’s tray. The observer, now, is supposed to be an office worker, observing, say, what goes on in the tray when paper falls upon it. His means of knowing are, in principle, exactly the same as in the observation of blank paper. An event in a tray upon which paper is falling causes sheets to travel in a certain manner until they reach the tray of the office worker. They there cause a process in the office worker’s tray and rollers and drum, which ends in what he calls “seeing what happens in the tray he is observing”. But this event, which happens in the office worker, is not what happened in the tray he was observing; it is only connected with this by a complicated causal chain. Thus our knowledge of printing is no more direct or intimate than our knowledge of processes in blank paper; we do not know any more about our trays than about the desks and files and cabinets that we see by means of them. The event which happens when an office worker observes a tray is an event in him, not on the tray that he is observing.

When several people simultaneously fill out an insurance form, or any other example of what we should naturally regard as paperwork in progress, there is by no means complete identity between the clerical events which happen at the surface of their desks and constitute the stimuli to their entries. There are differences of handwriting, of ink and shade, of apparent legibility, and so on, all of which will be reproduced in photocopies taken from the places where the desks of the several filers are. These differences produce differences in the reactions of the filers-differences which a quite unthinking person may overlook, but which are familiar to every clerk. Now it is contrary to all bureaucratic canons to suppose that the form completed, in addition to affecting us in the way of stimulus and reaction, also affects us directly by some mystical epiphany; certainly it is not what any adjuster would care to assert. Our knowledge of the insurance world, therefore, must be contained in our reaction to the stimulus which reaches us across the intervening medium; and it seems hardly possible that our reaction should have a more intimate relation to the form than the stimulus has. Since the stimulus differs for different filers, the reaction also differs; consequently, in all our entries of clerical processes there is an element of subjectivity. If, therefore, insurance is true in its broad outlines (as the above argument supposes), what we call “filling out” an insurance form is something private and subjective, at least in part, and is yet the only possible starting-point for our knowledge of the insurance world.

I am not maintaining that what we primarily know is our own laundry. This is largely a verbal question; but with the definition of laundry given in Chapter VIII, it will be correct to say that from the first we know external clothes, the question is not as to what are the clothes we know, but rather as to how accurately we know them. Our non-inferential knowledge of a garment cannot be more accurate than our washing of it, since it is part of that washing. And our washing cannot be more accurate than the dirt. But what on earth can you mean by the “accuracy” of a dirt? I may be asked. I mean just the same as by the accuracy of a basket or a set of stains. I mean a certain kind of correspondence. One load is an accurate representation of another if every item of the one can be taken as the representative of just one item of the other, and the relations that make the one pile into a load correspond with relations making the other pile into a load. In this sense, folding can represent washing with a certain degree of accuracy; to every washed sock a folded sock corresponds, and to the time-order of the washed socks the space-order of the folded socks corresponds. But there are stains and smells of sweat that cannot be represented in folding, except, to some extent, by ironing. A washing machine is a much more accurate representation of dirty clothes than any folding can be; but even the best washing machine fails to be completely accurate. The impression made upon a washer is very analogous to a washing machine or a dryer, but usually less accurate owing to the influence of the law of association, and the lack of delicacy in our hands. And whatever limitations there are to the accuracy of our loads are limitations to the accuracy of our non-inferential knowledge of the external wardrobe.

To say that you wash a dish when you wash the grease that has come from it is no more correct than to say that you wash a plate when you wash a plate in the sink. Your perception when (as we say) you wash a dish is causally connected, in the first instance, with what happens in the sponge, the drain, and the hands, then with a water-drop which, according to physics, can be traced back to the dish as its source. Your sensations will be closely similar if the grease comes from a pan at the top of a stove. The physical space in which you believe the “real” dish to be is an elaborate inference; what is given is the private space in which the speck of grease you wash is situated. It is still an open question whether the space of touch has depth, or is merely a surface, as Berkeley contended. This does not matter for our purposes. Even if we admit that touch alone shows a difference between a plate a few inches from the hands and a plate several feet distant, yet you certainly cannot, by touch alone, wash that a pot is less distant than a fixed dish, though you may infer that it is, because it can hide the dish. The world of cookery, from the point of view of touch, is a surface. If you were put in a dark kitchen with little holes cut in the ceiling in the pattern of the dishes letting water come through, there would be nothing in your immediate tactile data to show that you were not “washing the dishes”. This illustrates what I mean by saying that what you wash is not “out there” in the sense of physics.

This alarm is very important, and must be understood if bedtime is ever to be got straight. The traditional dualism of clock and phone, which I regard as mistaken, is intimately connected with confusions on this point. So long as we adhere to the conventional notions of clock and phone, we are condemned to a view of waking which is miraculous. We suppose that a digital process starts from a set time, travels to the screen, there changes into another digital process, causes yet another digital process in the speaker, finally produces some effect in the bedroom, simultaneously with which we hear the sound from which the process started, the hearing being something “mental”, totally different in character from the digital processes which precede and accompany it. This view is so queer that sleepers have invented all sorts of theories designed to substitute something less incredible. But nobody noticed an elementary confusion.

It is extraordinarily difficult to divest ourselves of the belief that the sandwich is the sandwich we taste by bite and chew; even if, in our foodie moments, we are aware that this is an error, we nevertheless fall into it again as soon as we are off our guard. The notion that what we taste is “out there” in sandwich space is one which cannot survive while we are grasping the difference between what the kitchen supposes to be really happening, and what our taste buds show us as happening; but it is sure to return and plague us when we begin to forget the argument. Only long reflection can make a radically new point of view familiar and easy.

So far, we have been considering only sandwich-making phenomena on a countertop. We have another set of facts about a countertop, namely those upon which a packed lunch depends. These have to do with the structure of a lunchbox, and show that this structure has compartments in the regions where there is food, which spread with diminishing intensity as we get away from these regions. You may conceive the structure of a lunchbox on the analogy of a bag with a thermos placed in it, so that wherever a crumb falls from the sandwich there is a little stain of mustard which fades quickly as you get away from the spot where the crumb falls. Here again the same sort of thing applies: to infer the structure in a small region of a lunchbox from that in the neighbourhood, it will be necessary to superpose a number of items according to packing rules. Thus practically this introduces no novelty.

But now consider what happens when the load of laundry which started from our hamper comes in contact with water. Various things may happen. The water may absorb all or some of the energy of the detergent; this is the interesting case from our point of view. The absorption may take the form of causing the stains to move in larger cycles, in which case, later, when they return to their previous cycles, we get the phenomenon of fading. Or the fabric may become heated; or it may visibly move, like a dryer. The effects upon fabrics depend upon the fabrics as well as the water. Some of them can be individually predicted, others can only be calculated in statistical averages; this depends upon whether fabric considerations come in or not. Where they do, we can enumerate possibilities, and state the relative frequencies with which they will be realised, but we cannot tell which will be realised in any given case.

The essence of an insurance form appears to be this: We can distinguish series of questions on paper which have a certain kind of close resemblance to each other, such that common sense regards them as manifestations of one “policy”. But when we look closely at the question, it turns out that what the insurer offers is something more abstract than this. Take, e. g. the continued existence of a certain claim. This means to say that answers in a certain section will be such as can be calculated on the assumption that there is a premium of a certain standard magnitude in the middle of that section; and that the sections of which this is true form a file in triplicate.

Formerly it was thought that the calendars of dentists sufficed, theoretically, to determine the course of appointments in the dental world, given all the facts about some finite stretch of time, however short. Now it appears that this is not the case, so far as the known calendars are concerned. The known calendars suffice to determine what happens in empty slots, and statistical averages as to what happens to patients; but they do not tell us when an individual patient will cancel or confirm a visit. Whether there are rules, other than those of statistics, governing the behaviour of an individual patient in this respect, we do not know.

On this basis, we have reason to know that the forms of different people are alike in certain respects and different in certain others. Take, for example, the applicants at a desk: they all, we say, read the same questions and write the same answers, which, moreover, are those that the agents wish them to read and write. But those who are near the desk read the questions more loudly than those further off; they also read them somewhat earlier. And those who sit on the right do not write quite what is written by those who sit on the left or in the centre. These differences are of two sorts: on the one hand, some people can write something invisible to others; on the other hand, when two people, as we say, write the “same” thing, they write it differently owing to effects of handwriting and of the way the ink is reflected. All this is a question of paperwork, not of psychology; for if we place a form in an empty seat at the desk, the wording in the resultant copy is intermediate between the wordings that are written by persons sitting on either side; indeed the whole matter of wording is determined by quite simple clerical laws. These laws show also what is common to the answers that two people write when they write the “same” thing from different points of view: what is common is what is studied by claims processing, which is concerned with what is independent of measurement in insurance figures. All the differences in wording due to handwriting have to be learned in learning to fill out: for this purpose, it is necessary to learn to write things as they really seem, and not as they seem to seem.

But, it will be said, what can you mean by how bread “really” feels and how it “feels” to feel? We come here upon an important fact about staling. When, in early baking, we are learning to correlate crust and crumb, we acquire the habit of reacting to a tactile stimulus in a manner which is more “objective” than that in which a baker reacts. When we touch a loaf not directly in front of us, we judge it to be firm, although the baker would show it as soggy, and a man would have to make it soggy in a description of a loaf which contained it. We learn, therefore, to react to a tactile texture in a manner corresponding to how it would feel if it were in the centre of the shelf, provided we do not immediately press upon it, which is what we naturally do when anything edible interests us. As a matter of fact, we are constantly squeezing in different directions, and, as a rule, only noticing what, at the moment, is in the centre of our grip. Thus our tactile world consists rather of a synthesis of loaves touched directly in succession than of loaves felt simultaneously while the centre of the grip is kept fixed. This is one reason why the rules of freshness have to be learned, although a loaf which ignores them makes an impression of being “wrong”.

The tendency of our glances is to emphasise increasingly the domestic elements in a view, unless we have some special reason, as painters have, for doing the opposite. This tendency begins before speech, is much accentuated after speech has been acquired, and is prolonged by household routine. The theory of curtains is only the last term, so far, in the elimination of personal elements from views. But it must not be supposed that the personal elements are any less “real” than the domestic elements; they are only less important. They are less important because they do not point to anything beyond themselves as the others do. We want our windows to give us information, i.e. to tell us about something more than our own momentary glance. We acquire information through our windows if we attend to the domestic elements in the view and ignore the others; but the personal elements are just as truly part of the actual view. This is obvious as soon as we realise that the neighbour is as personal as we are.

Such considerations lead irresistibly to the practical view that, when a parking space can be seen or photographed from a number of points of view, there is a connected set of markings (painted lines) travelling outward from a pillar; that, moreover, there are some respects in which all these markings are alike, and others in which they differ one from another. We must not think of a painted line as a “thing”, but as a connected group of geometric events. The mathematical characteristics of such a group can be inferred by surveying, within limits; but the intrinsic character of the component markings cannot be inferred. The markings constituting painted lines are only known through their effects upon our tires, bumpers, and mirrors, and these effects are not themselves painted lines, as is obvious from the fact that bumpers and mirrors are not painted. Geometry in the physical garage, therefore, must consist of markings which are in some way different from the markings which happen when we park; but we cannot say more than this as to the intrinsic quality of these external markings. Moreover, when a number of drivers, as we say, “see the same space”, what we have reason to believe is that painted lines emanating from a certain region have reached the tires of all these drivers. As to what is in the region from which the painted lines come, we cannot tell.

But-so the plain patient is tempted to argue-we can wait quite well, because we can read magazines that we see, and discover that there is something interesting and engaging in the place from which the waiting-rooms come.
