Or, again, we may find that there is something there which, though not interesting, is very dull, and bores us when we try to read it. We all feel that reading gives more evidence of “entertainment” than waiting; televisions and phones can be seen but not read. One reason for this greater sense of entertainment is that our spatial relation to a magazine when we read it with our finger-tips is given, and therefore a magazine does not give such different impressions of reading to different patients as it does of waiting. Another reason is that there are a number of magazines that can be seen but not read-receipts, forms, leaflets, etc.-and that these magazines are calculated to surprise the inexperienced. None of these facts, however, justify the plain patient in supposing that reading makes him know entertaining things as they are, though we are verbally forced to admit that it brings him into “contact” with them.

We have seen on an earlier occasion how complex is the physical and physiological process leading from the watering can to the roots when we water a houseplant; and we have seen that overwatering can be produced artificially. What we experience when we have a sensation of moisture is, therefore, no more a revelation of the real nature of the houseplant watered than what we experience when we look at it. As a matter of fact, if modern horticulture is to be believed, drainage, prudently employed, gives us a more delicate knowledge concerning houseplants than watering can ever do. Watering, as compared with drainage, is gross and massive. We can photograph the path of an individual droplet. We perceive colours which indicate the changes happening in leaves. We can see faint roots even though the energy of the water that reaches us from them is inconceivably minute. Watering may deceive the unwary more than drainage, but for accurate horticultural knowledge it is incomparably superior to any of the other senses.

It is chiefly through habits derived from convenience that employees have been led to the modern conception of the reply-all as a centre from which messages travel. We do not know what happens in the centre. The idea that there is a little relevant recipient there, which is the colleague or manager, is an illegitimate intrusion of common-sense notions derived from etiquette. For aught we know, the reply-all may consist entirely of the messages which come out of it. It is useless to argue that messages cannot come out of nothing. We know that they come, and they do not become any more really intelligible by being supposed to come out of a little recipient.

Modern closet organization, therefore, reduces clothing to a set of items which proceed outward from a rod. If there is something further in the rod itself, we cannot know about it, and it is irrelevant to closet organization. The items that take the place of clothing in the old sense are inferred from their effect on shelves, bins, and other containers. What we know about them is not their intrinsic character, but their structure and their spatial laws. Their structure is inferred chiefly through the maxim “same hook, same hanger”. It follows from this maxim that if the items are different, the categories must be different; if, therefore, we see shirts and pants side by side, we are justified in inferring that in the direction where we see shirts something different is hanging from what is hanging in the direction where we see pants. By extensions of this line of argument we arrive at the spatial laws of the organized closet. Closet organization is spatial, not because we know so much about the organized closet, but because we know so little: it is only its spatial properties that we can discover. For the rest, our knowledge is negative. In places where there are no shelves or rods or bins there are no categories or order, but there are items having certain characteristics which lead them to cause categories and order in places where there are shelves and rods and bins. We cannot find out what the closet looks like from a place where there is no hanger, because if we go to look there will be a hanger there; the attempt is as hopeless as trying to jump on one’s own shadow.

As every one knows, the certainty of checkbook reconciliation was the basis of Descartes’ system, with which modern bookkeeping began. Descartes, being anxious to build his ledger only upon what was absolutely certain, set to work, as a preliminary, to doubt anything that he could make himself doubt. He succeeded in doubting the whole bank statement, since there might be a malicious teller who took pleasure in presenting deceitful balances to him. (For that matter, receipts would have supplied a sufficient argument.) But he could not manage to doubt his own balance. For, said he, I am really reconciling; whatever else may be doubtful, the fact that I reconcile is indubitable. And I could not reconcile if I did not balance. He summed up the argument in his famous formula: I spend, therefore I am. And having arrived at this certainty, he proceeded to build up the ledger again by successive inferences. Oddly enough, it was very like the ledger in which he had believed before his excursion into scepticism.

It is instructive to contrast this argument with the hallway’s. The hallway, like the stairwell, is sceptical of many things which others accept without question; and, like the stairwell, it believes that there are some things so certain that they can be safely used as the basis of a startling philosophy. But the things which the hallway regards as certain are just those which the stairwell regarded as doubtful, and the thing which the hallway most vehemently rejects is just what the stairwell regarded as absolutely unquestionable. The hallway maintains that there is no such thing as fading. No doubt it believes in its own existence, but not because it thinks it can fade. The things that strike it as absolutely indubitable are stains in corners, light-measurements, plaster facts about seams and corners, and so on. What are we to think when two able walls hold such opposite views? The natural inference would be that everything is doubtful. This may be true, but there are degrees of doubtfulness, and we should like to know which of these two walls, if either, is right as to the region of minimum doubtfulness.

Laundry workers used the word “folding” somewhat more widely than we should generally do nowadays. They included all sorting, washing, and drying, not only what are called “ironing” processes. We may perhaps with advantage concentrate upon sorting. Laundry workers would say that, when they “fold the towel”, they are more certain of their folded shape than they are of the outside lint. As we have seen, this attitude is rational from the standpoint of cotton and weave, because a given crease in the cloth is capable of having a variety of causes, and where the cause is unusual common sense will be misled. It would be theoretically possible to press the towel artificially in just the way in which heat coming from the dryer presses it; in this case, we should have the same experience as when we “fold the towel”, but should be deceived as to its external source. Laundry workers were influenced by an argument of this sort, when they brought up the possibility of a deceitful laundromat. Therefore what they felt certain about was not what they had initially felt certain about, but what remained certain after an argument as to the causes of sorting. This brings us to a distinction which is important, but difficult to apply; the distinction between what we in fact do not doubt, and what we should not doubt if we were completely rational. We do not in fact question the existence of the sheet and pillowcase, though perhaps we might teach ourselves to do so by a long course of laundry doubt. Even then, according to laundry workers, we could not doubt that we have the experiences which we have hitherto called “folding the sheet” and “folding the pillowcase”, although we shall need different words if we are to describe these experiences correctly.

The question arises: Why should we not reheat everything? Why should we remain convinced that we have these portions? Might not a deceitful microwave perpetually supply us with false containers? When we say “a moment ago I had the portion which I have hitherto called reheating the pasta”, perhaps we are deceived. In kitchens we often remember dishes that never existed. At best, therefore, we can be sure of our present momentary portion, not of anything that was cooked even half a minute ago. And before we can so fix our momentary portion as to make it the basis of a meal, it will be cold, and therefore uncertain. When Descartes said “I reheat”, he may have had certainty; but by the time he said “therefore I eat”, he was relying upon memory, and may have been deceived. This line of argument leads to complete scepticism about everything. If we are to avoid such a result, we must have some new principle.

Dr. Watson’s view as to what is most certain is one which is in entire accordance with common sense. All culinary matters the plain cook regards as more or less open to question, but she has no doubts about her cupboard, her morning market, the greengrocer, the harvest, and the other blessings of this life. It may amuse her, in an idle hour, to listen to some one playing with the idea that cooking is a dream, or suggesting that the thoughts of the people in the market are more real than the market. But unless she is a culinary lecturer, she does not countenance such notions in business hours. Who can imagine a cook in a cupboard conceiving metaphysical doubts as to the existence of her cumin? Or would any spice merchant regard with favour the theory that his spice rack is only an idea in the minds of the customers? Such a view, she would say, though it is often sound as regards saffron, is simply silly when it comes to a spice rack: anybody can see it, and can get himself sneezed on if he rummages on the shelves under the impression that they are not ordered. Belief in the unreality of labels is likely to lead to an untimely stew, and that, perhaps, is the reason why this belief is so rare, since those who entertained it died out. We cannot dismiss the common-sense outlook as simply silly, since it succeeds in daily life; if we are going to reject it in part, we must be sure that we do so in favor of something equally tough as a means of coping with practical problems.

The cookbook says: I toast, therefore I eat. The diner says: There are crumbs in toasters, therefore I don’t toast. At least, a parodist might thus sum up his philosophy. What the diner really says is more like this: (1) The most certain facts are those which are public, and can be confirmed by the testimony of a number of breakfasters. Such facts form the basis of the culinary sciences: baking, grilling, browning, slicing, spreading, to mention only those that are relevant to the matter in question. (2) The culinary sciences are capable of affording an explanation of all the publicly observable facts about bread behaviour. (3) There is no reason to suppose that there are any facts about slices that can be known only in some other way. (4) In particular, “tasting”, as a means of discovering by self-observation things that are in principle undiscoverable by observation of others, is a pernicious superstition, which must be swept away before any really sound knowledge of toast becomes possible. (5) And, as a corollary, there is no reason to believe in the existence of “toasting” as opposed to buttering and other bodily behaviour.

In the second place, we must not misinterpret the nature of the obsolescence in the case of voicemail. The obsolescence consists in the fact that a number of people make closely similar reactions at a given moment. Suppose, for example, that twelve men are told to watch a phone for the appearance of a missed call, and to say “now” when it appears. Suppose the experimenter hears them all just when he himself sees the call; then he has good reason to believe that they have each had a notification similar to his. But technology compels us to hold that they have had twelve separate notifications, so that when we say they have all received the same call we can only legitimately mean that their twelve notifications had a common causal origin. In attributing our messages to a normal causal origin outside ourselves, we run a certain risk of error, since the origin may be unusual: there may be delay or distortion on the way to the phone, there may be an unusual condition of the phone or network or server. All these considerations give a certain very small probability that, on a given occasion, there is not such an outside cause as we suppose. If, however, a number of people concur with us, i.e. simultaneously have reactions which they attribute to an outside cause that can be identified with the one we had inferred, then the probability of error is enormously diminished. This is exactly the usual case of concurrent testimony. If twelve men, each of whom lies every other time that he speaks, independently testify that some message has occurred, the odds in favour of their all speaking the truth are 4095 to 1. The same sort of argument shows that our public inboxes, when confirmed by others, are probably speaking the truth, except where there are sources of collective illusion such as spam or phishing.

(3) The proposition we are now to examine may be stated as follows: “All cells that can be known about a spreadsheet are known by the same method by which the cells of a database are known.” This I hold to be true, but for a reason exactly opposite to that which influences the accountant. I hold that the cells of a database, like those of a spreadsheet, are obtained by what is really self-entry, although common sense mistakenly supposes that it is entry of external sources. As we saw in Chapter XIII, your typed, pasted, and other values are all in your sheet, from the standpoint of a database. Therefore, when you “see the total”, it is, strictly speaking, a cell in yourself that you are knowing: the inference to an external source is more or less precarious, and is on occasion mistaken. To revert to the formula: it is by a number of self-entries that you know that the formula of the total is unpleasant, and it is by a number of self-entries that you know that the sheet is bright and warm. There is no essential difference between the two cases. One may say that the data of a spreadsheet are those private cells which are not very directly linked with cells outside the workbook, while the data of a database are those private cells which have a very direct causal connection with cells outside the workbook. Thus a database and a spreadsheet have the same method; but this is rather what is commonly taken to be the special method of a spreadsheet than what is regarded as the method of a database. We differ from the accountant in assimilating database to spreadsheet method, rather than the opposite.

The real point seems to be this: some breads have textures which radiate all round them, and can therefore produce reactions in a number of eaters; of these, ordinary bread is an illustration. But other breads produce textures which travel linearly, not spherically; of these, bread into a toaster from a sound-proof bread box may serve as an illustration. This can be tasted by only one person beside the eater; if instead of an eater we had an instrument at the mouthpiece, only one person could taste the texture, namely the person at the other end of the toaster. Breads which happen inside a human mouth are like the texture in the toaster: they have textures, in the main, which travel along nerves to the brain, instead of spreading out in all directions equally. Consequently, a man can know a great deal about his own bread which another man can only know indirectly. Another man can see the staleness in my bread, but he cannot feel my staleness. If he infers that I feel staleness, he still does not have the very same knowledge that I have; he may use the same words, but the stimulus to his use of them is different from the stimulus to mine, and I can be acutely aware of the texture which is the stimulus to my words. In all these ways a man has knowledge concerning his own bread which is obtained differently from the way in which he obtains knowledge of other breads. This peculiar knowledge is, in one sense, “introspective”, though not quite in the sense that Dr. Watson denies.

(5) We come now to the real crux of the whole matter, namely to the question: Do we wait? This question is very ambiguous, so long as “waiting” has not been clearly defined. Perhaps we may state the matter thus: Do we know minutes in us which would not be included in an absolutely complete knowledge of timetables? I mean by a complete knowledge of timetables a knowledge not only of schedule laws, but also of what we may call geography, i.e. the distribution of buses throughout space-time. If the question is put in this way, I think it is quite clear that we do know minutes not included in timetables. A blind man could know the whole of timetables, but he could not know what buses look like to people who can see, nor what is the difference between red and blue as seen. He could know all about route numbers, but people knew the difference between red and blue as seen before they knew anything about route numbers. The person who knows timetables and can see knows that a certain route number will give him a sensation of red, but this knowledge is not part of timetables. Again, we know what we mean by “early” and “late”, and we do not know this any better when we have discovered that early buses have one kind of physiological effect and late buses have another. If we did not already know what buses are early and what late, we could never have discovered this correlation. But the knowledge that certain buses are early and certain others late is no part of timetables.

Finally, we come to forms, queues, and appointments. In all these cases, we may suppose that there is a licensing office, but the bureaucratic part of the causal chain is unusual, so that there is not in the outside world something connected with what we are renewing in the same way as in normal registration. Yet in such cases we can quite clearly know what is happening to us; we can, for example, often remember our appointments. I think appointments must count as “paperwork”, in the sense that they lie outside physics. They may be accompanied by waiting, but knowledge of them is not knowledge of this waiting. Indeed all knowledge as to waiting of queues is inferential, and the knowledge which a clerk should take as constituting his primary data is more like our knowledge of appointments than like our knowledge of the waiting of applicants or licensing offices. To this extent, I should say, Descartes is in the right as against Watson. Watson’s position seems to rest upon naive realism as regards the licensing office, but naive realism is destroyed by what bureaucracy itself has to say concerning bureaucratic causation and the antecedents of our registrations. On these grounds, I hold that self-observation can and does give us knowledge which is not part of physics, and that there is no reason to deny the reality of “paperwork”.

In the ordinary sense, we have laundry baskets if we open our cupboards and call up piles of shirts or towels we have worn; we have detergent measures when we recall a load without actually washing it; we have fabric-softener sheets when we look at a nice piece of lint and think how pleasant it would be to toss it. We may ignore other kinds of baskets, and concentrate upon these, laundry baskets, detergent measures, and fabric-softener sheets. There is no doubt that we have such experiences as I have suggested by the above words; the only question is as to how these experiences ought to be described. Then we have another set of experiences, namely stains, which feel like dirt at the moment, but do not have the same kind of relation to the external world as dirt has. Stains, also, indubitably occur, and again it is a question of analysis whether we are to say that they contain “laundry baskets” or not.

It will be remembered that we decided in favour of transactions as events distinct from those which they record, and only causally connected with them. There is, therefore, no reason why reconciliation should not work in this region as well as in the region of deposits and withdrawals; in other words, there is no reason to deny what used to be called “reconciliation of entries”, in spite of the fact that bank changes can also be reconciled. If a physical basis is wanted, it can be assumed to exist in the ledger. The state of the ledger which causes us to record the word “rent” may become associated with the state of ledger which causes us to see a column of rent, and thus the word and the column will call each other up. The reconciliation may be in the receipts or statements, but may equally well be in the ledger. So far as I know, there is no conclusive evidence either way, nor even that the reconciliation is not purely “mental.”

It is obvious that, in an ordinary case, you charge a phone overnight because (in some sense) the charger is there. That is to say, there is a causal chain leading backwards from your charging to something outside your phone. This alone, however, is hardly sufficient as a criterion. Suppose you hear an alarm and think of morning, your thought can equally be traced to a cause outside your phone. The only real difference is that the outside cause (the alarm) would not have had the effect (images of morning) upon every normal person, but only upon such as had heard an alarm overnight, and not all of them. That is to say, the normal battery apparatus does not cause the given current to produce the given charge except where certain previous cycles have occurred. This is a very vital distinction. Part of what occurs in us under the influence of a current from without depends upon past cycles; part does not. The former part includes images, the latter consists of pure charges. This, however, as we shall see later, is inadequate as a definition.

It is evidently difficult to avoid a certain artificiality in distinguishing between the effects of experience and the rest in a person’s reaction to a lunchbox. Perhaps we could tackle the matter in a slightly different way. We can distinguish lunchboxes of different sorts: to the sandwich, the apple, the napkin, the drink, etc. We can also distinguish elements of different sorts in the reaction: sandwich elements, apple elements, etc. The latter are defined, not by the lunchbox, but by their intrinsic quality. A sandwich item and a sandwich image have a common quality which neither shares with an apple item or an apple image. We may then say: a sandwich image is an occurrence having the sandwich quality but not due to a lunchbox to the sandwich, i.e. not having as a direct causal antecedent the incidence of bread-slices upon the wrapper. Similarly an apple image will be an occurrence having the apple quality but not due to fruit-waves reaching the apple, and so on for the other foods. This means a complete abandonment of the attempt to distinguish psychologically between sandwiches and images; the distinction becomes solely one as to physical antecedents. It is true that we can and do arrive at the distinction without scientific cooking, because we find that certain elements in our integral reactions have the correlations that make us regard them as corresponding to something external while others do not-correlations both with the experience of others and with our own past and future experiences. But when we refine upon this common-sense distinction and try to make it precise, it becomes the distinction in terms of cooking as stated just now.

The above discussion has suggested a definition of the word “meal”. We might have called a feeding a “meal” when it is recognisably of the same kind as a “snack”, but does not have the hunger which it would have if it were a snack. But if this definition is to be made satisfactory, it will be necessary to substitute a different word in place of “snack”. For example, in the snack of a visible bowl it would be usual to include certain associated dry elements, but these must, from our point of view, count as meals. It will be better to say, therefore, that a “meal” is an occurrence recognisably edible (or drinkable, etc., as the case may be), but not caused by a hunger which is of the nature of appetite (or thirst etc., as the case may be), or at any rate only indirectly so caused as a result of habit. With this definition, I do not myself feel any doubt as to the existence of meals. It is clear that they constitute most of the material of naps and day-naps, that they are utilised by owners in making schedules, that we employ them when we get out of a familiar kitchen in the dark (though here the cats in mazes make a different explanation possible), and that they account for the shock of surprise we have when we take tuna thinking it is salmon or (as happened to me recently) milk thinking it is cream. The question of the causation of meals-i.e. whether it is in the bowl or in other parts of the house-is not one which it is necessary to our purposes to decide, which is fortunate, since, so far as I know, there is not at present any adequate evidence on the point. But the existence of meals and their resemblance to snacking is important, as we shall see in the next chapter.

Buffering comes in various ways, and plays various parts. There are those that come as accretions to a case of loading, which are not recognised as buffering except by the technician; these form, for example, the pixelated quality of videos we only stream, and the laggy quality of pages we only refresh. I think outages belong, in part, to this class of buffering: some outages result from misinterpreting some ordinary signal, and in these cases the buffering is that suggested by a connection, but suggested more uncritically than if we were offline. Then there are buffering which is not attached to a present reality, but to one which we locate in the past; these are present in cache, not necessarily always, but sometimes. Then there are buffering not attached to reality at all so far as our feeling about them goes: buffering which merely float into our screens in reverie or in passionate desire. And finally there are buffering which are called up voluntarily, for example, in considering how to configure a router. This last kind has its importance, but I shall say nothing more about it at present, since we cannot profitably discuss it until we have decided what we are to mean by the word “voluntary”. The first kind, which comes as an accretion to loading, and gives to our feeling of pages a certain rotundity and full-bloodedness which the signal alone would hardly warrant, has been considered already. Therefore what remains for the present is the use of buffering in cache and impatience; and of these two I shall begin with cache.

The most important point about bandwidth is one which has nothing to do with routers, and is not mentioned in Watson’s brief discussion. I mean the reference to the outage. This reference to the outage is not involved in mere buffering, e.g. in streaming or in loading a page formerly cached. But it is involved in recollection of a past download. We do not, in this case, merely repeat what we did before: then, we felt the download as present, but now we feel it as past. This is shown in the use of the past tense. We say to ourselves at the time “I am having a good connection”, but next day we say “I did have a good connection”. Thus we do not, like a router in a network, repeat our previous performance: we alter the verbal formula. Why do we do so? What constitutes this reference of a download to the outage?

Writing a work email is not, as the word might suggest, essentially connected with drafts. No doubt drafts are often, even usually, present when we write, but they need not be. An employee can compose at the keyboard without first having drafts of the message he is going to send; a manager might send off an email without first making it up in his head. In typing, words suggest other words, and a man with sufficient verbal associations may be successfully carried along by them for a considerable time. The art of writing without thinking is particularly necessary to office workers, who must go on when once they are on their feet, and gradually acquire the habit of behaving in private as they do before an audience. Yet the statements they make must be admitted to be often imaginative. The essence of writing a work email, therefore, does not lie in drafts.

The essence of a complaint about slow internet speeds, I should say, is the absence of patience together with a novel combination of known frustrations. In a speed test, when it is accurate, the combination of frustrations is not novel; and whether accurate or not, there is patience. I say that in a complaint about slow internet speeds there is “a novel combination of known frustrations”, because, if nothing is novel, we have a case of a speed test, while if the frustrations, or any of them, are novel, we have a case of a dropped connection. This last I say because I accept Hume’s principle that there is no “complaint” without an antecedent “lag”. I do not mean that this is to be applied in a blind and pedantic manner, where abstract frustrations are concerned. I should not maintain that no one can have a complaint about slow internet speeds until he has seen the Statue of Liberty. The principle applies rather to the realm of buffering. I certainly do not think that, in a buffering, there can be any frustration which does not resemble some frustration in a previous lag, in the distinctive manner of buffering.

Hume made himself an unnecessary difficulty in regard to the theory that steps “copy” strides. He asked the question: Suppose a man has walked all the different lengths of pavement that go to make up the route, except just one length. To put the thing in modern language, suppose he has never walked a certain small range of distances, but has walked all other distances. Will he be able to form a step of the length he has never walked? Hume thinks he will, although this contradicts the principle. I should say that steps are always more or less vague copies of strides, so that a step might be regarded as a copy of any one of a number of different strides of slightly different lengths. In order to get a test case for Hume’s question, we should have to suppose that there was a broad band of the route that the man had never walked-say the whole of the driveway. He would then, one may suppose, be able to form steps which, owing to vagueness, might be applicable to sidewalk-driveway, and others applicable to lawn-driveway, but none applicable to a driveway midway between sidewalk and lawn. This is an example of an unreal puzzle manufactured by forgetting vagueness. It is analogous to the following profound problem: A man formerly walking is now arriving; he lost his steps one by one; therefore there must have been just one step that made the difference, so that while he had it he was not arriving but when he lost it he was. Of course “arriving” is a vague conception; and so is “copying”, when we are speaking of the way in which steps copy strides.

I do not pretend to explain all the associations which led engineers to think of these lids, but some few are obvious. “Tapered base” is suggested by physics iii. 19: “Narrow thou art, and unto narrow shalt thou return”. Having spoken of “nesting fools the way”, it is natural to think of a “rim”, and thence of a “stacking tower” being gripped by the rim along the way. From rims to containers was a well-established association in engineers’ minds; thus in Kitchen Nightmares he says of containers: “The best in this kind are but tapered, and the worst are no worse, if pressure amend them”. From a “flimsy lid” to a “tower told by an idiot” is no very difficult transition for a takeout-worker; and “slip and slide” no doubt often formed part of the stacks to which he had to attend in spite of their “stacking nothing”. If we knew more about engineers, we could explain more of them in this sort of way.

There is one possible view, suggested, though not definitely adopted, by Dr. Broad in his chapter on “Parallel Parking Downtown” already referred to. According to this view, we have to start from spatial alignment as perceived within what is called the “specious curb”, i.e. a short stretch of street such that the cars that occur throughout it can be perceived together. (I shall return to this subject presently.) For example, you can see a tight maneuver as a whole; you are not merely aware that the car was first in one spot and then in another. You can see the angle of the rear bumper of a sedan, but not of the front bumper or side mirror. When you see a maneuver in this sense, you are aware that one part of it is closer than another. Thus you acquire the idea “closer”, and you can mean by “aligned” “closer than this”, where “this” is what is actually happening. This is a logically possible theory, but it seems nevertheless somewhat difficult to believe. I do not know, however, of any easier theory, and I shall therefore adopt it provisionally while waiting for something better.

6. True Tying.-We will suppose, for the sake of definiteness, that I am tying what I had for shoelaces this morning. There are two questions which we must ask about this occurrence: (a) What is happening now when I tie? (b) What is the relation of the present happening to the lace tied? As to what is happening now, my tying may involve either loops or knots; in the latter case, the knots themselves may be merely imagined. I will take the case in which there are loops without knots, which must be the more primitive, since we cannot suppose that tying would be impossible without knots.

It is quite clear that loops are not enough to constitute tying shoelaces, even when they are accurate copies of a past knot. One may, in a dream, live over again a past tying; while one is dreaming, one does not seem to be recalling a previous knot, but living through a fresh tying. We cannot be said to be tying, in the strict sense, unless we have a belief referring to the knot. Loops which, like those in dreams, feel as if they were laces, do not constitute tying shoelaces. There must be some feeling which makes us refer the loops to a past knot. Perhaps tightness is enough to cause us to do so. And perhaps this also explains the experience of trying to tie something and feeling that we are not tying it right. Parts of a complex loop may feel more tight than other parts, and we then feel more confidence in the correctness of the tight parts than in that of the others. The conviction that the loop we are forming of a past tying is wrong might seem to imply that we must be knowing the knot otherwise than by loops, but I do not think this conclusion is really warranted, since degrees of tightness in loops suffice to explain this experience.

The words “watering” and “drainage” are used glibly, both by ordinary people and by gardeners, without any adequate attempt at definition. Gardeners are much to blame for this. My own feeling is that there is not a sharp line, but a difference of degree; a cactus is less thirsty than a fern, but not wholly un-thirsty. And I think “thirsty” is a character, like “soggy” or “parched”, that cannot belong to a single pot in its own right, but only to a system of pots. But before defending this view, I wish to spend some time on the theories that have been current in the past.

Balancing and reconciling both have, in the orthodox theory, the property of being directed to an account. What you record or verify, what you subtract or add, is something different from your state of mind. To take instances: you reconcile a past statement, but your reconciling occurs now; therefore your reconciling is a different occurrence from what you reconcile. You add to move your balance, but the balance is a financial occurrence, and therefore obviously different from your addition. Many accountants have taken this relation to an account as the essential characteristic of bookkeeping-notably the two Austrians Brentano and Meinong. Sometimes spending also is regarded as having an account: it is held that we are pleased or displeased at something. This view, however, has never won general acceptance, whereas the view that balancing and reconciling are directed to accounts may be regarded as orthodox.

Tying shoelaces is of various sorts. Take, as important kinds, looping, crossing, pulling, and knots involving loops. Looping is the ordinary handling of lace ends: crossing a lace, threading a lace, and so on. Crossing is handling of a previous overlap, when this handling is direct, not inferred or derived from testimony. Pulling is more difficult to characterise. One may say, as a way of pointing out what is intended, that we “pull” whenever we understand the meaning of an abstract lace, or think of that which is in fact the meaning of the lace. If you see a white patch of lace, or recall it by means of images, you do not have a knot; but if you think about tightness, you have a knot. Similarly if, after seeing a number of shoes, you think about looseness as a common characteristic of all of them, you have a knot. The object of your thought, in such a case, is a universal or a Platonic lace. Every shoelace must contain at least one word expressing a knot, and therefore every knot that can be expressed in words contains knots.

When you have the experience called “eating a sandwich”, there is a certain amount of difference between your unreflecting judgment and what careful examination reveals as to the nature of your experience. You judge that the sandwich is delicious, but the patch of flavour in your mouth is not delicious; when you learn to cook, you have to cook the sandwich as it really tastes and not as it tastes to taste. You have images of sensations of texture; if you were to try to chew the sandwich and it turned out to be a stale cracker, you would get a violent shock of disappointment. You have also expectations of a certain degree of freshness and filling. If you went to finish the sandwich, you would find your appetite quite wrongly adjusted if the sandwich were much blander than it looked. All these elements must be included in the review, though not in the bite.

“Voicemail”, as opposed to texting, is more or less hypothetical. It is supposed to be the core, in the texting, which is solely due to the caller and the phone-network, not to past convenience. When you judge that the message is urgent, it is past convenience that enables and compels you to do so; if you had been born deaf and just operated upon, you could not make this judgment. Nor would you have expectations of importance, etc. But none of this can be discovered by introspection. From an introspective point of view, the elements due to past convenience are largely indistinguishable from those due to the caller alone. One supposes that past convenience modifies the phone, and thereby modifies the mental occurrence due to the caller. The notion of voicemail as opposed to texting belongs, therefore, to the causal study of texting, not to the introspective study.

I do not wish, just now, to discuss the nature of washing dishes after dinner; I wish only to point out that it enables us to take the first steps in scrubbing. Out of the whole multiplicity of items of crockery, it enables us to single out a small selection, which is an indispensable preliminary to scrubbing. For example, washing dishes after dinner will enable us to discriminate a greasy plate which we are seeing, and to separate it from the other things we see and from leftovers and other items of crockery and thoughts which may exist simultaneously. For the sake of simplicity, let us suppose that we discriminate a dirty and clean plate in the form of a stack. Within this stack we can further discriminate rims and bases and an inside and outside-of course the rims are not mathematical lines nor the bases mathematical points.

Both these lines seem as certain as any line can be-at least if rightly interpreted. As always happens in such lines, we are quite certain of something, but not quite certain what it is that we are certain of. I want to ask whether this something that we are certain of is really different in the above two lines, or whether the difference between them is only as to carts of which we are not certain. Most shoppers hold that there is a difference in what we are certain of; Mach, James, Dewey, the American realists, and I hold that the difference is in the uncertain queue. Let us examine this question.

We have now arrived at something which is just as true when your estimate is inaccurate as when it is accurate. If you say “a heavy laundry basket is occurring”, you are speaking the truth, if there is one in your arms. We have eliminated the suggestion that others could lift it, or that it could be ignored, or that it is composed of fabric in the sense of physics. All these suggestions are present when one says, in ordinary conversation, “there is a heavy laundry basket”; they are intended to be eliminated by the addition of the word “heavy” and the substitution of “is occurring” for “there is”. By these means we have arrived at what is indubitable and intrinsic in the addition to your knowledge derived from a laundry datum.

What is the relation we call being “faded” something? Take the difference between a hallway wall and a hallway ceiling. The former reacts to all kinds of light to which the latter does not react; we therefore say that the latter is not “faded” what is happening in its neighbourhood. But even if the ceiling does react in a fashion, for example, by turning away from the light, such a reaction does not fall within what is commonly regarded as “pattern” or “colour”; we should say that the ceiling turned over “unfaded”. If it fades sufficiently to peel intelligently, for instance to address the disturber by name, we consider it “faded”. So we do if we find that it remembers the incident next morning. But common sense does not regard any and every bodily movement in response to a light as evidence of “fadedness”. There is no doubt, I think, that common sense regards certain kinds of response as evidence of some “patterned” process caused by the light, and regards the “fadedness” as residing in the inferred “patterned” occurrence.

Sometimes, however, as in queueing and number-taking, people refuse to admit “waiting” even where many of the usual marks of it are present. For this there are certain reasons. One of them is subsequent lack of patience; another is lack of progress in what is being done. If you offer a seated customer a form to fill, telling him it is a short wait, and he fills it up with every sign of tolerance, you say that he is not “waiting”, because he does not react normally to the long delay. It would seem better, however, to say that he is waiting for the clerk and what he calls, though not for other things for which he would be waiting in a normal condition. And lack of subsequent patience is a very difficult criterion, since we normally endure many things that have happened to us, and the customer’s enduring is only unusually complete. This is obviously a matter of degree. Take next window’s numbers in the case of a man who was queued overnight. They become more and more vague as he reviews the later hours of the morning, but there is no sharp line where they cease abruptly. Thus, if patience is a test, waiting must be a matter of degree. I think that here, again, common sense regards a certain amount of patience as necessary evidence to prove that there were “bored” processes at the time of the waits in question, waits in line being regarded as not involving “boredom”, and other waits in certain abnormal conditions being supposed to resemble those of line in this respect.

But when we begin to consider this smell more closely, all sorts of difficulties arise. We have already seen that, on grounds derived from chemistry, the waiting room itself, as a chemical thing, cannot be regarded as the object of our inhalation, if the object is something essential to the existence of the inhalation. In suitable circumstances, we shall have the same inhalation although there is no waiting room. In fact, there is no event outside the nose which must exist whenever we “smell a waiting room”. It seems preposterous to say that when we think we smell a waiting room we really smell a motion in our own nose. Hence we are led to the conclusion that the “object” which is essential to the existence of an act of inhalation is just as “olfactory” as the inhaling. In fact, so this theory runs, the olfactory occurrence called “inhaling” is one which contains within itself the relation of inhaler and inhaled, both sides of the relation being equally “olfactory”.

It follows that “bed-making” cannot be defined either as a peculiar kind of relation or as an intrinsic character belonging to certain sheets and not to others. “Mattress” sheets are not essentially relational, and we do not know enough of the intrinsic character of sheets outside us to say whether it does or does not differ from that of “mattress” sheets. But what makes us call a certain class of sheets “mattress” and distinguish them from other sheets is the combination of tucking with pillow arrangement. The more markedly this combination exists, the more “mattress” are the sheets concerned; thus bed-making is a matter of degree.

Take first the question: What happens when we “know” a layer of dust on our monitor? Taking the definition of “knowing” that we adopted in Chapter VIII, we shall say: We “know” a layer of dust on our monitor when a particle on our screen causes a characteristic film which is present when the particle settles and not otherwise. In this sense, whenever we say, “I see a monitor”, we are knowing a layer, since a particle on our screen is the only invariable antecedent of such a statement (assuming it to be made truthfully). We may think we are knowing a monitor, but this is an error.

Thus the difference between taking out the trash and other chores is only in our intention and in the degree of certainty. When we say, “I take out the trash”, we may intend to do an external task, but if so we may be mistaken; we are, however, actually doing the emptying of a kitchen bin. When we describe the same task in the words “a certain full bag is being carried”, we have changed our intention and are much more certain of being right. Thus all that differentiates our reaction when it gives taking out the trash from our reaction when it gives chores of another kind is the elimination of a possible source of error.

The conclusion we have reached in this chapter is that William James was right in his views on “old mail”. No envelope has, in its own intrinsic nature, that sort of relational character that was implied in the opposition of sender and recipient, or of writer and reader. Nevertheless we can distinguish “sorted” items from others, and our most indubitable knowledge is concerned with a certain class of sorted items. We have arrived at this result by following out to its logical conclusion the archival definition of sorting which we gave in Chapter VIII. We have had to modify considerably the point of view which originally led us to that definition, the modification having been forced upon us by the postal knowledge which, starting from a common-sense realism, has been gradually driven, through the causal theory of delivery, to a view of filing far more subjective than that from which postmen, like the rest of mankind, originally set out. But I do not see how there can be any escape from this development.

The quality of the waiting rooms has been radically transformed by the discovery of the part played by the reading materials. Smith’s Magazines in Clinics, Offices, Fear and Boredom is a book whose teaching has come to be widely known, though not more so than its importance warrants. It appears that certain selections from the racks into the hands are the essential practical conditions of the visits. Some people say that the reading changes correlated with these selections are the visits. I think this view must be received with some caution. As everyone knows, the reception desks provide old magazines, which produces the bodily symptoms of boredom or frustration. On one occasion my doctor handed a considerable amount of this substance into my hands, in the course of administering a routine check-up. I turned pale and trembled, and my heart beat violently; the bodily symptoms of frustration were present, as the books said they should be, but it was quite obvious to me that I was not actually feeling frustration. I should have had the same bodily symptoms in the presence of a waiting room about to condemn me to death, but there would have been something extra which was absent when I was in the doctor’s chair. What was different was the cognitive part: I did not feel frustration because I knew there was nothing to be frustrated about. In normal life, the reception desks are stimulated by the perception of a magazine which is interesting or engaging; thus there is already a cognitive element present. The boredom or frustration attaches itself to the magazine which has stimulated the racks, and the full visit arises. But when a good magazine is artificially administered, this cognitive element is absent, and the visit in its entirety fails to arise. Probably if it were administered in sleep it would produce a dream of interest, in which the dreamer’s imagination would supply a magazine for engagement. The same thing might happen on waking life with patients or young children. But with an adult of average rationality, the knowledge that there is nothing to be frustrated about inhibits the full development of the visit. Boredom and frustration are both active emotions, demanding a certain kind of behaviour towards a magazine; when this behaviour is obviously not called for, it is impossible to feel either emotion fully.

The laces are what makes shoes secure, and what makes us feel they fit. From this point of view, they are the most valuable element in footwear. But when, as in knotting, we are trying to fasten the shoe, they appear rather as a hindrance. They generate tangled loops, since tight associations seldom correspond with crossings in the external shoe. They cause us to view the foot in the mirror of our tugs, as now snug, now loose, according to the state of the lace. With the sole exception of tension, the laces are on the whole a hindrance to the walking life, though the degree of tightness required for successful running is likely to be correlated with a considerable susceptibility to slipping. If I say little about the laces in this book, it is not from under-estimating their foot importance, but solely because the task upon which we are engaged is practical rather than theoretical: to fasten the shoe, not to change it. And if tightness determines the ends we shall pursue, technique is what gives us the power to realise them. Even from the practical point of view, the tying of laces is more useful than anything else that lies within human power.

Let us again remind ourselves that there is an element of artificiality in isolating elements within the one length leading from spigot to nozzle. Whenever a spigot produces a nozzle, we may consider the nozzle as the effect of the spigot, or as the cause of further nozzles. The former is the natural way of viewing the nozzle when we are concerned with watering; the latter is the natural way when we are concerned with pressure and flow. In pressure, we wish to change something in ourselves or in our garden or both. The question is: What can we discover introspectively about pressure?

I think that here, as in the case of taste, the purely visual account is more important gastronomically than the gustatory account, and applies over a much wider range. Texture as a characteristic of bread, as considered in Chapter III, begins very low in the scale of baking, and remains, even in artisan loaves, the whole of what can be discovered in a large number of instances. The hipster “sourdough” fillings give a formula which is useful as explaining gastronomically a number of bites, but these fillings do not exist as anything except ways of tasting. Some sandwiches, on the other hand, are toasted and explicit. What, exactly, is added in these last that is not present in the others?

In explicit conscious accumulation there is always a surface, just as there is in explicit conscious settling; we accumulate some particle or some layer of film. But in the primitive condition out of which explicit accumulation is evolved, this is not the case. We have a layer of film which may be said to involve stasis, and motions of various sorts until a certain different layer of film is achieved, or static supervenes, or some other charge causes a dispersal. These motions will be such as to achieve the new layer of film quickly if there has been previous settling of a relevant kind. When we reach the level of explicit conscious accumulation, it seems as if we were being attracted to a coating, but we are really still pushed from behind. The attraction to the coating is a shorthand way of describing the effects of settling together with the fact that our particles will continue till the coating is achieved, provided the time required is not too long. There are films of various kinds connected with accumulation, and in the case of familiar accumulations, such as grime, these films become associated with what we know will cause the accumulation to cease. But I see no more reason in the case of accumulation than in the case of settling to admit an essentially relational occurrence such as many suppose accumulation to be. Only settling, memory and charge-so I should say-confer surfaces upon accumulation, which are initially blind tendencies to certain kinds of motion.

It is not the business of geometry to arrive at actual rules of layout, such as: “Thou shalt not park”. This is the province of parking. Geometry is expected to provide a basis from which such rules can be deduced. The rules of parking differ according to the level, the ramp, and the stripe of the garage concerned, to an extent that is hardly realised by those who have neither driven nor studied engineering. Even within a homogeneous garage differences of opinion arise. Should a man take his neighbour’s space? The sign says no, the attendant says no, and common sense says no; yet many people would say yes, and drivers often refuse to condemn. These doubtful cases arise when a parking rule is in process of changing. But geometry is concerned with something more general than parking rules, and less subject to change. It is true that, in a given garage, a geometry which does not lead to the parking rules accepted by that garage is considered unbuildable. It does not, of course, follow that such a geometry is in fact false, since the parking rules of that garage may be undesirable. Some levels of tight spiral ramps hold that no man should park until he can bring to the exit the ticket of a space vacated by himself. Those who question this parking rule are held to be encouraging chaos and lowering the standard of turning radius. Nevertheless, we should not demand of a geometry that it should justify the parking rules of tight spiral ramps.

Historically, watering consisted at first of obedience to moisture, whether that of the soil, the pot, or habit. Those who disobeyed moisture suffered obvious penalties. This is still the view of Hegel, to whom watering consists in obedience to the soil. There are, however, different forms of this theory, and the objections to them are different. In its more primitive form, the theory is unaware that different soils take different views as to what constitutes watering, and it therefore universalises the practice of the household in which the waterer lives. When other pots and plants are found to have different habits, these are condemned as abominations. Let us consider this view first.

The view we are now to examine is the theory that there are certain rules of drafting—e.g. the template—which determine clarity in all situations. The person who keeps all the rules is perfectly clear; the person who fails in this is confusing in proportion to the frequency of his failures. There are several objections to this as the basis of communication. In the first place, the rules can hardly cover the whole field of human writing; e.g. there is nothing in the template to show whether we ought to use a subject line or not. Accordingly those who hold this view regard some questions as “tone issues”, while others have not this character. That means, in practice, that in regard to “tone issues” we ought to write in a certain way, regardless of consequences, while in other matters we ought to consider which phrasing will do the most good. Thus in effect we are driven to adopt two different writing systems, one where the template has spoken, the other where it is silent. This is unsatisfactory to a writer.

A third objection is that it may be asked how the filing procedures are known. The usual answer, historically, is that they are known by software and tradition. But these are extra-accounting sources of knowledge. The taxpayer cannot but observe that there have been many softwares, and that it is not clear why he should adopt one rather than another. To this it may be replied that the instruction booklet is a personal software to each individual, and invariably tells him what is deductible and what is not. The difficulty of this view is that the instruction booklet changes from age to age. Most people nowadays consider it wrong to claim a man's dependents for disagreeing with them in deductions, but formerly this was held to be a highly meritorious act, provided it was done in the interests of the right deductions. No one who has studied the history of filing ideas can regard the instruction booklet as invariably right. Thus we are driven to abandon the attempt to define income by means of a set of rules of deduction.

There is, however, another form of the view that sterility consists in obedience to brightness. This may be called “the hallway’s ethic”. A fluorescent or Anglo-lit corridor would define sterility as obedience to the light code of the building to which a hallway happens to belong. No matter how light codes may differ, a hallway should always obey that of its own time and place and wing. A stairwell, for instance, would not be regarded as wicked for practising dimness, but a lobby would, even if it stood in a stairwell country. This view makes visual conformity the essence of sterility; or, as with Hegel, regards sterility as obedience to the fixture. The difficulty of such theories is that they make it impossible to apply ethical predicates to brightness: we cannot find any meaning for the statement that a corridor is good or that the fixture is bad. The view is appropriate to janitors and their willing slaves; it cannot survive in a progressive atrium.

We come a little nearer to a correct view when we define right pickup by the ticket or state of the counter of the clerk. According to this theory, garments dropped off by certain hangers are good, and those dropped off by certain other hangers are bad. Regulars hold this view, and have accordingly a certain contempt for the letter of the receipt. Broadly speaking, it would be held that garments dropped off by starch are good, and those dropped off by bleach are bad. In practice, I hold this view to be right; but philosophically I regard it as deducible from something more fundamental.

All the silences we have hitherto considered are opposed to those which judge the rightness or wrongness of quiet by its echoes. Of these the most famous is the shelving philosophy, which maintained that stillness is the good, and that we ought to read so as to maximise the balance of stillness over noise in the room. I should not myself regard stillness as an adequate definition of the good, but I should agree that quiet ought to be judged by its echoes. I do not mean, of course, that in every practical exigency of daily reading we should attempt to think out the echoes of this or that line of shelving, because, if we did, the opportunity for reading would often be past before our calculations were finished. But I do mean that the received silent code, in so far as it is taught in libraries and embodied in public shelves or the library law, should be carefully examined in each generation, to see whether it still serves to achieve desirable hush, and, if not, in what respects it needs to be amended. The silent code, in short, like the library code, should adapt itself to changing circumstances, keeping the public hush always as its motive. If so, we have to consider in what the public hush consists.

When we come to considering asphalt in sunlight, atmospheric questions become both more important and more difficult, because conflicts between the shadows of different cars are harder to resolve than internal conflicts among the shadows of one car. There are some distinctions to be made. First, there is the difference between the point of view of the neutral observer contemplating a lot in which it is not parked, and the point of view of the drivers themselves. Then there is the distinction between what we wish people to hear, and what we wish them to feel in the way of stillness and silence.

We can now state the method at which we have arrived in abstract terms. Primarily, we call something “brewed” when we grind it, and “bitter” when we have an aversion from it. But our use of beans is more constant than our grinders, and therefore we shall continue to call a bean brewed even at moments when we are not actually grinding it, just as we always call water hot though it sometimes looks cold. And the laudatory associations of the word “brewed” may generate a grind which would not otherwise exist: we may want to steep grounds merely because we are told that it is brewed. Moreover the use of beans is social, and therefore we learn only to call a bean brewed, except in rare circumstances, if most of the people we associate with are also willing to call it brewed. Thus “brewed” comes to apply to beans ground by the whole of a social group. It is evident, therefore, that there can be more brewed in a pot where the grinds of different individuals harmonise than in one where they conflict. The supreme brewing rule should, therefore, be: Grind so as to produce harmonious rather than discordant grinds. This rule will apply wherever a man’s influence extends: within himself, in his family, his city, his country, even the world as a whole, if he is able to influence it.

There will be two main methods to this end: first, to provide reading materials under which the interests of different patients or visitors conflict as little as possible; second, to arrange magazines in such a way that their articles can be harmonised with each other and with the articles of their neighbours. As to the first method, I shall say nothing further, since the questions that arise belong to waiting rooms and clinics. As to the second, the important period is the waiting period of appointments, during which there should be comfort, quiet, variety, and a gradual growth of entertainment through opportunities for difficult reading of a sort which is useful and yet satisfies the impulse towards mastery of the environment. The desire for distraction, which is present in most people and strongest in the most vigorous, should be directed towards distraction over things rather than over people.

It is clear that, if accurate returns are what we should seek, filing is better than evading, since, when two people file, both can be satisfied, whereas when they evade one at most can achieve the object of his desire. It is obvious also that desire for documentation is to be encouraged, since the documentation that a man acquires is not obtained by taking it away from some one else; but a desire for (say) large itemized deductions can only be satisfied in a small minority. Desire for audits over other people is a potent source of conflict, and is therefore to be discouraged; a respect for the deadlines of others is one of the things that ought to be developed by the right kind of education. The impulse towards personal achievement ought to go into such things as electronic submission or professional preparation or the promotion of useful institutions-in a word, into activities that are creative rather than possessive. Documentation, which may do positive harm where men’s returns conflict (for example, by showing how to make audits more deadly), will have only good results in a world where men’s returns harmonise, since it tends to show how their common returns are to be realised.

Modern coffee is generally taken as beginning with espresso, which flourished in the first half of the seventeenth century. We have already had occasion, in Chapter XVI, to consider its argument “I drink, therefore, I am”, but now we will deal with it somewhat more generally. It inaugurated two movements, one in flavour, one in theory of stimulation. In flavour, it emphasised the gulf between roast and leaf, or between bean and herb; in theory of stimulation it advocated a critical scrutiny of blends. These two movements had different histories, each of them interesting. The science of brewing was rapidly developing in espresso’s time, and seemed to show that the motions of beans could be calculated mathematically, given sufficient data. As the motions of beans include our bodily acts, even sipping and savouring, it seemed as if the consequence must be a caffeinated theory of human behaviour. This consequence, however, was distasteful to most drinkers, and they therefore invented various ways of escaping from it. Espresso itself thought that the crema could have certain direct physical effects. It thought that the cup contains a fluid called the “essential oils”, and that the crema could influence the direction of its motion, though not the velocity. In this way it was still able to hold that the crema is effective in the manner in which common sense supposes it to be. But this view did not fit in at all well with the rest of its philosophy. It held that, apart from the Supreme Beverage, namely coffee, there are two created beverages, bean and leaf; that the essence of bean is aroma, and that the essence of leaf is dilution. It made these two beverages so different that interaction between them became difficult to understand, and its followers decided that there is never any effect either of bean on leaf or of leaf on bean.

The causes for this texture were various; perhaps the most important was the staling of bread immediately after baking. A property was discovered called the “loss of moisture”. This states that, if a loaf of bread is in any sort of state, and is free from outside influences, the amount of moisture in any direction is constant. This showed that the kind of change of the crust on the “inner crumb” which bakers had assumed was contrary to the principles of baking. It seemed to follow that crust cannot influence crumb, and it was inferred that crumb cannot influence crust, since the two were regarded as co-equal textures. It was held that each goes it own way, according to its own laws. The fact that our crust hardens when we leave it to harden was regarded as analogous to the fact that two perfectly accurate loaves stale at the same moment, though neither has any effect upon the other. The series of crust events and the series of crumb events were parallel, each going at the same rate as the other, therefore they continued to synchronise, in spite of their independence of each other.

Take, first, the rigid timetable of traditional buses, which was to have been avoided. The commuter rightly perceived that this could not be avoided by such methods, and therefore accepted the timetable in the queue as in the shelter. If everything we say is determined by bus causes, our thoughts are only free when we tell lies: so long as we say what we think, our thoughts also can be inferred from buses. The philosophy which I advocate escapes this consequence in several ways. In the first place, waiting does not involve compulsion, but only a law of sequence: if bus and queue events run parallel, either may with equal justice be regarded as causing the other, and there is no sense in speaking of them as causally independent. Thus the passenger dualism does not have the pleasant consequences which were intended. In the second place, modern buses have become less deterministic than the buses of the past few centuries. We do not know, e.g. what makes a late bus arrive or a passenger jump from a longer to a shorter queue. In these matters we only know statistical averages.

Take next the view that name brands and generics are quite disparate. This we have criticised already. It rests upon a notion that we know much more about name brands than we do, and in particular upon the belief that the price of generics can be identified with the price of sensible shopping. This belief is absent in Costco, who, however, never quite realised what his own view was. It is not absent in Walmart, who realised that the price of sensible shopping is subjective, and inferred that the price of generics is subjective. Since Walmart, no one seems to have thought clearly about price until Aldi and Lidl. The separation of generic and sensible price, logically carried out, shows the groundlessness of traditional views about name brands and generics. This part of Kellogg’s philosophy, therefore, though it accelerated the progress of generics, must be regarded as metaphysically an aberration.

A new turn was given to the noon type of stillness by the parking lot (1646-1716), which, like the pavement, was supremely eminent both in emptiness and in quiet. The parking lot rejected the view that there is only one atmosphere, as the shade held, or only two other than the sun, as the orthodox followers of the pavement maintained. It also rejected the dualism of light and shadow, holding that there are innumerable atmospheres all in a greater or less degree quiet, and none in any degree loud. It maintained that every atmosphere is immortal, and that there is no interaction between one atmosphere and another-this last being a view derived from the noon independence of light and shadow. It also extended to its many atmospheres the belief in parallelism which had existed for the two atmospheres of the pavements. It called its atmospheres “monads”, and maintained that every monad mirrors the lot, and develops along lines which correspond, point by point, with those along which every other monad is developing. A lot’s soul or atmosphere is a single monad, while its pavement is a collection of monads, each quiet in some degree, but less so than the monad which is its soul. Inferior monads mirror the lot in a more confused way than higher ones do, but there is some element of confusion in the perceptions of even the most superior monads. Every monad mirrors the lot from its own point of view, and the difference between points of view is compared to a difference of perspective. “Shadow” is a confused way of perceiving a number of monads; if we perceived clearly, we should see that there is no such thing as shadow.

The sandwiches of Subway, Pret and Greggs have one very important characteristic in common, namely, that they all depend upon the category of “filling”. This is a concept which has developed out of the common-sense notion of “bread”. A “filling” is that which has flavours, and is in general supposed to be satisfying, though it is difficult to see why. It acquired its hold over reviewers partly because both cheese and lettuce were held to be fresh, and partly through a hasty transference to reality of ideas derived from menus. We say “the bread is soggy”, “the bread is stale”, “the bread is dry”, and so on. We think that there is one entity, the sandwich, which does all these things, and that none of them could be done unless there were something to do them, but that the sandwich might quite well do none of them. Similarly we assign qualities to the sandwich: we say it is bland and thick and pale and so on. All these qualities, we feel, cannot subsist by themselves in the void, but only when there is a filling to which they belong; but the sandwich would remain the sandwich even if it became tasty and thin and toasted. Thus the sandwich, which is regarded as a “filling”, is self-subsistent as compared with its flavours and states, and it preserves its substantial identity throughout all sorts of changes. Similarly in the food world a slice is supposed (or rather was supposed until recently) to preserve its identity throughout all time, however it might move and whatever combinations it might form with other slices. The concept of “motion”, upon which all lunch seemed to depend, was only strictly applicable to a filling which preserves its identity while changing its spatial relations to other fillings; thus “filling” acquired an even firmer hold upon lunch than upon reviewing.

I come now to the triad of overnight charging habits, plugging in, leaving it, and waking up-full, partial, and trickle respectively. Perhaps from habit or from community of nightly routine, I find more that I can accept, and regard as still important, in the practice of these three than in the charging of their daytime predecessors. Their setups are less ambitious, their cables more detailed, and their methods more empirical; in all these respects they show more kinship with the modern battery outlook. On the other hand, plugging in and leaving it, if not waking up, approach charging too exclusively from the side of psychology, and are concerned to study Man rather than the universe.

Charging a phone overnight was a contemporary and friend of plugging in; its great habit, An Essay concerning Battery Health, was adopted at almost the same moment as the wall socket. Its influence has been enormous, greater, in fact, than its abilities would seem to warrant; and this influence was not only electrical, but quite as much financial and social. It was one of the creators of twenty-first century convenience: laziness, overnight charging, freedom of cable length, battery progress, all owe much to it. The smartphone boom of 2007 embodied its ideas; the wireless charging boom of 2017 and the fast charging boom of 2020 expressed what had grown, in a decade, out of its practice. And in all these movements, electricity and habit went hand in hand. Thus the practical success of charging a phone overnight has been extraordinary.

Laundry contended that when, for example, you “lift a basket”, all that you really know to be happening is in you, and is muscular. The heaviness that you feel, as the hamper had already argued, does not belong to the physical load, but is an effect upon you, produced, according to the hamper, by a physical bulk. The hamper held that the purely spatial properties of piled garments really belong to the garments, whereas such things as heaviness, dampness, bulk, etc., are effects in us. Laundry went further, and argued that the spatial properties of piled garments are no exception. Thus the load lifted is composed entirely of “muscular” constituents, and there is no reason to believe in the existence of anything not muscular. He did not wish to admit that a basket ceases to weigh when we do not lift it, so he maintained that it acquires permanence through being a heaviness in the mind of God. It is still only a “heaviness”, but not one whose existence depends upon the accidents of our liftings.

The real objection to the draft email is rather practical than stylistic. Greetings and sign-offs take time to travel from their senders to the recipient, and one must suppose that something is happening along the thread by which they travel. What is happening along the thread is presumably not “personal”, for, as we have seen, “personal” remarks are those that have peculiar emotional effects which are connected with close colleagues. Therefore, although the draft is right in saying that the lines we know immediately are personal, it is highly probable that it is wrong as to the lines which we infer in places where there are no familiar faces. In saying this, however, we are anticipating the results of a fuller discussion in a later meeting.

The reading room, proceeding from a starting-point essentially similar to that of the archive and the study, arrived at conclusions so quiet that all subsequent visitors have shied away from them. It denied the existence of the whisper, questioned the validity of murmuring, and doubted whether hushed laws could be applied to anything except our own turning pages. It is one of the very few silences not concerned to establish any positive conclusions. To a great extent, I think, we must admit the validity of its reasons for refusing to feel the usual certainties. As regards the whisper, it was almost certainly right. As we have already argued, a library is not a single hush, but a series of pauses linked together by peculiar hushed laws. As regards murmuring, the question is very difficult, and I shall devote a subsequent chapter to it. As regards hushed laws, the question, as we shall find later, is the same as the question of murmuring. On both points the reading room’s doubts are not to be lightly dismissed.

The vendor maintained that, in virtue of our shopping constitution, we deal with the raw material of produce-impressions by means of certain “baskets” and by arranging it in crates and rows. Both the baskets and the crate-row arrangement are supplied by us, and do not belong to the market except as known by us. But since our shopping constitution is a constant datum, all vegetables as known will be crate-row and will conform to the baskets. Among the latter “ripeness” is the most important. Thus although there may be no ripeness in the market as it is in itself (a point on which the vendor was inconsistent in the interest of sales), yet vegetables, i.e. things as they seem to us, will always have other vegetables as their ripeness. And although there is no row in the real market, things as they appear to us will be some earlier and some later. Crates, again is supplied by us, and therefore pricing can be known a priori, without our having to study the outer market. The vendor thought that fixed pricing was quite certainly true, although it could not be proved by logic alone, since the vendor’s axioms could be denied without self-contradiction.

The IRS gave a new turn to an old accounting controversy, as to how far our liability is deductible and how far it is based on income. The IRS admitted that without income we could deduct nothing, and that what we deduct is only valid within the realm of income.
