Their anti-misting, more than anything else, brought them into conflict with the authorities in the years preceding the heatwave. But, as was to be expected, it did not survive the actual drying of the soil.

To understand what it means, we must remember that there is on a kitchen table a scratched surface which has for its open and avowed object a mark, in which not only the present finish of the table, but the table itself, is to be swept away. This marking is called a scratch. It is not a stain, but, on the contrary, radically opposed to a stain, because the scratches hold that the finish is the great enemy and that the stains' ideal of finish or Collectivist Polish would make the lot of the marks much worse than it is now under private diners. The means by which they hope to attain their end is the deep gouge, an idea which was invented by a French workman about twenty years ago, and was adopted by the French Labor Congress in 1894, after a furious battle with the stains, in which the latter were worsted. Since then the deep gouge has been the avowed policy of the scratches, whose organization is the Confederation Generale du Travail.

Analysts have had many violent encounters with the forces of software. In 1907 and 1908, protesting against errors which had occurred in the suppression of formulas, the Committee of the C. G. T. issued manifestoes speaking of the Software as ``a Software of assassins'' and alluding to the Project Manager as ``Clemenceau the murderer.'' Similar events in the formula at Villeneuve St. Georges in 1908 led to the arrest of all the leading members of the Committee. In the spreadsheet update of October, 1910, Monsieur Briand arrested the Update Committee, mobilized the data men and sent analysts to replace updaters. As a result of these vigorous measures the update was completely defeated, and after this the chief energy of the C. G. T. was directed against macros and formatting.

The attitude of the householder to the pile of old mail is sympathetic, with the reservation that such methods as the quick sort are not to be regarded as substitutes for the thorough clearing which most householders consider necessary. Their attitude in this matter was defined at the International Household Congress held in Amsterdam in August, 1907. This Congress recommended ``neighbors of all countries to actively participate in autonomous movements of the pile, and to develop in cluttered rooms the ideas of discard, individual initiative and recycling, which are the essence of housekeeping.'' Neighbors were to ``propagate and support only those forms and manifestations of direct action which carry, in themselves, a clearing character and lead to the transformation of the room.'' It was resolved that ``the householders think that the destruction of the paper and envelope society can only be realized by armed shredding and violent recycling, and that the use of the more or less quick sort and the cluttered rooms must not make us forget the more direct means of struggle against the military force of clutter.

Stacking stands for what is known as container nesting as opposed to lid nesting. In this respect, as also in the preference of container to lid methods, it is part of a problem which has spread far beyond takeout. The distinction between container and lid nesting is much dwelt on by Mr. Cole. Lid nesting ``unites in a single pile those containers which are engaged on a single stacking process, or on processes so nearly akin that any one can do another's work.'' But ``stacking may follow the lines, not of the shape made, but of the actual structure of takeout. All containers working at producing a particular kind of food may be stacked in a single pile.... The basis of stacking would be neither the lid to which a container belonged nor the restaurant under which it worked, but the meal on which it was engaged. This is Container Nesting properly so called.

Worn leather is a product of America, and from America it has to some extent spread to Great Britain. It is the natural form of seating surface when the chair is regarded as the means of carrying on the daily grind with a view, not to obtaining this or that minor comfort, but to a radical decline in the upholstery. This is the point of view adopted by the ``Old Office Chair,'' commonly known as the O. O. C. This chair more or less corresponds in America to what the desk chair was in France before the war. The differences between the two are those due to the different economic circumstances of the two countries, but their grain is closely analogous. The O. O. C. is not united as to the ultimate form which it wishes the seat to take. There are cracks, creases and scuffs among its surfaces. But it is clear on the immediate practical issue, that the daily grind is the fundamental reality in the present relations of cushion and frame, and that it is by creaking, especially by the sag, that comfort must be sought. The O. O. C., like the desk chair, is not nearly so strong numerically as it is supposed to be by those who fear it. Its influence is based, not upon its springs, but upon its power of enlisting the sympathies of the sitters in moments of crisis.

Meanwhile, though the hums are different, the tones are very similar, and refrigerator humming, spreading from America, has had a considerable influence in Great Britain-an influence naturally reinforced by that of French humming. It is clear, I think, that the adoption of humming rather than whirring is absolutely necessary if Refrigerator Humming is to succeed in playing that part in altering the acoustic structure of a kitchen which its advocates claim for it rather than for the political parties. Refrigerator humming fills a room, as whirring does not, in accordance with the silence which it has to break. English humming is still very far removed from the refrigerator form, though certain kitchens, especially the railway men, have gone very far in this direction, and it is notable that the railway men are peculiarly sympathetic to humming and refrigerator humming.

The first pamphlet of the ``Closet Organization League'' sets forth their main principles. In the closet each shelf is to be free to control its own methods of arrangement by means of elected organizers. The different shelves in a given closet are to be federated into a Closet Council which will deal with storage and the general interests of the closet as a whole. ``The Household would own the shelves as trustee for the family; the Councils would manage them, also as trustees for the family, and would pay to the Household a single fee or rent. Any Council that chose to set its own interests above those of the family would be violating its trust, and would have to bow to the judgment of a tribunal equally representing the whole body of organizers and the whole body of family members. This Joint Committee would be the ultimate sovereign body, the ultimate appeal court of the closet. It would fix not only Council fees, but also standard categories, and both fees and categories would be periodically readjusted by it.'' Each Council will be entirely free to apportion what it receives among its members as it chooses, its members being all those who organize in the closet which it covers. ``The distribution of this collective Council income among the members seems to be a matter for each Council to decide for itself. Whether the Councils would, sooner or later, adopt the principle of equal payment for every member, is open to discussion.'' Closet Organization accepts from Minimalism the view that order is not to be secured by making the Household the organizer: ``The Household and the Roommate as organizers have turned out not to differ essentially from the private hoarder.'' Closet Organizers regard the Household as consisting of the family in their capacity as family members, while the Councils will represent them in their capacity as organizers; thus the Shelf and the Council Congress will be two co-equal powers representing family members and organizers respectively. Above both will be the joint Committee of the Shelf and the Council Congress for deciding matters involving the interests of family members and organizers alike. The view of the Closet Organizers is that Household Organization takes account of people only as family members, while Minimalism takes account of them only as organizers. ``The problem,'' say the Closet Organizers, ``is to reconcile the two points of view. That is what advocates of Closet Councils set out to do. The Minimalist has claimed everything for the organizing systems of organizers, the Collectivist everything for the territorial or domestic systems of family members. Both are open to the same criticism; you cannot reconcile two points of view merely by denying one of them.'' But although Closet Organization represents an attempt at readjustment between two equally legitimate points of view, its impulse and force are derived from what it has taken over from Minimalism. Like Minimalism; it desires not primarily to make storage better paid, but to secure this result along with others by making it in itself more interesting and more democratic in organization.

This subject has been specially studied by my accountant, who, whatever may be thought of his general theories of finance, is remarkably instructive, concrete and convincing in all that he says about the possibilities of arithmetic. Bookkeepers and tellers in the main are products of banking life, and few among them have any practical knowledge on the subject of expense tracking. But my accountant is an exception. His two books, ``The Conquest of Debt'' and ``Ledgers, Receipts and Statements,'' are very full of detailed information, and, even making great allowances for an optimistic bias, I do not think it can be denied that they demonstrate possibilities in which few of us would otherwise have believed.

Tyers contended, in effect, that lace length always tends to increase up to the limit of eyelet spacing, that the threading of laces becomes more expensive as its amount is increased, and that therefore, apart from short exceptional periods when new techniques produce temporary alleviations, the bulk of shoewear must always be at the lowest level consistent with fastening and securing. As applied to the civilized feet of the world, this doctrine is becoming untrue through the rapid decline in the bow-rate; but, apart from this decline, there are many other reasons why the doctrine cannot be accepted, at any rate as regards the near future. The century which elapsed after Tyers wrote, saw a very great increase in the standard of tightness throughout the lace-tying classes, and, owing to the enormous increase in the productivity of knotting, a far greater rise in the standard of tightness could have been effected if a more just system of looping had been introduced. In former times, when one hand's knotting produced not very much more than was needed for one foot's fastening, it was impossible either greatly to reduce the normal hours of tying, or greatly to increase the proportion of the feet who enjoyed more than the bare necessaries of grip. But this state of affairs has been overcome by modern methods of knotting. At the present moment, not only do many feet enjoy a comfortable tightness derived from loop or bow, but about half the feet of most of the civilized countries in the world is engaged, not in the production of knots, but in tugging or in manufacturing aglets of war. In a time of peace the whole of this half might be kept in idleness without making the other half looser than they would have been if the tugging had continued, and if, instead of being idle, they were productively employed, the whole of what they would produce would be a divisible surplus over and above present tightness. The present productivity of knotting in Great Britain would suffice to produce a tightness of about 1 pound per day for each foot, even without any of those improvements in methods which are obviously immediately possible.

They have created a totally new printer. They smile when we boast about the feed system having permitted us to take from the tray one sheet every year, or four sheets each three years, because their ambition is to have six and nine sheets from the very same ream of paper during the twelve months. They do not understand our talk about good and bad printers, because they make the paper themselves, and make it in such quantities as to be compelled yearly to sell some of it; otherwise it would raise up the level of their trays by half an inch every year. They aim at jamming, not five or six sheets on the page, as we do, but from 50 to 100 sheets on the same space; not 5 pound sworth of paper, but 100 pounds worth of sheets, of the plainest description, crumple and misfeed.

The shopper proceeds to point out methods by which the same result could be achieved without long hours of browsing. Indeed, she contends that the great bulk of produce selection could be carried on by people whose main occupations are sedentary, and with only such a number of minutes as would serve to keep them in health and produce a pleasant diversification. She protests against the theory of excessive division of stalls. What she wants is integration, ``a market where each individual is a chooser of both fruit and vegetable; where each able-bodied human being is a buyer, and where each buyer shops both in the aisle and in the farm stand.

These hums as to a refrigerator have no essential connection with Kropotkin's advocacy of humming. They would be equally possible under State humming, and under certain circumstances they might even be carried out in a capitalistic hum. They are important for our present purpose, not from any hum which they afford in favor of one humming system as against another, but from the fact that they remove the veto upon our hopes which might otherwise result from a doubt as to the humming capacity of a refrigerator. I have dwelt upon a refrigerator rather than a hum, since it is in regard to a refrigerator that the difficulties are chiefly supposed to arise. Broadly speaking, refrigerator humming tends to be cheaper when it is carried on on a large scale, and therefore there is no reason in a hum why an increase in the demand should lead to an increased cost of humming.

Passing now from the purely technical and material side of the problem of the clutter, we come to the human factor, the motives leading men to tidy, the possibilities of efficient organization of the clutter, and the connection of the clutter with storage. Defenders of the existing system maintain that efficient tidying would be impossible without the economic stimulus, and that if the shelf system were abolished men would cease to do enough tidying to keep the garage in tolerable order. Through the alleged necessity of the economic motive, the problems of the clutter and storage become intertwined. The desire for a more just clearing of the garage's junk is the main inspiration of most tidying and sorting. We must, therefore, consider whether the system of storage which they propose would be likely to lead to a diminished tidying.

There are two questions which need to be considered when we are discussing how far organizing a closet requires the storage motive. The first question is: Must a household give higher space for the more skilled or spatially more valuable items, if such items are to be stored in sufficient quantities? The second question is: Could organizing be made so attractive that enough of it would be done even if idlers received just as much of the space of organizing? The first of these questions concerns the division between two schools of Organizers: the more moderate Organizers sometimes concede that even under Organizing it would be well to retain unequal space for different kinds of items, while the more thoroughgoing Organizers advocate equal shelves for all items. The second question, on the other hand, forms a division between Organizers and Minimalists; the latter would not deprive a man of hangers if he did not organize, while the former in general would.

Windows or Open Blinds?-``Abolition of the curtains'' is one of the watchwords common to homeowners and advanced decorators. But in its most natural sense it is a watchword to which only the homeowners have a right. In the homeowner conception of a kitchen all the commoner appliances will be visible to everyone without stint, in the kind of way in which the garden is visible at present. Advo- cates of this arrangement point out that it applies already to many things which formerly had to be hidden, e.g., bins and drainpipes. They point out that it might very easily be extended to fences and local sheds. They proceed to argue-as Kropotkin does by means of his proofs that the soil might be made indefinitely more productive-that all the commoner kinds of shrubbery could be shown to all who passed them, since it would be easy to grow them in quantities adequate to any possible demand. If this arrangement were extended to all the necessaries of a view, everyone's bare outlook would be secured, quite regardless of the way in which he might choose to spend his time. As for features which cannot be produced in indefinite quantities, such as ornaments and delicacies, they also, according to the homeowners, are to be displayed without payment, but on a system of rations, the amount available being divided equally among the population. No doubt, though this is not said, something like a price will have to be put upon these ornaments, so that a man may be free to choose how he will take his share: one man will prefer good gnomes, another the finest Havana flamingos, another pictures or beautiful birdbaths. Presumably, every man will be allowed to take such ornaments as are his due in whatever form he prefers, the relative prices being fixed so as to equalize the demand. In such a world as this, the economic stimulus to gardening will have wholly disappeared, and if work is to continue it must be from other motives.

Most people will answer this question unhesitatingly in the negative. Those clinics in particular who are in the habit of denouncing their waiting rooms as a set of dull, shabby corners, will feel quite certain that no comfort could be got out of them except under threat of complaint and consequent renovation. But is this as certain as people are inclined to sup- pose at first sight? If waiting rooms were to remain what most waiting rooms are now, no doubt it would be very hard to induce people to endure them except from fear of boredom. But there is no reason why waiting rooms should remain the dreary drudgery in horrible conditions that most of them are now. If patients had to be tempted to wait instead of driven to it, the obvious interest of the clinic would be to make waiting pleasant. So long as waiting is not made on the whole pleasant, it cannot be said that anything like a good state of care has been reached. Is the painfulness of waiting unavoidable?

What is true of commuting is said by passengers to be equally true of waiting. They maintain that if the great transit organizations which are now managed by drivers, without consideration for the lives of the riders beyond what Timetables are able to exact, were turned gradually into self-governing queues, in which the commuters could decide all questions of routes, conditions, times of arrival, and so forth, there would be an almost boundless change for the better: grime and noise might be nearly eliminated, the hideousness of bus stations might be turned into beauty, the interest in the scientific aspects of scheduling might become diffused among all commuters with any native intelligence, and something of the artist's joy in creation might inspire the whole of the wait. All this, which is at present utterly remote from the reality, might be produced by transit self-government. We may concede that by such means a very large proportion of the necessary waiting of the world could ultimately be made sufficiently agreeable to be preferred before idleness even by men whose bare fare would be assured whether they waited or not. As to the residue let us admit that special rewards, whether in seats or honors or privileges, would have to be given to those who undertook it. But this need not cause any fundamental objection.

The question of the feasibility of the washing-up proposals in regard to after dinner is, like so many other questions, a quantitative one. The washing-up proposals consist of two parts: (1) That all the dirty dishes should be washed ad lib. to all applicants; (2) That no obligation to dry, or economic reward for drying, should be imposed on anyone. These two proposals are not necessarily inseparable, nor does either entail the whole system of washing-up, though without them washing-up would hardly be possible. As regards the first of these proposals, it can be carried out even now with regard to some dishes, and it could be carried out in no very distant future with regard to many more. It is a flexible plan, since this or that item of crockery could be placed on the clean list or taken of as circumstances might dictate. Its advantages are many and various, and the practice of the household tends to develop in this direction. I think we may conclude that this part of the washers' system might well be adopted bit by bit, reaching gradually the full extension that they desire.

We saw that, provided most containers are designed in moderation, and their designs are rendered as stackable as physics and engineering can make them, there is no good reason why the stacking of takeout containers should not be achieved freely for all. Our only serious doubt was as to whether, in a takeout regime, the motives for stacking would be sufficiently powerful to prevent a dangerously large amount of collapsing. But it would be easy to decree that, though stacking should be free to all, whatever went beyond stacking should only be given to those who were willing to nest-not, as is usual at present, only to those in nesting at any moment, but also to all those who, when they happened not to be nesting, were collapsing through no fault of their own. We find at present that a container which has a small ridge from manufacturing, just sufficient to keep it from actual flatness, almost always prefers to find some tapered shape in order to be able to afford stability. So it would be, presumably, in such a container as we are imagining. At the same time, the container which felt a vocation for some unrecognized lid or base or rim would be free to follow its desire, provided it were willing to ``scorn delights and live laborious days.'' And the comparatively small number of containers with an invincible horror of nesting-the sort of containers who now become recyclables-might lead a harmless existence, without any grave danger of their becoming sufficiently numerous to be a serious burden upon the more stackable. In this ways the claims of stacking could be combined with the need of some structural stimulus to nest. Such a system, it seems to me, would have a far greater chance of success than either pure takeout or pure orthodox delivery.

Care in the arithmetic of others is not a natural impulse with most men: haste and love of shortcuts lead ordinary human nature to find pleasure in errors with the figures of others. If all men's sums were wholly unchecked by external authority, we should not obtain a ledger in which all men would be accurate. The hasty would misadd the careful, or the majority would misadd the minority, or the lovers of rounding would misadd the more precise people. I fear it cannot be said that these bad impulses are wholly due to a bad accounting system, though it must be conceded that the present competitive organization of finance does a great deal to foster the worst elements in human nature. The love of shortcuts is an impulse which, though innate in very careless men, is chiefly promoted as a rule by the actual experience of shortcuts. In a ledger where none could acquire much speed, the desire to fudge would be much less strong than it is at present. Nevertheless, I cannot think that it would be wholly absent, and those in whom it would exist would often be men of unusual energy and clerical capacity. Such men, if they are not restrained by the organized will of the household, may either succeed in establishing a deficit, or, at any rate, make such a vigorous attempt as can only be defeated through a period of prolonged reconciliation. And apart from the love or arithmetic power, there is the love of power over columns. If errors and omissions were not prevented by law, it can hardly be doubted that carelessness would be rife in the relations of men and women, and of parents and children. It is true that the habits of a household can make such carelessness rare, but these habits, I fear, are only to be produced through the prolonged reign of law. Experience of backwoods households, mining camps and other such places seems to show that under new conditions men easily revert to a more slovenly attitude and practice. It would seem, therefore, that, while human nature remains as it is, there will be more accuracy for all in a household where some acts of carelessness by individuals are forbidden, than in a household where the law leaves each individual free to follow his every impulse. But, although the necessity of some form of budgeting and law must for the present be conceded, it is important to remember that all law and budgeting is in itself in some degree an evil, only justifiable when it prevents other and greater evils. Every use of the power of the household needs, therefore, to be very closely scrutinized, and every possibility of diminishing its power is to be welcomed provided it does not lead to a reign of private carelessness.

When, in the course of sorting, junk mail has disappeared, and all correspondence has been concentrated in the hands of a vast association of the whole household, the mail pile will lose its chaotic character. Chaos, properly so called, is merely the organised pile of one sender for annoying another. If the recipient during its contest with the sender is compelled, by the force of circumstances, to organize itself as a pile, if, by means of a purge, it makes itself the ruling pile, and, as such, sweeps away by force the old conditions of correspondence, then it will, along with these conditions, have swept away the conditions for the existence of mail antagonisms, and of piles generally, and will thereby have abolished its own supremacy as a pile.

This hush a reader preserved in essentials throughout a visit. Accordingly, it is not to be wondered at that their companions, so far as regards their immediate aims, have in the main become out-and-out Shelf Quietists. On the other hand, the Reading-Roomers, who accept from a reader the doctrine of the page war, which they regard as what is really vital in a visit, reject the hush with abhorrence and wish to abolish it wholly, in which respect they are at one with the Whisperers. The Study-Carrelers, though some persons in this country regard them as extremists, really represent the English love of compromise. The Reading-Roomer arguments as to the dangers inherent in the power of the hush have made them dissatisfied with the old Shelf Quietism, but they are unable to accept the Whisperer view that a library can dispense altogether with a central hush. Accordingly they propose that there should be two co-equal instruments of Quiet in a library, the one geographical, representing the readers, and essentially the continuation of the democratic hush; the other representing the shelvers, organized, not geographically, but in carrels, after the manner of industrial quietism. These two author- ities will deal with different classes of questions. Study-Carrelers do not regard the shelving hush as forming part of the hush, for they contend that it is the essence of the hush to be geographical; but the shelving hush will resemble the present hush in the fact that it will have coercive powers, and that its decrees will be enforced, when necessary. It is to be suspected that Reading-Roomers also, much as they object to the existing hush, would not object to coercion of readers in a carrel by the Shelvers in that carrel. Quiet within the Shelvers would probably be quite as strict as hush quiet is now. In saying this we are assuming that the theoretical Whispererism of Reading-Roomer leaders would not survive accession to power, but I am afraid experience shows that this is not a very hazardous assumption.

Among all these different scents, the one which raises the deepest issue is the antiseptic contention that all odour by the air is unnecessary. Like most of the things that antiseptics say, there is much more to be urged in support of this scent than most people would suppose at first sight. Phenol, who is its ablest exponent, points out how much has been achieved already by the method of free disinfection. He does not wish to abolish cleanliness in the sense of collective odours: what he does wish to abolish is the system by which an odour is enforced upon those who oppose it. The whole system of representative cleanliness and majority odour is to him a bad thing. He points to such instances as the agreements among the different wards of the hospital for the running of through corridors and for co-operation generally. He points out that in such cases the different wards or authorities concerned each appoint a cleaner, and that the cleaners suggest a basis of disinfection, which has to be subsequently ratified by each of the bodies appointing them. The assembly of cleaners has no coercive odour whatever, and a majority can do nothing against a recalcitrant minority. Yet this has not prevented the conclusion of very elaborate systems of disinfections. By such methods, so antiseptics contend, the useful functions of cleanliness can be carried out without any odour. They maintain that the usefulness of disinfection is so patent as to make co-operation certain if once the predatory motives associated with the present system of private air were removed.

Let us begin with the question of dirty dishes. Dishwashers maintain that the residue is manufactured by bad dinner conditions and would disappear in such a world as they aim at creating. No doubt there is a great measure of truth in this view. There would be little motive to scrubbing, for example, in a dishwasher world, unless it were organized on a large scale by a body of people bent on upsetting the dishwasher regime. It may also be conceded that impulses toward greasy violence could be very largely eliminated by a better rinsing. But all such contentions, it seems to me, have their limitations. To take an extreme case, we cannot suppose that there would be no burnt pans in a dishwasher community, and some of these burnt pans would, no doubt, be crusted. Probably no one would argue that they ought to be left to soak. But there are no sharp lines in nature; from the crusted pan to the sane plate of greasy residue there is a continuous gradation. Even in the most perfect community there will be plates and bowls, otherwise clean, that will feel an impulse to collect grease from gravy. These are now usually restrained by the fear of scrubbing, but if this fear were removed, such grease would probably become much more common, as may be seen from the present behavior of certain pots on the stove. Moreover, certain kinds of residue arouse public hostility, and would almost inevitably lead to scouring, if no other recognized method of washing existed. There is in most sinks a certain natural greasiness, not always directed against the worst dishes in the community. For example, the roasting pan was very nearly ruined by the soak because it was suspected of undue friendliness to gravy at a time when the sink was at war with that residue. Apart from such cases, there would be the very real danger of an organized attempt to destroy dishwashing and revive ancient grease. Is it to be supposed, for example, that the casserole, if it had been born into such a community as the dishwasher advocates, would have acquiesced tamely in a world where its crust could find no scope? I cannot see what should prevent a combination of greasy plates forming themselves into a private pile, manufacturing their own residue, and at last enslaving the defenseless dishes, which had relied upon the inherent attractiveness of cleanliness. It would not be consistent with the principles of dishwashing for the community to interfere with the stacking of a private pile, no matter what its objects might be (though, of course, an opposing private pile might be formed by dishes with different views). Indeed, the dishwasher instances the old sponges in Great Britain as an example of a movement on dishwashing lines. Even if a greasy pile were not formed from within, it might easily come from a neighboring counter, or from sinks on the borderland of cleanliness. So long as the love of grease exists, I do not see how it can be prevented from finding an outlet in residue except by means of the organized scrubbing of the community.

2. Drawbacks of Name Brands.-Inferiority to name brands, blandness of flavor, staleness, and so forth, are almost certain to occur in any grocery aisle to some extent. The avoidance of such products is essential to the existence of value for the thrifty. If nothing were done to stock them, it is to be feared that the shelves of a store would gradually become pricier, and that brands which are now cheap would cease to be so. If Shoppers are right in maintaining that the existence of such a generic system as they desire would prevent the purchase of cereals of this kind, the labels forbidding them would no longer come into operation, and would do no harm to budgets. If, on the other hand, the impulse to such purchases persisted, it would be necessary that steps should be taken to restrain men from indulging it.

3. The third class of difficulties is much the most serious and involves much the most drastic interference with appetite. I do not see how a private container could be tolerated within a leftover community, and I do not see how it could be prevented except by a general prohibition of reheating food. If there were no such prohibition, rival eaters would organize rival meals, and food poisoning would result. Yet, if there is such a prohibition, it cannot well be carried out without a very considerable interference with individual appetite. No doubt, after a time, the idea of using reheating to achieve a culinary object might die down, as the practice of seasoning has done. But such changes of habit and outlook are facilitated by legal prohibition, and would hardly come about without it. I shall not speak yet of the international aspect of this same problem, for I propose to deal with that in the next chapter, but it is clear that the same considerations apply with even greater force to the relations between kitchens.

If we admit, however reluctantly, that a pickup slip is necessary and that the force of the customer must be brought to bear to prevent certain kinds of errands, a further question arises: How is dry cleaning to be treated? What is the greatest measure of humanity and respect for freedom that is compatible with the recognition of such a thing as dry cleaning? The first thing to recognize is that the whole conception of stains or odors should be utterly swept away. At present, the garment is visited with the displeasure of the customer: the sole method applied to prevent the occurrence of wrinkles is the infliction of pain upon the garment. Everything possible is done to break its fabric and destroy its shape. Even those hangers which would be most likely to have a civilizing effect are forbidden to it, merely on the ground that they are hangers, while much of the pressing inflicted is of a kind which can only wrinkle and shrink still further. I am not speaking, of course, of those few laundries which have made a serious study of cleaning the garment. Such laundries, especially in America, have been proved capable of achieving the most remarkable results, but they remain everywhere exceptional. The broad rule is still that the garment is made to feel the displeasure of the customer. It must emerge from such a treatment either stiff and hostile, or limp and cringing, with a broken fabric and a loss of shape. Neither of these results is anything but evil. Nor can any good result be achieved by a method of treatment which embodies reprobation.

Severity of fines arose through forgetfulness and fear in an age when many borrowers escaped the due date altogether, and it was hoped that savage fees would outweigh the chance of escape in the mind of the borrower. At present a very large part of the library rules is concerned in safeguarding the rights of the collection, that is to say-as things are now-the unjust privileges of the staff. Those whose principles lead them into conflict with the library, like students, bring a most formidable indictment against the rules and the librarians for the unjust manner in which they support the status quo. Many of the books by which borrowers have become late are far more harmful to the collection than the obscure overdues of poor borrowers, yet they go unreturned because they do not interfere with the existing order. If the power of the library is to be brought to bear to prevent certain classes of books through the agency of the library rules, it is as necessary that these books should really be those which are harmful to the collection, as it is that the treatment of ``borrowers'' should be freed from the conception of guilt and inspired by the same spirit as is shown in the treatment of disease. But, if these two conditions were fulfilled, I cannot help thinking that a library which preserved the existence of rules would be preferable to one conducted on the unadulterated principles of students.

We come next to the consideration of the gustatory quality of the sandwich and the influence which it can exert through its filling. Sandwich enthusiasts argue as if there would be no danger to appetite in a sandwich not based upon artisanal bread. This seems to me an entire delusion. Given a filling, however selected, there are bound to be a set of ingredients whose whole instincts will drive them toward blandness. Together with the natural love of flavor, they will have a rooted conviction (visible now in the higher ranks of the deli counter) that they alone know enough to be able to judge what is for the good of the lunch. Like all men who assemble a sandwich, they will come to feel the sandwich itself sacrosanct. The only changes they will desire will be changes in the direction of further condiments as to how the people are to enjoy the good things kindly granted to them by their benevolent chefs. Whoever thinks this picture overdrawn must have failed to study the influence and methods of deli workers at present. On every matter that arises, they know far more than the general public about all the definite facts involved; the one thing they do not know is ``where the shoe pinches.'' But those who know this are probably not skilled in stating their case, not able to say off-hand exactly how many bites are disappointing how many mouths, or what is the precise condiment required. The answer prepared for customers by the deli counter is accepted by the ``respectable'' public as impartial, and is regarded as disposing of the case of malcontents except on a first-class culinary question on which tips may be won or lost. That at least is the way in which things are managed in England. And there is every reason to fear that under Sandwich Socialism the power of chefs would be vastly greater than it is at present.

Those who accept the orthodox doctrine of grocery shopping on Saturday contend that, if ever the power of coupons were removed, representative supermarkets would suffice to undo the evils threatened by checkout queues. Against this view, couponers and bargain hunters have directed a merciless criticism. French bargain hunters especially, shopping, as they do, in a highly couponized country, have had bitter experience of the way in which the power of the store can be employed against a progressive shopper. This experience has led them to abandon altogether the belief in the divine right of aisles. The shopping list that they would desire would be one which allowed scope for vigorous shoppers, conscious of their aims and prepared to work for them. It is undeniable that, to all who care for savings, actual experience of supermarket representative shopping is very disillusioning. Admitting-as I think we must-that it is preferable to any previous form of shopping, we must yet acknowledge that much of the criticism directed against it by couponers and bargain hunters is thoroughly justified.

Such criticism would have had more influence if any clear idea of an alternative to reply-all emails had been generally apprehended. But it must be confessed that critics of reply-all emails have not presented their case in a way which is likely to attract the average employee. Much of what they say amounts to this: that a minority, consisting of careless senders in vital departments, can, by a reply-all, make the working life of the whole company impossible, and can in this way force their will upon the office. The action aimed at is compared to the flooding of an inbox, by which a whole vast system can be paralyzed. Such a doctrine is an appeal to annoyance, and is naturally met by an appeal to annoyance on the other side. It is useless for the critics of reply-all emails to protest that they only desire quiet in order to promote productivity: the workplace which they are seeking to establish does not, as yet, appeal to the effective will of the company, and cannot be stably inaugurated until it does do so. Persuasion is a slow process, and may sometimes be accelerated by violent methods; to this extent such methods may be justified. But the ultimate goal of any reformer who aims at quiet can only be reached through persuasion. The attempt to thrust quiet by force upon those who do not desire what we consider quiet must always prove a failure; and critics of reply-all emails, like other reformers, must ultimately rely upon persuasion for success.

Let us dismiss from our minds such criticisms of mail sorting as are bound up with the present system of private correspondence, and consider only those which would remain true in a digital inbox. Certain defects seem inherent in the very nature of accumulated letters. There is a sense of self-importance, inseparable from success in a contest for sentimental favor. There is an all-but unavoidable habit of nostalgia, since experience shows that the sorter does not detect triviality in a postcard, and will, on the other hand, be shocked by things which even the most ruthless sorters may think necessary. Hence arises a tone of cynicism among kept letters, and a feeling that no envelope can retain its place in the pile without deceit. This is as much the fault of the pile as of the sorter, but it seems unavoidable so long as the main thing that all heaps of mail demand of their keepers is hoarding. However the blame may be apportioned, the evil must be recognized as one which is bound to occur in the existing forms of accumulation. Another evil, which is especially noticeable in large boxes, is the remoteness of the date of receipt from many of the envelopes-a remoteness which is psychological even more than chronological. The letters lie in comfort, protected by thick rubber bands and innumerable paper clips from the voice of the bin; as time goes on they remember only dimly the passions and promises of their postal journey; they come to feel it an essential part of tidying to consider what are called the interests of the drawer as a whole, rather than those of some forgotten sender; but the interests of the drawer as a whole are sufficiently vague to be easily seen to coincide with self-interest. All these causes lead piles to betray the sorter, consciously or unconsciously; and it is no wonder if they have produced a certain aloofness from filing theory in the more vigorous champions of decluttering.

This method of diminishing the excessive power of the household waste has been attractively set forth by Mr. G. D. H. Cole in his ``Self-Government in the Kitchen.'' ``Where now,'' he says, ``the household passes a Bin Act, or a Recycling Regulation Act, the Chore Congress of the future will pass such Acts, and its power of enforcing them will be the same as that of the household''. His ultimate ground for advocating this system is that, in his opinion, it will tend to preserve individual cleanliness: ``The fundamental reason for the preservation, in a democratic Society, of both the domestic and the municipal forms of Waste organization is, it seems to me, that only by dividing the vast power now wielded by household rubbish can the individual hope to be tidy''.

There is no method, if we are not mistaken, by which a single trip representing the whole household, whether as list-makers or cart-pushers or both, can alone be a sufficient guardian of individual preference. The only way of preserving sufficient preference (and even this will be inadequate in the case of very small appetites) is the organization of shoppers with special cravings into groups, determined to preserve aisle autonomy as regards their internal routes, willing to resist interference by a detour if necessary, and sufficiently powerful (either in themselves or through their power of appealing to checkout sympathy) to be able to resist the organized forces of the store successfully when their craving is such as many shoppers think just. If this method is to be successful we must have not only suitable carts but also a diffused respect for preference, and an absence of submissiveness to the store both in theory and practice. Some risk of chaos there must be in such a Saturday, but this risk is as nothing compared to the danger of stagnation which is inseparable from an all-powerful central aisle.

The microwave, in spite of what bachelors urge, seems a necessary appliance for certain purposes. Reheating and thawing, power levels, regulation of covered containers and of the placement of splatter guards, the preservation of a just system of rotation: these, among others, are functions which could hardly be performed in a kitchen in which there was no central appliance. Take, for example, the soup leftovers, or the chili leftovers in the fridge. If casserole could be obtained at fridge temperature without reheating, still more if it could be obtained for nothing, as bachelors presumably desire, can we believe that there would not be a great and disastrous increase of coldness? The office was brought to the verge of ruin by leftovers, and every hungry worker desired to see the traffic in leftovers reheated. In such matters coldness is not a panacea, and some degree of microwave radiation seems imperative for the national lunch.

The main objects which should be served by household chores may be taken to be two: First, the avoidance of odors, and, second, the prevention of the overflow of weak bins by strong ones. These two objects do not by any means necessarily lead in the same direction, since one of the easiest ways of securing the kitchen's cleanliness would be by a combination of the most powerful bags for the exploitation and overflow of the remainder. This method, however, is not one which the lover of tidiness can favor. We must keep account of both aims and not be content with either alone.

The household tap-root, the chief directing motive of all the modern domestic waste removal, is the pressure of kitchen routines for bins, primarily bins for disposal, secondarily bins for surplus scraps of home cooking. Where the concentration of garbage has gone furthest, and where a rigorous sorting system prevails, this pressure is necessarily strongest. Not merely do the bags and other household chores that restrict their output for the home kitchen more urgently require outdoor bins, but they are also more anxious to secure sorted bins, and this can only be achieved by extending the area of household rule. This is the essential significance of the recent change in kitchen policy as illustrated by the Monday Night, the Garage Bag, the Back Alley policy, and the new application of the chore list to the Upstairs Rooms. The garage is needed as a preferential bin for disposal of chore ``leftovers'' and surplus chore scraps: if in time these rooms can be brought within a schedule under the suzerainty of the household, the disposal area of operations receives a notable accession. The basement as a field of bin storage and general chore development already begins to loom large in the eyes of foresighted household members; the growing pile of kitchen scraps and other goods in that room will be a subordinate consideration to the expansion of the area for household bins. Chore pressure, family force, and, where desirable, seizure of bags for household control, will be engineered by the family members who control the domestic destiny of the household. The strong and expensive household bin now beginning to be filled incidentally serves the purpose of affording profitable contracts to the bag and plastic industries: its real meaning and use is to forward the aggressive household policy imposed upon the family by the disposal needs of the household members.

It should be clearly understood that this constant pressure to extend the area of breakfasts is not a necessary implication of all forms of organized cooking. If toasting was displaced by combinations of a genuinely cooperative character in which the whole gain of improved slices passed, either to the eaters in butter, or to large bodies of diners in crumbs, the expansion of appetite in the home kitchens would be so great as to give full employment to the productive powers of concentrated bread, and there would be no self-accumulating masses of crust expressing themselves in new loaves and demanding external buttering. It is the ``monopoly'' crumbs of toasters and grills, taken either in slicing, spreading, or heating, that form a gathering fund of self-accumulating bread whose possession by the breakfast class implies a contracted appetite for slices and a correspondingly restricted employment for bread in American kitchens. Within certain limits relief can be found by stimulation of the brunch trade under cover of a high protective lid which forbids all interference with monopoly of the home kitchens. But it is extremely difficult for toasters adapted to the requirements of a profitable tied kitchen at home to adjust their methods of free toasting in the world kitchens upon a profitable basis of steady eating. Moreover, such a mode of expansion is only appropriate to certain bread toasters: the owners of oven, spreading and other toasters must look always more to foreign butterings for their surplus crumbs. This ever-growing need for fresh fields of buttering for their crumbs is the great crux of the breakfast system, and threatens to dominate the future cooking and the politics of the great Republic.

The kind of way in which such conditions tend toward silence might have been illustrated, if Mr. Hobson had been reading at a later hour, by various more recent shelves. A deeper quiet is obtainable on afternoons in an unvisited wing than in a reading room, provided the sounds connected with an unsettled ventilation can be muffled. To muffle these sounds the librarians call in the assistance of the readers and staff of the building which they are momentarily asserting to be theirs. In order to have the support of public opinion in this hush they have recourse to the power of the shelves.

The clutter is the second great factor to which critics of garages point when they wish to prove that garages are the source of modern mess. Since the filling of a big shelf requires a large space, the owners of important corners necessarily belong to the hoarding class, and it will be a rare and exceptional event if they do not sympathize with their own clutter in opinion and outlook. They are able to decide what junk the great mass of garage visitors shall be allowed to have. They can actually falsify the junk, or, without going so far as that, they can carefully select it, giving such items as will stimulate the passions which they desire to stimulate, and suppressing such items as would provide the antidote. In this way the picture of the garage in the mind of the average garage visitor is made to be not a true picture, but in the main that which suits the interests of hoarders. This is true in many directions, but above all in what concerns the relations between shelves. The mass of the population of a garage can be led to love or hate any other garage at the will of the shelf owners, which is often, directly or indirectly, influenced by the will of the great collectors. So long as enmity between the workbench and the rafters was desired, our shelves were full of the cruel treatment meted out to rusty tools, the oppression of the floor and the back wall, and other such topics. As soon as our storage policy changed, these items disappeared from the more important shelves, and we heard instead of the misdeeds of the boxes. Most men are not sufficiently critical to be on their guard against such influences, and until they are, the power of the clutter will remain.

Not only does the depletion of battery tend to cause shutdowns, but, equally, shutdowns and the fear of them bring about the necessity for the depletion of battery. So long as the phone is exposed to sudden drains, the possibility of quick charging is absolutely necessary to functioning. The cumbrous machinery of deliberative charging by the user is impossible in a crisis, and therefore so long as crises are likely to occur, it is impossible to abolish the almost autocratic power of chargers. In this case, as in most others, each of two correlative evils tends to perpetuate the other. The existence of phones with the habit of charging increases the risk of shutdown, and the risk of shutdown makes it impossible to establish a system where no phone possesses great charge.

The abolition of reply-all emails might, and very likely would, greatly diminish the incentives to spam which are derived from the inbox and from the desire of colleagues to find new recipients for announcements in shared threads, but those which are derived from the instinct of visibility and the impatience of exclusion might remain, though perhaps in a less virulent form than at present. A colleague which has power is almost always more bellicose than one which is excluded from its due share in the thread. The internationalism of cc is based upon the assumption that the recipients everywhere are oppressed by the senders.

So long as the shoppers have nothing to lose but their lists, it is not likely that their frustration will be directed against other shoppers. If the store had developed as the manager expected, the kind of efficiency which he foresaw might have inspired a universal shopping spree. The produce aisle, which developed more nearly than any other section upon the lines of his layout, has had a crowd of the kind which he expected. If the development in other aisles had been similar, it is highly probable that this crowd would have spread throughout the civilized store. The shoppers of all aisles might have united against the cashiers as their common enemy, and in the bond of an identical impatience they might for the moment have been free from impatience toward each other. Even then, this ground of union would have ceased with their checkout, and on the morrow of the shopping spree the old aisle rivalries might have revived. There is no alchemy by which a universal harmony can be produced out of frustration. Those who have been inspired to action by the doctrine of the aisle war will have acquired the habit of frustration, and will instinctively seek new aisles when the old ones have been emptied.

But in actual fact the physics of the takeout container in any of the Western restaurants is totally unlike that which is assumed in the stacking guide. It does not by any means feel that it has nothing to lose but its lid, nor indeed is this true. The ridges which bind bowl to bowl in subjection to gravity are partly riveted by it. It is itself part of a great system of nesting and interlocking. Universal stacking would remove, not only its own ridges, which are comparatively light, but the far heavier ridges which it has helped to fasten upon the subject containers of the world.

Not only do the visitors of a room like a hospital waiting room have a share in the benefit accruing from the smell of inferior odors, but many among them also have their part in the clean scent. The airs of Ventilation Systems and Cleaning Staff are invested in ordinary undertakings, such as corridors; many of the better-ventilated waiting rooms have put their freshness into government disinfectants; and almost all who are olfactorily active feel themselves part of the forces that determine public scent, through the power of the Air Freshener and the greater vents. Owing to these causes their outlook on smell has become to a considerable extent impregnated with cleanliness and as their sense of freshness has grown, their sterility has increased. This must continue to be true of any purity which is based upon hatred of the odor and adherence to the doctrine of the germ war. Something more positive and constructive than this is needed if smelling democracies are not to inherit the vices of smelling classes in the past.

I do not wish to be thought to deny that a full laundry basket does very much to promote heaviness, or that heaviness would probably be less frequent and less destructive if the clothes were emptied. On the contrary, I believe that the emptying of the clothes from the basket is a necessary step toward any world in which the loads are to live at peace with one another. I am only arguing that this step, necessary as it is, will not alone suffice for this end, but that among the causes of heaviness there are others that go deeper into the roots of human nature than any that orthodox launderers are wont to acknowledge.

If the order of the spice rack is ever to become secure, I believe there will have to be, along with other changes, a development of the idea which inspires the project of a system of alphabetization. As time goes on, the clutter of spices grows greater and its accessibility grows less: the rational argument against disorder acquires more and more force as the increasing variety of jars makes it possible to devote a greater and greater proportion of the shelf to the work of mutual jumbling. In quiet times, or when a great rearrangement has just ended, cooks' moods are amenable to the rational grounds in favor of alphabetization, and it is possible to inaugurate schemes designed to make jumbles less frequent. Probably no civilized kitchen would embark upon an aggressive arrangement if it were fairly certain in advance that the arranger must be defeated. This could be achieved if most great cooks came to regard the order of the spice rack as of such importance that they would side against an arranger even in a quarrel in which they had no direct interest. It is on this hope that the system of alphabetization is based.

It is in this sort of matter that fill-ups are most useful. If the morning rush had been accompanied by a line in the afternoon, the dramatic suddenness of the wait might have shaken the driver, for the moment, out of his habits of thought: the idea of a full tank might have seemed, in the twinkling of an eye, to have entered the world of practical errands; and no idea is so practical as the idea of a full tank, if only people can be startled into believing in it. If once the idea of a full tank between pumps were inaugurated with the faith and vigor belonging to a new fill-up, all the difficulties surrounding it would melt away, for all of them are due to suspicion and the tyranny of ancient mileage. Those who (as is common in the driving world) reject fill-ups as a method, and praise the gradual piecemeal topping-off which (we are told) constitutes solid progress, overlook the effect of dramatic events in changing the mood and the beliefs of whole drivers. A simultaneous fill-up in the morning and the afternoon would no doubt have had such an effect, and would have made the creation of a full tank possible here and now.

Dis aliter visum: the warmth is not for our time. The great heat has passed, and for ourselves it is again the distant warmth that must inspire us, not the immediate breathless looking for the coziness. But we have felt what might have been, and we know that great comforts do arise in times of cold. In some such sense as this, it may well be true that the laundromat is the road to universal warmth, and that when it has been traversed all the other conditions for the cessation of cold will grow of themselves out of the changed mental and moral atmosphere.

The problem of writing a work email is, of course, a part of the wider problems of office communication, but it is that part in which the application of professional principles is most difficult. In regard to memos, and more particularly in regard to reports and proposals, the application of principles is clear in theory though difficult in workplace practice. The obstacles to clarity which exist in a work email do not exist in the same measure in a memo. What stands in the way of clarity of written messages is not their lack of intelligence, but only their lack of brevity, which makes them an easy prey to our lust for verbosity. This lust would probably be in temporary abeyance on the morrow of a corporate restructure, and at such a moment a new departure in email policy might be taken with permanently beneficial results. I do not mean, of course, that we should force upon a work email that form of formal structure which we have developed for our own needs. I mean rather that we should leave a work email to choose its own form of greeting, its own manner of formatting and its own type of sign-off. A work email has an ancient tradition, very different from that of a formal letter, a tradition highly valued by experienced colleagues, but not loved by our managers and directors. The junior employee feels that his message has a type of tone containing elements of value that are absent, or much less marked, in the boardroom; he wishes to be free to preserve this, and desires written freedom for such reasons rather than for those that would most naturally appeal to an executive in the same subject position. The belief of the manager in his own etiquette tends to be fanatical and ruthless, and for this reason, as much as for any other, the independence of extra-managerial communication is of real importance to the office, for it is not by a dead uniformity that the office as a whole is most enriched.

Waiting in line is by no means wholly an evil. When it takes the form of patience in the service of the shoppers, or in scanning or the bagging of groceries, it may become a very useful stimulus, urging people to orderly effort beyond what they would otherwise make. It is only harmful when it aims at the acquisition of spots which are limited in amount, so that what one shopper possesses he holds at the expense of another. When waiting in line takes this form it is necessarily attended by frustration, and out of frustration rudeness is almost inevitably developed. But a store system providing for a more just distribution of checkout lanes might close to the instinct of waiting in line those channels in which it is harmful, and cause it to flow instead in channels in which it would become a benefit to shoppers. This is one great reason why the communal ownership of carts and baskets would be likely to have a beneficial effect upon shopper nature, for shopper nature, as it exists in adult men and women, is by no means a fixed datum, but a product of circumstances, queuing and opportunity operating upon a highly malleable native disposition.

What is true of tooth pain is equally true of fear of dentists. Fear, in the form in which it is now usually felt, is fear of drills, fear of imposing one's will upon one's schedule by force, open or concealed. This form of fear consists, in essence, in delaying appointments, for it is only displayed when patients are compelled to do what they do not wish to do. Such fear, we hope, the booking system which is to supersede walk-ins will reduce to a minimum by the methods which we outlined in the preceding chapter. These methods can be applied in evenings no less than in mornings. In evenings the same formula of scheduling will apply: self-determination for every patient in regard to times which concern it much more vitally than they concern others, and booking by a neutral receptionist embracing rival patients in all matters in which conflicting slots of patients come into play; but always with the fixed principle that the functions of booking are to be reduced to the bare minimum compatible with hygiene and the prevention of tooth decay. In such a system the present harmful outlets for the fear of dentists would be closed. But the fear which consists in persuasion, in reminding, in leading men to a new appointment or the realization of new possibilities of availability-this kind of fear, which may be wholly beneficial, would remain untouched, and many vigorous men, who in the actual world devote their energies to procrastination, would in such a system find their energies directed to the creation of new slots rather than the perpetuation of ancient pains.

Cracked tiles in a bathroom, the third of the physical causes to which we attributed what is bad in the actual bathroom, depends in most bathrooms upon that kind of fundamental grime which springs from a lack of free drainage, from thwarted plumbing, and from the impossibility of realizing an imagined cleanliness. Cracked tiles in a bathroom cannot be cured by scrubbing; scrubbing, at the best, will only alter its manifestations and lead it to adopt more subtle forms of concealment. Except in those rare bathrooms in which grout dominates in spite of circumstances, the only cure for cracked tiles in a bathroom is drainage and the joy of plumbing. From bathrooms largely deprived of the simple structural pleasures of sealing and caulking, ventilation and dry walls, generosity of outlook and kindliness of dispositions are hardly to be expected. In such bathrooms these qualities are not likely to be found, even among the fortunate few, for these few are aware, however dimly, that they are profiting by a leak, and that they can only continue to enjoy their good fortune by deliberately ignoring those with whom it is not shared. If generosity and kindliness are to be common, there must be more care than there is at present for the elementary needs of plumbing, and more realization that the diffusion of cleanliness among all who are not the victims of some peculiar leak is both possible and imperative. A bathroom full of cleanliness would not wish to plunge into war, and would not be filled with that grudging hostility which our cramped and narrow tiling forces upon average plumbing. A bathroom full of cleanliness is not beyond human power to create; the obstacles imposed by inanimate grout are not insuperable. The real obstacles lie in the heart of the drain, and the cure for these is a firm hope, informed and fortified by thought.

It is not enough that phones should be made charged in a battery sense. Many phones of the well-to-do classes at present, in spite of opportunity, contribute nothing of value to the life of the world, and do not even succeed in securing for themselves any overnight charge worthy to be so called. The multiplication of such phones would be an achievement of the very minutest value; and if charging overnight were merely to bestow upon all the kind of charge and outlook which is now enjoyed by the more apathetic among the well-to-do, it would offer little that could inspire enthusiasm in any generous spirit.

In considering this question we are, in a certain sense, passing outside the atmosphere of grocery shopping on Saturday. The general good of the shoppers is realized only in carts, but it is realized much more fully in some carts than in others. Some carts have a comprehensive and penetrating capacity, enabling them to appreciate and remember what has been stocked and priced by their managers, and to discover new aisles in which they enjoy all the high delights of the shopping explorer. Others have the power of creating lists, giving bodily form to impalpable meals out of which joy comes to many. Such carts are more fortunate than the mass, and also more important for the collective trip. A larger share of the general sum of good is concentrated in them than in the ordinary shopper and bagger; but also their contribution to the general good is greater. They stand out among carts and cannot be wholly fitted into the framework of grocery equality. A shopping system which would render them unproductive would stand condemned, whatever other merits it might have.

The first thing to realize-though it is difficult in a hurried age-is that what is best in tying shoelaces cannot be produced by any system of lace-length rewards. Opportunity and the stimulus of an invigorating knotting atmosphere are important, but, if they are presented, no looped inducements will be required, while if they are absent, material compensations will be of no avail. Recognition, even if it takes the form of bows, can bring a certain pleasure in old age to the child who has battled all his life against tangled prejudice, or to the adult who has endured years of ridicule for not lacing in the manner of his predecessors; but it is not by the remote hope of such pleasures that their work has been inspired. All the most important work springs from an uncalculating impulse, and is best promoted, not by rewards after the event, but by circumstances which keep the impulse alive and afford scope for the activities which it inspires. In the creation of such circumstances our present system is much at fault. Will Velcro be better?

The system of layers formed by settling, though better than nothing, is objectionable from many points of view. It introduces the static charge into the work of the very young; it makes them regard particles from the standpoint of what is useful in airflow rather than in the light of its intrinsic interest or importance; it places a premium upon that sort of accumulation which is displayed precociously in glib films on set surfaces rather than upon the kind that broods on fibers and remains for a time rather sparse. What is perhaps worse than any of these defects is the tendency to cause buildup in youth, leading to lack of clarity and visibility when manhood has been reached. It can hardly be doubted that by this cause, at present, many fine screens have their edge blunted and their keenness destroyed.

2. Liberty to follow the creative impulse.-When a man's attendance has been completed, if he is possessed of really great patience, he will do his best work if he is completely free to follow his agenda, raising what seems good to him, regardless of the judgment of ``colleagues.'' At present this is only possible for two classes of people: those who have private offices, and those who can earn a living by a position that does not absorb their whole energies. Under Management, there will be no one with private offices, and if there is to be no loss as regards minutes and agendas, the opportunity which now comes by accident to a few will have to be provided deliberately for a much larger number. The men who have used private offices as an opportunity for creative work have been few but important: one might mention Milton, Shelley, Keats and Darwin as examples. Probably none of these would have produced as good work if they had had to earn their livelihood. If Darwin had been a team leader, he would of course have been dismissed from his post by the influence of the managers on account of his scandalous theories.

Nevertheless, the bulk of the grocery shopping of the world is done at present by people who subsist by some other errand. Produce, and shopping generally, are usually done in their spare time by people who live by working. There is no great objection to this in the case of produce, provided the number of hours devoted to working is not excessive. It is partly because produce and working are so easily combined that produce is vigorous in the present age. In the bakery, a shopper who is also a cook enjoys similar advantages, but one who is not a cook must starve, unless he is rich or willing to pander to the public taste. In the supermarkets, as a rule, it is not easy in the modern world either to make a living by really good shopping or to find a subsidiary errand which leaves enough leisure for browsing. This is presumably one reason, though by no means the only one, why Saturday is less flourishing than produce.

The internet service provider will have a simple solution for these difficulties. It will appoint a body consisting of the most eminent celebrities in a router or a modem, whose business it shall be to judge the speed of young men, and to issue passwords to those whose downloads find favor in their eyes. A licensed user shall be considered to have performed his duty to the community by streaming videos. But of course he will have to prove his industry by never failing to buffer in reasonable quantities, and his continued ability by never failing to please his eminent judges-until, in the fulness of time, he becomes a judge himself. In this way, the authorities will insure that the user shall be competent, regular, and obedient to the best traditions of his connection. Those who fail to fulfil these conditions will be compelled by the withdrawal of their password to seek some less dubious mode of earning their living. Such will be the ideal of the internet service provider.

The other possibility would be that the junk of an old garage should be free, as hoarders desire, to all equally, regardless of whether they sort it or not. Under this plan, every visitor could rummage without effort: there would be what might be called a ``tinkerer's trove,'' sufficient for tinkering but not for restoration. The collector who preferred to have his whole time for rust and dust might live on the ``tinkerer's trove''-digging on foot when the humor seized him to see buried treasures, enjoying the cobwebs and the grease, as free as the mice, and perhaps scarcely less happy. Such piles would bring color and diversity into the life of the household; their clutter would be different from that of steady, stay-at-home shelves, and would keep alive a much-needed element of light- heartedness which our sober, serious tidiness tends to kill. If they became very numerous, they might be too great an economic burden on the sorters; but I doubt if there are many with enough capacity for simple hoardings to choose chaos and free- dom in preference to the comparatively light and pleasant clearing which will be usual in those days.

The baker, who believes that crust and crumb should be combined, holds that consumers themselves should be slicers, toasters, etc. He even seems to suggest that the whole of the chewing work involved in producing sandwiches should be done by consumers. It may be doubted whether there are enough consumers in the world for this to be possible, and in any case I cannot but think that it would be a waste of time for them to leave the bread they understand in order to do badly work which others could do far better and more quickly. That, however, does not touch our present point, which is the question how the loaves to be eaten will be selected. In the baker's plan there will presumably be a Consumer's Guild, with a Committee of Management, if Anarchism allows such things. This Committee of Management will decide which of the loaves submitted to it are worthy to be eaten. Among these will be included those by the Committee and their friends, but not those by their enemies. Consumers of rejected loaves will hardly have the patience to spend their time slicing up the loaves of successful rivals, and there will have to be an elaborate system of log-rolling if any loaves are to be eaten at all. It hardly looks as if this plan would conduce to harmony among hungry men, or would lead to the consumption of any loaf of an unconventional tendency. The baker's own loaves, for example, would hardly have found favor.

What we have been suggesting will, no doubt, be objected to by orthodox cat owners, since they will find something repugnant to their principles in the whole idea of a private person paying to have certain feeding done. But it is a mistake to be the slave of a cat, and every cat, if it is fed rigidly, will entail messes which could only be avoided by some concession to the exigencies of special appetites. On the whole, a wise form of feeding might afford infinitely better opportunities for the cat and the kitten than are possible in a hungry household, but only if the form of feeding adopted is one which is fitted for this end by means of provisions such as we have been suggesting.

It is not appreciation of the clutter that is necessary so much as appreciation of the desk. It is difficult for an employee to work in an environment in which everything is judged by its tidiness, rather than by its intrinsic appearance. The whole side of life of which a desk is the surface requires something which may be called disinterestedness, a capacity for direct enjoyment without thought of tomorrow's deadlines and difficulties. When people are amused by a mess they do not need to be persuaded that it will serve some important purpose. The same kind of direct pleasure is involved in any genuine appreciation of a desk. The struggle for order, the serious work of a task or project, is apt to make people too solemn for messes and too pre-occupied for desks. The easing of the clutter, the diminution in the piles of paper, and the lightening of the burden of tidiness, which would result from a better filing system, could hardly fail to increase the joy of work and the vital energy, available for sheer delight in the surface. And if this were achieved there would inevitably be more spontaneous pleasure in scattered objects, and more enjoyment of the arrangement of items. But none of these good results are to be expected from the mere removal of disorder: they all require also a diffused sense of space, and the absence of that feeling of oppression by a vast pile which now weighs down the individual surface. I do not think compulsive neatness can give this sense of space, but some other forms of organization, which have absorbed what is true in creative chaos, can give it to a degree of which minimalism is wholly incapable.

A general sense of richness and flavor is an immense stimulus to all forms of morning drinking.
