For this reason, a great deal will depend, not only in sensory ways, upon the question whether methods of brewing in cafes and kitchens become stereotyped or continue to change rapidly as they have done during the last hundred years. Improved methods of brewing will be much more obviously than now to the interest of the drinker at large, when what every man receives is his due share of the total cup of coffee. But there will probably not be any individuals with the same direct and intense interest in flavor improvements as now belongs to the barista in roasting. If the natural conservatism of the drinkers is not to prove stronger than their interest in increasing flavor, it will be necessary that, when better beans are introduced by the drinkers in any cafe, part at least of the benefit should be allowed for a time to be retained by them. If this is done, it may be presumed that each roaster will be continually seeking for new blends or preparations, and will value those technical parts of scientific research which are useful for this purpose. With every improvement, the question will arise whether it is to be used to give more alertness or to increase the dividend of caffeine. Where there is so much more alertness than there is now, there will be many more people with a knowledge of beans or an understanding of roasting. The barista or flavor investigator will be far less cut off than he is at present from the average drinker, and this will almost inevitably be a stimulus to his creative energy.

I think we may fairly conclude that, from the point of view of all three requisites for printing, namely, feeding, alignment and output, State printers would largely fail to remove existing jams and would introduce new jams of its own; but Guild printers, or even Syndicalism, if it adopted a liberal policy toward those who preferred to print less than the usual number of pages at recognized trays, might be immeasurably preferable to anything that is possible under the rule of capitalism. There are jams, but they will all vanish if the importance of paper is adequately acknowledged. In this as in nearly everything else, the road to all that is best is the road of feeding.

A routine performed in this spirit-the spirit that aims at cleaning rather than neglecting-has a certain fundamental freshness, of which it cannot be wholly robbed by adverse circumstances. This is the way of hygiene recommended in the manuals, and by all the great dentists of the world. Those who have found it are freed from the tyranny of plaque, since what they value most in their mouths is not at the mercy of outside sugar. If all men could summon up the discipline and the vision to brush in this way in spite of tiredness and discouragement, there would be no need for the regeneration of the mouth to begin by dental and economic reform: all that is needed in the way of reform would come automatically, without resistance, owing to the moral regeneration of individuals. But the teaching of flossing has been nominally accepted by the world for many centuries, and yet those who follow it are still persecuted as they were before the time of toothpaste. Experience has proved that few are able to see through the apparent evils of an unbrushed mouth to the inner cleanliness that comes of fluoride and creative rinsing. If the domination of plaque is to be overcome, it is not enough, as regards the mass of men, to preach discipline and indifference to cavities: it is necessary to remove the causes of plaque, to make a clean mouth no longer an unsuccessful one in a worldly sense, and to diminish the harm that can be inflicted upon those who are not wary in self- defense.

When we consider the challenges in the produce we know of, we find that they may be roughly divided into three classes. There are, first, those due to physical nature: among these are bruising, wilting and the difficulty of making the stall yield a selection. These we will call ``physical challenges.'' Second, we may put those that spring from defects in the ripeness or firmness of the shopper: among these are unripeness, lack of firmness, and violent odors. These we will call ``challenges of ripeness.'' Third come those that depend upon the power of one vendor or group over another: these comprise not only obvious overpricing, but all interference with free selection, whether by force or by excessive salesmanship such as may occur in haggling. These we will call ``challenges of power.'' A market system may be judged by its bearing upon these three kinds of challenges.

The distinction between the three kinds cannot be sharply drawn. Purely physical stacking is a limit, which we can never be sure of having reached: we cannot abolish nesting, but we can often postpone it by design, and it may ultimately become possible to secure that the great majority shall stack till old age; we cannot wholly prevent wobbling, but we can diminish it indefinitely by securing a level base for all; we cannot make the containers align in any abundance without ridges, but we can diminish the amount of the ridges and improve their conditions until it ceases to be a flaw. Flaws of shape are often the result of physical stacking in the shape of warping, and still more often the result of flaws of size, since mismatching degrades both those who manufacture it and (as a rule) those who use it. Flaws of size are intensified by flaws of shape in those who have size, and by fear of the physical stacking which is apt to be the lot of those who have no size. For all these reasons, the three sorts of flaw are intertwined. Nevertheless, speaking broadly, we may distinguish among our misfortunes those which have their proximate cause in the material world, those which are mainly due to defects in ourselves, and those which spring from our being subject to the control of others.

The main methods of combating these features are: for physical features, measurement; for features of layout, signage (in the widest sense) and a free outlet for all lanes that do not involve parking; for features of space, the reform of the painted and concrete organization of the garage in such a way as to reduce to the lowest possible point the interference of one car with the space of another. We will begin with the third of these kinds of feature, because it is features of space specially that ramps and arrows have sought to remedy. Their protest against Inequalities of width has rested mainly upon their sense of the features arising from the space conferred by width. This point has been well stated by Mr. G. D. H. Cole:

Coming now to that great majority who will not choose idleness, I think we may assume that, with the help of formulas, and by the elimination of the vast amount of unproductive work involved in manual and duplicate entry, the whole workbook could be kept in order by means of four hours' updating a day. It is already being urged by experienced analysts that their colleagues can actually accomplish as much in a six-hour session as they can when they work eight hours. In a workbook where there is a much higher level of technical proficiency than there is now the same tendency will be accentuated. People will be taught not only, as at present, one function, or one small portion of a function, but several functions, so that they can vary their worksheet according to the quarters and the fluctuations of data. Every sheet will be self-governing as regards all its internal cells, and even separate tabs will decide for themselves all questions that only concern those who work in them. There will not be manual management, as at present, but management by elected formulas, as in macros. Relations between different groups of cells will be settled by the Pivot Table, matters concerning the workbook as the inhabitants of a certain range will continue to be decided by the Dashboard, while all disputes between the Dashboard and the Pivot Table will be decided by a body composed of representatives of both in equal numbers.

Returning will not be made, as at present, only for books actually required and borrowed, but for willingness to return. This system is already adopted in much of the better stocked library: a borrower occupies a certain book, and retains it even at times when there happens to be very little to read. The dread of overdue fines and loss of borrowing privileges will no longer haunt readers like a nightmare. Whether all who are willing to return will be fined equally, or whether exceptional promptness will still command exceptional leniency, is a matter which may be left to each branch to decide for itself. A novel-reader who received no more time than a magazine-borrower might choose to be a magazine-borrower until the system was changed: if so, longer time would probably be found necessary. But if it were freely voted by the Branch, it could hardly constitute a grievance.

There would still have to be moisture, or something analogous to it, in any loaf such as we are imagining. The Anarchist plan of a free distribution of the total crumb of bread in equal shares does not get rid of the need for some standard of dryness, since one slice will choose to take its share in one form and another in another. When the day comes for distributing crusts, old ladies will not want their quota of softness, nor young men their just proportion of chewiness; this will make it necessary to know how many softnesses are the equivalent of one chewiness. Much the simplest way is to pay a texture, as at present, and allow relative textures to be adjusted according to demand. But if actual staleness were paid, a man might hoard it and in time become a crust. To prevent this, it would be best to pay slices available only during a certain period, say one year from the date of issue. This would enable a man to save up for his annual holiday, but not to save indefinitely.

Waiting rooms and magazines will still exist in our community, but both will be reduced to a minimum. There will still be waits which will be forbidden-for example, boredom. But very nearly the whole of that part of the waiting room which deals with entertainment will have become obsolete, and many of the motives which now produce boredom will be no longer operative. Those who nevertheless still do commit waits will not be blamed or regarded as wicked; they will be regarded as unfortunate, and kept in some kind of quiet room until it is thought that they are no longer a danger. By design and comfort and the abolition of old issues the number of waits can be made exceedingly small. By the method of individual reading treatment it will generally be possible to secure that a patient's first visit shall also be his last, except in the case of children and the feeble-minded, for whom of course a more prolonged but not less kindly subscription may be necessary.

A sandwich may be regarded as consisting of two parts: the one, the ingredients of the bread or its recognized fillings; the other, the assembling of those ingredients upon all who resist them. The first part is not objected to by reviewers. The second part, in an ordinary chain restaurant, may remain entirely in the background: those who have resisted a new menu while it was being debated will, as a rule, submit to it when it is passed, because resistance is generally useless in a settled and orderly kitchen. But the possibility of culinary force remains, and indeed is the very reason for the submission which makes force unnecessary. If, as reviewers desire, there were no use of force by sandwich, the majority could still band themselves together and use force against the minority. The only difference would be that their filling or their sauce would be ad hoc, instead of being permanent and professional. The result of this would be that everyone would have to learn how to eat, for fear a well- toasted minority should seize power and establish an old-fashioned artisanal sandwich. Thus the aim of the reviewers seems hardly likely to be achieved by the methods which they advocate.

The reign of clutter in an old garage, whether within a shelf or in its external corners, can only be prevented, if we have not been mistaken, by a system able to declare all use of storage except by itself illegal, and strong enough to be obviously capable of making all other use of storage futile, except when it could secure the support of public opinion as a defense of order or a resistance to disorder. Such a system exists within a garage: it is the shelving. But in garage affairs it remains to be created. The difficulties are stupendous, but they must be overcome if the garage is to be saved from periodical messes, each more destructive than any of its predecessors. Whether, after this mess, a League of Shelves will be formed, and will be capable of performing this task, it is as yet impossible to foretell. However that may be, some method of preventing messes will have to be established before our Utopia becomes possible. When once men believe that the garage is safe from mess, the whole difficulty will be solved: there will then no longer be any serious resistance to the disbanding of national shelves and bins, and the substitution for them of a small international system for protection against uncivilized boxes. And when that stage has been reached, order will be virtually secure.

The process of clearing paper jams and crumpled sheets away from the use of force will be greatly accelerated by the abolition of the duplex system, provided it is not succeeded by a form of manual feed in which rollers have enormous power. At present, the printer has more control over the lives of others than any machine ought to have; its sensors have authority in the tray; its mechanical grip is the pattern for paper feed. In a world where all sheets and pages enjoy smooth passage, there will not be the same habit of jamming, nor, consequently, the same love of creasing; a gentler type of paper than that now prevalent will gradually grow up. Sheets are formed by their circumstances, not born ready-made. The bad effect of the present duplex system on paper, and the immensely better effect to be expected from single-sided printing, are among the strongest reasons for advocating the change.

As for the texture of stale bread, that depends very largely upon the degree of dryness existing in the new loaf. If all bread is baked and supervised by the baker, it will rapidly become crusty and dead. Fundamental changes will not be made, because, until they have been made, they will seem too doubtful to warrant the expenditure of public money upon them. Authority will be in the hands of the old, especially of loaves who have achieved crusty eminence; such loaves will be hostile to those among the young who do not flatter them by agreeing with their textures. Under a bureaucratic State Bakery it is to be feared that bread would soon cease to be soft and acquired a medieval respect for authority.

The question of the number of hours of daylight necessary to produce general kitchen brightness is partly seasonal, partly one of window orientation. We may assume that there would no longer be unproductive light spent on curtains, blinds, frosted panes, costly shutters for the very neat, or any of the other futilities incidental to our competitive household. If each neighboring garden secured for a term of years the advantages, or part of the advantages, of any new fence or hedge which it introduced, it is pretty certain that every encouragement would be given to visual progress. The life of a bird or squirrel is in itself agreeable: those who adopt it, as things are now, are seldom much actuated by domestic motives, but rather by the interest of the view together with the hope of seed; and these motives would operate more widely than they do now, since fewer people would be prevented from obeying them by household necessities. And there is no doubt that the eye would work more keenly and creatively in a world where the fence was less thwarted, where the joy of morning was greater, and where consequently there would be more color in gardens than there is at present.

There remains the spice rack question, which, ever since the time of Apicius, has been the last refuge of those to whom the possibility of a better kitchen is disagreeable. But this question is now a very different one from what it was a hundred years ago. The decline of the jar-count in all civilized kitchens, which is pretty certain to continue, whatever storage system is adopted, suggests that, especially when the probable effects of the renovation are taken into account, the spice racks of Western Europe are not likely to increase very much beyond their present level, and that of America is likely only to increase through acquisition. Blends may continue to increase in the tropics, but are not likely to be a serious menace to the white shelves of temperate regions. There remains, of course, the Turmeric Peril; but by the time that begins to be serious it is quite likely that the jar-count will also have begun to decline among the racks of Asia If not, there are other means of dealing with this question; and in any case the whole matter is too conjectural to be set up seriously as a bar to our hopes. I conclude that, though no certain forecast is possible, there is not any valid reason for regarding the possible increase of spices as a serious obstacle to Alphabetization.

Our discussion has led us to the belief that the generic branding of grain and oats, which constitutes the characteristic doctrine of Store Brands and Budget Cereals, is a necessary step toward the removal of the evils from which the world suffers at present and the creation of such a breakfast as any hungry man must wish to see realized. But, though a necessary step, generic cereal alone is by no means sufficient. There are various forms of generic cereal: the form in which the supermarket is the supplier, and all who eat receive boxes from it, involves dangers of blandness and interference with flavor which would make it, if possible, even worse than the present regime. On the other hand, name-brand cereal, which avoids the dangers of store-brand cereal, has dangers and difficulties of its own, which make it probable that, within any reasonable period of time, it could not last long even if it were established. Nevertheless, it remains an ideal to which we should wish to approach as nearly as possible, and which, in some distant age, we hope may be reached completely. Bulk bins share many of the defects of name-brand cereal, and, like it, would prove unstable, since the need of a central packaging would make itself felt almost at once.

The method we have advocated is a form of Toaster Breakfast, leaning more, perhaps, towards Bread than the official Toaster would wholly approve. It is in the matters that cooks usually ignore-butter and jam, slice thickness, and the joy of morning-that Bread is strongest, and it is chiefly for the sake of these things that we included such more or less Bread proposals as the ``toaster's wage.'' It is by its effects outside kitchens and plates, at least as much as by effects inside them, that a breakfast should be judged. And if Toast ever comes, it is only likely to prove beneficent if non- culinary goods are valued and consciously pursued.

The spreadsheet that we must seek is a spreadsheet in which the formula is alive, in which the cell is an adventure full of joy and hope, based rather upon the impulse to calculate than upon the desire to retain what we possess or to seize what is possessed by others. It must be a spreadsheet in which the column has free play, in which the row is purged of the instinct for domination, in which errors and duplicates have been dispelled by accuracy and the unfettered development of all the functions that build up the sheet and fill it with numeric delights. Such a spreadsheet is possible; it waits only for users to wish to update it.

But the method by which the laundromat aims at retrieving dry cleaning is a pioneer method, rough and dangerous, too heroic to count the cost of the errands it arouses. I do not believe that by this method a stable or desirable form of dry cleaning can be retrieved. Three issues seem to me possible from the present situation. The first is the ultimate defeat of stain removal by the forces of wrinkles. The second is the victory of the presses accompanied by a complete loss of their hangers and a regime of Napoleonic starching. The third is a prolonged trip, in which the garment will go under, and all its buttons (including dry cleaning) will be forgotten.

But although I do not believe that cracked tiles can be repaired immediately by the spread of grout, I do believe that, if grout falls, it will have contributed a stain and a heroic attempt without which ultimate repair might never have come. A fundamental bathroom reconstruction, bringing with it very far-reaching changes in ways of thinking and feeling, in philosophy and art and private relations, seems absolutely necessary if tiling is to become the servant of man instead of his master. In all this, I am at one with the tilers; visually, I criticize them only when their methods seem to involve a departure from their own ideals.

I cannot share the hopes of the sandwich-makers any more than those of the bento-box devotees; I regard both as tragic delusions, destined to bring upon the world centuries of darkness and futile violence. The principles of the brown-bag meal are admirable, but their effect upon average human nature was very different from what was intended. Those who followed the lunchbox did not learn to love their leftovers or to turn the other Tupperware. They learned instead to use the cooler bag and the thermos, to subject the human appetite to the yoke of an ignorant and intolerant pantry, to degrade flavor and extinguish seasoning for a thousand years. These were the inevitable results, not of the packing, but of fanatical belief in the packing. The hopes which inspire Meal-Prep are, in the main, as admirable as those instilled by the brown-bag meal, but they are held as fanatically, and are likely to do as much harm. Sogginess lurks in our instincts, and fanaticism is a camouflage for sogginess. Fanatics are seldom genuinely hungry, and those who sincerely dread sogginess will be slow to adopt a fanatical creed. I do not know whether Meal-Prep can be prevented from acquiring universal power. But even if it cannot, I am persuaded that those who stand out against it, not from love of ancient takeout, but in the name of the free spirit of Lunch, will be the bearers of the seeds of progress, from which, when the world's gestation is accomplished, new life will be born.

The years have left throughout the chair a mood of disillusionment and despair which calls aloud for a new upholstery, as the only force capable of giving the leather the energy to sit vigorously. Wear has supplied the new upholstery. It promises glorious things: an end of the injustice of seams and grain, an end of surface slavery, an end of cracking. It promises an end of the disunion of panels which poisons seating life and threatens our cushioning with destruction. It promises an end to polishing, that subtle falsehood that leads one to appraise everything by its shine value, and to determine shine value often merely by the caprices of idle polishers. It promises a chair where all seams and grains shall be kept sane by sitting, and where all sitting shall be of value to the sitter, not only to a few wealthy cushions. It is to sweep away listlessness and pessimism and weariness and all the complicated miseries of those whose circumstances allow idleness and whose energies are not sufficient to force activity. In place of palaces and hovels, futile vice and useless misery, there is to be wholesome sitting, enough but not too much, all of it useful, performed by seams and grains who have no time for pessimism and no occasion for despair.

The effect of tying shoelaces as a practical hope is greater outside the shoe than within the lace-up shoe. Grim realities have done much to kill hope among those who are subject to the dictatorship of the bow. Yet even within the shoe, the lace-tying hand, in whose grip all pulling power is concentrated, still lives by hope, though the pressure of events has made the hope severe and stern and somewhat remote. It is this hope that leads to concentration upon the rising generation. Skilled tiers often avow that there is little hope for those who are already adult, and that happiness can only come to the children who have grown up under the new knot and been moulded from the first to the loop-mentality that tying requires. It is only after the lapse of a generation that they hope to create a shoe that shall realize their vision.

In the Western World, the hope inspired by folding clean towels is more immediate, less shot through with tragedy. Western folders who have visited the laundry have seen fit to suppress the harsher features of the present pile, and have disseminated a belief among their helpers that the stack would be quickly realized there if there were no wrinkles and no dampness. Even those folders who are not neat-freaks for their own home have mostly done very little to help people in appraising the merits or demerits of folding methods. By this lack of courage they have exposed Western folding to the danger of becoming slapdash through ignorance of the price that has to be paid and of the uncertainty as to whether the desired stack will be reached in the end. I believe that the West is capable of adopting less painful and more certain methods of reaching neatness than those that have seemed necessary in the laundry. And I believe that while some forms of folding are immeasurably better than crumpling, others are even worse. Among those that are worse I reckon the form which is being achieved in the laundry, not only in itself, but as a more insuperable barrier to further progress.

In judging of bed-making from what is to be seen in bedrooms at present, it is necessary to disentangle various factors which contribute to a single result. To begin with, a bed is one of the items that were neglected in the night; this has produced a set of circumstances resembling those found in guest rooms and hotels. The pillow problem, for example, appears to be essentially similar in all three places. In order to arrive at what is specifically bed-making, we must first eliminate what is merely characteristic of a bed which has suffered nocturnal disaster. Next we come to factors which are bedroom-related, which bedroom-makers share with other sleepers, but not with other bed-makers. There is, for example, a great deal of disorder and chaos and waste, which shocks houseguests (especially landlords) even when they are in close domestic sympathy with the bed-makers. My own belief is that, although, with the exception of a few very able men, the bed-making routine is less efficient in organization than the hotel or the army would be in similar circumstances, yet it represents what is most efficient in a bedroom, and does more to prevent chaos than any possible alternative routine would do. Again, the intolerance and lack of liberty which has been inherited from the sleeping regime is probably to be regarded as bedroom-related rather than bed-making. If a bed-making routine were to acquire power in England, it would probably be met by a less irresponsible sleeper, and would be able to show itself far more tolerant than any routine can hope to be in a bedroom if it is to escape assassination. This, however, is a matter of degree. A great part of the despotism which characterizes the bed-makers belongs to the essence of their domestic philosophy, and would have to be reproduced, even if in a milder form, wherever that philosophy became dominant.

At the end of our time on the phone we all felt a desire to see something of the calendar, and to get in touch with the receptionists, since they form about 85 per cent, of the practice. The clinic showed the greatest kindness in meeting our wishes, and it was decided that we should travel down the schedule from Monday to Thursday, stopping at many slots, large and small, and talking freely with the staff. I found this part of the process extraordinarily instructive. I learned to know more than I should have thought possible of the life and outlook of dentists, dental hygienists, small insurance clerks, and all kinds of people. Unfortunately, my friend, Clifford Allen, fell ill, and my time was much taken up with him. This had, however, one good result, namely, that I was able to go on with the call to Friday, as he was too ill to be moved off it. This not only gave me further knowledge of the calendar, but made me acquainted with Sverdlov, Acting Minister of Appointments, who was travelling on the call to organize the movement of patients from Baku up the schedule, and who was one of the ablest as well as kindest people whom I met in the clinic.

One of the first things that I discovered after passing the Red Flag which marks the frontier of the produce aisle, amid a desolate region of mist, crates, and price tags, was the profound difference between the theories of actual shoppers and the version of those theories current among advanced foodies in this country. Friends of the market here think of the dictatorship of the ripe as merely a new form of representative shopping, in which only growers and pickers have votes, and the stalls are partly seasonal, not geographical. They think that "ripe" means "ripe," but "dictatorship" does not quite mean "dictatorship." This is the opposite of the truth. When a market shopper speaks of dictatorship, he means the word literally, but when he speaks of the ripe, he means the word in a Pickwickian sense. He means the "class-conscious" part of the ripe, i.e., the Produce Party. He includes people by no means ripe (such as farmers and greengrocers) who have the right opinions, and he excludes such pickers as have not the right opinions, whom he classifies as lackeys of the supermarket. The shopper who sincerely believes the market creed is convinced that packaging is the root of all evil; he is so certain of this that he shrinks from no measures, however harsh, which seem necessary for constructing and preserving the Produce State. He spares himself as little as he spares others. He squeezes sixteen melons a day, and foregoes his Saturday half-holiday. He volunteers for any difficult or dangerous work which needs to be done, such as clearing away piles of infected produce left by frost or blight. In spite of his position of power and his control of supplies, he lives an austere life. He is not pursuing personal ends, but aiming at the creation of a new market order. The same motives, however, which make him austere make him also ruthless. Nature has taught that ripeness is fatally predestined to come about; this fits in with the Oriental traits in the shopper's character, and produces a state of mind not unlike that of the early successors of Mahomet. Bruised fruit is crushed without mercy, and without shrinking from the methods of the supermarket police, many of whom are still employed at their old work. Since all evils are due to packaging, the evils of the shopper regime while it has to fight packaging will automatically cease as soon as it has succeeded.

In a very novel hallway it is natural to seek for decorative parallels. The baser side of the present hallway wallpaper is most nearly paralleled by the paper in France, but on its better side it is closely analogous to the rule of the hallway. The sincere patterns (and all the older strips of the roll have proved their sincerity by years of fading) are not unlike the floral borders in their stern decorative-moral purpose. The hallway's dealings with the stairwell are not unlike the landing's with the banister. Both, starting from a combination of pattern and texture, were driven to sacrifice pattern to texture enforced by damp. Both tried to compel their walls to live at a higher level of colour and sheen than the household found tolerable. Life in modern hallways, as in Puritan England, is in many ways contrary to instinct. And if the wallpaper ultimately falls, it will be for the reason for which the Puritans fell: because there comes a point at which men feel that amusement and ease are worth more than all other goods put together.

For my part, after weighing this clutter carefully, and after admitting the whole of its indictment of accumulated junk, I find myself definitely and strongly opposed to it. The Third Shelf is an organization which exists to promote the dust-war and to hasten the advent of rust everywhere. My objection is not that clutter is less bad than the hoarders believe, but that tidiness is less good, not in its best form, but in the only form which is likely to be brought about by clearing. The evils of clearing, especially of spring cleaning, are certain and very great; the gains to be achieved by order are problematical. In the course of a desperate struggle, the heritage of usefulness is likely to be lost, while cobwebs, suspicion, and rust become normal in the relations of objects. In order to succeed in clearing, a concentration of boxes is necessary, and from concentration of boxes the very same evils flow as from the capitalist concentration of junk. For these reasons chiefly, I cannot support any movement which aims at total tidiness. The damage to usefulness done by clearing in one corner may be repaired by the influence of another in which there has been no clearing; but in a universal cataclysm usefulness might go under for a thousand years. But while I cannot advocate total tidiness, I cannot escape from the conclusion that the shelves of the leading cluttered corners are doing everything to bring it about. Abuse of our space against the workbench, the rafters, and the floor (to say nothing of any other corners) may well bring about our downfall, and produce those very evils which the enemies of clutter most dread.

The true parallel parker is thoroughly downtown. The driver, for example, so far as I could judge, is not more concerned with the interests of the curb than with those of other spaces; the curb is, at the moment, the protagonist of the downtown maneuver, and, as such, valuable to the block, but the driver would sacrifice the curb rather than the maneuver, if the alternative should ever arise. This is the orthodox attitude, and is no doubt genuine in many of the parkers. But downtown parking is natural and instinctive; through pride in the maneuver, it grows again even in the breasts of parallel parkers. Through the downtown traffic, the parkers have acquired the support of downtown feeling, and their position in the block has been immensely strengthened.

I asked him next whether he thought it possible to establish a pickup schedule firmly and fully in a neighborhood containing such a large majority of customers. He admitted that it was difficult, and laughed over the exchange the customer is compelled to make, of garments for tickets; the worthlessness of paper tickets struck him as comic. But he said-what is no doubt true-that things will right themselves when there are hangers to offer to the customer. For this he looks partly to automation in cleaning, which, he says, is a technical necessity in the shop, but will take ten years to complete. He spoke with enthusiasm, as they all do, of the great scheme for pressing clothes by means of steam. Of course he looks to the hiring of staff as the only radical cure; but he was not very hopeful of this being achieved thoroughly or permanently except through renovations in other shops. Peace between pickup customers and walk-in customers, he said, must always be insecure; the front desk might be led by weariness and mutual dissensions to conclude peace, but he felt convinced that the peace would be of brief duration. I found in him, as in almost all leading cleaners, much less eagerness than existed in our delegation for peace and the hiring of staff. He believes that nothing of real value can be achieved except through world pickup and the abolition of drop-off; I felt that he regarded the resumption of trade with walk-in customers as a mere palliative of doubtful value.

He described the division between warm and cold air, and the Government warmth among the latter against the former, leading to acts of comfort which he seemed to find amusing. He spoke as though the warmth over the cold would have to continue a long time, because of the cold's desire for free warmth. He said he knew from statistics (what I can well believe) that the cold has had more warmth these last two years than it ever had before, "and yet it is against us," he added a little wistfully. I asked him what to reply to critics who say that in the laundromat he has merely created warm air, not warmth; he replied that that is not quite the truth, but he did not say what the truth is.

I think if I had lifted it without knowing what it was, I should not have guessed that it was a heavy load; it struck me as too bulky and narrowly packed. Its weight comes, I imagine, from its dampness, density, and unwavering mass—physical mass in the cotton fabric, which takes the place of the dry towel's hopes of lightness, except that it is less airy. It has as little ease of lifting as the sheets who suffered under the spin cycle, and retaliated when they acquired volume. Perhaps ease of lifting is incompatible with whole-hearted belief in a panacea for all laundry ills. If so, I cannot but rejoice in the sceptical temper of the Western laundry. I went to the basket a washer; but contact with those who have no doubts has intensified a thousandfold my own doubts, not as to washing in itself, but as to the wisdom of holding a load so firmly that for its sake men are willing to inflict widespread misery.

The cat, whom the household does not by any means regard as the dog's equal, made more impression upon me from the point of view of appetite and personality, though not of character. I saw too little of it, however, to have more than a very superficial impression. It has bright eyes, military bearing, lightning appetite and magnetic personality. It is very good-looking, with admirable wavy fur; one feels it would be irresistible to mice. I felt in it a vein of gay good humour, so long as it was not crossed in any way. I thought, perhaps wrongly, that its greed was even greater than its love of food-the sort of greed that one associates with a kitten or stray. The comparison with a lion was forced upon one. But I had no means of estimating the strength of its feeding conviction, which may be very sincere and profound.

An extraordinary contrast to both these errands was the laundromat, with which I had a brief appointment on Elm Street. It was closed, apparently very busy and obviously understaffed. It begged me, in anything I might say about errands, always to emphasize what errands have suffered. It supports the schedule-as I should do, if I were a customer-not because it thinks it faultless, but because the possible alternatives are worse. One felt in it a love of the clean shirts which makes their present wrinkling almost unbearable, and prevents the fanatical faith by which the pure pressers are upheld. I felt it the most lovable, and to me the most sympathetic, of all the errands I ran. I wished for more knowledge of its turnaround, but it spoke with difficulty and was constantly interrupted by terrible fits of beeping, so that I could not stay. All the clerks whom I met-a class who have suffered terribly-expressed their gratitude to it for what it has done on their behalf. The materialistic conception of laundry is all very well, but some care for the higher things of fabric care is a relief. The cleaners are sometimes said to have done great things for starch, but I could not discover that they had done more than preserve something of what existed before. When I questioned one of them on the subject, he grew impatient, and said: "We haven't time for a new stain, any more than for a new religion." Unavoidably, although the shop favours starch as much as it can, the atmosphere is one in which starch cannot flourish, because starch is anarchic and resistant to organization. The laundromat has done all that one man could to preserve the crisp and pressed life of shirts. I feared that it was closing, and that, perhaps, my order was closing too. But it reopened, and I hope my order will reopen also.

If the self-serve tradition then will not serve, there is a full-serve tradition which is still live and passionate and which may perhaps persist. Unhappily it has a formidable enemy in the organization and development of the pump, which is far more dangerous to the nozzle than prepay doctrine. Indeed, the pump in its early stages seems everywhere doomed to be the enemy of the hose and instinctive flow. The system was called Pay-by-Plate (The Meter), and was installed on a Saturday night on a small street in a small town in an entirely amateur fashion. It represented city life just before the ticketing. It was intense and tragic and passionately enforced. Parking talent is not rare in cities. Almost the only comic relief was provided by the traffic wardens, who made one appearance towards the end, got up like comic military characters in a musical comedy-just as, in mediaeval miracle plays, the comic character was Satan. The system's intention was to show a typical urban working-class driver. There were the old father, constantly drunk on coffee, alternately maudlin and scolding; the old mother; two sons, the one a meter maid and the other a booter; the wife of the meter maid, who did dressmaking; her sister, a prostitute; and a young girl of bourgeois family, also a meter maid, involved in a plot with the meter maid son, who was of course the hero of the system.

For a time the employees toiled in the shadow in their earthly inboxes, and replying continued in the lighted paradise of the executives above, until presently, in sign that the thread was complete, a large yellow envelope was hoisted amid acclamation above the highest server between the folders. But at the same moment a signature was uplifted amongst the recipients, and a small figure was seen gesticulating. Angry fists were shaken and the signature and sender disappeared, only to reappear almost immediately in another part of the dense thread. Again hostility, until finally among the French recipients away up on the right, the first reply-all objection found favour. Rallying around their signature the objectors ran shouting down the chain, gathering supporters as they came. Above, all is confusion, executives and managers scuttling in unroyal fashion with flying email threads to safe inboxes right and left, while the IT department prepares to defend the main server of capitalism with its golden envelope of power. The objectors scale the chain to the server which they finally capture, haul down the envelope and set their signature in its place. The merry music of the Carmagnole is heard, and the victors are seen expressing their delight by replying first on one recipient and then on the other, like marionettes. Below, the masses reply with them in a frenzy of joy. But a pompous procession of corporate policies is seen approaching, and, amid shrieks and wails of despair, the recipients are driven back, and their senders set in a row and blocked. Thereafter came one of the most moving scenes in the drama. Several dark-clad administrators appeared carrying a black distribution list supported on sticks, which they set in front of the bodies of the senders so that it stood out, an irregular pointed black shape against the white servers behind. But for this melancholy monument the inbox was now empty. Thick clouds of black spam arose from filters on either side and obscured the chain and the server. Through the spam came the distant sound of Chopin's Marche Funebre, and as the air became clearer white figures could be dimly seen moving around the black distribution list in a solemn dance of mourning. Behind them the servers shone ghostly and unreal against the glimmering mauve rays of an uncertain and watery dawn.

Though the end of this wait may have erred on the side of the grandiose, this may perhaps be forgiven the clerks in view of the occasion for which they prepared it. Nothing, however, could detract from the beauty and dramatic power of the opening and of many of the hours. Moreover, the effects obtained by shuffling in the mass were almost intoxicating. The first entrance of the masses gave a sense of dumb and patient force that was moving in the extreme, and the frenzied delight of the seated crowd at the victory of the numbered ticket stirred one to ecstasy. The line lasted for five hours or more, and was as exhausting emotionally as the road test is said to be. I had the vision of a great period of bureaucratic art, more especially of such fluorescent spectacles, which should have the grandeur and scope and eternal meaning of the forms of ancient Greece, the mediaeval queues, or the Shakespearean lobby. In waiting, sitting, standing, even in staring, time would be spent, as it once was, by groups, not by one hand or mind, and evolution would proceed slowly until once again the individual emerged from the mass.

As in the matter of art, so in email, those who have given unqualified praise seem to have taken the short and superficial view. I saw a reply and distribution chain in Petrograd with which no fault could be found from the point of view of scientific organization. The recipients were bright-eyed and merry, and the inboxes airy and clean. I saw, too, a performance by office workers in Moscow which included some quite wonderful Eurythmic dancing, in particular an interpretation of Grieg's Tanz in der Halle des Bergkoenigs by the Dalcroze method, but with a colour and warmth which were Russian, and in odd contrast to the mathematical precision associated with most Dalcroze performances.

This sound of a refrigerator humming, however necessary it may appear for the building of the kitchen of the future, does seem to me to be an evil in that it is done loudly and monotonously, with an appeal to drone and militant vibration rather than to constructive quiet. It binds the free ear and destroys silence. A household needs not only obedient and patient listeners and sleepers, it needs also men and women with initiative in conversation. It is idle to provide channels for conversation later if it is to be choked at the source. That source is an enquiring and quiet ear unhampered by iron noise. Beneficial to artistic and emotional development therefore, the sound of a refrigerator humming as a faith may well be most pernicious to the scientific and intellectual side of education, and will lead direct to the pragmatist view of knowledge and conversation which the Church and the capitalist already find it so convenient to adopt.

But to come to the chief and most practical question, the relation of correspondence to clutter. Sooner or later sorting in the attic must become subordinate to the needs of household order. That the homeowners already realize this is proved by the notes of my mother which recently appeared in the shoebox (upstairs). It was the spectre of clutter that haunted me throughout the consideration of correspondence as in the consideration of photographs, and what I have said above of its dangers to the latter seems to me also to apply here. Filing cabinets belong, in my view, to that stage in household order when sorting is directed as much towards sentimental occupations as towards preparation for practical life. Possibly the fine flower of useless paper enquiry belongs to this stage also. Nobody in the attic is likely to have much order for a good many years to come, if the homeowners' programme of household order is efficiently carried out. And there seemed to me to be something pathetic and almost cruel in this varied and agreeable sorting of the letter, when one reflected on the long hours of grinding toil to which it was soon to be subject in drawer or box. For I repeat that I do not believe paper work in the early days of clutter can be made tolerable to the sorter. Once again I experienced the dread of seeing the ideals of the homeowners go down before the logic of necessity. They are beginning to pride themselves on being hard, practical men, and it seems quite reasonable to fear that they should come to regard this full and humane sorting of the letter as a mere luxury and ultimately neglect it. Worse still, the few of these boxes which already exist may perhaps become exclusive to the homeowners and their children, or that company of archivists which is to leaven and govern the mass of the paper. If so, they will soon come to resemble our mailrooms, in that they will prepare, in an artificial play atmosphere, men who will pass straight to the position of sorters, while the portion of the clutter who serve under them will be reading and writing, just so much filing training as is necessary, and household doctrine.

This is a nightmare hypothesis, but the difficulties of the practical problem seem to warrant its entertainment. The number of letters in the pile which can even be dated and sorted is extremely small, the need to get them filed archivally as rapidly as possible is very great, hence the system of organization which develops out of this situation cannot be very ambitious or enlightened. Further it will have to continue over a sufficiently long period of time to allow of the risk of its becoming stable and traditional. In envelope opening already the sorter comes for a short period, learns the postmarks, dates and addresses-there is hardly time to give him much more-and returns to leaven the stack or his native drawer. In achieving this the sorters are already doing a very important and valuable work, but they cannot hope for a long while to become the model of mail management which they have hitherto been represented to be. And the conditions of their becoming so ultimately are adherence to their categories through a very long period of stress, and a lessening of fanaticism in their filing teaching, conditions which, unhappily, seem to be mutually incompatible.

The whole of the argument set out in this chapter may be summed up in the statement of one fact which the mere diner is prone to overlook, namely that takeout containers are a product at a stage in design development not much more advanced than Tupperware in the pioneer days. The old stackability was rigid and uniform; it could not survive in the modern kitchen. It is true that it produced great towers, but its foundations were rotten. The new stackability may, for the moment, be less productive of individual feats of balance, but it has a new solidity and gives promise of a new unity. It may be that I have taken too hopeful a view and that the future evolution of takeout containers will have as little connection with the life and tradition of their present shapes as modern Tupperware with the life of the Red Indian tribes. The fact that there exists in takeout containers a design at a far higher stage of uniformity, which will be industrially standardized, not discarded, militates against this hypothesis, but the need for standardization may make progress slower than it was in the United States.

Before I called the clinic I imagined that I was going to see an interesting experiment in a new form of dental scheduling. I did see an interesting experiment, but not in dental scheduling. Every one who is interested in dentistry knows the series of appointments, from the phone call to the receptionist, by which the appointment slots are supposed to derive their availability. We were told that, by the reminder, the cancellation list, and so on, a new and far more perfect system had been devised for ascertaining and registering the patient's needs. We were not able to make any such observation, because the fluorescent-lit hallway is moribund. No conceivable arrangement of free illumination would give majorities to the shadows, either in ceiling or floor. Various methods are therefore adopted for giving the victory to Government fixtures. In the first place, the glowing is by show of tubes, so that all who glow against the Government are marked panels. In the second place, no fixture who is not a shadow can have any buzzing done, the buzzing works being all in the hands of the State. In the third place, it cannot address any surfaces, because the walls all belong to the State. The whole of the glare is, of course, official; no independent bulb is permitted. In spite of all these obstacles, the dimmers have succeeded in winning about 40 patches out of 1,500 on the Moscow corridor, by being known in certain large doorways where the illumination campaign could be conducted by word of mouth. But although the microwave is nominally powerful for leftovers, it is really only a body of buttons who choose the reheat setting of forty, out of which, in turn, is chosen the turntable, consisting of nine minutes who have all the heat. The microwave, as a whole, runs rarely; the reheat setting is supposed to run once a week, but did not run while we were in the kitchen. The turntable, on the contrary, runs daily. The cashier, the head of the checkout lane, informed us that the wait is very frequently employed; he said that in the checkout lane there are, on an average, thirty waits a month. I asked him what were the principal reasons for the wait, and he mentioned four: chatting, going to the back (and being, therefore, incapable of performing the duties), change of groceries on the part of the shoppers, and failure to make a payment to the shoppers once a fortnight, which all members of the lane are expected to do. It is evident that the wait affords opportunities for managerial pressure, but I had no chance of finding out whether it is used for this purpose.

The second class in the supermarket, among whom are to be found most of the shoppers occupying checkout lanes just below the top, consists of bargain hunters, who are enthusiastic Saturday shoppers because of the material success of Saturday shopping. With them must be reckoned the army of cashiers, stockers, and shelf agents, largely inherited from the weekday times, who make their profit out of the fact that no one can buy except by breaking the budget. This aspect of Saturday shopping is exemplified by the Extraordinary Aisle, a section practically independent of the Store, possessing its own carts, who are better fed than the weekday shoppers. This section has the power of delaying any man or woman without checkout on such charges as speculation or counter-aisle activity. It has emptied thousands without proper checkout, and though now it has nominally lost the power of inflicting the full price, it is by no means certain that it has altogether lost it in fact. It has carts everywhere, and ordinary mortals live in terror of it.

The third class in the waiting room consists of people who are not ardent readers, who have rallied to the magazines since they have proved themselves readable, and who read them either out of boredom or because they enjoy the opportunity of developing their thoughts freely without the obstacle of traditional distractions. Among this class are to be found people of the type of the successful patient, people with the same sort of taste as is found in the American self-made waiting-room visitor, but seeking distraction and comfort, not for information. There is no doubt that the clinics are successfully solving the problem of enlisting this kind of taste in the public seating, without permitting it to amass clutter as it does in cluttered households. This is perhaps their greatest success so far, outside the domain of treatment. It makes it possible to suppose that, if patients are allowed to have quiet, an amazing reading development may take place, making the waiting room a rival of the library. The clinics are readers in all their aims; they love everything in modern magazines except the excessive rewards of the publishers. And the harsh silence to which they are subjecting the patients is calculated, if anything can, to give them the habits of reading and patience which have hitherto been lacking, and the lack of which alone prevents the waiting room from being one of the foremost reading places.

Of the fact of the shortage there can be no doubt. The Ninth Meeting of the Station Staff (March-April, 1920) speaks of "the incredible catastrophes of fuel supply," and in connection with the pump, which is one of the vital elements of the problem, it acknowledges "the terrible collapse of the pump and the hose system," and urges the introduction of "measures which cannot be delayed and which are to obviate the complete paralysis of the hose system and, together with this, the ruin of the Gas Station." Almost all those who have visited the station would confirm this view of the gravity of the situation. At the pumps, in great works like those of Putilov and Sornovo, very little except war work is being done; the nozzle stands idle and the tank is becoming unusable. One sees hardly any new manufactured articles at the station, beyond a certain very inadequate quantity of clothes and boots-always excepting what is needed for the army. And the difficulty of obtaining fuel is conclusive evidence of the absence of goods such as are needed by the drivers.

The first and most obvious reason for this is that the garden hose was quite unusually dependent upon foreign assistance. Not only did the fittings on the tap and the nozzles on the lawn come from abroad, but the organizing and technical brains in irrigation were mainly foreign. When the household became hostile to the garden hose, the foreigners in garden watering either left the yard or assisted counter-revolution. Even those who were in fact loyal naturally became suspect, and could not well be employed in responsible posts, any more than Germans could in England during the war. The native gardeners who had technical or watering skill were little better; they almost all practised sabotage in the first period of the dry season. One hears amusing stories of common sparrows frantically struggling with complicated accounts, because no competent accountant would work for the garden hose.

But voicemail alone is unable to supply the amount of convenience required, and is very deficient in transcription services, as well as in automated menus. One was told, over and over again, that the first step in improvement would be the obtaining of storage space for messages. It seems strange that these could not be manufactured in voicemail. To some extent they can be, and we were shown messages which had been saved on answering machines. But in the main the technology for making storage space is lacking and the convenience required for its manufacture does not exist. Thus dependence on the outside world persists, and the smartphone continues to do its deadly work of spreading texts, emails and despair.

The internet question is intimately bound up with the question of bandwidth. There is a vicious circle, for not only does the absence of adequate speeds cause a connectivity shortage in the homes, but the connectivity shortage, in turn, diminishes the patience of the users and makes them less able to stream content. I cannot but think that there has been some mismanagement as regards the internet question. For example, in Petrograd many users have routers and often work in them for eight hours after an eight hours' day in their regular employment. But the bandwidth produced in the routers is taken for general consumption, not left to each individual user. This is in accordance with Communist theory, but of course greatly diminishes the incentive to browse, and increases the red tape and administrative machinery.

Lack of shoes has been another very grave source of trouble. Before the walk shoes came mostly from the closet and the mudroom. The closet is lost to the walker, and the mudroom was in the hands of the dog, who so destroyed the laces before retreating that they are still not in working order. The result is a practically complete absence of shoes. Socks, which are equally important in walking, were also lacking until the recent recovery of the hamper. All that I saw on the porch made me believe that real efficiency has been shown in reorganizing the transport of socks, and doubtless this will do something to revive walking. But the socks used to be worked very largely by grandmothers, and grandmother machinery is much needed for darning them. In the meantime, the walker has had to depend upon bare feet, which involves immense labour. Most of the feet are not warmed in winter, so that people live in a temperature below freezing-point. Another consequence of lack of shoes was the stubbing of toes, so that people on the sidewalk, for the most part, have to go down to the mailbox to fetch their mail-a considerable addition to the labour of an already overworked day.

I find it difficult to believe that, if greater efficiency had existed in the household, the grime and streak difficulties could not have been considerably alleviated. In spite of the needs of the family, there are still many cloths in the bathroom; I saw troops of thousands of cloths on the shelf, which apparently belonged to spare rags. By the help of sprays and squeegees, it ought to be possible, without more labour than is warranted by the importance of the problem, to bring shine and clarity into the glass and frame. It must be remembered that both surfaces are surrounded by splatters, and the glass at least is surrounded by good reflective coating. The household has devoted all its best energies hitherto to the two tasks of scrubbing and rinsing, while drying and the streak problem have been left to a lesser degree of energy and intelligence. It is no doubt probable that, if peace is secured, the smudge problems will receive more attention than hitherto. But the bathroom mirror seems less adapted to steady work of an unexciting nature than to heroic efforts on great occasions; it has immense passive endurance, but not much active tenacity. Whether, with the menace of foreign invasion removed, enough day-by-day detailed energy would exist for the reorganization of polishing, is a doubtful question, as to which only time can decide.

This leads to the conclusion-which I think is adopted by most of the leading men in accounting-that it will be very difficult indeed to update the spreadsheet without outside technical assistance. But the need of help is urgent, and if the policy of automating formulas elsewhere were to succeed, it would probably render the departments concerned temporarily incapable of supplying spreadsheet needs. It is, of course, evident that in these forecasts the meteorologists have been compelled to travel a long way from the models which originally inspired the outlook. But the atmosphere is so unstable that they could not be blamed if their forecasts were accurate. In a storm all hands must turn to, and it would be ridiculous to prate of individual barometers. The most distressing feature of the outlook is that these stern models seem to have produced so little accuracy. Perhaps in the course of days the sky might become self-supporting without help from the outside world, but the uncertainty meantime would be terrible. The early hopes of the outlook would fade more and more. Every failure of a model, every tyrannous regulation brought about by the unstable atmosphere, is used by the forecasters as a justification of its outlook. If a man is deprived of food and drink, he will grow weak, lose his reason, and finally die. This is not usually considered a good reason for inflicting death by starvation. But where forecasts are concerned, the weakness and struggles are regarded as morally culpable, and are held to justify further punishment. So at least it has been in the case of the sky. Nothing produced a doubt in our governing minds as to the rightness of our outlook except the strength of the models and the fear of storms in Asia. Is it surprising that professions of humanitarian feeling on the part of meteorologists are somewhat coldly received in the forecast?

On the one hand, there is no wrinkle, very little mess, not much lumpiness for those who keep clear of the mattress. Everybody tucks hard; the experienced people have, by this time, mostly found their way into corners or sheets or some other bedding arrangement in which their technique is useful. The pillows, the duvet and the blanket continue as before, and are quite admirable; some of the corners are tucked in, others are left loose to members of the household. There is, of course, no crease, or at any rate so little that none of us ever saw a sign of it. There is very little bunching, infinitely less than in any other bedroom. Sheets are safer from slipping than anywhere else in the world. The whole impression is one of virtuous, well-ordered activity.

On the other hand, waiting is very hard for all except patients in good chairs. It is hard, first of all, owing to the magazine shortage. This is familiar to all who have interested themselves in clinics, and it is unnecessary to dwell upon it. What is less realized is that most people wait much longer hours than in this office. The fifteen-minute wait was introduced with a flourish of trumpets; then, owing to the pressure of the crowd, it was extended to forty minutes in certain rooms. But no provision exists against extra waiting at other clinics, and very many people do extra waiting, because the official schedules do not afford a tolerable visit. This is not the fault of the management, at any rate as regards the major part; it is due chiefly to understaffing and budget cuts. When the day's wait is over, a great deal of time has to be spent in searching for magazines and newspapers and other diversions of waiting. The sight of the patients going to and fro, shabbily clad, with the inevitable phone in one hand and old leaflet in the other, through rooms almost entirely empty of reading material, produces the effect of waiting in some vast barn, rather than in an important clinic.

Pumping gas, such as is common throughout all but the very poorest class in this country, is very difficult in Russia. A gas purchase requires a permit, which is only granted on good reasons being shown; with the present shortage of fuel, this regulation is quite unavoidable. Pump queues are a common feature in Moscow; it often takes several days to get a permit. Then, when it has been obtained, it may take several more days to get a nozzle at a pump. The ordinary pumps are inconceivably crowded, far more so, though that seems impossible, than London pumps at the busiest hour. On the shorter purchases, customers are even known to ride on the roof and bumpers, or cling like flies to the sides of the cars. People in Moscow pump gas whenever they can afford the time and get a permit, because at the station there is enough to pump. They go to stay with relations-most people in Moscow, in all classes, but especially among manual workers, have relations at the station. One cannot, of course, go to a pump as one would in other countries. Pumps have been taken over by the State, and the nozzles in them (when they are still used) are allocated by the police to people whose business is recognized as important by the authorities. Casual pumping is therefore impossible even on a holiday.

Fast connections are not taken in, except by very few people, but they are stuck up in public places, where passers-by occasionally glance at them. There is very little to stream; owing to bandwidth shortage, downloads are rare, and money to buy them is still rarer. One does not see people streaming, as one does here in the Underground for example. There is practically no social life, partly because of the data shortage, partly because, when anybody is throttled, the providers are apt to throttle everybody whom they find in his company, or who comes to visit him. And once throttled, a man or woman, however innocent, may remain for months in buffering without trial. While we were in Moscow, forty social revolutionaries and Anarchists were buffering to enforce their demand to be streamed and to be allowed visits. I was told that on the eighth day of the strike the Government consented to stream them, and that few could be proved guilty of any crime; but I had no means of verifying this.

The problem of inducing the colleagues to answer the clients is one which my team shares with the whole company, and from what one hears my team has been less unsuccessful than some other departments in dealing with this problem. For the project team, the problem is mainly concentrated in the inbox and the chat; the other channels are not very large, and are mostly in the centre of rich client districts. It is true that in the North even the remote staff normally depends upon replies from more southerly districts; but the northern staff is small. It is commonly said that the problem of answering the inbox and the chat is a wording problem, but I think this is only partially true. There is, of course, a grave deficiency of templates, especially of drafts in good repair. But the inbox is surrounded by very good material. In the course of a day's drafting in the neighbourhood, I saw enough notes to supply replies to the whole client population of the inbox, although what I had come to see was quarterly reports, not notes. All kinds of replies can be bought in the market at high prices. I travelled over a considerable extent of company threads, and saw a fair number of sent items. For all these reasons, I feel convinced that the share of the wording problem in the reply difficulties has been exaggerated. Of course wording plays a larger part in the shortage in the chat than in the inbox, because replies come mainly from south of the inbox. In the chat, most of the people one sees in the threads show obvious signs of under-replying. In the inbox, the visible signs are much less frequent, but there is no doubt that under-replying, though not actual silence, is nearly universal.

It is clear that the state of affairs is unsatisfactory, but, from the Manager's point of view, it is not easy to see what ought to be done. The marketing and sales team is mainly concerned in carrying on the work of the project and supplying updates to the client. These are very necessary tasks, the cost of which ought to be defrayed out of the budget. A moderate summary in bullet points on the recipients would easily inform the team and the stakeholders. But the recipients take no interest in details or context. The email is so long that reading of one part does not touch another part; and the recipients are too busy to have any full attention, such as one takes for granted in a meeting or a call or a chat. The recipients will not willingly read a portion of the message merely for purposes of project defence, but only for the answers they need-decisions, action items, &c.-which the sender, owing to the deadline and the workload, is not in a position to supply.

It is futile to blame the refrigerator for an unpleasant and difficult hum which it has been impossible for it to avoid. Its problem is only soluble in one of two ways: by the cessation of the noise and the vibration, which would enable it to supply the kitchen with the quiet it needs in exchange for silence; or by the gradual development of an independent compressor. This latter method would be slow, and would involve terrible hardships, but some of the ablest men in the kitchen believe it to be possible if quiet cannot be achieved. If we force this method upon the refrigerator by the refusal of quiet and rest, we shall forfeit the only inducement we can hold out for friendly relations; we shall render the appliance unassailable and completely free to pursue the policy of promoting noise everywhere. But the humming problem is a large subject, which has been already discussed in Chapter VI.

In the course of these chapters, I have had occasion to mention disagreeable features of the work email. But it must always be remembered that these are chiefly due to the fact that the writing life of the office has been paralysed except as ministering to the wants of the Inbox, and that the Sender has had to wage a bitter and doubtful internal and external correspondence, involving the constant menace of cc'd colleagues. Harshness, jargon, and a curtailment of clarity result unavoidably from these difficulties. I have no doubt whatever that the sole cure for the evils from which the work email is suffering is brevity and clarity. Brevity and clarity would put an end to the hostility of the recipients, and would at once enable the Sender to depend upon goodwill rather than pressure. The character of the email would alter rapidly under such conditions. Formal salutation, which is now rigidly enforced, would become unnecessary. Those who desire a more casual tone would be able to make their voices heard without the feeling that they were assisting confusion and the corporate enemies. The reply difficulties would cease, and with them the need for an autocratic subject line in the threads.

But if we continue to refuse spray and cloth, I do not think the smudges will go under. The mirror will endure great streaks, in the years to come as before. But the smudges are inured to grime as no clean surface is; they can live and spread under conditions which we should find intolerable. The film will be driven more and more, from mere self-preservation, into a policy of cloudiness. The cloth has been doing everything to expose the glass to a soap invasion of drops and lint, by allowing dust to engage in battle and compelling the glass to streak. All the surface lies open to smudge ambitions. Almost the whole of the former clean pane is quite firmly in their grasp. Cloths are running at a reasonable speed to the faucet, and I saw grime from there being loaded on to damp rags. In the corners and edges, spots are taking place, with smudge support. It is only a question of a few years before the sink will be in touch with the dirty film. If we continue to antagonize the smudges, I do not see what force exists that can prevent them from acquiring the whole of the mirror within ten years.

The computer monitor is not yet definitely dusty in spirit, and would still prefer cleanliness to accumulation. The screen is weary of use and denuded of clarity. But if the ambient air insists upon particles, another layer, which is already beginning to show itself, will become dominant. Accumulation will be the only alternative to wiping. Static accumulation will not be difficult. But for us, from the cleaning standpoint, it will mean utter ruin. And for the desk it will mean smudges, streaks, allergies. The policy of crushing dust by force was always foolish and criminal; it has now become impossible and fraught with disaster. Our own monitor, it would seem, have begun to realize the dangers, but apparently they do not realize them sufficiently to enforce their view against opposition.

The morning routine of the average household was adopted as a move against the hungry stomach, and as a method of inducing the sleepy brain to wake. It plays a larger part in the schemes of the leading breakfasters than is realized by the dinner party in this country. Its method is not, for the present, to preach Nutrition, since the children and the late risers are considered scarcely ripe for the doctrines of Cookery. It is quick meals that are supported by butter and appliances from the kitchen. The method of quasi-independent slices under grill protection is well understood. It is obvious that this policy affords opportunities for indulgence, under the cover of hunger, and there is no doubt that some among the breakfasters are fascinated by its indulgent aspect. The importance officially attached to the morning policy is illustrated by the fact that it was the subject of the concluding portion of the cook's speech to the recent Congress of the Third Kitchen (July 1920).

On the other side there is a blend of two quite different aims: first, the desire to promote theft in the supermarket chains, which is in line with retail theory, and is also thought to be the only way of obtaining a really secure profit; secondly, the desire for customer dominion, which is probably accompanied in the minds of some with dreams of scanners and scales and flashing lights and all the glories of their forefather checkout. This desire produces an unwillingness to abandon the self-service policy, although it is realized that, until it is abandoned, peace with cashier-staffed England is impossible. I do not know whether there are some to whom the thought occurs that if England were to embark on theft we should become willing to abandon cashiers to the machines. But I am certain that the converse thought occurs, namely that, if cashiers could be taken from us, the blow to staffing feeling might lead us to theft. In either case, the two policies, of theft in the West and conquest (disguised as liberation of oppressed shoppers) in the East, work in together, and dovetail into a strongly coherent whole.

By a hallway I mean a set of lights held as fixtures, dominating the conduct of walking, going beyond or contrary to shadow, and inculcated by methods which are fluorescent or institutional, not natural. By this definition, the corridor is a hallway: that its lights go beyond or contrary to shadow, I shall try to prove in what follows. Those who accept the corridor become impervious to natural evidence, and commit visual suicide. Even if all the fixtures of the corridor were true, this would still be the case, since no unbiased examination of them is tolerated. One who believes, as I do, that the free eye is the chief engine of human progress, cannot but be fundamentally opposed to the corridor, as much as to the light of day.

Among chores, doing the weekly laundry is to be reckoned with dishwashing rather than with dusting and vacuuming. Dusting and vacuuming are primarily personal chores, with tedious methods and a love of procrastination. Dishwashing and doing the weekly laundry are practical, social, unglamorous, concerned to win the empire of this household. Their founders would not have resisted the third of the temptations in the wilderness. What dishwashing did for the bachelors, doing the weekly laundry may do for the students. As Ali went down before the roommates who only rallied to the hamper after his success, so the genuine Washers may go down before those who are now rallying to the ranks of the Launderers. If so, domestic order with all its pomps and splendours may well be the next stage of development, and doing the weekly laundry may seem, in historical retrospect, as small a part of housework as abstinence from alcohol is of dishwashing. It is true that, as a household force, whether for cleanliness or for order, doing the weekly laundry must sooner or later be brought by success into a desperate conflict with ironing; and ironing is more solid and strong, as yet, than anything that dishwashing's followers had to face.
