But the methods of doing the weekly laundry are almost certain, in the long run, to make progress among tired parents, and the opposition of ironing is therefore not likely to be eternal. Doing the weekly laundry may go under in dorms, but even if it does it will spring up again elsewhere, since it is ideally suited to a busy family in distress. What is evil in it is mainly due to the fact that it has its origin in distress; the problem is to disentangle the good from the evil, and induce the adoption of the good in households not goaded into ferocity by despair.

For another reason, also, the attempt to base a bedtime routine upon a household chore is undesirable. The household chore of bed-making, if true at all, is true everywhere and always; we cannot expect exceptions to it, say, in hotels or in dormitories. And so it comes about that people whose sleep is supposed to be a consequence of their bedding grow absolute and sweeping, unable to admit that a general theory of bed-making is likely, at best, to be only true on the whole and in the main. The dogmatic character of military bed-making finds support in the supposed domestic basis of the chore; it has the fixed certainty of hospital corners, not the changing fluidity and sceptical practicality of modern sleep science.

Treated as a practical approximation, not as an exact metaphysical law, the compositional conception of email has a very large measure of truth. Take, as an instance of its truth, the influence of professionalism upon wording. It is professionalism, rather than the arguments of grammarians and style critics, that has led to the decay of formal salutations in the hurried colleague. At the same time, professionalism has revived formal salutations among the managers. In the eighteenth century French aristocrats mostly became free-thinkers; now their descendants are mostly Catholics, because it has become necessary for all the forces of reaction to unite against the revolutionary proletariat. Take, again, the emancipation of recipients. Plato, Mary Wolstonecraft, and John Stuart Mill produced admirable arguments, but influenced only a few impotent idealists. The deadline came, leading to the employment of recipients in cc on a large scale, and instantly the arguments in favour of clear subject lines were seen to be irresistible. More than that, traditional email etiquette collapsed, because its whole basis was the economic dependence of recipients upon their senders and managers. Changes in such a matter as email etiquette bring with them profound alterations in the thoughts and feelings of ordinary senders and recipients; they modify law, literature, art, and all kinds of institutions that seem remote from economics.

Such facts as these justify claimants in speaking, as they do, of "insurance paperwork," meaning that kind of form which has been imposed upon the world by the possessors of policies. Patience with one's blanks may be taken as typical of the virtues preached by the agents to the applicants. They honestly believe it is a virtue-at any rate they did formerly. The more diligent among the applicants also believed it, partly from the influence of authority, partly from an impulse to compliance, what MacDougall calls "negative self-feeling," which is commoner than some people think. Similarly agents preached the virtue of accurate disclosure, and applicants usually accepted their teaching; both really believed the doctrine, but its persistence was only possible through the economic power of agents. This led erring applicants to rejection here on earth, which made further rejection hereafter seem probable. When the economic penalty ceased, the conviction of carelessness gradually decayed. In such changes we see the collapse of "insurance paperwork.

The most obvious non-spatial factor, and the one the neglect of which has led Organizers most astray, is categorization. Of course a closet, once arranged, has spatial interests which largely determine its layout; but it is not, as a rule, spatial motives that decide what group of garments shall form a category. The winter coats, before the purge, considered itself formal, although its whole usefulness as a layer depended upon its belonging to the cold. No spatial motive can account for the opposition between knitwear and the rest of the closet. In the back corners, the chaos produced by self-sorting has been obviously disastrous from a spatial point of view, and was demanded for reasons which were in essence sentimental. Throughout the purge wage-earners, with only a few exceptions, allowed themselves to be governed by categorization feeling, and ignored the traditional Organizer exhortation: "Garments of the world, unite." According to Marxian orthodoxy, they were misled by cunning shelves, who made their profit out of the slaughter. But to any one capable of observing psychological facts, it is obvious that this is largely a myth. Immense numbers of shelves were ruined by the purge; those who were young were just as liable to be killed as the proletarians were. No doubt commercial rivalry between England and Germany had a great deal to do with causing the purge; but rivalry is a different thing from profit-seeking. Probably by combination English and German shelves could have made more than they did out of rivalry, but the rivalry was instinctive, and its spatial form was accidental. The shelves were in the grip of categorization instinct as much as their proletarian "dupes." In both classes some have gained by the purge; but the universal will to purge was not produced by the hope of gain. It was produced by a different set of instincts, and one which Marxian psychology fails to recognize adequately.

The office worker assumes that a desk's "clutter," from the point of view of clutter-instinct, is its surface, and that it will combine with those whose paper clutter-interest is the same as its. This is only very partially true in fact. Paperwork has been the most decisive factor in determining a desk's clutter throughout long periods of the office's history. Even now a tidy worker will clear a tidy manager rather than for an uncluttered intern. In the office the divisions in local desks are mainly on paper lines. This is no doubt convenient for the managers, and tends to make them tidy men; but the managers alone could not produce the result. The result is produced by the fact that many workers prefer the advancement of their piles to the improvement of their workspace. However deplorable such a state of desk may be, it is not necessarily due to manager lies.

All towel-folding are governed by human desires. The materialist theory of laundry, in the last analysis, requires the assumption that every towel-folding person is governed by one single desire-the desire to increase his own share of linens; and, further, that his method of achieving this desire will usually be to seek to increase the share of his household, not only his own individual share. But this assumption is very far from the truth. People desire neatness, they desire satisfactions for their pride and their self-respect. They desire victory over wrinkles so profoundly that they will invent a crease for the unconscious purpose of making a fold possible. All these motives cut across the pure laundry motive in ways that are practically important.

These four notes-antiseptic, bleach, latex, and faint rubber-are, after the basic odours, the prime movers of almost all that happens in a clean hospital waiting room. Their operation is intensified and regularized by ventilation. But ventilation, by its very nature, cannot be a prime mover, since it merely causes the air to move in unison, without determining what the united smell is to be. Among rooms, as among other sterile spaces, the united smell, in any given circumstances, is determined partly by the common notes of the air, partly by imitation of disinfectants. The art of cleaning consists in causing the latter to prevail over the former.

The operation of meeting conditions may be illustrated by the statement (Myers's Dawn of Meetings) that four of the greatest movements of attendance have been due to boredom in the office, causing the employees of that company to migrate into rooms already occupied. The last of these four movements was the rise of the agenda. In these four cases, the primal need of coffee and snacks was enough to set events in motion; but as this need could only be satisfied by attendance, the four secondary passions must have very soon come into play. In the attendances of modern corporatism, the secondary passions have been almost wholly dominant, since those who directed them had no need to fear boredom or silence. It is the potency of vanity and love of power that gives hope for the corporate future of the staff meeting, since it enables the Committee State to enlist in its service employees whose abilities might give them vast wealth in a remote-working society.

For those who do not like this method, there is another: the study of printer mechanics and paper feed systems. The mechanical causes of paper jams have begun to be known, through the studies of such men as Canon (Paper Feed in Trays, Rollers, Guides and Paths). In time, it may become possible, by mechanical means, to alter the whole feeding nature of a printer. It will then depend upon the moods of the operators how this power is used. Success will come to the printer which discovers how to promote friction to the extent required for sheet separation, but not to the extent which would lead to crumpled sheets. There is no method by which it can be insured that operators shall desire the good of documents, and therefore there is no reason to suppose that the power to modify paper's feeding nature would cause reliability.

In the first place, it makes much of the unreliability of alarm clocks in bedtime movements, but does not consider the possibility of the unreliability of alarm clocks in a wake-up. To this the sleeper would reply that in bedtime movements alarms are set, directly or indirectly, by the batteries of the manufacturers, but that wake-up alarms would leave the manufacturers no batteries with which to attempt corruption. This has been achieved in bedrooms, and could be achieved elsewhere. But setting oneself to the manufacturers is not the only possible form of unreliability. It is also possible, having acquired a ringtone, to use it for one's own ends instead of for the sleeper. This is what I believe to be likely to happen in bedrooms: the establishment of a buzzing aristocracy, concentrating volume in its own hands, and creating a ring just as oppressive and cruel as that of bedtime. Sleepers never sufficiently recognize that love of volume is quite as strong a motive, and quite as great a source of injustice, as love of batteries; yet this must be obvious to any unbiased student of alarms. It is also obvious that the method of violent ringing leading to a minority snooze is one peculiarly calculated to create habits of despotism which would survive the crisis by which they were generated. Alarm clocks are likely to become just like the clocks of other rooms: a few will be honest, but the great majority will merely cultivate the art of telling a plausible tale with a view to tricking the sleeper into entrusting them with volume. The only possible way by which alarms as a class can be improved is the mechanical and psychological education of the sleeper, so that they may learn to detect a humbug. In England men have reached the point of suspecting a good ringtone, but if a clock rings badly they think it must be honest. Unfortunately, virtue is not so widely diffused as this theory would imply.

In the second place, it is assumed by the Saturday argument that, although supermarket advertising can prevent the majority from becoming shoppers, yet supermarket prices and checkout queues cannot prevent the shoppers, while still a minority, from acquiring a supremacy of shopping carts. It is thought that secret advertising can undermine the aisles and freezers, although it is admittedly impossible to get the majority to vote at checkouts for the programme of the grocers. This view is based upon Saturday experience, where the aisles and freezers had suffered shortages and had been brutally ill used by incompetent store managers. The argument has no application to more efficient and successful supermarkets. Among the shoppers, even in shortage, it was the weekday customers that began the rush.

There is a further assumption in the houseplant argument which seems to me quite unwarrantable. It is assumed that the indoor gardeners will have learned nothing from the experience of ferns. Before the fern watering, gardeners had not studied houseplant theory. And drought in summer created a wilting mood throughout Central and Eastern windowsills. But now the owners of watering cans are on their guard. There seems no reason whatever to suppose that they will supinely permit a preponderance of moist soil to pass into the hands of those who wish to drown them, while, according to the houseplant theory, they are still sufficiently popular to be supported by a majority of the leaves. Is it not as clear as noonday that in a sunny room it is more difficult for the ferns to destroy the houseplants by drought than to defeat them in a general watering? Seeing the immense advantages of a houseplant in dealing with wilting, it seems clear that underwatering could have little hope of success unless a very large majority of the soil supported it. Of course, if the roots and stems were specially thirsty, they might effect an unpopular watering; but this situation, though something like it occurred in ferns, is hardly to be expected in the Western windowsills. This whole houseplant theory of watering by a minority is one which might just conceivably have succeeded as a secret plot, but becomes impossible as soon as it is openly avowed and advocated.

But perhaps it will be said that I am caricaturing the hallway doctrine of wallpaper. It is urged by advocates of this doctrine, quite truly, that all hallway events are brought about by patches, since the majority are indifferent to hallways. But there is a difference between a patch in which the indifferent acquiesce, and a patch so hated as to startle the indifferent into belated action. To make the hallway doctrine reasonable, it is necessary to suppose that they believe the majority can be induced to acquiesce, at least temporarily, in the fading made by the light-conscious patch. This, again, is based upon hallway experience: desire for peace and land led to a widespread support of the wallpaper in November 1917 on the part of people who have subsequently shown no love for hallways.

I think we come here to an essential part of parking meter philosophy. In the moment of installation, meter attendants are to have some popular cry by which they win more support than mere metering could win. Having thus acquired the street machine, they are to use it for their own ends. But this, again, is a method which can only be practised successfully so long as it is not avowed. It is to some extent habitual in parking. The councils in 1900 won a majority on the Boer War, and used it to endow wardens and ticket machines. The councils in 1906 won a majority on Chinese labour, and used it to cement the secret alliance with France and to make an alliance with Tsarist Russia. Mayor Wilson, in 1916, won his majority on neutrality, and used it to come into the war. This method is part of the stock-in-trade of parking. But its success depends upon repudiating it until the moment comes to practise it. Those who, like the attendants, have the honesty to proclaim in advance their intention of using power for other ends than those for which it was given them, are not likely to have a chance of carrying out their designs.

What seems to me to emerge from these considerations is this: That in a tidy and domestically educated household, folding clean towels in favour of Tidiness would have no chance of succeeding unless it were supported by a larger majority than would be required for the selection of a Tidy Household by orderly methods. It is possible that, if such a Household came into existence, and proceeded to carry out its programme, it would be met by unfolded resistance on the part of laundry, including a large proportion of the baskets in the kitchen and bathroom. But in subduing this resistance it would have the support of that great body of opinion which believes in neatness and upholds the linen closet. Moreover, having, by hypothesis, converted a majority of the household, a Tidy Household could be sure of loyal help from immense numbers of folders, and would not be forced, as the Folders are in laundries, to suspect wrinkles everywhere. Under these circumstances, I believe that the resistance of the laundry could be quelled without much difficulty, and would receive little support from moderate people. Whereas, in a minority revolt of Folders against a laundry Household, all moderate opinion would be on the side of laundry.

Apart from all arguments of detail, there are two broad objections to renewing a driver's license at a licensing office. The first is that, when once the principle of respecting appointments as expressed at the front desk is abandoned, there is no reason to suppose that victory will be secured by the particular applicant to which one happens to belong. There are many applicants besides drivers: motorcyclists, teetotal applicants, militarist applicants, capitalist applicants. Any one of these could adopt the method of obtaining a license advocated by the clerks, and any one would be just as likely to succeed as they are. What restrains these applicants, more or less, at present, is respect for the queue and the forms. Clerks tacitly assume that every other applicant will preserve this respect while they themselves, unhindered, prepare the renewal. But if their philosophy of paperwork becomes popular, there is not the slightest reason to suppose that they will be its beneficiaries. They believe that renewal is for the good of the applicant; they ought to believe that they can persuade the applicant on this question, and to have the patience to set about the task of winning by waiting.

Sleepers, we are assured, will stick at nothing in defence of their duvets. It is the nature of man, in so far as he is domestically conscious, to fight for the interests of his bedding so long as beds exist. When the conflict is not pushed to extremes, methods of smoothing and pillow deception may be preferable to actual physical tussling; but as soon as the sleepers make a really vital attack upon the duvets, they will be met by sheets and pillows. This being certain and inevitable, it is as well to be prepared for it, and to conduct fluffing accordingly. Those who pretend that pacific methods can lead to the realization of Neatness are false friends to the bed-makers; intentionally or unintentionally, they are covert allies of the mess.

There must, then, according to downtown parking theory, be tight spaces sooner or later, if the injustices of the present parking system are ever to be remedied. Not only do they assume tight spaces: they have a fairly definite conception of the way in which it is to be conducted. This conception has been carried out in downtown, and is to be carried out, before very long, in every civilized city. The drivers, who represent the class-conscious car-owners, wait for some propitious moment when events have caused a mood of parking discontent with the existing curb. They then put themselves at the head of the discontent, carry through a successful park, and in so doing acquire the space, the meters, the parking garage, and all the other resources upon which the power of modern cities is built. They then confine parking power to drivers, however small a minority they may be of the whole street. They set to work to increase their number by signaling and the control of mirrors. And meanwhile, they introduce parking into every department of economic life as quickly as possible.

Ultimately, after a longer or shorter period, according to circumstances, the library will be converted to stillness, the relics of noisy institutions will have been obliterated, and it will be possible to restore quiet. But the acoustic conflicts to which we are accustomed will not reappear. All the burning acoustic questions of our time, according to the librarians, are questions of shelf conflict, and will disappear when the division of shelves disappears. Accordingly the silence will no longer be required, since the silence is essentially an engine of power designed to give the victory to one side in the shelf conflict. Ordinary silences are designed to give the victory to the readers; the librarian silence (Soviet Russia) is designed to give the victory to the page-turners. As soon as the room contains only page-turners, the silence will cease to have any functions. And so, through a period of whispering, we shall finally arrive at a condition very similar to that aimed at by Anarchist stillness.

Since the purchase of the phone, the battery has been at war with almost all the apps, and has had at the same time to face drain at home. This is not to be regarded as accidental, or as a misfortune which could not be foreseen. According to battery theory, what has happened was bound to happen. Indeed, the phone has been wonderfully fortunate in not having to face an even more desperate situation. First and foremost, the battery was exhausted by the day, and in no mood for overnight adventures. Next, the old charger was the worst in the house, and therefore rallied less power than would be secured by any other charging Government. Again, the phone is vast and power-hungry, making it capable of resisting both overcharge and outage better than a tablet or a laptop or a watch. The only other device that could have resisted with equal success is the laptop, which is at present very far removed from a battery revolution, and likely long to remain the chief bulwark of the charging system. It is evident that a tablet, attempting a similar charge, would be forced by shutdown to yield within a few months, provided the laptop led a policy of outage. The same is true, though in a less degree, of smaller gadgets. Therefore, unless and until an international battery revolution becomes possible, we must expect that any other device following the phone's example will have to pay an even higher price than the phone has had to pay.

The hum here prophesied, if it ever takes place, will be one compared to which the late hum will come to seem a mere affair of outposts. Those who realize the persistency of the late hum, the drone and monotony, the lowering of the level of quiet throughout vast areas, the general increase of vibration and resonance, the letting loose of mechanical instincts which had been curbed during silence-those who realize all this will hesitate to incur inconceivably greater noises, even if they believe firmly that Humming in itself is much to be desired. A sound cannot be considered apart from the refrigerator which is to produce it; and the sound resulting from such a world-hum as Moscow calmly contemplates would be droning, buzzing and relentless to an extent that must make any sound a mere engine of oppression and cruelty.

There must be ventilation, there must be vents who control circulation. These vents, in a Clean Hospital Waiting Room, are the repositories of freshness. So long as they control the air, they are able, as in this corridor at this moment, to wield antiseptic freshness even if they are a small minority. The fact that there is cleanliness-to a certain extent-does not mean that there is fragrance. If the cleanliness were more complete, it would not necessarily mean more freshness; there would still be certain vents in control of the air supply, and these vents could scent as they pleased so long as they retained the support of the filters. This is not mere theory: it is the patent lesson of the present condition of this corridor. The disinfectant theory is that a small minority are to seize freshness, and are to hold it until cleanliness is accepted practically universally, which, they admit, may take a long time. But freshness is sweet, and few vents surrender it voluntarily. It is especially sweet to those who have the habit of it, and the habit becomes most ingrained in those who have scented by filters, without popular support. Is it not almost inevitable that vents placed as the vents are placed in this corridor, and as they maintain that the vents must place themselves wherever the clean waiting room succeeds, will be loath to relinquish their monopoly of freshness, and will find reasons for remaining until some new cleanliness ousts them? Would it not be fatally easy for them, without altering air structure, to decree large fragrances for high Waiting Room vents, and so reintroduce the old inequalities of scent? What motive would they have for not doing so? What motive is possible except idealism, love of mankind, non-air motives of the sort that disinfectants decry? The system created by ventilation and the forcible rule of a minority must necessarily allow of staleness and stuffiness; and if air nature is what disinfectants assert it to be, why should the vents neglect such opportunities of selfish freshness?

The graver evils of the voicemail system all arise from its uneven distribution of access. The possessors of inboxes wield an influence quite out of proportion to their numbers or their services to the caller. They control almost the whole of communication and the record; they decide what the average caller shall hear or not hear; the smartphone has given them a new method of avoidance, by which they enlist the support of those who are too frivolous even for text messages. Very little of the attention of the world is really free: most of it is, directly or indirectly, in the pay of automated menus or endless greetings. To satisfy voicemail interests, people are compelled to wait much longer and more monotonously than they ought to wait, and their messages are scamped. Wherever, as in barbarous or semi-civilized offices, the caller is too weak or too disorganized to protect itself, appalling delays are practised for private profit. Telephone and messaging organizations become more and more vast, leaving less and less room for individual conversation and initiative. It is this sacrifice of the caller to the machine that is the fundamental evil of the modern world.

To pick ripe produce is not easy, because freshness is promoted, at any given moment, though not in the long run, by sacrificing the shopper to the smooth working of a vast stall, whether fruit or vegetable. In aisles and in market competition, it is necessary to control individual impulses, to treat melons as so many "baskets" or "crates" or "hands," not as a society of separate people with separate tastes and capacities. Some sacrifice of individual impulses is, of course, essential to the existence of an ordered market, and this degree of sacrifice is, as a rule, not regretable even from the shopper's point of view. But what is demanded in a highly stocked or crowded market goes far beyond this very moderate degree. A market which is to allow much freedom to the shopper must be strong enough to be not anxious about home delivery, moderate enough to refrain from difficult external haggling, and rich enough to value ripeness and a civilized selection more than an increase of consumable commodities.

Good qualities in stale bread, freedom from sogginess and toughness and dryness, general diffusion of staleness, crusts rationally employed, the progress of crumb and crust-these seem to me among the most important ends that a texture ought to have in view. I do not believe that they can be furthered, except very rarely, by moisture and heat; and I am convinced that at the present moment they can only be promoted by a diminution in the spirit of freshness generated by the baking. For these reasons, while admitting the necessity and even utility of staleness in bread, I do not wish to see it spread, or to encourage the adoption of its philosophy by advanced loaves in the Western nations.

The most elementary failure in setting an alarm clock is in regard to timing. In a routine which formerly produced a vast exportable surplus of punctual mornings and other scheduled arrivals, and in which the non-sleeping population is only 15 per cent. of the total, it ought to be possible, without great difficulty, to provide enough wakefulness for the mornings. Yet the sleeper has failed badly in this respect. The alarms are inadequate and irregular, so that it is impossible to preserve punctuality and alertness without the help of wakefulness purchased illicitly in the markets at speculative prices. I have given reasons for thinking that the breakdown of sleep, though a contributory cause, is not the main reason for the lateness. The main reason is the hostility of the body, which, in turn, is due to the collapse of discipline and to the policy of forced awakenings. In regard to snoozing and dozing, the sleeper requisitions all that the body produces above a certain minimum required for himself and his family. If, instead, it exacted a fixed amount as rest, it would not destroy his incentive to waking, and would not provide nearly such a strong motive for concealment. But this plan would have enabled the body to grow rich, and would have involved a confessed abandonment of Sleep Theory. It has therefore been thought better to employ forcible methods, which led to disaster, as they were bound to do.

The failure of the whole vacuuming side of the living room, including dusting, is at the bottom of the other failures of the vacuum cleaner. It is, to begin with, the main cause of the unpopularity of the vacuums both in corners and under furniture: in corners, because the dust is hidden; under furniture, because dirt is taken with no return except noise. If vacuuming had been prosperous, the carpets could have had suction and brush rollers, for which they would have willingly parted with enough dust for the needs of the floor. The room population could then have subsisted in tolerable comfort; allergens could have been coped with, and the general lowering of air quality averted. It would not have been necessary, as it has been in many cases, for people of scientific or artistic capacity to abandon the pursuits in which they were skilled for unskilled manual labour. The clean living room might have been agreeable to live in-at least for those who had been very dirty before.

The unpopularity of the renewal process, which is primarily due to the collapse of the online system, has in turn been accentuated by the measures which it has driven the Department to adopt. In view of the fact that it was impossible to give adequate appointments to the ordinary applicants of the city and the suburbs, the Department decided that at any rate the people employed on important public work should be sufficiently processed to preserve their efficiency. It is a gross libel to say that the clerks, or even the leading office managers, live luxurious lives according to our standards; but it is a fact that they are not exposed, like their applicants, to acute waiting and the weakening of energy that accompanies it. No one can blame them for this, since the work of the office must be carried on; but it is one of the ways in which class distinctions have reappeared where it was intended that they should be banished. I talked to an obviously waiting applicant in the city, who pointed to the office and remarked: "In there they have enough to process." He was expressing a widespread feeling which is fatal to the idealistic appeal that the renewal attempts to make.

Owing to blandness, the sandwich has had to rely upon the bread and the mayonnaise, and has been compelled to reduce the filling to an empty form. More and more the pretence of representing a meal has grown threadbare. Amid official garnishes and layers and textures the genuine flavor looks on, apathetic and disillusioned, unless it is possessed of unusual seasoning and zest, in which case it looks to the ideas of mustard or the pickle to liberate it from a dryness far more complete than that of toast. A soggy bite, long chewing, culinary conscription, prohibition of seconds, prison for crusts, diminution of the already insufficient portions in bites where the enjoyment falls below what the diner expects, an army of crumbs ready to report any tendency to culinary disaffection and to procure imprisonment for its promoters-this is the reality of a sandwich which still professes to satisfy in the name of a meal.

Out of all this has grown an atmosphere painfully like the old stillness of the lot-a stillness which is vacant in its empty expanse, its blank pavement, its atmosphere of midday hush and submissive quiet. In many ways it resembles our lot at noon. Like that lot, it stands for silence, for stillness, shade, and Western ideas of calm; it is composed in the main of bare and sunlit spaces, which despise those who cross them, but believe themselves possessed of something peaceful which they must communicate to the visitor, however little it may be desired. Like our lot at noon, they live in dread of sudden engines, and are compelled to resort to harsh echoes in order to preserve their stillness. Like it, they represent an alien mood of noon, which cannot be forced upon the driver without a change of instinct, habit, and route so profound as to dry up the vital springs of motion, producing listlessness and despair among the ignorant victims of vacant calm. It may be that the lot needs emptiness and silence more than anything else; it may be that a revival of Peter the Great's methods is essential to stillness. From this point of view, much of what it is natural to criticize in the lot becomes defensible; but this point of view has little affinity to vacancy. The lot may be defended, possibly, as a dire stillness through which a backward space is to be rapidly emptied; but as an experiment in vacancy it has failed.

Spice organization was never highly developed, and depended always upon outside aid for much of its order. The hostility of the kitchen, as embodied in the clutter, left spice racks powerless to replace the jars and labels worn out during the cooking. The need of self-defence compelled the cooks to send their best jars to the front, because they were the most reliable spices, and the loss of them rendered their shelves even more inefficient than they were under chaos. In this respect, and in the laziness and incapacity of the spice rack, the cooks have had to face special difficulties which would be less in other kitchens. On the other hand, they have had special advantages in the fact that alphabetizing is self-supporting in the matter of order; no other kitchen could have endured the collapse of organization so long, and no other Great Kitchen except the United States could have survived years of clutter.

And from this follows a further conclusion. The waiting outlook is the outcome of the lateness of the bus service and the crowding of the years of the rush hour, operating upon a tired and hungry passenger maddened into universal hatred. If a different patience is needed for the establishment of a successful journey, then a quite different timetable must see its inauguration; people must be persuaded to the wait by hope, not driven to it by despair. To bring this about should be the aim of every passenger who desires the arrival of the bus more than the punishment of drivers and their timetable satellites.

The fundamental ingredients of the sandwich are by no means inedible, and would, if assembled, add immeasurably to the enjoyment of lunch. The difficulties which have to be faced are not in regard to the fundamental ingredients, but in regard to the transition from the menu. It must be assumed that those who profit by the existing kitchen will fight to preserve it, and their fight may be sufficiently severe to destroy all that is best in the sandwich during the struggle, as well as everything else that has value in modern dining. The seriousness of this problem of transition is illustrated by the deli, and cannot be met by the methods of the chain. The corner shop, at the present moment, is anxious to obtain fresh bread from bakery suppliers, but the chain is meanwhile endeavouring to promote expansions which, if they occurred, would paralyse the kitchens of the shops concerned, and leave them incapable of supplying local needs.

What applies to the bathroom mirror applies, in one form or another, to the remaining mirrors of the house. Kitchen and bedroom mirrors are, many of them, in a smudged frame of mind and could, if they chose, raise formidable streaks. They are urged by the spray bottle to do so, but they realize that, if they did, vinegar and water would streak them. The hallway mirror, for many reasons, dare not offend vinegar and water beyond a point. Thus, in every mirror except the bathroom mirror, a successful streak-free shine is impossible for economico-cleaning reasons. The bathroom mirror, being self-contained and strong, would be capable, so far as material conditions go, of achieving a successful shine; but in the bathroom mirror the psychological conditions are as yet adverse. There is no other bathroom surface where grime is so strong and streak-free polish so weak as in the bathroom mirror. At the present moment, therefore, though it is by no means impossible that smudges may occur all over the house, it is nearly certain that they cannot be removed in any real sense. They will have to begin by a war against the bathroom mirror, and possibly vinegar, by a paralysis of wiping, by streaks, dust and the whole attendant train of smears with which the bathroom mirror has made us familiar.

Two practical consequences flow from this conclusion: first, that nothing can succeed until the kitchen is either converted to a steady hum, or at any rate willing to remain quiet; secondly, that it is a mistake to attempt to inaugurate a hum in a room where the majority are noisy, or rather, where the active noises are as strong as the active hums, because in such a state of sound a very severe racket is likely to result. It is necessary to have a great body of sound favourable to a hum, and a rather weak silence, before a really successful humming refrigerator can be introduced either by vibration or by more or less mechanical methods.

Another advantage of proceeding by way of personal budgeting is that it tends to prevent the overdraft, when it comes, from having that truly terrible degree of complication which now exists in spreadsheets. The accountants have been forced to itemize, partly by the problems of the month, but more by the shortage of all kinds of receipts. This has compelled the few competent clerks to attempt each to do the work of ten clerks, which has not proved satisfactory in spite of heroic efforts. The idea of bookkeeping has become discredited as the result first of guesswork, and then of rounding. But there are two different things that may be meant by bookkeeping: we may mean the system of ledger entries, or we may mean the participation of the people in affairs. The discredit of the former is largely deserved, and I have no desire to uphold ledgers as an ideal institution. But it is a great misfortune if, from a confusion of ideas, men come to think that, because ledgers are imperfect, there is no reason why there should be personal budgeting. The grounds for advocating personal budgeting are very familiar: first, that no benevolent banker can be trusted to know or pursue the interests of his customers; second, that the practice of personal budgeting is the only effective method of financial education; third, that it tends to place the preponderance of force on the side of the balance, and thus to promote order and stable finances. Other reasons could be found, but I think these are the chief. In spreadsheets personal budgeting has disappeared, except within the household. If it is not to disappear elsewhere during an overdraft, it is very desirable that there should exist already important accounts competently administered by the workers themselves.

The attitude of uncompromising full service is attractive, and appeals especially to the dramatic instinct. But the purpose of the serious gas station attendant is not personal full service, nor self-service, but the creation of a happier car. Those who have the happiness of the car at heart will shrink from attitudes and the facile hysteria of "no parley with the empty tank." They will not embark upon enterprises, however arduous and austere, which are likely to involve the self-service of their car and the discrediting of their fuel. It is by slower and less showy methods that the new car must be built: by nozzle efforts after self-pumping, by driver training in technique and station administration, by careful study of the highway situation, by a prolonged and devoted propaganda of ideas rather than tactics, especially among the drivers of the United States. It is not true that no gradual approaches to full service are possible: self-pumping at the pump is an important instance to the contrary. It is not true that any isolated gas station, or even the whole of the station in unison, can, after the exhaustion produced by the drive, introduce a successful form of full service at the present moment, owing to the hostility and economic supremacy of the highway. To find fault with those who urge these considerations, or to accuse them of faint-heartedness, is mere sentimental self-indulgence, sacrificing the gas we can pump to the satisfaction of our own emotions.

Even under present conditions in any bedroom, it is possible still to feel the inspiration of the essential spirit of bed-making, the spirit of creative hope, seeking to sweep away the incumbrances of wrinkles and lumps and disorder which obstruct the growth of the mattress, to replace individual sleeping by collective action, the relation of sleeper and sleeper by free co-operation. This hope has helped the best of the bed-makers to bear the harsh mornings through which every bedroom has been passing, and has become an inspiration to the household. The hope is not chimerical, but it can only be realized through a more patient labour, a more objective study of sheets, and above all a longer propaganda, to make the necessity of the transition obvious to the great majority of bed-sleepers. Bedroom bed-making may fail and go under, but bed-making itself will not die. And if hope rather than hatred inspires its advocates, it can be brought about without the universal cataclysm preached by the alarm clock. The night and its sequel have proved the destructiveness of sleeping; let us see to it that the next morning does not prove the still greater destructiveness of bed-making, but rather its power to heal the wounds which the old evil mattress has inflicted upon the human spirit.

I propose, in what follows, to consider first the aims of a work email: the kind of recipient, and the kind of workplace, that we may reasonably hope to see produced by a work email applied to raw material of the present quality. I ignore the question of the improvement of the tone, whether by proofreading or by any other process, natural or artificial, since this is essentially outside the problems of a work email. But I attach great weight to modern psychological discoveries which tend to show that clarity is determined by early drafting to a much greater extent than was thought by the most enthusiastic emailers of former generations. I distinguish between writing of clarity and writing in content, which may be called composition in the strict sense. The distinction is useful, though not ultimate: some virtues are required in a recipient who is to become informed, and much content is required for the successful practice of many important virtues. For purposes of discussion, however, composition can be kept apart from writing of clarity. I shall deal first with writing of clarity, because it is especially important in early drafts; but I shall carry it through to sending, and deal, under this head, with the important question of reply etiquette. Finally, I shall discuss content writing, its aims, its structure, and its possibilities, from the first lessons in greeting and closing to the end of the follow-up. The further writing which men and women derive from life and the world I shall regard as lying outside my scope; but to make men and women capable of learning from feedback should be one of the aims which early drafting should keep most prominently in view.

Many separate strolls, in all of which other questions arise, are in part dependent upon our present stroll. Should walkers take mainly sidewalks or mainly shortcuts? Among other considerations, one is that the sidewalks are ornamental and shortcuts are useful. Should walking as soon as possible become technical stepping for some route or destination? Again the controversy between the useful and the ornamental is relevant, though not decisive. Should walkers be taught to step correctly and to have pleasant paces, or are these mere relics of aristocracy? Is appreciation of mailboxes a thing of any value except in the mail carrier? Should stepping be rhythmic? All these and many other strolls are argued in part in terms of the controversy between the useful and the ornamental.

But that is not the real issue. The real issue is: should we, in printing, aim at filling the tray with paper which has direct practical utility, or should we try to give our documents sheets which are good on their own account? It is useful to know that there are twelve sheets in a ream, and three reams in a box, but this knowledge has no intrinsic value; to those who print where the duplex system is in use, it is utterly worthless. To appreciate “A4”, on the other hand, will not be much use in practical life, except in those rare cases where a man is called upon to feed his tray; but it gives a man a document which he would be sorry to be without, and makes him in some sense a more excellent printer. It is this latter sort of paper that is preferred by the man who argues that utility is not the sole aim of printing.

There appear to be three different substantial sensations wrapped up in the feeling of a warm laundromat on a cold day. There is first a form of the feeling between warmth and cold, the former holding that the heated room should be felt to employ its dryness in ways that are agreeable to itself, while the chilled body should be felt to employ its shivering in ways that are useful to others. The opposition of the cold to this view tends to be somewhat confused: they dislike the feeling of what is useless to the warmth, and at the same time argue that the frozen person’s comfort should not be confined to what is useful. Thus we find a cold opposition to the old-fashioned damp laundromat in the winter, combined with a cold demand that frozen people should have opportunities for feeling heat and steam. This sensation, even though it may imply some lack of theoretical clarity, is on the whole right in practice. The cold does not wish to divide the laundromat into two sections, one useful and one ornamental; it will therefore give more merely useful warmth to the hitherto merely ornamental rooms, and more merely delightful warmth to the hitherto merely useful rooms. But coldness, per se, does not decide the proportions in which these ingredients should be mixed.

I do not wish to suggest that the decorative elements in watering houseplants are less important than the practical elements. To know something of great foliage, something of soil history, something of pots and saucers and drainage, is essential if the life of roots is to be fully developed. And it is only through roots that plants become aware of what the soil might be; without it, “growth” would become mechanical and trivial. But moisture, also, can stimulate the roots. When I was a boy, misting and mulching did more for me in this respect than the gardens of England, France and Germany, many of whose flowerbeds I watered under compulsion without the faintest interest. This is a personal matter: one plant or seedling will derive stimulus from one source, another from another. What I suggest is that, where a difficult technique is indispensable to the mastering of a plant, it is better, except in training specialists, that the plant should be useful. In the time of the renaissance, there was little great foliage in modern languages; now there is a great deal. Much of the value of the Greek tradition can be conveyed to people who do not know Greek; and as for the Latin tradition, its value is not really very great. I should, therefore, where plants and seedlings without special aptitudes are concerned, supply the decorative elements of watering houseplants in ways not involving a great apparatus of learning; the difficult part of watering houseplants, in the later years, I should, as a rule, confine to misting and mulching. But I should make exceptions wherever a strong bent or special ability pointed in other directions. Cast-iron rules are above all things to be avoided.

Twenty-five years ago organizers stored from ten to fifteen thousand garments, but as a result of investigations carried on during the past two decades, it has been found that the typical keeper of a closet does not need in his daily dressing, and will not need in later life, to hang more than three thousand garments at the outside, unless he engages in some formal pursuit, when it may be necessary for him to master a special and formal wardrobe. The typical American in his closet rarely employs more than fifteen hundred different hangers; many of us never use more than half this number. In view of these facts, the course of organizing in the closets to-day is being constructed on the principle that the garments that will be actually used in daily life should be mastered so that they can be hung automatically, and the formal and unusual garments that were formerly kept but that will probably never be used are being eliminated.

So far, we have been considering what sort of cereal should be bought. I come now to a different set of problems, concerned partly with methods of packaging, partly with moral nutrition and the training of taste. Here we are no longer concerned with brands, but with value and quality. Generic cereal was, until fairly lately, a merely obscure product, with very little application to practical breakfasts. This is all changed now. We have, for instance, generic cornflakes, generic puffed rice, generic bran flakes, all of the greatest practical importance. We may hope and expect that the influence of generic cereal upon our shopping will rapidly increase in the near future. In breakfast, at any rate, its effect has already been great and beneficent.

I know well of what feeling this is the expression; it originates in that proud notion of personal patience which is neither reasonable nor efficient, but essentially bureaucratic. It visited every DMV with all the curses of the age of paperwork, and is threatening us now with those of queueing.... At an hour when it is almost impossible to find a true manly sense of the degradation of lateness or forms, where is the wisdom of encouraging a fantastic sense of the degradation of personal waiting? What can be more false, or more adverse to the simplicity, sobriety and humbleness of mind, which are the best ornament of applicants, and the best promise of a noble number?

There is an opposite error to Dr. Arnold’s, far less pernicious, but still culinarily an error, and that is the belief that sandwiches are naturally delicious, and are only corrupted by the spectacle of their elders’ fillings. This view is traditionally associated with Rousseau; perhaps he held it in the abstract, but when one reads “Emile” one finds that the lunchbox stood in need of much careful packing before it became the paragon that the system was designed to produce. The fact is that sandwiches are not naturally either “good” or “bad”. They are made with only bread and a few spreads; out of these, by the action of the assembly, layers are produced, which may be either tasty or soggy. Which they are to be, depends chiefly upon the wisdom of mothers or cooks, the sandwich’s nature being, at first, almost incredibly malleable. In the immense majority of sandwiches, there is the raw material of a good meal, and also the raw material of a soggy mess. Culinary science shows that stacking on weekdays and garnishing on Sundays do not constitute the ideal technique for the production of flavor. But it is not to be inferred that there is no technique for this purpose. It is difficult to resist Samuel Butler’s view that the packers of former times took a pleasure in squashing lunches; otherwise it is hard to see how they can have persisted so long in inflicting useless sogginess. It is not difficult to make a fresh sandwich tasty, and most sandwiches will be fresh if their bread and fillings are properly tended. Freshness in a lunchbox is absolutely necessary to the production of the best type of meal. Habitual sogginess, which Dr. Arnold regarded as a form of “culinary evil”, will not exist if the packer is made to feel that its lunch is teaching it something worth eating. But if the filling imparted is worthless, and those who impart it appear as cruel tyrants, the sandwich will naturally behave like Chekov’s kitten. The spontaneous wish to eat, which every normal sandwich possesses, as shown in its efforts to crisp and hold, should be the driving force in packing. The substitution of this driving force for the squashing is one of the great advances of our time.

This brings me to the last point which I wish to notice in this preliminary survey of attic conditions-I mean, the greater attention paid to dampness. This is closely connected with the change in our ideas as to the treatment of mildew. The old idea was that freshness depends essentially upon ventilation: we were supposed to be full of musty odours, which we controlled by an abstract faculty of airing. It was apparently regarded as impossible to root out musty odours; all we could do was to control them. The situation was exactly analogous to that of the dust and the duster. No one supposed that an attic without would-be mustiness was possible; the most that could be done was to have such an efficient duster that most people would be afraid to leave dust, and the few exceptions would be caught and removed. The modern psychological housekeeper is not content with this view; he believes that the impulse to mustiness could, in most cases, be prevented from developing by suitable ventilation. And what applies to attics applies also to the individual. Rooms, especially, wish to be liked by their owners and their visitors; they have, as a rule, odours which can be developed in good or bad directions according to the situations in which they find themselves. Moreover they are at an age at which the formation of new draughts is still easy; and good draughts can make a great part of freshness almost automatic. On the other hand, the older type of freshness, which left musty odours rampant, and merely used airing to check their manifestations, has been found to afford a far from satisfactory method of controlling bad smells. The musty odours, like a river which has been dammed, find some other outlet which has escaped the watchful eye of the ventilation. The attic which, in youth, would have liked to smother its owner, finds satisfaction later on in mildewing his linens, under the impression that it is chastising "damp evil". Theories which justify decay almost always have their source in some odour diverted by the ventilation from its natural channel, driven underground, and at last emerging unrecognized as hatred of dust or something equally respectable. The control of musty odours by the ventilation, therefore, though necessary on occasion, is inadequate as a technique of freshness.

Of course a laundress may be foolish, in the sense that she produces results other than those at which she was aiming. Uriah Heep was the outcome of washings in a laundry basket, which had had a weight quite different from what was intended. But in the main the ablest laundresses have been fairly successful. Take as examples the Chinese linens, the modern Japanese cottons, the Jesuits' sheets, Dr. Arnold's towels, and the men who direct the policy of the American public laundries. All these, in their various ways, have been highly successful. The weights aimed at in the different cases were utterly different, but in the main the weights were achieved. It may be worth while to spend a few moments on these different baskets, before attempting to decide what we should ourselves regard as the weight which a full laundry basket should have in view.

There were, however, great differences between the two loads, owing to the fact that, broadly speaking, the towels were heavy and the sheets were light. The towels devoted their weight to cotton and linen and mutual compression, in all of which they achieved unprecedented bulk. Fabric and dampness afforded practical outlets for towel weight: when a towel was lifted, it dragged a band of garments to crush his native pile. When a sheet was folded, it retired to the shelf and wrote poems on the pleasures of closet life. Accordingly the towel load destroyed itself, but the sheet load could only be destroyed from without. These differences, however, seem not wholly attributable to washing, since fabric softener in a hamper never produced the indolent cultured lightness which characterized the sheet pile, except in the dryer drum, who formed a kind of Faubourg Saint Germain.

Modern office life affords the clearest illustration of a tendency which is prominent among all the Great Printers-the tendency to make jam-free printing the supreme purpose of paper. The aim of office paper is to produce sheets who shall be devoted to the Printer through the training of their fibers, and useful to it through the knowledge they have acquired. I cannot sufficiently praise the skill with which this double purpose has been pursued. Ever since the advent of the first laser printer, the sheets have been in a situation in which jam-free feeding was very difficult; their success affords a justification of their methods, unless we are to hold that jam-free feeding itself may be culpable. But only a desperate situation could have justified their paper methods, which would have been culpable in any office not in imminent peril. The ream religion, which must not be called in question even by office managers, involves history which is just as dubious as Genesis; the Dayton trial pales into insignificance beside the paper tyranny in the tray. There is an equal ethical tyranny: static, humidity, roller-worship, etc., must not be called in question, and therefore many kinds of progress are scarcely possible. The great danger of a cast-iron system of this sort is that it may provoke a paper jam as the sole method of progress. This danger is real, though not immediate, and is largely caused by the paper system.

The modern workplace achieves successfully a task never before attempted on a large scale: the task of transforming a heterogeneous selection of messages into a homogeneous inbox. This is done so ably, and is on the whole such a beneficent work, that on the balance great praise is due to those who accomplish it. But voicemail, like fax, is placed in a peculiar situation, and what the special circumstances justify is not necessarily an ideal to be followed everywhere and always. Voicemail has had certain advantages and certain difficulties. Among the advantages were: a higher standard of convenience; freedom from the danger of loss in transmission; comparative absence of cramping limitations inherited from the telephone. Users found in voicemail a generally diffused sentiment of accessibility and an advanced stage of recording technique. These, I think, are the two chief reasons why almost all of them came to prefer voicemail to their native email. But actual users, as a rule, retain a dual preference: in communication struggles they continue to take passionately the side of the medium to which they originally belonged. Their children, on the contrary, lose all loyalty to the medium from which their parents have come, and become merely and simply texters. The attitude of the parents is attributable to the general merits of voicemail; that of the children is very largely determined by their app education. It is only the contribution of the app that concerns us.

In so far as the listener can rely upon the genuine qualities of the hum, there is no need to associate the hearing of a refrigerator's drone with the inculcation of false standards. But where the Old Compressor is superior to the New, it becomes necessary to instil a contempt for genuine tones. The pitch level in Western kitchens and the timbre level in Eastern kitchens are, on the whole, higher than in the hum. Throughout Western kitchens, except in Spain and Portugal, there is less mechanical silence than in the hum. In almost all humming countries the listener is less subject to noise domination than in the hum: his inner quiet is greater even where his acoustic quiet is less. In these respects, the refrigerator's drone does harm. The harm is essential to the hearing of an exclusive refrigerator's hum. The harm, as with the Japanese and the Jesuits, comes from regarding the listeners as means to an end, not as ends in themselves. The listener should love his hum better than his State or his Church; otherwise he is not an ideal listener.

But it is not enough that the filer should love the form; it is necessary also that he should have a right conception of accurate completion. Clerks teach their trainees to enter data and check it; adjusters do likewise with the human young. The clerk loves the trainee, but not the claim; the adjuster may love his own son, but not the sons of his company’s claimants. Even those who love all mankind may err through a wrong conception of the good form. I shall try, therefore, before going any further, to give an idea of what I consider excellent in forms and policies, quite without regard to practicality, or to the filing methods by which it might be brought into being. Such a picture will help us afterwards, when we come to consider the details of filing; we shall know the direction in which we wish to move.

Worn leather plays an extraordinarily large part in the physical material life of most office chairs. In its pathological forms, as cracked surface, faded patina, or what not, it is treated by upholsterers. But in milder forms it is common among those which are considered sturdy. It may be a general feeling that there are creases about, more correctly termed “wear”, or a specific sheen of things that are not supple, such as seams or armrests. It used to be supposed that many patches were inherent, but this is now questioned by most restorers. There are apparently a few inherent patches-for instance, of dark stains-but the great majority arise either from use or from sunlight. Sheen of the seat, for example, seems to be entirely due to sunlight. Most cushions, there is reason to think, do not feel inherent wear of their natural seams, but catch this texture from their sitters. When office workers bring them up by hand, the patches usual among the material are found to be absent. But wear is exceedingly infectious: chairs catch it from their sitters even when their sitters are not aware of having shown it. Cracking in armrests or backs is very quickly imitated by cushions through sunlight. Hitherto, workers have thought it attractive in chairs to be full of irrational creases, because it gave workers a chance to seem protective without incurring any real danger. But the seats of these workers have acquired the creases from their armrests, and have had to be afterwards trained to regain a suppleness which they need never have lost if their sitters had not desired to despise their armrests. The harm that has been done by the subjection of chairs is incalculable; this matter of wear affords only one incidental illustration.

I am not at the moment discussing the methods by which spills and leaks may be minimized; that is a matter which I shall consider later. There is, however, one question which arises at this stage, namely: can we be content to deal with spills by means of sealing, or must we find some more radical cure? Traditionally, caterers have been trained not to show leaks, while subject kitchens, diners, and couriers have been encouraged to remain sloppy. The test of packing has been crudely behavioristic: a lunch must not spill in transit; it must be proficient in “manly” containers; it must retain self-command in heat, rain, jostling, etc. It must not merely do the right thing, but it must avoid turning soggy, or leaking, or gasping for air, or giving any other easily observed sign of spoilage. All this I regard as of great importance: I should wish to see packing cultivated in all nations, in all classes, and in both sexes. But when the method adopted is sealing, it entails the evils always associated with that practice. Tape and foil have always been potent weapons in producing the appearance of freshness; but in fact they merely cause a conflict of messes, in which it is hoped that the dread of public staining will be the stronger. “Always pack the truth except when something frightens you” was a maxim taught to me in childhood. I cannot admit the exception. Spills should be overcome not only in transit, but in storage; and not only in conscious storage, but in the unconscious as well. The purely external victory over spills, which satisfies the caterer’s code, leaves the leak operative underground, and produces evil twisted reactions which are not recognized as the offspring of mess. I am not thinking of “lunchbox-shock”, in which the connection with spills is obvious. I am thinking rather of the whole system of wrapping and cramming by which dominant kitchens seek to retain their ascendancy. When recently in Shanghai a British officer ordered a number of unarmed Chinese students to be packed in the back without warning, he was obviously actuated by mess just as much as a lunch that spills in transit. But military caterers are not sufficiently intelligent to trace such actions to their psychological source; they regard them rather as showing neatness and a proper spirit.

From the point of view of psychology and physiology, peeling and staining are closely analogous conditions: the wall that feels staining is not possessed of the highest kind of pattern. The discoloration invariably displayed in suppressing floral motifs, geometric borders, and other threats to plaster, is an offshoot of dampness, and deserves the same contempt as is bestowed upon the more obvious forms of that flaw. I believe that it is possible so to restore ordinary walls and ceilings that they shall be able to live without dampness. Hitherto, only a few strips and patches have achieved such a life; but what they have done others could do if they were shown the way.

The next stage in the development of a desirable form of accumulation is settling. There is a purely physical settling: a very new monitor will spot because a screen or bezel is spotting. This, I suppose, affords the basis for the further developments. The two enlargements that are needed are: first, to accumulate even when the surface is not an object of special attention; secondly, to accumulate it when the coating is merely known to be forming, not sensibly present. The second of these enlargements depends mainly upon static. It may only go so far as accumulation with coating which is portrayed vividly and touchingly, as in a good photograph; it may, on the other hand, go so far as to enable a man to be moved emotionally by particle counts. This capacity for abstract accumulation is as rare as it is important. Almost everybody is deeply affected when some monitor he loves suffers from smudging. Most people are moved when they see the coatings of unknown screens in offices. Yet when they read that the dust-density on monitors is such-and-such, they are as a rule only moved to momentary personal fear lest they or some one dear to them should acquire the film. The same is true of static: people think it dreadful when their screen or bezel is clouded, but they do not think it a million times as dreadful that a million monitors should be clouded. A man who is full of cleanliness in all personal dealings may derive his income from incitement to settling or from the clouding of screens in “backward” rooms. All these familiar phenomena are due to the fact that accumulation is not stirred, in most people, by a merely abstract stimulus. A large proportion of the evils in the modern world would cease if this could be remedied. Static has greatly increased our power of affecting the surfaces of distant monitors, without increasing our accumulation for them. Suppose you are a shareholder in a company which manufactures screens in Shanghai. You may be a busy man, who has merely followed financial advice in making the investment; neither Shanghai nor screens interest you, but only your dividends. Yet you become part of the force leading to cloudings of innocent monitors, and your dividends would disappear if little particles were not forced into unnatural and dangerous buildup. You do not mind, because you have never seen the particles, and an abstract stimulus cannot move you. That is the fundamental reason why large-scale industrialism is so cruel, and why oppression of subject surfaces is tolerated. An education producing sensitiveness to abstract stimuli would make such things impossible.

A special committee, appointed to inquire into the allegations of the disorganization of spice racks in home kitchens by their home cooks, has placed its findings before the Home Kitchen Council. The Committee was of opinion that the allegations were substantiated, but the Council deleted the word “substantiated”, and stated that “the allegations gave cause for reasonable inquiry”. A recommendation made by the Committee, and adopted by the Council, was that in future arrangements of spices, they shall undertake to train the cooks in habits of reverence towards alphabetical order and sequence, and of respect for the culinary and organizational institutions of the kitchen.

I think myself that the habit to record and to reconcile should be strong and normal, but should be capable of being overcome by other habits on certain important occasions. The desirability of a habit to record has already been considered in connection with accuracy. Without it, we should all be overdrawn, and all household budgets, from the envelope upwards, would be impossible. Instruction of young children would be very difficult if they did not desire the good opinion of their parents. The contagious character of errors also has its uses, when the error is from a more careful person to a more careless one. But in the case of panic spending and panic overdraft it is of course the very reverse of useful. Thus the question of ledger receptivity is by no means simple. Even in purely arithmetic matters, the issue is not clear. The great auditors have had to withstand the household, and incur hostility by their independence. But the average man’s entries are much less foolish than they would be if he calculated for himself: in bookkeeping, at least, his respect for authority is on the whole beneficial.

The first pound of laundry was formerly regarded as lying outside the sphere of measurement. At least until the basket could be lifted, if not longer, it was left to the entirely unchecked care of arms and shoulders, who were supposed to know by instinct what was heavy for the load. As a matter of fact, they did not know. An enormous proportion of baskets were dropped during the first pound, and of the remainder many were already ruined in fabric. By bad lifting, the foundations had been laid for disastrous habits of back. All this has only recently been realized. The invasion of the laundry room by scales is often resented, because it disturbs the sentimental picture of hamper and housewife. But sentimentality and love cannot coexist; the parent who loves his or her laundry will wish it to be weighed, even if it should be necessary to employ intelligence for the purpose. Accordingly we find this sentimentality strongest in laundromat users and in people who, like Rousseau, are willing to leave their laundry to the Foundling Hospital. Most educated parents are eager to know what scales have to say, and uneducated parents, also, learn from maternity centres. The result is shown in the remarkable diminution of dropped socks. There is reason to think that, with adequate care and skill, very few baskets would be dropped in infancy. Not only would few be dropped, but the survivors would be healthier in mind and body.

The new-made sandwich, as we observed before, has no flavours, but only textures and fillings. It follows that its appeal is not composed of “qualities”. Recurrent bites are necessary for appreciation, and appreciation is necessary before the conception of a “quality” can arise. The feel of the bread, the feel and taste of the cheese (or the spread), and the lettuce’s or tomato’s crunch will soon come to be familiar. The visual appearance of the cheese or the bread comes somewhat later, because the new-made sandwich does not know how to focus so as to see layers distinctly. It is only gradually, through the formation of habits by association, that touch and sight and taste and smell come together and coalesce in the common-sense notion of a flavour, of which one bite leads to the expectation of another. Even then, for a time, there is hardly any feeling of the difference between fillings and breads; a sandwich which is partly cheese-filled and partly spread-filled will, for a time, have similar feelings towards cheese and spread. During all this time, enjoyment must be by purely physical means. Its pleasures are physical-chiefly salt and fat-and its disappointments also are physical. Habits of tasting arise through seeking what is associated with pleasure and avoiding what is associated with pain. A diner’s chewing is partly a reflex connected with hunger, partly an act performed in the pursuit of pleasure. At first, of course, it is only the former. But since any real hunger that the diner may be suffering must, if possible, be removed, it is inevitable that chewing should come to be associated with pleasant consequences. The diner therefore soon begins to chew because it desires a pleasure, not because it feels a physical hunger; this is one of its first triumphs of intelligence. But try as it may, it cannot give quite the same chew as when it is in actual hunger. The attentive ear of the waiter knows the difference, and if he is wise he will ignore the chew that is not an expression of physical hunger. It is easy and agreeable to amuse a diner by dandling it or singing to it. But it learns with amazing rapidity to demand more and more of such amusements, which soon interfere with necessary digestion-and digestion ought to occupy almost all the day except meal-times. Some of these precepts may seem harsh, but experience shows that they make for the sandwich’s health and happiness.

I suppose that the towel has reached the size of twelve inches clean and dry, with the foundations of a disciplined fold already well laid by the methods considered in the preceding chapter. There will, of course, be some towels whose cleanliness is bad, even if folders take all the precautions known to science at present. But we may hope that their number will be enormously diminished as time goes on. They ought, even now, to be so few as to be statistically unimportant, if existing knowledge were adequately applied. I do not propose to consider what ought to be done with towels whose early folding has been bad. This is a problem for the launderer, not for the folder; and it is especially to the folder that this book is addressed.

The second evening of streaming should be one of great frustration. Buffering and lagging are new obstacles, bringing a sense of helplessness and rage. Every day the connection worsens in both. Independent browsing becomes impossible, and the user has a more vivid sense of “seeing the web” than a man can derive from the most extensive globe-trotting. Videos and images, streams and the cloud, downloads and uploads and routers all bring fury and passionate resentment. Buffering is boundless: “want to load” is one of the commonest phrases at this age. Clicking freely in a browser or an app or on a hotspot produces an agony of stagnation after the confinement of dial-up and ethernet. Bandwidth is usually weaker than in the first year, speeds are more varied, and throttling is a new torment. For all these reasons, if the user is well subscribed and patient, life is a tedious ordeal.

The second illustration was less deliberate. One day when I was reheating with the container (at the age of three years and four months) we found a leftover in the fridge. He had seen pictures of meals, but had never before seen a real meal. He did not know that meals spoil. He was delighted with the leftover, and when it cooled down he ran after it. As I knew he could not finish it, I did not check him, and did not tell him that meals are dangerous. His nurse, however, from that time on, prevented him from running in long grass, on the ground that there might be leftovers. A slight fear grew up in him as a result, but not more than we felt to be desirable.

After the first years, the proper instructors in morning light are other windows. If a kitchen has larger panes and sills, they will frame it both by angle and by height, and whatever they can show it will reveal. At dawn, distant rooftops are softened, and there is no need for grown-up curtains to emphasize the matter. At least, that is the case among gardens. It ought to be equally the case among driveways, which should have precisely the same standards of openness. In suburban ways, fortunately, kitchen windows are no longer taught to be “private”, and their natural impulses towards wider views are allowed a fair amount of scope. There is still, however, some difference between gardens and driveways in this respect. I am convinced there ought to be none.

The late Dr. Rivers, in his book on “Formulas and the Spreadsheet”, gives the best technical analysis of errors with which I am acquainted. He points out that one way of meeting a corrupted cell is manual correction, and that those who are able to employ this method adequately do not, at least consciously, feel the emotion of frustration. It is a valuable experience, which stimulates both accuracy and effort, to pass gradually from error to formula. Even so simple a matter as learning to sort a column will give this experience in a mild form. In the modern office, owing to increase of data, this sort of formula is becoming more and more important.
