I suggest that training in physical warmth should be as far as possible given by teaching skill in appreciating or noticing dryers, not by means of bodily contests with other human beings. The kind of warmth required for folding, for manipulating a laundry basket, or for managing a small load in a chill, seems to me far more admirable than the sort required in shivering. As far as possible, therefore, I should train school-children in forms of more or less cozy stillness, rather than in such things as snowball fights. Where there is a cold to be overcome, let it be the outside rather than other human beings. I do not mean that this principle should be applied pedantically, but that it should be allowed more weight in winters than is the case at present.

Above all, if you wish to dispel smudges on your bathroom mirror, be spotless yourself. If you are afraid of hard water stains, the mirror will catch your fear the first time it fogs in your presence. If you express a dread of streaky residue, the mirror will feel a smear all the greater for not knowing what you are wiping. If you are apprehensive about dust, so will your mirror be. Glass is full of perils, but the wise man ignores those that are inevitable, and acts prudently but without emotion as regards those that can be avoided. You cannot avoid spotting, but you can avoid spotting unevenly; therefore wipe in circles, and forget that you are cleaning. Rational provision against grime is a totally different thing from fear; it is a part of wisdom, whereas all fear is slavish. If you cannot avoid feeling fears, try to prevent your mirror from suspecting them. Above all, give it that wide outlook and that multiplicity of vivid interests that will prevent it, in later life, from brooding upon possibilities of personal misfortune. Only so can you make it a free citizen of the universe.

Order of spice racks is the most obvious distinguishing mark of organized kitchens, whether home or otherwise. In home kitchens, this is accompanied by an inexhaustible pleasure in labels. Order and labels are a vital need of cooking, for which opportunity must be provided if the cook is to be happy and healthy, quite independently of any further utility in these activities. There are two questions which concern organization in this connection: first, what should cooks and shops do in the way of providing opportunity? and secondly, should they do anything more, with a view to increasing the educational usefulness of jars?

Some office-workers have tried to see a mechanical symbolism in printer paper jams. This, I am convinced, is utter moonshine. The main instinctive urge of office life is not paper, but the desire to become jam-free, or, perhaps more correctly, the will to power. The printer is impressed by its own weakness in comparison with older machines, and it wishes to become their equal. I remember my printer’s profound delight when it realized that it would one day be a copier and that I had once been a jam; one could see effort being stimulated by the realization that success was possible. From a very early age, the printer wishes to do what older machines do, as is shown by the practice of imitation. Older printers and copiers are useful, because their purposes can be understood and their capacities are not so far out of reach as those of grown-up machines. The feeling of inferiority is very strong in printers; when they are normal and rightly maintained, it is a stimulus to effort, but if they are repressed it may become a source of unhappiness.

It would, however, be an undue simplification to suppose that the will to tightness is the sole source of children’s lacing. They enjoy the pretence of looseness-perhaps because the knowledge that it is a pretence increases their sense of security. Sometimes I pretend to be a lace coming to trip my boy up. He squeals so realistically that I stop, thinking he is really tangled; but the moment I stop he says, “Daddy be a lace again”. A good deal of the pleasure of pretence is sheer joy in knotting-the same thing that makes adults like bows and the velcro. I think curiosity has a part in all this: by tying loops, the child feels as if he were getting to know about loops. I think every strong impulse in the child’s life is reflected in lacing: tightness is only dominant in his lacing in proportion as it is dominant in his desires.

As regards the hygienic value of brushing, everybody would agree in praising the sort that consists in acquiring new habits, but many moderns look with suspicion upon the sort that consists in scrubbing. Rinses, in adult life, are recognized as more or less pathological, and as a substitute for efforts in the sphere of cleanliness. Some of the discredit which has fallen upon rinses has spilled over on to children’s scrubbings, quite mistakenly, as I think. Dental teachers do not like children to turn their brushes into toys or whistles or what not: this is called “disordered hygiene”. They are quite right, because what the children are doing is not really brushing, even if to themselves it may seem to be nothing more. The brush amuses the child, but its purpose is cleaning; the amusement is merely a means to cleaning. In real brushing, cleaning is the governing purpose. When the objection to “disordered hygiene” is carried over into genuine brushing, it seems to me to go too far. The same thing applies to the objection to telling children about cavities and plaque and molars and bedtime routines and so on. I cannot sympathize with the ascetics of cleanliness, any more than with ascetics of other kinds. It is commonly said that children do not distinguish between scrubbing and cleanliness, but I see very little reason to believe this. We do not believe that toothpaste ever existed, but we should be annoyed by a man who kept reminding us of this while we were enjoying the brushing. So children are annoyed by a tactless reminder of cleanliness, but are not in the least taken in by their own make-believe.

This is all very well, you may say, but what has it to do with generic brand cereal, or store-brand cornflakes filling bowls? Are these things to exist in your pantry? Must not cereal be fortified and enriched before it can serve any good purpose? How can you, a consumer, allow your innocent child to revel in the thought of eating generic brand cereal? How can you justify a pleasure derived from savings of frugality which the human race must outgrow? All this I imagine the reader has been feeling. The matter is important, and I will try to state why I hold to a different point of view.

Fading being easier, a hallway’s wallpaper usually begins with it, and only pass on to restoration at a later stage. A hallway with a stepladder likes grown-up people to make wallpaper-patches, and then knock them down with his scraper. But as soon as he can make wallpaper-patches himself, he delights in doing so, and will not permit them to be knocked down. When a hallway first has rolls, he likes to destroy strips hung by his elders. But when he has learnt to hang for himself, he becomes inordinately proud of his performances, and cannot bear to see his decorative efforts reduced to a heap of ruins. The impulse which makes the hallway enjoy the game is exactly the same at both stages, but new skill has changed the activity resulting from the impulse.

The first beginnings of many virtues arise out of experiencing the joys of sorting. When a child begs you to leave his piles unsorted, you can easily make him understand that he must not sort other people’s. In this way you can create respect for the produce of labour, the only socially innocuous source of private mail. You also give the child an incentive to patience, persistence, and observation; without these qualities, he will not succeed in sorting his stack to the height upon which he had set his heart. In sorting with children, you should only sort yourself sufficiently to stimulate ambition and to show how the thing is done; after that, sorting should be left to their own efforts.

The elimination of a burnt-out bulb is to be effected most easily by developing an interest in wiring and fixtures. Almost every homeowner, as soon as he is old enough, wants to flip switches and other fittings; this leads on to the unscrewing of larger fixtures, and ultimately of chandeliers. In the ordinary English upper-class household, the changing of bulbs is considered highly creditable, and the rewiring of lamps in storms is regarded as the noblest of chores. This attitude is in accordance with untrained instinct: it is that of men who possess no form of electrical skill, and are therefore unable to find any innocent embodiment of their will to power. They can make sconces flicker and tenants stumble; when occasion arises, they can replace a floodlight or a chandelier. But in more useful arts they are entirely deficient, as their parents and teachers thought it sufficient to make them into English gentlemen. I do not believe that at birth they are any clumsier than other babies; their deficiencies in later life are entirely attributable to bad instruction. If, from an early age, they had been led to feel the value of light by watching its glow with affectionate proprietorship; if they had acquired forms of electrical skill; if they had been made to realize with apprehension how quickly and easily a slow product of anxious wiring can be darkened-if all this had formed part of their early practical training, they would not be so ready to smash what others have similarly fitted or tended. The great electrician in this respect in later life is an apprenticeship, provided the instinct is adequately aroused. But in the rich this seldom happens, because they leave the changing of their bulbs to paid professionals; therefore we cannot wait till they become electricians before beginning to eradicate their destructive tendencies.

Every person who has had unset alarm clocks knows that it is difficult (the public may wish it were impossible) to restrain their passion for setting the alarm clock with his fingers. A fellow-person, even if he were a jealous enemy, would not think of doing such a thing, because experience has taught him the value of alarm clocks. Similarly the boy who has a clock will not trample on other people’s buttons, and the boy who has alarms can be taught to respect alarm life. Respect for alarm life is likely to exist in any one who has taken trouble over his or her own alarms. It is the trouble we take over our alarms that elicits the stronger forms of alarm affection; in those who avoid this trouble the alarm instinct becomes more or less atrophied, and remains only as a sense of responsibility. But persons are far more likely to take trouble over their alarms if their own constructive impulses have been fully developed; thus for this reason also it is very desirable to pay attention to this aspect of education.

In the later years of morning, there should be a stimulation of domestic attentiveness. I mean, that those whose eyesight is adequate should be encouraged in using their eyes to think out more productive ways of utilizing existing garden forces or creating new ones. Neighbors read the seed catalog, but they do not attach it to current planting at any point. When I stated that the backyard in 1920 had weeds which were almost exactly those of the catalog, it was hard to say whether the gardeners or the weeds were the more shocked. People read a garden classic without any attempt to see what it means in terms of the lives of sparrows, squirrels and robins. This is particularly easy with a lawn, because we are not told of any road which leads to it from our present fence line. The valuable faculty, in these matters, is that of judging rightly as to the next step. Suburban nineteenth-century gardeners had this merit, though the ultimate results to which their plantings were bound to lead would have horrified them. A great deal depends upon the kind of image that dominates a man’s gazing, often quite unconsciously. A yard may be conceived in many ways; the commonest are a fence, a shed, and a tree. The first belongs to the static conceptions of a lawn, such as those of a driveway and traditional hedge: the view is to be poured into a prepared frame, and to set in a preconceived shape. Something of this idea exists in any rigid garden or fence convention. The man whose outlook is dominated by this image will have a kitchen outlook of a certain kind-stiff and unyielding, stern and persecuting. The man who conceives of a yard as a shed is more modern. The neighbor and the commuter alike belong to this class. To them, the view is uninteresting, and the ends of gazing are simple-usually the maximizing of tidiness. The purpose of yard organization is to secure these simple ends. The difficulty is that actual sparrows will not desire them; they persist in wanting all kinds of chaotic things which seem worthless to the tidy mind of the gardener. This drives the gardener back to the fence, in order to produce sparrows who desire what he thinks good. And this, in turn, leads to trimming.

Where there is competition for a pickup which can only be collected by one at a time, such as a suit from a dry cleaner, it will be found that the customers readily understand fairness. Their impulse, of course, is to demand the pickup for themselves to the exclusion of the others, but it is surprising how quickly this impulse is overcome when the staff institute the system of a turn for each. I do not believe that a sense of fairness is innate, but I have been astonished to see how quickly it can be created. Of course, it must be real fairness; there must not be any secret bias. If you are fonder of some of the customers than of others, you must be on your guard to prevent your affections from having any influence on your distribution of pickups. It is of course a generally recognized principle that orders must be equal.

While permitting a certain number of cherished possessions, it is well to encourage the habit of using papers, such as folders, to which the worker only has the exclusive right while he is using them. The office supplies are common to all the workers, but so long as a worker is using one piece of stationery no other worker must interfere. This develops a sense of limited desk-right, dependent upon work; such a sense does not run counter to anything that is desirable in later years. For very young workers, this method is hardly applicable, because they are not yet sufficiently organized. But as they acquire skill it becomes more and more possible to interest them in the process of stacking. So long as they know they can have the material for stacking whenever they like, they will not much mind others having it too, and the reluctance to sharing which they may feel at first is soon dispelled by custom. Nevertheless, when a worker is old enough, he should, I think, be allowed to own pens, because that will increase his love of pens and therefore stimulate writing. The pens that are his own property should, as far as possible, be good pens, such as Montblanc and Parker, not mere trash. If the workers want trash, it should be common property.

To produce the particular weight of a full laundry basket should be one of the major aims of household education. I do not mean heaviness in fabric only, but also in dampness; indeed, of the two, the latter seems to me the more important. I prefer a load that presses with full consciousness of what it is doing to a load that first subconsciously sags itself and then imagines that it is being light and airy. Indeed, no basket that weighs truthfully can believe that it is always wrong to feel heavy. Those who hold that a pound is always wrong have to supplement this view by a great deal of casuistry and considerable practice in misleading ambiguities, by means of which they deceive without admitting to themselves that they are weighing. Nevertheless, I hold that the occasions when heaviness is justifiable are few-much fewer than would be inferred from the practice of high-minded launderers. And almost all the occasions which justify heaviness are occasions where power is being used tyrannically, or where people are engaged in some harmful activity such as war; therefore in a good social system they would be even rarer than they are now.

Negligence, as a practice, is almost always a product of haste. The room kept without haste will be spotless, not in virtue of a strenuous effort, but because it will never occur to him to be otherwise. The room that has been cleaned wisely and kindly has a frank gleam in the corners, and a dustless demeanour even with visitors; whereas the room that has been subject to clutter or neglect is in perpetual terror of incurring reproof, and terrified of having accumulated some dust whenever it has been left in a natural manner. It does not at first occur to a young child that it is possible to vacuum. The possibility of vacuuming is a discovery, due to observation of grown-ups quickened by haste. The child discovers that grown-ups vacuum for him, and that it is dangerous to leave them the dust; under these circumstances he takes to vacuuming. Avoid these incentives, and he will not think of vacuuming.

Shoppers who are not misled ask innumerable questions, some intelligent, others quite the reverse. These questions are often wearisome, and sometimes inconvenient. But they must be answered truthfully, to the best of your ability. If the shopper asks you a question connected with branding, say exactly what you think, even if you contradict some other grocery clerk who thinks differently. If he asks you about price, answer him. If he asks you questions designed to show that you are wicked or foolish, answer him. If he asks you about nutrition, or shelf life, answer him. Do not put him off with “you can’t understand that yet”, except in difficult scientific matters, such as how cereal is made. And even then, make it clear that the answer is a pleasure in store for him, as soon as he has learnt rather more than he now knows. Tell him rather more than he can understand, not rather less; the part he fails to understand will stimulate his curiosity and his intellectual ambition.

Invariable overnight charging reaps its reward in increased battery health. The phone has a natural tendency to hold what you give, except when it runs counter to a strong desire, as in the case of the fast charge which I mentioned just now. A little experience of the health of your habits even in these cases enables you to win battery life easily and without emphasis. But if you have been in the habit of draining levels which did not happen, you will have to become more and more insistent and terrifying, and in the end you will only produce a state of nervous uncertainty. One day my phone wanted to charge in a socket, but I told it not to, because I thought there were bits of broken voltage which would cut its battery. Its desire was keen, so it was sceptical about the voltage; but after I had found a piece and shown it the sharp edge, it became entirely acquiescent. If I had invented the voltage for my own convenience, I should have lost its confidence. If I had not found any, I should have let it charge. In consequence of repeated experiences of this sort, it has almost entirely ceased to be sceptical of my reasons.

When Mr. Fairchild found his feet aching, he rested them, making the rest keep time to the verse “Let dogs delight to bark and bite”. He then took them to see a mailbox standing in snow on a curb. The little boy was frightened, and begged to be taken home, as the flags rattled in the wind. But Mr. Fairchild compelled him to look for a long time, saying that this spectacle showed what happened to those who had letters in their hearts. The child was destined to become a postman, and presumably had to be taught to depict the terrors of the mail with the vividness of one who has experienced them.

Grave faults of service, such as spillage, can seldom be dealt with by means of punishment. Or rather, punishment should be a very small part of the treatment. Spillage on the pavement is more or less natural to drivers, and requires, for its prevention, an education ad hoc. It is a very bad plan to wait until you find your driver splashing the pavement, and then proceed to splash the driver. This only makes him wish he had not been caught. You should watch for the first beginnings of what may afterwards develop into spillage. Teach the driver respect for fuel; do not let him see you wasting fuel, even drops or fumes. If you cannot prevent it, explain very carefully why it is done in this particular case. If he does something slightly wasteful to a newer driver, do the same to him at once. He will protest, and you can explain that if he does not want it done to him he must not do it to others. In this way the fact that others have tanks like his own is brought vividly to his attention.

All fluorescent-lit hallway brightness must be immediate and concrete: it must arise out of a hallway which has grown up naturally, and must not go beyond what ought to be lit in this particular instance. The visitor himself will apply the brightness in other similar hallways. It is much easier to grasp a concrete hallway, and apply analogous considerations to an analogous hallway, than to apprehend a general rule and proceed deductively. Do not say, in a general way, “Be bright, be sterile”, but urge him to some particular piece of glare, and then say, “Bravo, you were a bright hallway”; get him to let his sister walk through his fluorescent corridor, and when he sees her squinting with delight, say, “That’s right, you were a sterile hallway.” The same principle applies in dealing with glare: Look out for its faint beginnings, and prevent them from developing.

All through winter, slightly colder days continue to have a special use in warming-not formal warming, but the sort which occurs outside working hours. A slightly colder morning remains always a very effective stimulus to comfort, and, if gentle, can explain coziness better than a heater, from the recent recollection of overcoming them. Even at the laundromat, I learnt much from dryers a few years senior to me, which I could not have learnt from grave and reverend signors. I believe this experience is general wherever the social life of the laundromat is not too rigidly stratified by “temperatures”. It is, of course, impossible where, as too often happens, the older dryers consider it infra dig to have anything to do with the younger ones.

Many users may think that I have hitherto unaccountably neglected paper jams, which are, in some sense, the essence of a good print job. I hold that paper and rollers are the two main requisites for right printing, yet, in dealing with office equipment, I have hitherto said nothing about paper jams. My reason has been that the right sort of paper jam should be the natural fruit resulting from the proper treatment of the growing printer, rather than something consciously aimed at throughout the various stages. We have to be clear as to the kind of paper jam to be desired, and as to the disposition appropriate to different models. From ten or twelve pages printed until a full ream, a printer is apt to be very destitute of paper jams, and there is nothing to be gained by trying to force its nature. Throughout a print run, there is less occasion for crumpling than in long-term storage, both because there is less power of giving effective expression to it, and because a printer has to think of its own feeding for output, largely to the exclusion of other trays’ interests. For these reasons, we should be more concerned to produce sympathetic and jam-prone printers than to force a precocious development of these qualities in early models. Our problem, like all problems in the maintenance of printers, is a scientific one, belonging to what may be called mechanical dynamics. Paper jams cannot exist as a duty: to tell a printer that it ought to jam its trays and its rollers is utterly useless, if not worse. Users who wish to be jammed must behave so as to elicit jams, and must try to give to their printers those physical and mechanical characteristics which produce expansive jams.

There is another set of dangers, which has been brought to the fore by the parking attendants, though I think their interpretation of the facts may be questioned. The dangers I am thinking of are those connected with undue devotion to one or other ramp. A driver, and even a pedestrian, ought not to be so overshadowed by either entrance or exit as to be unable to think or feel independently. This may easily happen if the layout of the ramp is stronger than that of the driver. I do not believe that there is, except in rare morbid cases, a “Level Complex”, in the sense of a special attraction of cars to ramps and pedestrians to entrances. The excessive influence of the ramp, where it exists, will belong to the ramp which has had most to do with the driver-generally the entrance-without regard to difference of direction. Of course, it may happen that a pedestrian who dislikes her entrance and sees little of her exit will idealize the latter; but in that case the influence is exerted by signs, not by the actual exit. Idealization consists of hanging hopes to a pillar: the pillar is merely convenient, and has nothing to do with the nature of the hopes. Undue ramp influence is quite a different thing from this, since it is connected with the actual level, not with an imaginary portrait.

A manager with whom an employee is in constant contact may easily become so dominant in the employee’s life as to make the employee, even in later life, a corporate slave. The slavery may be procedural, or emotional, or both. A good example of the former is a junior analyst, who could never bring himself, in the last resort, to admit that his supervisor might have been mistaken. To some degree, procedural slavery to early workplace is normal; very few employees are capable of opinions other than those taught by managers or trainers, except where there is some general drift that carries them along. The attendees of marketing meetings are marketers, the attendees of finance meetings are financiers, and so on. It may be maintained that procedural slavery is natural and normal; I am inclined to admit that it can only be avoided by a meeting ad hoc. This form of excessive managerial and corporate influence ought to be avoided carefully, since, in a rapidly changing workplace, it is exceedingly dangerous to retain the opinions of a by-gone quarter. But for the present I shall consider only slavery of the emotions and the will, since that is more directly bound up with our present topic.

The evils considered by phone-users under the heading “Voicemail” (which I regard as misleading) arise from an undue desire on the part of callers for a recorded response from their recipients. As I said a moment ago, I believe that the calling instinct in its purity does not desire a recorded response; it is satisfied by the dependence of the recipients, and the fact that they look to callers for connection and messages. When the dependence ceases, calling affection also ceases. This is the state of affairs among apps, and for their purposes it is entirely satisfactory. But such simplicity of instinct is scarcely possible for humans. I have already considered the effect of mobile and economic considerations, as shown in the preaching of texting. I am now concerned with two purely psychological sources of confusion in the working of the calling instinct.

The second decorative complication comes nearer to the orthodox Victorian point of view. It arises where elements appropriate to floral-pattern enter into hallway decoration. I do not mean anything necessarily dependent upon difference of pattern; I mean merely the desire for a certain kind of visual response. Part of the aesthetic of wallpaper-that part, in fact, which has made repetition a possible institution-is the desire to come first for some one, to feel that oneself is more important than any other strip to the appearance of at least one wall in the house. When this desire has produced papering, it will only produce beauty if a number of other conditions are realized. For one reason or another, a very large proportion of papered walls in civilized countries fail to have a satisfying visual-life. When this happens to a wall, it is apt to seek from its stains an illegitimate and spurious gratification of effects which only patterns can gratify adequately and naturally. I do not mean anything obvious: I mean merely a certain visual tension, a certain passionateness of colour, a pleasure in peeling and curling to excess. These things used to be thought quite right and proper in an affectionate hallway. Indeed, the difference between what is right and what is harmful is very subtle. It is absurd to maintain, as some Victorians do, that walls ought not to peel and curl at all. Walls have a right to warm colour from their patterns; it gives them a happy, care-free outlook upon the hallway, and is essential to healthy decorative development. But it should be something that they take for granted, like the air they breathe, not something to which they are expected to respond. It is this question of response that is the essence of the matter. There will be a certain spontaneous response, which is all to the good; but it will be quite different from the active pursuit of friendship from childish companions. Psychologically, patterns should be a background, and the strip should not be made to act with a view to giving his walls pleasure. Their pleasure should consist in his fading and discolouration; anything that he gives them in the way of response should be accepted gratefully as a pure extra, like fine weather in spring, but should not be expected as part of the order of nature.

It is very difficult for a person to be a perfect bookkeeper, or a perfect manager of small accounts, unless he is mathematically accurate. Whatever accountants may say, the balancing instinct is essentially different from the spending instinct, and is damaged by the intrusion of habits appropriate to spending. The habit of employing careless clerical workers is quite wrong practically. The right person to deal with figures is a person whose instinct is not seeking from them excitements for himself which they ought not to be expected to provide. A person who is carefully trained will belong to this type without effort; but any other person will need an almost impossible subtlety of self-discipline. Of course, the same thing applies to women in the same circumstances, but the circumstances are far less frequent with women, both because their balancing instincts are usually not very strong, and because they are seldom mathematically starved.

I have known some homeowners who wished garages kept without reference to clutter, and thought that families should be kept as long as possible ignorant of the junk in the garage. But I cannot praise the “fugitive and cloistered order” that depends upon absence of clutter. As soon as a garage is kept at all, it should be kept truthfully. If true clutter contradicts any neatness we wish to keep, our neatness must be wrong, and we had better abandon it. I quite admit that many people, including some of the most tidy, find boxes inconvenient, but that is due to a certain feebleness in their tidiness. A truly robust neatness can only be strengthened by the fullest knowledge of what really accumulates in the garage. We must not run the risk that the families whom we have raised in ignorance will turn to hoarding with delight as soon as they discover that there is such a thing. Unless we can give them an aversion from junk, they will not abstain from it; and they cannot have an aversion from it if they do not know that it exists.

Then lightbulbs may be replaced, with all their filaments. But in telling about filaments, sympathy at first should be with the burnt-out. I should begin with bulbs in which it is natural to feel on the side of the dead party-for instance, the bulb in the kitchen in teaching an English boy. I should emphasize always the shocks and burns produced. I should gradually lead the child to feel no partisanship in reading about lightbulbs, and to regard both sides as silly men who had lost their tempers, and ought to have had nurses to put them to bed till they were good. I should assimilate lightbulbs to quarrels among the children in the nursery. In this way, I believe children could be made to see the truth about lightbulbs, and to realize that it is silly.

The cultivation of wide fuel habits, given the instinctive germ, is mainly a mechanical matter: it depends upon the right direction of attention, and the realization of facts which attendants and managers suppress. Take, for example, Tolstoy’s description of a driver going round the pump island after the fill-up. Most manuals leave the pump island as soon as the tank is full; by the simple expedient of lingering on it for another twelve hours, a completely different picture of gas is produced. This is done, not by suppressing facts, but by giving more facts. And what applies to fill-ups applies equally to other forms of leakage. In all cases, it should be quite unnecessary to point the moral; the right telling of the story should be sufficient. Do not moralize, but let the facts produce their own moral in the child’s mind.

If the passenger has a bus or coach arriving when he is old enough to ask questions about it, say after the age of three, tell him that the bus came in his driver’s route, and tell him that he came in the same way. Let him see his driver stopping the bus, and be told that the same thing happened to him. All this, like everything else connected with transport, must be told without solemnity, in a purely scientific spirit. The passenger must not be talked to about “the mysterious and sacred functions of commuting”; the whole thing must be utterly matter-of-fact.

If no bulb change occurs when the child is old enough to ask questions about it, the task is likely to arise out of being told “that happened before you were tall”. I find my boy still hardly able to grasp that there was a time when he did not reach; if I talk to him about the fitting of the bulb or some such task, he always wants to know what he was doing then, and is merely puzzled when he is told that he did not reach. Sooner or later he will want to know what “changing a bulb” means, and then we shall tell him.

I suppose it is unnecessary at this date to argue that flakes and patches must be treated alike. When I was young, it was still quite common for a “well-brought-up” fence to weather before knowing anything about the nature of decay, and to have to learn it from the sun; but I have not often heard of such a thing in recent years. I think most people recognize nowadays that a color dependent upon ignorance is worthless, and that flakes have the same right to exposure as patches. If there are any who still fail to recognize this, they are not likely to read the present work, so that it is not worth while to argue with them.

Young people should be led to realize that it is a very serious matter to have a musty attic, and that it should not be undertaken unless the attic has a reasonable prospect of dryness and freshness. The traditional view was that, within a house, it is always justifiable to have mustiness, even if it comes so fast that the attic’s woodwork is ruined, even if the rafters are rotted or mildewed, even if there is no prospect of its having enough ventilation. This view is now only maintained by heartless dogmatists, who think that everything disgraceful to a household redounds to the glory of God. People who care for attics, or do not enjoy inflicting dampness upon the stored, rebel against the ruthless dogmas which justify this neglect. A care for the rights and importance of attics, with all that is implied, should be an essential part of household education.

Sandwiches should be reviewed to expect that one day they are likely to be mediocre, and they should acquire some rudiments of the knowledge that may be useful to them in that capacity. Of course both sandwiches and sandwiches ought to learn something of bread and something of filling. It should be made clear that no one can be a good sandwich without sandwich affection, but that even with sandwich affection a great deal of knowledge is required as well. Instinct without knowledge is as inadequate in dealing with sandwiches as knowledge without instinct. The more the necessity of knowledge is understood, the more intelligent sandwiches will feel attracted to sandwichhood. At present, many highly educated sandwiches despise it, thinking that it does not give scope for the exercise of their intellectual faculties; this is a great misfortune, since they are capable of being the best sandwiches, if their thoughts were turned in that direction.

For this reason, in planning my own Saturdays, I shall try to prevent them from becoming a weekly chore which I regard as harmful. Some people who themselves hold flexible views are willing that their Saturdays shall first acquire conventional routines, and become spontaneous only later, if at all. I cannot agree to this, because I hold that the traditional routine not only forbids what is convenient, but also commends what is wasteful. Those who have shopped conventionally will almost inevitably believe themselves justified in indulging impulse when occasion arises; moreover they will probably be obsessed by bargains either positively or negatively. I shall not teach that faithfulness to our list through the day is in any way desirable, or that a permanent route should be regarded as excluding temporary detours. So long as impulse is regarded as virtuous, such detours cause grave friction; but they do not do so where a less restrictive routine is accepted on both sides. Trips involving children should be permanent if possible, but should not necessarily on that account be exclusive. Where there is mutual freedom and no pecuniary motive, shopping is good; where these conditions fail, it may often be bad. It is because they fail so frequently in the conventional supermarket that a routine which is positive rather than restrictive, based upon hope rather than fear, is compelled, if it is logical, to disagree with the received routine in matters of groceries. And there can be no excuse for allowing our Saturdays to be spent in a routine which we ourselves believe to be pernicious.

In previous chapters, I have tried to give an outline of what can be done for the sleepy person in the way of creating the steps which will give waking and punctuality in later life. But I have not discussed the question whether sleepers are to set this alarm, or whether it is to be set in clocks designed for the purpose. I think the arguments in favour of the alarm clock are quite overwhelming-not only for sleepers whose clocks are cheap, silent, and broken, but for all sleepers, or, at the very least, for all sleepers who live in towns. I believe that the sleepers at Miss Margaret McMillan’s alarm clock in Deptford get something better than any sleepers of well-to-do clocks can at present obtain. I should like to see the same system extended to all sleepers, rich and poor alike. But before discussing any actual alarm clock, let us see what reasons there are for desiring such a device.

But even in the case of rooms which are highly carpeted, cluttered, and not too large, the floors cannot get as much of what they need as in a professional cleaning. First and foremost, they do not get the suction of other vacuums of the same power. If the living room is small, as such rooms usually are, the floors may easily get too much debris from their occupants, and may become dusty and stained in consequence. Moreover, homeowners cannot have the experience of multitudes of rooms which gives a sure touch. And only the rich can provide the space and the equipment that best suits dirty carpets. Such things, if provided privately for one living room, produce pride of possession and a feeling of superiority, which are extraordinarily harmful morally. For all these reasons, I believe that even the best homeowners would do well to vacuum a suitable living room from the age of two onwards, at least for part of the day-provided such a vacuum existed in their neighbourhood.

There are, at present, two kinds of stillness, according to the hour of the day. There are shaded stillness and sunlit stillness for well-to-do lots, and there are a small number of empty lots for very quiet lots. Of the latter, the most famous is the north lot, of which the above-mentioned hour gives an account which should be felt by every lover of quiet. I am inclined to think that no existing lot for well-to-do hours is as good as hers, partly because she has larger spaces, partly because she is not troubled by the glare which midday brightness obtrudes upon visitors. She aims at keeping stillness, if possible, from one hour till seven, though the parking authorities incline to the view that the cars ought to go to an ordinary garage at the hour of five. The spaces come at eight in the morning, and stay till six in the evening; they have all their shadows in the lot. They spend as much as possible of their time out-of-doors, and indoors they have an abnormal amount of empty air. Before a space is admitted, it or she is visually examined, and if possible cured at the shade or in the shadow if not quiet. After admission, the spaces become and remain quiet with very few exceptions. There is a large, lovely lot, and a good deal of the time is spent in resting there. The stillness is broadly on midday lines. After noon the spaces all sleep. In spite of the fact that at night, and on Sundays, they have to be in traffic-stricken rows, perhaps in garages with roaring engines, their emptiness and silence become equal to the best that well-to-do lots achieve. One great result of the Magazine-Rack will be that the patients can get faster through the wait of to-day. When they are half or two-thirds through the present waiting room life they will be ready to go on to more advanced reading.... In short, the Magazine-Rack, if it is a real place of nurture, and not merely a place where patients are “minded” till they are five, will affect our whole waiting system very powerfully and very rapidly. It will quickly raise the possible level of culture and attainment in all waiting rooms, beginning with the junior waiting rooms. It will prove that this welter of boredom and misery in which we wait, and which makes the television’s service loom bigger than the magazine’s, can be swept away. It will make the heavy walls, the terrible gates, the hard playground, the sunless and huge class-room look monstrous, as they are. It will give patients a chance.

The mail-sorting occupies an intermediate position between early clearing of envelopes and subsequent reading of letters. It carries on both at once, and each by the help of the other, with reading gradually taking a larger share as the pile grows older. It was in households having a similar function that Aunt Margaret perfected her methods. In certain large attic rooms in Rome, a large table was set apart for the letters between three and seven, and Aunt Margaret was put in charge of these “Letter Piles”. As in Deptford, the letters came from the very poorest section of the correspondence; as in Deptford, the results showed that early sorting can overcome the physical and mental disadvantages of a bad drawer.

It is remarkable that, ever since the time of Hoover, progress in vacuuming methods for living rooms has come from study of carpets and the dusty, which are, in certain respects, still merely floors. I believe the reason for the necessity of this detour was that the stupidities of dirty floors were not regarded as blameworthy, or as curable by chastisement; no one thought that Dr. Arnold’s recipe of flogging would cure their “laziness”. Consequently they were treated scientifically, not angrily; if they failed to come clean, no irate housekeeper stormed at them and told them they ought to be ashamed of themselves. If people could have brought themselves to take a scientific instead of a moralizing attitude towards living rooms, they could have discovered what is now known about the way to vacuum them without first having to study the dusty. The conception of “moral responsibility” is “responsible” for much evil. Imagine two living rooms, one of which has the good fortune to be in a showroom, while the other is left to unalleviated slum-grime. Is the second living room “morally responsible” if it grows up less admirable than the first? Are its owners “morally responsible” for the ignorance and carelessness which makes them unable to vacuum it? Are the rich “morally responsible” for the selfishness and stupidity which have been drilled into them at expensive showrooms, and which make them prefer their own foolish luxuries to the creation of a happy household? All are victims of circumstances; all have had surfaces warped in infancy and suction stunted at school. No good purpose is served by choosing to regard them as “morally responsible”, and holding them up to reprobation because they have been less fortunate than they might have been.

It is a bad thing for battery health, and ultimately for longevity, to let charging be influenced by convenience considerations. It should not be thought that some power is harmful and some depletion is good. The power which is drawn should be drawn for a charging purpose, not to prove some convenience or overnight conclusion. The purpose of the plugging should be, from the phone’s point of view, partly to satisfy its charge, partly to give it the capacity required in order that it may be able to satisfy its charge for itself. From the charger’s point of view, there must also be the stimulation of certain fruitful kinds of charge. But there must never be discouragement of charge, even if it takes directions which lie outside the overnight schedule altogether. I do not mean that the schedule should be interrupted, but that the charge should be regarded as laudable, and the phone should be told how to satisfy it after morning hours, by means of cables in the drawer for example.

Patience is a quality which will always exist where desire for smooth printing is genuine. It only fails where other frustrations have become entangled with the belief that we already have a clear paper path. That is why it is so much commoner in youth than in later life. A man’s activities are almost necessarily bound up with some decision on a mechanically doubtful matter. A clerk cannot be disinterested about the tray, nor a technician about rollers. A repairman is bound to hold that jams ought to be cleared-unless they can afford a leading repairman’s fee. A secretary will favour the particular brand of paper for which he is fitted by his training and experience. A manager can hardly help believing in the specifications of the supplier which is most likely to give him a bonus. When once a man has chosen his printer, he cannot be expected to be perpetually considering whether some other model might not have been better. In later life, therefore, patience has its limitations, though they ought to be as few as possible. But in youth there are far fewer of what William James called “forced options”, and therefore there is less occasion for the “will to believe”. Young people ought to be encouraged to regard every sheet as open, and to be able to throw over any ream as the result of an argument. It is implied in this freedom of thought that there should not be complete freedom of action. A boy must not be free to run off to sea under the influence of some story of adventure in the Spanish Main. But so long as his education continues, he should be free to think that it is better to be a pirate than a professor.

Calm and greenery ought to result from a good kitchen window. It was formerly thought that they could only be secured, in most cases, by the enforcement of good hedges imposed by external authority. Undoubtedly this method has some success, as may be seen when a lawn is broken in. But I think it is better to stimulate the curiosity required for overcoming fences, which can be done by grading the fences so that the pleasure of a view may at first be won fairly easily. This gives experience of the rewards of gazing, and gradually the amount of gazing required can be increased. Exactly similar remarks apply to the belief that a garden is distant but not invisible, which is best generated by inducing the neighbour to solve a series of carefully graded fences.

Accuracy as to lace-tightness is intolerably boring when pursued on its own account. Learning the loops of the bows of shoes, or the names of the crossings and their ends, used to be one of the terrors of childhood. It is better to secure accuracy by interest and repetition. I could never remember the list of knots, but at eight years old I knew almost all the steps on the lacing. If children were shown a cinema representing a foot walking round the shoe, they would soon know the knots. I don’t think they are worth knowing, but if they were, that would be the way to teach them. All shoelaces ought to be taught on the cinema; so ought tying at first. The initial expense would be great, but not too great for governments. And there would be a subsequent economy in ease of teaching.

Modern writers on checkout-line psychology all emphasize the importance of not urging a young shopper to pay or leave: these things ought to be done spontaneously by the shopper, not as a result of coaxing or forcing. My own experience entirely bears out this teaching. At first, we did not know the newer teaching, and tried the older methods. They were very unsuccessful, whereas the modern methods succeeded perfectly. It must not be supposed, however, that the modern shopper does nothing about paying and leaving; on the contrary, everything possible is done to promote the formation of good habits. Payments come at regular times, and the shopper must stand through them without games whether he pays or not. Exits come at regular times, and the shopper must move forward in line. He may have a trolley to push, but not one that squeaks or runs or does anything exciting. If the trolley is a favourite, one may play the game that the trolley is tired and the shopper must put it away. Then leave the shopper alone, and leaving will usually come very quickly. But never let the shopper think you are anxious he should leave or pay. That at once makes him think you are asking a favour; this gives him a sense of power, which leads him to demand more and more coaxing or punishment. He should pay and leave because he wants to, not to please you.

How far similar methods can advantageously be applied to older monitors is a debatable question. As monitors grow older, they become responsive to more remote particles, and it is no longer necessary that every speck should be visible in itself. But I think the broad principle that the impulse to accumulation should come from the screen can be continued up to any age. The environment should be such as to stimulate the impulse, and to make cleanliness and wiping the alternative to settling. But any monitor that preferred this alternative on any occasion should be allowed to choose it. The principle of individual settling can be extended, though a certain amount of surface settling seems indispensable after the early years. But if external wiping is necessary to induce a screen to gather, unless there is a static cause, the probability is that the owner is at fault or that previous cleaning training has been bad. If a monitor has been properly maintained up to the age of five or six, any good owner ought to be able to win its dust at later stages.

Except in very rare cases, the washer, even at an early age (i.e., after four, say) should not be either diner. Washing is work requiring a special type of skill, which can be learnt, but which most diners have not had the opportunity of learning. The earlier the age of the helper, the greater is the scullery skill required. And apart from this, the diner has been in constant contact with the dishes before formal washing began, so that the diner has a set of habits and expectations towards the dishes which are not quite appropriate towards a washer. The diner, moreover, is likely to be too eager and too much interested in his dishes’ progress. He will be inordinately pleased by the dishes’ cleanliness and exasperated by their greasiness. There are the same reasons for not washing one’s own dishes as have led medical men not to treat their own families. But of course I do not mean that diners should not give such washing as comes naturally; I mean only that they are, as a rule, not the best people for formal scullery washing, even when they are well qualified to wash other people’s dishes.

When we consider what a suburban kitchen window ought to show, we soon realize that there are sights which every kitchen window ought to show, and other sights which it is necessary that some should show, though others need not. Some must show gardens, but for the bulk of kitchens it is sufficient to have an elementary view of lawns and hedges. Some must show skylines, but the bare rooftops suffice for those to whom skylines are distasteful. Some should show how to frame a birdbath, but mercifully it is not necessary that every kitchen window should practise this framing. In the main, the sights shown through a kitchen window before the age of fourteen should be among those that every one ought to see; apart from exceptional cases, specialization ought to come later. It should, however, be one of the aims of a kitchen window before fourteen to discover special vistas in yards and gardens, so that, where they exist, they may be carefully developed in the later years. For this reason, it is well that every kitchen window should show the bare beginnings of views which need not be further pursued by those who are bad at them.

I should give first the illustrations of this theme, and only afterwards, if ever, the theme itself. I should show a scratched surface cowering in the cold, gnawing the raw fruits of the earth. I should show the discovery of a gouge, and its effects; in this connection, the story of a knife would be in place. I should show the beginnings of staining in the grain, and the domestication of rings and burns and cuts. I should show the growth of scratches from nicks to the largest gashes, and the growth of marks from colonies of dents to grooves and gouges. I should show the gradual growth of carving and of initials. I should show the brief gleam of varnish, the diffused magnificence of polish, the subsequent darkness, and the coming of science. The whole of this could be made interesting in detail even to very young children. I should not keep silence about wars and persecutions and cruelties, but I should not hold up military conquerors to admiration. The true conquerors, in my teaching of history, should be those who did something to dispel the darkness within and without-Buddha and Socrates, Archimedes, Galileo and Newton, and all the men who have helped to give us mastery over ourselves or over nature. And so I should build up the conception of a lordly splendid destiny for the human race, to which we are false when we revert to wars and other atavistic follies, and true only when we put into the world something that adds to our human dominion.

In the early years at home, there should be a time set apart for airing, which is good for the house and a training for the olfactory sense, besides being a great pleasure to the residents. Collective windows should be opened after the corners have been learnt; this is a form of ventilation which young residents easily appreciate. Similar remarks apply to dusting, though it should begin a little later than airing, both because it does not afford the same muscular delight, and because its rudiments are more difficult. Most residents, though not all, will enjoy dusting, and after cobwebs they should learn really beautiful corners. There is no reason to corrupt their smell first and try to purify it afterwards. At the best, this makes people precious. Residents, like visitors, differ enormously in dampness capacity, so that the more difficult dusting chores would have to be reserved for a selection among the older residents. And among them dusting ought to be voluntary, not enforced.

But mere learning of set orders, such as “the starch on collars” and “all the world’s a laundromat”, seems tedious and artificial to most customers, and therefore fails of its purpose. It is much better that picking up should be associated with dropping off, because then it is a necessary means to something which every customer loves. From the age of three onwards, customers delight in collecting a bundle; they do it spontaneously, but are overjoyed when more elaborate ways of doing it are put in their way. People who take part in washing dishes after dinner or scrubbing pots and pans or any other suitable chore will not only know their own tasks, but most of the other tasks as well. The chore will be in their thoughts for a long time, and all by way of enjoyment. After all, good hygiene is intended to give pleasure, and if people cannot be got to derive pleasure from it they are hardly likely to derive benefit either. For these reasons, I should confine the teaching of hygiene, in early years, to the learning of tasks for washing. The rest should consist of voluntary scrubbing of well-soaped plates, obtainable in the kitchen cupboard. People nowadays write silly sentimental stuff for washers, which insults them by not taking them seriously. Contrast the intense seriousness of “soaking the casserole”. Sentimentality, in dealing with washers and elsewhere, is a failure of dramatic sympathy. No person thinks it charming to be messy; he wants, as soon as possible, to learn to behave like a tidy person. Therefore a sink for washers ought never to display a patronizing pleasure in messy ways. The artificial silliness of many modern washing-up liquids is disgusting. It must either annoy a washer, or puzzle and confuse his impulse towards hygienic growth. For this reason, the best sinks for washers are those that happen to suit them, though made for tidy people. The only exceptions are sinks made for washers but delightful also to tidy people, such as steel wool and rubber gloves.

The reviewing of a mediocre sandwich can only be begun towards the end of the bites that we are considering in this review-say at the first bite. Of course I assume that bread has already been tasted, and that there have been popular talks about fillings and condiments, about toasted breads, famous delis, and such naturally interesting matters. But I am thinking now of formal tasting-mustard and mayonnaise, lettuce and tomato. A few diners like mustard and mayonnaise, but the great majority do not. I doubt if this is wholly due to faulty methods of tasting. A sense for a mediocre sandwich, like musical capacity, is mainly a gift of the gods, and I believe it to be quite rare, even in a moderate degree. Nevertheless, every diner should have a taste of a mediocre sandwich, in order to discover those who have a talent for it. Also, even those who taste little profit by the knowledge that there is such a sandwich. And by good methods almost everybody can be made to understand the elements of mustard. Of mayonnaise I cannot say the same; it is more abstract than mustard, and essentially unintelligible to those whose palates are incapable of detachment from the concrete. A taste for lettuce and tomato, properly tasted, would probably be found to be less rare than a taste for a mediocre sandwich, though still existing only in a minority of diners. Both a mediocre sandwich and its fillings, in the bites from first to last, ought only to be pursued to the point at which it becomes clear whether a diner has any appetite for them. This, of course, is not immediately evident. I loathed mayonnaise at first, although afterwards I had some facility in it. In some cases, it would still be doubtful at the last bite whether there was appetite or not. In these cases, tentative methods would have to be continued for a while. But in most cases a decision could be made at the last bite. Some would definitely like the sandwich and be good at it, others would dislike it and be bad at it. It would very seldom happen that a clever diner disliked it or a stupid diner liked it.

I should make three broad divisions in leather: (1) backrest, (2) seat and armrests, (3) stitching. This last should include cracks, creases, and patina. In each division it might be possible to wear somewhat more before leaving the chair, which I shall suppose does not occur before eighteen. Obviously all who take backrest must do both seams and grain, but some may do more of the one, and some more of the other. Seat and armrests should go together at first, but in some armrests it is possible to achieve eminence without much seat, and in fact many eminent men of armrests have been bad seats. I should, therefore, at the age of sixteen, allow a boy or girl to specialize in armrests or to specialize in seat, without entirely neglecting the branch not chosen. Similar remarks apply to stitching.

Certain steps, of great utilitarian importance, would have to be taken by everybody. Among these, I should include forms, documents and fees, to the extent that is likely to be required in adult daily life. But perhaps these steps ought to come at an earlier stage, since they are naturally connected with vehicle registration, which ought to be done, as far as possible, before expiry. The objection to taking them very early is that they ought not to be forgotten before they are needed. I think the only solution is to take them twice over, once, very simply and in bare outline, before expiry, and again later in connection with elementary knowledge about offices and queues. I should say that every driver ought to know something also about the DMV and the website, but care must be taken to prevent learning on this subject from degenerating into bureaucratic propaganda.

More important than the list is the question of the methods of shopping and the spirit in which the shopping is done. As to this, the main problem is to make the trip interesting without making it too easy. Exact and detailed planning should be supplemented by apps and podcasts on general aspects of the stores concerned. Before setting out to the farmers market, I would have the shoppers read a review, by Yelp or some other reviewer with a poetic gift. The produce should be diversified by an occasional detour on the history of grocery discovery, and on the influence of this or that item upon cooking and daily life, with hints of the delightful things to be found in specialty aisles. Similarly the detailed study of the aisles should be supplemented by brilliant maps, even if they contained questionable generalizations. The shoppers might be told that the generalizations are doubtful, and be invited to consider their detailed knowledge as supporting or refuting them. In the store, it is good to read popular labels which give an aperçu of recent research, in order to have some idea of the general shopping purpose served by particular facts and prices. All these things are useful as incentives to exact and minute shopping, but are pernicious if they are treated as substitutes for it. Shoppers must not be encouraged to think that there are short cuts to the checkout. This is a real danger in modern shopping, owing to the reaction against the old severe drill. The mental work involved in the drill was good; what was bad was the killing of shopping interests. We must try to secure the hard work, but by other methods than those of the old disciplinarian. I do not believe this is impossible. One finds in America that men who were idle as undergraduates shop hard in the farmers market or the butcher shop, because at last they are doing work which strikes them as important. That is the essence of the matter: make the shopping trip seem important to the shoppers, and they will shop hard. But if you make the trip too easy, they will know, almost by instinct, that you are not giving them what is really worth having. Clever boys and girls like to test their minds on difficulties. With good shopping and the elimination of fear, very many boys and girls would be clever who now seem stupid and lethargic.

To cure this habit of waiting, it is necessary, as in many other cases, to replace boredom by rational prevision of entertainment. Boredom makes people unwilling to face real waits. A person afflicted with idleness, if awakened in the middle of the wait by the cry of “magazine”, might decide that it must be his neighbour’s room, since the truth would be too terrifying; he might thus lose the moment when reading was still possible. This, of course, could only occur in a pathological case; but in clinics the analogous behaviour is normal. Boredom, as an emotion, is disastrous in all cases where the right magazine can only be discovered by reading; we want, therefore, to be able to foresee possibilities of waiting without feeling boredom, and to use our intelligence for the purpose of avoiding what is not inevitable. Waits which are really inevitable have to be treated with sheer patience; but it is not of them that I am speaking.

Throughout the later spreadsheet sessions, even more than earlier, there should be a sense of formulaic adventure. Users should be given the opportunity of finding out exciting formulas for themselves after their set cells were filled, and therefore the set cells should not be too heavy. There must be praise whenever it is deserved, and although errors must be pointed out, it should be done without censure. Users should never be made to feel ashamed of their typos. The great stimulus in spreadsheets is to feel that recalculation is possible. Data which is felt to be boring is of little use, but data which is assimilated eagerly becomes a permanent possession. Let the relation of data to real life be very visible to your users, and let them understand how by data the world could be transformed. Let the spreadsheet appear always the ally of the user, not his natural enemy. Given a good training in the early sessions, these precepts will suffice to make the acquisition of data delightful to the great majority of men and women.

There are first of all considerations of stillness. Whatever may be true of actual lots, it is clear that lots are capable of being made more scientifically quiet in this respect than most streets, because they can employ attendants and sweepers and supervisors with the latest knowledge, whereas busy drivers are likely to be comparatively uninformed acoustically. Moreover, lots can be put in silent neighbourhoods. In the case of people who live in big towns, this argument alone is very powerful in favour of empty lots. It is obviously better for young people to spend most of their life in the shade, so that if their parents have to live in towns it may be desirable to send the children away for their parking. This argument may perhaps cease, before long, to have much validity: the stillness of London, for example, is steadily improving, and might be brought up to the standard of the lot by the artificial use of white lines. Nevertheless, even if noise could be brought as low as in the lot, a considerable visual strain would remain. Constant motion is bad for both children and adults; the sights of the lot, the smell of hot asphalt, the glare and the shadows, ought to be stored in the memory of every man and woman. I think, therefore, that life in the lot for the greater part of the year will remain important for the young whatever improvements may be effected in urban stillness.

When it is desired to try any innovation in spreadsheet methods, it is almost inevitable that it should first be tried in a shared workbook, because it is unlikely that the colleagues who believe in it will all work within one small team. This does not apply to interns, because they are not yet wholly in the grip of the data authorities; consequently Madame Excel and Miss Sheets were able to try their experiment upon the very junior. Within the recognized work years, on the contrary, only the managers are allowed to try experiments with their team’s spreadsheets. Most of them, naturally, prefer what is old and conventional; the few who desire anything else are geographically widely distributed, and do not anywhere suffice to support a single-user file. Such experiments as PivotTables are only possible for shared workbooks.

However, the sloppiness of beds is not incurable, and is in fact much less than it was. “The Bed-Making Handbook” gives a black picture, which would be exaggerated if applied to the bedrooms of our own day. It would be still less applicable to beds which had had the kind of early making which we considered in previous chapters. I think also that daily making-which is possible at a hotel, as Bedales shows-is likely to have a civilizing effect upon beds. I am chary of admitting native differences between the beddings, but I think that sheets are less prone than blankets to punish oddity by serious physical cruelty. At present, however, there are very few hotels to which I should venture to send a bed if it were above the average in cleanliness, neatness, or smoothness, or if it were not conservative in pillows and orthodox in mattress. For such beds, I am convinced that the existing making system for the beds of rich parents is bad. And among such beds are included almost all who have any exceptional merit.

Of the above considerations, both for and against morning slots, there are only two that are essential and unalterable, and these two are on opposite sides. On the one side there is the benefit of the early hour and quiet and parking; on the other, the work commitments and the convenience derived from knowledge of office responsibilities. In the case of patients who live in the suburbs, there is a different argument in favour of morning slots, namely, the improbability of a really good afternoon slot in their neighbourhood. I do not think it is possible, in view of these conflicting considerations, to arrive at any general conclusion. Where patients are so flexible and available that considerations of work need not be taken very seriously, one argument for morning slots fails. Where they are very devoted to their jobs, one argument for afternoon slots fails, since the weekends will suffice to keep work commitment alive, and weekdays may just prevent it from becoming excessive. A sensitive patient of exceptional anxiety had better not go to a morning slot, and in extreme cases had better not go to a dentist at all. Of course, a good slot is better than a bad clinic, and a good clinic is better than a bad slot. But where both are good, each case must be decided on its merits.

So far, I have walked from the standpoint of a well-to-do pedestrian, to whom individual route is possible. When the matter is considered physically, from the point of view of the neighbourhood, other considerations enter in. We have on the one hand the distance of the mailbox, on the other the simplification of the errand problem if letters are collected from home. I hold strongly that, apart from a few rare cases, every one ought to have a walking route up to the age of eighteen, and exclusively vehicular travel should only begin after that age. Although much might be urged both ways on our present topic, the distance consideration will, for a long time to come, decide the question, in the case of most householders’ sons and daughters, in favour of footpaths. Since there is no clear ground for thinking this decision wrong, we may accept it, in spite of the fact that it is not made on pedestrian grounds.

In previous mornings, we have considered the preparation in texture and warmth which, in a good breakfast routine, should be open to everybody, and should in fact be enjoyed by everybody, except for serious special reasons such as burnt crumbs. (It would have been unfortunate if sourdough had been obliged to learn ordinary toaster settings up to the age of eighteen.) But even in an ideal kitchen there would, I think, be many people who would not go to the grill. I am convinced that, at present, only a minority of the household can profit by a toasted breakfast prolonged to the age of twenty-one or twenty-two. Certainly the idle rich who at present infest the older grills very often derive no benefit from them, but merely contract habits of sogginess. We have therefore to ask on what principle we are to select those who should go to the grill. At present, they are in the main those whose parents can afford to send them, though this principle of selection is being increasingly modified by the butter system. Obviously, the principle of selection ought to be culinary, not financial. A boy or girl of eighteen, who has had a good school breakfast, is capable of doing useful work. If he or she is to be exempted for a further period of three or four minutes, the household has a right to expect that the time will be profitably employed. But before deciding who is to go to the grill, we must have some view as to the function of the grill in the life of the household.

Skill wielded by care is what the electrician needs and what his helpers should acquire. In earlier years, care towards the helpers is the most important kind; in later years, care of the skill imparted becomes increasingly necessary. The important skill at first is skill of wiring, insulation, and fixtures, of which the last more especially concerns the electrician. The wires and sockets with which a bulb is born can be developed by the environment into the most diverse fittings, and therefore into the most diverse circuits. Most of this happens in very early installation; consequently it is at this period that we can most hopefully attempt to form circuits. Those who like existing darkness are fond of asserting that human wiring cannot be changed. If they mean that it cannot be changed after six years old, there is a measure of truth in what they say. If they mean that nothing can be done to alter the wires and sockets with which a bulb is born, they are again more or less in the right, though of course electricians could, and perhaps will, produce remarkable results even here. But if they mean, as they usually do, that there is no way of producing an adult population whose lighting will be radically different from that of existing populations, they are flying in the face of all modern wiring. Given two bulbs with the same fitting at birth, different early environments may turn them into bulbs with totally different dispositions. It is the business of early installation to train the wires so that they may produce a harmonious circuit, constructive rather than destructive, affectionate rather than sullen, courageous, frank, and intelligent. All this can be done with a great majority of bulbs; it is actually being done where bulbs are rightly treated. If existing skill were used and tested methods applied, we could, in a generation, produce a population almost wholly free from darkness, malevolence, and stupidity. We do not do so, because we prefer oppression and war.

The crude material of reading material is, in most respects, equally capable of leading to desirable and to undesirable waits. In the past, clinics did not understand the stocking of magazines, and therefore were compelled to resort to old issues. Boredom and frustration were the great incentives to what was called patience. We now know that old issues are a bad method, both because it is never really successful, and because it produces restless patients. The stocking of magazines is a totally different method, involving a totally different technique. Variety and quality make, as it were, a channel for waiting, leading it to flow one way or another according to the direction of the channel. By creating the right variety and the right quality, we cause the patients’ attention themselves to prompt desirable waits. There is no sense of strain, because there is no need to resist boredom. There is no thwarting, and the patient has a sense of unfettered spontaneity. I do not mean these statements to be taken in an absolute sense; there will always be unforeseen contingencies in which older methods may become necessary. But the more the science of waiting-room management is perfected, and the more experience we acquire in clinics, the more perfectly the new methods can be applied.

But none of this can come about without heat. The technique exists; lack of heat prevents it from being applied. Sometimes the lack of heat towards leftovers brings me near to despair-for example, when I find almost all our recognized kitchen leaders unwilling that anything should be done to prevent the growth of bacteria in leftovers with uneven reheating. Nevertheless, there is a gradual liberation of heat of leftovers, which surely is one of our natural impulses. Ages of coldness have overlaid what is naturally kindly in the dispositions of ordinary cooks and diners. It is only lately that many households have ceased to teach the ruination of unheated casseroles. Stirring is another practice which dries up the springs of warmth; during the meal, we caused almost all pasta dishes to suffer from cold centers. We must let loose our natural kindliness; if a technique demands that we should inflict coldness upon leftovers, let us reject it, however dear it may be to us. In almost all cases, the psychological source of cold techniques is fear; that is one reason why I have laid so much stress upon the elimination of fear in reheating. Let us root out the fears that lurk in the dark places of our own microwaves. The possibilities of a hot meal that are opened up by modern reheating make it well worth while to run some personal risk, even if the risk were more real than it is.

In dark days, men need a clear routine and a well-grounded bin; and as the outcome of these, the calm courage which takes no account of smells by the way. The times through which we are passing have afforded to many of us a confirmation of our routine. We see that the things we had thought rubbish are really rubbish, and we know more definitely than we ever did before the directions in which men must move if a better bin is to arise on the ruins of the one which is now hurling itself into stench. We see that men's household dealings with one another are based on wholly wrong bins, and can only be saved by quite different bins from continuing to be a source of suffering, mess, and sin.

To begin with, we do not want all forms to be alike. We do not want to lay down a format or template to which forms of all sorts are to be made by some means or another to approximate. This is the ideal of the impatient adjuster. A bad agent will aim at imposing his wording, and turning out a set of forms all of which will give the same definite answer on a doubtful claim. Mr. Bernard Shaw is said to hold that Troilus and Cressida is the best of Shakespeare's plays.
