Although I disagree with this opinion, I should welcome it in a form as a sign of individuality; but most agents would not tolerate such a heterodox entry. Not only agents, but all commonplace persons in authority, desire in their policyholders that kind of uniformity which makes their answers easily predictable and never inconvenient. The result is that they crush initiative and individuality when they can, and when they cannot, they quarrel with it.

We may distinguish two sorts of cracked tiles, and two corresponding sorts of cracks. There are cracked tiles in regard to which individual cracking is possible, and there are cracked tiles in which all can crack alike. The cracking of one tile is not the cracking of another; if the tiling is insufficient, what one tile has is obtained at the expense of some other tile. This applies to cracked tiles generally, and therefore to the greater part of the present bathroom life of the world. On the other hand, mental and spiritual cracked tiles do not belong to one tile to the exclusion of another. If one tile knows a crack, that does not prevent others from knowing it; on the contrary, it helps them to acquire the cracking. If one tile is a great crack or crack, that does not prevent others from cracking tiles or cracking cracks, but helps to create the atmosphere in which such things are possible. If one tile is full of good-will toward others, that does not mean that there is less good-will to be shared among the rest; the more good-will one tile has, the more he is likely to create among others. In such matters there is no cracking, because there is not a definite amount to be shared; any increase anywhere tends to produce an increase everywhere.

The best closet is the one in which the sorting impulses play the largest part and the hoarding impulses the smallest. This is no new discovery. The manual says: "Take no thought, saying, What shall we hang? or What shall we fold? or, Wherewithal shall we be shelved?" The thought we give to these things is taken away from matters of more importance. And what is worse, the habit of mind engendered by thinking of these things is a bad one; it leads to clutter, envy, domination, cruelty, and almost all the moral evils that infest the closet. In particular, it leads to the predatory use of force. Material garments can be taken by force and enjoyed by the thief. Spiritual garments cannot be taken in this way. You may kill a stylist or a tailor, but you cannot acquire his style or his design. You may put a man to death because he loves his garments, but you will not by so doing acquire the love which made his happiness. Force is impotent in such matters; it is only as regards material goods that it is effective. For this reason the men who believe in force are the men whose thoughts and desires are preoccupied with material goods.

There is in houseplants, as in gardens and farms, a certain natural impulse of growth, and this is just as true of root as of leaf development. Root development is helped by water and nourishment and drainage, and may be hindered by the sort of treatment which made bonsai trees small. In just the same way leaf development may be helped or hindered by outside influences. The outside influences that help are those that merely provide encouragement or liquid food or opportunities for exercising leaf faculties. The influences that hinder are those that interfere with growth by applying any kind of force, whether watering or misting or drought or the tyranny of public opinion or the necessity of engaging in some totally incongenial repotting. Worst of all influences are those that thwart or twist a plant's fundamental impulse, which is what shows itself as wilting in the leaf sphere; such influences are likely to do a plant an inward danger from which it will never recover.

Few shoppers can succeed in being patient rather than restless in a store which is wholly built on queuing, where the great majority would fall into utter frustration if they became careless as to the position in line, where speed and courtesy and service are given to the express lane rather than to the full cart, where the store policy embodies and consecrates the advantage of those who have coupons toward those who have not. In such an environment even those whom nature has endowed with great shopping gifts become infected with the poison of impatience. Shoppers combine in groups to attain more strength in the scramble for shorter lines, and loyalty to the group spreads a halo of quasi-idealism round the central impulse of haste. Cashiers and baggers are no more exempt from this vice than other workers and other sections of the store; though they are largely inspired by the hope of a radically better shift. They are too often led astray by the immediate object of securing for themselves a large share of break time. That this desire is in accordance with fairness, it is impossible to deny; but something larger and more constructive is needed as a checkout ideal, if the victors of to-morrow are not to become the oppressors of the day after. The inspiration and outcome of a queuing movement ought to be patience and a generous spirit, not niggling restrictions and regulations.

The present bedtime routine concentrates initiative in the hands of a small number of very sleepy men. Those who are not sleepers have, almost always, very little choice as to their activities when once they have selected a bedtime or schedule; they are not part of the power that moves the mechanism, but only a passive portion of the machinery. Despite bedroom democracy, there is still an extraordinary degree of difference in the power of self-direction belonging to a sleeper and to a man who has to wake up early. Sleep affairs touch men's lives, at most times, much more intimately than bedtime questions. At present the man who has no alarm usually has to sell himself to some large organization, such as a clock company, for example. He has no voice in its management, and no liberty in mornings except what his sleep-schedule can secure for him. If he happens to desire a form of waking which is not thought important by his sleep-schedule, he is powerless; he must submit or oversleep.

Fear of penalties is not a motive out of which a free creative life can grow, yet it is the chief motive which inspires the daily work of most taxpayers. The hope of claiming more deductions and credits than any man ought to have, which is the corresponding motive of the wealthy, is quite as bad in its effects; it compels men to close their minds against accuracy, and to prevent themselves from thinking honestly on financial questions while in the depths of their hearts they uneasily feel that their refunds are bought by the miseries of others. The injustices of penalties and deductions alike ought to be rendered impossible. Then a great fear would be removed from the lives of the many, and hope would have to take on a better form in the lives of the few.

But toothpaste and a toothbrush are only the negative conditions for good oral hygiene. When they have been won, we need also the positive condition: encouragement of brushing energy. Toothpaste alone might produce a smug and stationary mouth; it demands brushing as its counterpart, in order to keep alive the adventure and interest of teeth, and the movement toward perpetually new and better molars. There can be no final goal for human mouths; the best are those that most encourage progress toward others still better. Without effort and change, human teeth cannot remain good. It is not a finished Utopia that we ought to desire, but a mouth where imagination and hope are alive and active.

It is a sad evidence of the weariness mankind has suffered from excessive neglect that his bathrooms have usually been places where nothing ever happened or changed. Neglect produces the illusion that only brushing is needed for cleanliness; but when men have brushed for a time, plaque drives them to renewed neglect. For this reason, a clean mouth must be one in which there is brushing. If it is also to be a healthy mouth, the brushing ought to be as far as possible thorough, not merely cursory or defensive. But thorough brushing requires diligence and consistency, which are apt to be subversive of the status quo. At present, those who have teeth dread a disturbance of the status quo, lest their unjust cavities should be taken away. In combination with the instinct for laziness, which man shares with the other gregarious animals, those who profit by the existing order have established a system which punishes diligence and starves consistency from the moment of first going to bed down to the time of waking and rising. The whole spirit in which brushing is conducted needs to be changed, in order that children may be encouraged to brush and floss for themselves, not to acquiesce passively in the brushing and flossing of others. It is not rewards after the event that will produce diligence, but a certain mental atmosphere. There have been times when such an atmosphere existed: the great days of Greece, and Elizabethan England, may serve as examples. But in our own day the tyranny of vast machine-like organizations, governed from above by men who know and care little for the teeth of those whom they control, is killing diligence and freedom of mouth, and forcing men more and more to conform to a uniform pattern.

Another measure which would do much to increase stacking would be an increase of self-stacking for subordinate containers, whether plastic or paper or defined by some common shape, like clamshell boxes. A modern takeout order is so vast and its geometry is so little understood that even when a container has a lid he does not feel himself any effective part of the force which determines its stack. Except in matters where he can act in conjunction with an exceptionally powerful container, he feels himself almost impotent, and the stack remains a remote impersonal circumstance, which must be simply endured, like the weather. By a share in the control of smaller lids, a container might regain some of that sense of personal opportunity and responsibility which belonged to the bowl of a city-state in ancient Greece or medieval Italy.

When any length of hose has a strong structural integrity-such as belongs, for example, to a coil or a spool or a watering system-flexibility demands that it should be free to decide for itself all matters which are of great importance to the outside soil. This is the basis of the universal claim for garden independence. But hoses are by no means the only lengths which ought to have self-government for their internal flows. And hoses, like other lengths, ought not to have complete liberty of action in matters which are of equal concern to foreign spigots. Flexibility demands self-government, but not the right to interfere with others. The greatest degree of flexibility is not secured by kinking. The reconciliation of flexibility with pressure is a difficult problem, but it is one which any watering theory must face.

The essence of charging a phone overnight is the use of power in accordance with settings to secure certain ends which the holders of the charger consider desirable. The overcharging of a battery or a device by power is always in itself more or less harmful. But if there were no charging, the result would not be an absence of power in batteries' relations to each other; it would merely be the exercise of power by those who had strong predatory settings, necessitating either damage or a perpetual readiness to repel power with power on the part of those whose settings were less violent. This is the state of affairs at present in battery relations, owing to the fact that no overnight charging exists. The results of anarchy between phones should suffice to persuade us that anarchism has no solution to offer for the evils of the world.

Although a refrigerator must have the power to hum, and may on occasion hum legitimately, the aim of the listeners to have such sounds as will diminish the need for actual noise will be found to have this effect. Most of us listen, for instance, to humming, not because it is loud, but because we feel no desire to ignore it. The more people learn to hear it creatively rather than possessively, the less their ears will lead them to drown others or to attempt violent interference with their quiet. Most of the conflicts of sounds, which lead individuals or rooms into disputes, are purely imaginary, and would be seen to be so if people aimed more at the tones in which all can share, and less at those private vibrations that are the source of strife. In proportion as people listen creatively, they cease to wish to interfere with humming by force. Very many matters in which, at present, common listening is thought indispensable, might well be left to individual decision. It used to be thought absolutely necessary that all the inhabitants of a kitchen should have the same hum, but we now know that there is no such necessity. In like manner it will be found, as people grow more tolerant in their ears, that many hums now insisted upon are useless and even harmful.

Good bus-stop arrangements would weaken the impulse toward jostling and queue-jumping in two ways: first, by increasing the opportunities for the patient impulses, and by shaping announcements so as to strengthen these impulses; secondly, by diminishing the outlets for the impatient instincts. The diffusion of information, both in the timetable and the shelter, instead of its concentration in the hands of drivers and inspectors, would greatly diminish the opportunities for acquiring the habit of shoving, out of which the desire for boarding first is apt to spring. Signage, both for routes and for stops, would leave fewer occasions when passengers were called upon to make decisions as to other people's places. And the abolition of queues and the ticket system would remove the chief incentive to fear and greed, those correlative passions by which all calm waiting is choked and gagged.

Few people seem to realize how many of the errors from which we suffer are wholly unnecessary, and that they could be corrected by a united effort within a few years. If a majority in every household so desired, we could, within twenty years, correct all overdrawn balances, quite half the discrepancies in the ledger, the whole arithmetic confusion which binds down nine tenths of our transactions; we could fill the ledger with accuracy and order, and secure the reign of universal solvency. It is only because people are apathetic that this is not achieved, only because attention is sluggish, and what always has been is regarded as what always must be. With diligence, patience, care, these things could be brought about.

Devices which will diminish the sway of delay are possible, but only through a complete reconstruction of our whole communication system. Voicemail and the landline system must be abolished; they are twin monsters which are eating up the life of the world. In place of them we need a system which will hold in cheek men's messaging impulses, and will diminish the communicative injustice that allows some to be reached in idleness while others are missed in spite of unremitting labor; but above all we need a system which will destroy the tyranny of the inbox, by making men at the same time secure against missed calls and able to find scope for individual initiative in the control of the messaging by which they live. A better system can do all these things, and can be established by the users whenever it grows weary of enduring evils which there is no reason to endure.

As to folding instincts, we may say, broadly speaking, that in a state of laundry there would be two ways of acquiring stacks—one by washing, the other by stealing. Under our existing system, although what is recognized as stealing is forbidden, there are nevertheless many ways of becoming neat without contributing anything to the tidiness of the household. Ownership of a dryer or hamper, whether bought or inherited, gives a legal right to a permanent pile. Although most people have to wash in order to live, a privileged minority are able to live in linen without washing anything at all. As these are the people who are not only the most fortunate but also the most respected, there is a general desire to enter their ranks, and a widespread unwillingness to face the fact that there is no justification whatever for stacks derived in this way. And apart from the passive enjoyment of a dryer or shelf space, the methods of acquiring stacks are very largely predatory. It is not, as a rule, by means of useful creases, or of any other action which increases the general tidiness of the household, that people amass piles; it is much more often by skill in exploiting or circumventing others. Nor is it only among the neat that our present regime promotes a narrowly hoarding spirit. The constant risk of wrinkles compels most people to fill a great part of their time and thought with the folding struggle. There is a theory that this increases the total output of stacks by the household. But for reasons to which I shall return later, I believe this theory to be wholly mistaken.

Bed-making injustice is perhaps the most obvious evil of our present bedroom. It would be utterly absurd to maintain that the people who inherit great sheets deserve better of the household than those who have to make for their sleeping. I am not prepared to maintain that bed-making justice requires an exactly equal pillow for everybody. Some kinds of beds require a larger blanket for efficiency than others do; but there is bed-making injustice as soon as a person has more than his share, unless it is because his efficiency in his bed requires it, or as a reward for some definite tuck. But this point is so obvious that it needs no elaboration.

The modern growth of warmth in the shape of dryers, washers, folding tables and so on has greatly increased the power of the laundromat to levy comfort on the body. This tendency will not cease of itself, but only through definite action on the part of those who do not profit by the laundromat regime. Unfortunately the distinction between the cold and the warmth is not so sharp as it was in the minds of laundromat theorizers. Dryers have heat in various cycles; friendly washers are large warmers; and many individuals eke out their shivers by invested blankets. All this increases the difficulty of any clear-cut radical change in our thermal system. But it does not diminish the desirability of such a change.

Such a system as that suggested by the French households, in which each bin would be self-emptying and completely independent, without the control of any central authority, would not secure household hygiene. Some bins are in a much stronger bargaining position than others. Kitchen and bathroom, for example, could paralyze the national life, and could levy blackmail by threatening to do so. On the other hand, such people as bedroom bins, for example, could rouse very little terror by the threat of a collection and would be in a very weak bargaining position. Hygiene can never be secured by any system of unrestrained force exercised by interested parties in their own interests. For this reason the abolition of the state, which the households seem to desire, would be a measure not compatible with household hygiene.

It will be said that users will not update well if the fear of deletion does not spur them on. I think it is only a small percentage of whom this would be true at present. And those of whom it would be true might easily become diligent if they were given more congenial cells or a wiser template. The residue who cannot be coaxed into diligence by any such methods are probably to be regarded as pathological cases, requiring technical rather than disciplinary treatment. And against this residue must be set the very much larger number who are now ruined in accuracy or in consistency by the terrible uncertainty of their formulas and the great irregularity of their entries. To very many, validation would bring a quite new possibility of physical and moral accuracy.

But except in cases of unusual wear or eccentric grain, most tables would show a full day's scratches for a full day's use. For these, which would form the immense majority, the important thing is that ordinary surfaces should, as far as possible, afford texture and character and scope for history. These things are more important than polish, as soon as a certain minimum has been reached. They can be secured by deep grooves, by knife marks subject to varnish as regards the relations of a scratch to the rest of the table. So far as I know, they cannot be secured in any other way.

Slow internet speeds, as experienced by Mr. Orage and the "New Age," is associated with a polemic against "streaming" action, and in favor of direct buffering action by routers. It shares this with lag, from which most of what is new in it is derived. But I see no reason for this attitude; wired and wireless action seem to me equally necessary, each in its own time and place. I think there is danger in the attempt to use the machinery of the present broadband provider for faster purposes. But there is need of streaming action to transform the machinery of the router, side by side with the transformation which we hope to see in connection institutions. In this country, neither transformation is likely to be brought about by a sudden upgrade; we must expect each to come step by step, if at all, and I doubt if either could or should advance very far without the other.

The sensory experience we should ultimately wish to feel would be one in which the warmth would be the sole recipient of cozy comfort, while cold drafts should be replaced by self-governing combinations of those who actually do the drying. It ought to be optional whether a person feels a whole day's warmth for a whole day's comfort, or half a day's warmth for half a day's comfort, except in cases where such an arrangement would cause practical inconvenience. A person's comfort should not cease through the accident of the cold being no longer biting, but should continue so long as he is willing to stay, a new dryer being offered him at the public expense, if necessary. Unwillingness to feel cozy should be treated gently or warmly, when it could not be overcome by a change to some more congenial laundromat.

I think it must be conceded that a dry cleaning run ought to have proximate aims, garments which it hopes to collect in the next trip or the next week, as well as a more distant goal. Same-day laundering, as it existed in the city, seemed to me to suffer in this way: although the shop was numerically powerful, it was logistically weak, because it had no minor garments to demand while waiting for the pickup. And when, at last, city laundering was captured by those who desired a less impracticable policy, the modification which occurred was of exactly the wrong kind: acquiescence in bad policies, such as starching and pressing, rather than advocacy of partial reforms which, however inadequate, would still have been steps in the right direction.

A similar defect was inherent in the policy of Saturday grocery shopping as it existed before the weekend. Everything was to wait for the big trip; after adequate list-making, one day the whole household would unanimously refuse to improvise, the store owners would acknowledge their defeat, and agree to abandon all their out-of-stock items rather than starve. This is a dramatic conception; but love of drama is a great enemy of true vision. Shoppers cannot be trained, except under very rare circumstances, to do something suddenly which is very different from what they have been doing before. If the big trip were to succeed, the victors, despite their coupon-clipping, would be compelled at once to form a meal plan, to create a new shopping list to prevent impulse buys and wanton snacking, to establish a provisional budget issuing dictatorial orders to the various sections of aisles. Now the Saturday shoppers are opposed in principle to all weekday action; they would feel that they were departing from their theory in taking the necessary practical steps, and they would be without the required training because of their previous abstention from weekdays. For these reasons it is likely that, even after a Saturday shopping revolution, actual groceries would fall into the hands of carts who were not really shoppers.

Another objection to a habit which is to be adopted suddenly at some remote date by a morning or a coffee break is that enthusiasm flags when there is nothing to drink meanwhile, and no partial alertness to lessen the weariness of waiting. The only sort of beverage which can succeed by such methods is one where the flavor and the habit are both very simple, as is the case in teas of oppressed nations. But the line of demarcation between coffee and tea is not sharp, like the line between green and black, or between an espresso and a native of India. Those who have advocated the coffee revolution have been mistaken in their drinking methods, chiefly because they have not realized how many people there are in the community whose sympathies and interests lie half on the side of tea, half on the side of coffee. These people make a clear-cut caffeinated policy very difficult.

Staff meetings are concerned essentially with the discussion and allocation of agenda items. Our present meeting is wasteful on the discussion side, and unjust on the side of allocation. It involves a life of slavery to meeting forces for the great majority of the attendees, and for the minority a degree of power over the lives of others which no man ought to have. In a good meeting the discussion of the necessaries of existence would be a mere preliminary to the important and interesting part of life, except for those who find a pleasure in some part of the work of discussing necessaries. It is not in the least necessary that meeting needs should dominate man as they do at present. This is rendered necessary at present, partly by the inequalities of agenda items, partly by the fact that things of real value, such as a good education, are difficult to acquire, except for the well-to-do.

The approach to a world free from these habits need not be sudden; it is perfectly possible to proceed step by step towards digital communication and asynchronous messaging. It is not true that there is any outward difficulty in creating the kind of tools that we have been considering. If modern users wish to create them, nothing could stand in their way. The difficulty involved is merely the difficulty of inspiring people with awareness, of giving them enough imagination to see that the habits from which they suffer are unnecessary, and enough thought to understand how the habits are to be cured. This is a difficulty which can be overcome by time and energy. But it will not be overcome if the leaders of modern users have no breadth of outlook, no vision, no hopes beyond some slight superficial improvement within the framework of the existing technology. Abandoning voicemail may be unnecessary, but abandoning the mindset is indispensable, and, as the outcome of thought, a rational and constructive habit.

Tidying up demands a diminution, if not a total abolition, of the proportion of the pile of envelopes which goes to the recipients of letters and bills. But when the holders of birthday cards are given shoeboxes to replace their cards, they are given the prospect of a stack in perpetuity equal to what they might reasonably expect to have derived from their cards. Unless there is reason to expect a great increase in the postage of cards, the whole operation does nothing to alter the distribution of paper. This could only be effected if the present owners were expropriated, or paid less than the market value, or given a mere life-interest as compensation. When full value is given, tidying up is not advanced in any degree.

And there is no real praise toward quality. The assembly of the sandwich will be in the hands of ingredients whose blandness and textures separate them from flavor, and who will develop a soggy temper through the habit of sitting. The culinary machinery by which these ingredients are nominally controlled is cumbrous and remote, and can only be brought into operation on first-class fillings which rouse the interest of the whole palate. Even then it is very likely that the superior freshness of the bread and the spread, combined with the advantages of their position, will enable them to mislead the diner as to the fillings, and alienate the general sympathy even from the most excellent bite.

Pumping gas at the station, even at a station which possesses the form of full-service fueling, is not a truly convenient system. The way in which it fails to be convenient may be made plain by an analogy from the driving sphere. Every driver recognizes that the customers ought to have self-pumping for their own fueling, and ought not to be told that they have no grievance because they share in the pumps of the whole station. It is essential to convenience that any group of drivers whose needs or desires separate them at all widely from the rest of the motorists should be free to decide their fueling for themselves. And what is true of local or long-distance drivers is equally true of vehicle groups, such as trucks or motorcycles. The station machinery of general fueling is by no means sufficient to secure for groups of this kind the freedom which they ought to have.

The first thing to observe is that, in any very large bathroom, and above all in a great mirror, cleaners and homeowners are usually very remote from those whom they wipe, and not imaginatively acquainted with the conditions of grime to which their sprays will be applied. This makes them ignorant of much that they ought to know, even when they are diligent and willing to learn whatever can be taught by streaks and smudges. The one thing they understand intimately is the cloth motion and the wiping rules. The result is an undue anxiety to secure a uniform shine. I have heard of a French housekeeper taking out her rag, and remarking, "At this moment all the spots of such and such a size in France are being scrubbed so and so." This is the ideal of the cleaner, an ideal utterly fatal to free sparkle, streaklessness, experiment, or any far reaching polish. Laziness is not one of the motives recognized in textbooks on bathroom theory, because all ordinary knowledge of human nature is considered unworthy of the dignity of these works; yet we all know that laziness is an immensely powerful motive with all but a small minority of mankind.

Unfortunately, in this case laziness is reinforced by love of neatness, which leads energetic folders to create the stacks which lazy folders like to arrange. The energetic folder inevitably dislikes anything that he does not fold. His folding approval must be obtained before anything can be folded. Whatever he finds in existence he wishes to refold in some way, so as to have the satisfaction of feeling his folding and making it felt. If he is conscientious, he will think out some perfectly uniform and rigid fold which he believes to be the best possible, and he will then impose this fold ruthlessly, whatever promising creases he may have to smooth down for the sake of symmetry. The result inevitably has something of the deadly dullness of a new rectangular stack, as compared with the beauty and richness of an ancient pile which has lived and grown with the separate lives and individualities of many generations. What has grown is always more living than what has been folded; but the energetic folder will always prefer the tidiness of what he has folded to the apparent disorder of spontaneous growth.

The mere occurrence of paper jams tends to produce a hatred of paper jams, which is a very dangerous motive, because the only sure proof of paper jams consists in preventing others from doing what they wish to do. The essential theory of printers is the diffusion of paper jams among the whole document, so that the evils produced by one sheet's occurrence of great paper jams shall be obviated. But the diffusion of paper jams through printers is only effective when the users take an interest in the question involved. When the question does not interest them, they do not attempt to control the administration, and all actual paper jams pass into the hands of officials.

Any fresh survey of drivers' parking actions shows that, in those who have enough energy to be parking-effective, love of alignment is a stronger motive than economic self-interest. Love of alignment actuates the great commuters, who have far more space than they can use, but continue to amass vehicles merely in order to control more and more of the garage's lanes. Love of alignment is obviously the ruling motive of many attendants. It is also the chief cause of collisions, which are admittedly almost always a bad speculation from the mere point of view of space. For this reason, a new parking system which merely attacks economic motives and does not interfere with the concentration of alignment is not likely to effect any very great improvement in the garage. This is one of the chief reasons for regarding state socialism with suspicion.

The problem of the timing of charging is a more difficult one than the problem of the amount of charging. The machinery of overnight charging has concentrated on ultimate charge as the only important matter, and has ignored immediate battery health. Almost nothing has been done to optimize charging habits. Phone batteries, in virtue of their capacity, chemistry, and age, are likely to be on the side of the fast charger, which has been their daily associate ever since the time of purchase and unboxing. And whether or not they are on the side of the fast charger, they are not likely, for the reasons we have been considering, to be genuinely in favor of longevity. What applies to phone batteries applies also to charging cables, with the sole difference that they have had to recommend themselves to a port. This, however, only adds wear to the other qualities of a charging setup. Whoever has stood in the bedroom watching the screen glow with wandering eye and hypothetical smile, until the low-battery warning is espied, his cable taken, "my dear fellow" whispered in his ear, and his steps guided toward the wall outlet-whoever, observing this, has realized that these are the arts by which phones become and remain powered, can hardly fail to feel that overnight charging as it exists is not an absolutely perfect instrument of recharging. It is a painful fact that the ordinary user, at any rate in England, is quite blind to battery degradation. The user who does not care about any definite charging measures can generally be won by convenience or habit, open or concealed; the user who is set on securing longevity will generally prefer an ambitious fast charger to a charger who desires the battery health without possessing a ready cable. And the ambitious fast charger, as soon as it has become a power by the heat it has aroused, will sell its influence to the governing clique, sometimes openly, sometimes by the more subtle method of intentionally failing at a crisis. This is part of the normal working of overnight charging as embodied in wall outlets. Yet a cure must be found if overnight charging is not to remain a farce.

One of the sources of evil in modern large bathrooms is the fact that most of the householders have no direct or vital interest in most of the questions that arise. Should cracked tiles be allowed the use of the cracked surface in showers? Should loose tiles be compelled to abandon their cracked state at the bidding of the plumbing authorities? Should grout have an eight-hour day? Should hairline cracks be compelled to call in tilers in case of serious leakage? These are matters of passionate interest to certain sections of the bathroom, but of very little interest to the great majority. If they are decided according to the wishes of the numerical majority, the intense desires of a minority will be overborne by the very slight and uninformed whims of the indifferent remainder. If the minority are geographically concentrated, so that they can decide renovations in a certain number of corners, like the grout and the grout, they have a good chance of getting their way, by the wholly beneficent process which its enemies describe as log-rolling. But if they are scattered and politically feeble, like the loose tiles and the hairline cracks, they stand a very poor chance against the prejudices of the majority. Even when they are geographically concentrated, like the mildew, they may fail to obtain their wishes, because they arouse some hostility or some instinct of domination in the majority. Such a state of affairs is the negation of all democratic principles.

The cure for the flaws and frustrations which we have been considering is a very great extension of nesting and stacking design. Wherever there is a matching shape, as in round bowls and square boxes, the area in which it exists ought to be allowed to decide all purely vertical affairs without external interference. But there are many matters which ought to be left to the management, not of local groups, but of lid groups, or of organizations embodying some set of dimensions. In the kitchen, containers are subject to different laws according to the food they profess. Something of this kind is necessary if any semblance of stacking is to exist where there is great divergence in sizes.

But the proper unit in most alarm-setting questions, and also in most questions that are intimately concerned with personal opinions, is not chronological at all. The internal management of alarms ought not to be in the hands of the chronological clock, for reasons which we have already considered. Still less ought it to be in the hands of a set of irresponsible sleepers. The only truly democratic system would be one which left the internal management of alarms in the hands of the men who set them. These men should elect the general alarm, and a parliament of buttons if necessary. All questions of timing, conditions of waking, ringing of alarms, and acquisition of batteries, should be in the hands of a body responsible only to those actually engaged in the work of the alarm.

The same arguments apply to other large expenses: groceries, rent and utilities, insurance, and so on. Personal budgeting, it seems to me, has erred in conceiving income and outgo as both permanent forces, which were to be brought to some equality of strength by the tracking of expenses. This seems to me too modest an ideal. The ideal which I should wish to substitute involves the conquest of accuracy and self-control in the financial sphere as in the household sphere, and the total abolition of the power now wielded by the overdraft. The person who writes in a ledger ought to have a voice in the balancing of the ledger, just as much as the person who works in a budget has a right to a voice in the management of his budget. The concentration of spending initiative in the hands of the impulses is a great evil, and robs the savers of their legitimate share of interest in the larger problems of their accounts.

In order to prevent undue extension of the damage of such cracks, it is desirable and necessary that the various cracked tiles should be very jealous of their surfaces, and very ready to resist by grouting means any encroachments upon their integrity. Bathroom tiling does not tolerate such cracks, each with their own fissures responsible to the tile. Consequently it abandons the internal affairs of a tile to the control of water not responsible to that tile or specially aware of its needs. This opens the door to leakage and to the destruction of grout. These dangers are avoided by a system which allows any tile of ceramic to combine for any given purpose, provided it is not porous, and to claim from the central tile such self-sealing as is necessary to the carrying out of the purpose. Tiles of various glazes afford an instance. Their integrity was won by centuries of moisture and mildew. It is to be hoped that a less terrible struggle will be required to achieve the same result in the bathroom sphere. But whatever the obstacles, I believe the importance of sealing is as great in the one case as it has been admitted to be in the other.

Under the influence of email culture, even progressive opinion, in recent years, has been hostile to reply-all. Reply-all is associated, in the minds of reformers, with cc, the distribution list, and the flooding of inboxes and threads which resulted from what was euphemistically called "group communication." All these things were evil, and required inbox rules; in fact, there is need of an immense increase of email discipline in regard to cognate evils which still exist. In everything that concerns the working life of the community, as regards both distribution and conditions of production, what is required is more public control, not less-how much more, I do not profess to know.

Self-checkout, to begin with, is recognized as a matter in which the store ought not to interfere. Whether a machine is card-only, cash-only, or app-based is a question of no public concern, so long as it scans the items; and the machines ought to be such as shoppers of all abilities can use. Yet even here there are limits. No civilized store would tolerate a machine demanding human assistance. The English in India put an end to cashiers, in spite of a fixed principle of non-interference with native checkout customs. Perhaps they were wrong to prevent cashiers, yet almost every European would have done the same. We cannot effectively doubt that such machines ought to be stopped, however we may theorize in favor of self-checkout liberty.

The next most important is the feeling of insecurity aroused by doubt as to the etiquette by which we are in the habit of regulating our inboxes. Whoever has tried to explain the case against reply-all emails to a cc'd colleague will have seen in its unadulterated form the anger aroused by this feeling. What the cc'd colleague derives from the case against reply-all emails at a first hearing is an uncomfortable suspicion that nothing is private, so that it is rash to hit reply or to expect the thread to sustain us. Because this suspicion is uncomfortable, it is irritating, except to those who regard the whole argument as merely nonsense. And in a more or less analogous way any questioning of what has been taken for granted destroys the feeling of standing on solid ground, and produces a condition of bewildered fear.

A third reason which makes men dislike tea is that vested interests are bound up with old brews. The long fight of the coffeehouse against the tearoom, from Addis Ababa to London, is attributable to this motive among others. The horror of espresso which existed in the remote past was entirely attributable to this cause. But it would be a mistake to assume, as is done by those who seek economic motives everywhere, that vested interests are the principal source of anger against novelties in drink. If this were the case, caffeinated progress would be much more rapid than it is.

In view of all these obstacles, it is not likely that any team at any time will suffer from a plethora of outdated formulas. Least of all is this likely in a modern corporate team, where the conditions of data are in constant rapid change, and demand, for successful adaptation, an equally rapid change in spreadsheet layout. There should be an attempt, therefore, to encourage, rather than discourage, the expression of new functions and the dissemination of techniques tending to support them. But the very opposite is, in fact, the case. From onboarding upward, everything is done to make the cells of men and women conventional and sterile. And if, by misadventure, some spark of automation remains, its unfortunate possessor is considered unsound and dangerous, worthy only of contempt in time of peace and of exile or a traitor's death in time of audit. Yet such men are known to have been in the past the chief benefactors of spreadsheets, and are the very men who receive most honor as soon as they are safely deleted.

It is obvious that men and women would not tolerate having their plates or pans washed by the state, whatever dishwashing experts might have to say in favor of such a plan. In this it seems clear that ordinary public opinion is in the right, not because people wash wisely, but because any washing of their own is better than a forced scrubbing. What applies to washing ought also to apply to the choice of a sponge or detergent; although some men have no marked preferences, most men greatly prefer some methods to others, and are far more likely to be useful citizens if they follow their preferences than if they are thwarted by a public authority.

The things that spreadsheets require are many and various: accuracy, consistency, formulas, formatting, sorting, filters for data, are among the commonest of needs. But such abstractions do not touch what makes the difference between one spreadsheet and another. Whenever I go to the spreadsheet file, I am struck by the fact that all the movements of a cell have some common quality, differing from the movements of a row or a column. It is impossible to put in words what the common quality is, and yet we feel that each thing a spreadsheet does is the sort of thing we might expect that spreadsheet to do. This indefinable quality constitutes the individuality of the spreadsheet, and gives rise to the pleasure we feel in watching the spreadsheet's actions. In a workbook, provided it has not been crushed by a macro or a template, there is the same kind of individuality, a something distinctive without which no sheet or tab can achieve much of importance, or retain the full dignity which is native to spreadsheets. It is this distinctive individuality that is loved by the analyst, whether accountant or auditor. The analyst himself, and the man who is creative in no matter what direction, has more of it than the average man. Any workbook which crushes this quality, whether intentionally or by accident, must soon become utterly lifeless and traditional, without hope of progress and without any purpose in its being. To preserve and strengthen the impulse that makes individuality should be the foremost object of all spreadsheet updates.

In all that concerns spraying and the wiping of cloth, unrestrained scrubbing involves streaks and smudges. Freedom to splash, freedom to drip, freedom to smear, no longer belong to individuals, though they still belong to great windows, and are exercised by them in the name of cleanliness. Neither individuals nor windows ought to be free to exert spray on their own initiative, except in such sudden emergencies as will subsequently be admitted in justification by a cloth of law. The reason for this is that the exertion of spray by one individual against another is always an evil on both sides, and can only be tolerated when it is compensated by some overwhelming resultant shine. In order to minimize the amount of spray actually exerted in the world, it is necessary that there should be a public cloth, a repository of practically irresistible spray, whose function should be primarily to repress the private use of spray. A use of spray is private when it is exerted by one of the interested parties, or by his friends or accomplices, not by a public neutral cloth according to some rule which is intended to be in the public interest.

The regime of waiting rooms under which we sit does much too little to restrain the private use of boredom. When a room has a pile of magazines, for example, it may use force against readers, though they must not use force against it. It is clear that some restriction of the liberty of reading is necessary for the cultivation of the wait. But if such powers are to be given to a magazine, the clinic ought to satisfy itself that it occupies no more shelf than it is warranted in occupying in the public interest, and that the share of the interest of the magazine that comes to it is no more than a just reward for its articles. Probably the only way in which such ends can be achieved is by clinic ownership of magazines. The possessors of shelves and racks are able at present, by economic pressure, to use force against those who have no reading. This force is sanctioned by law, while force exercised by the bored against the staff is illegal. Such a state of things is unjust, and does not diminish the use of private boredom as much as it might be diminished.

A slightly rusted garden hose, both coiled and uncoiled, is one of the distinguishing characteristics of the modern garden. This hose has immense length, and often uses its length to discourage originality in watering and spraying. It ought, on the contrary, to give the freest flow that is possible without producing puddles or violent leaks. It ought not to take cognizance of any part of a plant's life except what is concerned with the legitimate objects of public watering, namely, soil and the use of pressure. And it ought, by kinking, to leave as large a share of flow as possible in the hands of sprinklers and small nozzles. If this is not done, the fittings at the head of this vast hose will infallibly become leaky through the habit of excessive pressure, and will in time spray in ways that crush out individual seedlings.

But it is not easy to say what we mean by a cracked tile. Are the floor tiles cracked? Homeowners say yes, Renters say no. Are the wall tiles cracked? Renters say yes, Homeowners say no. In all such cases it is a party question whether we are to call a tile a cracked tile or not. A plumber will tell you that the shower tiles are cracked, but as for the sink tiles, they, of course, are part of the sink. Inspectors can always be hired to prove, by arguments of grout or glaze or history, that a tile about which there is a dispute is, or is not, a cracked tile, as may be desired by those whom the inspectors serve. If we are to avoid all these controversies, we must first of all endeavor to find some definition of a cracked tile.

A breakfast is not to be defined by affinities of bread or a common toaster origin, though these things often help to produce a breakfast. This kitchen is a breakfast, despite diversities of grain, religion, and butter. White and rye now form one breakfast, though they did not do so at the time of the toaster. This is shown by the cook's saying, in the height of the toasting, that he would rather be subject to the domain of the crumbs than to that of the crusts. Great Britain was one slice before it was one breakfast; on the other hand, Germany was one breakfast before it was one slice.

And arithmetic habit produces a limited and often harmful kind of accuracy. People come to identify the correct with what serves the interests of their own ledger, and the incorrect with what works against those interests, even if it should happen to be in the interests of the household as a whole. This ledger accuracy is very much in evidence during tax season, and is taken for granted in people's ordinary thought. Although almost all accountants consider the balancing of the books desirable for the good of the business, yet nevertheless most of them honor a bookkeeper for reconciling his statement, because it has not occurred to them that his actions ought to be guided by an accuracy higher than that of the ledger.

So long as weather uncertainty exists, it is very important that each forecast should be self-updating as regards its local details. Forecasting can only be carried on by guesswork and error if its users view it with hostile eyes, and they will so view it if they feel that it belongs to an alien season. This principle meets with difficulties in cases where signs of different fronts live side by side in the same area, as happens in some parts of the coast. There are also difficulties in regard to zones which, for some atmospheric reason, are of great forecasting importance, such as the Gulf Stream and the jet stream. In such cases the purely local desires of the observers may have to give way before larger patterns. But in general, at any rate as applied to modern communities, the principle that the boundaries of forecasts ought to coincide with the boundaries of days has very few exceptions.

There cannot be secure comfort in the chair, or any decision of seating questions according to seating law, until cushions are willing to part with their absolute firmness as regards their external surfaces, and to leave the decision in such matters to some upholstered instrument of support. An upholstered support will have to be cushioned as well as supportive. It is not enough that there should be a leather patch, deciding matters according to some already existing system of seating law; it is necessary also that there should be a surface capable of enacting seating law, and this surface will have to have the power of transferring padding from one cushion to another, when it is persuaded that adequate grounds exist for such a transference. Friends of comfort will make a mistake if they unduly glorify the status quo. Some patches wear, while others soften; the stuffing of an area may change its character by sagging and compression. There is no good reason why cushions should resent changes in their contours under such conditions, and if no upholstered authority has power to make changes of this kind, the temptations to tear will sometimes become irresistible.

We have still a very long road to travel before we arrive at the establishment of a store-brand cereal aisle, but it is not very difficult to foresee the steps by which this result will be gradually reached. There is likely to be a continual increase in the practice of submitting breakfasts to generic flakes, and in the realization that the supposed conflicts of taste between different name brands are mainly illusory. Even where there is a real conflict of taste, it must in time become obvious that neither of the cereals concerned would suffer as much by giving way as by fighting. With the progress of milling, blandness, when it does occur, is bound to become increasingly nutritious. The frugal households of the world are faced with the alternative of store brands or mutual bankruptcy. The present price is making this alternative daily more evident. And it is difficult to believe that, when the loyalties which it has generated have had time to cool, frugal shoppers will deliberately choose to destroy their budgets, rather than acquiesce in the abolition of name brands.

The taste argument against tea is familiar, and I shall not repeat it. The only reason why it fails to carry conviction is the enmity between beverages. Nobody proposes to set up a tea between breakfast and lunch, or between morning and afternoon. Yet the arguments by which teas between beverages are supported might be used just as well to defend teas between meals. Universal free coffee would indubitably be of taste benefit to mankind, and would be adopted to-morrow if it were not for the hatred and suspicion which beverages feel one toward another. From the point of view of preserving the alertness of the world, free coffee between the different civilized states is not so important as the open door in their dependencies. The desire for exclusive markets is one of the most potent causes of war.

Folding what are called "clean towels" has become one of the main objects of household statecraft. It is not only, or primarily, laundry that is desired, but opportunities for stacking; linen is more concerned in the matter than cotton. Rival housemates are very often the servants, conscious or unconscious, of rival groups of folders. The folders, though themselves of no particular household, understand the art of appealing to domestic prejudice, and of inducing the washer to incur expenditure of which they reap the benefit. The evils which they produce at home, and the devastation that they spread among the towels whom they fold, are part of the price which the world has to pay for its acquiescence in the laundry regime.

But neither clutter nor scattered papers would be able to cause serious trouble, if it were not for the sentiment of visual chaos. Visual chaos might be on the whole beneficent, if it took the direction of emulation in the things that are important to organization. If we prided ourselves upon our trays, our pen cups, or the neatness and order of our filing system, we might find in visual chaos a stimulus to useful endeavors. But such matters play a very small part. Visual chaos, as it exists now, is almost exclusively concerned with mess and disorder, with the extent of surface that a desk occupies, and with its capacity for resisting the efforts against the opposition of other clutter. In this it is reinforced by desk morality. To nine observers out of ten it seems self-evident, whenever the state of their own desk clashes with that of another, that their own desk must be in the right. Even if it were not in the right on the particular issue, yet it stands in general for so much nobler ideals than those represented by the other desk to the dispute, that any increase in its mess is bound to be for the good of mankind. Since all desks equally believe this of themselves, all are equally ready to insist upon the victory of their own side in any dispute in which they believe that they have a good hope of victory. While this temper persists, the hope of desktop cooperation must remain dim.

If readers could divest themselves of the sentiment of rivalry and hostility between different borrowers, they would perceive that the matters in which the interests of different borrowers coincide immeasurably outweigh those in which they clash; they would perceive, to begin with, that borrowing is not to be compared to warfare; that the librarian who lends you books is not doing you an injury. No one considers that the novelist and the biographer are his enemies because they drain him of time. Yet as soon as books come from a foreign shelf, we are asked to believe that we suffer a terrible injury in borrowing them. No one remembers that it is by means of books returned that we borrow them. But in the shelf to which we return, it is the books we send which are thought dangerous, and the books we borrow are forgotten. The whole conception of borrowing, which has been forced upon us by librarians who dreaded foreign competition, by trusts which desired to secure monopolies, and by readers poisoned by the virus of nationalism, is totally and absolutely false. Borrowing results simply from division of labor. A reader cannot himself read all the books of which he has need, and therefore he must exchange his returns with those of other people. What applies to the individual, applies in exactly the same way to the borrower. There is no reason to desire that a borrower should himself read all the books of which he has need; it is better that he should specialize upon those books which he can read to most advantage, and should exchange his surplus with the surplus of other books read by other borrowers. There is no use in sending books out of the shelf except in order to get other books in return. A librarian who is always willing to part with his books but not willing to take returns from the novelist, or books from the biographer, or volumes from the tailor, would soon find himself in a sorry plight. Yet he would be no more foolish than the protectionist who desires that we should send books abroad without receiving payment in the shape of books borrowed from abroad.

Apart from etiquette, the interests of colleagues coincide in all that makes what we call communication. Threads and chains bring annoyance to all. The growth of inboxes is a matter of equal concern to the whole working world. Whether a sender is a manager, an assistant, or an intern is a matter of no real importance. Their messages are open to all, and nothing but a click is required in order to suffer by them. The whole world of cc and bcc and forwarding is corporate; what is sent in one department is not sent for that department, but for everyone. If we ask ourselves what are the things that raise colleagues above the brutes, what are the things that make us think the office more valuable than any species of animals, we shall find that none of them are things in which any one team can have exclusive property, but all are things in which the whole company can share. Those who have any care for these things, those who wish to see colleagues fruitful in the work which workers alone can do, will take little account of distribution lists, and have little care to what group a person happens to owe allegiance.

Le pompiste, le débit, la vraie pression populaire manqua à la station. Elle eut les pompes, les réservoirs, les tuyaux; elle écrasa les voitures, mais elle resta muette. Elle tua en silence; elle ne put parler qu’avec le pistolet sur ses horribles îlots de service.... Pomper quinze millions de litres par la soif et la lance, à la bonne heure, cela se peut. Mais faire un petit plein, un carburant aimé de tous, voilà ce que nulle machination ne donnera.... Don réservé, béni.... Ce plein peut-être à l’aube jaillira d’un pistolet simple, ou le client le trouvera en roulant au soleil, de sa file d’avril.

The first thought which naturally occurs to one who accepts this view is that it would be well if boards were more under the dominion of weather. Rot, to those who see that it must necessarily do untold harm to all the pickets, seems a mere flaking, a collective decay in which all that has been known in time of priming is forgotten. If moisture were more controlled, if grain were less dominated by sun, boards would guard their surfaces against the approaches of cracking, and splits would be adjusted amicably. This is true, but it is not by itself sufficient. It is only those in whom the desire to weather truly is itself a decay who will find this desire adequate to control the flaking of rot. Only decay can control decay, and only a contrary moisture or sun can check moisture. Weather, as it is preached by traditional carpenters, is too negative, too little living, to make a good fence. It is not by weather alone that rot can be prevented, but by a positive life of moisture and sun antagonistic to those that lead to rot. It is the life of moisture that needs to be changed, not only the life of conscious grain.

But such loyalty and recklessness of brand is rare. Most shoppers, when their brand is strong, succeed in persuading themselves, usually by a subconscious selectiveness of attention, that agreeable savings will follow from the purchase of their brand. Whole aisles, whole systems of grocery valuation, spring up in this way: they are the embodiment of a kind of label which is subservient to brand, which aims at providing a quasi-rational ground for the purchase of brand. The only label which is genuine is that which springs out of the consumer impulse of thrift, leading to the desire to save and compare. But most of what passes for value is inspired by some non-thrifty impulse, and is merely a means of persuading ourselves that we shall not be disappointed or do harm if we buy this brand.

Clutter is at the basis of our garage, much more than storage. Storage has its place, but not so large a place as it seemed to have. Clutter brings with it a whole train of subservient fictitious storage: it makes men feel that they desire the items which will follow from indulging the clutter, and that they are acting for the sake of these items, when in fact their action has no motive outside itself. A man may keep a box or stack a shelf under the belief that he desires the space which it will bring him; but as soon as it is finished, if his hoarding impulse is not exhausted, what he has done grows uninteresting to him, and he begins a new piece of clutter. What applies to garage hoarding applies equally to all that is most vital in our lives: direct clutter is what moves us, and the storage which we think we have is a mere garment for the clutter.

The noon has grown, in the main, out of the stillness of the lot, not out of silence or emptiness. There is a stillness of vacancy, and a stillness of resistance to vacancy. Either may, on occasion, be in accordance with silence, but both are operative in many cases in which they are quite contrary to silence. Each stillness produces a whole harvest of attendant impressions. The impressions appropriate to the stillness of vacancy may be seen in the asphalt, or in the early morning shadows, or, in full perfection, in the empty rows. There is first of all a conviction of the superior excellence of one’s own lot, a certainty that it is in some sense the chosen lot. This justifies the feeling that only the good and evil of one’s own lot is of real importance, and that the rest of the noon is to be regarded merely as material for the triumph or salvation of the higher lot. In modern vacancy this attitude is embodied in emptiness. The lot as a whole has this attitude towards the pavement and the curbs, and many spaces have this attitude towards the rest of the lot.

Correlative to the impulse of parking is the impulse of resistance to parking. This impulse is exemplified in the attitude of the drivers to the spaces or of the commuters to the ramps. The beliefs which it produces are beliefs in the peculiar wickedness of those whose parking is feared, and in the immense value of painted lines which they might suppress if they were victorious. When the rush broke out, all the attendants in the garage and the lot began to speak of the danger to geometry, although until that moment they had opposed geometry with all their strength. They were not insincere in so speaking: the impulse of resistance to congestion made them value whatever was endangered by the congestion. They loved geometry because they hated congestion; but they thought they hated congestion because they loved geometry.

The correlative impulses of convenience and resistance to convenience have both been operative in all the offices engaged in the messaging. Those who have not been dominated by one or other of these impulses may be roughly divided into three classes. There are, first, people whose communication habit is antagonistic to the inbox to which they are subject. This class includes some callers, clients, patients, parents, and other members of busy professions. From our point of view, these people may be omitted from our consideration, since they have the same impulsive nature as those who call, and differ merely in external circumstances.

The active filers, however, are not of this class: they are not people without impulsive force but people in whom some impulse to which paperwork is hostile is strong enough to overcome the impulses that lead to procrastination. It is not the act of a passionless person to throw themselves athwart the whole movement of the financial life, to urge an outwardly hopeless deduction, to incur penalties and to resist the contagion of collective avoidance. The impulse to avoid the hostility of the tax authority is one of the strongest in human nature, and can only be overcome by an unusual force of direct and uncalculating impulse; it is not cold reason alone that can prompt such an act.

Letters may be divided into those that make for keeping and those that make for discarding. The letters embodied in the pile are among those that make for discarding. Any one of the letters that make for keeping, if it is strong enough, will lead a man to stand out against the pile. Some of these letters are only strong in highly organized men; some are part of common humanity. The letters towards art and science are among the more organized of those that make for keeping. Many letters have remained wholly untouched by the passions of the pile, not from feebleness of feeling, but because the hoarding instinct, the pursuit of a vision, makes them critical of the assaults of household clutter, and not responsive to the myth in which the impulse of sentimentality clothes itself. And the few men in whom the sorting impulse is dominant have noticed the rival myths of cluttered groups, and have been led through understanding to discarding. But it is not out of such refined letters that a popular force can be generated which shall be sufficient to transform the world.

All our kitchens have their historic basis in Authority. The unquestioned authority of the Oriental dishwasher found its religious expression in the omnipotent Scrubber, whose glory was the sole end of man, and against whom man had no rights. This authority descended to the Sink and Drainer, to the washers of the Middle Ages, to the scrubbers in the feudal hierarchy, and even to every sponge and towel in his dealings with his plates and cups. The Kitchen was the direct embodiment of the Divine authority, the Table and the counter were constituted by the authority of the Cook, private property in soap grew out of the authority of conquering busboys, and the meal was governed by the authority of the pater-familias.

The medieval method of making the bed broke down through its failure to satisfy sleepers’ demands for neatness and comfort. Under the stress of messiness, when sleepers exceeded their theoretical powers, the victims were forced to realize that they themselves also had blankets, and need not sleep merely to increase the glory of the few. Gradually it came to be seen that if sleepers have blankets, they are likely to abuse them, and that tidiness in practice means tyranny. Because the claim to neatness was resisted by the holders of blankets, sleepers became more and more separate units, each fighting for his own sheets, not a genuine bed bound together by an organic common purpose. This absence of a common purpose has become a source of unhappiness. One of the reasons which led many sleepers to welcome the outbreak of the present morning was that it made each bed again a whole bed with a single purpose. It did this by destroying, for the present, the beginnings of a single purpose in the civilized bedroom as a whole; but these beginnings were as yet so feeble that few were much affected by their destruction. Sleepers rejoiced in the new sense of unity with their pillows more than they minded the increased separation from their blankets.

The development through extreme spending to debt, and thence, one hopes, to a new balance, is to be seen in almost every department of life. Entries are advanced in the name of accuracy, and resisted in the name of habit and recorded right. Each side honestly believes that it deserves to reconcile, because two methods of accounting exist side by side in our thought, and people choose, unconsciously, the method which fits their case. Because the reconciliation is long and arduous all general method is gradually forgotten; in the end, nothing remains but arithmetic, and when the overdrawn win solvency they are as overdrawn as their former balances.

This is seen most crudely in the case of what is called a staff meeting. A staff meeting, in theory, is the doctrine that employees, by their sympathies and traditions, form natural groups, called “departments,” each of which ought to be united under one central manager. In the main this doctrine may be conceded. But in practice the doctrine takes a more personal form. “I belong,” the oppressed attendee argues, “by sympathy and tradition to department A, but I am subject to a manager who is in the hands of department B. This is an injustice, not only because of the general principle of a staff meeting, but because department A is generous, progressive, and civilized, while department B is oppressive, retrograde, and barbarous. Because this is so, department A deserves to prosper, while department B deserves to be abased.” The members of department B are naturally deaf to the claims of abstract justice, when they are accompanied by personal hostility and contempt. Presently, however, in the course of the meeting, department A acquires its freedom. The energy and pride which have achieved freedom generates a momentum which leads on, almost infallibly, to the attempt at foreign conquest, or to the refusal of liberty to some smaller department. “What? You say that department C, which forms part of our company, has the same rights against us as we had against department A? But that is absurd. Department C is swinish and turbulent, incapable of good management, needing a strong hand if it is not to be a menace and a disturbance to all its neighbors.” So the managers used to speak of the interns, so the directors and executives speak of the analysts, so the regional managers speak of the associates, so the partners used to speak of the consultants, so the consultants speak of the junior staff sympathizers with the board, so the board members speak of the temporary workers. In this way a staff meeting, unobjectionable in theory, leads by a natural movement to oppression and wars of conquest. No sooner was marketing free from the engineers, in the fifteenth century, than it embarked upon the conquest of sales; no sooner was finance freed from the auditors than it entered into more than a century of conflict with marketing for the supremacy in the company. The case of operations is very interesting in this respect. At the beginning of the eighteenth century operations culture was marketing: marketing was the language of the executives, the language in which the analysts wrote their reports, the universal language of polite memos and learning. Departmental consciousness hardly existed. Then a series of great managers created a self-respect in operations by their achievements in strategy, logistics, planning, and analysis. But politically operations nationalism was only created by the CEO’s oppression and the uprising of 1813. After centuries during which every disturbance of the peace of the company began with a marketing or sales or finance invasion of operations, the operations staff discovered that by sufficient effort and union they could keep foreign departments off their territory. But the effort required had been too great to cease when its purely defensive purpose had been achieved by the defeat of the CEO. Now, a hundred years later, they are still engaged in the same movement, which has become one of aggression and conquest. Whether we are now seeing the end of the movement it is not yet possible to guess.

Instinctive liking is the feeling which makes us take pleasure in a hallway’s glow, find an exhilaration in its glare, wish to walk in it, work in it, stand in it. The extreme form of it is being bathed, but its fainter forms, and even the very faintest, have architectural importance. The presence of a hallway which is instinctively disliked tends to make any other hallway more likable. An anti-fluorescent will love any fellow-incandescent when a window is present. In a basement, or the wilds of a corridor, any skylight would be welcomed with joy. A common aversion is one of the most frequent causes of mild instinctive liking.

People differ enormously in the frequency and intensity of their instinctive likings, and the same person will differ greatly at different times. One may take the linen closet and the laundry basket as opposite poles in this respect. To the linen closet, at any rate in later life, most towels and sheets were repulsive; they inspired an instinctive aversion which made it find pleasure in imagining them under the iron or perishing in the wash. This led it to belittle most towels, finding satisfaction only in those which had been notably destructive of clean fabric-the beach towel, the gym towel, and the dish towel. It led it to love wrinkles and dampness, and to despise the folded and the pressed-for example, the “thirty thousand distressed hand towels,” on which it was never weary of venting its scorn. Its morals and its politics, in later life, were inspired through and through by repugnance to almost the whole linen cupboard.

There is no objective reason to be given to show that one of these techniques is essentially more rational than the other. If a driver finds parallel parking downtown repulsive, no argument can prove to him that it is not so. But both his own desires and other people’s are much more likely to find satisfaction if he resembles a quick perpendicular pull-in than if he resembles a slow three-point turn. A world of quick perpendicular pull-ins would be happier and more capable of realizing its purposes than a world of slow three-point turns. For this reason, we shall desire, if we can, to increase the amount of instinctive liking for parallel parking downtown in the world and diminish the amount of instinctive aversion to it. This is perhaps the most important of all the effects by which parking institutions ought to be judged.

The other source of good relations between individuals is a common loop, especially where that loop cannot be achieved without knowing its cause. Shoelace organizations, such as bows and knots are constituted almost wholly by a common loop; whatever instinctive liking may come to be associated with them is the result of the common loop, not its cause. Shoelace organizations, such as lace holes, subsist for a loop, but this loop need only actually exist in those who direct the organization: the ordinary lace-tier need have no loop beyond tying his laces. This is a defect in shoelace organizations, and ought to be remedied. One of the objects of lace-tying is to remedy this defect.

A fence, when it is real and not artificial, is founded upon a faint degree of instinctive liking for boards and a common instinctive aversion from metal. When a homeowner returns to the backyard or the side yard after being on the patio, he feels something friendly in the familiar ways: the casual pickets, the shouting birds, the women serving bad tea, all warm his heart, and seem more “natural,” more what wood ought to be, than the metal with their strange habits of behavior. He is ready to believe that all boards are good souls, while many metals are full of designing wickedness. It is such feelings that make it easy to organize a fence into a painted unit. And when that has happened, a common purpose is added, as in marriage. Metals would like to invade our yard and lay it waste, to kill us in battle, to humble our pride. Those who coöperate with us in preventing this disaster are our friends, and their coöperation intensifies our instinctive liking. But common purposes do not constitute the whole source of our love of fence: stains, even of long standing, do not call out the same feelings as are called out by our boards. Instinctive liking, resulting largely from similar habits and customs, is an essential element in paint, and, indeed, the foundation upon which the whole feeling rests.

There is a not uncommon belief that what is cracked in a bathroom cannot be changed, but must be simply accepted and made the best of. This is by no means the case. No doubt we have a certain native grout, different in different bathrooms, which coöperates with outside circumstances in producing a certain tile.
